Normal blood vessel — the three-layer frame

PATH.5001src p.6
Exam Lock
Why this revision slide is not optional
  • Every entity in this lecture is defined by which layer it damages: atheroma = intima; Mönckeberg = media; fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia = intima; hyaline and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis = small vessel wall.
  • Robbins Basic Pathology, 11th Ed. Chapter 8, p.275 — regional specialisations of the vasculature.
L01 · Arteriosclerosis8

The whole spectrum of vessel pathology, on one line

PATH.5001src p.7
  • Narrowing / obstruction (stenosis) → Arteriosclerosis (chronic) or thrombosis / embolism (acute), Prinzmetal angina (acute vasospasm)
  • Weakening (aneurysm, dissection) → rupture → haemorrhage
  • Inflammation (vasculitis – infectious vs non-infectious) → vessel wall damage
L01 · Arteriosclerosis9

Arteriosclerosis — the umbrella term

PATH.5002src p.8–9
Arteriosclerosis literally means “hardening of the arteries”; it is a generic term for arterial wall thickening and loss of elasticity.Lecture 01, slide 8

Four members of the family — the comparison the objective asks for

TypeVessel sizeLesion / morphologyClinical significance
AtherosclerosisLarge and medium arteriesIntimal lesions called atheroma. From the Greek for “gruel” and “hardening”.Most frequent and clinically important pattern
ArteriolosclerosisSmall arteries and arteriolesTwo variants: hyaline (protein deposition) and hyperplastic (SMC proliferation)Morphological changes due to hypertension — benign vs malignant (not neoplastic) — and diabetes
Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosisMedium-sized arteriesCalcific deposits in the media, usually centred on the internal elastic laminaNot clinically significant — lesions do not encroach on the lumen. Age > 50
Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasiaMedium-sized arteriesHealing response to inflammation or mechanical injury; SMC- and ECM-rich lesionTransplant-associated arteriopathy, stents, balloon angioplasty
L01 · Arteriosclerosis10

Pattern lock — telling the four apart in one question stem

PATH.5002
If the stem says…It is…Because
“calcification of the media of the radial artery, incidental finding on X-ray, patient 78, pulses normal”Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosisMedia, does not narrow the lumen, no ischaemia
“onion-skin concentric thickening, BP 220/130, fibrinoid necrosis”Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosisMalignant hypertension, SMC proliferation
“homogeneous pink hyaline thickening of arterioles in a long-standing diabetic”Hyaline arteriolosclerosisProtein deposition, benign HTN and diabetes
“restenosis 6 months after balloon angioplasty”Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasiaHealing response to mechanical injury
“yellow raised intimal lesion in the abdominal aorta with a lipid core”AtherosclerosisIntimal atheroma in a large elastic artery
Trap
The trap in this set
  • Mönckeberg is the one that is radiologically dramatic and clinically silent. A stem that describes impressive calcification but normal pulses and no ischaemia is steering you away from atherosclerosis, not toward it.

Atherosclerosis — definition and risk

PATH.5003src p.10–11
Thickening / hardening of arteries due to the formation of intimal lesions called “atheromas” (or atheromatous or atherosclerotic plaques) that obstruct the vascular lumen and can rupture to cause sudden occlusion.Lecture 01, slide 10
Modifiable risk factorsNon-modifiable (constitutional)Additional important risk factors
1. Hyperlipidemia
2. Hypertension
3. Cigarette smoking
4. Diabetes mellitus
5. Obesity		1. Increasing age
2. Male gender
3. Family history
4. Genetic abnormalities
5. Inherited causes (e.g. familial hypercholesterolemia)		Inflammation · Metabolic syndrome · Homocysteinemia · Lipoprotein-a

Natural history — as given

  • Underlies the pathogenesis of coronary, cerebral, and peripheral vascular disease
  • Causes more morbidity and mortality (roughly half of all deaths) in the Western world than any other disorder
L01 · Arteriosclerosis12

Pathogenesis — the response-to-injury hypothesis, in order

PATH.5003src p.13–18
Step 1 · injury
  • Increased vascular permeability, enhanced leucocyte adhesion, altered gene expression
  • Hemodynamic disturbances: ostia of exiting vessels, branch points, posterior abdominal aorta — non-laminar flow
  • Hypercholesterolemia: ↑ LDL and lipoprotein-a, ↓ HDL
  • Inflammation · Smoking
Steps 2–4 · lipid + cell
  • LDL aggregates and/or is oxidised by ROS → collects within macrophages → foam cells → release IL-1 → promote inflammation
  • Activated macrophages engulf lipids, oxidise them, release ROS, cytokines and growth factors for SMCs
  • Activated T-lymphocytes release interferon-γ → activate macrophages, ECs and SMCs
Steps 5–6 · remodelling
  • Intimal SMC proliferation and ECM deposition convert the earliest lesion, a fatty streak, into a mature fibrofatty atheroma
  • Growth factors: PDGF (from adherent platelets, macrophages, ECs, SMCs), FGF, TGF-α
L01 · Arteriosclerosis13

Morphology — fatty streak vs plaque, and where they sit

PATH.5004src p.19–22
Fatty streak
  • Flat yellow macules that coalesce to form longer streaks (1 cm or longer)
  • Made of lipid-filled macrophages
  • Not raised; no obstruction
  • Seen in the aorta of almost everyone
Atheromatous plaque
  • (F) fibrous cap · (C) central lipid core · (L) lumen
  • Thinning of the media under the most advanced plaque
  • Neovascularisation and calcification
  • Raised, white-yellow, encroaches on the lumen

Vessel involvement — in descending order of how extensively involved

1 · Lower abdominal aorta and iliac arteries→2 · Coronary arteries→3 · Popliteal arteries→4 · Internal carotid arteries→5 · Vessels of the circle of Willis
Exam Lock
Memory line for the order
  • A-C-P-I-C — the vessels get smaller and more proximal-to-distal as you go down the list; the abdominal aorta below the renals is the single most involved segment, which is why AAA is infrarenal.

Complications — five, numbered as taught

PATH.5004PATH.5005PATH.5006src p.23–27
#ComplicationMechanismClinical consequence
1Stenosis of medium-sized vesselsProgressive luminal narrowing. Atherosclerosis is asymptomatic until occlusion is > 70%Angina pectoris · Peripheral vascular disease · Ischemic bowel disease
2Rupture, ulceration or erosionExposure of thrombogenic substances causing thrombus formation → partial or complete obstruction of the lumenAcute myocardial infarction (“heart attack”) · TIA / stroke
3Haemorrhage into a plaqueRupture of the overlying fibrous cap, or of the thin-walled vessels in areas of neovascularisationSudden plaque expansion → acute occlusion
4Aneurysm formationAtherosclerosis-induced pressure or ischaemic atrophy of the underlying media with loss of elastic tissue → weakness → potential ruptureAbdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)
5AtheroembolismPlaque rupture discharges atherosclerotic debris into the bloodstream → microemboliCholesterol emboli syndrome · blue toe syndrome
L01 · Arteriosclerosis16

Cholesterol emboli syndrome — the whole table, verbatim

PATH.5005src p.27–28
Pathogenesis
Disruption of atherosclerotic plaque releasing cholesterol crystals into circulation.
Consequence
Arterial blockage, leading to tissue or organ damage.
Common causes
Post-cardiac catheterization and other vascular procedures OR it can occur spontaneously.
Pathological hallmark
Presence of cholesterol cleft in the embolus.
Clinical manifestation
According to affected blood vessel: acute kidney injury, bowel ischemia, pancreatitis, retinal plaque, stroke
Cutaneous — livedo reticularis
Reticular, lacy skin discoloration / erythema that blanches on pressure
Cutaneous — blue toe syndrome
Acute onset of purple painful digits with intact peripheral pulses because it affects vessels of small diameter
Trap
Why “intact pulses” is the whole question
  • Blue toe syndrome looks like acute limb ischaemia but the pulses are normal — the emboli are microscopic. A stem with painful blue toes and absent pulses is large-vessel occlusion, not atheroembolism.
  • The other giveaway is timing: days after a catheterisation, often with a rising creatinine and eosinophilia.

Prevention strategies

Primary — modification of risk factors
  • Stop smoking
  • Exercise
  • Weight loss
  • Control hypertension
  • Lower LDL and raise HDL — diet and statins
Secondary
  • Aspirin (antiplatelet)
  • Statins
  • Beta blockers (limit cardiac demand)
  • CABG (coronary artery bypass graft)
  • Carotid endarterectomy

Hypertension — where the lecture pivots

PATH.5007src p.32
Systemic and local tissue blood pressures are maintained within a narrow range to prevent untoward consequences. Low pressures (hypotension) → inadequate organ perfusion → dysfunction or tissue death. High pressure (hypertension) → end organ damage → one of the major risk factors for atherosclerosis.Lecture 01, slide 32

ACC/AHA guidelines — as printed

CategorySystolic (mm Hg)Diastolic (mm Hg)
Normal BP< 120and< 80
High normal BP120–129and< 80
Stage I hypertension130–139or80–89
Stage II hypertension≥ 140or≥ 90
Hypertensive crisis (severe)> 180and/or> 120
L01 · Arteriosclerosis19

Regulation of blood pressure

PATH.5007src p.33–34
  • Cardiac output = determined by blood volume and heart rate
  • Peripheral resistance of arterioles and capillaries: controlled by humoral factors like angiotensin, prostaglandins and nitrous oxide, and neural factors like α and β adrenergic
Bottom Line
Carry this forward
  • When you reach Diuretics, Antihypertensives I and II, hold each drug against this equation: diuretics and aldosterone antagonists cut volume → CO; β-blockers cut HR → CO; ACE-I/ARB, CCBs, α-blockers and direct vasodilators cut PR.

L01 · Arteriosclerosis21

Practice — arteriosclerosis and the plaque

PATH.5005

A 62-year-old man has a coronary angiogram after two episodes of chest pain at rest. A 40% eccentric lesion in the LAD is described as having a thin fibrous cap, a large lipid core and dense macrophage infiltration at the lesion shoulders. Which feature best predicts his risk of acute myocardial infarction?

  1. AThe 40% degree of luminal stenosis
  2. BThe thin fibrous cap with a large lipid core
  3. CThe eccentric rather than concentric shape
  4. DThe location in the left anterior descending artery
  5. EThe presence of medial calcification
Answer
B. Vulnerable plaques have thin fibrous caps, large lipid cores, and increased inflammation with fragile neovascularisation; shoulder areas are more susceptible. Degree of stenosis predicts angina (symptoms begin above ~70% occlusion) but not rupture — most infarcts arise from non-critical lesions.
PATH.5005

Three days after cardiac catheterisation a 70-year-old develops painful, purple discolouration of several toes. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable and symmetric. Creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 2.1 mg/dL. What is the pathological hallmark of the responsible lesion?

  1. AFibrinoid necrosis of the arteriolar wall
  2. BCholesterol clefts within the embolus
  3. CConcentric onion-skin intimal thickening
  4. DCalcification of the internal elastic lamina
  5. EFoam cells in a non-raised intimal macule
Answer
B. Blue toe syndrome with intact pulses, days after an arterial procedure, with acute kidney injury = cholesterol emboli syndrome. The pathological hallmark is the presence of a cholesterol cleft in the embolus.
L01 · Arteriosclerosis22

Practice — arteriosclerosis and the plaque (cont.)

PATH.5002

A radial artery from a 79-year-old shows heavy calcification of the media centred on the internal elastic lamina. The lumen is patent and the patient has no ischaemic symptoms. Which process is this?

  1. AAtherosclerosis
  2. BHyaline arteriolosclerosis
  3. CMönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis
  4. DHyperplastic arteriolosclerosis
  5. EFibromuscular intimal hyperplasia
Answer
C. Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis: calcific deposits in the media of medium-sized arteries, usually centred on the internal elastic lamina, in patients older than 50. The lesions do not encroach on the vessel lumen and are not clinically significant.
L01 · Arteriosclerosis23

Practice — pathogenesis and hypertension

PATH.5003

Which cell is directly responsible for converting a fatty streak into a mature fibrofatty atheroma?

  1. AThe endothelial cell, by increasing permeability
  2. BThe macrophage, by engulfing oxidised LDL
  3. CThe T lymphocyte, by releasing interferon-γ
  4. DThe smooth muscle cell, by proliferating and depositing ECM
  5. EThe platelet, by adhering to denuded endothelium
Answer
D. Intimal SMC proliferation and ECM deposition lead to the conversion of the earliest lesion, a fatty streak, into a mature fibrofatty atheroma. The other four cells all contribute signals (PDGF, IL-1, IFN-γ) — but the structural conversion is the smooth muscle cell's work.
PATH.5007

A 44-year-old woman has a blood pressure of 168/104 mm Hg on three occasions, an unexplained hypokalaemia and an abdominal bruit. Under the lecture's classification, which category and cause does this pattern point to?

  1. APrimary hypertension — increased peripheral resistance
  2. BSecondary hypertension — renal (renal artery stenosis)
  3. CSecondary hypertension — neurogenic
  4. DPrimary hypertension — stress, hormonal, neural
  5. ESecondary hypertension — increased vasoactive hormones
Answer
B. 95% of hypertension is primary, but the stem gives a renovascular signature: young-ish patient, abdominal bruit, hypokalaemia from secondary hyperaldosteronism. Renal causes — glomerulonephritis and renal artery stenosis — head the secondary list.
PATH.5007

Under the ACC/AHA table used in this lecture, a reading of 136/78 mm Hg is classified as:

  1. ANormal BP
  2. BHigh normal BP
  3. CStage I hypertension
  4. DStage II hypertension
  5. EHypertensive crisis
Answer
C. Stage I hypertension is 130–139 systolic or 80–89 diastolic. Because the categories are joined by *or* above the high-normal band, the systolic value alone (136) fixes the stage.

Lecture 01 — summary sheet

Everything below appears again in the Cardiovascular summary sheet at the end of the block.

Bottom line

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Arteriosclerosis is a family of four wall-thickening processes; only atherosclerosis builds an intimal atheroma, and the atheroma's danger is decided not by its size but by cap thickness, core size and inflammation.

Exam Locks

Exam Lock
The five that get asked
  • Atherosclerosis is asymptomatic until occlusion is > 70% — that number is the boundary between silent disease and angina.
  • Mönckeberg does not narrow the lumen and is not clinically significant.
  • Fatty streaks are not raised, cause no obstruction, and are present in almost everyone's aorta.
  • Vessel order: lower abdominal aorta and iliacs → coronaries → popliteal → internal carotid → circle of Willis.
  • BP = CO × PR, and hypertension is 95% primary / 5% secondary.

Traps

Trap
Three ways this lecture is made to look harder than it is
  • Confusing hyaline (protein, benign HTN + diabetes) with hyperplastic (SMC onion-skin, malignant HTN) arteriolosclerosis.
  • Assuming the tightest stenosis causes the infarct — the vulnerable plaque usually is not the tightest one.
  • Reading blue toes as large-vessel occlusion when the stem hands you intact pulses.

CLSK · Peripheral Vascular System27

The three bedside tests you will be marked on

CPD.0.0188src p.48–50
Capillary refill — technique
Place pressure on arteriolar capillaries by pressing down on the nail so it blanches, then let go and note the time it takes for the pink colour to return. Do at least one nail on each limb. Results can be affected if the room temperature is low.
Capillary refill — values
≤ 2 s normal · > 3 s abnormal
Allen's test — indication
Test to determine the patency of the collateral arterial blood supply to the hand.
Allen's test — technique
Locate the radial and ulnar artery with index and 3rd digit → patient makes a tight fist → compress both radial and ulnar arteries firmly with your thumbs → patient opens the hand, the palm should be pale → release the ulnar side to test ulnar patency, then repeat releasing the radial.
Allen's test — meaning
Ensures patency of the ulnar artery before puncturing the radial artery for blood samples. Persisting pallor indicates occlusion of the ulnar/radial artery or its distal branches.
Buerger's test — technique
Patient supine; raise both feet to 60–90° for up to 2 minutes; observe for maximal pallor with emptying of the superficial veins. Then sit up and dangle the feet over the edge of the bed.
Buerger's test — normal timings
Return of pinkness ≈ 10 seconds or less; filling of the veins of the feet and ankles ≈ 15 seconds.
Buerger's test — positive
If the leg becomes blue, then red, the test is positive.
CLSK · Peripheral Vascular System28

Ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI)

CPD.0.0188src p.51
  • Patient supine · Doppler probe + sphygmomanometer · ABPI = P_leg / P_arm · leg is normally higher
ABPI valueInterpretationAction
above 1.2Abnormal — vessel hardening from PVDRefer or measure toe pressure
1.0 – 1.2Normal rangeNone
0.90 – 0.99AcceptableNone
0.80 – 0.89Some arterial diseaseManage risk factors
0.50 – 0.79Moderate arterial diseaseRoutine specialist referral
under 0.50Severe arterial diseaseUrgent specialist referral
Trap
Why a high ABPI is bad news, not good news
  • An ABPI above 1.2 does not mean excellent perfusion — it means the vessels are too calcified to compress (classically diabetes, chronic kidney disease). That is why the action is to measure the toe pressure instead.
CLSK · Peripheral Vascular System29

Acute vs chronic arterial insufficiency

CPD.0.0185src p.52–56
Acute — caused by
  • Embolus
  • Thrombus
Acute — symptoms
  • Acute pain
  • Tingling & numbness of the limb
  • Paralysis
  • Pale blue limb
  • Pulseless & cold
  • Gangrene
Chronic — causes
  • Outside wall: tumor
  • Within wall: Raynaud's disease, Buerger's disease
  • Within lumen: embolus, thromboembolism, atherosclerosis

Chronic arterial insufficiency — risk factors (verbatim)

  • Family history (genetic predisposition to heart disease & stroke) · Age (> 60) · Diabetes · Smoking · Hypertension · Atherosclerosis · Hyperlipidemia (cholesterol & triglycerides)
  • Lifestyle factors (obesity, poor diet & a sedentary lifestyle)
  • Trousseau syndrome (cancer-associated thrombosis) · Protein C & S deficiency · Pregnancy · Oral contraceptive pills
Chronic arterial insufficiency — symptomsChronic arterial insufficiency — signs
Intermittent claudication · Rest pain (severe cases) · Paresthesia · Paralysis · Pallor · Cold · Hair loss · Skin changes (thin, shiny, taut, flaky)Decreased / absence of pulse · Decreased capillary refill · Ulcers · Gangrene

Other arterial system disorders named: Raynaud's disease · Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) · Leriche syndrome.

Investigations, and the aneurysm sites you are expected to name

Arterial vs neurogenic claudication
  • Arterial claudication is reproducible at a fixed walking distance, relieved by standing still, with absent pulses. Neurogenic (spinal stenosis) claudication is relieved by flexion — leaning on a shopping trolley, cycling — and the pulses are normal.

Venous system — components, examination, special tests

CPD.0.0185CPD.0.0188src p.62–71
Key components
  • Deep veins
  • Superficial veins
  • Perforating veins
  • Venous valves
Primary functions
  • Blood transport — returns deoxygenated blood to the heart (except pulmonary veins, which carry oxygenated blood)
  • Blood reservoir — a capacitance system that can store large volumes of blood
  • Regulation — assists in controlling blood pressure and body temperature
Examination
  • Inspection: size, shape, symmetry, edema, varicosity, colour, pigmentation, ulcer
  • Palpation: temperature, tenderness, veins, edema, size of calf muscle
  • Special tests: manual compression, Trendelenburg, calf circumference, Homan's sign

The three venous pathologies named

EntityFindings (verbatim)
Varicose veinsDilated, tortuous veins · incompetent valves of superficial or deep veins
Superficial thrombophlebitisTender · red · firm and cordlike · varicose veins
Chronic venous insufficiencyEdema · warm · ulcers around the medial malleolus · brown pigmentation · normal pulses

The comparison that gets asked every time — arterial vs venous insufficiency

CPD.0.0185src p.73
FeatureChronic arterial insufficiencyChronic venous insufficiency
PainClaudicationAbsent
PulsesAbsentPresent
ColourPaleNo change
TemperatureColdWarm
SkinShiny, atrophic; loss of hair; nails brittleStasis dermatitis; skin thick
MusclesWastingNo wasting
EdemaAbsentPresent

Bottom Line
Two words decide it
  • Pulses and ulcer site. Pulseless + toe/pressure-point ulcer = arterial. Pulses present + medial malleolus + brown pigmentation = venous.

Deep vein thrombosis

CPD.0.0185CPD.0.0188src p.74–77
Deep venous thrombosis is the formation of clot in the venous circulation in the extremity or pelvic region.CLSK PVS, slide 38
Predisposing factors
  • Reduced mobility / immobility
  • Obesity
  • Smoking
  • Oral contraceptives
  • Trauma
  • Malignancy
  • Surgery
  • Infections
  • Heart failure
  • Family history
Symptoms & signs
  • Legs swollen
  • Warm
  • Tender
  • Asymmetrical calf muscle
  • Discoloration
  • Complication: pulmonary embolism
Special tests
  • Calf circumference
  • Homan's sign
  • Wells score
Calf circumference — technique
Palpate the tibial tuberosity and measure 10 cm below. From this point measure the calf circumference. Normal = difference < 3 cm; positive = difference > 3 cm.
Homan's sign — technique
Patient supine, knee extended, passively dorsiflex the foot at the ankle; calf discomfort = positive.
Homan's sign — the caveat printed on the slide
Sensitivity 10–54%, specificity 39–89%. Danger — dislodgment of thrombus. Done for teaching purposes.
Trap
Do not treat Homan's sign as a rule-out
  • The lecture prints its own numbers to make the point: a sensitivity as low as 10% means a negative Homan's sign tells you almost nothing. The Wells score plus D-dimer is what excludes DVT in a low-risk outpatient.
CLSK · Peripheral Vascular System34

Wells score and “EAT CHIPS”

CPD.0.0185src p.78–79
  • The Wells' DVT criteria can be used in the outpatient and emergency department setting. By risk stratifying to low risk (Wells' score < 2) and a negative D-dimer, the clinician can exclude the need for ultrasound to rule out DVT.
  • Note: the Wells' score is less useful in hospitalized patients (Silveira PC, 2015).

“EAT CHIPS” — criteria for predicting the probability of developing a pulmonary embolism

LetterCriterionPoints
EEdema in the leg or any other symptoms of DVT3
AAlternative diagnosis being less likely3
TTachycardia1.5
CCancer1
HHemoptysis1
IImmobilization1.5
PPrevious history of DVT or PE1.5
SSurgery (major) in the past month1.5

Significance of the Modified Wells criteria: < 2 points = low risk for PE; 2–6 points = moderate risk; > 6 points = high risk.

Clinical approach to leg swelling

Directed Learning Activity — links BPM1 CPR, CLSK Peripheral Vascular, and PVS Simulations 1 & 2.

Department of Clinical Skills  ·  source pp. 94–112

Objectives — verbatim

  • Mention the causes of unilateral peripheral edema. CPD.0.0176
  • Determine the difference between edema and lymphedema. CPD.0.0177
  • Discuss the differential diagnosis along with differentiating signs/symptoms and diagnostic tests in a patient with peripheral edema. CPD.0.0178

64-year-old man comes to the clinic with bilateral swelling of the lower extremities for the last 35 years. His physical examination shows dark brown patches, venous varicosities below the knees. His legs are warm, non-tender, with grade 3 pitting edema up the knees.The case the session is built on
DLA · Clinical approach to leg swelling37

Pathophysiology — five mechanisms, and only five

CPD.0.0176src p.97–98
Sodium and water retention→Increased capillary permeability→Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure→Lowered oncotic pressure→Lymphatic obstruction

Edema of a limb — swelling caused by excess fluid trapped in your body's tissues.

Exam Lock
Map every differential back to one of the five
  • CHF → hydrostatic · nephrotic and cirrhosis → oncotic · cellulitis → permeability · filariasis and post-radiotherapy → lymphatic obstruction · NSAIDs and CCBs → Na⁺ and water retention.

Edema vs lymphedema — the discriminating table

CPD.0.0177src p.99, 103
FeatureEdemaLymphedema
CauseFluid accumulation due to venous or systemic conditionsLymphatic dysfunction or obstruction
PittingUsually pitting (except in late stages)Non-pitting
SymmetryOften bilateralCan be unilateral or bilateral but asymmetric
Skin changesMinimal unless chronicThickened, fibrotic skin (woody texture)
Response to elevationImproves with limb elevationDoes not improve significantly
Associated symptomsMay have pain, redness, or warmth (if inflammatory)Heaviness, tightness, and reduced range of motion
Lymphedema: painless, firm edema that characteristically causes squaring of the toes and a dorsal hump on the foot. In contrast to venous edema, lymphedema varies little during the day and ulceration is uncommon unless there is secondary infection.DLA slide 103
DLA · Clinical approach to leg swelling39

Differential diagnosis of peripheral edema

CPD.0.0178src p.101–102
Acute
  • Deep vein thrombosis
  • Compartment syndrome
  • Cellulitis
  • Ruptured gastrocnemius muscle tear
Gradual
  • Medications
  • Lipedema
  • Lymphedema
  • Chronic venous insufficiency
  • Systemic process
ConditionKey signs / symptomsDiagnostic tests
Congestive heart failureBilateral edema, dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles on lung auscultationBNP, echocardiogram, chest X-ray
Chronic venous insufficiencyEdema worse at end of the day, varicose veins, skin hyperpigmentation, venous ulcersDoppler ultrasound (venous reflux study)
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)Unilateral swelling, pain, erythema, positive Homan's signD-dimer, venous ultrasound
Nephrotic syndromeGeneralized edema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemiaUrinalysis, serum albumin, kidney function tests
Cirrhosis / liver diseaseAscites, jaundice, spider angiomas, bilateral edemaLiver function tests, abdominal ultrasound
LymphedemaChronic, non-pitting edema, thickened skin, often unilateralLymphoscintigraphy, ultrasound

DLA · Clinical approach to leg swelling40

Management of lymphedema

CPD.0.018src p.104
Non-pharmacological
  • Compression therapy (graded compression stockings or bandaging)
  • Manual lymphatic drainage (specialized massage to improve lymph flow)
  • Exercise therapy (low-impact activities to improve circulation)
  • Skin care (to prevent infections and complications)
  • Weight management (to reduce pressure on lymphatic vessels)
Medical
  • Diuretics are generally NOT recommended as they do not address the underlying lymphatic dysfunction
  • Antibiotics if secondary cellulitis is present
Surgical (severe cases)
  • Lymphatic bypass surgery (to improve drainage)
  • Debulking procedures (for advanced fibrotic lymphedema)
Trap
The single most testable line on this slide
  • Diuretics do not treat lymphedema. The fluid is not there because of a hydrostatic/oncotic imbalance — the drainage route is blocked. A stem offering furosemide for a woody, non-pitting, post-mastectomy arm is the distractor.
DLA · Clinical approach to leg swelling41

Practice — the faculty's own question set (Vascular Pathology, NCRS Lecture 1)

Reproduced from the practice-question block printed inside this session; answer key p.112.

faculty Q1

A 58-year-old man had a myocardial infarction 1 year ago, which was the first major illness in his life. He now wants to prevent another acute coronary event and is advised to begin a program of exercise and to change his diet. After one year, a reduction in the level of which of the following analytes in the serum would be the best indicator of the success of his diet and exercise regimen?

  1. AHDL cholesterol
  2. BLDL cholesterol
  3. CGlucose
  4. DFree fatty acids
  5. ETriglycerides
Answer
B. Faculty answer key: B. LDL is the causal lipoprotein in atherogenesis — lowering LDL (not raising it) is the endpoint. A *reduction* in HDL would be harmful, which is why option A is a trap.
faculty Q3

A 50-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of exercise-induced angina pectoris. BP 145/85, HR 79 and slightly irregular. Coronary angiography shows a fixed 75% narrowing of the anterior descending branch of the left coronary artery. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes for 20 years and his serum cholesterol is typically over 230 mg/dL. Which of the following is the earliest event that gives rise to narrowing of the artery?

  1. AAlteration in vasomotor tone
  2. BConversion of smooth muscle cells to foam cells
  3. CEndothelial dysfunction
  4. D“Danger signals” delivered to macrophages by oxidized HDL
  5. EModification of hepatic lipoprotein receptors
Answer
C. Faculty answer key: C. The response-to-injury hypothesis begins with endothelial injury and dysfunction. Note the distractor in B — foam cells derive from macrophages, not smooth muscle cells, and they are not the earliest event.
DLA · Clinical approach to leg swelling42

Practice — the faculty's own question set (Vascular Pathology, NCRS Lecture 1) (cont.)

faculty Q8

A 42-year-old man dies after a motor vehicle accident. At autopsy the aorta shows multiple flat, yellow lesions that do not significantly narrow the vascular lumen; microscopy shows numerous lipid-filled macrophages within the intima. Which of the following best describes the vascular lesion?

  1. AFatty streak
  2. BAtherosclerotic plaque
  3. CFibromuscular intimal hyperplasia
  4. DFibrofatty atheroma
  5. EMönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis
Answer
A. Faculty answer key: A. Flat (not raised) + no luminal narrowing + lipid-filled macrophages in the intima = fatty streak. The word that eliminates B and D is “do not significantly narrow”.
DLA · Clinical approach to leg swelling43

Directed Learning Activity — history first, ECG second, and one alarm symptom that changes everything.

Dr Michon Sukhoo-Pertab · Department of Clinical Skills  ·  source pp. 113–150

Learning objectives — verbatim

  • Define palpitations.
  • Discuss the differential diagnoses for palpitations including cardiac and non-cardiac etiologies. CPD.0.0181
  • Outline an approach to history taking for a patient presenting with palpitations. CPD.0.0182
  • Describe and discuss the relevant physical examination and expected findings for a patient presenting with palpitations. CPD.0.0183

DLA · Clinical approach to palpitations44

What palpitations are — and are not

CPD.0.0181src p.116–119
It is the unpleasant awareness of the heartbeat. Patients use various terms to describe palpitations such as skipping, racing, fluttering, pounding, or stopping of the heart. Palpitations may be irregular, rapidly slow down or accelerate, or arise from the increased forcefulness of cardiac contraction. Palpitations do not necessarily mean heart disease.DLA Palpitations, slide 116

Differential diagnoses — the full three-column table

CardiovascularPsychiatricOther systemic causes
Disturbance in electrical activity (arrhythmias): Atrial fibrillation · Atrial flutter · Multifocal atrial tachycardia · Premature supraventricular contractions · Premature ventricular contractions · Sinus tachycardia · Supraventricular tachycardia · Ventricular tachycardia · Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome · Sick sinus syndrome

Changes in structure of the heart: Atrial septal defects · Ventricular septal defects · Cardiomyopathy · Congestive heart failure · Congenital heart disease e.g. Tetralogy of Fallot · Pericarditis · Valvopathies		Panic disorder or panic attacks
Agoraphobia
Any other phobia
Generalized anxiety disorder
Somatization disorder
Depression		Hyperthyroidism · Hypoglycemia · Fever · Sepsis · Dehydration · Hypovolemia · Electrolyte imbalances e.g. hyperkalemia · Anemia · Mastocytosis · Idiopathic · Pregnancy · Pulmonary disease / pulmonary embolism · Vasovagal syndrome · POTS

Drugs and medications: alcohol, caffeine, theophylline, digitalis, beta-agonists, phenothiazine

The lecture flags atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter and anxiety with an asterisk as the most common causes in adults.

DLA · Clinical approach to palpitations45

Alarming symptoms — the four that change management

CPD.0.0182src p.125
Alarming symptomConcern
Palpitations associated with syncope or presyncopeSuggest ventricular tachycardia (VT) or supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) that is sufficiently rapid to reduce effective cardiac output.
Family history of sudden cardiac death or known arrhythmiaRaises concern for idiopathic VT arising from the right ventricular outflow tract, Brugada syndrome, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, or the prolonged QT syndrome.
Use of any medications known to prolong the QT intervalSuch as methadone, antiarrhythmic agents, or antipsychotics. Acquired prolongation of the QT interval can lead to serious ventricular arrhythmias.
Personal history of heart disease — CAD, congenital or valvular heart disease, hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathyPredictor of serious arrhythmia. Absence of a personal history of heart disease symptoms such as chest pain or dyspnea is less helpful because these are often present in panic disorder.
Exam Lock
The one-line rule the session is built to teach
  • Syncope in association with palpitations should prompt a work-up for serious arrhythmia — and the diagnosis of an anxiety disorder does not preclude the diagnosis of an arrhythmia.
DLA · Clinical approach to palpitations46

History → diagnosis: the pattern table

CPD.0.0182src p.124, 128
Key clinical findingSuggested diagnosis
Single skipped beatsBenign ectopy
Feeling of being unable to catch one's breathVentricular premature contractions
Single pounding sensationsVentricular premature contractions
Rapid regular pounding in the neckSupraventricular arrhythmias
Palpitations worse at nightBenign ectopy or atrial fibrillation
Positional palpitationsAtrioventricular nodal tachycardia
Palpitations since childhoodSupraventricular tachycardia
Rapid, irregular rhythmAtrial fibrillation
Palpitations terminated by vagal maneuversSupraventricular tachycardia
Palpitations associated with emotional distressPsychiatric etiology
Medications and recreational drug useDrug-induced palpitations

Interview framework: allow the patient to describe symptoms in their own words before closed questions; the focus is to identify patients who require diagnostic testing for serious arrhythmia; identification of a psychiatric disorder benefits the patient even if unrelated.

DLA · Clinical approach to palpitations47

Physical examination findings → diagnosis

CPD.0.0183src p.133
Physical examination findingSuggested diagnosis
Mid-systolic click of mitral valve prolapseSuggests a supraventricular arrhythmia
Harsh holosystolic murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy along the left sternal border, increases with the Valsalva maneuverSuggests atrial fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia
Crescendo mid-diastolic murmurSuggests a possible atrial myxoma
Displaced and enlarged cardiac point-of-maximal impulse (PMI)Suggests dilated cardiomyopathy, which increases the likelihood of VT and atrial fibrillation
Tremulousness, brisk deep tendon reflexes, or fine hand tremorSigns of hyperthyroidism → increased sympathetic response → sinus tachycardia
Dilated pupils, or skin or nasal septal perforationsSigns of stimulant drug use → increased sympathetic response → sinus tachycardia
Visible neck pulsations associated with palpitationsIncrease the likelihood of atrioventricular nodal reentry tachycardia
Positive stand testSuggests postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome
DLA · Clinical approach to palpitations48

Investigations and the ECG patterns you must recognise

CPD.0.0184src p.135, 141–146
12-lead ECG
Gold standard diagnostic technique for a patient with palpitations. Can be done at the physician's office or through ambulatory monitoring devices.
Ambulatory ECG monitoring
Performed with the goal of correlating a transitory symptom with arrhythmia; the choice of monitoring should be guided by the yield.
Directed studies
Cardiovascular disease → echocardiogram · palpitations on exertion / suspected myocardial ischemia → exercise stress test · anemia → CBC, iron studies · thyrotoxicosis → thyroid panel · pheochromocytoma → 24-hour urine VMA · DKA → complete metabolic panel
RhythmRateP wavePRQRS
Sinus tachycardia> 100/min, regularNormal size and configuration, precedes each QRS; may be superimposed on the preceding T waveNormal, constantNormal duration and configuration
Atrial fibrillationAtrial indiscernible; ventricular ~130/min, irregularly irregularAbsent — replaced by fine fibrillatory wavesIndiscernible0.08 s (narrow)
Ventricular tachycardia~187/min, regularAbsentUnmeasurable0.16 s — wide and bizarre; T wave opposite in direction to the QRS

VT is defined as three or more PVCs in a row with a ventricular rate above 100/min; may be monomorphic or polymorphic, sustained or non-sustained. Torsades de pointes is a special variation of polymorphic VT.

DLA · Clinical approach to palpitations49

Case resolution — and the caveats the session ends on

src p.137–138
The patient experienced a syncopal episode in association with his palpitations, raising concern for an arrhythmia significant enough to decrease cardiac output and prevent adequate cerebral perfusion. The patient's family history and the association of his syncope with a high catecholamine state (exercise) also suggest a ventricular tachycardia (VT), such as an idiopathic VT. … during an exercise (treadmill) ECG test, the patient went into VT and experienced syncope.DLA Palpitations, slide 137

Caveats — verbatim

  • No single element of the history can reliably distinguish between arrhythmic and non-arrhythmic causes of palpitations.
  • Palpitations in and of themselves are neither sensitive nor specific for arrhythmia.
  • Many arrhythmias are asymptomatic and will not correlate with symptoms reported during ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring.
  • Most outpatients with palpitations do not have an arrhythmia and unreliably perceive their own cardiac activity.
  • Syncope in association with palpitations should prompt a work-up for serious arrhythmia.
  • Physicians tend to underdiagnose arrhythmias in patients with psychiatric disorders and palpitations.
  • The diagnosis of an anxiety disorder does not preclude the diagnosis of an arrhythmia.
DLA · Clinical approach to palpitations50

Practice — palpitations

CPD.0.0182

A 25-year-old man with well-controlled panic disorder reports 6 months of rapid, regular palpitations occurring only during his morning jog. Three days ago he developed tunnel vision at the end of a run and lost consciousness. His aunt died suddenly while swimming 5 years ago. Examination and resting ECG are normal. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

  1. AReassurance and referral back to psychotherapy
  2. B24-hour Holter monitor only
  3. CExercise (treadmill) ECG test
  4. DThyroid function tests
  5. ESerum electrolytes and magnesium
Answer
C. The palpitations are reproducibly exertional and accompanied by syncope with a family history of sudden death — a catecholamine-driven ventricular arrhythmia. Holter monitoring was unrevealing in the case; the treadmill test reproduced VT with syncope. Panic disorder can cause palpitations but would not cause syncope.
CPD.0.0184

An 80-year-old woman describes a rapid, irregular heartbeat with no clear start or stop. Her pulse is irregularly irregular. Her ECG shows absent P waves replaced by fine fibrillatory waves and a narrow QRS at 130/min. Which single ECG feature most reliably separates this from multifocal atrial tachycardia?

  1. AThe ventricular rate above 100/min
  2. BThe narrow QRS complex
  3. CThe complete absence of discrete P waves
  4. DThe irregular R-R interval
  5. EThe unmeasurable QT interval
Answer
C. MAT also has an irregular rhythm and a narrow QRS, but it has discrete P waves of ≥ 3 different morphologies. Atrial fibrillation has no discrete P waves at all — they are replaced by fibrillatory waves. The lecture itself notes that AF, flutter and MAT can be difficult to separate.
DLA · Clinical approach to palpitations51

Practice — palpitations (cont.)

CPD.0.0183

Which physical finding on this session's table would most specifically raise the possibility of an atrial myxoma as the cause of palpitations?

  1. AMid-systolic click
  2. BHarsh holosystolic murmur increasing with Valsalva
  3. CCrescendo mid-diastolic murmur
  4. DDisplaced enlarged PMI
  5. EVisible neck pulsations
Answer
C. The session's table pairs the crescendo mid-diastolic murmur with atrial myxoma. The mid-systolic click is mitral valve prolapse (SVT); the Valsalva-augmented holosystolic murmur is HCM.
DLA · Clinical approach to palpitations52

src p.155
CodeObjective (verbatim)

Clinical presentations of hypertension

PATH.5010PATH.5012src p.157–160
PresentationDefinition (verbatim)
Benign hypertensionAsymptomatic
Hypertensive crisisBP > 180/120
— Hypertensive urgencySevere hypertension without end-organ damage
— Hypertensive emergencySevere hypertension with end-organ damage
Malignant hypertension> 200/120 mm Hg commonly with advanced bilateral retinopathy (flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, or papilledema)
Hypertensive encephalopathySevere blood pressure elevation with lethargy, seizures, cortical blindness, and coma in absence of other explanations
Hypertensive thrombotic microangiopathySevere blood pressure elevation with hemolysis (breakdown of RBCs) and thrombocytopenia (lowered platelet count) in absence of other explanations
Other emergenciesSevere BP elevation associated with cerebral hemorrhage, acute stroke, acute coronary syndrome, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, aortic aneurysm/dissection, and severe preeclampsia and eclampsia
Exam Lock
The single sentence that separates the two
  • In malignant hypertension, the vascular damage is acute. In benign hypertension, vascular damage is chronic. Everything else — the morphology, the organ damage, the urgency of treatment — follows from that one word.
L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection55

Hyaline vs hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis — the pair that gets asked

PATH.5010PATH.5012src p.161–164
Hyaline arteriolosclerosisHyperplastic arteriolosclerosis
SettingChronic (“benign”) hypertension — and diabetesSudden and severe elevation in blood pressure (malignant hypertension)
MechanismHemodynamic stress → plasma protein leakage and smooth muscle cell matrix productionThickened reduplicated basement membrane (PAS positive) and smooth muscle cell hyperplasia
MorphologyDeposition of homogenous pink material (hyaline) in the vessel wall causing wall thickening and luminal narrowingConcentric laminated “onion skin” thickening with luminal narrowing
Accompanied by—Fibrinoid necrosis (necrotising arteriolitis)
End resultImpairment of blood supply to the tissue and ischemic changesAcute ischemic injury

Organ by organ — what each arteriolosclerosis produces

OrganLesion
KidneyHyaline arteriolosclerosis → benign nephrosclerosis · Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis → malignant nephrosclerosis
BrainBoth hyaline and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis seen → can cause hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhages
RetinaHyperplastic arteriolosclerosis → cotton wool spots
L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection56

Hypertension and the vessel — three levels of damage

PATH.5010PATH.5012src p.160–161
  1. Accelerates atherosclerosis
  2. Degenerative changes in large and medium arteries
    • Cerebrovascular hemorrhage
    • Aortic dissection
  3. Small vessel changes
    • Hyaline arteriolosclerosis: seen in chronic (“benign”) hypertension
    • Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis: seen in malignant hypertension

Complications, by organ (verbatim)

  • Kidney — renal failure; nephrosclerosis (arteriolosclerosis of renal vessels)
  • Heart — left ventricular failure, ischemic heart disease
  • Retina — impairment of vision
L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection57

Morphology of the heart in hypertension — and cor pulmonale

PATH.5010PATH.5012PATH.5016src p.165–167
Systemic (left-sided) hypertensive heart diseaseIsolated pulmonary (right-sided) hypertensive heart disease
• Left ventricular hypertrophy in the absence of other cardiovascular pathology
• Clinical history or pathologic evidence of hypertension in other organs (e.g., kidney)
• Sequence: Hypertension → left ventricular hypertrophy → ischemic heart disease → left ventricular failure		• Also called “Cor Pulmonale” (cor – heart, pulmonale – lung): right heart disease due to lung parenchymal / vascular diseases
• Right ventricular and right atrial hypertrophy
• Sequence: Pulmonary hypertension → right ventricular failure due to back pressure → cor pulmonale
Acute cor pulmonaleChronic cor pulmonaleMorphology
Due to massive pulmonary emboli. Right ventricle is dilated but no hypertrophy.COPD — most common cause. Others: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, cystic fibrosis, or marked obesity.Right ventricular hypertrophy · often right atrial hypertrophy ± dilatation

Pulmonary hypertension is high blood pressure in the blood vessels that supply the lungs (pulmonary arteries). Seen in left heart failure, congenital heart disease, valvular disorders, lung diseases. Morphology: spectrum of changes from fibrotic intimal thickening to medial hyperplasia.

Trap
The distinction the objective is actually testing
  • Acute cor pulmonale dilates; chronic cor pulmonale hypertrophies. A saddle embolus gives you a thin, ballooned RV at autopsy — not a thick one. There has been no time to hypertrophy.
L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection58

Aneurysms — types by what makes the wall

PATH.5013PATH.5014src p.169–170
ClassificationDefinition (verbatim)Common causes
TRUEAll layers involved, classified on basis of shape — saccular (discrete outpouchings) or fusiform (diffuse and circumferential dilations; most common)• Atherosclerotic
• Hypertension
• Syphilitic
• Mycotic: infective
• Vasculitic: polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki's disease
• Congenital: defect in media — Marfan's syndrome, Berry aneurysm
• Iatrogenic: arteriovenous aneurysms for chronic renal failure patients for dialysis
FALSEDefect in wall leading to an extravascular hematoma communicating with intravascular space. Ruptured wall creating a collection of blood (hematoma) bounded externally by adherent extravascular tissues — “pulsating hematoma”
L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection59

Aneurysms: pathogenesis — one imbalance, three routes

PATH.5013src p.171–173
An imbalance between the synthesis and degradation of the extracellular matrix (ECM) → compromise of the structural integrity of arterial media → cystic medial degeneration.Lecture 03, slide 171
Excessive connective tissue degradation
  • Atherosclerosis
Inadequate or abnormal connective tissue synthesis
  • Marfan / Scurvy
Loss of smooth muscle cells
  • Ischaemia of the media — see below

Why the location differs by cause — the mechanism slide

CauseWhat it does to the mediaWhere the aneurysm forms
Atherosclerosis / atheromatous plaqueIschemia of the inner media by increasing diffusion distanceAbdominal aortic aneurysm
HypertensionNarrowing of the lumen of the vasa vasorum → ischemia of the outer media → loss of SMCs and aortic degenerationAscending aortic aneurysm
Exam Lock
The morphology term to attach
  • Cystic medial degeneration — marked elastin fragmentation with areas devoid of elastin that resemble cystic spaces, against the regular layered pattern of elastic tissue in normal media.
L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection60

The five named aneurysms — location, cause, complication

PATH.5013PATH.5014src p.174–182
AneurysmLocationPathogenesisSignature complication / clue
Abdominal aortic aneurysmAbdominal aorta and common iliac arteries; most distal to the renal arteries and proximal to the bifurcationAtherosclerosis. Males >>> females; older, rarely below age 50; smokersRisk of rupture is directly related to the size of the aneurysm. Usually fusiform, may be saccular; lined by raised, ulcerated and calcified (complicated) plaque and thrombi
Syphilitic aneurysmAscending thoracic aortaTertiary syphilis → inflammatory response to the spirochete → obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum → ischemic injury of the elastic tunica media → medial destruction, chronic inflammation and scarring“Tree bark” appearance of the intima; may narrow or occlude coronary ostia; aortic valve ring dilation → valvular insufficiency → massive LV hypertrophy = cor bovinum (cow's heart)
Marfan's syndromeAscending aorta and arch of aortaAutosomal dominant; mutation in the gene for fibrillin-1, required for normal elastic tissue development → elastic fibers become incompetent to resist normal stressCystic medial degeneration → aneurysms, aortic dissection, valve lesions. Elongated axial bones, tall slender body, lower body > upper body length, long thin extremities and fingers; subluxation of the lens (ciliary body is rich in fibrillin)
Berry aneurysmCircle of Willis — most common site: anterior cerebral artery branches; small and saccularNot present at birth but develop over time because the arterial media is congenitally attenuatedClinically silent until they rupture — often during increased intracranial pressure (straining at stool or sexual orgasm) → subarachnoid hemorrhage → severe headache, coma. Association: autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)
Mycotic aneurysmAnywhere — usually smallNot a true aneurysm. Weakening and rupture of the vessel wall by a microbial infection. Called mycotic (a misnomer) because initially people thought it was caused by fungal infectionA dislodged septic embolus, usually as a complication of infective endocarditis, damages the wall → hemorrhage and abscess at the site of rupture. Usually clinically silent
L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection61

Abdominal aortic aneurysm — clinical features in full

PATH.5014src p.175–177
Presentation
  • Asymptomatic
  • Discovered incidentally on physical examination as an abdominal mass (often palpably pulsating) that simulates a tumor
  • Rarely as an emergency with shock due to rupture
  • Rupture into the peritoneal cavity or retroperitoneal tissues with massive, potentially fatal hemorrhage
Branch-vessel obstruction → downstream ischemic injury
  • iliac → leg
  • renal → kidney
  • mesenteric → gastrointestinal tract
  • vertebral arteries → spinal cord
Also
  • Embolism from atheroma or mural thrombus

CT: bright contrast material in the blood filling the open aortic lumen, whereas the surrounding mural thrombus has decreased (darker) attenuation. A total aortic diameter of 7–8 cm is in great danger of rupture.

L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection62

Aortic dissection

PATH.5015src p.183–184
Separation / dissection of the layers of media due to structural weakening with a blood-filled channel within the aortic wall (between the middle and outer third of aortic wall).Lecture 03, slide 183
Epidemiology
  • Common in males, aged 40 to 60 years, with antecedent hypertension
  • Younger patients with syndromic diseases affecting the aorta (e.g. Marfan syndrome)
Etiopathogenesis
  • Hypertension
  • Abnormality of connective tissue: Marfan's and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes
Microscopy
  • Elastic tissue fragmentation
  • Accumulations of amorphous proteoglycan-rich ECM

DeBakey / proximal-distal classification — based on the portion affected

Proximal lesions (Type A dissection)Distal lesions (Type B dissection)
ExtentMore common, involve the ascending aortaInvolve the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery
PrognosisHigh mortalityBetter prognosis
ManagementNeeds rapid medical and surgical treatmentCan be managed conservatively
L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection63

Aortic dissection — clinical features and complications

PATH.5015src p.185–188

Classic clinical symptoms (verbatim)

  • Sudden onset of excruciating pain
  • Usually beginning in the anterior chest
  • Radiating to the back between the scapulae
  • Moving downward as the dissection progresses
  • Absent / weak peripheral pulses
  • Pain can be confused with that of myocardial infarction (MI).

Complications

ComplicationMechanism
Most common cause of deathRupture of the dissection and bleeding into the pericardial, pleural, or peritoneal cavities
Retrograde dissection into the aortic rootDisrupts the aortic valve annulus → cardiac tamponade and aortic insufficiency
Extension into branch vesselsGreat arteries of the neck, or the coronary, renal, mesenteric or iliac arteries → vascular obstruction and ischemic consequences
— coronary arteriesMyocardial infarction
— spinal arteriesTransverse myelitis

Gross: an opened aorta with a proximal dissection originating from a small, oblique intimal tear associated with an intramural hematoma. The intimal tear occurred in a region largely free of atherosclerotic plaque; the distal edge of the hematoma lies at the edge of a large area of atherosclerosis, which arrested the propagation of the dissection. If the hematoma re-enters the lumen through a second distal intimal tear it creates a “double-barreled aorta”, which over time becomes endothelialized, forming a chronic dissection.

Trap
Why plaque protects here but causes AAA elsewhere
  • Atherosclerosis causes abdominal aneurysm by starving the inner media — but a dense plaque is also a mechanical barrier that arrests a propagating dissection. That is why the tear itself occurs in relatively plaque-free aorta.
L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection64

Practice — hypertension and the vessel wall

PATH.5010

A 38-year-old man presents with BP 226/128 mm Hg, headache and blurred vision. Fundoscopy shows flame-shaped haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and papilloedema. Creatinine is 3.4 mg/dL. A renal biopsy is most likely to show which arteriolar change?

  1. AHomogeneous pink hyaline thickening of the arteriolar wall
  2. BConcentric laminated onion-skin thickening with fibrinoid necrosis
  3. CCalcification centred on the internal elastic lamina
  4. DFibromuscular intimal hyperplasia of the interlobar arteries
  5. EAmyloid deposition in the arteriolar wall
Answer
B. Malignant hypertension (> 200/120 with retinopathy and end-organ damage) produces hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis — onion-skin concentric thickening, PAS-positive reduplicated basement membrane, smooth muscle hyperplasia, accompanied by fibrinoid necrosis (necrotising arteriolitis) — i.e. malignant nephrosclerosis. Hyaline change belongs to chronic benign hypertension and diabetes.
PATH.5016

A 66-year-old man with severe COPD has a raised JVP, hepatomegaly and pedal edema. At autopsy the right ventricular free wall is 8 mm thick and the right atrium is enlarged; the left ventricle is normal. What is the diagnosis, and what distinguishes it from the acute form?

  1. ASystemic hypertensive heart disease; the acute form spares the atrium
  2. BChronic cor pulmonale; the acute form shows RV dilation without hypertrophy
  3. CChronic cor pulmonale; the acute form shows biventricular hypertrophy
  4. DAcute cor pulmonale; the chronic form is caused by pulmonary embolism
  5. ERestrictive cardiomyopathy; the acute form follows myocarditis
Answer
B. Chronic cor pulmonale: RV (± RA) hypertrophy, COPD is the most common cause. Acute cor pulmonale follows massive pulmonary emboli and shows a dilated RV with no hypertrophy — there has been no time to remodel.
L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection65

Practice — aneurysm and dissection

PATH.5014

A 24-year-old man, 196 cm tall with arachnodactyly and upward lens subluxation, dies suddenly. The ascending aorta is dilated and shows elastin fragmentation with cystic spaces devoid of elastin. Which protein is defective?

  1. AType III collagen
  2. BFibrillin-1
  3. CElastin
  4. DType I collagen
  5. ELysyl oxidase
Answer
B. Marfan syndrome — autosomal dominant mutation in the gene for fibrillin-1, required for normal elastic tissue development. The aneurysm sits at the ascending aorta and arch; the histology is cystic medial degeneration; the ocular sign is lens subluxation because the ciliary body is rich in fibrillin.
PATH.5014

A 52-year-old man with a two-week history of fever and a new murmur develops sudden severe abdominal pain. Imaging shows a small saccular dilation of the superior mesenteric artery. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Which aneurysm type is this, and by what mechanism?

  1. ATrue saccular aneurysm from atherosclerosis of the SMA
  2. BBerry aneurysm from congenital medial attenuation
  3. CMycotic aneurysm from a dislodged septic embolus damaging the wall
  4. DFalse aneurysm from iatrogenic catheter injury
  5. ESyphilitic aneurysm from obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
Answer
C. Fever + new murmur + S. aureus bacteraemia = infective endocarditis; a dislodged septic embolus weakens the arterial wall — a mycotic aneurysm, which the lecture is explicit is not a true aneurysm and is a misnomer (not fungal).
L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection66

Practice — aneurysm and dissection (cont.)

PATH.5015

A 58-year-old hypertensive man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the interscapular region and a 24 mm Hg difference in systolic pressure between arms. CT shows a dissection flap beginning 2 cm above the aortic valve. Which statement is correct?

  1. AThis is a distal (Type B) lesion and can be managed conservatively
  2. BThis is a proximal (Type A) lesion, is more common, carries high mortality and needs rapid medical and surgical treatment
  3. CThe dissection plane lies between the intima and the inner third of the media
  4. DThe most common cause of death is myocardial infarction from coronary extension
  5. EThe intimal tear characteristically arises within a heavily calcified plaque
Answer
B. Ascending involvement = proximal / Type A: more common, high mortality, requires rapid medical and surgical treatment. The plane is between the middle and outer third of the media; the most common cause of death is rupture into the pericardial, pleural or peritoneal cavities; and the tear typically occurs in aorta largely free of plaque.
L03 · Hypertension, Aneurysms & Dissection67

Lecture 03 — summary sheet

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Hypertension damages vessels two ways — slowly (hyaline → benign nephrosclerosis) or suddenly (hyperplastic + fibrinoid necrosis → malignant nephrosclerosis) — and a weakened media then fails either by ballooning outward (aneurysm) or splitting along its length (dissection).
Exam Lock
The eight that get asked
  • Malignant HTN = > 200/120 with end-organ damage; urgency vs emergency is decided by end-organ damage, not by the number.
  • Hyaline = chronic/benign + diabetes. Hyperplastic = malignant, onion-skin, PAS+, fibrinoid necrosis.
  • Cor pulmonale: acute dilates (PE), chronic hypertrophies (COPD).
  • AAA is infrarenal, atherosclerotic, male, > 50, smoker — and rupture risk tracks size.
  • Syphilis → ascending thoracic aorta, tree bark, cor bovinum.
  • Berry → circle of Willis, ACA branches, ADPKD, SAH on straining.
  • Mycotic is not a true aneurysm — septic embolus, usually from infective endocarditis.
  • Type A > Type B in frequency; Type A needs surgery; dissection plane = middle/outer third of media.
Trap
Three traps
  • Calling a pulsating haematoma a true aneurysm — it is a false aneurysm; the wall is adherent tissue, not vessel.
  • Attributing an ascending aneurysm to atherosclerosis — atherosclerosis starves the inner media and gives you the abdominal aneurysm; hypertension narrows the vasa vasorum and gives you the ascending one.
  • Reading dissection pain as MI. Both are severe anterior chest pain — the discriminators are radiation between the scapulae, absent or unequal pulses, and a normal-to-high blood pressure.

Chest pain — characterising the pain

CPD.0.0215src p.202–203
The frame used
  • O Onset
  • P Provocation / palliation
  • Q Quality
  • R Radiation / region / regularity
  • S Severity
  • T Timing
SOCRATES equivalents
  • Site — “Can you point to where you experience the pain?”
  • Onset — “Did the pain come on suddenly or gradually? … at rest or whilst you were exerting yourself?”

  • Ask open-ended questions first, then move to focused questioning

L04 · CLSK Cardiovascular System70

Clinical relevance of exacerbating and relieving factors — chest pain

CPD.0.0215src p.204
FactorWhat it tells you (verbatim)
Deep inspirationOften aggravates pain from the pleura or pericardium. E.g. pleurisy (pleuritic pain) from a pulmonary embolism or pericarditis.
ExertionMay worsen the pain from myocardial infarction or aortic dissection. Rest may ease the pain from cardiac ischemia, often gradually.
PositionPatients with pericarditis often feel worse when supine (lying) and better when sitting up. Patients with musculoskeletal pain may feel worse in certain positions. The pain of myocardial infarction is usually unaffected by changes in position — but this is not always the case.
Food intakePain on swallowing may help localize the problem to the gastrointestinal tract. Chest pain after a meal may indicate gastrointestinal pathology but can also occur with myocardial infarction or ischemia.
NitroglycerinIf chest pain decreases with nitrates, a cardiac etiology should be suspected; however, esophageal spasm may also respond to this therapy.
Trap
Nitroglycerin response is not a diagnostic test
  • The slide says so explicitly. Oesophageal spasm relaxes to nitrates too — “it got better with GTN” does not confirm ischaemia, and “it did not” does not exclude it.

Types of chest pain — the definitions to reproduce

CPD.0.0215src p.207
TypeDefinition (verbatim)
Angina pectorisDiscomfort in the chest and/or adjacent areas (jaw, shoulder, back, arm), usually, but not always, due to myocardial ischemia.
— Typical anginaSubsternal chest discomfort with all three: characteristic oppressive quality (described as “pressure”, “squeezing”, or “heaviness”, but almost never sharp or stabbing) and duration (typically minutes) · provoked by exertion or emotional stress · relieved by rest or nitroglycerin (within several minutes).
— Atypical chest painChest discomfort that meets 2 of the typical angina characteristics.
— Non-cardiac painChest pain that meets 1 or none of the typical angina characteristics.
PleuriticSudden and intense sharp, stabbing, or burning pain in the chest when inhaling and exhaling. Exacerbated by deep breathing, coughing, sneezing, or laughing. Pleuritic inflammation near the diaphragm — pain can be referred to the neck or shoulder. It is inflammation of the parietal pleura.
Exam Lock
3 / 2 / ≤1
  • The count is the whole classification: 3 features = typical, 2 = atypical, 1 or 0 = non-cardiac. Learn the three features as a set — quality, provocation, relief.

Dyspnea — definition and the words patients use

CPD.0.0216src p.213–215
Dyspnea is defined as a subjective experience of breathing discomfort… Because dyspnea can only be perceived by the patient's experience, adequate assessment by the clinician relies on the patient's description.Lecture 4, slide 23
  • Patient phrasings to expect: “I feel short of breath” · “I'm having difficulty breathing” · “I can't catch my breath” · “I feel like I'm suffocating.”
  • Dyspnea usually indicates pulmonary or cardiac disease but can also be the presenting symptom of metabolic derangements, hematologic disorders, toxic ingestions, psychiatric conditions, or simple deconditioning.

“Can be bluntly assessed by assessing if the patient is able to speak in full sentences without having to take a breath.”

The examination — sequence, positioning, landmarks

CPD.0.0392src p.220–224
Approach
Patient preparation, comfort and dignity → hand hygiene → general appearance and vital signs → cardiovascular system (inspection, palpation, auscultation, special tests) → other systems as the differential requires.
Sequence of positions
1. Supine with head of table elevated at 30° — inspection, palpation and beginning of auscultation. 2. Left lateral decubitus — brings the ventricular apex closer to the chest wall; for palpation and auscultation of the apex. 3. Supine at 30° — continued palpation and auscultation. 4. Sitting, leaning forward, after full exhalation — brings the left ventricular outflow tract closer to the chest wall and improves detection of aortic regurgitation.
Chest wall locationValve
Right second intercostal space or cardiac baseAortic valve
Left second and third intercostal spaces close to the sternum, but also at higher or lower levelsPulmonic valve
At or near the lower left sternal borderTricuspid valve
At and around the cardiac apexMitral valve
L04 · CLSK Cardiovascular System78

Carotid pulses — and the rules that protect the patient

CPD.0.0392src p.225
  • Inspect each carotid pulse.
  • Auscultate before you palpate — carotid atherosclerosis narrows the arteries, so it is important to auscultate the carotid arteries prior to palpating the carotid pulse.
  • Other than atherosclerosis, bruits are also caused by a tortuous carotid artery, external carotid arterial disease, aortic stenosis, the hypervascularity of hyperthyroidism, and external compression from thoracic outlet syndrome.
  • Do not palpate both arteries at the same time or overstimulate the carotid sinus — this can cause cerebral hypoperfusion resulting in syncope.
  • Most feared complication of carotid artery palpation is the dislodgment of an atherosclerotic plaque causing a stroke.
  • Causes of decreased pulsations: decreased stroke volume from shock or MI, and local atherosclerotic narrowing or occlusion.
  • Thrills in aortic stenosis are transmitted to the carotid arteries from the suprasternal notch or second right intercostal space.

CPD.0.0392src p.228
Clinical correlateClinical findings (verbatim)
MI or ACSDiaphoretic · hypotensive/hypertensive · tachypneic · tachycardic/bradycardic
CHFTachycardic · tachypneic · hypoxemic (decreased O₂ saturation)

Pericarditis and cardiac tamponadeTachycardia and hypotensive with a narrow pulse pressure (e.g. < 35 mm Hg) · BP may remain normal or be slightly elevated until hemodynamic collapse occurs · may be febrile

L04 · CLSK Cardiovascular System80

JVP, hepatojugular reflux, heaves, thrills and the PMI

CPD.0.0392src p.229–233
JVP — where and why
Best assessed from pulsations in the right internal jugular vein, which is directly in line with the superior vena cava and right atrium. JVP closely parallels right atrial pressure, i.e. central venous pressure (CVP). The sternal angle lies about 5 cm above the level of the right atrium and should be added to your measurement to get the CVP.
JVP values
0–5 cmH₂O (CVP 4–10) = within reference · > 3 cmH₂O (CVP > 8) = elevated, can be normal or abnormal · > 5 cmH₂O (CVP > 10) = consider heart failure, hypervolemia, pulmonary embolism, tricuspid stenosis, chronic pulmonary hypertension, SVC obstruction, cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis
Hepatojugular reflux
For diagnosis of cardiac insufficiency in patients with CVP > 8 cmH₂O; especially in the absence of overt congestion — commonly seen in early heart failure. Press the RUQ firmly upward under the costal margin for ≥ 10–15 seconds. Positive if the jugular venous column rises and persists while abdominal pressure continues. Seen with severe right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, right ventricular infarction.
Heaves
Sustained impulses that rhythmically lift your fingers, usually produced by an enlarged ventricle (commonly right ventricular hypertrophy) and occasionally by ventricular aneurysms. Use the ulnar border of the hand at the left parasternal border.
Thrills
Buzzing or vibratory sensation caused by underlying turbulent flow — usually indicative of a palpable murmur. Use the ball of the hand at the aortic, pulmonic, tricuspid and mitral areas.
PMI
The brief early pulsation of the LV as it moves anteriorly during systole. Normally 4th or 5th left ICS at the MCL; diameter discrete, ≤ 2 cm (< 2.5 cm, pinpointed with one finger); amplitude brisk and tapping (non-sustained); duration ≤ ⅔ of systole. A diffuse PMI (usually > 3 cm) may indicate left ventricular enlargement.
Location of thrillThink about
Base of the heart, 2nd ICS just right of the sternum, during systole (aortic area)Aortic stenosis
At the apex during systole (mitral area)Mitral regurgitation
Left of the sternum at the 2nd ICS (pulmonic area)Pulmonic stenosis
Left of the sternum at the 4th ICS (tricuspid area)Small muscular ventricular septal defect (Roger disease)

4/6Louder than S1 and S2, with palpable thrill4/4Very loud
5/6With thrill; heard when the stethoscope is partly off the chest
6/6With thrill; heard with the stethoscope entirely off the chest

Murmur maneuvers — the supplemental table that shows up in comprehensives

CPD.0.0392src p.252
ManeuverEffect on cardiac parametersEffect on murmurs
Inspiration↑ RV preload · ↓ LV preload · no effect on LV afterload↑ intensity of murmurs arising from the right side of the heart; ↓ intensity of murmurs arising from the left side
Valsalva maneuver / standing↓ RV preload · ↓ LV preload · ↓ LV afterload↑ intensity of MVP (with early mid-systolic click) and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmurs; ↓ intensity of murmurs arising from the left side
Squatting / lying down quickly / raising the leg↑ RV preload · ↑ LV preload · no effect on LV afterload (afterload may increase with squatting)↑ intensity of all murmurs; ↓ intensity of MVP (with late mid-systolic click) and HCM murmurs. Tetralogy of Fallot: severity of tet spells and associated murmurs decrease with squatting. MVP: click occurs later in systole
Exam Lock
The two that move the other way
  • HCM and MVP are the exceptions: less filling makes them louder, more filling makes them softer. Everything else follows preload.

Marked in the deck as post-lecture supplemental material: not currently taught in the clinical skills physical examination sessions, but may arise in Comprehensive Examination questions.

Recording the findings — the model normal write-up

CPD.0.0392src p.247
CVS: JVP 3 cmH₂O (CVP 8 cmH₂O). Negative hepatojugular reflux. Absent carotid artery bruits. Carotid pulses: 2+, brisk upstroke, rounded summit and less abrupt downstroke. Chest wall appears symmetrical, no surgical scars, no visible precordium hyperactivity. No heaves or thrills, PMI 5th LICS MCL. S1 and S2 present and regular. No S3 but S4 present. No murmurs.Lecture 4, slide 47 — the example write-up
Bottom Line
Use this as your template
  • Note the order: JVP → hepatojugular reflux → carotids (auscultate, then palpate) → inspection → palpation (heaves, thrills, PMI) → auscultation (S1, S2, extra sounds, murmurs) — exactly the sequence of the examination itself. Write in that order and you cannot forget a component.
L04 · CLSK Cardiovascular System86

Practice — CVS history and examination

CPD.0.0215

A 58-year-old woman describes 4 months of substernal heaviness that comes on climbing two flights of stairs, lasts about 5 minutes, and goes away when she stops. Under the classification used in this lecture, how is this chest pain classified?

  1. ANon-cardiac chest pain
  2. BAtypical chest pain
  3. CTypical angina
  4. DPleuritic chest pain
  5. ENeuromuscular chest pain
Answer
C. All three features are present: characteristic oppressive quality lasting minutes, provoked by exertion, and relieved by rest. Three of three = typical angina. Two of three = atypical; one or none = non-cardiac.
CPD.0.0216

A 63-year-old man is short of breath when he sits up and feels better lying flat. Which of the following should be at the top of the differential?

  1. ACongestive heart failure
  2. BCOPD
  3. CLeft atrial myxoma
  4. DUnilateral pleural effusion
  5. ESevere anemia
Answer
C. SOB in the upright position relieved by lying supine is platypnea, associated with left atrial myxoma or hepatopulmonary syndrome. Orthopnea and PND (the reverse pattern) are the ones associated with CHF; trepopnea is the lateral-decubitus one associated with unilateral pleural effusion.
L04 · CLSK Cardiovascular System87

Practice — CVS history and examination (cont.)

CPD.0.0392

You auscultate a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border. It becomes louder when the patient performs a Valsalva maneuver and softer when he squats. Which lesion behaves this way?

  1. AAortic stenosis
  2. BMitral regurgitation
  3. CVentricular septal defect
  4. DHypertrophic cardiomyopathy
  5. ETricuspid regurgitation
Answer
D. Valsalva and standing decrease preload; almost every murmur gets softer — except HCM and mitral valve prolapse, which get louder. Squatting increases preload and does the reverse. AS, MR, VSD and TR all follow the normal preload rule.
CPD.0.0392

A 71-year-old with long-standing uncontrolled hypertension has a fourth heart sound at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position. What does this sound indicate?

  1. ARapid ventricular filling into a compliant, dilated ventricle
  2. BAtrial contraction against a stiff, non-compliant left ventricle
  3. CDelayed closure of the pulmonic valve
  4. DTurbulent flow across a stenotic aortic valve
  5. EPericardial inflammation
Answer
B. S4 is the atrial kick in late diastole — blood entering a stiffened (non-compliant) LV against high atrial pressure. It is the sound of severe LVH from uncontrolled hypertension or severe aortic stenosis, and is usually a sign of diastolic heart failure. Option A describes S3.

Cardiovascular Pathology: Vasculitides

Lecture 05 — eight named vasculitides, sorted by vessel size, then age, then serology.

Dr. Omnia Haboura · Department of Pathology  ·  source pp. 255–303

Lesson plan — as given

Framework

  • 3. Pathogenesis of immune-mediated vasculitis
The three tiers

Objectives — verbatim

  • PATH.5020 — Distinguish the different vasculitides based on etiology, vessels affected, clinical presentation: Giant cell arteritis, Takayasu, Polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki, Buerger, Wegener granulomatosis, Microscopic polyangiitis, Churg Strauss syndrome
  • PATH.5021 — Distinguish the different vasculitides based on morphology, complications, diagnostic investigations: (same eight)
L05 · Vasculitides89

What a vasculitis is, and how it announces itself

PATH.5020src p.261–262
Inflammation of and damage to blood vessels → vessel lumen compromised → ischemia of tissue supplied by the vessel.Lecture 05, slide 261
Constitutional — from systemic inflammation
  • Fever
  • Myalgia
  • Arthralgia
  • Malaise
  • Raised ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate)
Site-specific — depending on the vascular bed involved
  • Pneumonitis
  • Renal infarction
  • Mesenteric ischemia
  • Glomerulonephritis
  • Cutaneous purpura
  • Sinusitis
  • Conjunctivitis and iritis
  • Peripheral neuritis
  • …and many more
Exam Lock
The clinical decision this lecture is really about
  • Pathogenesis is either immune-mediated or direct infection, and it is very important to differentiate between them: immunosuppressives are used for immune-mediated conditions and will be counterproductive in an infectious pathology.
L05 · Vasculitides90

Pathogenesis of immune-mediated vasculitis — four mechanisms

PATH.5020src p.263–264
#MechanismHypersensitivityDetailDiseases
1Deposition of immune complexesType IIICirculating immune complexes formed due to hypersensitivity to drugs, or following infections, or against self-antigens, are deposited in the vessel walls and cause inflammation and vessel wall damageVasculitis in SLE and rheumatoid arthritis · Polyarteritis nodosa (associated with Hepatitis B) · Drug induced
2Autoantibodies against endothelial cell and smooth muscle cell antigensType IIUnknown mechanism of formation; react against vessel wall and cause inflammation and damageBest seen in Kawasaki disease
3T-cell mediated ± granulomatous response—Autoreactive T cellsGiant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis · Wegener's granulomatosis and Churg-Strauss syndrome · allograft rejection vasculitis
4Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)Type IIHeterogeneous group of autoantibodies targeting components in the cytoplasm of neutrophil and monocyte lysosomes (enzymes in primary granules)See the ANCA split below
L05 · Vasculitides91

p-ANCA vs c-ANCA — the serology that names the disease

PATH.5020src p.264
  • Those that target the granules around the nucleus are called p-ANCA (p = perinuclear). Target is usually myeloperoxidase (MPO), so MPO-ANCA. Seen in Churg-Strauss syndrome and microscopic polyangiitis.
  • Those that target the granules diffusely spread in the cytoplasm are called c-ANCA (c = cytoplasmic). Target is usually proteinase-3 (PR3), so PR3-ANCA. Seen in Wegener's granulomatosis.

PATH.5020src p.265
Large vessels — aorta and its branchesMedium vessels — main visceral arteries, veins, branchesSmall vessels — intraparenchymal arteries and veins, arterioles, capillaries and venules
1. Giant cell arteritis
2. Takayasu arteritis		1. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)
2. Kawasaki disease
3. Buerger's disease		1. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's)
