L05 · Vasculitides93

Large vessel — Giant cell arteritis

PATH.5020PATH.5021src p.266–269
Vessels
  • Most commonly: temporal artery (also called “temporal arteritis”)
  • Vertebral arteries, ophthalmic arteries
  • Arch of aorta (also called “giant cell aortitis”)
Epidemiology
  • Most common form of vasculitis among elderly adults in the United States and Europe
  • Age > 50 years
  • More common in females
Pathogenesis
  • T cell mediated response to an unidentified antigen in the vessel wall
  • Pro-inflammatory cytokines especially IFN-γ and IL-17 (targets for treatment)
  • ± anti-endothelial cell antibodies
Clinical featuresMorphology
• Headache — along the course of the superficial temporal artery, painful and rope-like thickened on palpation
• Facial pain and jaw claudication (painful chewing)
• Ocular symptoms ranging from diplopia to blindness
• Associated with polymyalgia rheumatica — stiffness, aching, and pain in the muscles of the neck, shoulders, lower back, hips, and thighs
• Most commonly characterised clinically by the complex of fever, anemia, high ESR, and headaches		• Segmental involvement
• Focal, nodular thickening with reduction of lumen due to intimal hyperplasia
• Granulomatous inflammation of intima and inner media
• Multinucleated giant cells
• Fragmentation of internal elastic lamina
Trap
Why “segmental” matters clinically
  • Because involvement is segmental, a temporal artery biopsy can miss the lesion — a negative biopsy does not exclude the diagnosis, and treatment is not delayed for it when vision is at risk.
L05 · Vasculitides94

Large vessel — Takayasu arteritis

PATH.5020PATH.5021src p.270–272
Vessels & epidemiology
  • Aortic arch and great vessels
  • Most prevalent in adolescent girls and young women
  • Age usually < 50 years
  • Possible autoimmune etiology
Site-specific clinical features
  • Pulses are weaker / absent in affected vessels — “Pulseless disease”: arm claudication, BP discrepancies
  • Ocular symptoms: visual disturbances, retinal hemorrhages, blindness
  • Neurological symptoms: dizziness, focal weakness, hemiparesis
Morphology
  • Histological findings very similar to giant cell arteritis
  • Destruction and collagenous fibrosis of the arterial media associated with mononuclear infiltrates and inflammatory giant cells

Arteriography: aortic arch angiogram showing reduced flow of contrast into the great vessels and narrowing of the brachiocephalic, carotid, and subclavian arteries; cross-sections of the right carotid show marked intimal thickening and luminal narrowing.

Exam Lock
Giant cell vs Takayasu — the only reliable separator
  • The histology is essentially the same. Age is the discriminator: > 50 = giant cell; < 50 = Takayasu. Territory helps — temporal/ophthalmic vs aortic arch and great vessels.
L05 · Vasculitides95

Medium vessel — Polyarteritis nodosa

PATH.5020PATH.5021src p.273–277
Vessels involved
  • Medium-sized arteries of kidney > heart > liver > gastrointestinal tract
  • Lungs are spared
  • Young adults are affected more commonly
Pathogenesis
  • Immune complex mediated damage following Hepatitis B (HB surface antigen–antibody complexes) — ⅓ of cases
  • Rest of the cases: cause unknown
Site-specific clinical features
  • Kidney: hypertension, hemorrhage, infarction
  • Heart: myocardial infarction, pericarditis, heart failure
  • Liver and GIT: abdominal pain, mesenteric ischemia and infarcts
  • Rashes, gangrene, peripheral neuropathy

Morphology

  • Transmural inflammation (trans- throughout; mural- wall)
  • Fibrinoid necrosis
  • Predilection for branching points in vessels
  • Patchy involvement — only parts of the circumference uninvolved
  • Later stages: fibrosis
  • Different stages of activity are present at the same time (acute and chronic) — evidence of ongoing injury
  • Superimposed small aneurysms (nodular appearance on angiogram — hence the name) ± thrombosis

Diagnosis: angiogram of the superior mesenteric artery shows arterial wall irregularity — “pearls on a string” indicating distal microaneurysm formation — and abrupt termination in small distal arteries.

L05 · Vasculitides96

Medium vessel — Kawasaki disease

PATH.5020PATH.5021src p.278–280
Vessels & epidemiology
  • Coronary arteries primarily
  • Young children under 4 years of age
  • Common cause of acquired cardiac disease in children in the USA and endemic in Japan
Pathogenesis
  • Delayed hypersensitivity reaction to some vascular antigens
  • Subsequent cytokine production and B cell activation results in autoantibodies to endothelial cells and smooth muscle cells which precipitates the vasculitis
  • This is the pattern of vasculitis observed in some children infected with COVID-19
Morphology & management
  • Histopathology very similar to polyarteritis nodosa
  • Transmural necrotising inflammation
  • More acute inflammatory cells, less fibrinoid necrosis
  • Superimposed aneurysms ± thrombosis
  • Management: intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) + aspirin

Clinical features — the diagnostic criteria, verbatim

Fever ≥ 5 days plus ≥ 4 of the following: Conjunctivitis — bilateral non-exudative · Mucositis — injected/fissured lips, oral erythema and blistering, “strawberry tongue” · Cervical lymphadenopathy — ≥ 1 lymph node > 1.5 cm in diameter (also called “mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome”) · Erythema of palms and soles and/or edema of hands and feet, periungual desquamation · Rash — generalized, polymorphous, often beginning in the perianal area, desquamation after weeks.Lecture 05, slide 279
Trap
The exception written into the criteria
  • Children who fall short of the full criteria but have cardiac abnormalities on echocardiogram meet the diagnosis of Kawasaki disease. If untreated, 20% develop cardiovascular sequelae — coronary arteritis, aneurysm rupture and hemorrhage, myocardial infarction.
L05 · Vasculitides97

Medium vessel — Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans)

PATH.5020PATH.5021src p.281–283
Vessels & who
  • Tibial and radial arteries (extending into veins and nerves)
  • Young male smokers less than 40 years
Pathogenesis
  • Smoking tobacco — direct endothelial injury → inflammation and thrombosis
  • Endothelial dysfunction including reduced endothelium-dependent vasodilation and release of prothrombotic substances
  • Genetic predisposition in Indians, Israelis and Japanese
Clinical features
  • Raynaud phenomenon and cold sensitivity
  • Pain in foot induced by exercise (instep claudication)
  • Superficial nodular phlebitis (venous inflammation)
  • Pain at rest due to neural involvement
  • Ulceration, gangrene, and autoamputation of fingers and toes

Morphology — read the name

Part of the nameWhat it means histologically
Thromb-Thrombus → contains microabscesses of neutrophils and is surrounded by granulomatous inflammation
-angiitisSegmental inflammation of the vessel → both acute and chronic inflammatory cells
obliteransOcclusion of the vessel → obliteration of lumen → ischemia and infarction of digits supplied and skin → ulceration and gangrene
AlsoInflammation extends to contiguous nerves and veins — all three encased in fibrous tissue. Angiogram: tortuous and narrowed collateral vessels — corkscrew appearance; segmental occlusion of small and medium-sized arteries
L05 · Vasculitides98

Small vessel vasculitis — the three-way table the exam is built from

PATH.5020src p.285
  • Small vessels like arterioles, venules and capillaries · ANCA positive · called PAUCI-IMMUNE (no demonstrable immune complex deposition)
FeatureWegener's granulomatosisChurg-Strauss syndromeMicroscopic polyangiitis
Other namesGranulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)Allergic granulomatosis and angiitis / Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA)Hypersensitivity or leukocytoclastic vasculitis
Common organsUpper and lower respiratory tract; kidneyGIT, kidney, skin, respiratory tractLungs; kidney; skin — not upper respiratory tract
ANCA typec-ANCA / PR3-ANCAp-ANCA / MPO-ANCAp-ANCA / MPO-ANCA
AsthmaAbsentPresentAbsent
GranulomaPresentPresentAbsent
Exam Lock
Three questions separate all three
  • Upper airway involved? → Wegener's. Asthma and eosinophilia? → Churg-Strauss. Neither, plus no granuloma, all lesions the same age? → microscopic polyangiitis.
L05 · Vasculitides99

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's granulomatosis)

PATH.5020PATH.5021src p.286–288

The triad, verbatim

  1. Necrotizing granulomas of the upper-respiratory tract (ear, nose, sinuses, throat) or the lower-respiratory tract (lung) or both
  2. Necrotizing or granulomatous vasculitis affecting small- to medium-sized vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles, and arteries), most prominently the lungs and upper airways but other sites as well
  3. Focal necrotizing, often crescentic, glomerulonephritis
Who
  • Typical patient is a middle-aged man
  • Age ~ 40 years; males > females
  • Pathogenesis: c-ANCA / PR3-ANCA mediated
Site-specific clinical features
  • Sinusitis, pneumonitis; hemoptysis
  • Mucosal ulcerations (nose, palate, or pharynx)
  • Hematuria
  • Rashes, myalgia, neuritis
  • Rapidly fatal if left untreated — 80% mortality within 1 year
Morphology
  • Ulcerative lesions surrounded by granulomas with geographic necrosis and accompanying vasculitis
  • Necrotizing granulomas surrounded by a zone of proliferating fibroblasts with giant cells and leukocyte infiltrate
  • Respiratory tract: sinusitis, bilateral nodular infiltrates with cavitations
  • Kidney: crescentic glomerulonephritis
  • Later — organization and fibrosis
L05 · Vasculitides100

Churg-Strauss syndrome and microscopic polyangiitis

PATH.5020PATH.5021src p.289–291
Churg-Strauss syndromeMicroscopic polyangiitis (MPA)
EpidemiologyCan occur at any age · slight female preponderanceMean age of onset 50–60 years · slight male preponderance
Pathogenesisp-ANCA / MPO-ANCA mediatedp-ANCA / MPO-ANCA mediated · antibody responses to antigens such as drugs (e.g. penicillin), microorganisms (e.g. streptococci), heterologous proteins, or tumor proteins
PathologyNecrotizing granulomatous inflammation — both in vessel wall and extravascularFibrinoid necrosis; all lesions are the same age
Clinical featuresRespiratory tract — attacks of asthma; allergic rhinitis and sinusitis · Skin — palpable purpura · GIT — bleeding · Kidney (uncommon compared to other small vessel vasculitis) — hematuria and proteinuria · neuropathy, myocarditis and cardiomyopathyHemoptysis, hematuria and proteinuria · bowel pain or bleeding · muscle pain or weakness · palpable cutaneous purpura · either recover fully or death
DiagnosisPulmonary infiltrates on imaging · tissue eosinophilia as well as peripheral blood eosinophilia · serology: raised IgE levels—
Exam Lock
“All lesions the same age” is the MPA lock
  • PAN shows different stages of activity at the same time; MPA shows lesions all of the same age. That single phrase is how a histology stem separates them.

Vasculitis in other disorders: SLE · rheumatoid arthritis · malignancies · antiphospholipid syndrome · Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis — common in children) · infection related — bacteria, fungi (Aspergillus, Mucor).

Practice — the lecture's own eight clinical cases

Case 1

A 60-year-old woman has a 1-month history of headache, jaw claudication, pain over the shoulder and lower back pain. Physical examination shows rope-like thickening of the temporal artery. Labs show anemia and elevated ESR. Which histopathological finding is seen in her temporal artery?

  1. ATransmural fibrinoid necrosis with lesions of different ages
  2. BGranulomatous inflammation of intima and inner media with multinucleated giant cells and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina
  3. CThrombus containing neutrophil microabscesses surrounded by granulomatous inflammation
  4. DNecrotizing granulomas with geographic necrosis and crescentic glomerulonephritis
  5. EFibrinoid necrosis with no granulomas, all lesions the same age
Answer
B. Case 1 — giant cell arteritis. Age > 50, female, rope-like temporal artery, jaw claudication, polymyalgia rheumatica (shoulder and lower back pain), anemia and high ESR. Morphology: segmental, intimal hyperplasia, granulomatous inflammation with giant cells, fragmented internal elastic lamina.
Case 2

A 25-year-old woman has a 1-month history of flu-like symptoms and difficulty with vision. Examination shows weak pulses in her upper extremities; an aortic arch angiogram shows narrowing of the carotid and subclavian arteries. What will the carotid artery show?

  1. ADestruction and collagenous fibrosis of the media with mononuclear infiltrates and inflammatory giant cells
  2. BCholesterol clefts within an embolus
  3. COnion-skin hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis
  4. DTransmural inflammation at vessel branch points with microaneurysms
  5. ELeukocytoclastic vasculitis without granulomas
Answer
A. Case 2 — Takayasu arteritis. Age < 50, young woman, pulseless disease with aortic-arch branch narrowing. Histology is very similar to giant cell arteritis: media destruction and collagenous fibrosis, mononuclear infiltrate, inflammatory giant cells. Age and territory are the separators.
L05 · Vasculitides103

Practice — the lecture's own eight clinical cases (cont.)

Case 3

A 30-year-old man has 1 month of recurrent abdominal pain, worse after meals, and rashes over the forearm. He had Hepatitis B infection 2 months ago. What will the mesenteric artery show?

  1. AGranulomatous inflammation of the intima and inner media
  2. BTransmural inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis at branching points, patchy, with different stages of activity present at the same time
  3. CNecrotizing granulomas of the upper airway
  4. DEosinophil-rich granulomatous inflammation
  5. EConcentric onion-skin thickening with fibrinoid necrosis
Answer
B. Case 3 — polyarteritis nodosa. Young adult, ⅓ of cases follow Hepatitis B, mesenteric ischaemia (post-prandial abdominal pain) and rash. Morphology: transmural inflammation, fibrinoid necrosis, predilection for branching points, patchy, lesions of different ages, superimposed microaneurysms.
L05 · Vasculitides104

Practice — vasculitides, continued

Case 4

A 3-year-old boy has 3 weeks of chest pain, rashes, and edema of the hands and feet. Examination shows painful cervical lymphadenopathy, a sore and swollen tongue and multiple oral ulcers. What is seen in the coronary artery, and what is the treatment?

  1. AGranulomatous arteritis with giant cells; high-dose corticosteroids
  2. BTransmural necrotising inflammation with more acute inflammatory cells and less fibrinoid necrosis; IVIG and aspirin
  3. CThrombus with microabscesses; smoking cessation
  4. DPauci-immune necrotising vasculitis; cyclophosphamide
  5. EHyaline arteriolosclerosis; blood pressure control
Answer
B. Case 4 — Kawasaki disease. Under 4, fever with conjunctivitis, mucositis / strawberry tongue, cervical node > 1.5 cm, erythema and oedema of the extremities. Histopathology is very similar to PAN but with more acute inflammatory cells and less fibrinoid necrosis. Management is IVIG + aspirin — one of the few paediatric indications for aspirin.
Case 5

A 35-year-old man who smokes 2 packs daily for 15 years has 1 month of severe lower-extremity pain, cold sensitivity in his hands, rest pain, and gangrene of the great toe. What will the tibial artery show?

  1. ACholesterol emboli with clefts
  2. BSegmental inflammation with luminal thrombosis containing neutrophil microabscesses surrounded by granulomatous inflammation, extending to contiguous nerves and veins
  3. CNecrotising granulomas with geographic necrosis
  4. DFibrinoid necrosis with eosinophilic infiltrate
  5. EMedial calcification centred on the internal elastic lamina
Answer
B. Case 5 — Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans). Male smoker under 40, Raynaud + instep claudication + rest pain + digital gangrene. The three parts of the name are the three findings: thrombus with microabscesses, segmental angiitis, obliteration of the lumen — with nerves and veins encased in the same fibrous tissue.
L05 · Vasculitides105

Practice — vasculitides, continued (cont.)

Case 6

A 30-year-old man has 2 months of flu-like symptoms, haematuria and weight loss. He has a nasal ulcer, and chest X-ray shows a cavitary lesion in the left lung. Which serology and lung-biopsy finding fit?

  1. Ap-ANCA/MPO; eosinophil-rich granulomas
  2. Bc-ANCA/PR3; necrotising granulomas with geographic necrosis and accompanying vasculitis
  3. Cp-ANCA/MPO; fibrinoid necrosis without granulomas
  4. DAnti-GBM; linear immunofluorescence
  5. EANA; immune-complex deposition
Answer
B. Case 6 — granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's). The triad: upper-airway necrotising granulomas (nasal ulcer), lower-airway granulomatous vasculitis (cavitating nodule), and focal necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis (haematuria). Serology is c-ANCA / PR3-ANCA. Untreated, 80% mortality within 1 year.
Case 7

A 30-year-old woman with asthma since age 10 has 2 weeks of flu-like symptoms and cannot extend her left wrist and some fingers (wrist drop). She has palpable purpura on both hands and eosinophilia. Which diagnosis, and what additional serology supports it?

  1. AMicroscopic polyangiitis; anti-GBM
  2. BGranulomatosis with polyangiitis; c-ANCA
  3. CChurg-Strauss syndrome (EGPA); p-ANCA/MPO with raised IgE
  4. DPolyarteritis nodosa; hepatitis B surface antigen
  5. EHenoch-Schönlein purpura; IgA deposition
Answer
C. Case 7 — Churg-Strauss. Asthma + eosinophilia + mononeuritis multiplex (wrist drop) + palpable purpura. Serology: p-ANCA / MPO-ANCA, plus raised IgE and tissue as well as peripheral blood eosinophilia. Asthma is the feature that is present in Churg-Strauss and absent in both Wegener's and MPA.
L05 · Vasculitides106

Practice — vasculitides, continued (cont.)

Case 8

A 20-year-old man has 2 days of muscle pain and a raised, non-blanchable rash over both lower limbs. A week earlier he had a sore throat treated with oral penicillin. What does the skin biopsy show?

  1. AGranulomatous inflammation with giant cells
  2. BFibrinoid necrosis with all lesions of the same age and no granulomas
  3. CTransmural necrosis with lesions of different ages
  4. DEosinophilic granulomas in the vessel wall
  5. EImmune complexes with IgA deposition
Answer
B. Case 8 — microscopic polyangiitis. Antibody responses to antigens such as drugs (penicillin) or microorganisms (streptococci). Pathology: fibrinoid necrosis, all lesions the same age, no granulomas — that combination separates MPA from both PAN (different ages) and Churg-Strauss (granulomas + eosinophils).
L05 · Vasculitides107

Lecture 05 — summary sheet

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Sort by vessel size, confirm with age, and prove it with serology and the presence or absence of granulomas and eosinophils.
Exam Lock
The seven locks
  • GCA > 50, Takayasu < 50 — the histology will not separate them for you.
  • PAN spares the lungs and is HBV-associated in ⅓ of cases; lesions are of different ages.
  • MPA lesions are all the same age and there are no granulomas.
  • Kawasaki = fever ≥ 5 days + 4 of 5 criteria; coronary aneurysms in 20% if untreated; IVIG + aspirin.
  • Buerger = male smoker < 40, tibial/radial, corkscrew collaterals, autoamputation.
  • c-ANCA/PR3 = Wegener's. p-ANCA/MPO = Churg-Strauss and MPA.
  • All three small-vessel vasculitides are pauci-immune — ANCA-positive but no immune-complex deposition.
Trap
Two traps
  • Treating a negative temporal artery biopsy as excluding giant cell arteritis — involvement is segmental.
  • Reaching for immunosuppression before excluding infectious vasculitis — the lecture calls this out explicitly as counterproductive.
L05 · Vasculitides108
PHAR

Cardiovascular Drugs 1 / Diuretics

Six classes, six sites along one nephron. Learn the transporter and every action, adverse effect and clinical use falls out of it.

Lucy Clunes PhD  ·  source pp. 304–368

Lecture objectives — verbatim

  • PHAR.0220 Describe the normal regulation of fluid and electrolytes by the kidneys.
  • PHAR.0221 Describe the location and function of major ion transporters and channels on renal epithelial membranes.
  • PHAR.0222 Explain how sodium transport influences the reabsorption of other ions and water in the kidney.
  • PHAR.0223 Explain how abnormal renal function can cause hypertension or edema.
  • PHAR.0224 Describe the mechanism of action of the different classes of diuretics.
  • PHAR.0225 Describe the changes that occur with electrolyte transport, water reabsorption and hemodynamics when specific diuretics inhibit kidney function.
  • PHAR.0226 Explain how thiazides and loop diuretics can cause metabolic alkalosis.
  • PHAR.0227 Explain how diuretic therapy can lead to hyponatremia.
  • PHAR.0228 Describe the metabolic imbalances with diuretic therapy on glucose, urate, lipids, calcium, magnesium and potassium.
  • PHAR.0229 Describe the clinical consequences of interactions between diuretics and drugs such as cardiac glycosides, oral hypoglycemics, NSAIDs and angiotensin inhibitors.
  • PHAR.0230 Describe why reduced renal perfusion can limit the use of thiazide diuretics.
  • PHAR.0231 Describe the therapeutic uses of diuretics.
By definition, diuretics are drugs that increase the rate of urine flow; however, clinically useful diuretics also increase the rate of excretion of Na⁺ (natriuresis) and of an accompanying anion, usually Cl⁻.Reading notes accompanying the lecture
PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)109

Segments of the nephron — the table everything else hangs on

PHAR.0220PHAR.0221src p.320–321
SegmentFunctionsWater permeabilityPrimary transporters & drug targets
GlomerulusFormation of glomerular filtrateExtremely highNone
Proximal tubuleReabsorption of Na⁺/K⁺/Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ (65%), NaHCO₃ (85%), glucose & amino acids (~100%). Secretion & reabsorption of organic acids & bases (including most diuretics). Isosmotic reabsorption of H₂OVery highNa⁺/H⁺ (NHE3), carbonic anhydrase, acid and base transporters
Thin descending loop of HenlePassive reabsorption of H₂OHighAquaporins
Thick ascending loop of HenleActive reabsorption of Na⁺/K⁺/Cl⁻ (15–25%); secondary reabsorption of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺Very lowNa⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ (NKCC2)

PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)110

Sites of action — the whole class list on one nephron

PHAR.0224PHAR.0225src p.327
Trap
Why the biggest reabsorber is not the strongest diuretic
  • The proximal tubule reclaims 65% of filtered sodium, so acetazolamide ought to be the most powerful diuretic. It is not — most of the excess fluid delivered out of the proximal tubule can be reabsorbed more distally, particularly in the loop of Henle. The loop is the high-ceiling site because nothing downstream can compensate for it.
PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)111

When do we need a diuretic?

PHAR.0223PHAR.0224src p.322–326
Edematous states — ↑ NaCl reabsorption → water retention & ↑ blood volume
  • Heart failure
  • Hepatic ascites
  • Nephrotic syndrome
  • Premenstrual edema
Non-edematous states
  • Hypertension
  • Hypercalcemia
  • Diabetes insipidus
The class list
  • Loop: furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide
  • Thiazides: hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, metolazone
  • K⁺-sparing: spironolactone, eplerenone, triamterene, amiloride
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: acetazolamide
  • Osmotic agents: mannitol
  • ADH antagonist: conivaptan

Diuretics are inhibitors of renal ion transporters that decrease the reabsorption of Na⁺ at different sites in the nephron (natriuretics). Major clinical uses: managing abnormal fluid retention (edema), or treating hypertension (reduce blood volume).

PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)112

Loop (high-ceiling) diuretics — furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide

PHAR.0224PHAR.0227PHAR.0228PHAR.0231src p.328–333
Site & target
Act in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle; block the NKCC2 Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransporter → ↑ [Na⁺], [Cl⁻] and [K⁺] in tubular fluid → H₂O excretion
Efficacy
Highest efficacy in removing Na⁺ & Cl⁻ from the body
Clinical applications
Diuretics of choice for managing edema associated with heart failure, hepatic or renal disease · moderate-severe hypertension · hypercalcemia · hyperkalemia · acute pulmonary edema
Pharmacokinetics
Oral & parenteral · t½ = 2–4 h
Actions
  • Increased urine output
  • Increased K⁺ excretion
  • Increased Ca²⁺ excretion
  • Increased Mg²⁺ excretion
  • Increased prostaglandin synthesis
  • Decreased renal vascular resistance
  • Increased renal blood flow
Adverse effects
  • Ototoxicity
  • Hyperuricemia
  • Acute hypovolemia
  • Hypokalemia
  • Hypomagnesemia
  • Allergic reactions
Urine composition
  • ↓ excretion: uric acid
  • ↑ excretion: Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, urine volume
Exam Lock
Calcium is the whole loop-vs-thiazide question
  • Loops lose calcium (they abolish the lumen-positive potential that drives paracellular Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ reabsorption) → used in hypercalcemia. Thiazides keep calcium → used in hypercalciuria / recurrent stones. Loops Lose calcium; Thiazides Take it back.
PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)113

Thiazides — hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, metolazone

PHAR.0224PHAR.0225PHAR.0226PHAR.0230PHAR.0231src p.334–340
Site & target
Act predominantly in the distal convoluted tubule; block the NCCT Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter → ↑ [Na⁺] and [Cl⁻] in tubular fluid → H₂O excretion
Clinical applications
Hypertension (alone or in combination) · heart failure (mild–moderate) · hypercalciuria — inhibit Ca²⁺ excretion, particularly useful for kidney stones · diabetes insipidus (produce hyperosmolar urine) · premenstrual edema
Pharmacokinetics
Orally effective · t½ = 40 h, take 1–3 weeks to produce a stable effect
Renal-function caveat
In moderate-to-severe CKD (e.g. GFR < 30 mL/min) thiazides should be replaced by loop diuretics. (Objective PHAR.0230)
Chlorthalidone
Long duration of action: t½ = 40–60 h — used to treat hypertension once daily
Metolazone
Most potent; causes Na⁺ excretion in advanced kidney failure
Actions
  • Increased Na⁺ & Cl⁻ excretion
  • Increased K⁺ excretion
  • Increased Mg²⁺ excretion
  • Decreased urinary Ca²⁺ excretion
  • Decreased peripheral vascular resistance — initially due to a decrease in blood volume; with continued therapy volume recovery occurs although the hypotensive effects remain
Adverse effects — the “hypos and hypers”
  • Hypokalemia
  • Hyponatremia
  • Metabolic alkalosis
  • Hyperuricemia
  • Hyperglycemia
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • Hypersensitivity
  • Sexual dysfunction
Urine composition
  • ↓ excretion: uric acid, Ca²⁺
  • ↑ excretion: Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺, urine volume
PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)114

Where the thiazide adverse effects come from — the mechanisms named in the reading

PHAR.0226PHAR.0227PHAR.0228PHAR.0229
Adverse effectMechanism (verbatim from the reading)
HypokalemiaIncreased delivery of Na⁺ to the distal tubule → enhanced exchange of Na⁺ for K⁺ → greater excretion of K⁺
HyponatremiaReports of fatal or near-fatal hyponatremia, attributed to inappropriate secretion of ADH. Plasma electrolytes should be monitored.
HyperuricemiaCompetition for the organic secretory pathway in the proximal tubule by thiazides and uric acid. Can precipitate gout in some patients.
HypercalcemiaThiazides inhibit sodium reabsorption but at the same time increase the reabsorption of calcium
HyperglycemiaThiazides decrease glucose tolerance and latent diabetes mellitus may be unmasked. Appears to involve reduced insulin secretion (due to depletion of K⁺) and alterations in glucose metabolism.
HyperlipidemiaMay increase plasma LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol and total triglycerides (~5–15% increase); may return toward baseline after prolonged therapy
Metabolic alkalosis (objective PHAR.0226)Increased urinary excretion of K⁺ and titratable acid, from increased distal Na⁺ delivery — the same mechanism as loop diuretics
Exam Lock
Loop-specific extras the reading adds
  • Loops abolish the lumen-positive potential from K⁺ recycling → ↑ Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ excretion; loop diuretics should be avoided in postmenopausal osteopenic women because increased Ca²⁺ excretion may have deleterious effects on bone metabolism. Loops also induce COX-2 expression — the prostaglandins mediate part of the diuretic/natriuretic action, which is why NSAIDs blunt them.
PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)115

Potassium-sparing diuretics — two mechanisms, one effect

PHAR.0224PHAR.0228PHAR.0231src p.341–348
Aldosterone antagonists — spironolactone, eplerenoneNa⁺ channel inhibitors — amiloride, triamterene
SiteCollecting tubule / ductLate distal tubule and collecting duct
MechanismAntagonise aldosterone at intracellular cytoplasmic receptor sites — prevents translocation of the receptor complex to the nucleus → ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption and ↓ K⁺ excretionDirectly block the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) → decreasing Na⁺/K⁺ exchange. Advantage: they do not rely on the presence of aldosterone.
Clinical applicationsHeart failure (spironolactone) — adjunct to prevent cardiac remodeling; severe HF, NYHA class III–IV, to increase survival and reduce hospitalization when added to standard therapy · hypertension (adjunct) · primary hyperaldosteronism (diagnosis & treatment) · edema associated with excessive aldosterone excretion · cirrhosis with edema or ascites · nephrotic syndrome · hypokalemiaSmall increases in NaCl excretion; usually employed for their antikaliuretic actions to offset the effects of other diuretics. Usually used in combination (not very efficacious). Can prevent K⁺ loss associated with thiazides & furosemide.
Adverse effectsGastric upset & peptic ulcers · endocrine effects (antiandrogen) · hyperkalemia · nausea, lethargy, mental confusion (rare)Hyperkalemia · hyponatremia · leg cramps · GI upset · dizziness, pruritus, headache & minor visual changes
NoteSpironolactone has affinity for progesterone and androgen receptors where it acts as an antagonist → gynecomastia, impotence, menstrual irregularities. Eplerenone has low affinity for these receptors and is less likely to produce these effects.Triamterene is metabolised in the liver but renal excretion is a major route of elimination for the active form and metabolites; amiloride is eliminated predominantly by urinary excretion of intact drug.

Urine composition for both: ↓ excretion of K⁺; ↑ excretion of Na⁺ and urine volume.

PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)116

Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, osmotic agents, ADH antagonists

PHAR.0224PHAR.0228PHAR.0229PHAR.0230PHAR.0231src p.349–365
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors — acetazolamideOsmotic — mannitolADH antagonist — conivaptan
Site / MOAProximal tubular epithelial cells. Inhibits intracellular carbonic anhydrase → decreases ability to exchange Na⁺ for H⁺ → decreases activity of Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase (diuresis) → HCO₃⁻ is retained in the lumen, increasing urinary pHEverywhere. Raises osmotic pressure of the plasma, drawing H₂O out of body tissues → osmotic diuresis. Does not affect Na⁺ excretion directly; the only drug that truly increases urine volume.Collecting duct. Antagonist at V1 and V2 receptors. V1R = increases smooth muscle contraction; V2R = increases H₂O permeability and reabsorption (upregulates aquaporins)

PharmacokineticsOral & well absorbed; IV for acute closed-angle glaucoma · t½ = 3–6 h · increases urine pHIV only (only a small amount absorbed from the GI tract)IV only · metabolised by and a potent inhibitor of CYP 3A4
Adverse effectsMetabolic acidosis · hyponatremia · hypokalemia · crystalluria · malaise, fatigue, depression, headache, GI upset, drowsiness, paresthesiaExtracellular volume expansion and hyponatremia — mannitol extracts water from cells, so before the diuresis there is expansion of extracellular volume; headache, nausea and vomiting are common · tissue dehydration · acidosisInfusion site reactions · thirst · atrial fibrillation · GI & electrolyte disturbances · nephrogenic diabetes insipidus if serum Na⁺ is not monitored closely (conivaptan can cause severe hypernatremia)
Contraindications—Congestive heart failure · pulmonary edemaHypovolemic hyponatremia · renal failure

Practice — diuretics

PHAR.0231

A 68-year-old woman with recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones and hypertension needs a single agent that helps both problems. Which diuretic, and by what mechanism?

  1. AFurosemide — blocks NKCC2 and increases calcium excretion
  2. BHydrochlorothiazide — blocks NCCT and increases calcium reabsorption
  3. CAcetazolamide — inhibits carbonic anhydrase and alkalinises the urine
  4. DSpironolactone — antagonises aldosterone and reduces calcium loss
  5. EAmiloride — blocks ENaC and reduces calcium excretion
Answer
B. Thiazides inhibit sodium reabsorption in the DCT but increase the reabsorption of calcium — this fall in calcium excretion is useful in recurrent kidney stones due to hypercalciuria, and they are first-line for hypertension. Furosemide does the opposite and would make her stones worse.
PHAR.0228

A patient on high-dose intravenous furosemide for decompensated heart failure develops sudden bilateral hearing loss and tinnitus. Which adverse effect is this, and which other diuretic class shares the sulfonamide hypersensitivity risk?

  1. ACrystalluria; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
  2. BOtotoxicity; thiazides
  3. CNephrogenic diabetes insipidus; ADH antagonists
  4. DTissue dehydration; osmotic agents
  5. EMetabolic acidosis; potassium-sparing agents
Answer
B. Ototoxicity is the signature loop-diuretic adverse effect (worse with rapid IV infusion and with aminoglycosides). Both loops and thiazides are sulfonamide-based and carry hypersensitivity risk — the reading lists hypersensitivity for both.
PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)119

Practice — diuretics (cont.)

PHAR.0228

A man with cirrhosis and ascites is started on spironolactone and develops tender gynaecomastia. What is the mechanism, and which agent avoids it?

  1. AInhibition of ENaC; switch to triamterene
  2. BAntagonism at progesterone and androgen receptors; switch to eplerenone
  3. CInhibition of 5α-reductase; switch to amiloride
  4. DIncreased prolactin from dopamine blockade; switch to furosemide
  5. EAromatase induction; switch to chlorthalidone
Answer
B. Spironolactone has affinity for progesterone and androgen receptors, where it acts as an antagonist — gynecomastia, impotence, menstrual irregularities. Eplerenone has low affinity for these receptors and is less likely to produce these effects.
PHAR.0224

Why is acetazolamide a weak diuretic despite acting where 65% of filtered sodium is reabsorbed?

  1. AIt is poorly absorbed orally
  2. BFluid escaping the proximal tubule is reabsorbed more distally, particularly in the loop of Henle
  3. CCarbonic anhydrase is not expressed in the human proximal tubule
  4. DIt is rapidly metabolised by CYP3A4
  5. EIt causes compensatory aldosterone release within hours
Answer
B. The reading states it directly: a proximally acting diuretic might be expected to induce large losses, but most of the excess fluid delivered out of the proximal tubule can be reabsorbed more distally, particularly in the loop of Henle. Downstream compensation is what caps its ceiling.
PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)120

Practice — diuretics (cont.)

PHAR.0230

A 74-year-old with GFR 22 mL/min and volume overload is prescribed hydrochlorothiazide with little effect. What is the correct change, and why?

  1. AIncrease the hydrochlorothiazide dose; the t½ is long
  2. BSwitch to a loop diuretic; thiazides should be replaced by loops in moderate-to-severe CKD
  3. CAdd acetazolamide to alkalinise the urine
  4. DSwitch to mannitol to raise plasma osmolality
  5. EAdd conivaptan to block V2 receptors
Answer
B. Objective PHAR.0230: in moderate-to-severe CKD (e.g. GFR < 30 mL/min) thiazides should be replaced by loop diuretics. The one thiazide-like exception the lecture names is metolazone, the most potent, which causes Na⁺ excretion in advanced kidney failure.
PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)121

Diuretics — summary sheet

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Each class is defined by one transporter at one segment: CA-inhibitor/PCT, NKCC2/thick ascending limb, NCCT/DCT, aldosterone-receptor or ENaC/collecting duct — and the electrolyte disturbance is simply what that segment normally handles.
Exam Lock
The six locks
  • Loops lose calcium (→ hypercalcaemia treatment); thiazides keep it (→ stone prevention).
  • Both loops and thiazides cause hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis by increasing distal Na⁺ delivery.
  • Spironolactone = antiandrogen effects; eplerenone does not.
  • Acetazolamide = metabolic acidosis + alkaline urine; used for glaucoma, epilepsy, mountain sickness.
  • Mannitol is contraindicated in CHF and pulmonary oedema — it expands the extracellular volume first.
  • Conivaptan is IV-only, a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor, contraindicated in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia.
Trap
Three traps
  • Giving a thiazide when GFR < 30 — it will not work; use a loop (or metolazone).
  • Combining an ACE inhibitor or ARB with spironolactone/amiloride and not checking potassium — hyperkalaemia.
  • Forgetting that NSAIDs blunt loop diuretics by blocking the COX-2/prostaglandin arm of their action.
PHAR · Diuretics (Cardiovascular Drugs 1)122

Dr. Omnia Haboura · Department of Pathology  ·  source pp. 369–411

Objectives — verbatim

  • PATH.5025 Recapitulate the normal anatomy and physiology of heart.
  • PATH.5026 Explain the compensation mechanism that helps the heart to meet inward demand.
  • PATH.5027 Correlate the common symptoms, signs and investigations with the pathogenesis and morphology of common heart diseases listed in the module.

  • PATH.5032 Recapitulate the physiology of cardiac output, Frank–Starling law, and the concepts of preload and afterload.

L07 · Heart Failure123

Normal heart — the numbers you are expected to have

PATH.5025src p.375–378
Normal weight
Males 300–360 g · Females 250–320 g — can go up to 1000 g in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Normal ventricular thickness
Left 1.2–1.5 cm · Right 0.3–0.5 cm
Pericardium
Visceral and parietal pericardium; the pericardial cavity holds 30–50 mL of fluid and acts as a shock absorber
Layers
Epicardium (including visceral pericardium with main vessels of coronary circulation) · Myocardium (specialized muscle cells, fibroblasts, endothelial cells) · Endocardium (with an ill-defined subendocardial layer that contains Purkinje fibers)
Valvular system
Two atrioventricular valves — mitral and tricuspid; two semilunar valves — aortic and pulmonary. Maintain unidirectional blood flow, lined by endothelium; scanty blood flow — thin enough to be nourished by diffusion from blood within the heart
Coronary circulation
Right and left coronary arteries are end arteries; collaterals open up when arteries narrow; most blood flow to myocardium is during diastole
Exam Lock
Two numbers that decide autopsy questions
  • A left ventricle over 1.5 cm is hypertrophied. A heart over ~360 g (male) is enlarged. And because valves are avascular and nourished by diffusion, they heal by scarring, not regeneration — which is why rheumatic valve disease is progressive.
L07 · Heart Failure124

Compensation — three mechanisms, in the order the heart uses them

PATH.5026PATH.5029PATH.5032src p.379–381
MechanismDetail
Activation of neurohormonal systemsEndogenous catecholamines · renin–angiotensin–aldosterone
Frank-Starling lawIncreased force of contraction with myofiber stretching (due to increased end-diastolic volume)
Myocardial hypertrophyConcentric or eccentric

The cardiovascular system attempts to compensate for increased hemodynamic burden or reduced myocardial contractility through these mechanisms.

Cardiac hypertrophy — cellular adaptations

  • Increase in size of the cardiac myocytes
  • Upregulation of genes coding for proteins: actin, myosin (fetal isoforms) → increased sarcomeres
  • Usually not accompanied by an increase in vascularization
  • Relative decrease in capillary density → ischemia → fibrosis → reduced diastolic relaxation
  • Coupled with increased metabolic and oxygen needs → cardiac decompensation

Histology: note the increases in both cell size and nuclear size in the hypertrophied myocytes, while the interstitial cells remain small.

L07 · Heart Failure125

Concentric vs eccentric hypertrophy

PATH.5029src p.382
Trap
The line students miss
  • There can be significant hypertrophy without any increase in thickness of the walls. In eccentric hypertrophy the mass rises in proportion to the dilatation, so wall thickness can measure normal while the heart weighs 600 g.
L07 · Heart Failure126

PATH.5027PATH.5028PATH.5030src p.383–384
PathologyFeature
Failure of pumpSystolic dysfunction — improper contraction · Diastolic dysfunction — improper relaxation
Obstruction to flowLesions preventing the valve from opening · increased ventricular chamber pressure. The myocardium has to overwork to pump against obstruction
Regurgitant flowValvular pathology resulting in backward flow → results in volume overload
Shunted flowInappropriate flow from one chamber to another → pressure and volume overload
Disorders of cardiac conductionArrhythmias
Rupture of heart / cardiac vesselsLoss of continuity in circulation
InflammatoryIschemia / infarctionCongenitalHypertensiveMechanical / electrical dysfunctionNeoplastic
Infectious and non-infectious causes: myocarditis · pericarditis · endocarditis (valvular disease)Ischemic heart disease: angina pectoris · myocardial infarction (MI) · sudden cardiac death · chronic heart diseaseDevelopmental anomalies of the heart: left to right shunt · right to left shunt · obstructive diseases of heartHypertensive heart disease: systemic hypertension affecting left heart · pulmonary hypertension affecting right heartCardiomyopathies: dilated · hypertrophic · restrictiveBenign neoplasms · malignancies · secondaries

Everything in this table converges on one endpoint: heart failure.

How heart disease presents, and what you order

PATH.5027src p.385–386
Common clinical presentations
  • Acute chest discomfort / pain
  • Dyspnea, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND)
  • Palpitation
  • Syncope, especially exertional syncope
  • Leg swelling
Physical examination
  • Change in pulse / blood pressure
  • Raised jugular venous pressure (JVD)
  • Displaced apex (PMI)
  • Cardiac murmurs
  • Systolic / diastolic sounds
  • Pericardial friction rub

12-lead ECGSTEMI · arrhythmias e.g. atrial fibrillation · pericarditis

Exercise / stress ECGStable angina

L07 · Heart Failure128

Heart failure — definition and the five axes

PATH.5031src p.388
Inability of the heart, working at normal or elevated filling pressure, to pump enough blood to meet the metabolic demands of the body. Endpoint for many cardiac diseases. Most cases develop gradually and insidiously. Also called Congestive Heart Failure (CHF).Lecture 07, slide 388

It can be classified as

Systolic vs diastolic→High output vs low output→Left sided vs right sided→Forward vs backward→Compensated vs decompensated
Bottom Line
Why five axes and not one taxonomy
  • These are not competing classifications — they are five independent questions about the same patient. A single case is, for example, systolic, low-output, left-sided, backward, decompensated. Answer all five and you have described the failure completely.
L07 · Heart Failure129

Systolic vs diastolic dysfunction

PATH.5031src p.389
Systolic dysfunctionDiastolic dysfunction
DefectInability to contract properlyInability of the heart to relax and fill properly
CausesLoss of myocyte, as in myocardial infarction · pressure overload, as in hypertension · volume overload, as in valvular regurgitation · decreased contractility, as in myocarditis, dilated cardiomyopathyMassive ventricular hypertrophy · myocardial fibrosis · amyloidosis (extracellular deposition of amyloid) · constrictive pericarditis
Also calledHeart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) — left ventricular ejection fraction ≥ 50%

Both can coexist.

L07 · Heart Failure130

Left vs right, forward vs backward — one picture

PATH.5031PATH.5033src p.390–393

Isolated right-sided heart failure due to lung pathology is called cor pulmonale.

L07 · Heart Failure131

High vs low output, compensated vs decompensated, and the clinical features

PATH.5026PATH.5027PATH.5031src p.394–396
Definition
High-output failureOccurs due to increased demands like anemia, hyperthyroidism, thiamine deficiency, and pregnancy. Symptoms of heart failure occur in spite of a well-functioning heart (high cardiac output).
Low-output failureDecreased cardiac output. The majority of cardiac diseases result in a low-output cardiac failure.
Compensated heart failureDilated ventricle is able to maintain the cardiac output to meet the needs of the body, in spite of excessive need and a defective pump or decreased blood volume, because of compensatory mechanisms
Decompensated heart failureIn spite of the compensatory mechanisms, the failing myocardium is no longer able to propel sufficient blood to meet the needs of the body — even at rest, once the compensatory mechanisms have failed
Left ventricular failureRight ventricular failure
Features of backward failure: dyspnea on exertion · orthopnea · paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND)
Features of forward failure: fatigue · cardiogenic shock · irritability, restlessness, syncope		Systemic venous congestion
Distended neck vein (JVD)
Enlarged tender liver
Pedal edema

Exam Lock
Two named appearances
  • Heart failure cells = hemosiderin-laden macrophages in the lung, from left failure. Nutmeg liver = chronic passive congestion with hemorrhagic centrilobular necrosis, from right failure. If a stem gives you one, it is telling you which side failed.
L07 · Heart Failure133

Introduction to ischemic heart disease

PATH.5027PATH.5028PATH.5034src p.400–401
Imbalance between coronary arterial supply of nutrients and oxygen and the requirement of the heart. Frequently referred to as coronary artery disease (CAD).Lecture 07, slide 400
Epidemiology
  • Leading cause of mortality in the US and other industrialized nations
  • Each year 7.5 million die of IHD worldwide
  • May affect any age, but most common in older individuals
  • Males > females (except after 80 years, M = F)
Etiology
  • Atherosclerosis — 90% of cases
  • Other rare causes of ischemia:
  • • Decreased oxygen content of the blood — anemia, carbon monoxide poisoning, pneumonia, or CHF
  • • Lowered systemic blood pressure / volume — shock
  • • Increased cardiac demand — hypertrophy, exercise
  • • Vasculitis · aortic dissection
IHD syndromes
  • 1. Angina pectoris (chest pain): stable · unstable · Prinzmetal
  • 2. Acute myocardial infarction (MI)
  • 3. Chronic IHD with CHF
  • 4. Sudden cardiac death (SCD)
Exam Lock
The definition of acute coronary syndrome used in this module
  • The term acute coronary syndrome is applied to any of the three catastrophic manifestations of IHD: unstable angina, MI, and sudden cardiac death.
L07 · Heart Failure134

Pathogenesis — the two percentages that separate stable from unstable

PATH.5034PATH.5035src p.402–405
  • Insufficient coronary perfusion relative to myocardial demand. In the majority of cases this is due to either or both of: 1. pre-existing (“fixed”) atherosclerotic occlusion of the coronary arteries · 2. acute plaque change with superimposed thrombosis and/or vasospasm.
  • If an atherosclerotic lesion progressively occludes a coronary artery at a slow rate over the years, collateral perfusion can protect against MI, even if the original vessel becomes completely occluded.
  • Vasoconstriction directly compromises lumen diameter and can also cause plaque disruption.
Stable plaque / stable anginaUnstable plaque / unstable anginaMyocardial infarction
LesionFixed (stable) lesion obstructing > 70% of vascular cross-sectional area — CRITICAL STENOSISObstruction of 90% of cross-sectional areaUnpredictable and sudden conversion of a stable plaque into an unstable plaque
ConsequenceThreshold for symptomatic ischemia precipitated by exercise — EXERTIONAL ANGINA. Compensatory vasodilation is no longer sufficient to meet myocardial demandInadequate flow even at rest. Collateral circulation will mitigate stenosis; neovascularization indicates increased inflammationRupture, superficial erosion, ulceration, fissuring, deep hemorrhage → unstable angina, myocardial infarction and sudden death

> 90% of patients with IHD have atherosclerotic lesions that cause stable fixed narrowing of one or more coronary arteries.

L07 · Heart Failure135

Practice — the lecture's own four IHD cases

Case 2

A 60-year-old man has 10 minutes of severe diffuse chest pain radiating to the left shoulder. He has had the same pain repeatedly when walking uphill or climbing stairs; it is relieved by rest or by vasodilators. ECG shows no ST elevation; troponin and CK-MB are normal. Angiography shows a fixed lesion obstructing > 70% of the vascular cross-sectional area. What is the diagnosis?

  1. AUnstable angina
  2. BStable angina from a fixed critical stenosis
  3. CPrinzmetal (variant) angina
  4. DNon-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
  5. EST-elevation myocardial infarction
Answer
B. Case 2 — stable angina. The lecture's own numbers: a fixed lesion obstructing > 70% is critical stenosis and is the threshold for exertional angina; enzymes and ST segments are normal because there is no infarction.
Case 3

The same 60-year-old returns with 20 minutes of worsening chest pain that began at rest while watching TV, only slightly relieved by vasodilators. ECG shows no ST elevation; troponin and CK-MB are normal. Angiography shows a ruptured plaque with thrombus formation. What is the diagnosis?

  1. AStable angina
  2. BUnstable angina
  3. CST-elevation myocardial infarction
  4. DChronic ischemic heart disease
  5. ESudden cardiac death
Answer
B. Case 3 — unstable angina: pain at rest, incomplete relief, ruptured plaque with thrombus, but normal troponin and no ST elevation, so no infarction has occurred yet. Unstable angina is one of the three manifestations grouped as acute coronary syndrome.
L07 · Heart Failure136

Practice — the lecture's own four IHD cases (cont.)

Case 4

A third presentation: 30 minutes of sharp chest pain radiating to the left shoulder that began suddenly at rest with no relief from vasodilators. ECG shows ST-segment elevation and troponin is elevated. Angiography shows a ruptured plaque with superimposed thrombus completely occluding the left coronary artery. What changed?

  1. AThe stenosis progressed slowly past 90%
  2. BA stable plaque converted suddenly and unpredictably into an unstable plaque, with thrombotic occlusion
  3. CCoronary vasospasm without atherosclerosis
  4. DIncreased demand from left ventricular hypertrophy
  5. EAnemia reduced the oxygen content of the blood
Answer
B. Case 4 — myocardial infarction. The lecture's phrase is exact: “unpredictable and sudden conversion of a stable plaque into an unstable plaque” by rupture, superficial erosion, ulceration, fissuring or deep hemorrhage. Elevated troponin is what separates this from Case 3.
PATH.5031

A 55-year-old woman with severe iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 5.8 g/dL) develops dyspnoea, oedema and a hyperdynamic circulation. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart with an ejection fraction of 62% and a high cardiac output. Which classification applies?

  1. ALow-output systolic failure
  2. BHigh-output failure
  3. CDiastolic failure from amyloidosis
  4. DCor pulmonale
  5. ECompensated failure with reduced EF
Answer
B. High-output failure occurs due to increased demands — anemia, hyperthyroidism, thiamine deficiency, pregnancy — and the defining feature is that symptoms of heart failure occur in spite of a well-functioning heart with a high cardiac output.
L07 · Heart Failure137

Lecture 07 — summary sheet

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Compensation (neurohormonal → Frank-Starling → hypertrophy) buys time at the cost of an under-vascularised, stiff myocardium; when it runs out, the heart fails forward into the organs it should perfuse and backward into the veins that drain into it.
Exam Lock
The seven locks
  • Concentric = pressure = sarcomeres in parallel. Eccentric = volume = sarcomeres in series.
  • HFrEF = systolic; HFpEF = diastolic, EF ≥ 50%.
  • The commonest cause of right-sided failure is left-sided failure; isolated right failure from lung disease is cor pulmonale.
  • Heart failure cells (lung, hemosiderin) = left. Nutmeg liver = right.
  • High-output failure: anemia, hyperthyroidism, thiamine deficiency, pregnancy.
  • Stable angina ≈ > 70% fixed stenosis; unstable ≈ 90% or plaque rupture.
  • Acute coronary syndrome = unstable angina + MI + sudden cardiac death.
Trap
Two traps
  • Assuming hypertrophy means a thicker wall — in eccentric hypertrophy the wall thickness can be normal.
  • Assuming the heart is failing because it is weak — in high-output failure the pump is fine and the demand is the problem.

Blood pressure has four anatomic control points. Every drug in this lecture attacks one of them.

Hypertension is the most common cardiovascular disease and a major risk factor for many adverse cardiovascular events… One of the main obstacles in the treatment of hypertension is the largely asymptomatic nature of the disease.Reading notes
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)139

Definition, categories and the control points

PHAR.0232PHAR.0233PHAR.0234src p.417–420
  • Sustained systolic BP > 130 mmHg or sustained diastolic BP > 80 mmHg
  • Results from: increased peripheral vascular smooth muscle tone → increased arteriolar resistance & reduced capacitance of the venous system. In most cases the cause is unknown.
  • Regardless of origin, the increase in arterial blood pressure is caused by either an increase in peripheral vascular resistance or an increase in cardiac output; the kidney contributes by regulating intravascular fluid volume.
BP categorySBP (mm Hg)DBP (mm Hg)
Normal< 120and< 80
Elevated120–129and< 80
Hypertension — Stage 1130–139or80–89
Hypertension — Stage 2≥ 140or≥ 90

Current guidelines recommend that the BP goal should be < 130/80 mmHg. For older patients (> 60 per JNC8, or > 80 per ASH guidelines) a systolic pressure up to 150 mm Hg is now regarded as acceptable.

Anatomic sites of BP control — all antihypertensive agents act at one or more

1 · Pump output of heart→2 · Capacitance venules→3 · CNS — sympathetic nerves→4 · Volume (kidneys): renin → angiotensin → aldosterone→+ Resistance arterioles
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)140

Treatment strategy — what is first-line and why

PHAR.0234PHAR.0235src p.426–427, 459–460
Strategy
  • Goal is to reduce CV and renal morbidity and mortality
  • Stage 1 — often controlled with a single drug
  • Stage 2 — often requires multiple drugs
  • Lifestyle recommendations are made to all hypertensive patients
First-line agents
  • ACE inhibitors
  • ARBs
  • Calcium channel blockers
  • Thiazide diuretics
Second-line and other
  • Second line: β-blockers, aldosterone antagonists
  • Other: loop diuretics, α-blockers, direct vasodilators, central α₂-agonists, renin inhibitors
Compelling indicationStandard pharmacotherapyAdd-on pharmacotherapy
Heart failureLoop diuretics (volume overload), then ARNI + β-blocker + MRA + SGLT2iIvabradine, vericiguat, hydralazine/isosorbide dinitrate (if black), digoxin (SVT)
Post-myocardial infarctionβ-blocker; then add ACEI or ARBAldosterone antagonist
Coronary artery diseaseβ-blocker; then add ACEI or ARBCCB, diuretic
Diabetes mellitusACEI or ARBCCB or thiazide
Chronic kidney diseaseACEI or ARBCCB or thiazide
Prior ischemic strokeACEI or ARBCCB or thiazide, β-blocker
Exam Lock
Special considerations with black patients (current guidelines, verbatim)
  • Hypertension occurs at a younger age and is often more severe; black patients are particularly vulnerable to strokes and hypertensive kidney disease — 3–5 times as likely to have renal complications and end-stage kidney disease. They usually respond well to calcium channel blockers and diuretics but have smaller blood pressure reductions with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and β-blockers. Appropriate combination therapies provide powerful responses that are similar in black or white patients.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)141

ACE inhibitors — captopril, enalapril, lisinopril

PHAR.0235PHAR.0236PHAR.0237src p.429–436, 463–465
Mechanism
Inhibit ACE (angiotensin converting enzyme), which cleaves angiotensin I to form angiotensin II → ↓ peripheral vascular resistance · ↓ Na⁺ & H₂O retention · ↑ bradykinin levels · do not reflexively increase cardiac output, rate or contractility
Extra actions from the notes
Also block the degradation of bradykinin and stimulate secretion of other vasodilating substances such as prostaglandin E₂ and prostacyclin. Because the AT1 negative-feedback loop is not fully activated, renin and angiotensin I levels rise.
Clinical applications
Hypertension — first-line, most effective in white and/or young patients; + diuretic gives similar effectiveness in non-black and black patients · first-line for hypertension caused by unilateral renal artery stenosis (renin-dependent) · preserve renal function in diabetic or non-diabetic nephropathy (diminish proteinuria and stabilise renal function) · effective in chronic heart failure · standard of care following MI, started 24 h after the end of infarction
Pharmacokinetics
All approved for once-daily dosing except captopril, usually dosed two or three times daily
Adverse effects
  • Dry hacking cough
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Hypotension
  • Angioedema (rare but life-threatening)
  • Acute renal failure in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis
  • Rash, fever, altered taste
Contraindications
  • Pregnancy — 1st trimester: risk of congenital malformations; 2nd and 3rd trimesters: fetal hypotension, anuria & renal failure (Cat C then Cat D)
  • Bilateral renal artery stenosis
  • History of angioedema with a previous ACEI, or hereditary/idiopathic angioedema
  • Hyperkalemia
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)142

Why ACE inhibitors protect the kidney — and when they destroy it

PHAR.0236src p.433–434
ArterioleConstricted byDilated by
AfferentEpinephrine, norepinephrineProstaglandins, kinins
EfferentAngiotensin IIACE inhibitors, ARBs
  • In diabetes and hypertension, angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole → glomerular hypertension → proteinuria → decline in GFR → renal failure. ACE inhibitors and ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole, dropping intraglomerular pressure — this is why they diminish proteinuria and stabilise renal function.
  • The same mechanism is the danger: in bilateral renal artery stenosis (or unilateral stenosis of a solitary kidney) the whole GFR depends on efferent constriction. Remove it and you get acute renal failure.
Trap
The paradox to hold in one sentence
  • The short-term creatinine rise on starting an ACE inhibitor and the long-term renal protection have the same cause — efferent dilation. A modest early rise is expected; a large one means you have unmasked stenosis.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)143

ARBs and the renin inhibitor

PHAR.0235PHAR.0237src p.437–442, 465–468
ARBs — losartan, valsartanRenin inhibitor — aliskiren
StatusFirst-line agents; alternatives to ACEIs in intolerant patientsAlternative agent — not a first-line drug, because of the lack of long-term studies evaluating CV event reduction
MechanismBlock angiotensin-2 type 1 (AT1) receptors → ↓ BP by causing arteriolar & venous dilation; block aldosterone secretion → ↓ Na⁺ & H₂O retention; ↓ diabetic nephropathy. DO NOT increase bradykinin levels.Blocks the RAAS at its point of activation — inhibits the enzyme activity of renin and prevents conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I → inhibits production of both angiotensin II and aldosterone → reduced plasma renin activity, vasodilation, ↓ BP
PharmacokineticsAll drugs in the class have similar antihypertensive efficacyOrally active nonpeptide; half-life ~24 hours, dosed once daily
Adverse effectsLowest incidence of side effects compared with other antihypertensives; similar to ACE inhibitors but no dry cough (no effect on bradykinin) and angioedema risk significantly lower. Hypotension · hyperkalemia · rare acute renal failure. Losartan reduces plasma uric acid by inhibiting the URAT1 transporter — useful in gout.Similar to ACE inhibitors; no dry cough; angioedema risk significantly lower
ContraindicationsPregnancy · bilateral renal artery stenosisPregnancy · bilateral renal artery stenosis · hyperkalemia
Trap
Two combinations the notes tell you not to make
  • A combination of an ACEI and an ARB is not recommended — each is beneficial in kidney disease, but together they increase harm.
  • Adding aliskiren to an ACEI or ARB might increase cardiovascular and renal events in patients with diabetes and should be avoided.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)144

Calcium channel blockers

PHAR.0235PHAR.0236PHAR.0237src p.443–453, 468–470
  • First-line agents, particularly in black and/or elderly patients. Used to treat hypertension, angina and arrhythmias. Have an intrinsic natriuretic effect (no need for a diuretic).
  • MOA: block the voltage-sensitive L-type Ca²⁺ channel → less Ca²⁺ entry → less calcium-induced calcium release from stores → ↓ free cytosolic Ca²⁺ → myofibril / vascular relaxation.
Verapamil (diphenalkylamine)Diltiazem (benzothiazepine)Dihydropyridines — nifedipine, amlodipine
SelectivityBoth cardiac & vascular smooth muscle, slightly more selective towards the myocardium; greatest depressant effect on the heart, can decrease heart rate and cardiac outputEffects in both cardiac & vascular smooth muscle; good side-effect profileGreater affinity for vascular Ca²⁺ channels than cardiac; more likely to evoke reflex tachycardia
Used to treatAngina, supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, hypertension, migraine & cerebral vasospasmAngina, hypertension, supraventricular tachyarrhythmias & cerebral vasospasmPrimarily hypertension — coronary & peripheral vasodilatation
Adverse effectsConstipation (~7%), negative inotropic effects, gingival hyperplasiaNegative inotropic effectsHypotension, peripheral edema (especially feet & ankles), dizziness, headache, fatigue, gingival hyperplasia, flushing, reflex tachycardia (especially short-acting preparations)
Exam Lock
Two safety lines
  • High doses of short-acting dihydropyridines can increase the risk of MI (excessive vasodilation and reflex cardiac stimulation) — sustained-release preparations are preferred.
  • Non-dihydropyridines (verapamil & diltiazem) are relatively contraindicated in patients taking β-blockers, or with 2nd or 3rd degree AV block, or severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Patients with bradycardia, conduction defects or heart failure should not be given CCBs, especially verapamil and diltiazem.

Hypertensive crisis — the definitions and the treatment goals

PHAR.0235src p.479–480
The term hypertensive crisis refers to clinical syndromes characterized by severe (typically acute) elevations in blood pressure, generally considered to be a diastolic pressure > 120 mmHg. This abrupt increase in blood pressure, if not treated, can lead to acute vascular injury and derivative end-organ damage.Reading notes
DefinitionTreatment
Hypertensive emergencySevere hypertension (DBP > 150 mm Hg with SBP > 210 mm Hg in an otherwise healthy person, or DBP > 120 mm Hg in individuals with pre-existing complications) with signs of damage to target organs (brain, CV system, kidneys)ICU. Arterial line monitoring. Progressive (not abrupt) reduction with a short-acting, titratable IV drug: (a) lower BP by no more than 25% within minutes to 1 h — appropriate goal 100–110 mm Hg DBP; (b) if stable, further reduction toward 160/100 within 2–6 h, and gradual reduction to normal over the next 8–24 h. Abrupt decreases must be avoided.
Hypertensive urgencyVery high blood pressure without signs of target-organ damageIdeally managed by adjusting maintenance therapy — adding a new antihypertensive drug and/or increasing the dose of a present medication

Practice — antihypertensives I

PHAR.0236

A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria is started on lisinopril. Two weeks later his creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.9 mg/dL and he is oliguric. Which underlying lesion does this suggest, and why?

  1. ADiabetic nephropathy; ACE inhibitors accelerate glomerulosclerosis
  2. BBilateral renal artery stenosis; GFR depended on angiotensin II–mediated efferent constriction
  3. CAcute tubular necrosis; ACE inhibitors are directly tubulotoxic
  4. DInterstitial nephritis; a class effect of ACE inhibitors
  5. ERenal vein thrombosis; ACE inhibitors are prothrombotic
Answer
B. In bilateral renal artery stenosis, perfusion pressure is low and filtration is maintained by angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole. An ACE inhibitor removes that constriction → acute renal failure. Bilateral stenosis is a listed contraindication; unilateral stenosis, by contrast, is a first-line indication.
PHAR.0237

A patient on enalapril develops a persistent dry hacking cough. What is the mechanism, and what is the appropriate substitution?

  1. AAccumulation of angiotensin II; switch to a β-blocker
  2. BAccumulation of bradykinin; switch to an ARB such as losartan
  3. CReflex bronchoconstriction; switch to a dihydropyridine
  4. DHyperkalemia; switch to a thiazide
  5. EDirect airway irritation; switch to aliskiren
Answer
B. ACE also degrades bradykinin; inhibiting it raises bradykinin (and prostaglandin E₂ / prostacyclin), producing the cough and contributing to angioedema. ARBs block the AT1 receptor downstream and do not affect bradykinin, so they do not cause the cough and carry a much lower angioedema risk.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)152

Practice — antihypertensives I (cont.)

PHAR.0237

A 66-year-old man with hypertension and gout needs a single antihypertensive. Which agent has the additional benefit of lowering plasma uric acid, and by what mechanism?

  1. AHydrochlorothiazide — increases urate secretion
  2. BLosartan — inhibits the URAT1 transporter
  3. CVerapamil — reduces renal urate reabsorption
  4. DLisinopril — increases bradykinin-mediated uricosuria
  5. EAmlodipine — increases renal blood flow
Answer
B. Losartan reduces plasma uric acid levels by inhibiting the URAT1 transporter — can be useful in patients with gout. Thiazides do the opposite: they cause hyperuricemia by competing for the proximal organic secretory pathway and can precipitate gout.
PHAR.0237

A 72-year-old woman with hypertension develops bilateral ankle swelling on amlodipine. Her JVP is normal, there are no crackles, and BNP is normal. What is the mechanism and best next step?

  1. AHeart failure from negative inotropy; stop the drug and start a loop diuretic
  2. BPrecapillary arteriolar dilation without venular dilation causing a local pressure gradient; consider reducing the dose or switching class — a diuretic will not fix it
  3. CHypoalbuminaemia; check urinary protein
  4. DLymphatic obstruction; refer for lymphoscintigraphy
  5. EVenous thrombosis; start anticoagulation
Answer
B. Dihydropyridine peripheral edema, especially feet and ankles, is a listed adverse effect and is not volume overload — it is a local Starling-forces problem from selective arteriolar dilation, which is why it responds poorly to diuretics. A normal JVP, clear chest and normal BNP exclude heart failure.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)153

Practice — antihypertensives I (cont.)

PHAR.0235

A 44-year-old man presents with BP 240/140, headache, papilloedema and a creatinine of 2.8. He is admitted to the ICU. What is the correct blood pressure target in the first hour?

  1. ANormalise the blood pressure to < 130/80 immediately
  2. BReduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 25%, aiming for a diastolic of about 100–110 mm Hg
  3. CReduce to 160/100 within the first 15 minutes
  4. DWithhold treatment until oral therapy can be started
  5. EReduce systolic pressure to below 120 mm Hg within 2 hours
Answer
B. Hypertensive emergency (severe hypertension with target-organ damage): lower BP by no more than 25% within minutes to 1 hour (goal DBP 100–110), then toward 160/100 within 2–6 h, then gradually to normal over 8–24 h. Abrupt decreases must be avoided — they cause watershed hypoperfusion.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)154

Antihypertensives I — summary sheet

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Four first-line classes — ACEI, ARB, CCB, thiazide — chosen by the compelling indication in front of you: kidney or diabetes → RAAS blockade; black or elderly → CCB or thiazide; post-MI or heart failure → β-blocker plus RAAS blockade.
Exam Lock
The eight locks
  • ACEI = cough + angioedema + hyperkalaemia; ARB = the same minus the cough.
  • Both are contraindicated in pregnancy and bilateral renal artery stenosis — and both are first-line for unilateral renal artery stenosis.
  • Never combine ACEI + ARB; never add aliskiren to either in diabetes.
  • Verapamil → constipation and the greatest cardiac depression; dihydropyridines → ankle oedema and reflex tachycardia.
  • Do not combine verapamil or diltiazem with a β-blocker (AV block, negative inotropy).
  • Nitroglycerin for emergencies with cardiac ischaemia; esmolol for aortic dissection; fenoldopam for renal failure; phentolamine for catecholamine excess.
  • Nitroprusside → cyanide toxicity → sodium thiosulfate.
  • Clonidine must never be stopped abruptly — rebound hypertension.
Trap
Three traps
  • Reading a creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor as a reason to abandon RAAS blockade — a modest rise is the mechanism working; a large one means stenosis.
  • Treating dihydropyridine ankle oedema with a diuretic.
  • Giving a short-acting dihydropyridine at high dose — the notes say it can increase the risk of MI.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs I (Cardiovascular Drugs 2)155
