The three anginas — the lecture's own three cases, side by side

PATH.5040src p.494–497
Paroxysmal and usually recurrent attacks of substernal or precordial chest discomfort/pain caused by transient (15 seconds to 15 minutes) myocardial ischemia that is insufficient to induce myocyte necrosis. Ischemia induces the release of adenosine, bradykinin, and other molecules that stimulate sympathetic and vagal afferent nerves.Lecture 09, slide 494
Stable (typical) anginaUnstable (crescendo) anginaVasospastic (Prinzmetal / variant)
TriggerPhysical activity, emotional excitement, stress — increased demandProgressively less effort; often occurs at restOccurs at rest, awakens the patient from sleep
MechanismReduction of coronary perfusion because of fixed stenosis — no myocardial necrosisDisruption of plaque with superimposed thrombosis and possibly vasospasmCoronary artery spasm producing transient squeezing chest pain; mechanism not clear. Can occur in atherosclerotic as well as normal coronary arteries.
Duration / reliefTransient recurrent attacks; relieved by rest or vasodilatorsPersistent, more prolonged, not easily relieved by rest; may respond to vasodilatorsDoes not disappear with rest; responds to vasodilators
ECGNo ST elevationNo ST elevationST-segment elevation during the episode — indicative of transmural ischemia
EnzymesTroponin and CK-MB not elevatedTroponin and CK-MB not elevatedTroponin and CK-MB not elevated
AngiographyFixed ~70% narrowing (e.g. LAD)Ruptured plaque with thrombusNo significant narrowing
SignificanceMost common formHarbinger of subsequent MI — “pre-infarction angina”—
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease157

The three anginas — the lecture's own three cases, side by side (cont.)

PATH.5040src p.494–497
Exam Lock
The one that breaks the pattern
  • Prinzmetal angina gives ST elevation with normal troponin and normal arteries. Every other combination of those three findings points somewhere else — ST elevation *with* raised troponin is an infarct; no ST elevation with raised troponin is NSTEMI.
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease158

Myocardial infarction — epidemiology and pathogenesis

PATH.5040src p.499–500
Epidemiology
  • Roughly 1.5 million individuals suffer an MI in the USA each year
  • Approximately 610,000 deaths annually
  • M:F 5:1 at age 45–54 · M:F 2:1 at age 55–80 · no difference after 80
Etiology
  • 90% — atherosclerosis
  • 10% — vasospasm, emboli, vasculitis, dissection, amyloidosis, sickle cell disease
Pathogenesis of the 90%
  • Acute thrombosis leading to coronary occlusion, from disruption of a pre-existing plaque in which:
  • ⅔ have < 50% stenosis
  • 85% have < 70% stenosis
  • The remaining 10%: vasospasm — isolated, intense and relatively prolonged, with or without coronary atherosclerosis · emboli — from a left-sided mural thrombus · unexplained — disease of small intramural coronary vessels like vasculitis, or hematological abnormalities like sickle cell anemia.
Trap
The most counter-intuitive number in the lecture
  • Two-thirds of infarcts arise from plaques causing less than 50% stenosis. The plaque that kills you is usually not the one that was causing your angina. That is why plaque stability, not plaque size, is the object of the previous lecture.
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease159

The first hour — what dies, and when

PATH.5044src p.501
Myocardial responseFeatureTime
BiochemicalCessation of aerobic metabolism → drop in ATP and accumulation of lactic acid in myocytesSeconds
ATP reduced to 50% of normal10 min
ATP reduced to 10% of normal40 min
FunctionalLoss of contractility< 2 min
MorphologicalReversible cell injury (cellular swelling)< 20 min
Irreversible cell injury (coagulative necrosis)20–40 min
Microvascular injury> 1 hr
Exam Lock
The two-minute / twenty-minute rule
  • Contractility stops at < 2 minutes — that is why a wall-motion abnormality appears on echocardiography long before any necrosis. Irreversible injury begins at 20–40 minutes — that is the window reperfusion is racing.
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease160

Transmural vs subendocardial infarction

PATH.5042src p.502
Transmural infarctionSubendocardial infarction
ExtentInvolve the full thickness of the ventricular wall in the distribution of a single coronary artery (regional) — also called STEMILimited to the inner one third, or at most one half, of the ventricular wall — also called NSTEMI
Vessel pathologyUsually associated with acute plaque changes and superimposed, completely occlusive thrombosis. Can also occur with cocaine abuseAssociated with diffuse stenosing coronary atherosclerosis or with prolonged hypotension (global / circumferential infarctions); may occur due to transient/partial arterial obstruction (regional)
Severity—Less serious than transmural infarction
ECGST elevation; Q wave after 6 hours of onsetNo specific changes, no ST elevation, maybe T-wave depression

Microscopic infarctions are also seen.

Bottom Line
Why the subendocardium goes first
  • It is the last territory perfused — the coronaries run epicardium → endocardium and most flow occurs in diastole. Any global insult (shock, prolonged hypotension, severe anaemia) starves that layer first, which is why a circumferential subendocardial infarct means hypoperfusion, not a single blocked artery.
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease161

Morphologic timeline of infarction

PATH.5044src p.504–506
TimeGrossHistology (light microscopy)
< 4 hrsNoneNone
4–12 hrsOccasionally dark mottlingOnset of coagulative necrosis
12–24 hrsDark mottling (red-blue)Coagulative necrosis
1–3 daysMottling (yellow/tan centre)Heavy neutrophilic infiltrate
3–7 daysCentral softening (yellow/tan) · hyperemic borderMacrophages appear · breakdown of myofibers
7–10 daysMaximum softening (no myocytes / no collagen)Well-developed phagocytosis · extensive macrophages
> 2 monthsScarring completeDense collagenous scar

“Wavy fibers” at the periphery of the infarct result from contractions of viable myocardium stretching and buckling adjacent, non-contractile dead fibers. Myocyte vacuolization reflects intracellular accumulation of salt and water within the sarcoplasmic reticulum and marks myocytes that are viable but poorly contractile. Because cardiac myocytes are terminally differentiated, no cardiomyocyte proliferation is seen — only hypertrophy of the remaining cells.

L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease162

Reperfusion injury

PATH.5045src p.508–509
Reperfusion of ischemic tissue can cause rebound myocardial damage → reperfusion injury. It is estimated that up to 50% (or more) of the ultimate infarct size can be attributed to its effects.Lecture 09, slide 508
Gross
Typically a hemorrhagic infarct as a consequence of vascular injury and leakiness
Microscopy
Irreversibly damaged myocytes after reperfusion develop contraction band necrosis — prominent hyper-eosinophilic cross-striations spanning myofibers
Why contraction bands form
An influx of calcium across plasma membranes heightens actin-myosin interactions. In the absence of ATP, the sarcomeres cannot relax and get stuck in an agonal tetanic state.
Mechanisms
Mitochondrial dysfunction · increased cytosolic calcium leading to hypercontracture of myofibrils · free radicals · endothelial injury · leukocyte aggregation · platelet and complement activation
Exam Lock
Contraction band necrosis has three homes
  • Reperfused infarct · catecholamine excess (cocaine, pheochromocytoma) · around the edge of any infarct. All three are the same mechanism — calcium flooding a myocyte with no ATP.
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease163

Clinical features and diagnosis of MI

PATH.5046src p.511–514
Clinical features
  • Chest pain — retrosternal, crushing in nature; may radiate to the neck, jaw, epigastrium, shoulder, or left arm; persistent > 30 min (unlike angina); not significantly relieved by vasodilators (nitroglycerine) or rest
  • Dyspnea
  • Rapid weak pulse
  • Diaphoresis, nausea and vomiting, arrhythmia, left ventricular failure, and cardiogenic shock
Silent MI — why some patients have no symptoms
  • Occurs in as many as 25% of cases
  • Asymptomatic MI discovered only by ECG changes and laboratory tests
  • Patients may experience few if any symptoms (no chest pain)
  • Common in elderly patients
  • Underlying diabetes mellitus / hypertension
MarkerBehaviour
Troponins (I and T)Most sensitive and specific marker. Normally not detectable in circulation. Rises in 2–4 hrs, peaks at 48 hrs, persists for 7–10 days
Creatine kinase isoenzymesA dimer composed of M & B subunits: MM, MB, BB. CK-MB is the most specific for the heart among the CKs. Rises in 2–4 hrs, peaks at 24–48 hrs, disappears by ≈ 72 hrs. Useful for detection of reinfarction.
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)Rises in 24 hrs, peaks at 3–6 days, returns to baseline within 8–12 days
MyoglobinNot used in clinical practice
InvestigationFindings
ECGTransmural (STEMI): ST elevation, Q wave after 6 hours of onset. Subendocardial (NSTEMI): no specific changes, no ST elevation, maybe T-wave depression
EchocardiogramUseful in detecting complications · evaluate ventricular function and wall-motion abnormalities · can identify pericardial effusion, valve regurgitation and cardiac tamponade
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease164

Clinical features and diagnosis of MI (cont.)

PATH.5046src p.511–514
Exam Lock
Why CK-MB still matters
  • Troponin stays up for 7–10 days, so it cannot tell you whether a patient who reinfarcts on day 4 has a *new* event. CK-MB clears by 72 hours, so a second rise is a second infarct.
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease165

Predicting the infarct from the vessel

PATH.5043src p.522–530
Involved myocardiumST-segment elevation or abnormal Q waveOccluded vessel
Anteroseptal wallV1–V2Left anterior descending (LAD) and right coronary arteries
Anteroapical wallV3–V4LAD
Anterolateral wallV5–V6LAD or circumflex artery (LCX)
Lateral wallI, aVLLCX
Inferior wallII, III, aVFRight coronary artery (RCA)
Posterior wallV7–V9; reciprocal changes in leads V1–V3Posterior descending artery (PDA)
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease166

Predicting the infarct from the vessel (cont.)

PATH.5043src p.522–530
InfarctComplications the lecture attaches
Right ventricular MI — RCA (including the PDA if right dominant)Hypotension · JVD · bradyarrhythmia
Inferior wall MI — PDAMitral regurgitation (papillary muscle rupture)
Left ventricular MI — LADLeft ventricular septum rupture · anterior wall rupture · left ventricular aneurysm · heart failure
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease167

Complications of MI — the five categories

PATH.5047src p.515–518
#CategoryDetail
1IschemicExtension of the infarction
2ArrhythmicMost common cause of sudden cardiac death. Factors that can cause arrhythmias following MI: myocardial irritability and conduction disturbances · electrolyte imbalance · hypoxia
3EmbolicMural thrombus → systemic emboli. Stroke (most common), limb ischemia, renal infarction or mesenteric ischemia can occur
4aMechanical — contractile dysfunctionLeft ventricular failure; if severe, cardiogenic shock (10–15% of cases); progressive heart failure (chronic IHD)
4bMechanical — papillary muscle dysfunctionMitral / tricuspid valve incompetence — from rupture, or fibrosis or shortening. Global ventricular dilation can also cause mitral valve insufficiency
4cMechanical — myocardial ruptureOccurs between 3–7 days, when lysis of necrotic myocardium is maximal and much of the infarct has converted to soft, friable granulation tissue. Ventricular free wall rupture → cardiac tamponade. Ventricular septum rupture → VSD.
4dMechanical — ventricular aneurysmLate complication of large transmural infarcts. Scar-tissue wall bulges during systole; mural thrombus, arrhythmias and heart failure may occur. Unlikely to rupture due to the tough fibrotic wall.
5aInflammatory — acute pericarditisAcute fibrinous / fibrinohemorrhagic, due to direct irritation of the pericardium in transmural infarcts. Usually day 2 or 3 post MI
5bInflammatory — Dressler syndromeAutoimmune; occurs several weeks post-MI; autoantibodies that target damaged pericardial antigens
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease168

The summary table — time, morphology and the complication of that day

PATH.5044PATH.5047src p.531
TimeGrossHistology (LM)Complications
< 4 hrsNoneNoneArrhythmia and CHF can occur at any time · cardiogenic shock
4–12 hrsOccasionally dark mottlingOnset coagulative necrosisArrhythmia
12–24 hrsDark mottling (red-blue)Coagulative necrosisArrhythmia
1–3 daysMottling (yellow/tan centre)Heavy neutrophilic infiltrateFibrinous pericarditis
3–7 daysCentral softening (yellow/tan) · hyperemic borderMacrophages appear · breakdown of myofibersRupture of ventricular free wall (cardiac tamponade), papillary muscle (mitral regurgitation), or interventricular septum (shock)
7–10 daysMaximum softening (no myocytes / no collagen)Well-developed phagocytosis · extensive macrophagesRupture of free wall, papillary muscle, or interventricular septum
> 2 monthsScarring completeDense collagenous scarAneurysm · mural thrombosis · Dressler syndrome (autoimmune pericarditis)
Exam Lock
The single most examinable relationship in this lecture
  • Peak macrophage activity (days 3–7) = maximum softening = maximum rupture risk. The heart is weakest exactly when the patient feels best, which is why day-4 sudden deterioration after an uncomplicated MI is rupture until proven otherwise.
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease169

Chronic ischemic heart disease and sudden cardiac death

PATH.5040PATH.5041src p.519–520
Chronic ischemic heart diseaseSudden cardiac death
DefinitionInsidious onset of CHF in patients who may or may not have past episodes of MI or anginal attacksUnexpected death due to cessation of normal cardiac electrical activity with hemodynamic collapse. Can occur without symptoms or within 1–24 hours of the onset of symptoms
Pathogenesis / causesCardiac decompensation owing to exhaustion of the compensatory hypertrophy of non-infarcted viable myocardium, or severe coronary obstructive disease → diffuse myocardial dysfunction. Arrhythmia and intercurrent MI are common and fatalIn adults: CAD is the most common cause. In younger victims: cardiomyopathy and myocarditis · myocardial hypertrophy · channelopathies · mitral valve prolapse · pulmonary hypertension
Morphology / mechanismGross: enlarged and heavy heart due to hypertrophy and dilation · discrete gray-white scars of healed previous infarcts · patchy fibrous thickening of mural endocardium. Histology: myocardial hypertrophy · diffuse subendocardial vacuolization (myocytolysis) · scars of previously healed infarctsUltimate mechanism is a lethal arrhythmia — ventricular fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, and asystole.
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease170

Practice — angina and infarct diagnosis

Case 3

A 45-year-old man is woken at 3 a.m. by severe chest pain that does not resolve with rest but goes away with sublingual nitrate. ECG during the episode shows ST-segment elevation; troponin and CK-MB are normal. Angiography the next day shows no significant narrowing. What is the diagnosis?

  1. AStable angina
  2. BUnstable angina
  3. CNSTEMI
  4. DVasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina
  5. EAcute pericarditis
Answer
D. Case 3 in the lecture — Prinzmetal angina. Occurs at rest and wakes the patient, ST-segment elevation during episodes (transmural ischaemia), normal enzymes, and no significant narrowing on angiography because the mechanism is coronary artery spasm. It responds to vasodilators and can occur in atherosclerotic or normal coronaries.
PATH.5047

A patient with an acute MI dies on day 4. At autopsy the infarct centre is soft and yellow-tan with a hyperaemic border, and there is 400 mL of blood in the pericardial sac. Which histological finding explains the rupture?

  1. ADense collagenous scar with contraction bands
  2. BPeak macrophage activity with breakdown of myofibers and no collagen yet laid down
  3. CHeavy neutrophilic infiltrate with intact myofibers
  4. DCoagulative necrosis with wavy fibres at the periphery
  5. EGranulation tissue with abundant new collagen
Answer
B. Days 3–7: macrophages appear and break down myofibers, but collagen has not yet been laid down — maximum softening, maximum rupture risk. Free-wall rupture → haemopericardium and cardiac tamponade. Neutrophils dominate days 1–3; dense scar takes > 2 months.
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease171

Practice — angina and infarct diagnosis (cont.)

PATH.5043

Four days after an inferior STEMI a patient develops a new loud holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, with flash pulmonary oedema. Which vessel was occluded and what has ruptured?

  1. ALAD; interventricular septum
  2. BRCA/PDA; posteromedial papillary muscle
  3. CLCX; anterolateral papillary muscle
  4. DLAD; ventricular free wall
  5. ERCA; right ventricular free wall
Answer
B. The lecture pairs inferior wall MI (PDA) with mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture. The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply from the PDA, so it is the vulnerable one. A septal rupture (LAD) gives a harsh murmur at the left sternal border with a step-up in oxygen saturation.
PATH.5046

A 78-year-old diabetic woman is found to have Q waves in II, III and aVF on a routine ECG. She reports no chest pain, ever. What phenomenon is this and how common is it?

  1. APericarditis; ~5% of cases
  2. BSilent MI; as many as 25% of cases
  3. CPrinzmetal angina; ~10% of cases
  4. DChronic ischemic heart disease; ~50% of cases
  5. EReperfusion injury; ~30% of cases
Answer
B. Silent MI occurs in as many as 25% of cases — asymptomatic infarction discovered only by ECG changes and laboratory tests, common in the elderly and in patients with diabetes mellitus or hypertension (autonomic neuropathy blunting afferent pain signalling).
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease172

Practice — mechanism and complication

PATH.5045

After successful primary PCI a patient's infarct is grossly haemorrhagic, and microscopy shows prominent hyper-eosinophilic cross-striations spanning myofibers. What are these bands and why do they form?

  1. AWavy fibres; buckling by adjacent viable myocardium
  2. BContraction band necrosis; calcium influx driving actin-myosin interaction with no ATP to permit relaxation
  3. CCoagulative necrosis; loss of nuclei with preserved outlines
  4. DMyocyte vacuolization; salt and water in the sarcoplasmic reticulum
  5. EGranulation tissue; new capillaries and fibroblasts
Answer
B. Contraction band necrosis is the microscopic signature of reperfusion injury: an influx of calcium heightens actin-myosin interactions and, in the absence of ATP, the sarcomeres cannot relax and get stuck in an agonal tetanic state. Up to 50% or more of final infarct size may be attributable to reperfusion injury.
PATH.5042

A hypotensive patient in septic shock survives, but troponin is elevated and the ECG shows T-wave depression without ST elevation. Autopsy of a similar case shows necrosis confined to the inner third of the ventricular wall, circumferentially. What is the mechanism?

  1. AComplete occlusive thrombus in a single epicardial artery
  2. BGlobal hypoperfusion of the last-perfused layer, on a background of diffuse stenosing atherosclerosis
  3. CCoronary vasospasm in a normal artery
  4. DEmbolus from a left ventricular mural thrombus
  5. EVasculitis of small intramural vessels
Answer
B. A circumferential subendocardial infarct is not the territory of one artery — the lecture attributes it to diffuse stenosing coronary atherosclerosis or prolonged hypotension. The subendocardium is the last region perfused, so it dies first in any global insult. ECG shows no ST elevation, maybe T-wave depression (NSTEMI).
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease173

Practice — mechanism and complication (cont.)

PATH.5047

Six weeks after a large anterior MI a patient develops fever, pleuritic chest pain and a pericardial friction rub, with a raised ESR. What is this, and how does it differ from the pericarditis of day 2–3?

  1. AFibrinous pericarditis; both are due to direct pericardial irritation
  2. BDressler syndrome; it is autoimmune, from autoantibodies targeting damaged pericardial antigens, whereas the early form is direct irritation in transmural infarcts
  3. CVentricular aneurysm with mural thrombus; the early form is embolic
  4. DReinfarction; the early form is arrhythmic
  5. EConstrictive pericarditis; the early form is haemorrhagic
Answer
B. Two pericarditides follow MI. The early one (day 2–3) is acute fibrinous/fibrinohaemorrhagic, from direct irritation of the pericardium in transmural infarcts. Dressler syndrome occurs several weeks post-MI and is autoimmune — autoantibodies targeting damaged pericardial antigens.
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease174

Lecture 09 — summary sheet

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Angina is ischaemia without necrosis; infarction is ischaemia past 20–40 minutes; and after that a single clock — neutrophils days 1–3, macrophages and softening days 3–7, scar at 2 months — predicts every complication.
Exam Lock
The nine locks
  • Prinzmetal: ST elevation, normal troponin, normal arteries.
  • ⅔ of infarcts arise from plaques with < 50% stenosis.
  • Contractility stops < 2 min; irreversible injury 20–40 min.
  • Transmural = STEMI = one artery; subendocardial = NSTEMI = inner ⅓, often global hypoperfusion.
  • Troponin: rises 2–4 h, peaks 48 h, persists 7–10 d. CK-MB clears by 72 h → detects reinfarction.
  • Rupture day 3–7 (free wall → tamponade; septum → VSD; papillary muscle → MR).
  • Aneurysm is late and rarely ruptures — the fibrotic wall is tough.
  • Arrhythmia is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death post-MI.
  • Dressler = weeks later, autoimmune.
Trap
Three traps
  • Calling ST elevation with a normal troponin an infarct — check whether it is vasospasm.
  • Attributing a circumferential subendocardial infarct to a single vessel.
  • Expecting the largest plaque to be the culprit lesion.
L09 · Ischemic Heart Disease175

PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs II (Cardiovascular Drugs 3)176

Diuretics revisited — the role each plays in hypertension

PHAR.0236PHAR.0243src p.535–538
AgentRole in hypertension
ThiazidesFirst-line agents, particularly in black and/or elderly patients. Counteract the Na⁺ & H₂O retention caused by other antihypertensive drugs.
Loop diureticsAct promptly in patients with poor renal function or heart failure. Used primarily in patients who do not respond to thiazide therapy adequately.
Potassium-sparingOffset the K⁺ loss in urine caused by thiazide or loop diuretics. Used in combination with other diuretics.
Aldosterone antagonists — spironolactoneReduces K⁺ excretion → risk of hyperkalemia, more prominent in chronic kidney disease or with concurrent ACEI, ARB or other K⁺-sparing diuretics. Used in hypertension & heart failure; can be used as part of first-line therapy in patients with hypertension and severe left ventricular dysfunction.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs II (Cardiovascular Drugs 3)177

β-blockers and α-blockers in hypertension

PHAR.0237PHAR.0243src p.539–545
β-blockers — propranolol, metoprolol, atenolol, pindololα₁-blockers — prazosin, doxazosin
StatusAdd-on therapy only to first-line agents in primary prevention patients. First-line only for coronary artery disease, heart failure, or post-MI.Seldom used in essential hypertension — because of the side-effect profile, development of tolerance, and the advent of safer antihypertensives. Reserved as alternative agents for unique situations such as men with benign prostatic hyperplasia.
PharmacologyPropranolol — non-selective β1 & β2 antagonist. Metoprolol & atenolol — selective β1 antagonists (most widely used). Pindolol — non-selective β1 & β2 partial agonist with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity.Competitively block α₁-adrenoceptors → ↓ peripheral vascular resistance and arterial BP by relaxing both arterial and venous smooth muscle. Cause minimal changes in cardiac output, renal blood flow & GFR → no long-term tachycardia. Na⁺ & H₂O retention does occur.
Adverse effectsSee Antihypertensives I — bronchoconstriction with non-selective agents, masking of hypoglycaemia, fatigue and reduced sexual functionOrthostatic hypotension (may lead to syncope) on first dose or large dose increases — a β-blocker may be necessary to blunt the short-term reflex tachycardia · dizziness, drowsiness, headache, lack of energy, nausea, palpitations · doxazosin shown to increase the rate of congestive heart failure
Labetalol — mixed α and β blocker
Oral & parenteral. Used in hypertension management and is safe in pregnancy; IV labetalol gives rapid reduction in BP → useful in hypertensive emergencies. Advantage: the fall in BP from α₁-blockade is not associated with a reflex increase in heart rate or cardiac output. Adverse effect: orthostatic hypotension on first use or at high doses.

Central α₂ agonists — clonidine vs methyldopa

PHAR.0236PHAR.0239PHAR.0237src p.546–549
ClonidineMethyldopa
MechanismReduces sympathetic outflow by acting on presynaptic α₂ adrenergic autoreceptors → ↓ peripheral vascular resistance & cardiac output → ↓ BPα₂ agonist converted centrally to α-methyldopamine and α-methylnorepinephrine to diminish sympathetic outflow in the CNS → ↓ peripheral resistance & BP (cardiac output is not reduced)
Renal effectDOES NOT reduce renal blood flow or GFRDOES NOT reduce renal blood flow or GFR
UseHypertension management including hypertensive crises (other drugs with fewer side effects are now generally preferred)Usually treatment of choice for pregnancy-induced hypertension (other drugs with fewer side effects are now generally preferred for other patients)

Rebound hypertension following abrupt withdrawal — avoid concomitant use with β-blockers.Sedation, drowsiness, dizziness, nausea, headache, weakness, fatigue, sexual dysfunction, hyperprolactinemia · nightmares, mental depression, vertigo (infrequent) · reversible lupus-like syndrome · positive Coombs test in 10–20% on long-term treatment (> 1 year), which can result in hemolytic anemia, hepatitis & drug fever
Exam Lock
Why both preserve renal blood flow
  • Central sympatholysis lowers pressure without constricting the renal vasculature. That is why these two survive in patients where renal perfusion matters — and why methyldopa remains the classic choice in pregnancy, where uteroplacental flow must be preserved.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs II (Cardiovascular Drugs 3)179

Direct vasodilators

PHAR.0237PHAR.0239src p.550–554
  • Not used as first-line antihypertensives. Direct-acting smooth muscle relaxants. Produce reflex tachycardia and increase plasma renin → Na⁺ & H₂O retention. Major side effects can be blocked if combined with a diuretic & a β-blocker.
HydralazineMinoxidil
Route & siteOral or IV; acts mainly on arteriolesCauses direct peripheral vasodilatation of arterioles; oral
UsePregnancy-induced hypertension / pre-eclampsia; last-line therapy in the management of hypertensionOral treatment for severe-malignant hypertension refractory to other treatments
Adverse effectsFluid retention & reflex tachycardia are common · reversible lupus-like syndrome · headache, nausea, sweating, flushing. Usually administered with a β-blocker and a thiazide.Reflex tachycardia & fluid retention may be severe — combine with a loop diuretic & β-blocker · hypertrichosis, which is why it is also used topically to treat male pattern baldness
Trap
Two drugs, one lupus-like syndrome
  • Hydralazine and methyldopa both produce a reversible lupus-like syndrome. Methyldopa additionally produces a Coombs-positive haemolytic anaemia — the two are frequently offered as distractors for each other.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs II (Cardiovascular Drugs 3)180

Pulmonary hypertension

PHAR.0244PHAR.0245src p.555–558
An increase in blood pressure in the pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein or pulmonary capillaries.Lecture, slide 555
DrugClass & mechanismNotes / adverse effects
EpoprostenolSynthetic PGI₂ (prostacyclin). Lowers peripheral, pulmonary, and coronary resistance. Given via continuous infusion.Flushing, headache, jaw pain, diarrhea and arthralgias

Exam Lock
Objective PHAR.0245 — why nitrate + sildenafil is dangerous
  • Both act on the same pathway: nitrates donate NO which raises cGMP, and sildenafil blocks the PDE5 that degrades cGMP. Together they cause runaway cGMP accumulation → profound, refractory hypotension — potentially fatal. This same pairing reappears in the Antianginal Drugs lecture.

Hypertensive crises — definitions, causes and the management protocol

PHAR.0238src p.562–568
Hypertensive emergencyHypertensive urgency
DefinitionSevere hypertension with signs of damage to target organs (brain, CV system, kidneys). DBP > 150 mmHg (with SBP > 210 mmHg) in an otherwise healthy person, or DBP > 120 mmHg in individuals with pre-existing complications (e.g. cerebral hemorrhage, aortic stenosis)Very high BP without target-organ damage. Acute complications unlikely, so immediate BP reduction is not required
ManagementImmediate BP reduction with IV drugs. Admission to ICU; drugs applied by IV line; arterial line to measure BP; progressive reduction using a short-acting titratable IV drug. Avoid abrupt decreases in BP — can lead to MI, stroke or visual changes.
(a) Lower BP by no more than 25% within min–1 h; appropriate goal 100–110 mmHg DBP.
(b) If stable, further reduction toward 160/100 within 2–6 h, and gradual reduction to normal over the next 8–24 h		Patients should be started on a 2-drug oral combination with close evaluation continued on an outpatient basis

Causes of hypertensive emergency

Vascular / renal
  • Essential hypertension
  • Renal parenchymal disease
  • Renovascular disease
Endocrine & obstetric
  • Pregnancy (eclampsia)
  • Endocrine: pheochromocytoma, Cushing's, renin-producing tumors
Drugs & CNS
  • Drugs: cocaine, crack, sympathomimetics, amphetamines, MAO inhibitors, tyramine
  • Drug withdrawal: clonidine, nifedipine
  • CNS disorders: injury, stroke, tumor
  • Autonomic hyperreactivity

Practice — antihypertensives II

PHAR.0239

A 29-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation has BP 176/118, headache and proteinuria. Which two agents are named in this lecture as the pregnancy choices for acute lowering and for chronic control?

  1. AEnalapril acutely; losartan chronically
  2. BHydralazine acutely; methyldopa chronically
  3. CNitroprusside acutely; aliskiren chronically
  4. DDiazoxide acutely; bosentan chronically
  5. EAmlodipine acutely; spironolactone chronically
Answer
B. Hydralazine is the drug of choice for hypertensive emergencies in pregnancy related to eclampsia, and methyldopa is usually the treatment of choice for pregnancy-induced hypertension. Labetalol is the commonly used β-blocker in pregnancy. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aliskiren and bosentan are all contraindicated in pregnancy.
PHAR.0238

A patient with a phaeochromocytoma has a hypertensive crisis. Which agent is the drug of choice, and why is starting with a β-blocker alone dangerous?

  1. AEsmolol; because α-blockade causes reflex tachycardia
  2. BPhentolamine; unopposed α-stimulation after β-blockade worsens vasoconstriction
  3. CNitroglycerin; because venodilation reduces preload
  4. DFenoldopam; because it preserves renal blood flow
  5. EDiazoxide; because it opens potassium channels
Answer
B. Phentolamine — a non-selective α blocker — is named as the drug of choice for catecholamine-related emergencies: pheochromocytoma, cocaine and amphetamine toxicity, clonidine withdrawal and MAOI interactions. β-blockade first leaves α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs II (Cardiovascular Drugs 3)186

Practice — antihypertensives II (cont.)

PHAR.0238

A 61-year-old man with hypertensive emergency has a creatinine of 4.2 mg/dL. Which IV agent both lowers blood pressure and maintains or increases renal perfusion?

  1. ASodium nitroprusside
  2. BFenoldopam
  3. CEsmolol
  4. DDiazoxide
  5. ENicardipine
Answer
B. Fenoldopam is a peripheral dopamine-1 receptor agonist: it evokes arteriolar dilation while maintaining or increasing renal perfusion and promoting natriuresis, which is why the lecture calls it particularly beneficial in renal insufficiency. Its one contraindication is glaucoma.
PHAR.0245

A man taking sildenafil for pulmonary hypertension is given sublingual nitroglycerin for chest pain and becomes profoundly hypotensive. What is the mechanism?

  1. ABoth drugs block calcium channels
  2. BNitrates raise cGMP and sildenafil blocks the PDE5 that degrades it, so cGMP accumulates unopposed
  3. CSildenafil inhibits the hepatic metabolism of nitrates
  4. DBoth drugs are α-adrenergic antagonists
  5. ESildenafil causes reflex bradycardia that compounds nitrate venodilation
Answer
B. Objective PHAR.0245. Nitrates donate NO → guanylyl cyclase → ↑ cGMP; sildenafil inhibits PDE5, the enzyme that breaks cGMP down. Given together, cGMP accumulates without limit → profound, refractory vasodilation and hypotension. Nitrates are an absolute contraindication with PDE5 inhibitors.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs II (Cardiovascular Drugs 3)187

Practice — antihypertensives II (cont.)

PHAR.0237

A patient on long-term methyldopa develops fatigue and jaundice; haemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL with a raised reticulocyte count. Which test is most likely to be positive, and in what proportion of long-term users does it occur?

  1. AAntinuclear antibody; ~50%
  2. BDirect Coombs test; 10–20% of patients treated for over a year
  3. CAnti-histone antibody; ~5%
  4. DCold agglutinins; ~30%
  5. EG6PD assay; ~1%
Answer
B. Methyldopa causes development of a positive Coombs test in 10–20% of patients on long-term treatment (> 1 year), which can result in haemolytic anaemia, hepatitis and drug fever. It also causes a reversible lupus-like syndrome — as does hydralazine.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs II (Cardiovascular Drugs 3)188

Antihypertensives II — summary sheet

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • In a crisis the drug is chosen by the organ that is failing — ischaemia → nitroglycerin, dissection → esmolol, kidneys → fenoldopam, catecholamines → phentolamine, pregnancy → hydralazine or labetalol.
Exam Lock
The seven locks
  • Emergency = target-organ damage → IV, ICU, ≤ 25% drop in the first hour.
  • Urgency = no organ damage → two oral drugs, outpatient follow-up.
  • Pregnancy: methyldopa (chronic), hydralazine (eclamptic crisis), labetalol (β-blocker of choice). No ACEI/ARB/aliskiren/bosentan.
  • Nitroprusside → cyanide → sodium thiosulfate; t½ 1–2 min, IV only.
  • Fenoldopam preserves renal perfusion; contraindicated in glaucoma.
  • Labetalol does not cause reflex tachycardia; nicardipine and diazoxide do.
  • Sildenafil + nitrate = contraindicated (cGMP accumulation).
Trap
Three traps
  • Stopping clonidine abruptly, or pairing it with a β-blocker — rebound hypertension.
  • Using doxazosin as monotherapy for hypertension — it increases the rate of congestive heart failure.
  • Correcting a hypertensive emergency too fast — the complication is MI, stroke or visual loss.
PHAR · Antihypertensive Drugs II (Cardiovascular Drugs 3)189

L11 · Valvular Heart Disease190

Stenosis vs insufficiency, and the valve apparatus

PATH.5051src p.586–587
  • The valve apparatus: 1 valve cusps · 2 valve commissure · 3 valve ring (annulus) · 4 chordae tendineae · 5 papillary muscle.
StenosisInsufficiency (regurgitation, incompetence)
Failure of a valve to open completely, obstructing forward flow.
Acquired valvular stenosis is almost always due to a primary leaflet abnormality and is virtually always a chronic process (degeneration, calcification, inflammation and scarring).		Failure of a valve to close completely, allowing regurgitation (backflow) of blood.
Can result from intrinsic disease of the valve leaflets (e.g. endocarditis) or disruption of the supporting structures (the aorta, mitral annulus, tendinous cords, papillary muscles, or ventricular free wall) without primary leaflet injury.
Can appear abruptly, as with chordal rupture, or insidiously as a consequence of leaflet scarring and retraction.

Valvular disease comes to clinical attention due to stenosis, insufficiency, or both — producing abnormal heart sounds called murmurs.

Exam Lock
The asymmetry to remember
  • Stenosis is always the leaflet, and always chronic. Regurgitation can be leaflet or apparatus, and can be acute — which is why a ruptured chord or papillary muscle presents as sudden flash pulmonary oedema, while stenosis never does.
L11 · Valvular Heart Disease191

The four common valvular lesions — causes, symptoms, signs

PATH.5051src p.588–589
LesionCommon causesSymptomsSigns
Mitral stenosisPost-inflammatory scarring (rheumatic heart disease)Dyspnea (pulmonary edema), orthopnea and hemoptysisLate low-pitched diastolic murmur and crepitations in lung
Mitral regurgitation1. Post-inflammatory scarring (rheumatic) · 2. Infective endocarditis · 3. Mitral valve prolapseDyspnea (pulmonary edema), palpitations and fatiguePansystolic murmur radiating to axilla
Aortic stenosisSenile calcific aortic stenosis; less commonly post-inflammatory scarring (rheumatic heart disease)Angina, syncope, congestive heart failureEjection systolic murmur loudest at base, radiating to neck after S1
Aortic regurgitation1. Syphilitic aortitis · 2. Marfan syndrome · 3. Rheumatoid arthritisVolume overload congestive heart failureBounding pulses, early diastolic murmur, laterally displaced apex beat
Bottom Line
Two mnemonics that carry the table
  • Aortic stenosis = Angina, Syncope, CHF — “ASC” in the order severity is reached. Mitral stenosis pushes pressure backwards into the lungs — so haemoptysis and orthopnoea, with a left atrium that enlarges and fibrillates.
L11 · Valvular Heart Disease192

Rheumatic heart disease — acute rheumatic fever

PATH.5052src p.590–594
Immunologically mediated, multisystem inflammatory disease classically occurring a few weeks after group A streptococcal infections of throat and skin.Lecture 11, slide 590
Epidemiology
  • More common in developing countries and crowded, economically depressed areas of the western world
  • Acute RF typically appears 10 days to 6 weeks after a group A streptococcal infection in about 3% of patients
  • Occurs most often in children between 5 and 15 years of age, but first attacks can occur in middle to later life
Etiopathogenesis
  • Host immune responses to group A streptococcal antigens that cross-react with host proteins following throat infections or sometimes skin infections
  • Type-2 hypersensitivity reaction
  • Streptococci are not seen in the lesion.

Morphology of acute rheumatic carditis

  • Focal inflammatory lesions found in all three layers — hence pancarditis
  • Small vegetations along the line of closure, mainly in the mitral valve and rarely in aortic and tricuspid valves — verrucae, small (1–2 mm)
  • Distinctive lesions in the heart — Aschoff bodies (pathognomonic feature): foci of T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, and plump activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells — abundant cytoplasm, central round-to-ovoid nuclei (occasionally binucleate), with chromatin condensed into a central, slender, wavy ribbon, hence “caterpillar cells”
L11 · Valvular Heart Disease193

Rheumatic fever — the Jones criteria and chronic RHD

PATH.5053src p.596–598

Major Jones criteria — verbatim, with the mnemonic printed on the slide

LetterMajor criterion
JMigratory polyarthritis of the large Joints
♥Pancarditis (myocarditis, pericarditis, or endocarditis)
NSubcutaneous Nodules (typically on extensor surfaces of extremities)
EErythema marginatum, an irregular circinate skin rash
SSydenham chorea, a neurologic disorder with involuntary rapid movements
  • Pharyngeal cultures for streptococci are negative by the time the illness begins.
  • Antibodies to one or more streptococcal enzymes, such as streptolysin O and DNase B, can be detected in the sera.
  • Predominant clinical manifestations are carditis and arthritis, the latter more common in adults than in children.
  • Diagnosis requires evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection plus two major manifestations, or one major and two minor manifestations (fever, arthralgia, or elevated acute-phase reactants).
Chronic mitral valvulitis → mitral stenosisChronic aortic valvulitis
• Fibrous thickening and calcification of the leaflets
• Fusion of the commissures and shortening of the chordae tendineae
• Fixed narrow opening — “fish mouth”, “button hole”		• Cusps are thickened, firm and adherent to each other
• Valve orifice is reduced to a rigid, triangular channel

Complications of acute rheumatic fever: left atrium progressively dilates → mural thrombi → embolus · congestive heart failure · arrhythmias · infective endocarditis.

L11 · Valvular Heart Disease194

Calcific aortic stenosis and the myxomatous mitral valve

PATH.5052PATH.5053src p.600–606
Calcific aortic stenosisMyxomatous mitral valve (mitral valve prolapse)
WhoMore common over 65 years of age. Congenital bicuspid aortic valve occurs in ~1% of the population and stenoses at 40–50 yearsWomen affected almost 7-fold more than men, between 20–40 years of age
MechanismA previously normal or congenital bicuspid aortic valve undergoes wear and tear with calcification. Chronic progressive injury → valvular degeneration and calcification. Bicuspid valves incur greater mechanical stress than normal tricuspid valves, which may explain their accelerated stenosis.Intrinsic defect of connective tissue, as in Marfan syndrome. Leaflets are “floppy”, weak and prolapse — they balloon back into the left atrium during systole
ClinicalAngina pectoris — increased requirement of hypertrophied myocardium · syncope — poor perfusion of the brain · death usually occurs due to congestive heart failure or arrhythmiasMost patients are asymptomatic (incidental detection) · palpitations, fatigue or atypical chest pain · mid-systolic click — abrupt tension on leaflets and chordae when the valve tries to close
GrossMounded calcified masses on the outflow surfaces of the cusps that ultimately prevent cuspal opening. Free edges of the cusps are usually not involved. Nodular masses of calcium heaped up within the sinuses of Valsalva; on a bicuspid valve, one cusp has a partial fusion at its centre called a rapheSoft mitral valve cusps with mucoid thickening · ballooning of the leaflets into the left atrium · chordae tendineae elongated and fragile — may rupture in severe cases · mitral annulus may be dilated · concomitant tricuspid valve involvement in 20–40%
MicroscopyDystrophic calcification. Functional valve area decreased by large nodular calcific deposits → measurable outflow obstruction → progressively increasing pressure overload on the LVThinning of the fibrosa layer, expansion of the spongiosa layer — excessive loose, edematous, faintly basophilic ground substance within the middle layer of the leaflets and chordae (myxomatous degeneration)
ComplicationsCongestive heart failure, arrhythmiasInfective endocarditis · ventricular arrhythmias (may lead to sudden cardiac death) · thromboembolic stroke · occasionally part of a syndrome characterised by scoliosis and high arched palate
L11 · Valvular Heart Disease195

Calcific aortic stenosis and the myxomatous mitral valve (cont.)

PATH.5052PATH.5053src p.600–606
Trap
Why the free edges matter
  • In calcific aortic stenosis the calcium sits on the outflow surface and the free edges are spared; in rheumatic aortic disease the commissures fuse and the free edges are thickened. That single feature separates senile from rheumatic aortic stenosis on a gross photograph.

Infective endocarditis — definition, classification, predisposing factors

PATH.5054src p.608–610
Microbial infection of the heart valves or the mural endocardium that leads to the formation of vegetations composed of thrombotic debris and organisms, often associated with destruction of the underlying cardiac tissues.Lecture 11, slide 608
AcuteSubacute
Valves affectedPreviously normalPreviously deformed
Organisms involvedHighly virulent, like Staphylococcus aureusLess virulent, like Viridans streptococci
Speed of destructionRapidInsidious
Extent of destruction++++++
Clinical pictureHigh-grade fever with chills · changing cardiac murmur · features of septicemiaLow-grade fever; malaise · changing cardiac murmurs · weight loss and splenomegaly
Predisposing factorDetail
Previously damaged valveRheumatic valvular disease · mitral valve prolapse · congenital defects · degenerative calcific aortic stenosis
Prosthetic heart valves10–20% of cases
Intravenous drug abuseTricuspid valve
Transient bacteremiaDental procedures, urinary catheterization, endoscopy

Pathogenesis

Endothelial injury→Fibrin thrombi→Invasion by microorganism→Microbial multiplication→Shed into bloodstream

Fibrin deposition + platelet aggregation + microbial proliferation = infected vegetations.

L11 · Valvular Heart Disease197

Infective endocarditis — clinical features, morphology, Duke criteria

PATH.5054src p.611–615
Fever & constitutionalLocalDistant (embolic)Immune complex
PUO (pyrexia of unknown origin) · arthralgia · myalgia · anemia · increased ESR · increased CRPValvular dysfunction: murmur · heart failureThromboembolism > infection > sepsis · splinter hemorrhages and Janeway lesions · mycotic aneurysmGlomerulonephritis · Osler nodes and Roth spots
SignDescription
Splinter haemorrhagesLinear hemorrhagic lesions on the nail bed
Janeway lesionsPainless, flat, erythematous lesions on palms or soles
Osler nodesPainful, raised, violaceous lesions on finger or toe pads
Roth spotsRetinal hemorrhagic lesions with pale centers

Morphology

Acute IE
  • Most common valves involved — mitral and aortic; in IV drug abuse — tricuspid
  • Classic hallmark = vegetations on heart valves: friable, bulky, potentially destructive lesions containing fibrin, inflammatory cells, and bacteria
  • Single or multiple; may involve more than one valve
  • Occasionally erode into the underlying myocardium and produce an abscess (ring abscess)
  • Prone to embolization → embolic fragments with virulent organisms → abscesses → septic infarcts or mycotic aneurysms
Subacute IE
  • Associated with less valvular destruction
  • Microscopically: granulation tissue at their bases (indicative of healing)
  • Fibrosis and calcification
  • Chronic inflammatory infiltrate

NBTE and Libman-Sacks endocarditis

PATH.5055src p.617–619
Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE)Libman-Sacks endocarditis (LSE)
SettingDebilitated patients, such as those with cancer — hence the name “marantic endocarditis”. Associated with endothelial abnormalities, hypercoagulable states, adenocarcinomasSmall (1 to 4 mm), sterile vegetations in the setting of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) — “LSE seen in SLE”
MechanismSmall thrombotic vegetation on the leaflets of previously normal valvesImmune complex deposition
SiteMitral valve involved most commonly; multiple, 1 to 5 mm small vegetationsVegetations can occur anywhere on the valve surface, on the chordae, or even on the atrial or ventricular endocardium, and in the pockets of the aortic valve
DestructivenessVegetations are not invasive; no destruction of valve. Nodules composed of eosinophilic material (fibrin) and a delicate layer of aggregated platelets. Photomicrograph shows bland thrombus with virtually no inflammation, only loosely attached to the cuspSterile — no organisms
Clinical relevanceUsually asymptomatic, but becomes clinically relevant when there is embolizationMay cause valvular insufficiency; risk of embolization
Exam Lock
Three sterile-vegetation tells
  • Cancer + bland thrombus + no inflammation = NBTE. SLE + vegetations on *both* surfaces = Libman-Sacks. Previous rheumatic fever + tiny warty nodules on the line of closure = RHD.
L11 · Valvular Heart Disease201

Prosthetic valve disease

PATH.5056src p.621
Mechanical valvesTissue valves (bioprostheses)
Material—Porcine, bovine or human
AnticoagulationLife-long anticoagulation needed (bleeding tendency)None needed
ComplicationsThrombo-embolism · infective endocarditis · RBC destruction (hemolysis)Less durable — need replacement after a few years; matrix deterioration, rigidity, calcification → stenosis; can perforate · infective endocarditis

60% of patients develop complications within 10 years.

Bottom Line
How the choice is actually made
  • Mechanical = durability bought with anticoagulation. Bioprosthetic = freedom from warfarin bought with a second operation. That trade-off is why mechanical valves go to younger patients and bioprostheses to older ones or to those who cannot be anticoagulated.
L11 · Valvular Heart Disease202

Practice — the lecture's own six cases

Case 1

A 10-year-old boy has one week of fever, chest pain and joint pain; his parents report a throat infection 3 weeks earlier. He has a subcutaneous nodule on the extensor surface of his right forearm and a raised ESR. What histological lesion is pathognomonic in his heart?

  1. AVerrucae along the line of closure alone
  2. BAschoff bodies containing Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells
  3. CBland fibrin thrombus with no inflammation
  4. DDystrophic calcification of the sinuses of Valsalva
  5. EExpansion of the spongiosa with myxoid ground substance
Answer
B. Case 1 — acute rheumatic fever. The Aschoff body is the pathognomonic feature: T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, and plump activated macrophages (Anitschkow cells) whose chromatin condenses into a slender wavy ribbon — “caterpillar cells”. Verrucae are present but not pathognomonic.
Case 3

A 70-year-old man has syncope and exertional chest pain. Echocardiography shows a thickened, calcified aortic valve with left ventricular hypertrophy. Where will the calcium be found, and what is spared?

  1. AAlong the commissures, with the free edges thickened and fused
  2. BMounded on the outflow surfaces of the cusps, with the free edges usually not involved
  3. COn the atrial surface of the leaflets, with the chordae elongated
  4. DOn both surfaces of the leaflet and on the chordae
  5. EWithin the myocardium, sparing the valve entirely
Answer
B. Case 3 — calcific aortic stenosis: mounded calcified masses on the outflow surfaces of the cusps, heaped within the sinuses of Valsalva, with the free edges usually not involved. Commissural fusion with thickened free edges would indicate a rheumatic aetiology.
L11 · Valvular Heart Disease203

Practice — the lecture's own six cases (cont.)

Case 4

A tall, thin 35-year-old woman with scoliosis and a high arched palate has palpitations; echocardiography shows mitral cusps protruding into the left atrium during systole. Which layer of the valve is abnormal?

  1. AThe fibrosa is expanded and the spongiosa thinned
  2. BThe fibrosa is thinned and the spongiosa expanded with myxoid ground substance
  3. CThe atrialis is calcified
  4. DAll three layers are replaced by granulation tissue
  5. EThe endothelium is denuded with platelet-fibrin thrombus
Answer
B. Case 4 — myxomatous mitral valve / mitral valve prolapse, here with a Marfan-like connective tissue phenotype. Microscopy: thinning of the fibrosa layer, expansion of the spongiosa layer with loose, oedematous, faintly basophilic ground substance.
Case 5

A 30-year-old man has 3 weeks of fever, chest pain, palpitations and low urine output. He had a tooth extracted a month ago. Echocardiography shows nodules at the line of closure with destruction of the mitral valve. Which organism is most likely, and why is the urine output low?

  1. AStaphylococcus aureus; septic renal infarction
  2. BViridans streptococci; immune-complex glomerulonephritis
  3. CCandida albicans; direct fungal invasion of the kidney
  4. DEnterococcus faecalis; obstructive uropathy
  5. ECoagulase-negative staphylococci; drug-induced interstitial nephritis
Answer
B. Case 5 — subacute infective endocarditis after a dental procedure: Viridans streptococci on a valve that becomes deformed, insidious course over weeks. The renal impairment is one of the immune-complex phenomena listed alongside Osler nodes and Roth spots — glomerulonephritis.
L11 · Valvular Heart Disease204

Practice — the lecture's own six cases (cont.)

Case 6

A 75-year-old man with colon carcinoma has small nodules at the line of closure of the mitral valve on routine echocardiography, with no valve destruction. What is the diagnosis and the histology?

  1. ALibman-Sacks endocarditis; immune complexes on both leaflet surfaces
  2. BNon-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis; bland thrombus with virtually no inflammation, loosely attached to the cusp
  3. CSubacute infective endocarditis; granulation tissue at the base
  4. DChronic rheumatic heart disease; commissural fusion
  5. EAcute rheumatic fever; Aschoff bodies
Answer
B. Case 6 — NBTE (marantic endocarditis): small thrombotic vegetations on previously normal valves in a debilitated patient with an adenocarcinoma / hypercoagulable state. The nodules are fibrin and platelets, not invasive, with no destruction of the valve and no inflammation.

Learning objectives — verbatim

  • List each of the risk factors associated with infective endocarditis and outline their role/contribution to the likely development of infective endocarditis. MICR.63
  • Identify the most common clinical findings for a suspected case of infective endocarditis. MICR.64

  • Identify the types of valves affected by infective endocarditis and correlate the underlying infectious cause with the time frame. MICR.67
  • Explain the relationship between the type of valve and the most common associated source of infection. MICR.68
  • Outline the basic biological features of staphylococci, including the normal location of the organism and the gram stain characteristics. MICR.69
  • Identify the role of each virulence factor — the capsule, surface adhesins and biofilm formation — and explain how each contributes to the pathogenicity of S. aureus in infective endocarditis. MICR.70
  • Compare and contrast the two major staphylococcal species associated with infective endocarditis. MICR.71
  • Explain the biochemical features of and risk factors associated with the relevant streptococci responsible for causing IE. MICR.72
  • Differentiate between the two major bacterial causes of IE based on laboratory tests and grouping methods. MICR.73
L12 · Cardiovascular Infections 1206

How a vegetation is built — the five steps

MICR.62src p.628–629

Endocarditis is inflammation of the inner layer of the heart, usually on the valves — mitral (M) and aortic (A); occasionally tricuspid (< 10%), often with IV drug use. It is a non-transmissible infection.

1 · Initial damage — mechanical or endothelial injury→2 · Platelet and fibrin thrombus (NBTE)→3 · Bacteraemia — introduction of bacteria→4 · Bacterial adhesin→5 · Biofilm formation → vegetation
Exam Lock
Why NBTE is step 2 of infective endocarditis
  • The sterile platelet–fibrin thrombus of NBTE is the scaffold that circulating bacteria adhere to. That is why the pathology and microbiology lectures describe the same lesion from two directions, and why any condition producing endothelial injury is a risk factor.
L12 · Cardiovascular Infections 1207

Features to consider, epidemiology and risk factors

MICR.63MICR.67src p.630–632
1 · Etiologic agent
  • Bacterial
  • Fungal, etc.
2 · Type of valve
  • Native valve (~72%) — acute or subacute
  • Prosthetic valve (~21%) — early: days to months after surgery; late: 12 months to years after surgery
3 · Source of infection
  • Community-acquired infection
  • Nosocomial / health-care-acquired infection
  • Antibiotic resistance
  • Opportunistic pathogens
Cardiac risk factorsNon-cardiac risk factors
History of prior IE · prosthetic valve · cardiac device · congenital / valvular heart diseaseIV drug use · indwelling IV line · immunosuppression (therapy, HIV etc.) · recent dental or surgical procedure · hemodialysis

Most risk factors are either associated with direct damage to the endothelium or with increasing the introduction of microorganisms into the blood. Peak incidence: men, age > 65.

L12 · Cardiovascular Infections 1208

Diagnosing IE — clinical, microbiological, imaging

MICR.64MICR.66src p.633–638
  • Diagnosis is a combination of: 1. clinical presentation (signs & symptoms) · 2. microbiology — blood culture · 3. imaging — echocardiogram. The modified Duke criteria should be used as a diagnostic guide together with clinical judgment.
1 · Clinical presentation
  • Fever (80%)
  • Heart murmur (85%)
  • Embolic phenomenon (> 50%)
  • Petechiae (20–40%)
  • Skin manifestations (18–50%)
  • Splenomegaly (20–57%)
  • Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions and Roth spots are uncommon but pathognomonic for IE
2 · Blood culture
  • 2 bottles — one aerobic and one anaerobic — constitutes one set
  • 3 sets enable detection of 96–98% of cases of bacteraemia
  • Bacteraemia is usually continuous
  • Samples ideally taken prior to initiation of antibiotics
  • In up to 10% of cases there is no growth in standard conditions → “blood culture-negative endocarditis”
3 · Imaging
  • Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE)
  • Transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE/TEE) — higher sensitivity for vegetations and prosthetic valves

“In patients with infective endocarditis, the history is highly variable. Symptoms commonly are vague, emphasizing constitutional complaints, or complaints may focus on primary cardiac effects or secondary embolic phenomena.”

L12 · Cardiovascular Infections 1209

Microbial causes — native vs prosthetic valve

MICR.67MICR.68src p.641–642
SettingCausal agents
Native valve endocarditis (NVE)Staphylococcus spp. · Streptococcus spp. · Enterococcus spp. · HACEK organisms · difficult-to-culture pathogens: fungi, parasites, intracellular bacteria
Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (< 1 year post-surgery, usually in the first 2 months)Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus spp. (CoNS) · S. aureus
Late prosthetic valve endocarditis (> 1 year post-surgery)Same as native valve endocarditis

80% of cases = Staphylococcus and Streptococcus spp. — in descending order: staphylococcus, viridans streptococci, coagulase-negative staphylococci, enterococci, HACEK, then fungi/parasites/uncultivable bacteria.

Exam Lock
The time-based rule for prosthetic valves
  • Early PVE (< 1 year, usually < 2 months) = skin flora introduced at surgery → coagulase-negative staphylococci and S. aureus. Late PVE (> 1 year) behaves like native-valve disease — the organism comes from the community, not the theatre.
L12 · Cardiovascular Infections 1211

Staphylococci — species, biochemistry, virulence

MICR.69MICR.70MICR.71src p.643–650
SpeciesMost common clinical presentationsWhere you'll see it
Staphylococcus aureusSkin and soft tissue infections, endocarditis, food poisoning, septicemiaSkin, muscle, bone; cardiovascular; gastrointestinal
Staphylococcus epidermidisEndocarditis, indwelling device infections, prosthetic joint infectionsCardiovascular
Staphylococcus saprophyticusUrinary tract infection — “honeymoon cystitis”Urogenital tract
S. aureusS. epidermidis
BiochemistryCatalase-positive · coagulase-POSITIVE · mannitol-POSITIVE · beta-hemolyticCatalase-positive · coagulase-NEGATIVE · mannitol-NEGATIVE · novobiocin sensitive
Role in IEOne of the most common causes of both NVE and PVE. Aggressive disease with increased risk of embolism, stroke, persistent bacteremia and deathOne of the main causes of early PVE; major cause of infections associated with inserted medical devices and prostheses. Most frequently isolated species from human skin
Virulence factorsPolysaccharide capsule — 90% of endocarditis strains produce one, which resists phagocytosis · surface adhesins (MSCRAMM): clumping factor A (ClfA, a fibrinogen-binding protein), fibronectin binding protein A and B, collagen binding protein · hemolysins: α-hemolysin (α-toxin), a pore-forming exotoxin causing cellular lysis · biofilm formation, which protects from the host immune system and is recalcitrant to antibioticsSurface adhesins: fibrinogen binding protein · biofilm formation

Biochemical tests to differentiate: coagulase test — positive = S. aureus, negative = S. epidermidis. Mannitol salt agar (MSA) is selective (7.5% sodium chloride) and differential (mannitol): S. aureus mannitol +, S. epidermidis mannitol −.

L12 · Cardiovascular Infections 1212

Streptococci and the identification algorithm

MICR.71MICR.72MICR.73src p.651–654
SpeciesInfectionsWhere you'll see it
Streptococcus pyogenes“Strep throat” · cellulitis · erysipelas · rheumatic fever / heart disease · scarlet feverRespiratory & haematopoietic; skin & musculoskeletal; cardiovascular
Streptococcus agalactiaeNeonatal meningitisNervous system and special senses
Streptococcus pneumoniaePneumoniaRespiratory and haematopoietic
Streptococcus mutansDental caries · endocarditisRespiratory; cardiovascular
Streptococcus sanguinisEndocarditisCardiovascular
Viridans streptococci — features
  • Members of the normal microbiota of the mouth and upper respiratory tract
  • Usually alpha-hemolytic on blood agar
  • Optochin resistant
  • Catalase negative
  • Responsible for both NVE and PVE
Which is which
  • S. sanguinis — most common cause of IE due to strep
  • S. mutans — primary etiological agent of dental caries (60–90%) and dental plaques
  • S. mitis, S. oralis, S. sobrinus
Risk factors & pathogenicity
  • Oral / dental procedures, gingival inflammation, dental caries, periodontal disease
  • Surface adhesins enable interactions with salivary, serum and extracellular matrix components, host cells and other microbes, allowing colonization and infection

The identification algorithm

Gram-positive cocci→Catalase test→Positive → Staphylococci → coagulase test → + S. aureus / − S. epidermidis, S. saprophyticus→Negative → Streptococci → grouping: Lancefield classification, haemolysis pattern, capsular polysaccharides, antibiotic sensitivity
L12 · Cardiovascular Infections 1213

Practice — infective endocarditis microbiology

MICR.68

A 58-year-old man with no history of heart disease has 4 days of high fever and chills, worsening confusion, and sudden left-sided hemiparesis. He had a recent deep skin infection. He has a grade III murmur and bibasal crepitations. Which organism, and which form of endocarditis?

  1. AViridans streptococci; subacute IE on a deformed valve
  2. BStaphylococcus aureus; acute IE on a previously normal valve
  3. CStaphylococcus epidermidis; early prosthetic valve endocarditis
  4. DHACEK organisms; culture-negative endocarditis
  5. EEnterococcus faecalis; subacute IE after genitourinary instrumentation
Answer
B. Case 1 — a previously normal valve, a highly virulent organism seeded from a deep skin infection, rapid destruction and an embolic stroke within days = acute IE due to S. aureus. S. aureus carries an increased risk of embolism, stroke, persistent bacteraemia and death.
MICR.67

A 75-year-old man has 14 days of low-grade fever, fatigue and painful bumps on his hands and feet. He had a mitral valve replacement 4 years ago and a recent colonoscopy. He has Osler nodes, splinter haemorrhages and petechiae. What category of endocarditis is this?

  1. AEarly prosthetic valve endocarditis — coagulase-negative staphylococci
  2. BLate prosthetic valve endocarditis — organisms as for native valve disease
  3. CNon-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis
  4. DLibman-Sacks endocarditis
  5. EAcute native valve endocarditis
Answer
B. Case 2 — the valve was replaced 4 years ago, so this is late PVE (> 1 year), whose organisms are the same as native valve endocarditis (viridans streptococci, S. aureus, enterococci, HACEK) rather than the perioperative skin flora that cause early PVE. Osler nodes are painful; Janeway lesions are painless.
L12 · Cardiovascular Infections 1214

Practice — infective endocarditis microbiology (cont.)

MICR.71

Two sets of blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in clusters. The isolate is catalase-positive, coagulase-negative, mannitol-negative and novobiocin-sensitive. Which organism and which clinical context?

  1. AS. aureus; native valve acute IE
  2. BS. epidermidis; device-related or early prosthetic valve IE
  3. CS. saprophyticus; urinary tract infection
  4. DS. sanguinis; post-dental IE
  5. ES. pneumoniae; pneumonia
Answer
B. Catalase + (staphylococcus), coagulase − (not S. aureus), mannitol − and novobiocin sensitive = S. epidermidis — the most frequently isolated species from human skin, a major cause of early PVE and of infections associated with inserted devices, via fibrinogen-binding adhesins and biofilm. Novobiocin resistance would indicate S. saprophyticus.
MICR.65

Under the Modified Duke criteria as taught in this lecture, a patient with one positive echocardiogram showing an intracardiac mass, a temperature of 38.4 °C, IV drug use and a Janeway lesion has how many major and minor criteria, and what is the diagnostic category?

  1. A2 major, 1 minor — definite IE
  2. B1 major, 3 minor — definite IE
  3. C1 major, 2 minor — possible IE
  4. D0 major, 3 minor — possible IE
  5. E1 major, 1 minor — possible IE
Answer
B. Major: the positive echocardiogram (1). Minor: temperature > 38 °C, predisposing risk factor (IV drug use), vascular phenomenon (Janeway lesion) = 3. 1 major + 3 minor = definite IE.
L12 · Cardiovascular Infections 1215

Valvular disease and CV infections — block summary

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Four vegetations, told apart by size, site, destructiveness; and one organism rule — virulent organism on a normal valve = acute; low-virulence organism on a deformed valve = subacute.
Exam Lock
The ten locks
  • AS = angina, syncope, CHF; ejection systolic to the carotids. MR = pansystolic to the axilla. MS = late diastolic. AR = early diastolic + bounding pulses.
  • Aschoff body with Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells is pathognomonic for rheumatic carditis.
  • Rheumatic MS: commissural fusion + short chordae → fish-mouth orifice.
  • Calcific AS: calcium on the outflow surface; free edges spared.
  • MVP: thin fibrosa, expanded spongiosa; women 7:1; mid-systolic click.
  • IE hallmark = vegetation that destroys the valve; ring abscess; IVDU → tricuspid.
  • Osler = painful (immune); Janeway = painless (embolic).
  • NBTE = cancer/hypercoagulable, bland, non-destructive. Libman-Sacks = SLE, both surfaces.
  • 3 sets of blood cultures detect 96–98%; 10% are culture-negative.
  • Early PVE < 1 y = CoNS/S. aureus; late PVE > 1 y = native-valve organisms.
Trap
Three traps
  • Assuming a negative pharyngeal culture excludes rheumatic fever — cultures are negative by the time the illness begins; you need anti-streptolysin O or anti-DNase B.
  • Calling every mitral vegetation infective — check whether the valve is destroyed.
  • Forgetting mitral valve prolapse as a predisposing lesion for infective endocarditis.
L12 · Cardiovascular Infections 1216

SG01 · CVS & PVS Physical Examination217

Neck examination — carotids and JVD

CPD.0.0192CPD.0.0193src p.660–662
Carotid pulsations
Inspect the neck in the carotid triangle bilaterally. The common carotid artery is medial to the sternocleidomastoid. Aortic valve insufficiency can lead to heart failure and is characterised clinically by head bobbing — Corrigan's sign, also referred to as dancing carotids.
Carotid bruits
Ask the patient to stop breathing for approximately 15 seconds; use the diaphragm to auscultate both carotids. Auscultate before palpating.
JVD technique
Raise the head of the examining table to 30–45° and stand on the right side. Ask the patient to turn the head to the left and use tangential lighting to identify internal jugular pulsations on the right. Look between the attachments of the SCM on the sternum and clavicle.
Conditions associated with JVD
Right-sided heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, and cardiac tamponade
Internal jugular pulsationsCarotid pulsations
Rarely palpable
Soft biphasic undulating quality, usually with two elevations and a characteristic inward deflection (x descent)
Pulsations eliminated by light pressure on the vein just above the sternal end of the clavicle
Height of pulsations changes with position, normally dropping as the patient becomes more upright
Height of pulsations usually falls with inspiration		Palpable
A more vigorous thrust with a single outward component
Pulsations not eliminated by pressure on veins at the sternal end of the clavicle
Height of pulsations unchanged by position
Height of pulsations not affected by inspiration
SG01 · CVS & PVS Physical Examination218

Precordium — palpation, stethoscope, S2 splitting, gallops

CPD.0.0194CPD.0.0197CPD.0.0198src p.663–666
PMI technique
Patient supine, head of the bed 30–45°; palpate over the left midclavicular line in the 4th–5th intercostal space with an open palm. If not felt supine, turn the patient into the left lateral decubitus position. Localise with one digit and count intercostal spaces from the sternal angle.
What shifts it
Pregnancy or a high left diaphragm may shift the apical impulse upward and to the left. Lateral displacement toward the anterior axillary line from ventricular dilatation is seen in heart failure and cardiomyopathy.
Diaphragm vs bell
Diaphragm — relatively high-pitched sounds of S1 and S2, the murmurs of aortic and mitral regurgitation, and pericardial friction rubs; press firmly. Bell — low-pitched S3 and S4 and the murmur of mitral stenosis; apply lightly, just enough to produce an air seal; use at the apex then move medially along the lower sternal border.
Type of splitDescriptionCauses
Physiological splitAortic closure (A2) precedes pulmonary closure (P2) during inspiration: inspiration → fall in intrathoracic pressure → increased venous return to the right heart → prolonged RV systole → delayed P2; pooling of blood in the pulmonary circulation → shortened LV systole → premature A2Especially pronounced among young individuals
Wide splitAn exaggerated physiological split, more pronounced during inspiration. Caused by any condition that increases right ventricular afterload or decreases left ventricular preloadPulmonary hypertension · pulmonary valve stenosis · RBBB · massive pulmonary embolism · severe mitral regurgitation
SoundOriginTimingOccurrence
S3Rapid ventricular filling and sudden deceleration of blood when the ventricle reaches its elastic limit. Heard best with the bell in the mitral area, patient in left lateral positionEarly diastolic, immediately after S2. Ventricular gallop — cadence of the word “Ken-tuc-ky” (Ken = S1, tuc-ky = S2, S3)Physiological: young individuals < 40 years, athletes, pregnant women. Pathological: chronic mitral regurgitation · aortic regurgitation · heart failure · dilated cardiomyopathy · thyrotoxicosis
S4Late diastolic atrial contraction against a stiff ventricleLate diastolic (presystolic)See Lecture 4 — severe LVH, ischaemia, hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathy
SG01 · CVS & PVS Physical Examination219

Peripheral vascular examination — the numbers you must state

CPD.0.0396CPD.0.0397CPD.0.0398CPD.0.0399src p.676–684
AssessmentTechnique & values
Pulse amplitude grading0 = absent/not palpable · +1 = diminished/difficult to palpate/thready/weak · +2 = expected/easy to palpate (normal) · +3 = full/increased · +4 = bounding/strong
RateIf the rhythm is regular, palpate the radial artery for 30 seconds and multiply by 2. If irregular, or unusually fast or slow, palpate for 60 seconds.
Pulsus parvus / tardusPulsus parvus = weak pulses, usually seen with atherosclerotic PVD. Pulsus tardus = delayed upstroke.
Calf circumferencePalpate the tibial tuberosity and measure 10 cm below; measure and repeat on the other limb. Normal difference between the calves is less than 3 cm. Unilateral calf and ankle swelling suggests venous thromboembolic disease.
Pitting edema gradingPress with your thumb for at least 5 seconds over dorsal feet, behind each medial malleolus, and over shins. Grade +1 — up to 2 mm depression, rebounding immediately · Grade +2 — 3–4 mm, rebounding < 15 s · Grade +3 — 5–6 mm · Grade +4 — deeper, prolonged
Capillary refillPress on the nail until it blanches (about 5–10 seconds), release, and note the time to colour return. At least one nail bed on each limb. Normal is within 2 seconds.
Allen's testReturn of colour in 3–5 seconds. Persisting pallor indicates occlusion of the artery or its distal branches. Absent or diminished pulses at the wrist occur in acute embolic occlusion and in Buerger disease.
Buerger's testRaise both feet to 45° for 1–2 minutes. Development of pallor indicates peripheral arterial pressure cannot overcome gravity. The angle at which pallor develops is the Buerger's angle. In a healthy individual the entire leg should remain pink even at 90°; a Buerger's angle of less than 20° indicates severe limb ischaemia.
Homan's signA non-specific and insensitive clinical sign for DVT. Teaching point only.
TemperatureAcute arterial occlusion → the limb distal to the occlusion becomes cold, pale and pulseless. Bilateral coldness is usually environmental or anxiety. Asymmetric warmth and redness over the calf signal cellulitis. Asymmetric coolness of the feet has a positive likelihood ratio of > 6 for PAD.
SG01 · CVS & PVS Physical Examination220

The two model write-ups you are expected to reproduce

CPD.0.0394CPD.0.0198src p.672, 684
Cardiovascular System: There is no visible carotid pulsation, and carotid bruits are absent. The carotid pulse is 2+ in amplitude; rate and rhythm are regular, and there is a smooth contour with a quick upstroke and a gradual downstroke. There is no JVD. The JVP is 2 cmH₂O, and the CVP is 7 cmH₂O. The chest wall is symmetrical with no skin or musculoskeletal abnormalities. The point of maximal impulse is in the 5th left intercostal space (LICS) in the mid-clavicular line (MCL). There are no heaves at the right parasternal border. There are no thrills in the aortic, pulmonic, tricuspid, and mitral areas. S1 and S2 are present and regular in rate and rhythm. No S3, S4, murmurs, or abnormal heart sounds are heard.SG01 CVS checklist
Peripheral Vascular System — UE: No skin discoloration, no visible varicosities, lesions, or ulcers present. No localized warmth or coolness. No edema. Radial and brachial pulse 2+, regular, synchronous and symmetrical. Capillary refill < 2 sec, Allen's test negative. LE: No change in skin color, no visible varicosities, lesions, or ulcers present. Temperature adequate. Calf circumference — L 10 cm R 11 cm. No pedal edema. Femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses 2+…SG01 PVS checklist
Bottom Line
Learn the write-ups, not just the manoeuvres
  • The rubric marks verbalising as well as performing. Reciting these two paragraphs in order forces you through every required step — and the order of the paragraph is the order of the examination.

Objectives — verbatim
