L13 · Myocarditis, Cardiomyopathies & Pericardial Disease225

Myocarditis

PATH.5061PATH.5062src p.845–850
Primary inflammatory process causing myocardial inflammation — mostly idiopathic, less often due to an infection-causing organism, i.e. Coxsackie B6 virus and rarely trichinosis and fungi. Should be distinguished from conditions such as IHD, in which myocardial inflammation is secondary to other causes.Lecture 13, slide 846
TypeCause & settingHistologyClinical / complications
Viral myocarditisMost common cause of myocarditis in the US, self-limiting. Coxsackie A & B6 and enteroviruses account for most casesGross: dilated flabby heart, mural thrombi may be present. Histology: interstitial inflammation mainly lymphocytes and a few plasma cells, with focal necrosis of myocytes adjacent to inflammatory cellsFlu-like symptoms · fatigue, dyspnea, palpitations, chest pain, fever · may mimic acute MI · may present with heart failure or arrhythmia. Investigation: PCR for viral nucleic acids. Complication: may end up as dilated cardiomyopathy.
Fungal myocarditisOccurs in immunocompromised individuals — Candida, AspergillusMixed inflammatory infiltrate composed of neutrophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells—
Hypersensitivity myocarditisMethyldopa and sulfonamidesLymphocytes, macrophages and abundant eosinophilsMild and self-limiting
Giant cell myocarditisIdiopathic; might be of immune origin (autoreactive T cells)Granulomatous inflammation with many giant cells, lymphocytes, eosinophils and plasma cellsHeart failure due to arrhythmias

Some parasites can cause myocarditis — trichinosis, Trypanosoma, Toxoplasma.

Exam Lock
The four infiltrates
  • Lymphocytes → viral. Neutrophils + lymphocytes + plasma cells → fungal. Eosinophils → hypersensitivity (methyldopa, sulfonamides). Giant cells → giant cell myocarditis. The cell in the infiltrate *is* the answer.
L13 · Myocarditis, Cardiomyopathies & Pericardial Disease226

The four cardiomyopathies

PATH.5061src p.852
Primary disease of the myocardium of unknown etiology ending up with heart failure, after excluding coronary artery disease, congenital heart diseases, valvular diseases and hypertensive heart diseases. Rarely secondary to known causes like hemochromatosis, alcohol and amyloidosis.Lecture 13, slide 852

Classification: I. Dilated · II. Hypertrophic · III. Restrictive · IV. Arrhythmogenic.

L13 · Myocarditis, Cardiomyopathies & Pericardial Disease227

Dilated vs hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

PATH.5061PATH.5062src p.854–861
Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)
DefinitionProgressive cardiac dilatation leading to progressive heart failure (ejection fraction < 25%). Most common form of cardiomyopathy — 90% of cases.Primary myocardial hypertrophy of the left ventricle with marked reduction in diastolic filling, and in one-third of cases with left ventricular outflow obstruction
PhysiologySystolic dysfunction — flabby, hypocontractingPrimarily diastolic dysfunction — thick-walled, overweight and hypercontracting, in striking contrast to DCM
Genetics / etiologyIdiopathic (small number) · genetic: autosomal dominant mutation affecting cytoskeletal protein (most common titin) and X-linked mutation in the dystrophin gene · chemotherapy: doxorubicin · alcohol · end result of viral myocarditis, thiamine deficiency and postpartumAutosomal dominant with variable expression. Missense point mutations in genes encoding sarcomeric proteins → gain of function: β-myosin heavy chain (most common), myosin-binding protein C, cardiac troponin T
Who / clinicalMost commonly affects individuals 20–50 years. Progressive CHF refractory to therapy, usually end stage by the time of diagnosis. Secondary mitral regurgitation and abnormal rhythms are common; embolism from mural thrombi. Treatment: cardiac transplantMassively hypertrophied LV with reduced stroke volume → CHF · increased O₂ demand → angina · decreased cardiac output → exertional dyspnea · harsh ejection systolic murmur · sudden death due to arrhythmias — one of the most common causes of sudden, otherwise unexplained death in young athletes
GrossDilation and hypertrophy of all chambers · flabby and heavy (2–3× normal weight) · mural thrombosis → embolizationMassive myocardial hypertrophy without dilation · asymmetric septal hypertrophy, most prominent in the subaortic region · on longitudinal section a banana-like configuration of the ventricular cavity · endocardial plaque/sclerosis in the left outflow tract
MicroscopyInterstitial and endocardial fibrosis · small subendocardial scars replacing individual cells or groups of cells · combination of hypertrophied and atrophied myocardial cellsMarked myocyte hypertrophy with myofiber disarray — haphazard arrangement of hypertrophied, abnormally branching myocytes · interstitial fibrosis
L13 · Myocarditis, Cardiomyopathies & Pericardial Disease228

Restrictive and arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy

PATH.5061PATH.5062src p.863–867
Restrictive cardiomyopathyArrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy
DefinitionPrimary myocardial disease due to impaired diastolic fillingCardiomyopathy that classically manifests with right-sided heart failure and rhythm disturbances, and can cause sudden cardiac death
EtiologyPrimary / idiopathic: major types — endomyocardial fibrosis and Loeffler endomyocarditis. Similar pathology can be seen secondary to amyloidosis, sarcoidosisAutosomal dominant with variable penetrance. Mutations in genes coding for desmosomal junctional proteins at the intercalated disk (plakoglobin) and proteins that interact with the desmosome — intermediate filaments like desmin — leading to desmosomes detaching after strenuous exercise
MorphologyBoth atria dilated due to impaired ventricular filling and pressure overload · ventricles approximately normal size (or slightly enlarged) · ventricular cavities not dilated · myocardium largely unremarkableThe right ventricle is markedly dilated with focal, almost transmural replacement of the free wall by adipose tissue and fibrosis
ClinicalExertional dyspnea · fatigue · congestive heart failure with prominent right heart failure · chest pain · arrhythmiasRight-sided heart failure, arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death
Named associationsEndomyocardial fibrosis (EMF): children and young adults, Africa and the tropics; dense fibrosis of endocardium and subendocardium from apex to AV valves — looks as if molten wax has been poured; reduced volume and compliance.
Loeffler endomyocarditis: worldwide; endocardial fibrosis with large mural thrombi; peripheral hypereosinophilia with abnormal degranulated eosinophils; major basic protein (MBP) from eosinophil granules → endocardial damage, necrosis and fibrosis		Naxos syndrome: arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy + hyperkeratosis of plantar and palmar skin surfaces, associated with plakoglobin mutations
L13 · Myocarditis, Cardiomyopathies & Pericardial Disease229

Pericardial diseases

PATH.5065PATH.5066PATH.5067src p.869–875
  • Normally the pericardial sac contains less than 50 mL of thin, clear and straw-coloured fluid. The parietal pericardium may be distended by serous fluid (pericardial effusion), blood (hemopericardium), pus (purulent pericarditis) or lymph (chylous pericarditis). Effects depend on the rapidity of fluid accumulation — if a large amount accumulates suddenly → cardiac tamponade.
Classification by etiologyClassification by type of exudate
Primary pericarditis: may be limited to virus

Secondary pericarditis:
• MI, cardiac surgery
• Uremia — the most common systemic disorder associated with pericarditis
• Radiation-induced
• Rheumatic fever
• Autoimmune: SLE
• Metastatic malignancies		Fibrinous: “bread and butter” — irregular, shaggy. Seen in RHD, uremia, post-MI
Fibrinous and hemorrhagic: seen in malignancy
Fibrinopurulent (suppurative): seen in bacterial pericarditis
Caseous: tuberculosis
Acute pericarditisChronic pericarditis
FeaturesAtypical chest pain not related to exertion; worsens on reclining and relieved by leaning forward · high-pitched friction rub · if large effusion → cardiac tamponade: 1. faint distant heart sounds · 2. distended neck veins · 3. declining cardiac output · 4. shockIdiopathic or tuberculosis. In extreme cases the heart is so completely encased by dense fibrosis that it cannot expand normally during diastole — constrictive pericarditis. Clinical features are similar to restrictive cardiomyopathy: a combination of right-sided venous distention and low cardiac output. CT shows a thickened, calcified pericardium encasing the heart.
Exam Lock
Beck's triad is in the slide, unnamed
  • Faint distant heart sounds + distended neck veins + declining cardiac output (hypotension) is Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade. The lecture lists all three and adds shock as the endpoint.
L13 · Myocarditis, Cardiomyopathies & Pericardial Disease230

Practice — the lecture's own five cases

Case 1

A 25-year-old woman has 2 days of fever and severe chest pain radiating to her left shoulder, not related to exercise. She recovered from “flu” two weeks earlier and has felt weak since. Angiography shows no coronary blockage. Which infiltrate would a biopsy show, and what is the main complication?

  1. AEosinophils; drug hypersensitivity
  2. BLymphocytes with focal myocyte necrosis; may end up as dilated cardiomyopathy
  3. CGiant cells and granulomas; sudden cardiac death from arrhythmia
  4. DNeutrophils, lymphocytes and plasma cells; fungal dissemination
  5. EAmyloid deposits; restrictive physiology
Answer
B. Case 1 — viral myocarditis (Coxsackie A & B6, enteroviruses): interstitial inflammation of mainly lymphocytes with focal necrosis of myocytes adjacent to the inflammatory cells; gross shows a dilated flabby heart. It may mimic acute MI and may end up as dilated cardiomyopathy.
Case 3

A 20-year-old footballer dies suddenly. His uncle died suddenly at 25. Autopsy shows a thick myocardial wall without dilation, asymmetric septal hypertrophy and myocardial disarray. Which protein is most commonly mutated?

  1. ATitin
  2. BDystrophin
  3. Cβ-myosin heavy chain
  4. DPlakoglobin
  5. EDesmin
Answer
C. Case 3 — hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: autosomal dominant, missense gain-of-function mutations in sarcomeric proteins, of which β-myosin heavy chain is the most common (then myosin-binding protein C and cardiac troponin T). Titin and dystrophin belong to DCM; plakoglobin and desmin to ARVC.
L13 · Myocarditis, Cardiomyopathies & Pericardial Disease231

Practice — the lecture's own five cases (cont.)

Case 4

A 65-year-old woman with 25 years of rheumatoid arthritis has exertional dyspnoea, syncope and fatigue; echocardiography shows impaired ventricular diastolic filling, and post-mortem shows amyloid in the myocardium. What will the chamber sizes look like?

  1. ADilation and hypertrophy of all four chambers
  2. BBoth atria dilated with ventricles of approximately normal size and undilated cavities
  3. CAsymmetric septal hypertrophy with a banana-shaped ventricular cavity
  4. DRight ventricle dilated and replaced by fat
  5. EThickened, calcified pericardium encasing normal chambers
Answer
B. Case 4 — restrictive cardiomyopathy secondary to amyloidosis: both atria dilated from impaired ventricular filling and pressure overload, with the ventricles approximately normal size and the cavities not dilated. Option E describes constrictive pericarditis, which produces very similar physiology — that is the classic distractor.
Case 5

A 50-year-old man has a month of dyspnoea, chest pain and palpitations with a raised JVP, tender hepatomegaly and pedal oedema. He dies suddenly; post-mortem shows a dilated right ventricle with focal replacement of myocardium by adipose tissue and fibrosis. Which syndrome should be considered, and which skin finding would support it?

  1. ANaxos syndrome; hyperkeratosis of plantar and palmar surfaces
  2. BMarfan syndrome; arachnodactyly
  3. CLoeffler endomyocarditis; eosinophilic dermatitis
  4. DChagas disease; chagoma at the bite site
  5. ECarney complex; lentigines
Answer
A. Case 5 — arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, from mutations in desmosomal proteins (plakoglobin) or desmin, so that desmosomes detach after strenuous exercise. Naxos syndrome = ARVC + hyperkeratosis of plantar and palmar skin surfaces, associated with plakoglobin mutations.
L13 · Myocarditis, Cardiomyopathies & Pericardial Disease232

Practice — the lecture's own five cases (cont.)

PATH.5066

A patient with end-stage renal failure has pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward and a high-pitched friction rub. What type of exudate is expected, and what is the underlying category?

  1. ACaseous; primary tuberculous pericarditis
  2. BFibrinous (“bread and butter”); secondary pericarditis due to uraemia
  3. CFibrinopurulent; secondary bacterial pericarditis
  4. DFibrinous and haemorrhagic; malignant pericarditis
  5. ESerous; primary viral pericarditis
Answer
B. Uraemia is the most common systemic disorder associated with pericarditis — a secondary pericarditis with a fibrinous “bread and butter” exudate, the same exudate seen in rheumatic heart disease and post-MI. Haemorrhagic points to malignancy, caseous to TB, fibrinopurulent to bacteria.

L14 · Cardiovascular Infections 2234

Rheumatic heart disease and IE — the link

MICR.74src p.881
S. pyogenes (GAS) — beta-haemolytic, bacitracin sensitive→“Strep throat”→M protein → antibodies generated→Molecular mimicry — cross-reaction with host antigens→Type II hypersensitivity → damage (heart, joints)→Risk factor for infective endocarditis
Bottom Line
Why this closes the loop
  • Rheumatic damage deforms the valve, and a deformed valve is the substrate for subacute endocarditis by low-virulence organisms such as viridans streptococci. The same organism genus causes both, by two entirely different mechanisms — immune mimicry, then direct colonisation.
L14 · Cardiovascular Infections 2235

Enterococci and HACEK organisms

MICR.75MICR.76src p.882–887
Enterococcus spp.HACEK organisms
MembersE. faecalis — most commonly isolated, causes 85–90% of enterococcal infections, particularly ICU infections. E. faecium — 5–10% of enterococcal infections, higher levels of antibiotic resistanceHaemophilus spp. · Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans · Cardiobacterium hominis · Eikenella corrodens · Kingella kingae
FeaturesMembers of the normal enteric microbiota · Gram-positive cocci · diplococci, short-medium length chains · catalase negative · coagulase negative · ferments mannitol (like S. aureus) · gamma haemolysisCommensals of the oropharyngeal tract · Gram-negative coccobacilli · slower growing · fastidious · responsible for ~5% of community-acquired NVE
Pathogenicity / notesSurface adhesion proteins to attach to GI or GU epithelial cells and native and prosthetic heart valves · biofilm formation · antibiotic resistance — most isolates show intrinsic resistance to several antibiotics, with increasing vancomycin resistance (E. faecium > E. faecalis). Risk factors: genitourinary and gastrointestinal procedures.Most common HACEK organisms to cause IE: Haemophilus aphrophilus → Aggregatibacter aphrophilus, frequently found in dental plaque and gingival scrapings; Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, forming colonies with a star-shaped interior on solid media. Modern blood culture instruments now reliably detect HACEK organisms within a 5-day incubation period. Cases are often associated with dental disease (periodontitis), oral infections/surgery or dental procedures.
L14 · Cardiovascular Infections 2236

The biochemistry table for the Gram-positive cocci that cause IE

MICR.75src p.885
OrganismCoagulase testCatalase testMSAMost common haemolysis on blood agar
Staphylococcus aureus++YellowBeta-haemolytic
Staphylococcus epidermidis−+RedNon / gamma haemolytic
Streptococcus sanguinis−−No growthAlpha-haemolytic
Enterococcus faecalis−−YellowNon / gamma haemolytic

MSA = mannitol salt agar. Note the trap: E. faecalis ferments mannitol like S. aureus — but it is catalase negative.

Exam Lock
Two tests separate all four
  • Catalase splits staph from strep/enterococcus. Then coagulase splits S. aureus from S. epidermidis, and MSA/haemolysis splits S. sanguinis (alpha, no growth on MSA) from E. faecalis (gamma, yellow on MSA).
L14 · Cardiovascular Infections 2237

Culture-negative infective endocarditis

MICR.77MICR.78src p.888
Frequency
Reported in ≈ 5% of IE cases (the pathology lecture quotes up to 10% for no growth in standard conditions)
Reasons
Antecedent administration of antimicrobial therapy · fastidious bacteria or non-bacterial pathogens, e.g. fungi and parasites — Bartonella spp., Coxiella spp., Aspergillus spp.
Solution
Further microbiological testing · serology · molecular testing: PCR
Trap
Why this objective exists (MICR.78)
  • A negative culture is not a negative diagnosis. If you stop at “no growth”, you miss Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) and Bartonella — organisms with specific serological tests and specific therapy. The most common reason for no growth is simply that antibiotics were given first.
L14 · Cardiovascular Infections 2238

Myocarditis and pericarditis by pathogen

MICR.79MICR.80MICR.81src p.890–900
MyocarditisPericarditis
ScaleIncidence approximately 1.5 million cases worldwide per year; overall incidence unknown and probably undiagnosedAcute pericarditis is the most common disorder affecting the pericardium; may have a self-limited duration of 1–3 weeks
PresentationHighly variable — from subclinical to sudden cardiac death. Children: viral prodrome common; respiratory distress, resting tachycardia/arrhythmias, dyspnea, syncope, heart failure symptoms. Adults: viral prodrome common; chest pain, palpitations/arrhythmias, heart failure symptoms — differential diagnosis: acute coronary syndrome, separated by ECG and cardiac biomarkersFever · chest pain that is sharp, sudden in onset, worse with inspiration, improves with sitting up and leaning forward · pericardial friction rub · serial ECG changes · ± pericardial effusion
Microbial etiologyViral causes are most common. Bacterial causes are uncommon and usually seen in the context of overwhelming sepsis. Parasites are an important cause in low-income countries and for immigration. Fungal causes are increasing with advances in medical practices.Viruses: Coxsackievirus A and B, CMV, EBV, hepatitis viruses, measles, mumps, herpes virus 6, parvovirus B19, HIV, varicella zoster. Bacteria: Gram-positive and Gram-negative spp., rarely Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Fungi (immunocompromised): Blastomyces dermatitidis, Candida spp., Histoplasma capsulatum
DiagnosisPCR, biomarkers, imagingInitial history and physical exam (pericardial friction rub) · electrocardiogram · cardiac biomarkers · blood cultures · imaging: chest X-ray, echocardiogram · evaluation for pericardial effusion
L14 · Cardiovascular Infections 2239

Myocarditis and pericarditis by pathogen (cont.)

MICR.79MICR.80MICR.81src p.890–900

The named organisms of myocarditis

CategoryOrganism and detail
ViralEnterovirus spp. — Coxsackievirus B. 5% of all symptomatic coxsackievirus infections induce some degree of heart disease. Coxsackievirus B3 is a common cause of primary myocardial disease in humans and is associated with a high mortality rate. The virus uses the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor (CAR) on the surface of myocytes to enter the cell. Myocardial injury results from direct viral assault and the host immune response.
FungalCandida, Aspergillus — most commonly associated with immunocompromised / immunosuppressed patients; most cases follow systemic mycoses (disseminated fungal infections).
ParasiticTrypanosoma — American trypanosomiasis / Chagas' disease; zoonotic tropical disease of the Americas; intracellular flagellated protozoan; mainly vector-borne; high-grade parasitaemia and direct tissue parasitism; up to 30% of patients develop chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy → dilated cardiomyopathy. Toxoplasma — worldwide zoonosis; obligate intracellular protozoan; distinct clinical syndromes in the immunocompromised. Risk depends on immune status, geographic location and exposure.

Practice — CV infections 2

Case 1

A 5-year-old boy has 2 days of chest pain and decreased energy, with tachypnoea and intercostal retractions, resting tachycardia, an irregular rhythm and weak peripheral pulses. He had a recent gastrointestinal illness and has no cardiac history. Which organism and receptor are involved?

  1. AStreptococcus pyogenes; M protein
  2. BCoxsackievirus B; the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor (CAR)
  3. CStaphylococcus aureus; clumping factor A
  4. DTrypanosoma cruzi; direct tissue parasitism
  5. ECoxiella burnetii; intracellular replication
Answer
B. Case 1 — viral myocarditis in a child after a gastrointestinal (enteroviral) prodrome. Coxsackievirus B, especially B3, enters myocytes via the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor (CAR); injury comes from direct viral assault and the host immune response.
Case 2

A 32-year-old man has sudden sharp anterior chest pain, worse on deep inspiration and when lying down, relieved by sitting forward. He is diaphoretic and tachycardic with a pericardial friction rub and recent cold symptoms. Which is the most likely category of cause?

  1. ABacterial, from overwhelming sepsis
  2. BViral
  3. CFungal, from disseminated mycosis
  4. DMycobacterial
  5. EParasitic
Answer
B. Case 2 — acute viral pericarditis. The lecture lists a long viral differential (Coxsackievirus A and B, CMV, EBV, hepatitis, measles, mumps, HHV-6, parvovirus B19, HIV, VZV); bacteria are uncommon, TB is rare, and fungi occur in the immunocompromised. The positional chest pain and friction rub are the signature.
L14 · Cardiovascular Infections 2242

Practice — CV infections 2 (cont.)

MICR.78

Blood cultures from a patient with a new murmur remain sterile after 5 days. He keeps goats and has had intermittent fevers for months. What is the diagnostic strategy?

  1. ARepeat standard cultures for a further 21 days
  2. BSerology and PCR for fastidious organisms such as Coxiella and Bartonella
  3. CEmpiric antifungal therapy
  4. DAssume the diagnosis is rejected under the Duke criteria
  5. ERepeat echocardiography weekly until vegetations appear
Answer
B. Culture-negative IE (~5% of cases) is caused by prior antibiotics or by fastidious / non-bacterial pathogens — Bartonella, Coxiella (Q fever, classically animal exposure), Aspergillus. The stated solution is further microbiological testing: serology and molecular testing (PCR). Modern instruments already detect HACEK within 5 days, so slow growth no longer explains it.
MICR.75

A blood isolate is a Gram-positive coccus in short chains: catalase negative, coagulase negative, gamma-haemolytic, and it turns mannitol salt agar yellow. The patient had a recent urological procedure. Which organism?

  1. AStaphylococcus aureus
  2. BStreptococcus sanguinis
  3. CEnterococcus faecalis
  4. DStaphylococcus epidermidis
  5. EAggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans
Answer
C. Enterococcus faecalis: catalase −, coagulase −, gamma haemolysis, and ferments mannitol like S. aureus (yellow MSA) — the deliberate trap in the lecture's table. Enterococci are enteric flora and the named risk factors are genitourinary and gastrointestinal procedures.

Normal fetal circulation and the transition at birth

PATH.5071src p.909
Fetal circulationFetal to adult transition
• Blood returning to the heart is oxygenated (placenta)
• Pulmonary resistance is high, so shunts go right → left in the fetus, bypassing the lungs

Physiologic right-to-left shunts:
• Foramen ovale — in the interatrial septum; allows blood to cross the atria and bypass the pulmonary circulation during fetal development
• Ductus arteriosus — arises from the pulmonary artery and joins the aorta just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery		At birth the baby breathes → the lungs inflate → pulmonary resistance (right-sided pressure) falls
• Blood flow stops through the foramen ovale (flap valve)
• Ductus arteriosus closes by 15 hours of life
• Prostaglandins maintain patency (keep it open); PGs are produced in the placenta and metabolized in the lungs
• At birth, reduced production / increased breakdown
Exam Lock
Why prostaglandins are the whole story
  • Made in the placenta, destroyed in the lungs. Cut the placenta and inflate the lungs and PG levels collapse — the duct closes. That is why PGE₁ keeps a duct open (transposition, preductal coarctation) and indomethacin closes it (isolated PDA).
L15 · Congenital Heart Disease & Cardiac Neoplasms245

Congenital heart disease — overview, etiology, classification

PATH.5071PATH.5072src p.910–912
Abnormalities of the heart or great vessels that are present at birth. Arise from faulty embryogenesis during gestational weeks 3 to 8, when major cardiovascular structures form and begin to function. Usually produce clinically important manifestations only after birth — uncovered by the transition from fetal to perinatal circulation. Roughly one-half are diagnosed in the first year of life; milder forms may not be discovered until adulthood.Lecture 15, slide 910
Types
  • Septal defects, or “holes in the heart”
  • Stenotic lesions, either at the level of valves or the entire cardiac chamber
  • Outflow tract anomalies, including inappropriate routing of the great vessels from the ventricles, or anomalous coronary arteries
Environmental etiology
  • Congenital rubella infection
  • Teratogens — including some therapeutic drugs
  • Gestational diabetes
  • Folate supplementation during early pregnancy reduces CHD incidence
Genetic etiology
  • DiGeorge syndrome (deletion 22q)
  • Turner syndrome → coarctation of aorta
  • Trisomies 13, 15, 18, 21 — trisomy 21 is the most common known genetic cause of congenital heart disease; 40% of patients have a defect — AV canal, ASD, VSD (endocardial cushion)
ShuntsObstructive
Abnormal connections between chambers / blood vessels. Allow flow down a pressure gradient from left (systemic) to right (pulmonary) circulation, or vice versa.Abnormal narrowing of chambers / valves / blood vessels. Complete obstruction = atresia. Coarctation of aorta · pulmonary stenosis and atresia · aortic stenosis and atresia (hypoplastic left heart syndrome)
L15 · Congenital Heart Disease & Cardiac Neoplasms246

Left-to-right vs right-to-left — the master comparison

PATH.5072PATH.5073src p.913–914, 929
Left → right shunts (acyanotic — “D”)Right → left shunts (cyanotic — “T”)
LesionsAtrial septal Defect · Ventricular septal Defect · Patent Ductus arteriosusTetralogy of Fallot · Transposition of great arteries · Truncus arteriosus · Tricuspid atresia · Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection
HaemodynamicsIncreased pulmonary blood flow (plethoric lung fields on CXR). A normally low-volume, low-resistance side becomes a high-volume, high-pressure side. Initially the pulmonary artery undergoes fibrotic intimal thickening, medial hypertrophy and vasoconstriction; later, changes of pulmonary hypertension set in; the right ventricle undergoes hypertrophyPulmonary circulation bypassed. Poorly oxygenated blood shunts into the systemic circulation → hypoxemia and cyanosis, which can cause polycythemia and clubbing
Endpoint / riskEventually pulmonary vascular resistance equals or exceeds systemic levels → the shunt reverses and becomes right-to-left (cyanotic) = EISENMENGER SYNDROME. Once irreversible pulmonary hypertension develops, the structural defects are irreparable.Emboli from peripheral veins can travel to the systemic circulation — paradoxical embolism

The three left-to-right shunts

PATH.5072src p.915–920
Atrial septal defect (ASD)Ventricular septal defect (VSD)Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)
DefinitionAbnormal and fixed opening between the left and right atrial septumIncomplete closure of the ventricular septum allowing free communication between the left and right ventriclesDuring intrauterine life the ductus permits flow from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing the unoxygenated lungs. In healthy term infants it constricts and is functionally closed within 1 to 2 days of birth
EpidemiologyUsually asymptomatic until adulthood — the most common congenital cardiac malformation diagnosed in adults. Incidence: 10% of all congenital heart diseasesMost common form of congenital heart disease. Associated with trisomy 21, 13, 18 and fetal alcohol syndromeFemales >> males. Higher incidence with maternal rubella infection. Accounts for about 7% of CHD; 90% of these are isolated defects
Types / anatomySecundum ASD (90%) — deficient septum secundum formation near the centre of the atrial septum · Primum (5%) — adjacent to the AV valves, often with AV valve abnormalities and/or a VSD · Sinus venosus (5%) — near the entrance of the superior vena cavaMost commonly (90%) membranous. Most VSDs close spontaneously in childhood.—
MurmurOften present as a result of excessive flow through the pulmonary valve and/or through the ASDPansystolic murmurCharacteristic continuous, harsh, “machinery-like” murmur
Complications / managementEisenmenger physiology if untreatedPulmonary hypertension; CHF. Large unclosed VSDs almost universally lead to irreversible pulmonary vascular disease, ultimately resulting in shunt reversal and cyanosis — Eisenmenger complex.Because the shunt is initially left-to-right, there is no cyanosis. The shunt may reverse, leading to lower-extremity cyanosis — differential cyanosis: blue toes, normal fingers. May need to be kept open with prostaglandin E if associated with other malformations (coarctation, TGA). Closes with indomethacin.
L15 · Congenital Heart Disease & Cardiac Neoplasms248

The right-to-left shunts

PATH.5073src p.922–929
Tetralogy of FallotTransposition of great arteriesTruncus arteriosus
AnatomyFour cardinal features: 1. ventricular septal defect · 2. obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract (subpulmonic stenosis) · 3. an aorta that overrides the VSD · 4. right ventricular hypertrophyAorta arises from the right ventricle and pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle — ventriculoarterial discordance → parallel circulationsFailure of partitioning of the embryologic truncus into aorta and pulmonary artery, due to failure of neural crest cells to drive formation of the aorticopulmonary septum. A single great artery receives blood from both ventricles
Embryology / associationResults embryologically from anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum; RVH is a secondary consequence of pressure overload. Associated with Down syndrome and DiGeorge syndromeAssociated with maternal diabetes. Incompatible with postnatal life unless a shunt (VSD or PDA) is present — the more common presentation. In utero the foramen ovale and ductus ensure mixing; after birth they close → no mixing → severe refractory progressive cyanosisAssociated with DiGeorge syndrome (microdeletion chromosome 22, 22q11). There is an underlying VSD which turns the right and left ventricles into a single chamber → mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood
ClinicalMost common cyanotic congenital heart disease, usually present by 6 months. More outflow obstruction → more right-to-left shunting → more cyanosis → more severe ToF; the more severe the subpulmonic stenosis, the more hypoplastic the pulmonary arteries. Cyanotic disease with reduced pulmonary blood flow. “TET SPELLS” with vigorous crying, feeding or agitation · dyspnoea on exertion, syncope · polycythaemia → cerebral thrombosis · right-to-left shunt increases risk of infective endocarditis and systemic embolizationOutcome depends on the degree of blood mixing, tissue hypoxia, and the ability of the RV to maintain the systemic circulation. VSD present in about ⅓ of casesToo much blood may flow to the lungs — flooding makes it difficult to breathe; may lead to pulmonary hypertension

Exam Lock
Two counting mnemonics from the lecture
  • Acyanotic = the three D's (ASD, VSD, PDA). Cyanotic = the T's — and the number of letters counts the anatomy: 1 vessel (truncus), 2 switched (transposition), 3 (tricuspid atresia), 4 (tetralogy), 5 (total anomalous pulmonary venous connection).

Obstructive lesions — coarctation of the aorta

PATH.5072src p.930–933
  • Narrowed aortic lumen. Associated with Turner's syndrome. 50% of cases are an isolated cardiac anomaly; the rest are associated with a bicuspid aortic valve; remaining cases are associated with PDA, VSD, ASD. Twice as common in males as in females.
Preductal (infantile)Postductal (older children and adults)
DuctHas PDANo PDA
PresentationCongestive heart failure—
CyanosisSelective cyanosis of the lower extremities (via the PDA)No selective cyanosis is seen
Pulses / BPFemoral pulses are weaker than those of the upper extremitiesHypertension of the upper extremities; blood pressure is low and pulses are weak in the lower extremities
Other—Notching of ribs due to collaterals · intermittent claudication — arterial insufficiency

Postductal coarctation is a segmental narrowing of the aorta; the dilated ascending aorta and major branch vessels lie to the left of the coarctation, and the lower extremities are perfused predominantly by dilated, tortuous collateral channels.

Trap
Two lower-limb cyanoses that are not the same
  • Preductal coarctation gives lower-limb cyanosis because deoxygenated blood reaches the descending aorta through the PDA. Differential cyanosis in a reversed PDA gives the same picture for the same reason — but with a normal aortic arch. The clue is the blood pressure difference between arms and legs, which belongs to coarctation.

Cardiac neoplasms

PATH.5074PATH.5075src p.934–937
  • Primary tumors of the heart are rare; the most common are metastatic neoplasms. Clinical presentation: sudden onset of severe, rapidly progressive heart failure without apparent cause and/or arrhythmia; silent until they impair function.

Primary cardiac neoplasms in descending order of frequency (combined pediatric and adult populations)

1 · Myxomas→2 · Fibromas→3 · Lipomas→4 · Papillary fibroelastomas→5 · Rhabdomyomas
Cardiac myxomaMetastatic tumors
Frequency / whoMost common primary cardiac tumor in adults. Female preponderance; age 30–60 yearsOccur in roughly 5% of patients dying of cancer
Location90% of myxomas arise in the atria: left-to-right ratio approximately 4:1. Often calcify and at times can be seen on X-rayMost frequent primaries: lung and breast carcinomas, melanomas, leukemias and lymphomas
ClinicalMost are asymptomatic · some may fragment and embolize · ball-valve obstruction of the atrioventricular valve → syncopal episodes, sudden deathRoutes: retrograde lymphatic extension from the mediastinum (mostly carcinomas) · hematogenous seeding (many tumors) · direct contiguous extension (intrathoracic tumors) · venous extension (tumors of the kidney or liver). Symptoms depend on myocardial or pericardial involvement, or space-occupying lesions in the mediastinum
MorphologyGross: lobulated pedunculated or sessile mass with a gelatinous appearance; the pedunculated form moves during systole into the AV valve opening → intermittent obstruction that may be position-dependent. Microscopy: multinucleated stellate cells in an edematous mucopolysaccharide-rich stroma, with characteristic peculiar vessel-like or gland-like structures—

Exam Lock
Position-dependent syncope is the myxoma question
  • A left atrial mass that obstructs the mitral orifice only in certain positions produces syncope on standing or bending, a crescendo mid-diastolic murmur (from the palpitations DLA), and constitutional symptoms from IL-6. It is the one cardiac tumour with a classic bedside story.

Practice — congenital heart disease

PATH.5072

A 32-year-old woman is found to have a fixed, widely split S2 and a systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border. Echocardiography shows a defect near the centre of the atrial septum. Which type is this, and what proportion of ASDs does it represent?

  1. APrimum ASD; 5%
  2. BSecundum ASD; 90%
  3. CSinus venosus defect; 5%
  4. DMembranous VSD; 90%
  5. EPatent foramen ovale; 25%
Answer
B. Secundum ASD — resulting from deficient septum secundum formation near the centre of the atrial septum — accounts for 90% of all ASDs. Primum defects (5%) sit adjacent to the AV valves; sinus venosus defects (5%) sit near the SVC entrance. ASD is the most common congenital cardiac malformation diagnosed in adults.
PATH.5072

A neonate has cyanosis of the toes but pink fingers, with a continuous machinery murmur. What is the mechanism?

  1. AA right-to-left shunt through an ASD
  2. BReversal of flow through a patent ductus arteriosus, delivering deoxygenated blood distal to the left subclavian artery
  3. CAn overriding aorta above a VSD
  4. DVentriculoarterial discordance with parallel circulations
  5. EA single great artery receiving blood from both ventricles
Answer
B. Differential cyanosis — blue toes, normal fingers — is the PDA slide's own phrase. The duct joins the aorta just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, so when the shunt reverses, only the lower body receives deoxygenated blood. Head and right arm stay pink.
L15 · Congenital Heart Disease & Cardiac Neoplasms254

Practice — congenital heart disease (cont.)

PATH.5073

A 4-month-old becomes deeply cyanosed while crying and improves when the mother holds his knees to his chest. Why does that manoeuvre work?

  1. AIt reduces pulmonary vascular resistance and increases pulmonary flow
  2. BIt increases peripheral vascular resistance and so decreases the right-to-left shunt across the VSD
  3. CIt increases venous return and dilates the right ventricular outflow tract
  4. DIt closes the patent ductus arteriosus
  5. EIt reduces systemic oxygen demand
Answer
B. Tetralogy of Fallot: squatting or knees to chest increases peripheral vascular resistance and thus decreases the magnitude of the right-to-left shunt across the ventricular septal defect, sending more blood through the obstructed outflow to the lungs. The severity of a tet spell tracks the degree of subpulmonic stenosis.
PATH.5073

A newborn of a diabetic mother has severe refractory cyanosis from day 2. Echocardiography shows the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left. What is the immediate pharmacological priority?

  1. AIndomethacin to close the ductus arteriosus
  2. BProstaglandin E to keep the ductus arteriosus open and preserve mixing
  3. CBeta-blockade to relieve infundibular spasm
  4. DDiuresis to reduce pulmonary flooding
  5. EDigoxin to improve right ventricular contractility
Answer
B. Transposition of the great arteries creates parallel circulations and is incompatible with postnatal life unless a shunt (VSD or PDA) is present. In utero the foramen ovale and duct provide mixing; once they close there is none. PGE keeps the duct open — indomethacin would be lethal here.
L15 · Congenital Heart Disease & Cardiac Neoplasms255

Practice — congenital heart disease (cont.)

PATH.5072

A 16-year-old girl of short stature with a webbed neck has upper-limb hypertension, weak femoral pulses and rib notching on chest X-ray. Which lesion, which syndrome, and which associated valve abnormality should be sought?

  1. APreductal coarctation; Turner syndrome; pulmonary stenosis
  2. BPostductal coarctation; Turner syndrome; bicuspid aortic valve
  3. CPatent ductus arteriosus; Down syndrome; mitral valve prolapse
  4. DAortic stenosis; Marfan syndrome; aortic regurgitation
  5. ETruncus arteriosus; DiGeorge syndrome; truncal valve incompetence
Answer
B. Postductal coarctation: upper-limb hypertension, weak low-pressure lower limbs, rib notching from collaterals, intermittent claudication. Associated with Turner's syndrome, and in the non-isolated half of cases with a bicuspid aortic valve. Preductal coarctation presents in infancy with CHF and lower-limb cyanosis through a PDA.
L15 · Congenital Heart Disease & Cardiac Neoplasms256

Lecture 15 — summary sheet

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • The direction of the shunt sets the colour, the volume load sets the long-term damage, and every unrepaired left-to-right shunt is on a path to Eisenmenger.
Exam Lock
The eight locks
  • ASD = most common CHD diagnosed in adults; secundum is 90%.
  • VSD = most common CHD overall; 90% membranous; most close spontaneously.
  • PDA = machinery murmur; PGE keeps it open, indomethacin closes it; reversal gives differential cyanosis.
  • Eisenmenger = the shunt reverses when pulmonary resistance ≥ systemic; the defect is then irreparable.
  • Tetralogy = most common cyanotic CHD; the degree of subpulmonic stenosis sets the severity; squatting helps.
  • Transposition = parallel circulations; survival depends on a shunt; maternal diabetes.
  • Truncus = DiGeorge / 22q11, one great artery over a VSD.
  • Coarctation = Turner, bicuspid aortic valve, rib notching (postductal), lower-limb cyanosis (preductal).
Trap
Three traps
  • Calling a left-to-right shunt “cyanotic” — it is acyanotic until it reverses.
  • Forgetting that trisomy 21 is the most common genetic cause of CHD, with a defect in 40%.
  • Missing cardiac myxoma as a cause of positional syncope and embolic stroke in a middle-aged woman.
L15 · Congenital Heart Disease & Cardiac Neoplasms257
PHAR

Cardiovascular Drugs 4 / Drugs Used in Heart Failure

Four pillars that change mortality, and a long tail of drugs that change symptoms. Know which column each drug sits in.

Lucy Clunes PhD  ·  source pp. 940–1015

Lecture objectives — verbatim

  • PHAR.0246 Describe the basic pathophysiology of heart failure and the cardiac and extracardiac compensatory mechanisms that are activated.
  • PHAR.0247 Explain the difference between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction in congestive heart failure.
  • PHAR.0248 Describe the American Heart Association and New York Heart Association Classifications of Heart Failure.
  • PHAR.0249 Describe the therapy goals in heart failure.
  • PHAR.0250 Describe the mechanism of action, pharmacokinetic properties, adverse effects and clinical indications of drugs used in heart failure.
  • PHAR.0251 Explain the beneficial effects of ARNIs/ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, aldosterone antagonists, vasodilators, inotropic agents, SGLT2 inhibitors, I_f channel blockers, sGC stimulators and β-blockers in systolic heart failure.
  • PHAR.0252 Explain the beneficial effects of calcium channel blockers and β-blockers in diastolic heart failure.
  • PHAR.0253 Compare and contrast the management of acute and chronic heart failure.
Heart failure is a common clinical problem and occurs when cardiac output is inadequate to provide the oxygen needed by the body. It is a highly lethal condition, with a 5-year mortality rate of approximately 50%. The most common cause of HF in the US is coronary artery disease, with hypertension also an important factor.Reading notes
PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)258

Pathophysiology — four determinants and the compensations that turn toxic

PHAR.0246PHAR.0247src p.968–977
Symptoms
  • Tachycardia
  • Decreased exercise tolerance
  • Dyspnea
  • Peripheral & pulmonary edema
  • Cardiomegaly
Risk factors
  • Hypertension
  • Coronary artery disease (coronary atherosclerosis)
  • Myocardial infarction / valvular disease
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Cardiomyopathy (alcohol, familial, arrhythmia/thyroid induced, amyloidosis/sarcoidosis)
  • Use of cardiotoxins
  • Obesity
HFrEF vs HFpEF
  • HFrEF (systolic failure) — mechanical pumping action (contractility) and the ejection fraction are reduced
  • HFpEF (diastolic failure) — stiffening and loss of adequate relaxation
DeterminantDetail from the lecture and notes
PreloadForce stretching the ventricles. Force of contraction depends on the length the myocardial cells are stretched (Frank-Starling). But preload can be too high: preloads greater than 20–25 mm Hg result in pulmonary congestion due to volume overload, and at that point increasing preload decreases stroke volume.
AfterloadThe force against which the ventricles must act; dependent on vascular resistance (aortic BP). As cardiac output falls in HF, a compensatory increase in vascular resistance occurs.
ContractilityEven in chronic HF, positive inotropic agents are capable of producing some increase in contractility.
Heart rateAs the heart fails and stroke volume diminishes, heart rate rises through sympathetic activation of β1-adrenoceptors.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)259

Pathophysiology — four determinants and the compensations that turn toxic (cont.)

PHAR.0246PHAR.0247src p.968–977

The compensations, and why they are the disease

↓ Cardiac output→↑ SNS (β1 → HR & contractility; α1 → vasoconstriction)→↓ renal blood flow → renin → RAAS → ↑ resistance + Na⁺/H₂O retention→Frank-Starling + ventricular hypertrophy and remodeling→Vicious cycle → death
Exam Lock
Why the mortality drugs are all anti-compensatory
  • Chronic activation of the SNS and RAAS is associated with cardiac tissue remodeling, which prompts additional neurohumoral activation — a vicious cycle. Every drug that prolongs survival (ARNI/ACEI/ARB, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) blocks a compensation. Every drug that only relieves symptoms (diuretics, digoxin) treats the consequence.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)260

Classification — NYHA and AHA stages

PHAR.0248PHAR.0249src p.978–982
NYHA classLevel of impairment
INo symptom limitation with ordinary physical activity
IIOrdinary physical activity somewhat limited by dyspnea (e.g. long-distance walking, climbing two flights of stairs)
IIIExercise limited by dyspnea with moderate workload (e.g. short-distance walking, climbing one flight of stairs)
IVDyspnea at rest with very little exertion
AHA stageDescriptionExamples
AHigh risk for developing heart failureHypertension, diabetes mellitus, CAD, family history of cardiomyopathy
BAsymptomatic heart failurePrevious MI, LV dysfunction, valvular heart disease
CSymptomatic heart failureStructural heart disease, dyspnea & fatigue, impaired exercise tolerance
DRefractory end-stage heart failureMarked symptoms at rest despite maximal medical therapy

The bulk of patients with HF fall under Stage C; once Stage C is reached, severity is usually described according to the NYHA scale, which correlates fairly well with prognosis.

Therapeutic strategy and lifestyle

  • Treatment is directed at (1) reducing symptoms and slowing progression of disease, and (2) managing acute episodes.
  • Lifestyle: light aerobic exercise · low dietary Na⁺ (2 g sodium diet) · smoking/alcohol cessation · achieving ideal weight · 2 L fluid restriction · NSAIDs, alcohol and calcium-channel blockers should be avoided if possible (may exacerbate HF) · address comorbid conditions.
  • The first step in managing chronic HF is to determine the etiology or precipitating factors — treating an underlying disorder (e.g. anemia, hyperthyroidism) may remove the need for treating HF.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)261

The four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT)

PHAR.0249PHAR.0250PHAR.0251src p.985–1005
PillarDrugsWhy it worksKey adverse effects / cautions
1 · ARNI (or ACEI/ARB)Sacubitril / valsartanIn HF the natriuretic peptide system is activated alongside RAAS and works antagonistically to it — vasodilation, natriuresis, diuresis, lower BP and sympathetic tone, reduced aldosterone. Natriuretic peptides are broken down by neprilysin. Sacubitril blocks neprilysin, prolonging their favourable effects. Because neprilysin also breaks down angiotensin II, sacubitril can never be used alone — it must always be combined with an ARB. Preferred over ACEI in new guidelines; absolute 4.7% reduction in CV death or HF hospitalisation vs ACEI.Hypotension · hyperkalemia · angioedema · teratogenic (valsartan component) · worsening renal function with NSAIDs · cough (very small %). Contraindicated: history of angioedema with ACEI/ARB; recent ACEI use (< 36 hours); severe hepatic impairment; pregnancy; diabetics on aliskiren
2 · β-blockersBisoprolol · carvedilol · metoprololReverse cardiac remodeling; 30–40% reduction in mortality and hospitalisation in NYHA II–IV. Main benefit in HFrEF is inhibition of renin release, plus preventing the deleterious effects of norepinephrine on cardiac muscle fibres (remodeling, hypertrophy). Recommended for all stable patients with reduced LVEF, and for asymptomatic Stage B.Can get initial exacerbation of symptoms — start at low dose and increase gradually over several weeks. Bradycardia, reduced exercise capacity, hypotension, AV block. Use cautiously in decompensated HF; contraindicated in cardiogenic shock. Considerable care with verapamil (additive negative inotropy)
3 · MRASpironolactone · eplerenonePatients with advanced heart disease have elevated aldosterone from angiotensin stimulation and reduced hepatic clearance. Aldosterone antagonism prevents Na⁺ retention, myocardial hypertrophy and hypokalemia. Benefits are thought to be relatively independent of the diuretic effect and due to a beneficial influence on cardiovascular remodeling. Decrease morbidity and mortality in severe HF.Hyperkalemia — especially with ACEI/ARB/ARNI, K⁺ supplements or renal failure · GI disturbances (gastritis, peptic ulcer) · CNS effects (lethargy, confusion) · endocrine abnormalities (gynecomastia, decreased libido, menstrual irregularities — less with eplerenone). Contraindicated at eGFR ≤ 30 or serum K⁺ ≥ 5.0 mEq/L

The four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) (cont.)

PHAR.0249PHAR.0250PHAR.0251src p.985–1005
PillarDrugsWhy it worksKey adverse effects / cautions
4 · SGLT2 inhibitorsDapagliflozin · empagliflozinRecommended in symptomatic chronic HFrEF to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and CV mortality irrespective of the presence of diabetes. Mechanism remains unclear: osmotic diuresis and natriuresis, decreases in arterial pressure and stiffness, reduction of preload/afterload → blunting of cardiac stress → less hypertrophy and fibrosis, and a shift to ketone-based myocardial metabolism.Increased incidence of genital and urinary tract infections (glycosuria) · osmotic diuresis → volume depletion, increased serum creatinine. PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)263

Diuretics, ACE inhibitors and ARBs in heart failure

PHAR.0250PHAR.0251src p.983–997
AgentRole and evidence
Loop diuretics (furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide)Usually necessary to restore and maintain euvolemia. Unlike thiazides, loop diuretics maintain their effectiveness in the presence of impaired renal function. The treatment goal is to eliminate clinical evidence of fluid retention using the lowest dose possible to maintain euvolemia.
Thiazide diureticsRelatively weak; used alone infrequently in HF. May be added to a loop diuretic in patients with persistent volume overload or refractory edema.
BothWith the exception of MRAs, there is no evidence of a mortality benefit with loop or thiazide diuretics. They do not alter disease progression or prolong survival, so they are not mandatory for patients without fluid retention.
ACE inhibitors (captopril, enalapril, ramipril)Improve symptoms, decrease long-term remodeling, decrease incidence of hospitalization and MI, and prolong survival in HF with reduced LVEF (Stage C). Recommended for all patients with symptomatic HF and for asymptomatic patients with decreased LVEF or a history of MI; suggested for those at high risk (Stages A and B). Used in patients who are not candidates for ARNIs.
ARBs (candesartan, valsartan)Potent competitive antagonists of the angiotensin type I receptor; do not affect bradykinin levels. Substitute for patients who cannot tolerate ACE inhibitors (severe cough or angioedema).

PHAR.0250PHAR.0251src p.1006–1014, 955–961
DrugMechanismWhen it is usedAdverse effects & contraindications
Ivabradine (I_f channel inhibitor)Specific inhibitor of the I_f current involved in sinoatrial nodal activity → reduces heart rate without affecting contractilityHeart rate independently predicts outcomes in HFrEF; lower heart rate (< 70 bpm) is directly related to improved outcomes in chronic HFrEF in sinus rhythm. Before initiating, the β-blocker dose should be optimised/maximised — it is an adjunct, or for those who cannot tolerate the maximum β-blocker doseBradycardia · atrial fibrillation · sinus arrest · QT prolongation · torsade de pointes. Vericiguat (soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator)Guanylate cyclase has two forms — soluble (the receptor for NO) and a transmembrane receptor for natriuretic peptides; both raise cGMP. Vericiguat stimulates sGC independently of NO → cGMP → protein kinase G → ↓ fibrosis, hypertrophy and inflammation in the heart; ↓ inflammation and ↑ vasodilation in vessels; ↓ fibrosis and ↑ renal blood flow in the kidneyAdd-on therapy in HFrEF with recently decompensated or worsening heart failure, high-risk HFrEF, especially after rehospitalisation. Does not prolong survival but does reduce hospitalisation.Postural dizziness, headache · orthostatic hypotension / syncope · nausea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea · anemia. Contraindicated with PDE-5 inhibitors (severe hypotension and syncope) and with long-acting nitrates; avoid in severe anemia
Hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrateNitrates dilate veins and venules → ↓ cardiac preload. Hydralazine dilates arterioles → ↓ systemic arteriolar resistance and afterload. Concurrent use produces sustained improvement in LVEF and decreases morbidity/mortalityRecommended for patients who cannot tolerate ARNI/ACEI/ARB or have CKD, and in African American patients with advanced heart failure as an adjunct to standard therapy. A fixed-dose combination is available; dosed 3 times dailyHypotension · reflex tachycardia and Na⁺ & H₂O retention · headache, dizziness, GI disturbances

PHAR.0250PHAR.0251src p.1006–1014, 955–961
DrugMechanismWhen it is usedAdverse effects & contraindications
Digoxin (cardiac glycoside)Inhibits Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase → rise in cytosolic Na⁺ → reduces the transmembrane gradient that drives Ca²⁺ exit via the Na⁺-Ca²⁺ exchanger during repolarisation → Ca²⁺ accumulation in the myocyte → more Ca²⁺ released during calcium-induced calcium release → positive inotropyDecreases the symptoms of HF, increases exercise tolerance and decreases the rate of hospitalization. IT DOES NOT INCREASE SURVIVAL. Indicated in HF with supraventricular tachyarrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, to help control ventricular response rateNarrow therapeutic window — toxicity is one of the most common adverse drug reactions. Cardiac: arrhythmias — atrial tachycardias, atrial fibrillation, AV block, ectopic ventricular beats. GI: anorexia, nausea, vomiting. CNS: headache, fatigue, confusion, blurred or yellow vision, altered colour perception, halos on dark objects. Excreted by the kidney; half-life substantially increased in advanced renal disease and the elderly
PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)266

Digoxin toxicity — electrolytes and treatment

PHAR.0250PHAR.0251src p.960–961
Potassium
Potassium decreases the affinity of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase for digoxin — so hypokalemia increases digoxin binding and enhances both the therapeutic and the toxic effects. Hyperkalemia has the opposite effect.
Treatment of digoxin toxicity
1. Withdraw the drug (if possible) or lower the dose. 2. Adjust electrolyte status (K⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺). 3. Treat ventricular tachyarrhythmias with lidocaine and/or Mg²⁺. 4. If toxicity is severe, treat with digitalis antibodies (digoxin immune Fab / Digibind), which bind and inactivate the drug.
Trap
The interaction that kills
  • Every drug that causes hypokalaemia — loop diuretics, thiazides — makes digoxin more toxic at the same serum level. A patient stabilised on digoxin who is started on furosemide can become toxic without a dose change. Check the potassium, not just the digoxin level.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)267

HFpEF and acute decompensated heart failure

PHAR.0250PHAR.0252PHAR.0253src p.946–947, 962–964
HFpEF (diastolic failure)Acute decompensated heart failure
GoalsReduce HF symptoms, increase functional status, reduce risk of hospitalization, improve quality of life, prevent disease progression, and effectively manage underlying comorbidities. The treatment of systolic failure follows clear clinical guidelines based on numerous trials; diastolic failure is more difficult.Treat volume overload and congestive symptoms; decrease preload; support the circulation
TherapyLifestyle and behavioral modifications are a cornerstone — exercise training, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation and weight loss improve cardiorespiratory fitness and quality of life. Use of MRAs may also be appropriate provided a framework for careful laboratory surveillance is in place. β-blockers and calcium channel blockers slow the rate and lengthen diastole, improving filling (objective PHAR.0252).Loop diuretics — the most important intervention. Then inotropic agents: inamrinone, milrinone, dopamine, dobutamine, glucagon

HFpEF and acute decompensated heart failure (cont.)

PHAR.0250PHAR.0252PHAR.0253src p.946–947, 962–964
Acute inotropeMechanismNotes
Inamrinone, milrinone (PDE III inhibitors)Inhibit myocardial PDE activity → increase cAMP → positive inotropic and arterial and venous vasodilating effectsIV, short-term therapy in intractable heart failure. Long-term therapy with PDE inhibitors has been shown to increase mortality. Adverse effects: arrhythmia, hypotension, thrombocytopenia

Also causes release of norepinephrine from nerve terminalsUsed in shock (MI, open heart surgery, renal failure, cardiac decompensation) persisting after adequate fluid replacement
DobutamineAt therapeutic levels β1 stimulation predominates → potent inotropic effect with little change in heart rate; net vascular effect is usually vasodilation (β2)Less arrhythmogenic than dopamine

Exam Lock
Objective PHAR.0253 in one line
  • Chronic HF = block the compensations (ARNI, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) and relieve congestion (loop diuretic). Acute decompensated HF = relieve congestion first (IV loop diuretic), then support the pump short-term (milrinone, dobutamine) — never long-term, because PDE inhibitors increase mortality.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)269

Practice — heart failure pharmacology

PHAR.0250

A 64-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 28%) on lisinopril, carvedilol and furosemide is to be switched to sacubitril/valsartan. What must happen first, and why?

  1. AStart immediately; there is no interaction
  2. BWait at least 36 hours after the last ACE inhibitor dose, because of the increased risk of angioedema
  3. CStop the β-blocker first, because of additive bradycardia
  4. DStop the furosemide, because of additive hypotension
  5. ECheck the LVEF again after 6 months
Answer
B. Neprilysin also breaks down bradykinin; inhibiting it with sacubitril causes bradykinin to accumulate. Adding it to an ACE inhibitor (which already blocks bradykinin degradation) markedly raises angioedema risk, so sacubitril cannot be used with an ACEI, or dosed within less than 36 hours of one.
PHAR.0251

Six months after starting sacubitril/valsartan, a patient's BNP has risen although he is clinically improved. What explains this, and which test should be used instead?

  1. AWorsening heart failure; repeat BNP in a week
  2. BNeprilysin inhibition prevents BNP degradation, falsely elevating it; use NT-proBNP
  3. CRenal impairment falsely elevates BNP; use serum creatinine
  4. DThe valsartan component raises BNP; use troponin
  5. EVolume overload; increase the diuretic
Answer
B. BNP is degraded by neprilysin, so ARNIs can cause misleading elevations. NT-proBNP is not degraded by neprilysin, so it is the more clinically useful marker for monitoring HF during ARNI therapy.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)270

Practice — heart failure pharmacology (cont.)

PHAR.0250

A patient with HFrEF in sinus rhythm has a resting heart rate of 82 bpm on the maximum tolerated dose of bisoprolol. Which agent should be added, and what must be true for it to work?

  1. ADigoxin; the patient must be in atrial fibrillation
  2. BIvabradine; the patient must be in sinus rhythm
  3. CVerapamil; the patient must have preserved ejection fraction
  4. DAmiodarone; the patient must have ventricular ectopy
  5. EDobutamine; the patient must be hypotensive
Answer
B. Ivabradine inhibits the I_f current in the sinoatrial node, so it only works in sinus rhythm — being out of sinus rhythm is a listed contraindication. It is an adjunct after the β-blocker dose has been optimised, and is contraindicated alongside verapamil or diltiazem (CYP3A4).
PHAR.0250

A 78-year-old on digoxin and furosemide develops nausea, confusion and describes yellow-tinged vision with halos around lights. Her ECG shows atrial tachycardia with AV block. Which single laboratory value most likely precipitated this?

  1. ASerum sodium
  2. BSerum potassium (low)
  3. CSerum calcium (low)
  4. DSerum magnesium (high)
  5. ESerum albumin
Answer
B. Hypokalaemia — caused here by the loop diuretic — increases digoxin binding to the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase because potassium decreases the enzyme's affinity for digoxin, enhancing both therapeutic and toxic effects. Treatment: withdraw/reduce, correct K⁺, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, lidocaine and/or Mg²⁺ for ventricular tachyarrhythmias, and digoxin immune Fab if severe.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)271

Practice — heart failure pharmacology (cont.)

PHAR.0251

Which statement about drugs used in HFrEF is correct?

  1. ALoop diuretics prolong survival and are mandatory in all patients
  2. BDigoxin reduces symptoms and hospitalisation but does not increase survival
  3. CLong-term milrinone improves mortality in intractable heart failure
  4. DSGLT2 inhibitors are only beneficial in patients with diabetes
  5. Eβ-blockers should be started at full dose to gain benefit quickly
Answer
B. Digoxin decreases symptoms, increases exercise tolerance and decreases hospitalisation — but does not increase survival. Diuretics have no mortality benefit except MRAs; long-term PDE III inhibition increases mortality; SGLT2 inhibitors benefit HFrEF irrespective of diabetes; and β-blockers must be started low and titrated over weeks.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Heart Failure (Cardiovascular Drugs 4)272

Heart failure drugs — summary sheet

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Four drugs change the trajectory — ARNI, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor — and everything else in the lecture makes the patient feel better without making them live longer.
Exam Lock
The eight locks
  • Sacubitril must always be paired with an ARB — neprilysin inhibition also raises angiotensin II.
  • No ACEI within 36 hours of an ARNI (angioedema).
  • Monitor NT-proBNP, not BNP, on an ARNI.
  • β-blockers: start low, go slow; contraindicated in cardiogenic shock.
  • MRAs stop at eGFR ≤ 30 or K⁺ ≥ 5.0.
  • SGLT2i help regardless of diabetes; contraindicated in T1DM and eGFR < 25.
  • Ivabradine needs sinus rhythm; digoxin needs a symptom or AF, and never claims survival.
  • Hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate: intolerant of RAAS blockade, CKD, or African American patients with advanced HF.
Trap
Three traps
  • Treating HFpEF as if it were HFrEF — the four pillars were trialled in reduced ejection fraction.
  • Giving a calcium channel blocker or NSAID in HFrEF — both are on the avoid list.
  • Reading a rising BNP on an ARNI as decompensation.

Antiarrhythmic Drugs 1

The action potential first, the arrhythmia mechanisms second, the drug classes third. In that order the Vaughan-Williams classes stop being arbitrary.

Dr. Lucy Clunes  ·  source pp. 1044–1155

Lecture objectives — verbatim

  • PHAR.0254 Describe the ionic basis of the action potential in different types of cardiac cells (sinus node, AV node, atrium, His bundle, Purkinje cell, ventricle cell).
  • PHAR.0255 Describe the electrophysiology of normal cardiac rhythm.
  • PHAR.0256 Discuss the relationship between cellular cardiac electrical activity and the ECG.
  • PHAR.0257 Describe the pathophysiologic mechanisms of cardiac arrhythmias (abnormal automaticity, triggered rhythms, reentrant rhythms and abnormal impulse conduction).
  • PHAR.0258 List antiarrhythmic drugs and classify them according to the Vaughan-Williams classification into classes I, II, III and IV, including other miscellaneous agents.
  • PHAR.0259 List the primary channel or receptor mechanisms by which class I, II, III and IV antiarrhythmic drugs produce their effects.
  • PHAR.0260 Describe the effects of the different antiarrhythmic agents on the cardiac action potential and the ECG.
  • PHAR.0261 Describe the routes of administration, biotransformation and excretion of antiarrhythmic drugs.
  • PHAR.0262 Describe the adverse effects and contraindications of antiarrhythmic drugs.
All cardiac cells have the property of automaticity — the ability to generate action potentials — and rhythmicity, the ability to generate these potentials in a regular, repetitive manner. Cardiac arrhythmia is defined as loss of cardiac rhythm.Reading notes
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs I274

The two action potentials, phase by phase

PHAR.0254PHAR.0255src p.1076–1085
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs I275

The two action potentials, phase by phase (cont.)

PHAR.0254PHAR.0255src p.1076–1085
PhaseFast response (myocardial)Slow response (SA / AV node)
0Rapid upstroke & depolarization — Na⁺ channels open → fast inward current; the upstroke ends as Na⁺ channels are inactivated. Threshold ≈ −50 mVUpstroke — Ca²⁺ channels open → slow conduction velocity
1Initial repolarization — Na⁺ channels inactivate; K⁺ channels rapidly open and close → transient outward current—
2Plateau — voltage-sensitive Ca²⁺ channels open → slow inward (depolarizing) current balancing slow outward (polarizing) movement of K⁺—
3Repolarization — Ca²⁺ channels close, K⁺ channels open → outward current. Net result: gain of Na⁺ and loss of K⁺, corrected by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPaseCa²⁺ channels inactivated and increased activation of K⁺ channels → increased K⁺ efflux
4Resting potential — increasing depolarization due to a gradual increase in Na⁺ permeability brings the cell to the threshold of the next action potentialSlow spontaneous depolarization due to I_f (mixed Na⁺/K⁺ inward current) — the “funny” current

Channel states: resting (openable above threshold), open, and inactivated (at positive potentials and during sustained depolarization). The inactivated channel cannot be activated until it cycles back to the resting state — the basis of the refractory period and of use-dependence.

PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs I276

Reading the ECG, and the electrical events behind it

PHAR.0256src p.1087–1089
StepNormal value / what to check
1. RateNormal 60–100 bpm
2. RhythmRegular or irregular? Is there a P wave before every QRS? Is there a QRS after every P wave?
3. P wavesPresent? Consistent shape? Normal duration (< 120 ms)?
4. PR intervalNormal 120–200 ms
5. QRS complexNormal < 120 ms
6. ST segmentST elevation or depression? T-wave changes (peaked or inverted)?
7. QT intervalNormal < 440 ms (men), < 460 ms (women)

Specific patterns to look for

  • STEMI: ST elevation in 2+ contiguous leads · Atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular RR intervals, no P wave · Atrial flutter: sawtooth pattern · Ventricular tachycardia: wide complex, fast · Wolff-Parkinson-White: delta wave and short PR
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs I277

Mechanisms of arrhythmia — and how each is treated

PHAR.0257src p.1090–1108
  • All arrhythmias result from (a) disturbances in impulse formation, (b) disturbances in impulse conduction, or (c) a combination. They may be supraventricular (atrial or AV junctional) or ventricular.
MechanismWhat happensHow antiarrhythmics treat it
Abnormal automaticityThe SA node sets the pace, but if other cardiac sites show enhanced automaticity they generate competing stimuliMost antiarrhythmics suppress automaticity by blocking Na⁺ or Ca²⁺ channels to reduce the ratio of these to K⁺ → decrease the slope of phase 4 depolarization and/or raise the threshold of discharge to a less negative voltage → ↓ frequency of discharge
Re-entrant circuitsNormal impulses are conducted down bifurcated pathways to activate the entire ventricular surface. Re-entry occurs if a unidirectional block creates an abnormal conduction pathway, with abnormally slow retrograde conduction around a non-excitable area. Re-entry is the most common cause of arrhythmias.Slow conduction and/or increase the refractory period — i.e. convert the unidirectional block into a bidirectional block
Early afterdepolarizations (EADs)Occur during the inciting action potential (phase 2 or 3); triggered by conditions that prolong the action potential (e.g. drugs that prolong the QT interval). Phase 2 EADs are carried by inward Ca²⁺; phase 3 EADs by partially recovered Na⁺ channels. If sustained, they lead to torsades de pointes.Slow conduction and/or increase the refractory period — make cells less excitable
Delayed afterdepolarizations (DADs)Occur shortly after repolarization is complete (interrupting phase 4). Mechanism not well understood; classically calcium overload, as in digoxin toxicityAs above
Accessory tract pathwaysAn extra conduction route bypassing the AV nodeSlow conduction and/or increase the refractory period — goal: enhance conduction through ‘normal’ pathways

Factors that can precipitate arrhythmias: ischemia · hypoxia · acidosis or alkalosis · electrolyte abnormalities · excessive catecholamine exposure · autonomic influences · drug toxicity (especially antiarrhythmics).

PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs I278

Therapy of cardiac arrhythmias, and the Vaughan-Williams classification

PHAR.0258PHAR.0259src p.1110–1113
Tachyarrhythmias
  • Antiarrhythmic drugs
  • External electrical cardioversion
  • Ablation of arrhythmic pathways and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators have an increasing role
Bradyarrhythmias
  • Cardiac pacing is the treatment of choice
  • Atropine and sympathomimetics have been used
Devices
  • Pacemaker — prevents the heart beating too slowly
  • ICD — for ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation; monitors the rhythm and delivers energy to restore normal beating
  • Catheter ablation — high-frequency energy through a catheter disconnects the pathway causing the abnormal rhythm
ClassTargetDrugs
I — fast channel blockersNa⁺IA quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide · IB lidocaine, mexiletine · IC flecainide, propafenone
II — β-blockersβ-adrenoceptorPropranolol, metoprolol, esmolol
III — inhibitors of repolarizationK⁺Amiodarone / dronedarone, sotalol, dofetilide
IV — calcium channel blockersCa²⁺Verapamil, diltiazem
MiscellaneousVariousDigoxin, adenosine, magnesium, atropine
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs I279

Therapy of cardiac arrhythmias, and the Vaughan-Williams classification (cont.)

PHAR.0258PHAR.0259src p.1110–1113
Exam Lock
Use / state-dependence — one idea that explains the whole class
  • Drugs bind more rapidly to open or inactivated Na⁺ channels, so they have a greater effect in tissues that are more frequently depolarizing. Cells discharging at abnormally high frequency are preferentially blocked — which is why an antiarrhythmic can suppress a tachycardia while barely touching normal myocardium, and why toxicity appears in hypoxia and acidosis, when normal cells behave abnormally.
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs I280

Digoxin as an antiarrhythmic — mechanism, interactions, toxicity

PHAR.0262PHAR.0263src p.1046–1062
Direct actions
Shortens the action potential and refractory period in atrial and ventricular myocardial cells (via increased intracellular Ca²⁺, which stimulates K⁺ channels); prolongs the effective refractory period and diminishes conduction velocity in the AV node through direct AV-nodal blockade and vagomimetic properties — inhibition of Ca²⁺ currents in the AV node and activation of ACh-mediated K⁺ currents in the atrium
Net antiarrhythmic action
1. Slows AV conduction and 2. prolongs the effective refractory period of the AV node → decreases the fraction of atrial impulses conducted through the node and increases the PR interval → useful in atrial flutter/fibrillation by controlling ventricular rate
Pharmacokinetics
Very potent (narrow safety margin) · widely distributed including CSF · t½ ≈ 36–40 h · accumulates in muscle → large Vd, so a loading dose is required
Contraindications
Diastolic or right-sided heart failure · uncontrolled hypertension · bradyarrhythmias · non-responders or intolerant patients
IonInteraction with digoxin
K⁺Digoxin and K⁺ inhibit each other's binding to the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → hyperkalemia reduces digoxin activity; hypokalemia facilitates digoxin activity and toxicity
Ca²⁺Accelerates overloading of Ca²⁺ stores → facilitates toxic actions of digoxin, especially arrhythmias
Mg²⁺Opposite to Ca²⁺ — magnesium antagonises the effects of calcium
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs I281

Digoxin as an antiarrhythmic — mechanism, interactions, toxicity (cont.)

PHAR.0262PHAR.0263src p.1046–1062
Precipitating factors
  • Hypokalemia
  • Drug accumulation / relative overdose
  • Hypomagnesemia or hypercalcemia
  • Hyperthyreosis
  • Abnormal renal function
  • Respiratory disease
  • Acid-base imbalances
  • Age above 65, low body weight, fever
Predisposing factors & drugs
  • K⁺-depleting diuretics
  • Corticosteroids
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Hypoxia
  • Renal failure
  • Myocarditis
  • Drugs: quinidine, verapamil & amiodarone
Treatment
  • Recognise toxicity: GI (nausea, vomiting, anorexia); neuro (confusion, weakness, visual changes); cardiac (bradycardia, AV block, ventricular arrhythmias)
  • Stop digoxin; review drug interactions
  • Check serum digoxin level, electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺), renal function
  • Mild-moderate: monitor closely, correct electrolytes
  • Severe: digoxin-specific antibody fragments; lidocaine/phenytoin for ventricular arrhythmias; temporary pacemaker for bradyarrhythmias
  • AVOID DC cardioversion — it can provoke VF.
Trap
The three drugs that raise digoxin levels
  • Quinidine, verapamil and amiodarone. All three are themselves antiarrhythmics, so the combination that seems most rational — adding a rhythm drug to a rate drug — is exactly the one that pushes digoxin into its toxic range.

PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs II283

Class I — the three subclasses on one page

PHAR.0259PHAR.0262src p.1195–1219
  • Class I drugs block fast inward Na⁺ channels → decreased Na⁺ entry slows the rate of rise of phase 0 → decreased excitability and conduction velocity. The subclasses differ by rate of binding and dissociation: IA intermediate · IB most rapid · IC slowest.
Class IAClass IBClass IC
DrugsQuinidine · procainamide · disopyramideLidocaine · mexiletineFlecainide · propafenone
Action potentialSlow the rate of change of phase 0; slow conduction, prolong the action potential and increase the ventricular effective refractory period; prolong phase 3 by inhibiting K⁺ channelsSlow phase 0 and decrease the slope of phase 4; shorten phase 3 repolarization; little effect on depolarization in normal cellsMarkedly depress phase 0 → marked slowing of conduction, but little effect on duration or the ventricular effective refractory period; prominent effects even at normal heart rates
ECG↑ QRS, ↑ QT, ↑ ERP (moderate Na⁺ block + prolonged repolarization)Small ↑ QRS; clinically insignificant ↓ QT (mild Na⁺ block, shortened repolarization)Significant ↑ QRS, no change in repolarization
Clinical useAtrial fibrillation; supraventricular and ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Largely replaced by safer antiarrhythmics because of proarrhythmic risk. Procainamide still maintains a niche as the drug of choice for stable pre-excited atrial fibrillation.Lidocaine: acute ventricular arrhythmias from MI or cardiac manipulation; digitalis-induced arrhythmias. Its use for VT has declined because IV amiodarone is superior. Little effect on atrial or AV junctional arrhythmias. Mexiletine: oral derivative for severe ventricular arrhythmiasSevere symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias resistant to other therapy; severe symptomatic supraventricular arrhythmias and prevention of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Propafenone also maintains sinus rhythm in symptomatic AF
Signature toxicityAnticholinergic effects — tachycardia, dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision, constipation; diarrhoea, nausea, headache, dizzinessLidocaine: wide toxic-therapeutic ratio; CNS effects (drowsiness, slurred speech, agitation); no negative inotropic effect; toxic doses → convulsions, coma. Mexiletine: mainly CNS & GINegative inotropy (aggravates CHF); CNS and GI effects. Flecainide and propafenone are associated with the potential for fatal ventricular arrhythmias in persons with structural heart disease.
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs II284

Class I — the three subclasses on one page (cont.)

PHAR.0259PHAR.0262src p.1195–1219
Exam Lock
Why lidocaine works only where the tissue is sick
  • Class IB drugs are less prominent blockers of Na⁺ channels at rest but effectively block channels in depolarized tissue. In ischaemic tissue, cells are partly depolarized because they lack sufficient ATP to run the sodium pump, so their Na⁺ channels spend more time inactivated — and IB drugs have the greatest affinity for the inactivated state. That is the whole reason lidocaine is a post-MI drug.
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs II285

Class IA drug by drug

PHAR.0259PHAR.0262src p.1198–1207
QuinidineProcainamideDisopyramide
Extra actionsConcomitant class III activity (blocks K⁺ channels); pro-arrhythmic; being replaced by Ca²⁺ antagonistsDerivative of the local anaesthetic procaine; blocks Na⁺ channels in the activated state; blocks K⁺ channels; antimuscarinicStrong negative inotropic effect (greater than quinidine and procainamide); strong antimuscarinic properties; causes peripheral vasoconstriction; blocks K⁺ channels
