PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs II286

Class II and Class IV — the two rate-control classes

PHAR.0259PHAR.0262PHAR.0264src p.1220–1245
Class II — β-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol, esmolol)Class IV — calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem)
MechanismInhibit sympathetic tone, affecting predominantly slow-response tissues (SA and AV nodes). Reduce heart rate and myocardial contractility (β1); slow conduction through the myocardial conducting system; reduce the rate of spontaneous depolarization in pacemaker cells (decreased slope of phase 4); little effect on the action potential in most myocardial cells. ECG: ↑ PRDecrease inward Ca²⁺ current → decreased rate of phase 0 depolarization; slow conduction in tissues dependent on Ca²⁺ current (SA & AV nodes). Bind only to open, depolarized channels — use/state-dependent — preventing repolarization before the drug dissociates; slow conduction and prolong the effective refractory period. ECG: ↑ PR
Why sympathetic tone is proarrhythmicβ1 stimulation causes: ↑ automaticity (enhanced phase 4 spontaneous depolarization) · ↑ membrane excitability (shortened refractoriness in phases 2 and 3) · ↑ rate of impulse conduction (accelerated phase 0 upstroke velocity) · ↑ delayed afterpolarizationsVerapamil is relatively selective for the myocardium and is less effective as a systemic vasodilator. Diltiazem has intermediate myocardial selectivity, between verapamil and the dihydropyridines. Major effects: ↓ contractility (negative inotropy), ↓ heart rate (negative chronotropy), ↓ conduction velocity (negative dromotropy)
Clinical applicationsReduce the incidence of sudden arrhythmic death after MI · control of supraventricular tachycardias (atrial fibrillation & flutter, AV nodal re-entrant tachycardias) · certain ventricular tachycardias, e.g. catecholamine-induced arrhythmias and digoxin toxicity. Esmolol — short-acting β1-selective antagonist, t½ ≈ 9 min, given IV for acute arrhythmias during surgery or emergenciesMore effective against atrial than ventricular arrhythmias. Supraventricular tachycardia is the major arrhythmia indication; reduction of ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation and flutter; also hypertension and angina. They are 2nd line to adenosine for conversion of PSVT, because adenosine is more effective with fewer side effects.
Adverse effects & contraindicationsBradycardia, hypotension, CNS effects. Contraindicated in acute CHF, severe bradycardia or heart block (negative inotropy) and severe hyperactive airway disease (β2 blockade)Negative inotropes · transient decrease in BP · CNS effects (headache, fatigue, dizziness) · GI effects (constipation, nausea) · excessive bradycardia and AV nodal block. Verapamil can increase the concentrations of digoxin, dofetilide, simvastatin and lovastatin.
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs II287

Class III — the K⁺ channel blockers

PHAR.0259PHAR.0262PHAR.0270src p.1225–1239
  • Block repolarizing K⁺ channels → prolong the action potential (and the QT interval) without altering phase 0 or the resting membrane potential → prolong the effective refractory period. All have the potential to induce arrhythmias.
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs II288

Class III — the K⁺ channel blockers (cont.)

PHAR.0259PHAR.0262PHAR.0270src p.1225–1239
AmiodaroneDronedaroneSotalolDofetilide
MechanismStructurally related to thyroxine (contains iodine). Complex: class I, II and III (and some IV) effects, with K⁺ channel blockade dominant. Decreases AV conduction and sinus node function; blocks mostly inactivated Na⁺ channels; weak Ca²⁺ blocker; inhibits adrenergic stimulation (α and β blocking). Antianginal as well as antiarrhythmicRelated to amiodarone but with NO iodine content → decreased adverse effects but decreased efficacy. K⁺ blockade dominant, with Na⁺, Ca²⁺ and β-blocking effectsPotent non-selective β-blocker that also inhibits the rapid outward K⁺ current → prolongs repolarization and action potential duration, lengthens the refractory periodPotent and pure K⁺ channel blocker
Clinical applicationsOne of the most commonly employed antiarrhythmics despite its side-effect profile. Ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias. Drug of choice for acute VT refractory to cardioversion shock. Low doses maintain sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillationAtrial fibrillation / flutterLife-threatening ventricular arrhythmias; maintenance of sinus rhythm in patients with AF/flutter who are currently in sinus rhythm. Because of pro-arrhythmic effects, do not use for asymptomatic arrhythmias.Conversion of atrial fibrillation/flutter to sinus rhythm, and maintenance of sinus rhythm in chronic AF/flutter of longer than one week's duration after conversion
PharmacokineticsOral (very well absorbed) and IV. t½ several weeks (25–60 days) — extensively distributed in adipose tissue, loading dose required; full clinical and adverse effects may take 6 weeks—Use with caution in renal impairmentExcreted in urine (~80% unchanged)

The two orientation tables, and atrial fibrillation (cont.)

PHAR.0265PHAR.0266PHAR.0267PHAR.0268PHAR.0269src p.1256–1258, 1132–1134

Drug therapy for atrial fibrillation — from the reading notes

  • Atrial fibrillation is the commonest arrhythmia encountered clinically — a rapid, irregularly irregular atrial rhythm. Symptoms include palpitations and sometimes weakness, dyspnea and presyncope. Atrial thrombi often form, causing a significant risk of embolic stroke. Diagnosed with an ECG.
  • Rate control: β-blockers should not be used to acutely control the ventricular response in patients with HF (negative inotropy), and should be used with caution in bronchospasm or COPD. Verapamil and diltiazem should be used with caution in HF, also for negative inotropy. Digoxin is the least effective but should be used in patients with reduced EF or CHF. Amiodarone can be used as a rate-control agent in patients refractory to, or with contraindications to, β-blockers, calcium channel blockers or digoxin; IV amiodarone for critically ill patients or acute rate control in CHF.
  • Rhythm control: flecainide, propafenone, dofetilide and amiodarone are currently the recommended drugs for conversion of atrial fibrillation to normal sinus rhythm; the choice depends on patient tolerance.
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs II293

Practice — antiarrhythmics

PHAR.0262

A 68-year-old man on long-term amiodarone develops a dry cough and progressive exertional dyspnoea; chest imaging shows reticular changes. Which two baseline tests should have been performed before starting the drug, and which organs does it classically affect?

  1. ARenal function and ECG; kidney and heart
  2. BThyroid function and pulmonary/liver assessment; thyroid, lung, liver, cornea and skin
  3. CFull blood count and coagulation; bone marrow
  4. DLipid profile and glucose; pancreas and liver
  5. ESpirometry alone; lung
Answer
B. Amiodarone contains iodine and is structurally related to thyroxine — serum TSH should be tested before initiation. Classic long-term toxicities: interstitial pulmonary fibrosis, hyper-/hypothyroidism, liver toxicity, photosensitivity, corneal deposits and blue-grey skin discoloration, plus neurological effects. More than 50% of long-term users stop it.
PHAR.0264

A patient with a narrow-complex regular tachycardia at 180 bpm is given a rapid IV bolus of a drug with a 15-second half-life and converts to sinus rhythm after a brief flush and chest discomfort. Which drug, and which structure does it act on most?

  1. AVerapamil; the SA node
  2. BAdenosine; the AV node
  3. CDigoxin; the atrium
  4. DLidocaine; the His-Purkinje system
  5. EEsmolol; the ventricle
Answer
B. Adenosine — a P1 purinergic agonist that opens a G-protein-coupled K⁺ channel and inhibits cAMP-mediated Ca²⁺ influx, causing hyperpolarization. The AV node is more sensitive than the SA node, which is why it terminates AV-nodal re-entrant PSVT. Flushing, burning, chest pain and bronchoconstriction in asthmatics are the expected effects.
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs II294

Practice — antiarrhythmics (cont.)

PHAR.0262

A patient with a previous anterior myocardial infarction and an ejection fraction of 32% is started on flecainide for symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. What is the concern?

  1. AIt will prolong the QT and cause torsades
  2. BClass IC drugs carry the potential for fatal ventricular arrhythmias in persons with structural heart disease, and are negatively inotropic
  3. CIt will cause a lupus-like syndrome
  4. DIt will raise the digoxin level
  5. EIt will cause cinchonism
Answer
B. Flecainide and propafenone are associated with the potential for fatal ventricular arrhythmias in persons with structural heart disease, and flecainide's negative inotropy aggravates CHF. Class IC markedly depresses phase 0 with slow dissociation, so the QRS widens significantly even at normal rates. Lupus-like syndrome is procainamide; cinchonism is quinidine.
PHAR.0262

Which class IA drug is described as the drug of choice for stable pre-excited atrial fibrillation, and which chronic adverse effect occurs in 25–30% of long-term users?

  1. AQuinidine; thrombocytopenic purpura
  2. BProcainamide; reversible lupus-like syndrome
  3. CDisopyramide; urinary retention
  4. DMexiletine; tremor
  5. ESotalol; torsades de pointes
Answer
B. Procainamide — the lecture states it “still maintains a specific niche as the drug of choice for the management of stable pre-excited atrial fibrillation”. Its chronic toxicity is a reversible lupus-like syndrome in 25–30%; it is metabolised in part to NAPA, which adds a class III effect.
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs II295

Practice — antiarrhythmics (cont.)

PHAR.0259

Which single feature separates class IB from class IA on the ECG, and why?

  1. AIB widens the QRS more, because it dissociates slowly
  2. BIB produces only a small QRS increase and a clinically insignificant QT decrease, because it dissociates rapidly and shortens phase 3
  3. CIB prolongs the PR interval, because it blocks the AV node
  4. DIB has no ECG effect at all
  5. EIB prolongs the QT, because it blocks potassium channels
Answer
B. IA blocks Na⁺ and K⁺ → ↑ QRS, ↑ QT, ↑ ERP. IB has the most rapid binding and dissociation, shortens phase 3 repolarization, and so gives only a small QRS increase with a clinically insignificant QT decrease. IC dissociates most slowly → significant QRS increase with no change in repolarization.
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs II296

Antiarrhythmics — summary sheet

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Match the class to the phase — I blocks phase 0 Na⁺, II slows phase 4, III blocks phase 3 K⁺, IV blocks phase 0 Ca²⁺ in the nodes — and then match the tissue: nodes for II and IV, ventricle for IB, atrium and accessory pathways for IA, IC and III.
Exam Lock
The ten locks
  • IA ↑ QRS, ↑ QT, ↑ ERP. IB small ↑ QRS, insignificant ↓ QT. IC significant ↑ QRS.
  • Binding speed: IB fastest, IA intermediate, IC slowest.
  • Lidocaine works on ischaemic (depolarised) tissue and has no negative inotropy.
  • Flecainide/propafenone are lethal in structural heart disease.
  • Quinidine → cinchonism + raises digoxin. Procainamide → lupus-like. Disopyramide → antimuscarinic + negative inotropy.
  • Amiodarone: t½ 25–60 days, loading dose, > 50% long-term adverse effects, check TSH first.
  • Dronedarone has no iodine — fewer effects, less efficacy — contraindicated in decompensated HFrEF and permanent AF.
  • Sotalol = β-blocker + K⁺ blocker; lowest adverse-effect rate but torsades.
  • Adenosine is first line for PSVT; CCBs are second line.
  • Magnesium is the treatment for torsades.
Trap
Three traps
  • Giving a β-blocker or verapamil for acute rate control in decompensated heart failure.
  • Forgetting that quinidine, verapamil and amiodarone all raise digoxin.
  • DC cardioversion in digoxin toxicity — it can provoke ventricular fibrillation.
PHAR · Antiarrhythmic Drugs II297
PHAR

Antianginal Drugs

One equation — supply vs demand — and four drug classes, each attacking a different term in it.

Dr. Lucy Clunes  ·  source pp. 1296–1351

Lecture objectives — verbatim

  • PHAR.0272 Describe the pathophysiology of the three major forms of angina.
  • PHAR.0273 Describe the mechanism of action and pharmacokinetic properties of drugs used in the management of angina.
  • PHAR.0274 Compare and contrast the therapeutic and adverse effects of nitrates, β-blockers and calcium channel blockers used for treating angina.
  • PHAR.0275 Explain why the combination of a nitrate with a β-blocker or a calcium channel blocker may be more effective than either alone.
  • PHAR.0276 Describe the effects of each antianginal drug or drug class on the determinants of myocardial oxygen consumption and/or oxygen supply.
  • PHAR.0277 Describe the use of antianginal drugs in classic (effort-related), vasospastic and unstable angina pectoris.
  • PHAR.0278 Describe the mechanism of action and adverse effects of sildenafil.
  • PHAR.0279 Explain why the combination of a nitrate with sildenafil is potentially dangerous.
The primary cause of angina is an imbalance between the oxygen demand of the heart and the oxygen supplied to it via the coronary vessels — caused by an increase in myocardial oxygen demand (determined by heart rate, ventricular contractility, and ventricular wall tension) or by a decrease in myocardial oxygen supply.Reading notes
PHAR · Antianginal Drugs298

Angina — definition, classification and the four types

PHAR.0272src p.1314–1318
  • Angina pectoris is the principal clinical manifestation of CAD, characterised by pre-cordial pressure-like discomfort resulting from myocardial ischemia. Transient episodes that do not cause cellular death, lasting ~15 seconds to ~15 minutes. The immediate cause is an imbalance between myocardial O₂ supply and demand.
  • When the myocardium becomes hypoxic, pain receptors within the heart are triggered → the classical presentation of chest pain. Decreased coronary blood flow (vasospasm, fixed stenosis, thrombus) or increased oxygen consumption (↑ heart rate, contractility, afterload, preload).
ClassDescription
0Asymptomatic
1Angina with strenuous exercise
2Angina with moderate exercise
3Angina with mild exertion — 1. walking 1–2 level blocks at a normal pace · 2. climbing 1 flight of stairs at a normal pace
4Angina at any level of physical exertion
TypeCauseKey featureVessel picture
Stable anginaFixed atherosclerotic plaquePredictable with exertion; relieved by restLumen narrowed by plaque; inappropriate vasoconstriction
Unstable anginaPlaque rupture + thrombosis (partial)Occurs at rest, increasing frequencyRuptured plaque, platelet aggregation, thrombus formation, unopposed vasoconstriction
Prinzmetal / variant anginaCoronary artery spasmTransient ST elevation; not exertion-relatedNo overt plaques; intense vasospasm
Microvascular anginaSmall vessel dysfunctionNormal coronaries with typical angina symptoms—

Normal for comparison: patent lumen, normal endothelial function, platelet aggregation inhibited.

The four drug classes against the supply-demand equation

PHAR.0273PHAR.0274PHAR.0276src p.1320–1345
  • Treatment rationale — increase oxygen delivery (coronary vasodilators, antithrombotic drugs) and decrease oxygen demand (vasodilators reducing afterload and preload; cardiac depressants reducing heart rate and contractility).
PHAR · Antianginal Drugs300

The four drug classes against the supply-demand equation (cont.)

PHAR.0273PHAR.0274PHAR.0276src p.1320–1345
ClassDrugsMechanismCardiovascular actionClinical use
NitratesNitroglycerin · isosorbide dinitrate · isosorbide mononitrateMimic endogenous NO. NO is produced by vascular endothelial cells and acts through guanylyl cyclase → cGMP, which stimulates a cGMP-dependent protein kinase that activates myosin light chain phosphatase, dephosphorylating myosin light chains → relaxation. NO also inhibits platelet aggregation (antithrombotic) and leukocyte-endothelial interactions (anti-inflammatory)Systemic: vasodilation with venous dilation > arterial dilation → ↓ venous pressure, small ↓ arterial pressure. Cardiac: ↓ preload and afterload (↓ wall stress) → ↓ oxygen demand. Coronary: prevents/reverses vasospasm, vasodilation, improves subendocardial perfusion → ↑ oxygen deliveryVariant angina · stable & unstable angina · IV nitroglycerin for unstable angina and acute heart failure · sublingual or spray nitroglycerin is first-line for acute anginal symptoms · isosorbide mononitrate orally for prophylaxis
β-blockersAtenolol · metoprolol · propranololBlock β1 receptors → reduce heart rate and contractilityO₂ demand reduced during exercise and at rest; reduce the frequency and severity of angina attacks. No reflex tachycardia, because of their negative inotropic/chronotropic actions. β-blockers decrease mortality after MI. Propranolol non-selective; metoprolol and atenolol cardioselectiveRecommended in all patients (unless contraindicated) with stable angina who have had an ACS or who have left ventricular dysfunction

Calcium channel blockersAmlodipine · nifedipine · diltiazem · verapamilImprove symptoms by coronary and peripheral vasodilatation and by reducing contractility; the degree of each varies with the type of blockerDihydropyridines (nifedipine, amlodipine): minimal effect on cardiac conduction or heart rate; short-acting dihydropyridines should be avoided unless combined with a β-blocker (increased mortality). Verapamil: slows AV conduction directly → ↓ HR, contractility, BP and O₂ demand; greater inotropic effects than dihydropyridines, weaker vasodilator. PHAR · Antianginal Drugs302

Nitrates — pharmacokinetics, tolerance, and the sildenafil interaction

PHAR.0275PHAR.0278PHAR.0279src p.1326–1330, 1351
Nitroglycerin
Undergoes significant first-pass metabolism → taken sublingually, transdermally, buccally or IV. Fast-acting: 2–5 minutes to onset; effect usually lasts ~30 minutes. Longer-acting 12–24 h preparations available (e.g. transdermal patches)
Isosorbide mononitrate
Longer onset and duration than nitroglycerin — more useful for long-term prophylaxis. Onset > 1 h; nearly 100% oral bioavailability; metabolites have longer half-lives and significant activity
Tolerance
Develops rapidly — vessels desensitize to vasodilation. Overcome by a daily nitrate-free interval of 10–12 h: e.g. nitroglycerin patches on for 12 h, off for 12 h.
Adverse effects
Headache (cerebral vasodilation) · high doses: postural hypotension, facial flushing, reflex tachycardia · tolerance. Hypotension is the most serious toxicity; both excessive hypotension and tachycardia can worsen angina by increasing oxygen demand.
Contraindication
Sildenafil, tadalafil
Exam Lock
Objectives PHAR.0275, 0278 and 0279 on one slide
  • Why nitrate + β-blocker (or CCB) is better than either alone: nitrates ↓ preload but cause reflex tachycardia and increased contractility; β-blockers and rate-limiting CCBs ↓ heart rate and contractility but increase end-diastolic volume. Together, each cancels the other's compensatory penalty.
  • Why nitrate + sildenafil is dangerous: sildenafil inhibits PDE5, the enzyme that breaks down cGMP; nitrates raise cGMP. Combined, cGMP accumulates unopposed → profound hypotension.

Trap
Two β-blocker traps in angina
  • β-blockers are contraindicated in variant angina — non-selective agents such as propranolol can exacerbate vasospasm by blocking β2-mediated vasodilation. Treat vasospasm with CCBs or nitrates.
  • NEVER discontinue a β-blocker abruptly — it causes rebound hypertension or angina.
PHAR · Antianginal Drugs305

Practice — antianginal drugs

PHAR.0273

A 62-year-old man with stable angina on a nitroglycerin patch worn continuously reports the patch no longer helps. What has happened and what is the fix?

  1. AHe has developed coronary steal; switch to a beta-blocker
  2. BNitrate tolerance; institute a daily nitrate-free interval of 10–12 hours
  3. CThe patch dose is too low; double it
  4. DHe has developed a PDE5 interaction; stop sildenafil
  5. EThe angina has become unstable; admit for angiography
Answer
B. Nitrate tolerance develops rapidly as vessels desensitize to vasodilation, and is overcome by a daily nitrate-free interval of 10–12 hours — patches on for 12 h, off for 12 h. Increasing the dose without a nitrate-free window makes tolerance worse.
PHAR.0277

A 54-year-old man has chest pain at rest, at night, with transient ST elevation and normal coronary arteries on angiography. Which drug should be avoided, and why?

  1. ANitroglycerin; it worsens coronary steal
  2. BPropranolol; non-selective β-blockade removes β2-mediated vasodilation and can exacerbate vasospasm
  3. CAmlodipine; dihydropyridines cause reflex tachycardia
  4. DDiltiazem; it slows AV conduction
  5. EAspirin; it inhibits prostacyclin
Answer
B. This is variant (Prinzmetal's) angina — coronary spasm without overt plaque. The reading is explicit: non-selective β-blockers such as propranolol can exacerbate variant angina by blocking β2-mediated vasodilation. Treat with nitroglycerin and calcium channel blockers, which are all equally effective here.
PHAR · Antianginal Drugs306

Practice — antianginal drugs (cont.)

PHAR.0275

Why does adding a β-blocker to a nitrate produce better angina control than either drug alone?

  1. AThe β-blocker prevents nitrate tolerance
  2. BThe β-blocker abolishes the nitrate's reflex tachycardia and increased contractility, while the nitrate offsets the β-blocker's increase in end-diastolic volume
  3. CThe nitrate increases β-receptor density
  4. DTogether they block both calcium and sodium channels
  5. EThe nitrate prevents β-blocker withdrawal rebound
Answer
B. Objective PHAR.0275. The lecture's own table: nitrates alone → reflex increase in HR and contractility and ↓ EDV; β-blockers/CCBs alone → ↓ HR and contractility but ↑ EDV. Combined → HR down, contractility unchanged, EDV none-or-decreased — each drug cancels the other's penalty.

DLA · Cardiac Arrhythmias 1 & 2308

What an arrhythmia is, and what causes it

PATH.50078PATH.50079src p.1353–1358
  • A normal resting heart beats with a regular rhythm (60–100/min); each beat starts by depolarization of the sinus node → normal sinus rhythm. Anything else is called an “arrhythmia” — a pathological change in the rhythm of the heart. May be asymptomatic, symptomatic, or cause sudden cardiac death; picked up on physical examination or ECG. Symptoms: lightheadedness, syncope (if cardiac output falls), sudden death (after an MI).

Etiology — “HIS DEBS”

LetterCauseDetail
HHypoxiaOxygen-deprived myocardium due to pulmonary disorders, severe lung disease, acute pulmonary embolus
IIschemia / irritabilityIschemic heart disease, MI, myocarditis, inflammation
SSympathetic stimulation↑ sympathetic tone — hyperthyroidism, CHF, pheochromocytoma, sympathomimetic drugs
DDrugsAntiarrhythmics, antianginals, antihypertensives, antiemetics, gastrointestinal stimulants, antibacterials, narcotics, antipsychotics, digoxin, anaesthetic agents, bronchodilators, alcohol
EElectrolyte disturbancesPotassium (hyper/hypo), calcium (hyper/hypo), magnesium (hyper/hypo)
BBradycardiaA very slow heart rate can predispose to arrhythmias
SStretchHypertrophy/enlargement of the heart leads to cellular, electrical and myocardial remodeling
Diagnosis
1. ECG — primary investigation to view the electrical activity of the heart. 2. Holter monitoring — continuous ECG over long periods, useful to diagnose paroxysmal arrhythmias.
The normal ECG
P wave atrial depolarization · PR segment AV node and bundle of His delay · QRS complex ventricular depolarization · ST segment ventricles completely depolarized · T wave ventricular repolarization. PR interval = start of atrial depolarization to start of ventricular depolarization. QT interval = ventricular depolarization, contraction and repolarization.
Counting boxes
1 small box = 0.04 s; 1 big box = 5 small boxes = 0.2 s. PR interval = 3–5 small boxes · QRS = 2–3 small boxes · QT = 9–11 small boxes
DLA · Cardiac Arrhythmias 1 & 2309

Bradyarrhythmias — decreased automaticity and the AV blocks

PATH.50083src p.1362–1367
EntityMechanismECG signatureCauses
Decreased automaticityPhase 4 of the SA node action potential becomes gradual → slow heart rate or pauseSinus bradycardia or heart blockIncreased vagal tone (sleeping, athletes, inferior wall MI) · slow AV conduction (β-blockers / calcium channel blockers / digoxin) · slow metabolism of nodal cells (hypothermia, hypothyroidism, electrolyte imbalance — hyperkalaemia, raised intracranial pressure — Cushing's triad)
First degree blockA conduction delay through the AV node, but all electrical signals reach the ventriclesRegular RR intervals throughout; increased PR intervalExcess vagal tone · aging · ischemia · cardiomyopathy
Second degree — Mobitz I (Wenckebach)Gradual increase in refractoriness at the AV node blocks some but not all atrial impulses. Block above the bundle of HisProgressive prolongation of the PR interval until a QRS is droppedExcess vagal tone · myocardial infarction · digoxin toxicity
Second degree — Mobitz IIThe impulse sometimes fails to pass through the AV node or bundle of His; conduction of the conducted beats is always the same (constant PR). Block below the bundle of HisAll-or-nothing conduction — QRS complexes dropped without prolongation of the PR intervalMyocardial infarction · degeneration of the His-Purkinje system
Third degree — complete AV blockNo atrial impulses pass through the AV node; the ventricles generate their own impulse — an ‘escape mechanism’ from a focus within the ventricle at a regular, slow rateComplete heart block with AV dissociation — atria and ventricles driven by independent pacemakersInfarction · digitalis toxicity · degenerative changes · infectious/inflammatory processes
DLA · Cardiac Arrhythmias 1 & 2310

Bradyarrhythmias — decreased automaticity and the AV blocks (cont.)

PATH.50083src p.1362–1367
Exam Lock
Above vs below the bundle of His
  • Mobitz I is above the His bundle — the node is fatiguing, so the PR stretches before it fails, and the block is usually benign and vagally responsive. Mobitz II is below it — an all-or-nothing infranodal failure that progresses to complete block, which is why it needs a pacemaker.

DLA · Cardiac Arrhythmias 1 & 2313

Atrial fibrillation — rate vs rhythm control, and anticoagulation

PHAR.0267PHAR.0268PHAR.0269PHAR.0270src p.1309–1312
  • Commonest arrhythmia encountered clinically. Can be paroxysmal (intermittent) or persistent (chronic). For most patients it is not immediately life-threatening; management focuses on symptom control and prevention of long-term morbidity and mortality.
Rate controlRhythm control
Control of ventricular rate while allowing atrial fibrillation to continue. Generally involves drugs that act on the AV node to slow conduction — negative dromotropic agents:
• Ca²⁺ channel blockers
• β-blockers
• Digoxin (in patients with reduced EF or CHF)
• Amiodarone (when other agents can't be used)		Restore and maintain sinus rhythm. Achieved either by synchronized direct current or by drugs — both methods must be preceded by anticoagulation:
• Class IC antiarrhythmics
• Class III antiarrhythmics

Studies show little difference between the two strategies in terms of symptom control or clinical events; the choice depends on patient characteristics and preference.

Prevention of thromboembolic events

  • IV anticoagulants — unstable patients who require immediate cardioversion.
  • Direct oral anticoagulants — in stable patients, cardioversion should be delayed for 3–4 weeks until adequate anticoagulation has been achieved.
  • Control of ventricular rate should be undertaken while the patient is waiting for cardioversion.
  • Oral anticoagulants are usually continued for at least 4 weeks after the procedure.
DLA · Cardiac Arrhythmias 1 & 2314

Practice — the DLA's own questions, plus rhythm recognition

DLA 1 question

A 58-year-old woman with coronary artery disease presents with 18 hours of palpitations, BP 100/70, pulse 150. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Flecainide is given, which works by prolonging the QRS duration. Which ECG intervals does this drug affect?

  1. AThe PR interval only
  2. BThe QRS complex only
  3. CThe QT interval only
  4. DThe QRS complex, and therefore the QT interval which contains it
  5. EThe PR and QT intervals
Answer
D. The DLA's own question. Flecainide is class IC — it markedly blocks Na⁺ channels and produces a significant increase in QRS with no change in repolarization. Because the QT interval contains the QRS, widening the QRS necessarily lengthens the measured QT even though phase 3 is untouched.
DLA 2 question

A 39-year-old man has 12 hours of palpitations after several days of binge drinking. He is dehydrated, BP 125/75, pulse 110. The ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves and a narrow QRS. Which cause from the mnemonic fits, and what is the rhythm?

  1. ASinus tachycardia; sympathetic tone
  2. BAtrial flutter; re-entry around the tricuspid annulus
  3. CAtrial fibrillation; ethanol (the 'E' of PIRATES)
  4. DMultifocal atrial tachycardia; pulmonary disease
  5. EAVRT; a concealed accessory pathway
Answer
C. Irregularly irregular + absent P waves + narrow QRS = atrial fibrillation. The binge drinking is the classic “holiday heart” presentation — E for ethanol in PIRATES: Pulmonary disease, Ischemia, Rheumatic heart disease, Age/Anemia/Atrial myxoma, Thyrotoxicosis, Ethanol, Sepsis.
DLA · Cardiac Arrhythmias 1 & 2315

Practice — the DLA's own questions, plus rhythm recognition (cont.)

PATH.50083

A rhythm strip shows progressive lengthening of the PR interval until a QRS is dropped, then the cycle repeats. Where is the block, and what are the classic causes?

  1. ABelow the bundle of His; His-Purkinje degeneration
  2. BAbove the bundle of His; excess vagal tone, myocardial infarction, digoxin toxicity
  3. CAt the SA node; hypothermia
  4. DAt the accessory pathway; congenital
  5. EComplete AV dissociation; digitalis toxicity
Answer
B. Mobitz type I (Wenckebach): gradual increase in refractoriness at the AV node, so the PR progressively prolongs until a beat is dropped. The block is above the bundle of His. Causes: excess vagal tone, myocardial infarction, digoxin toxicity. Mobitz II drops beats without PR prolongation and sits below the His bundle.
PATH.50085

A patient on a macrolide antibiotic and a tricyclic antidepressant develops a polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia whose QRS amplitude twists around the baseline. What is the rhythm, what predisposes to it, and what is the treatment?

  1. AVentricular fibrillation; hyperkalaemia; defibrillation
  2. BTorsades de pointes; QT prolongation from the 'ABCDE' drug classes and hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia; magnesium
  3. CMonomorphic VT; myocardial scar; amiodarone
  4. DAtrial flutter with aberrancy; re-entry; adenosine
  5. EAVRT; accessory pathway; ablation
Answer
B. Torsades de pointes — polymorphic VT on a background of a prolonged QT. Causes: congenital; hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia; and drugs — AntiArrhythmics (IA/IC/III), AntiBiotics (macrolides), AntipsyChotics, AntiDepressants (TCAs), AntiEmetics. Magnesium is the treatment (from the antiarrhythmics lecture).
DLA · Cardiac Arrhythmias 1 & 2316

Angina and arrhythmias — block summary

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Angina is one equation with four levers; arrhythmia is one strip read in a fixed order — rate, rhythm, P wave, PR, QRS, ST, QT — and each abnormal answer names a mechanism.
Exam Lock
The eight locks
  • Nitrates dilate veins > arteries → ↓ preload; the reflex tachycardia is why you pair them with a β-blocker.
  • Nitrate-free interval of 10–12 h prevents tolerance.
  • Nitrate + sildenafil = contraindicated.
  • β-blockers are contraindicated in variant angina and must never be stopped abruptly.
  • Ranolazine is last-line and prolongs the QT.
  • Mobitz I: PR lengthens then drops, above the His. Mobitz II: drops without warning, below the His.
  • WPW = short PR + delta wave + wide QRS (bundle of Kent).
  • PIRATES for AF; ABCDE drugs + low K/Mg/Ca for torsades.
Trap
Two traps
  • Giving a short-acting dihydropyridine alone — increased mortality unless combined with a β-blocker.
  • Cardioverting a stable patient in AF without 3–4 weeks of anticoagulation first.

The clinical reasoning skeleton — what you are actually being graded on

CPD.0.0219CPD.0.0220src p.1389, 1397–1399

SG03 — leg swelling: the interview framework and the mimics table

CPD.0.0218CPD.0.0219src p.1391–1404

Interview framework

  1. Determine onset and location
    • Is the swelling acute (< 72 hours) or chronic (> 72 hours)?
    • Is it unilateral (one leg) or bilateral (both legs)?
  2. If unilateral — ask about signs of infection
    • Redness
    • Warmth
    • Pain
  3. If bilateral — ask about underlying disease
    • Cardiovascular: heart failure symptoms (shortness of breath, fatigue)
    • Liver: history of liver disease or alcohol use
    • Kidney: foamy urine, decreased urination
    • Malnutrition: poor diet or weight loss
    • Medications: calcium-channel blockers or steroids
    • Venous insufficiency: varicose veins, leg heaviness
  4. Check for alarm symptoms.

SG04 — shortness of breath: stepwise approach and causes by system

CPD.0.0226CPD.0.0227src p.1415–1427
  1. Check stability first (ABCs) — airway, breathing, circulation. Red flag: if the patient cannot speak a full sentence without stopping to breathe, this may indicate severe respiratory distress.
  2. Classify the time course — acute develops over hours to a few days; chronic develops gradually and lasts more than 4 weeks.
  3. Characterize the dyspnea — what makes it worse, what makes it better, when does it occur (at rest, with exertion, lying flat)? Associated symptoms: chest pain, wheezing, cough, fever, leg swelling, palpitations.
  4. Assess risk factors — including family history. A family history of premature coronary disease is significant when a first-degree relative has had significant coronary heart disease before age 50 if male or age 60 if female.

Exam Lock
Deep inspiration is the fastest discriminator at the bedside
  • Pain that worsens on deep inspiration is pleuritic — PE, pneumothorax, pericarditis, pleuritis, musculoskeletal. Pain unaffected by breathing or position but reproduced by exertion is ischaemic. Pain relieved by sitting forward is pericarditis.
SG03 · SG04 · SG06 — Cardiovascular simulations & SOAP327

Practice — the small-group differentials

CPD.0.0218

A 34-year-old woman has 2 days of unilateral right calf pain and swelling after a long flight. The calf is 4 cm larger than the left, warm and tender, with no fever or sharply demarcated erythema. Which diagnosis heads the SG03 list, and which physical measurement supports it?

  1. ACellulitis; sharply demarcated erythema
  2. BDeep vein thrombosis; calf circumference difference greater than 3 cm measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity
  3. CRuptured Baker's cyst; a palpable popliteal mass
  4. DChronic venous insufficiency; medial malleolar pigmentation
  5. EErythema nodosum; bilateral anterior shin nodules
Answer
B. Acute (< 72 h), unilateral, no infective features, with a recognised risk factor. The measurement the checklist requires: palpate the tibial tuberosity, measure 10 cm below, and compare — a difference of more than 3 cm is a positive result. Erythema nodosum is bilateral and on the anterior shins; erysipelas is sharply demarcated.
CPD.0.0226

A 68-year-old man with breathlessness has bilateral pitting oedema, orthopnoea and PND. Which additional history question best separates the cardiac from the hepatic and renal causes on the SG04 list?

  1. AAsk about calf pain
  2. BAsk about frothy urine and facial swelling, and about alcohol use and liver disease
  3. CAsk about cold intolerance
  4. DAsk about recent travel
  5. EAsk about medication allergies
Answer
B. Bilateral oedema opens the systemic differential. The workbook's own cues: kidney → swelling of the face, haematuria, frothy urine, oliguria; liver → history of liver disease or alcohol use; cardiac → SOB, PND, orthopnoea, past ischaemic heart or chronic lung disease; and hypothyroidism → cold intolerance, weight gain, mood changes.
SG03 · SG04 · SG06 — Cardiovascular simulations & SOAP328

Practice — the small-group differentials (cont.)

CPD.0.0232

A 46-year-old man has sharp anterior chest pain, worse on deep inspiration and lying flat, better sitting forward, with a rub. Which of the SG06 differentials fits, and which one would be excluded by the positional relief?

  1. ACostochondritis; excluded: GERD
  2. BPericarditis; excluded: myocardial infarction, whose pain is usually unaffected by position
  3. CGERD; excluded: aortic dissection
  4. DAortic dissection; excluded: myocarditis
  5. EACS; excluded: pericarditis
Answer
B. Pericarditis: pleuritic, positional, relieved by sitting forward, with a friction rub. The CLSK lecture states it directly — the pain of myocardial infarction is usually unaffected by changes in position, though not always. Aortic dissection radiates between the scapulae with unequal pulses.

Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation

Dr Bhaktavatsalam Peta · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology. Two halves that mirror each other: drugs used to reduce clotting, and drugs used in bleeding disorders. Every drug in the first half has a matching antidote in the second.

PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation333

Hemostasis occurs in four phases — and the drug classes map onto them one-to-one

PHAR.0280src p.1521

Learn this frame first. Every drug in this lecture is an intervention on phase 2, 3 or 4.

PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation334

Phase 1 — vascular spasm · Phase 2 — the platelet plug (primary hemostasis)

PHAR.0280src p.1521–1522
Following injury to the vessel wall, the initial event is vasoconstriction, which is a transient, locally-induced phenomenon.Vascular spasm

The platelet's master switch

↑ intracellular cAMP
inhibition of platelet function — adhesion, aggregation, secretion
↑ cytosolic Ca²⁺
platelet activation

This one line explains four drug classes. The chemical signals that promote aggregation do so by decreasing cAMP or increasing Ca²⁺; therefore anything that raises cAMP (PGI₂, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, P2Y12 blockade) is antiplatelet.

Resting vs injured endothelium

Intact, healthy endothelium
  • Platelets remain unactivated
  • Endothelium releases prostacyclin (PGI₂) and nitric oxide
  • Both act as inhibitors of platelet aggregation
Damaged endothelium
  • Subendothelial layer is exposed — basal lamina of endothelial cells and smooth muscle cells
  • Platelets bind collagen via GPVI and vWF via GPIb
  • → adhesion to the subendothelium → activation

Release reaction — what comes out of the granules

  • ADP · Ca²⁺ · ATP · serotonin · vWF · platelet factor 4 (PF4) are secreted from platelet granules.
  • Most chemical signals released by activated platelets — such as ADP and thromboxane A₂ — recruit and activate more platelets.
  • Activation exposes GP IIb/IIIa, whose ligand is fibrinogen. Fibrinogen forms bridges between adjacent platelets — this is the final common pathway of aggregation.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation335

Phase 3 — coagulation · Phase 4 — fibrinolysis · and the endothelium's own brakes

PHAR.0280 · PHAR.0281src p.1523–1524

Secondary hemostasis

  • The coagulation cascade is a sequence of enzymatic events; the coagulation factors are generally serine proteases circulating as inactive zymogens.
  • Thrombin, a serine protease, catalyses the conversion of fibrinogen → fibrin — the last step of the cascade.
  • Subsequent cross-linking of fibrin strands stabilises the clot and forms the hemostatic plug.

Anticoagulant factors secreted by the endothelium after vascular injury

Endothelial factorWhat it does
Prostacyclin (PGI₂)Eicosanoid; increases cAMP within platelets → inhibits platelet activation. Also a vasodilator — relaxes vascular smooth muscle by increasing cAMP.
Antithrombin IIIInhibits the clotting-factor proteases — thrombin, IXa and Xa. This is the target heparin exploits.
Proteins C and SVitamin-K-dependent anticoagulant proteins. Remember this: it is the reason warfarin can cause skin necrosis.
Tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI)Inhibits the extrinsic pathway.
Tissue-type plasminogen activator (t-PA)Starts tertiary hemostasis — the endogenous molecule that alteplase reproduces.

Vitamin K sits on both sides of the balance
  • Vitamin K is required for factors II, VII, IX and X *and* for the anticoagulant proteins C and S (PHAR.0281). A drug that blocks vitamin K therefore lowers procoagulants and anticoagulants — and the anticoagulants fall first.

Check — hemostasis and the map

PHAR.0280

A drug raises intracellular cAMP inside the platelet. What is the predicted effect on platelet function, and which endogenous mediator works the same way?

  1. AActivation; thromboxane A₂
  2. BInhibition; prostacyclin (PGI₂)
  3. CInhibition; ADP
  4. DActivation; prostacyclin (PGI₂)
  5. ENo effect; nitric oxide acts only on smooth muscle
Answer
B. Elevation of intracellular cAMP results in the inhibition of platelet function — adhesion, aggregation and secretion. PGI₂, secreted by healthy endothelium, is the endogenous mediator that raises platelet cAMP (and also vasodilates by raising cAMP in smooth muscle). ADP and TXA₂ do the opposite: they decrease cAMP or increase Ca²⁺.
PHAR.0283

Which receptor pair does the platelet use to adhere to exposed subendothelium, and which receptor is the final common pathway for aggregation?

  1. AGPIIb/IIIa for collagen and GPIb for fibrinogen; final pathway GPVI
  2. BGPVI for collagen and GPIb for vWF; final pathway GP IIb/IIIa
  3. CP2Y12 for ADP and GPVI for vWF; final pathway GPIb
  4. DGPIb for collagen and GPVI for vWF; final pathway P2Y12
  5. EPAR-1 for thrombin and GPVI for collagen; final pathway GPIb
Answer
B. The reading is explicit: platelets have collagen receptors (GPVI) and vWF receptors (GPIb), and activation of GP IIb/IIIa — the fibrinogen receptor — is the final common pathway for platelet aggregation. That is why GP IIb/IIIa blockers are the most complete antiplatelets.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation339

Check — hemostasis and the map (cont.)

PHAR.0282

A 66-year-old is admitted with an occlusive thrombus in the left anterior descending artery. Which compositional feature best explains why an antiplatelet, not warfarin, is the chronic secondary prevention?

  1. AArterial thrombi are fibrin-rich and warfarin cannot reach fibrin
  2. BArterial thrombi are platelet-rich, forming on a ruptured plaque under high shear
  3. CWarfarin is contraindicated after any myocardial infarction
  4. DArterial thrombi contain no fibrinogen
  5. EAntiplatelets dissolve established arterial thrombi
Answer
B. Arterial ("white") thrombi are platelet-rich and form on ruptured plaque; venous ("red") thrombi are fibrin-rich and form in stasis. The composition dictates the class. Note option 5's trap: antiplatelets and anticoagulants prevent thrombus formation but are ineffective against pre-existing clots — only thrombolytics lyse them.

Platelet aggregation inhibitors · Anticoagulants · Thrombolytics

Platelet aggregation inhibitors — the four subclasses

PHAR.0283src p.1525 · 1547–1550
Platelet aggregation inhibitors decrease formation or action of chemical signals that promote platelet aggregation. These agents are beneficial in the prevention and treatment of occlusive cardiovascular diseases, maintenance of vascular grafts and arterial patency, and as adjuncts in the therapy of MI.Reading notes
  1. Cyclooxygenase inhibitors — aspirin
  2. ADP receptor (P2Y12) blockers — clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor, cangrelor
  3. Phosphodiesterase inhibitors — dipyridamole, cilostazol
  4. Blockers of GP IIb/IIIa receptors — abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation342

Aspirin — irreversible acetylation, and why the platelet never recovers

PHAR.0283src p.1525 · 1551–1555
  • Thromboxane A₂ causes platelets to change shape, release their granules and aggregate.
  • Aspirin inhibits TXA₂ synthesis by irreversible acetylation of COX.
  • The anuclear platelet cannot synthesise new proteins — therefore it cannot synthesise new enzyme during its 10-day lifetime.

Uses — verbatim

  • To reduce the risk of death and MI in patients with coronary artery disease.
  • To reduce the risk of death and recurrent stroke in patients who had an ischemic stroke or a TIA.
Exam Lock
The anuclear-platelet argument is the whole answer
  • Any question asking *why aspirin's antiplatelet effect outlasts its plasma half-life*, or *why 5–7 days must elapse before surgery*, is answered by the same sentence: irreversible COX acetylation in a cell that cannot make new protein, so the effect lasts the platelet's 10-day lifetime and recovers only as new platelets are produced.
Trap
Aspirin is not the same as the other NSAIDs here
  • In the MI appendix the lecture states that nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (except aspirin) should be discontinued — reversible COX inhibitors compete for the same site and can blunt aspirin's irreversible effect, and they carry their own cardiovascular risk.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation343

P2Y12 (ADP receptor) blockers — clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor, cangrelor

PHAR.0283src p.1526 · 1557–1565
  • ADP is a mediator of platelet aggregation. P2Y12 is one of the two subtypes of ADP receptor on the platelet surface. P2Y12 is coupled to Gi.
  • These drugs are antagonists of P2Y12. Blockade increases cAMP — therefore they reduce platelet aggregation by inhibiting ADP binding.
DrugProdrug?MechanismRoute
ClopidogrelProdrugIrreversible antagonist of P2Y12Oral
PrasugrelProdrugIrreversible antagonist of P2Y12Oral
TicagrelorDrugReversible antagonist of P2Y12Oral

Reproduced from the lecture's own summary table (source pp. 1562–1564).

Uses

  • Treatment of acute coronary syndromes (ACS).
  • Preventive treatment of patients at risk of thromboembolism, myocardial infarction or stroke.
Bottom Line
Two axes, four drugs
  • Prodrug vs drug on one axis; reversible vs irreversible on the other. Clopidogrel and prasugrel are the prodrugs and the irreversible pair; ticagrelor and cangrelor are the active drugs and the reversible pair. Cangrelor is the only IV agent — which is why it is the one used when you need P2Y12 blockade *now* in the cath lab.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation344

Clopidogrel pharmacogenetics — the CYP2C19 story, in the three forms it is examined

PHAR.0284 · PHAR.0285src p.1559–1561
Question the exam asksThe lecture's answer
Why is clopidogrel's effect variable between patients?Clopidogrel is a prodrug converted to an active metabolite mainly by CYP2C19. Patients who are CYP2C19 poor metabolizers have lower plasma levels of the active metabolite — alternative treatments should be considered for them.
Which common drug must not be co-prescribed, and why?Omeprazole, a CYP2C19 inhibitor, reduces plasma levels of the active metabolite of clopidogrel. Concurrent use of clopidogrel and omeprazole should be avoided. More generally: concomitant use of clopidogrel and CYP2C19 inhibitors should be avoided.
Why does prasugrel not have this problem?Prasugrel is also a prodrug and requires hepatic activation by several P450 enzymes, but polymorphisms have no effect on prasugrel activation. Its activation is more efficient: most of the absorbed prasugrel undergoes activation, versus only 15% of absorbed clopidogrel
Exam Lock
15% and "no effect"
  • Two numbers carry this objective: only 15% of absorbed clopidogrel is activated, and polymorphisms have no effect on prasugrel. If a stem gives you a poor metabolizer on a PPI with recurrent stent thrombosis, the answer is to switch agent — prasugrel or ticagrelor — not to raise the clopidogrel dose.

Blockers of platelet GP IIb/IIIa receptors

  • The GP IIb/IIIa receptor is the receptor for fibrinogen. Activation of this receptor is the final common pathway for platelet aggregation.

Check — antiplatelets

PHAR.0285

A 61-year-old with a drug-eluting stent is on clopidogrel and develops reflux. Which acid-suppressing strategy is contraindicated by this lecture, and what is the mechanism?

  1. ARanitidine, because it induces CYP2C19
  2. BOmeprazole, because it inhibits CYP2C19 and lowers the active metabolite of clopidogrel
  3. COmeprazole, because it displaces clopidogrel from plasma proteins
  4. DAny PPI, because they irreversibly acetylate COX
  5. EPantoprazole, because it is a P2Y12 agonist
Answer
B. Concurrent use of clopidogrel and omeprazole should be avoided — omeprazole is a CYP2C19 inhibitor, and CYP2C19 is the enzyme that converts the clopidogrel prodrug to its active metabolite. Less active metabolite, less P2Y12 blockade, more stent thrombosis.
PHAR.0283

Which single agent blocks the final common pathway of platelet aggregation, and what is its molecular nature?

  1. AAspirin — a small-molecule irreversible COX acetylator
  2. BClopidogrel — a thienopyridine prodrug
  3. CAbciximab — a chimeric mouse–human monoclonal antibody against GP IIb/IIIa
  4. DDipyridamole — a phosphodiesterase inhibitor
  5. EFondaparinux — a synthetic pentasaccharide
Answer
C. GP IIb/IIIa is the fibrinogen receptor and its activation is the final common pathway for aggregation. Abciximab is the chimeric mouse–human monoclonal antibody against it; eptifibatide and tirofiban are the other two blockers. All three are adjuncts to PCI.
PHAR.0283

  1. ADipyridamole
  2. BCilostazol
  3. CTicagrelor
  4. DAbciximab
  5. EAspirin plus extended-release dipyridamole
Answer
B. Cilostazol — a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that promotes vasodilation and inhibits aggregation — is the agent listed for intermittent claudication. Aspirin + extended-release dipyridamole is the combination for secondary prophylaxis of cerebrovascular disease.

Anticoagulants — the four subclasses, and the heparin family

PHAR.0286 · PHAR.0287src p.1528 · 1573–1577
  1. Indirect thrombin and factor Xa inhibitors — UFH, LMWH (enoxaparin), fondaparinux
  2. Vitamin K antagonists — warfarin
  3. Direct thrombin inhibitors — parenteral (desirudin, bivalirudin, argatroban) and oral (dabigatran)
  4. Direct factor Xa inhibitors — apixaban, rivaroxaban

What heparin is

  • Heparin is an injectable, rapidly acting anticoagulant often used acutely to interfere with the formation of thrombi.
  • A heterogeneous mixture of straight-chain, sulfated mucopolysaccharides, isolated from bovine lung or porcine intestinal mucosa.
  • Normally occurs as a macromolecule complexed with histamine in mast cells.
UFHLMWH (e.g. enoxaparin)

PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation348

Heparin's mechanism — one geometric rule generates the entire UFH/LMWH table

PHAR.0286 · PHAR.0287src p.1528–1529 · 1578–1583
  • Antithrombin III inhibits the clotting-factor proteases thrombin (IIa), IXa and Xa — but in the absence of heparin it does so very slowly.
  • Binding of heparin to ATIII accelerates the inhibition: heparin functions as a cofactor for the antithrombin–protease reaction.
  • UFH efficiently inactivates both thrombin and factor Xa. LMWH efficiently inhibit Xa but have less effect on thrombin — the short chain cannot form the ternary complex needed to inactivate IIa.

The two-line version
  • aPTT → intrinsic + common → UFH and parenteral DTIs. PT/INR → extrinsic + common → warfarin. Everything modern (LMWH, fondaparinux, DOACs) is predictable and unmonitored; that predictability *is* the selling point.

Uses

  • Pulmonary embolism
  • Myocardial infarction

Adverse effects

EffectDetail and management
BleedingExcessive anticoagulant action is treated by discontinuance of the drug. If bleeding occurs, protamine sulfate is given.

PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation351

HIT type II — the self-amplifying loop, and why you cannot simply stop the heparin

PHAR.0288 · PHAR.0290src p.1530 · 1588–1601
Exam Lock
Management of HIT (PHAR.0290) — verbatim
  • Patients are treated by discontinuance of heparin and administration of a direct thrombin or factor X inhibitor (argatroban, bivalirudin, dabigatran, apixaban, rivaroxaban) or fondaparinux.
Trap
Stopping heparin alone is the wrong answer
  • HIT type II is a prothrombotic state — the antibodies activate platelets. Removing the trigger does not remove the circulating immune complexes or the activated platelets, so an alternative anticoagulant must be started. Note also that warfarin alone is not on the list.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation352

Fondaparinux — the pentasaccharide alone

PHAR.0286 · PHAR.0287src p.1602 · 1538
  • Synthetic pentasaccharide — the sequence of five carbohydrates that binds to antithrombin III.
  • Specific inhibitor of Xa, with negligible antithrombin (IIa) activity.
  • Approved for prevention and treatment of DVT.
  • Also listed in this lecture's summary as a treatment option in HIT.
Bottom Line
Why fondaparinux is the cleanest illustration of the mechanism
  • It is *only* the ATIII-binding pentasaccharide — no chain at all. So by the ternary-complex rule it must be a pure anti-Xa agent with no effect on thrombin. UFH → both; LMWH → mostly Xa; fondaparinux → Xa only. The gradient follows chain length exactly.
Trap
Protamine does not fully rescue these
  • Protamine sulfate partially reverses LMWH and is inactive against fondaparinux.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation353

Check — heparins

PHAR.0287

Why does LMWH inhibit factor Xa efficiently but have little effect on thrombin?

  1. ALMWH does not bind antithrombin III
  2. BThe short chain cannot bridge ATIII and thrombin into a ternary complex, which Xa inactivation does not require
  3. CLMWH binds thrombin's exosite rather than its active site
  4. DThrombin is not inhibited by antithrombin III
  5. ELMWH is a direct thrombin inhibitor
Answer
B. Both bind ATIII through the same pentasaccharide. The difference is purely geometric: inactivation of IIa requires a ternary complex in which the heparin chain binds ATIII and thrombin simultaneously — LMWH is too short. The ternary complex is not necessary to accelerate inactivation of Xa by ATIII. Note ATIII does inhibit thrombin, IXa and Xa — just very slowly without heparin.
PHAR.0290

Day 7 of UFH for a DVT: platelets have fallen from 240 to 62 ×10⁹/L and the patient has a new right-leg arterial occlusion. What is the correct management?

  1. AStop heparin and observe
  2. BStop heparin and transfuse platelets
  3. CStop heparin and start argatroban
  4. DStop heparin and start warfarin monotherapy
  5. EContinue heparin and add aspirin
Answer
C. This is HIT type II — immune-mediated, and characteristically thrombocytopenia *with* thrombosis. The lecture's management is discontinue heparin and give a direct thrombin or factor X inhibitor (argatroban, bivalirudin, dabigatran, apixaban, rivaroxaban) or fondaparinux. Observation alone leaves a prothrombotic state untreated. Contrast HIT type I: common, mild, nonimmunologic, within the first 5 days.

Check — heparins (cont.)

PHAR.0286

A pregnant woman at 26 weeks is diagnosed with a proximal DVT. Which agent does this lecture identify, and what disqualifies the main alternative?

  1. AWarfarin; heparin cannot be used in pregnancy
  2. BHeparin; warfarin crosses the placenta and is pregnancy category X
  3. CRivaroxaban; it is the only DOAC studied as monotherapy
  4. DAlteplase; the clot is established
  5. EAspirin; the thrombus is platelet-rich

B. Heparin is listed as the drug of choice during pregnancy. Warfarin crosses the placenta and can cause a hemorrhagic disorder in the fetus and serious birth defects; it should never be administered during pregnancy — category X. Option 4's trap: thrombolysis is reserved for acute massive PE, not routine DVT.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation355

Warfarin — the vitamin K cycle and the delay it creates

PHAR.0281 · PHAR.0286src p.1531 · 1605–1607
  • Factors II, VII, IX and X undergo a vitamin-K-dependent post-translational modification in which glutamic acid residues are carboxylated to γ-carboxyglutamic acid.
  • Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase — treatment results in the production of inactive clotting factors, because they lack the γ-carboxyglutamyl side chains.
  • Warfarin was initially used as a rodenticide.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation356

Warfarin — the timing numbers, and why the heparin bridge exists

PHAR.0286 · PHAR.0291src p.1532 · 1607–1610

Time to peak effect72 – 96 h

Exam Lock
The bridging rule, verbatim
  • For treatment of acute venous thromboembolism, heparin, LMWH, or fondaparinux is usually continued for at least 5 days after warfarin therapy is begun, and until the INR is in the therapeutic range on 2 consecutive days. This overlap allows for adequate depletion of the vitamin-K-dependent coagulation factors.
Bottom Line
Why the delay, in one sentence
  • Warfarin stops new factor synthesis; it does nothing to factors already circulating. The onset is therefore governed by the half-life of the longest-lived factor (up to 60 h) — which is exactly why a fast parenteral agent must cover the first days.

Warfarin — uses, adverse effects and reversal

PHAR.0286 · PHAR.0289 · PHAR.0292src p.1610–1613

Uses

  • Prevention and treatment of DVT and PE, following an initial course of heparin — "to prevent the progression or recurrence of acute DVT or pulmonary embolism".
  • Prevention and treatment of thromboembolic complications associated with atrial fibrillation.

Adverse effects and their management

Adverse effectManagement (verbatim)
Hemorrhage — the main adverse effectMinor bleeding: withdrawal of the drug, or oral vitamin K. Severe bleeding: greater doses of vitamin K. For rapid reversal: fresh/frozen plasma.
Warfarin-induced skin necrosisOccurs in patients with deficiencies of protein C or S. Warfarin lowers proteins C or S before it lowers factor X and factor II — the result is thrombosis. Treatment: discontinuation of warfarin and reversal with vitamin K if needed; UFH or LMWH should be given to patients with thrombosis.
Fetal harmWarfarin crosses the placenta → hemorrhagic disorder in the fetus and serious birth defects. Never administer during pregnancy. Pregnancy category X.
Exam Lock
Skin necrosis is a protein C/S problem, not a bleeding problem
  • The paradox resolves once you remember PHAR.0281: proteins C and S are vitamin-K-dependent anticoagulants with short half-lives, so warfarin creates a transient hypercoagulable window before the procoagulant factors fall. That is why the treatment includes heparin, not more warfarin.

PHAR.0292

On day 3 of warfarin (started without a parenteral agent) a woman develops painful purpuric skin lesions over the breast and thigh that progress to necrosis. What is the underlying mechanism and the correct treatment?

  1. AWarfarin hypersensitivity; give corticosteroids
  2. BProtein C or S deficiency — these fall before factors II and X, causing thrombosis; stop warfarin, give vitamin K if needed, and give UFH or LMWH
  3. CExcess anticoagulation; give fresh frozen plasma alone
  4. DHIT type II; give argatroban
  5. EVitamin K excess; restrict dietary vitamin K
Answer
B. Warfarin-induced skin necrosis occurs in patients with deficiencies of protein C or S; warfarin lowers proteins C or S before it lowers factor X and factor II — the result is thrombosis. Treatment is discontinuation of warfarin and reversal with vitamin K if needed; UFH or LMWH should be given to patients with thrombosis. It is a clotting problem being treated with an anticoagulant — that is the counter-intuitive step.
PHAR.0293

A patient on warfarin for AF is started on a new drug and the INR climbs from 2.4 to 6.1. Which of these could be responsible?

  2. BCarbamazepine
  3. CPhenytoin
  4. DMetronidazole
  5. EBarbiturates
Answer
D. Metronidazole is on the lecture's list of drugs that inhibit warfarin metabolism, thereby potentiating anticoagulation — INR rises, bleeding risk rises. The other four (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, barbiturates) are the four inducers that reduce anticoagulation. Full inhibitor list: cimetidine, chloramphenicol, disulfiram, fluconazole, metronidazole, TMP-SMX.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation364

Check — warfarin, DTIs and DOACs (cont.)

PHAR.0295

A 58-year-old with an unprovoked proximal DVT wants to avoid injections entirely. Which regimen is supported, and which DOAC would NOT satisfy the request?

  1. ADabigatran monotherapy; rivaroxaban would need a lead-in
  2. BRivaroxaban or apixaban monotherapy; dabigatran would require a parenteral lead-in
  3. CWarfarin monotherapy; all DOACs need a lead-in
  4. DFondaparinux monotherapy; all oral agents need a lead-in
  5. EAny DOAC; none require pre-treatment
Answer
B. Rivaroxaban and apixaban are the only direct oral anticoagulants that have been studied and approved as monotherapy (no pre-treatment with heparin) for the treatment of VTE. Dabigatran requires parenteral anticoagulants transitioning to dabigatran, and warfarin requires a ≥ 5-day bridge.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation365

Thrombolytics and their mirror image — the plasmin axis

PHAR.0296src p.1535 · 1624–1625
  • Anticoagulants prevent formation of thrombi but are ineffective against pre-existing clots.
  • Thrombolytic drugs lyse blood clots and restore the patency of obstructed vessels before distal tissue necrosis occurs.
  • They act by converting plasminogen to plasmin.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation366

Fibrin-specific vs non-fibrin-specific — and the five agents

PHAR.0296 · PHAR.0297src p.1536–1537 · 1626–1629
Non-fibrin-specificFibrin-specific
AgentsStreptokinase · urokinaseAlteplase · reteplase · tenecteplase
OriginStreptokinase: protein produced by β-hemolytic streptococci. Urokinase: human enzyme synthesized by the kidney and found in the urine.t-PA is a serine protease produced by human endothelial cells. Alteplase is recombinant t-PA; reteplase and tenecteplase are recombinant variants with longer half-lives.
BehaviourCatalyse systemic fibrinolysisLow affinity for free plasminogen in the plasma; preferentially activate plasminogen bound to fibrin in a thrombus or hemostatic plug. They accumulate onto the thrombus, degrading fibrin without evoking systemic fibrinolysis.
Preferred?—Fibrin-specific agents are preferred.

Alteplase's biological half-life is 3–6 minutes — which is why reteplase and tenecteplase, engineered for longer half-lives, are convenient for bolus dosing in STEMI.

Appendix 1 — management of myocardial infarction

PHAR.0298 · PHAR.0299src p.1539–1540

Initial management

  • A 12-lead ECG should be performed and interpreted at the site of first medical contact (FMC).
  • Give: Aspirin · Oxygen · Nitroglycerin · Morphine.
  • Intravenous morphine should be avoided if possible and reserved for patients with an unacceptable level of pain.
  • Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (except aspirin) should be discontinued.

Revascularization strategies

StrategyWhat it isAdjunctive therapy
Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)Improve blood supply to the ischemic tissue — most commonly ballooning the narrow segment or deploying a stent to keep the artery open.Antiplatelet: aspirin + an ADP receptor blocker; plus a GP IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist in high-risk patients. Anticoagulant: UFH or bivalirudin.
Fibrinolytic therapyOnly for STEMI.Fibrin-specific agents preferred.
Trap
"MONA" is not a priority order
  • The lecture lists aspirin, oxygen, nitroglycerin and morphine — but explicitly de-emphasises morphine (avoid IV morphine if possible) and removes non-aspirin NSAIDs. Reflex mnemonics are exactly where these two modifiers get lost.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation369

Appendix 2 — secondary prevention of ischemic stroke

PHAR.0300src p.1541–1542

Lifestyle modifications (verbatim)

  • Regular aerobic activity is indicated.
  • Sodium intake should be reduced; a Mediterranean-type diet is recommended.
  • In patients who are overweight or obese, weight loss is recommended to improve the ASCVD risk factor profile.
  • Patients who smoke should be advised to quit; heavy drinkers should eliminate or reduce alcohol consumption.

Antiplatelet therapy

  • For patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIA, antiplatelet agents are recommended to reduce the risk of recurrent stroke and other cardiovascular events.
  • Options: aspirin monotherapy · clopidogrel monotherapy · aspirin + dipyridamole.
  • Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel) is NOT recommended long term due to the risk of hemorrhage. Short term, dual antiplatelet therapy may be used.
Exam Lock
Long term vs short term is the whole point
  • DAPT after a noncardioembolic stroke/TIA is a short-term strategy only; extending it long term trades ischemic benefit for hemorrhage. Note also the word noncardioembolic — a cardioembolic stroke (e.g. AF) is an anticoagulation problem, not an antiplatelet one.

Summary 2 — the ten discriminators this lecture is examined on

src p.1521–1642
  1. Arterial = platelet-rich → antiplatelet. Venous = fibrin-rich → anticoagulant.
  2. ↑ cAMP inhibits platelets; ↑ Ca²⁺ activates them. Every antiplatelet mechanism reduces to this.
  3. Aspirin is irreversible in an anuclear cell → effect lasts the platelet's 10-day lifetime.
  4. Clopidogrel is a CYP2C19 prodrug — only 15% activated; avoid omeprazole; poor metabolizers need a different agent. Prasugrel is unaffected by polymorphisms.
  5. Ternary complex is needed for IIa, not for Xa → UFH hits both, LMWH mostly Xa, fondaparinux Xa only.
  6. aPTT → UFH and parenteral DTIs. PT/INR → warfarin. Nothing → LMWH, fondaparinux, DOACs.
  7. HIT II: stop heparin AND start a DTI/Xa inhibitor or fondaparinux. Stopping alone is wrong.
  8. Warfarin: peak 72–96 h; bridge ≥ 5 days and until INR therapeutic ×2 days; category X; skin necrosis = protein C/S.
  9. Only rivaroxaban and apixaban are monotherapy for VTE. Dabigatran needs a parenteral lead-in.
  10. Alteplase for ischemic stroke within 3–4.5 hours; reteplase and tenecteplase are STEMI only.
Bottom Line
If you have five minutes before the exam
  • Read the drug table on the previous slide top-to-bottom once, then answer this question out loud for each row: *what is its antidote, and what does it get monitored with?* Almost every coagulation question is one of those two axes.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation375

Block exam — Drugs used in disorders of coagulation

PHAR.0296 · PHAR.0297 · PHAR.0300

A 72-year-old presents 2 hours after sudden right hemiparesis and expressive aphasia. CT shows no hemorrhage. Which drug is indicated, and what property makes it preferable to streptokinase?

  1. ATenecteplase; it has the longest half-life
  2. BAlteplase; it is fibrin-specific, with low affinity for free plasma plasminogen, so it acts on the thrombus without evoking systemic fibrinolysis
  3. CUrokinase; it is human-derived and therefore non-antigenic
  4. DStreptokinase; it produces the most complete systemic lysis
  5. EAspirin plus clopidogrel; the thrombus is platelet-rich
Answer
B. Alteplase is the only agent this lecture lists for acute ischemic stroke, started within 3–4.5 hours of onset in a patient with a measurable neurologic deficit. It is fibrin-specific: low affinity for free plasminogen, preferential activation of fibrin-bound plasminogen, accumulation onto the thrombus, degradation of fibrin without evoking systemic fibrinolysis. Reteplase and tenecteplase are listed for acute STEMI only.
PHAR.0286

Which statement about antithrombin III is correct as this lecture presents it?

  1. AATIII inhibits thrombin, IXa and Xa rapidly, and heparin slows this down
  2. BATIII inhibits thrombin, IXa and Xa very slowly in the absence of heparin; heparin acts as a cofactor that accelerates the reaction
  3. CATIII is inhibited by heparin, releasing free thrombin
  4. DATIII is a vitamin-K-dependent factor
  5. EATIII is secreted by platelets during the release reaction
Answer
B. Antithrombin III inhibits clotting factor proteases — thrombin, IXa and Xa. In the absence of heparin, antithrombin III inhibits them very slowly. Binding of heparin to antithrombin III accelerates the inhibition; heparin functions as a cofactor for the antithrombin–protease reaction. ATIII is an endothelial anticoagulant factor (with PGI₂, proteins C and S, TFPI and t-PA); the vitamin-K-dependent proteins are II, VII, IX, X, C and S.
PHAR.0289 · PHAR.0302

A man on long-term warfarin for AF requires urgent surgery for a bleeding duodenal ulcer; INR is 6.8. What achieves the fastest correction?

  1. AOral vitamin K
  2. BParenteral vitamin K alone
  3. CFresh-frozen plasma
  4. DProtamine sulfate
  5. EIdarucizumab
Answer
C. Vitamin K works by allowing new γ-carboxylated factors to be synthesised, so reversal following administration of vitamin K takes approximately 24 h. For rapid reversal — immediate hemostasis — fresh/frozen plasma is infused, because it supplies the factors directly. Protamine antagonises heparin, not warfarin; idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation376

Block exam — Drugs used in disorders of coagulation (cont.)

PHAR.0289 · PHAR.0302

Which pairing of anticoagulant and its reversal agent is INCORRECT?

  1. AUnfractionated heparin — protamine sulfate
  2. BDabigatran — idarucizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody Fab fragment
  3. CRivaroxaban — andexanet alfa, a modified factor Xa decoy
  4. DFondaparinux — protamine sulfate
  5. EWarfarin — vitamin K
Answer
D. Protamine can partially reverse the anticoagulant effects of LMWHs but is inactive against fondaparinux. The other four pairings are exactly as the lecture gives them. Remember protamine works electrostatically — a cationic, arginine-rich protein complexing anionic heparin — and fondaparinux is too small a pentasaccharide for that interaction to neutralise.
PHAR.0287

Which of these is a property of LMWH relative to UFH, per the lecture's comparison?

  1. ALower bioavailability and shorter half-life
  2. BHigher bioavailability, longer half-life, less frequent dosing, equal efficacy
  3. CGreater effect on thrombin than on factor Xa
  4. DRequires routine aPTT monitoring
  5. EMolecular weight 5,000–30,000
Answer
B. LMWH have equal efficacy to UFH, higher bioavailability, longer half-life, and less frequent dosing requirements, and are replacing UFH in many clinical settings. Their MW is 1,000–5,000 (UFH is 5,000–30,000), they efficiently inhibit Xa but have less effect on thrombin, and monitoring is not usually necessary (anti-Xa assay if needed).
PHAR.0298 · PHAR.0299

A patient undergoing PCI for NSTEMI is high-risk. According to Appendix 1, which combination of adjunctive antithrombotic therapy is described?

  1. AAspirin alone plus warfarin
  2. BAspirin + an ADP receptor blocker + a GP IIb/IIIa antagonist, with UFH or bivalirudin
  3. CFibrinolytic therapy plus fondaparinux
  4. DClopidogrel alone with LMWH
  5. EAspirin + dipyridamole with argatroban
Answer
B. For PCI the lecture gives Antiplatelet therapy: aspirin + ADP receptor blocker; additionally a GP IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist in high-risk patients. Anticoagulant therapy: UFH or bivalirudin. Note also that fibrinolytic therapy is only for STEMI, which rules out option 3 for an NSTEMI.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation377

Block exam — Drugs used in disorders of coagulation (cont.)

PHAR.0301 · PHAR.0303

A haemophilia A patient has persistent oral bleeding after a dental extraction despite factor replacement. Which adjunct does this lecture name, and what is its mechanism?

  1. AProtamine sulfate; complexes anionic heparin
  2. BTranexamic acid; inhibits plasminogen activation
  3. CVitamin K; restores γ-carboxylation
  4. DAlteplase; converts plasminogen to plasmin
  5. EAndexanet alfa; decoy factor Xa
Answer
B. Aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid inhibit plasminogen activation and are used as adjunctive therapy in hemophilia, and therapy for bleeding from fibrinolytic therapy. They are the exact mirror of the thrombolytics on the plasmin axis. Note the lecture's own line on plasma fractions: factor VIII deficiency and factor IX deficiency account for most of the heritable coagulation defects.
PHAR.0286

Which statement about the timing of warfarin therapy is correct?

  1. APeak anticoagulant effect occurs within 6 hours
  2. BThe anticoagulant effect is apparent within 24 h, peaks at 72–96 h, and a single dose lasts 2–5 days
  3. CA single dose lasts 12 hours because factor VII has a short half-life
  4. DThe onset is immediate because warfarin inactivates circulating factors
  5. EOverlap with heparin is unnecessary if the INR is above 2 on day 1
Answer
B. The coagulation factors involved have half-lives of 6–60 hours; the anticoagulant effect is apparent within 24 h; peak effect may take 72–96 h; a single dose lasts 2–5 days. Warfarin does not touch circulating factors — it blocks synthesis of functional new ones, which is why the overlap rule exists: heparin/LMWH/fondaparinux for at least 5 days after warfarin is begun and until the INR is therapeutic on 2 consecutive days.
PHAR.0291

Which pairing of monitoring test and pathway is correct?

  1. AaPTT — extrinsic and common; PT/INR — intrinsic and common
  2. BaPTT — intrinsic and common; PT/INR — extrinsic and common
  3. CBoth test the common pathway only
  4. DaPTT — extrinsic only; PT — intrinsic only
  5. EAnti-Xa assay is required for all DOACs
Answer
B. The aPTT is a test of the integrity of the intrinsic and common pathways (used for UFH and parenteral DTIs); the PT — expressed as the INR — is a test of the extrinsic and common pathways (used for warfarin, every 2–4 weeks). DOACs do not require monitoring; LMWH potency can be assessed with an anti-factor Xa assay but this is not routine.
PHAR · Drugs Used in Disorders of Coagulation378

Block exam — Drugs used in disorders of coagulation (cont.)

PHAR.0286 · PHAR.0290

Which drug is a synthetic pentasaccharide with negligible antithrombin activity, approved for prevention and treatment of DVT and usable in HIT?

  1. AEnoxaparin
  2. BFondaparinux
  3. CBivalirudin
  4. DDabigatran
  5. EUnfractionated heparin
Answer
B. Fondaparinux — a synthetic pentasaccharide, the sequence of five carbohydrates that bind to antithrombin III, a specific inhibitor of Xa with negligible antithrombin activity, approved for prevention and treatment of DVT. The lecture's summary table lists its uses as VTE and HIT. Enoxaparin is a LMWH (a chain, not a bare pentasaccharide); bivalirudin and dabigatran are direct thrombin inhibitors.
