L17 · Introduction to Renal Pathology381

Review of the kidney, and the three compartments

PATH.6001PATH.6003src p.1021–1022
Anatomy
  • Part of the urinary system: upper (2 kidneys + 2 ureters), lower (bladder + urethra)
  • Bilateral retroperitoneal organs divided into cortex and medulla
  • 135–160 g in weight
  • 10–12 cm long, 5–7 cm wide, 2–3 cm thick
Functions
  • Filters blood to form urine
  • Reabsorption and secretion of molecules and electrolytes
  • Endocrine function — renin, EPO, prostaglandins
  • Acid-base balance
  • Vitamin D activation
  • Excretion of waste products such as nitrogen
Causes of renal disease, by compartment
  • 1. Glomerular disorders — usually immune mediated damage
  • 2. Tubules and interstitium — usually toxic, ischemic or infectious in etiology
  • 3. Vasculature — local or systemic disorder
Exam Lock
The compartment triad is the diagnostic algorithm
  • Glomerulus → immune. Tubule/interstitium → toxic, ischaemic, infectious. Vessels → local or systemic vascular disease. Every lecture that follows sits in exactly one of these three rows, and the urinalysis tells you which.
L17 · Introduction to Renal Pathology382

Acute kidney injury — the pre-renal / renal / post-renal split, by BUN:Cr

PATH.6003src p.1023
CategoryThink…BUN : CrCauses
Pre-renalINADEQUATE BLOOD FLOWmore than 20 : 1Heart failure · sepsis · severe bleeding (trauma, surgery, gastrointestinal bleeds, chronic bleeding) · volume depletion · certain drugs like NSAIDs that reduce renal perfusion
Renal / intra-renal / intrinsic (congenital or acquired)RENAL PARENCHYMA10–15 : 1, or less than 20 : 1Glomerular disease · tubulo-interstitial disease · renal vessel disease
Post-renalURINARY TRACT OBSTRUCTION10–20 : 1Tumors · benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) · nephrolithiasis
Bottom Line
Why pre-renal raises the ratio
  • Urea is reabsorbed with sodium and water; creatinine is not. When perfusion falls, avid proximal reabsorption drags urea back with it, so BUN rises out of proportion to creatinine — hence a ratio above 20:1. Once the tubule itself is injured, that reabsorption fails and the ratio falls back toward 10–15:1.
L17 · Introduction to Renal Pathology383

Acute vs chronic kidney disease

PATH.6003PATH.6004src p.1024–1026
Acute kidney diseaseChronic kidney disease
TempoDevelops suddenly and lasts a short time, often only a few days or weeksDevelops slowly and may worsen over months to years
DefinitionRapid decline of GFR within hours to days · dysregulation of fluid and electrolyte balance · retention of metabolic wastes · azotemia (elevation of blood nitrogen products)Reduced GFR persistently less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m² for at least 3 months from any cause, with persistent albuminuria · anemia · symptoms of uremia
Normal reference—Normal GFR is 120 (women) and 130 (men) mL/min/1.73 m²
Context—Seen as a complication of comorbid conditions such as diabetes, hypertension and autoimmune diseases. Can progress to end-stage renal disease — GFR less than 5% of normal
Biopsy / imaging—Renal biopsies are rarely taken in patients with known chronic kidney failure. Clinical imaging may show small, shrunken kidneys; a predominance of glomerulosclerosis or interstitial fibrosis argues strongly for chronic disease

General clinical symptoms and signs of renal disease

  • Edema · hematuria (“blood in urine”) · pruritus (itchy skin) · jaundice · pallor · changes in urine output (polyuria, oliguria, urinary frequency, urinary urgency) · changes in urine appearance · hypertension · skin changes (sallow appearance) · myopathy · peripheral neuropathy
L17 · Introduction to Renal Pathology384

Clinical manifestations, by compartment

PATH.6003src p.1027–1028
Glomerular pathologies
  • Asymptomatic proteinuria / hematuria
  • Acute nephritic syndrome
  • Nephrotic syndrome
Tubular pathologies
  • Urinary tract infections
  • Nephrolithiasis
  • Renal tubular function defects
Glomerular & tubular
  • Acute renal failure (acute kidney injury)
  • Chronic renal failure (chronic kidney disease)

Urinary tract infection — the introduction

  • Risk is higher in females than males. Can affect the upper or lower urinary tract — may infect the kidney (pyelonephritis) or bladder (cystitis). Upper urinary tract involvement can lead to urosepsis. Many microbes can cause a UTI.
  • Symptoms: dysuria · urinary frequency and urgency · cloudy appearing urine · hematuria · strong-smelling urine · fever · shivering or chills.
L17 · Introduction to Renal Pathology385

Interpreting the labs

PATH.6002PATH.6005src p.1029–1032
UrinalysisSerum
Gross: colour and appearance
Chemical: specific gravity, osmolarity
Urine dipstick: + proteins (proteinuria/albuminuria) · + glucose (glucosuria) · + lipids (lipiduria) · + bilirubin (bilirubinuria) · + ketones (ketonuria) · + blood (hematuria)
Sediments: cells, casts, crystals, stones		Metabolic acidosis
Hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia
Anemia
BUN and creatinine elevation
Hyperkalemia

Renal function tests check whether the glomerulus and tubules are functioning properly — they measure glomerular permeability, tubular reabsorption, tubular secretion, renal acidification, and concentration and dilution.

GFR
The volume of fluid filtered from the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's space per unit time (mL/min). Calculated by measuring the renal clearance of any substance that has a steady level in blood, is freely filtered, and is not reabsorbed or secreted by renal tubules.
Inulin vs creatinine
Inulin clearance is used to determine GFR but is not routinely performed in the clinical setting. eGFR is done with creatinine clearance — creatinine is a good approximation but slightly over-estimates GFR because there is moderate secretion of creatinine. Consider dietary meat (protein) intake, muscle mass volume, and medications that interfere with tubular secretion of creatinine.
Renal clearance
The volume of plasma from which a substance is completely cleared in urine per unit time: C = (U × V) / P, where U = urinary concentration, V = urinary flow rate, P = plasma concentration. C < GFR → net reabsorption (or the substance is not freely filtered); C > GFR → net secretion.
BUN and creatinine
BUN is produced by the metabolism of protein and amino acids, hydrolyzed by the liver, and excreted by the kidneys. Serum creatinine is the product of muscle metabolism and relates to the concentration of creatine in muscle.
Azotemia vs uremia
Both result from an increase in BUN and creatinine. Azotemia is related largely to decreased GFR — divided into pre-renal (hypoperfusion) and post-renal (urine flow obstructed distal to the kidney). Uremia = azotemia + clinical signs and symptoms of renal demise: failure of renal excretory function, with metabolic and endocrine alterations.

PATH.6002src p.1033–1036

ImmunofluorescenceDetects deposition of antibody-antigen complexes — IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, C1q, kappa, lambda and albumin. C4d is routinely performed on renal transplant biopsies. Glomerular diseases are more related to immunologic reactions.Green on a black background
Electron microscopyAssessment of the integrity of the basement membrane, podocyte foot processes, and capillary fenestraeVarying shades of black and grey
When a renal biopsy IS performedWhen a renal biopsy should NOT be performed
• To make a diagnosis of a suspected glomerular or any other renal pathology
• To monitor treatment effects and disease progress		• Advanced renal disease with small shrunken kidneys on ultrasound
• Young child with nephrotic syndrome
• Clinical picture and systemic findings are fairly specific and definitive (diabetes mellitus, post-streptococcal infection)
• Normal creatinine, normal complement, normal blood pressure, and limited proteinuria (< 1 g/day)
Trap
Why the child with nephrotic syndrome is not biopsied
  • In a young child, nephrotic syndrome is minimal change disease until proven otherwise — it responds to steroids, and light microscopy would be normal anyway. Biopsy is reserved for failure to respond.

Glomerular disorders — the five pathological changes and where immune complexes sit

PATH.6005src p.1037–1039
  1. Basement membrane thickening
  2. Proliferation of mesangial cells and endothelial cells inside the glomeruli
  3. Proliferation of parietal cells around the glomeruli (crescents)
  4. Fibrosis and sclerosis in the mesangium
  5. Inflammatory infiltrate

More than one of these changes can be seen in a single condition.

Site of immune complex depositionClassic disease
Isolated subepithelial humpsAcute glomerulonephritis (post-streptococcal)
Regularly spaced subepithelial depositsMembranous nephropathy
Subendothelial depositsLupus nephritis and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Mesangial depositsIgA nephropathy

EN = endothelium; EP = epithelium; GBM = glomerular basement membrane; LD = lamina densa; LRE = lamina rara externa; LRI = lamina rara interna; MC = mesangial cell; MM = mesangial matrix.

Exam Lock
Deposit location is the single most efficient fact in the renal block
  • Subepithelial humps → post-strep. Regular subepithelial → membranous. Subendothelial → lupus and MPGN. Mesangial → IgA. Learn these four before any of the individual diseases and half of the nephritic lecture becomes recall.
L17 · Introduction to Renal Pathology388

Nephrotic vs nephritic — the distinction the whole block turns on

PATH.6003PATH.6005src p.1040–1042
Nephritic syndromeNephrotic syndrome
Glomerular injury is due to acute inflammation (“itis” = “itic” syndrome)
• Hypertension
• Oliguria
• Hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts (tea/cola coloured urine; Tamm-Horsfall protein forms the cast matrix)
• Proteinuria < 3.5 g/day
• Periorbital and pedal edema		Glomerular injury is due to cytokine-mediated podocyte damage, leading to their effacement, loss and detachment, along with derangement of the filtration barrier with destruction of the negative charge of the GBM
• Proteinuria > 3.5 g/day
• Hypoalbuminemia and generalized pitting edema = anasarca (puffy pale face, swollen lips, periorbital and pretibial edema)
• Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria
• Hypercoagulability due to loss of antithrombin III
L17 · Introduction to Renal Pathology389

Practice — renal evaluation

PATH.6003

A 72-year-old man with severe gastroenteritis has a creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL and a BUN of 62 mg/dL. Urinalysis is bland. Which category of acute kidney injury does the BUN:creatinine ratio point to, and why?

  1. AIntrinsic renal; the tubules cannot reabsorb urea
  2. BPre-renal; the ratio is above 20:1 because avid tubular reabsorption returns urea with sodium and water
  3. CPost-renal; obstruction traps urea proximally
  4. DIntrinsic renal; glomerular disease raises the ratio
  5. EPost-renal; the ratio is characteristically above 20:1
Answer
B. BUN:Cr ≈ 26:1. The lecture's own thresholds: pre-renal is more than 20:1 (think inadequate blood flow — volume depletion here), intrinsic renal 10–15:1, post-renal 10–20:1. A bland urinalysis supports pre-renal rather than tubular injury.
PATH.6005

A renal biopsy shows immune complexes as regularly spaced deposits on the subepithelial side of the glomerular basement membrane. Which disease does this pattern indicate?

  1. AIgA nephropathy
  2. BMembranous nephropathy
  3. CPost-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
  4. DLupus nephritis
  5. EMembranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Answer
B. Regularly spaced subepithelial deposits = membranous nephropathy. Post-streptococcal GN gives isolated subepithelial humps; lupus nephritis and MPGN give subendothelial deposits; IgA nephropathy gives mesangial deposits.
L17 · Introduction to Renal Pathology390

Practice — renal evaluation (cont.)

PATH.6003

A patient's urine is tea-coloured with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts; proteinuria is 1.8 g/day and blood pressure is 168/98. Which syndrome, and what is the underlying mechanism?

  1. ANephrotic syndrome; cytokine-mediated podocyte effacement
  2. BNephritic syndrome; glomerular injury due to acute inflammation
  3. CAcute tubular necrosis; ischaemic tubular injury
  4. DPost-renal obstruction; back-pressure injury
  5. EChronic kidney disease; glomerulosclerosis
Answer
B. RBC casts + dysmorphic RBCs + hypertension + sub-nephrotic proteinuria = nephritic syndrome, whose mechanism is acute inflammation (“itis” → “itic”). Nephrotic syndrome would give bland urine, > 3.5 g/day proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia and hypercoagulability.
PATH.6002

Which of these is a listed contraindication to renal biopsy in this lecture?

  1. AA 45-year-old with new proteinuria of 4 g/day and normal-sized kidneys
  2. BA 4-year-old with nephrotic syndrome
  3. CAn adult with an unexplained rise in creatinine over 3 weeks
  4. DA transplant recipient with suspected rejection
  5. EAn adult with haematuria and RBC casts
Answer
B. The lecture lists four situations where biopsy should not be performed: advanced disease with small shrunken kidneys, a young child with nephrotic syndrome, a clinical picture that is already specific (diabetes, post-streptococcal), and normal creatinine, complement and BP with proteinuria < 1 g/day.
L17 · Introduction to Renal Pathology391

Lecture 17 — summary sheet

Bottom Line
One sentence
  • Ask three questions in order: which compartment (glomerulus, tubule/interstitium, vessel), acute or chronic (tempo, kidney size, GFR for 3 months), and nephrotic or nephritic (bland urine and > 3.5 g vs RBC casts and hypertension).
Exam Lock
The seven locks
  • Pre-renal BUN:Cr > 20:1; intrinsic 10–15:1; post-renal 10–20:1.
  • CKD = GFR < 60 for ≥ 3 months with albuminuria; ESRD = GFR < 5% of normal.
  • Creatinine slightly OVERestimates GFR because it is moderately secreted.
  • Azotemia = raised BUN and creatinine. Uremia = azotemia + symptoms.
  • Deposits: subepithelial humps = post-strep; regular subepithelial = membranous; subendothelial = lupus/MPGN; mesangial = IgA.
  • Nephrotic loses antithrombin III → hypercoagulable.
  • RBC casts are nephritic and nothing else.
Trap
Two traps
  • Reading a normal creatinine as a normal GFR in a frail, low-muscle-mass patient.
  • Biopsying a child with nephrotic syndrome, or a pair of small shrunken kidneys.

Hyperlipidemia: elevation of plasma cholesterol and/or TGs, or a low HDL level. Causes may be primary (genetic) or secondary.Definition, PHAR.0304
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs393

Lipids and cardiovascular risk — the three sentences that matter

PHAR.0305src p.1701–1703
  • There is a link between elevated plasma lipid concentrations and the risk of cardiovascular disease.
  • Increased risk of cardiovascular mortality is most closely linked to elevated LDL and decreased HDL.
  • In addition, hypertriglyceridemia represents an independent risk factor.
Exam Lock
The one number from this section
  • The relationship between LDL and CHD risk is log-linear: for every 30 mg/dL reduction in LDL, the relative risk for CHD is reduced by about 30%. This is the quantitative justification for treating to a target rather than to a threshold.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs394

Primary hyperlipidemias — the Fredrickson classification, verbatim

PHAR.0304 · PHAR.0306src p.1704–1708

Primary causes include monogenic diseases, genetic polymorphisms, and gene–environment interactions. The nomenclature is confusing because the same genetic defect can contribute to a number of phenotypic syndromes; Fredrickson's scheme divides them into five phenotypic groups based on patterns of elevation of lipoproteins.

TypeDiseaseLipid profileEtiology
IFamilial hyperchylomicronemia↑ ChylomicronsDeficiency in LPL or apoC-II
IIAFamilial hypercholesterolemia↑ LDLDecreased or no functional LDL receptor expression
IIBFamilial combined hyperlipidemia↑ LDL and ↑ VLDLOverproduction of VLDL by liver
IIIFamilial dysbetalipoproteinemia↑ IDLAbnormal apoE
IVFamilial hypertriglyceridemia↑ VLDLOverproduction and/or impaired catabolism of VLDL
VFamilial mixed hypertriglyceridemia↑ VLDL and ↑ chylomicronsOverproduction and/or decreased clearance of VLDL and chylomicrons
Bottom Line
Read the type from the particle
  • Chylomicrons → I (the LPL/apoC-II machine is broken). LDL alone → IIA (the receptor is broken). LDL + VLDL → IIB. IDL → III (apoE is the remnant ligand). VLDL → IV. VLDL + chylomicrons → V. The particle names the defect.

The unifying mechanism — one loop, five ways into it

PHAR.0307src p.1716–1718 · 1750 · 1755 · 1764 · 1776
Bottom Line
Why this diagram is worth memorising instead of five mechanisms
  • Four of the six classes lower LDL by the same final step — depleting hepatocyte cholesterol so that LDL receptors are upregulated and plasma LDL is cleared. They differ only in *how* they deplete it. PCSK9 inhibitors are the exception and act on receptor degradation, which is exactly why the lecture calls them complementary to statins.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs398

Statins — mechanism, potency ranking and pleiotropic effects

PHAR.0307 · PHAR.0309 · PHAR.0312src p.1711 · 1714–1723
Statins are the lipid-lowering agents of first choice for treatment of most patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and can decrease the incidence of major coronary events and death. In selected high-risk patients, use of non-statins may be considered if statin therapy has not achieved >50% reduction in LDL.Management principle
  • The class: atorvastatin, fluvastatin, lovastatin, pitavastatin, pravastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin.
  • Competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase — the enzyme that catalyses the first committed step of cholesterol biosynthesis.
  • Statins are more effective than other drugs in lowering LDL; they also cause a decrease in plasma TG and a small increase in HDL.

Potency ranking — verbatim

  1. Rosuvastatin — most effective in lowering LDL
  2. Atorvastatin — next most effective
  3. Simvastatin and pitavastatin
  4. Lovastatin, pravastatin and fluvastatin — least effective

All statins reduce cardiovascular risk, and the magnitude of the reduction is related to the magnitude of LDL reduction. The effectiveness of statins at lowering TG is similar to their effectiveness at lowering LDL; the largest TG reductions are seen with rosuvastatin and atorvastatin.

Pleiotropic effects (PHAR.0312) — the four the lecture lists

Vascular
  • Improve endothelial function
  • Stabilize atherosclerotic plaque
Haemostatic / inflammatory
  • Decrease platelet aggregation
  • Reduce inflammation
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs399

Statins — uses, the four benefit groups, adverse effects and monitoring

PHAR.0307 · PHAR.0309 · PHAR.0314src p.1724–1727

Uses

  • Drugs of choice for LDL reduction. Reduce cardiovascular mortality.
  • Lower LDL levels in all types of hyperlipidemias.
  • High-dose statin therapy is started immediately after ACS, regardless of lipid levels.
  • Homozygotes for familial hypercholesterolemia lack functional LDL receptors and thus benefit much less from statin therapy.
  • Contraindicated in pregnancy.

Who should be treated with a statin — the four major statin benefit groups

  1. Patients with clinical ASCVD.
  2. Patients aged 40–75 years with diabetes and LDL ≥ 70 mg/dL.
  3. Patients with LDL ≥ 190 mg/dL.
  4. Patients aged 40–75 years with LDL ≥ 70 mg/dL and ≥ 7.5% 10-year ASCVD risk.
Source note
Guideline source (verbatim from the slide)
  • 2018 AHA/ACC/AACVPR/AAPA/ABC/ACPM/ADA/AGS/APhA/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol.

Adverse effects and monitoring

Adverse effectDetailMonitoring
Elevation of aminotransferasesUsually not associated with other evidence of liver toxicity.Measure at baseline, at 1–2 months, then every 6–12 months.
Myopathy and rhabdomyolysisRare. Rhabdomyolysis may cause myoglobinuria, leading to renal injury.CK at baseline. If muscle pain or weakness appears, measure CK immediately and discontinue the drug if activity is significantly elevated.
Exam Lock
The two statin sentences most likely to be tested
  • High-dose statin immediately after ACS regardless of lipid levels — the benefit is not a lipid-number benefit. And homozygous FH benefits much less — no functional LDL receptor means the drug's final common pathway is missing, which is precisely why PCSK9 inhibitors appear in the FH row of the treatment table.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs401

Check — statins and the LDL receptor loop

PHAR.0307

A 52-year-old starts rosuvastatin. Which sequence correctly describes how plasma LDL falls?

  1. AStatin blocks LDL receptors → LDL is not taken up → hepatic cholesterol falls
  2. BStatin inhibits HMG-CoA reductase → intracellular cholesterol is depleted → HMG-CoA reductase and LDL receptors are upregulated → LDL clearance from blood increases
  3. CStatin binds circulating LDL directly and promotes biliary excretion
  4. DStatin inhibits PCSK9 → LDL receptors recycle → LDL clearance increases
  5. EStatin blocks NPC1L1 → dietary cholesterol absorption falls → LDL falls
Answer
B. Statins are competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase, the first committed step of cholesterol biosynthesis. Depletion of intracellular cholesterol leads to upregulation of HMG-CoA reductase, and upregulation of the LDL receptor; upregulation of LDL receptors results in increased clearance of LDL from the blood. Option 4 is the PCSK9 mechanism; option 5 is ezetimibe.
PHAR.0309

Which patient benefits LEAST from statin monotherapy, and why?

  1. AA 60-year-old with clinical ASCVD — statins do not affect established plaque
  2. BA homozygote for familial hypercholesterolemia — no functional LDL receptors, so the final common pathway of statin action is absent
  3. CA 45-year-old diabetic with LDL 120 — diabetes blocks HMG-CoA reductase inhibition
  4. DA patient with hypertriglyceridemia — statins do not lower TG at all
  5. EA patient with low HDL — statins raise HDL substantially
Answer
B. Homozygotes for familial hypercholesterolemia lack functional LDL receptors and thus benefit much less from statin therapy. Note the distractors' errors: statins stabilize plaque (pleiotropic effect), their TG-lowering efficacy is similar to their LDL-lowering efficacy, and the HDL rise is described as small (5–15%).
PHAR.0307

Which monitoring plan matches this lecture's recommendation for a patient starting atorvastatin?

  1. ACK every month indefinitely; no liver testing
  2. BAminotransferases at baseline, 1–2 months, then every 6–12 months; CK at baseline and immediately if muscle pain or weakness appears
  3. CAminotransferases weekly for 3 months
  4. DNo monitoring is required for any statin
  5. ECK and aminotransferases every 2 weeks for the first year
Answer
B. Aminotransferase activity should be measured at baseline, at 1–2 months, and then every 6–12 months. CK should be measured at baseline. If muscle pain or weakness appears, CK should be measured immediately and the drug discontinued if activity is significantly elevated. Rhabdomyolysis is rare but can cause myoglobinuria → renal injury.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs402

Niacin (nicotinic acid) — four mechanistic steps, then a long adverse-effect list

PHAR.0307 · PHAR.0308src p.1728–1734

Niacin favorably affects virtually all lipid parameters: it decreases VLDL, LDL and Lp(a) and increases HDL.

Niacin inhibits adenylyl cyclase in adipocytes (Gi-coupled) → ↓ cAMP → PKA inactive→Hormone-sensitive lipase inactive → reduced breakdown of TG to free fatty acids→Transport of fatty acids to the liver is reduced → reduced hepatic TG synthesis→↓ VLDL production and release → ↓ LDL production
  • Separately, niacin increases LPL activity, promoting clearance of TG from chylomicrons and VLDL.
  • The catabolic rate for HDL is decreased → HDL increases.

Uses

  • Niacin is the most effective drug for raising HDL.
  • Useful in patients with combined hyperlipidemia and low HDL levels.
  • Niacin has many adverse effects which limit its use.
  • Addition of niacin to statin therapy has not been shown to reduce ASCVD risk.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs403

PHAR.0307src p.1735–1738

Exam Lock
Niacin's profile in one line
  • Flush (aspirin-preventable, prostaglandin-mediated) · hyperglycemia · hyperuricemia/gout · hepatotoxicity. A diabetic with gout is the patient in whom niacin is hardest to justify — especially since adding niacin to a statin has not been shown to reduce ASCVD risk.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs404

Fibrates — gemfibrozil and fenofibrate

PHAR.0307 · PHAR.0308src p.1739–1743
  • Fibrates lower VLDL levels and increase HDL levels.
  • They activate peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-α (PPAR-α), expressed primarily in liver and brown adipose tissue.
  • Activation of PPAR-α leads to a decrease in plasma TG and an increase in plasma HDL.

How the TG falls — three components

  1. Increased expression of lipoprotein lipase
  2. Decreased hepatic expression of apoC-III
  3. Increased hepatic oxidation of fatty acids
Trap
Fibrates may RAISE LDL
  • Fibrates may increase LDL, particularly if the TG level is greater than 400 mg/dL. In the lecture's summary table the LDL column for fibrates is written as ↑ or ↓ — the only class with an ambiguous entry.

Uses

  • Drug of choice in severe hypertriglyceridemia.
  • Reasonable consideration in moderate hypertriglyceridemia.
  • As monotherapy, fibrates offer the highest TG reduction, followed by niacin, ω-3 fatty acids, statins, and ezetimibe.

Adverse effects

  • Mild GI disturbances.
  • Myositis — patients with renal insufficiency may be at risk; rhabdomyolysis has occurred rarely.
  • Lithiasis — fibrates increase biliary cholesterol excretion, therefore they may cause gallstones.
  • Minor elevations of aminotransferases and alkaline phosphatase.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs405

Statin + fibrate — the interaction objective (PHAR.0311), spelled out

PHAR.0311src p.1744
GemfibrozilFenofibrate
Effect on statin handlingInhibits hepatic uptake of statins, thus increasing plasma concentration of statins. Competes for the glucuronosyl transferases that metabolize most statins.Does not inhibit statin metabolism.
ConsequenceLevels of both drugs may be increased when co-administered — this increases the risk of rhabdomyolysis.Much less likely to increase risk of rhabdomyolysis.
Practical ruleAvoid with a statin where possibleThe fibrate to pair with a statin
Exam Lock
If a question pairs a fibrate with a statin, the answer hinges on which fibrate
  • Both drugs independently cause myositis; the danger is pharmacokinetic and belongs to gemfibrozil alone — two mechanisms (blocked hepatic uptake and competition for glucuronosyl transferases), both raising statin levels. Fenofibrate does not do this. Add renal insufficiency to the stem and the risk rises further.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs406

Bile acid-binding resins — cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam

PHAR.0307src p.1745–1753

Physical properties (they explain everything else)

  • Large molecular weights (> 10⁶): neither absorbed nor metabolized. Insoluble in water. Totally excreted in the feces.

Mechanism

Most bile salts secreted are normally reabsorbed (enterohepatic circulation)→Resins bind bile acids in the intestinal lumen and prevent their reabsorption; the insoluble resin–bile acid complex is excreted in the feces→Reduced bile acid concentration → hepatocytes increase conversion of cholesterol to bile acids→Intracellular cholesterol decreases → ↑ HMG-CoA reductase and ↑ hepatic LDL receptors→Liver uptake of LDL increases → plasma LDL falls. HDL rises modestly.

Uses, adverse effects and interactions

Detail
UsesUseful only in hyperlipidemias involving isolated increases in LDL. Used with statins or niacin to increase LDL reduction. Drugs of choice for pregnant women and for children. Little effect in individuals who completely lack functional LDL receptors.
Adverse effectsGI: bloating, nausea, cramping and constipation. Colesevelam produces fewer GI adverse effects than cholestyramine or colestipol. They may increase TG — contraindicated in hypertriglyceridemia. In patients who have hypertriglyceridemia as well as elevated LDL, VLDL levels may increase.
InteractionsCholestyramine and colestipol reduce absorption of several drugs and liposoluble vitamins.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs407

Ezetimibe and the ω-3 fatty acid esters

PHAR.0307src p.1754–1761

Ezetimibe — cholesterol absorption inhibitor

  • Inhibits absorption of dietary and biliary cholesterol in the small intestine. It is a prodrug, conjugated to an active glucuronide in the liver and small intestine.
  • Molecular target: the intestinal transport protein NPC1L1, which takes up cholesterol from the lumen. Cholesterol absorption is reduced by 54%.
  • Reduced delivery of intestinal cholesterol to the liver → ↑ HMG-CoA reductase and ↑ LDL receptors → enhanced LDL clearance from plasma.
  • Effective even in the absence of dietary cholesterol, because it inhibits reabsorption of cholesterol excreted in the bile.
EzetimibeDetail
EfficacyMaximal efficacy for lowering LDL is about 20%.
Place in therapyUseful in combination with a statin in patients unable to reach their LDL goal on statin monotherapy. The first non-statin drug that should be considered as an adjunct to a statin. Only used as monotherapy in patients who do not tolerate statins.
Adverse effectsLow incidence of reversible impaired hepatic function, with a small increase in incidence when given with a statin. Myositis has been reported rarely.
InteractionsBile-acid sequestrants inhibit absorption of ezetimibe — the two agents should not be administered together.

ω-3 fatty acid esters

  • EPA and DHA reduce TG synthesis and increase fatty acid oxidation in the liver; HDL levels may modestly increase.
  • Three prescription formulations are FDA-approved: two contain both EPA and DHA, one contains only EPA.
  • Formulations containing both EPA and DHA increase LDL-C. EPA-only products do not increase LDL-C.
  • Indicated to reduce TG levels in adult patients with hypertriglyceridemia.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs408

PCSK9 inhibitors — two modalities against one protease

PHAR.0307 · PHAR.0310src p.1762–1775
PCSK9 is a protease produced by the liver. PCSK9 binds to the LDL receptor and targets it for lysosomal degradation. If PCSK9 is inhibited the LDL receptor can recycle to the surface of the hepatocyte — therefore, more LDL receptors are available.Mechanism
Monoclonal antibodiessiRNA
DrugsAlirocumab · evolocumabInclisiran
NatureHumanized antibodies directed against PCSK9Small interfering RNA directed to PCSK9 mRNA — binds PCSK9 mRNA and prevents protein translation of PCSK9
Route and scheduleSC injections, every 2 or 4 weeksSC at month 0, month 3, then every 6 months. Should be administered by a healthcare provider.
EfficacyReduce LDL by 70% as monotherapy and by 60% in patients on statin therapy.Added to maximally tolerated statin therapy, reduced LDL by about 50%.
IndicationsReduce LDL in heterozygous or homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia; reduce risk of MI and stroke in patients with ASCVD. Alone or in combination; usually given with diet and maximally tolerated doses of statins.Adjunct to diet and maximally tolerated statin therapy in adults with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia or ASCVD who require additional LDL lowering.
Exam Lock
Why PCSK9 inhibitors and statins add up
  • Statins upregulate LDL receptors, and PCSK9 inhibitors increase LDL receptors on the membrane of the hepatocyte — PCSK9 inhibitors are complementary to statins. Two different points in the receptor's life cycle: synthesis versus recycling.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs409

ATP-citrate lyase inhibitor — bempedoic acid

PHAR.0307 · PHAR.0313src p.1776 · 1694
  • ACL is involved in hepatic cholesterol synthesis.
  • Bempedoic acid inhibits ACL → reduction in LDL-C → upregulation of LDL receptors, increasing clearance of LDL-C from circulation.
  • Approved for use alone or in a fixed-dose combination with ezetimibe.
  • Adverse effects: URTI, muscle spasms, back and extremity pain, elevated hepatic enzymes and uric acid levels. Drug interaction with statins.
Source note
From the reading notes (source p. 1694)
  • Indication: add-on to maximally tolerated statin ± ezetimibe, used in ASCVD and heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) when LDL is still above target. Lowers LDL by ~15–20%.
Bottom Line
Bempedoic acid is a statin one step earlier in the pathway
  • ACL sits upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in hepatic cholesterol synthesis, and bempedoic acid is a prodrug activated by an enzyme not present in skeletal muscle — which is the clinical reason it appears in statin-intolerant patients. Note it still elevates uric acid, like niacin.

Combinations and the suggested therapy table

Block exam — antihyperlipidemic drugs

PHAR.0311

A 58-year-old on simvastatin is started on a fibrate for TG of 780 mg/dL and develops severe muscle pain with CK 12,000 U/L. Which fibrate was most likely used, and what are the two mechanisms?

  1. AFenofibrate; it inhibits CYP3A4 and displaces statins from albumin
  2. BGemfibrozil; it inhibits hepatic uptake of statins and competes for the glucuronosyl transferases that metabolize most statins
  3. CFenofibrate; it activates PPAR-γ in skeletal muscle
  4. DGemfibrozil; it directly inhibits HMG-CoA reductase in muscle
  5. EEither fibrate; the risk is identical
Answer
B. Gemfibrozil inhibits hepatic uptake of statins, thus increasing plasma concentration of statins, and competes for the glucuronosyl transferases that metabolize most statins. As a consequence, levels of both drugs may be increased when they are co-administered — this increases the risk of rhabdomyolysis. Fenofibrate does not inhibit statin metabolism and is much less likely to increase risk of rhabdomyolysis. Fibrates act on PPAR-α, not γ.
PHAR.0307

A patient starting niacin reports intense facial flushing after each dose. What is the mediator, and what prevents it?

  1. AHistamine; give an H1 antihistamine
  2. BProstaglandins; give aspirin before the niacin dose
  3. CBradykinin; switch to an ARB
  4. DNitric oxide; give a nitrate antagonist
  5. ESerotonin; give a 5-HT3 antagonist
Answer
B. Administration of aspirin prior to niacin decreases the flush, which is prostaglandin-mediated. The flush is intense, cutaneous, after each dose, and occurs when the drug is started or the dose increased. Niacin's more serious effects are hepatotoxicity and hyperglycemia (via insulin resistance), plus ↑ uric acid → gout.
PHAR.0313

A woman planning pregnancy has LDL 205 mg/dL. Which agent is supported by this lecture?

  1. AAtorvastatin
  2. BColesevelam
  3. CGemfibrozil
  4. DEvolocumab
  5. EEzetimibe
Answer
B. Statins are absolutely contraindicated — category X. Resins are the drugs of choice for pregnant women and for children, and among them colesevelam is category B ("appears to be safe in animal reproductive studies"). Fibrates, niacin, ezetimibe and cholestyramine/colestipol are all category C; PCSK9 inhibitors have not been tested and are not approved in pregnancy.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs416

Block exam — antihyperlipidemic drugs (cont.)

PHAR.0307

Which lipid abnormality would make bile acid-binding resins a poor choice?

  1. AIsolated elevated LDL
  2. BElevated LDL with triglycerides of 620 mg/dL
  3. CFamilial hypercholesterolemia in a child
  4. DElevated LDL in pregnancy
  5. ELow HDL with normal LDL and TG
Answer
B. Resins may increase TG — they are contraindicated in hypertriglyceridemia, and in patients with hypertriglyceridemia as well as elevated LDL, VLDL levels may increase. They are useful only in hyperlipidemias involving isolated increases in LDL, and are the drugs of choice for pregnant women and children — which is why the other options are appropriate uses.
PHAR.0307

Which mechanism correctly describes inclisiran?

  1. AA humanized monoclonal antibody that binds PCSK9 protein
  2. BA small interfering RNA that binds PCSK9 mRNA and prevents translation of PCSK9
  3. CAn antisense oligonucleotide against apoB mRNA
  4. DA competitive inhibitor of ATP-citrate lyase
  5. EAn NPC1L1 transport inhibitor
Answer
B. Inclisiran is a small interfering RNA (siRNA) directed to PCSK9 mRNA; it binds to PCSK9 mRNA and prevents protein translation of PCSK9, resulting in decreased PCSK9 and LDL. It is given SC at month 0, month 3, and then every 6 months, by a healthcare provider, and added to maximally tolerated statin therapy it reduces LDL by about 50%. The antibodies are alirocumab and evolocumab; ACL is bempedoic acid; NPC1L1 is ezetimibe.
PHAR.0307 · PHAR.0310

A 63-year-old with clinical ASCVD is on maximally tolerated rosuvastatin with LDL still 118 mg/dL. Which is the first non-statin agent this lecture says should be considered?

  1. ANiacin
  2. BEzetimibe
  3. CGemfibrozil
  4. DCholestyramine
  5. EEvolocumab
Answer
B. Ezetimibe is the first non-statin drug that should be considered as an adjunct to a statin, with maximal LDL-lowering of about 20%. Note the lecture's separate warning that addition of niacin to statin therapy has not been shown to reduce ASCVD risk, and that PCSK9 inhibitors sit further down the ladder — reserved in the treatment table for familial hypercholesterolemia not responsive to oral therapy and for high-risk ASCVD.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs417

Block exam — antihyperlipidemic drugs (cont.)

PHAR.0304

Which Fredrickson type is caused by an abnormal apoE, and which lipoprotein accumulates?

  1. AType I; chylomicrons
  2. BType IIA; LDL
  3. CType III; IDL
  4. DType IV; VLDL
  5. EType V; VLDL and chylomicrons
Answer
C. Type III — familial dysbetalipoproteinemia — ↑ IDL, caused by abnormal apoE. ApoE is the ligand for remnant clearance, so remnants (IDL) accumulate. For contrast: type I = ↑ chylomicrons from deficiency in LPL or apoC-II; IIA = ↑ LDL from decreased or no functional LDL receptor; IIB = ↑ LDL and VLDL from hepatic VLDL overproduction; IV = ↑ VLDL; V = ↑ VLDL and chylomicrons.
PHAR.0307

Which statement about ezetimibe is correct?

  1. AIt is only effective when dietary cholesterol intake is high
  2. BIt inhibits NPC1L1, reduces cholesterol absorption by 54%, and remains effective without dietary cholesterol because it also blocks reabsorption of biliary cholesterol
  3. CIt should be combined with a bile-acid sequestrant for additive effect
  4. DIt lowers LDL by about 50% as monotherapy
  5. EIt is an irreversible inhibitor of HMG-CoA reductase
Answer
B. Ezetimibe inhibits the intestinal transport protein NPC1L1; cholesterol absorption is reduced by 54%; it is also effective in the absence of dietary cholesterol because it inhibits reabsorption of cholesterol excreted in the bile. Maximal LDL lowering is about 20%, and bile-acid sequestrants inhibit absorption of ezetimibe — the two should not be administered together.
PHAR.0308

Which combination of "best-in-class" claims matches the lecture's percentage table?

  1. AStatins best for HDL; niacin best for LDL; fibrates best for TG
  2. BPCSK9 monoclonals best for LDL; niacin best for HDL; fibrates best for TG
  3. CEzetimibe best for LDL; resins best for HDL; statins best for TG
  4. DInclisiran best for HDL; ω-3 best for LDL; niacin best for TG
  5. EStatins best for all three parameters
Answer
B. From the table: evolocumab/alirocumab ↓ LDL 60–70% (largest); niacin ↑ HDL 20–35% — and the lecture states outright that niacin is the most effective drug for raising HDL; fibrates ↓ TG 30–60%, and as monotherapy fibrates offer the highest TG reduction, followed by niacin, ω-3 fatty acids, statins, and ezetimibe.
PHAR · Antihyperlipidemic Drugs418

Block exam — antihyperlipidemic drugs (cont.)

PHAR.0312

Which is a pleiotropic effect of statins as listed in this lecture?

  1. AIncreased lipoprotein lipase expression
  2. BStabilization of atherosclerotic plaque
  3. CInhibition of adenylyl cyclase in adipocytes
  4. DPPAR-α activation
  5. EInhibition of NPC1L1
Answer
B. The four pleiotropic effects given are: improve endothelial function, decrease platelet aggregation, stabilize atherosclerotic plaque, and reduce inflammation. ↑ LPL belongs to niacin and fibrates; ↓ adenylyl cyclase in adipocytes is niacin; PPAR-α is fibrates; NPC1L1 is ezetimibe.

Nephrotic syndrome — definition and pathogenesis

PATH.6006src p.1161–1162
Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria (usually defined as > 3.5 g/24 hr) → hypoalbuminemia, edema.Definition

Pathogenesis

  • Primary or secondary damage to podocytes (visceral epithelial cells).
  • Podocyte slit diaphragms serve as the diffusion barrier to plasma proteins — attributed to the negative charge of the basement membrane.
  • Podocyte damage is associated with effacement of foot processes and loss of the negative charges on the basement membrane.
Exam Lock
Two barriers, two failures
  • The filtration barrier is both a size barrier (slit diaphragm) and a charge barrier (anionic GBM). Albumin is anionic, so charge loss alone lets albumin through — which is why minimal change disease produces massive selective proteinuria with a normal light microscope. Structural collapse (FSGS, membranous) adds size failure, and the proteinuria becomes non-selective.
L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes422

The four consequences of heavy proteinuria

PATH.6006 · PATH.6007src p.1163–1166
L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes423

PATH.6006 · PATH.6007src p.1163–1166
What is lost / madeConsequenceClinical or laboratory finding
Albumin lostHypoalbuminemia → decreased intravascular oncotic pressure → shifting of plasma fluid from capillary into interstitial space — "third spacing"EDEMA — generalized edema or edema of serosal spaces. Pre-tibial pitting edema · periorbital edema · pulmonary edema
Compensatory increase in hepatic protein synthesisIncreased lipoproteinsHYPERLIPIDEMIA and LIPIDURIA. Urinalysis: oval fat bodies, fatty casts, lipid droplets — seen with Sudan III stain, and the Maltese cross under polarized light

Exam Lock
PATH.6007 in one sentence
  • The thrombotic risk in nephrotic syndrome is two-hit: antithrombotic factors are lost in the urine through the damaged glomerulus, and the liver's compensatory protein synthesis increases pro-thrombotic factors. Renal vein thrombosis is the named complication — and it is listed again under membranous nephropathy.

Membranous nephropathy (membranous glomerulonephritis)

PATH.6008src p.1168–1169
Characterized by diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall due to the deposits of antigen–antibody complexes along the subepithelial side of the basement membrane.Definition
Epidemiology
  • Peak incidence between the ages of 30 and 60 years
  • Male to female ratio of 2:1
  • Extremely rare in children
Etiology
  • 75% of cases are primary and 25% secondary

Primary

  • Caused by antibodies against antigens — Phospholipase A2 Receptor (PLA2R) — on podocytes.
  • Leads to complement activation on the surface of podocytes and generates the membrane attack complex (C5–C9) → damages podocytes.

Secondary — caused by either endogenous or exogenous antigens

Endogenous antigens
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
  • Malignancies like lung, colon, melanoma
  • Other autoimmune conditions like autoimmune thyroiditis
Exogenous antigens
  • Drugs: gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs, captopril
  • Infections: hepatitis B, malaria, syphilis, schistosomiasis
L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes426

Membranous nephropathy (membranous glomerulonephritis) (cont.)

PATH.6008src p.1168–1169
Exam Lock
PLA2R + membrane attack complex
  • Membranous is an in situ immune-complex disease: the antibody meets its antigen (PLA2R) *on the podocyte itself*, which is why the deposits are subepithelial. The injury is done by C5–C9, not by neutrophils — which is why the light microscope shows thickening without hypercellularity and the urine is nephrotic rather than nephritic.
L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes427

Membranous nephropathy — clinical features, prognosis and morphology

PATH.6008src p.1170–1175

Clinical features

  • Present predominantly with nephrotic syndrome, microscopic hematuria (50% of cases), and hypertension.

Prognosis / complications

OutcomeFrequency
Persistent proteinuria60% of patients
End-stage renal disease40% develop it
Partial or total remission of proteinuria10–30% of patients
Renal vein thrombosisA named complication

Poor prognosis: male · > 50 years of age · > 10 g/day proteinuria.

What is happening to the GBM

  1. GBM thickening is caused by subepithelial deposits.
  2. These deposits are separated from each other by small, spike-like protrusions of GBM matrix that form in reaction to the deposits.
  3. As the disease progresses, spikes close over the deposits, incorporating deposits into the GBM.
  4. Incorporated deposits may be broken down and eventually disappear.
Light microscopy
Thickening of the glomerular basement membrane. Silver stain: "spike and dome" appearance of reactive GBM deposition between immune complex deposits.
Immunofluorescence
Typical granular deposits of immunoglobulins and complement along the GBM — IgG+ and C3+.
Electron microscopy
Basement membrane thickening with subepithelial deposits and spikes.
L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes428

Minimal change disease

PATH.6008src p.1176–1178
No glomerular abnormality seen on light microscopic examination.Definition
  • Most frequent cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.
  • Sometimes follows a respiratory infection or routine prophylactic immunization.
  • Etiopathogenesis: some immune dysfunction from cells such as lymphocytes → injures podocytes → increasing permeability of the glomerular basement membrane leading to proteinuria.
  • Glomerular abnormality (podocyte damage) can only be seen on electron microscopy.

Clinical features

  • Usually follows a respiratory infection and prophylactic immunization.
  • Most common between ages 1 and 7.
  • Abrupt development of the nephrotic syndrome in an otherwise healthy child.
  • Periorbital edema and generalized edema (anasarca).
  • Protein loss usually confined to smaller plasma proteins, chiefly albumin — selective proteinuria.
  • No hypertension. Renal function is preserved in most of these patients.
  • Association with other atopic disorders.
  • Increased incidence in Hodgkin lymphoma with known T cell-mediated immunity defects.
  • More than 90% of children respond to a short course of corticosteroid therapy.
L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes429

Minimal change disease (cont.)

PATH.6008src p.1176–1178

Histopathology

Light microscopy
Normal basement membranes and absence of proliferation — no increased cellularity.
Immunofluorescence
No pattern.
Electron microscopy
Effacement or fusion of foot processes and absence of deposits.
Exam Lock
The three negatives are the diagnosis
  • No LM finding · no IF pattern · no deposits on EM. All that is left is foot-process effacement. Add no hypertension, preserved renal function, selective proteinuria and >90% steroid response and MCD becomes the most "negative" disease in the lecture — which is exactly how it is recognised.
L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes430

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

PATH.6008src p.1179 · 1181
Focal
< 50% of glomeruli involved
Segmental
Part of the glomerulus involved
Sclerosis
Hyalinosis and sclerosis in the glomeruli
  • A disorder of podocytes (like minimal change disease).
  • Can be idiopathic ("primary") or secondary to some other condition.
  • Primary FSGS: idiopathic (a specific cause is unknown), and an important cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults.

Etiology of secondary FSGS

  • HIV infection
  • Morbid obesity
  • Chronic reflux nephropathy
  • Heroin use
  • Malignancies (like lymphoma)

Pathogenesis of secondary FSGS — hyperfiltration injury

Reduction in renal mass due to any renal disease→Compensatory hypertrophy and hyperfiltration of remaining glomeruli to maintain GFR→Intraglomerular hypertension and systemic hypertension (hyperfiltration injury)→Focal and segmental sclerosis in glomeruli

At the cellular level: podocyte derangement ranging from foot-process effacement to proliferation of visceral epithelial cells · increases in mesangial matrix · loss of endothelial cells and obliteration of capillary lumens by sclerosis.

L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes431

FSGS vs minimal change disease — the six differences, verbatim

PATH.6008src p.1180 · 1182–1183
#Clinical features of FSGS differ from MCD in the following ways
1Acute or sub-acute onset of nephrotic syndrome
2Higher incidence of microscopic hematuria, reduced GFR (renal insufficiency), and hypertension
3Proteinuria is more often non-selective (more than just albumin)
4Poor response to corticosteroid therapy
5Degree of proteinuria is an important prognostic indicator
6Most common glomerular disorder that progresses to chronic kidney disease
FSGS — light microscopy
Collapse of capillary loops, increase in matrix, and segmental deposition of plasma proteins along the capillary wall. Low-power view shows focal sclerosis involving one of three glomeruli; involvement of a segment of a glomerulus with sclerosis and hyaline deposit.
FSGS — immunofluorescence
Negative / no pattern; sometimes granular for IgM and C3.
FSGS — electron microscopy
Diffuse effacement of foot processes, and there may also be focal detachment of the podocytes — the basement membrane is now denuded or naked. Effacement is seen in both sclerotic and non-sclerotic areas.
Trap
A child with nephrotic syndrome who does not respond to steroids
  • This is the single most common way the pair is tested. MCD: >90% of children respond to a short course of corticosteroids. FSGS: poor response to corticosteroid therapy. Add hematuria, hypertension or a reduced GFR to the stem and the answer moves from MCD to FSGS even before the biopsy is described.
L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes432

Diabetic nephropathy

PATH.6008src p.1184–1187
  • Describes the renal lesions that develop in patients with diabetes mellitus.
  • After cardiac causes (MI), renal failure is the most common cause of death in diabetic patients.
  • Due to the effects of long-standing hyperglycemia — diabetics with disease of more than 10 years' duration.
  • Severe glomerulosclerosis leads to nephrotic syndrome, characterized by proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema.

Clinical course — the timeline the exam tests

StageTimingFinding
HyperfiltrationInitiallyHyperglycemia leads to hyperfiltration (increased GFR) and increased glomerular hydrostatic pressure → polyuria and nocturia
Incipient nephropathyAfter 7–13 yearsMicroalbuminuria 30–300 mg/24 hr
Overt nephropathyAfter 10–20 yearsMacroalbuminuria > 300 mg/24 hr
Progressive diseaseLaterPersistent and progressive proteinuria, hypertension, declining renal function

Urine protein is used as an important screening tool to track the progression of renal injury.

Histopathology

  1. GBM thickening — identified on EM first (the earliest feature)
  2. Mesangial widening
  3. Tubular BM thickening
  • Nodular glomerulosclerosis — Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules: distinctive glomerular lesions described as ball-like (ovoid or spherical) deposits of a laminated matrix in the periphery of the glomerulus containing trapped mesangial cells.
  • Hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
  • Grossly: granular, contracted kidneys.
L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes433

Renal amyloidosis

PATH.6008src p.1188–1190
  • Most commonly seen in patients undergoing prolonged dialysis (β2-microglobulin).
  • Grossly: kidneys may be of normal size and color; in advanced cases shrunken because of ischemia — vascular narrowing induced by the deposition of amyloid within arterial and arteriolar walls.
  • Microscopically: amyloid is deposited primarily in the glomeruli (in the mesangium). Mesangial deposition and deposits along the basement membranes → capillary narrowing, obliteration and distortion of the glomerular tuft.

Clinical features

  • The kidney is the most commonly involved organ of systemic amyloidosis.
  • Renal insufficiency is present in 50% at the time of diagnosis.
  • Most common clinical presentation is proteinuria, mainly composed of albumin.

Diagnosis and natural history

  • Biopsy of the organ involved.
  • Very poor prognosis.
  • Many die of end-organ failure from amyloid deposition.

Light microscopy, PAS stain: the glomerular architecture is almost totally obliterated by the massive accumulation of amyloid.

Block exam — the nephrotic syndromes

PATH.6008

A 4-year-old develops periorbital swelling and anasarca two weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. Urine protein is 5 g/24 hr and is almost entirely albumin. BP is normal and creatinine is normal. What will the renal biopsy show?

  1. AThickened GBM with spike-and-dome on silver stain; granular IgG and C3
  2. BNormal light microscopy, no immunofluorescence pattern, and effacement of foot processes on EM
  3. CSegmental sclerosis in fewer than half the glomeruli with granular IgM and C3
  4. DKimmelstiel-Wilson nodules and hyaline arteriolosclerosis
  5. EAmyloid deposits in the mesangium on PAS stain
Answer
B. Minimal change disease — the most frequent cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, most common between ages 1 and 7, often follows a respiratory infection or prophylactic immunization, with selective proteinuria (chiefly albumin), no hypertension, and preserved renal function. The biopsy is a triple negative: no LM finding, no IF pattern, and effacement or fusion of foot processes with absence of deposits on EM.
PATH.6008

The same child is given a short course of corticosteroids and does not respond; repeat urinalysis now shows microscopic hematuria, and BP is 128/86. Which diagnosis becomes most likely, and which feature of the proteinuria supports it?

  1. AMinimal change disease; proteinuria is selective
  2. BFocal segmental glomerulosclerosis; proteinuria is more often non-selective
  3. CMembranous nephropathy; proteinuria is selective
  4. DDiabetic nephropathy; microalbuminuria
  5. EAmyloidosis; proteinuria mainly albumin
Answer
B. The lecture lists the six ways FSGS differs from MCD: acute or sub-acute onset · higher incidence of microscopic hematuria, reduced GFR and hypertension · proteinuria more often non-selective · poor response to corticosteroid therapy · degree of proteinuria is an important prognostic indicator · most common glomerular disorder that progresses to chronic kidney disease. Steroid failure plus hematuria plus hypertension is three of the six.
L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes438

Block exam — the nephrotic syndromes (cont.)

PATH.6008

A 54-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome has a biopsy showing diffusely thickened capillary walls; silver stain shows spikes projecting between deposits, and immunofluorescence is granular for IgG and C3 along the GBM. Which antigen underlies the primary form, and what does the injury?

  1. AType IV collagen α3 chain; neutrophil proteases
  2. BPhospholipase A2 receptor on podocytes; the membrane attack complex C5–C9
  3. CDNA–anti-DNA complexes; cytotoxic T cells
  4. Dβ2-microglobulin; macrophage phagocytosis
  5. EStreptococcal M protein; immune complex neutrophil influx
Answer
B. Membranous nephropathy. Primary disease is caused by antibodies against antigens (Phospholipase A2 Receptor, PLA2R) on podocytes, which leads to complement activation on the surface of podocytes and generates the membrane attack complex (C5–C9) → damages podocytes. 75% of cases are primary and 25% secondary. Because the injury is complement-mediated rather than neutrophil-mediated, the LM shows thickening without hypercellularity.
PATH.6008

Which secondary cause of membranous nephropathy is an EXOGENOUS antigen in this lecture's scheme?

  1. ASystemic lupus erythematosus
  2. BMelanoma
  3. CAutoimmune thyroiditis
  4. DPenicillamine
  5. EColon carcinoma
Answer
D. The lecture splits secondary causes into endogenous antigens — SLE, malignancies (lung, colon, melanoma), other autoimmune conditions like autoimmune thyroiditis — and exogenous antigens — drugs like gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs, captopril, and infections like hepatitis B, malaria, syphilis, schistosomiasis**==.
L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes439

Block exam — the nephrotic syndromes (cont.)

PATH.6007

A nephrotic patient develops flank pain and a CT shows thrombus in the right renal vein. Which two mechanisms does this lecture give for the hypercoagulability?

  1. APolycythemia and hyperviscosity
  2. BLoss of anti-thrombotic factors in the urine, plus increased hepatic synthesis of pro-thrombotic factors
  3. CPlatelet activation by circulating immune complexes
  4. DAntiphospholipid antibodies generated against the GBM
  5. EReduced hepatic clearance of activated factor X
Answer
B. There is loss of anti-thrombotic factors in the urine due to glomerular damage, and the liver's compensatory increase in protein synthesis produces an increase in pro-thrombotic factors — giving an increased risk of thrombosis, illustrated in the lecture with a CT showing right renal vein thrombosis. Renal vein thrombosis is also listed as a complication of membranous nephropathy.
PATH.6006

Which urinary finding in nephrotic syndrome is produced by the liver's compensatory response, and how is it identified?

  1. ARed cell casts, seen on phase-contrast microscopy
  2. BOval fat bodies and fatty casts, showing a Maltese cross under polarized light
  3. CWhite cell casts, seen with Wright stain
  4. DBroad waxy casts, seen with Sudan III
  5. EHyaline casts, seen with silver stain
Answer
B. Hypoalbuminemia → compensation by the liver → increased protein synthesis → hyperlipidemia → lipiduria. Urinalysis shows oval fat bodies, fatty casts and lipid droplets, seen with Sudan III stain, with the classic Maltese cross under polarized light. Red cell casts belong to the nephritic syndromes of the next lecture.
L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes440

Block exam — the nephrotic syndromes (cont.)

PATH.6008

A 63-year-old with 18 years of type 2 diabetes has 4 g/24 hr proteinuria. Which is the EARLIEST structural change, and by which modality is it identified?

  1. AKimmelstiel-Wilson nodules on PAS light microscopy
  2. BGBM thickening, identified on electron microscopy first
  3. CHyaline arteriolosclerosis on silver stain
  4. DTubular basement membrane thickening on immunofluorescence
  5. EMesangial widening on light microscopy
Answer
B. The lecture lists the earliest features in order: 1. GBM thickening (identified on EM first), 2. mesangial widening, 3. tubular BM thickening. Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules — ball-like deposits of a laminated matrix in the periphery of the glomerulus containing trapped mesangial cells — and hyaline arteriolosclerosis are later, and grossly the kidneys become granular and contracted.
PATH.6008

Which statement about the timeline of diabetic nephropathy matches the lecture?

  1. AMicroalbuminuria appears within the first year
  2. BMicroalbuminuria (30–300 mg/24 hr) appears after 7–13 years; macroalbuminuria (>300 mg/24 hr) after 10–20 years
  3. CGFR falls from the outset
  4. DMacroalbuminuria precedes microalbuminuria
  5. ENephropathy occurs only in type 1 diabetes
Answer
B. Initially, hyperglycemia leads to hyperfiltration (increased GFR) and increased glomerular hydrostatic pressure → polyuria and nocturia. After 7–13 years of disease: microalbuminuria 30–300 mg/24 hr appears in incipient nephropathy. After 10–20 years: macroalbuminuria >300 mg/24 hr, overt nephropathy. Note that GFR rises first — option 3 inverts the sequence. Urine protein is the important screening tool for tracking progression.
L19 · Glomerular Diseases Part 1 — The Nephrotic Syndromes441

Block exam — the nephrotic syndromes (cont.)

PATH.6008

A patient on haemodialysis for nine years develops nephrotic-range proteinuria. Biopsy shows material in the mesangium that obliterates the glomerular tuft. Which protein is implicated, and what is the prognosis?

  1. ALight chains; good response to steroids
  2. Bβ2-microglobulin; very poor prognosis, with many dying of end-organ failure
  3. CSerum amyloid A; excellent prognosis with dialysis
  4. DPLA2R; 10–30% remission
  5. EFibrinogen; resolves after transplant
Answer
B. Renal amyloidosis is most commonly seen in patients undergoing prolonged dialysis (β2-microglobulin). The kidney is the most commonly involved organ of systemic amyloidosis, renal insufficiency is present in 50% at the time of diagnosis, diagnosis is by biopsy of the organ involved, and the prognosis is very poor — many die of end-organ failure from amyloid deposition.
PATH.6008

Which grouping correctly separates the nephrotic entities by immune complex deposits?

  1. A(+) MCD and FSGS; (−) membranous, amyloidosis, diabetic
  2. B(+) membranous, amyloidosis, diabetic; (−) MCD, FSGS
  3. C(+) membranous only; (−) all others
  4. D(+) FSGS and diabetic; (−) MCD, membranous, amyloidosis
  5. EAll five are immune-complex diseases
Answer
B. The lecture's classification is: (+) immune complex deposits — membranous nephropathy, amyloidosis, diabetic nephropathy; (−) immune complex deposits — minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. This is also the immunofluorescence result: granular IgG and C3 along the GBM in membranous, no pattern in the podocyte diseases (FSGS sometimes granular for IgM and C3), no specific pattern in diabetic nephropathy.

Learning objective — verbatim

  • PATH.6015 Compare and contrast the relative frequency, etiology, pathogenesis, clinical presentation, course, prognosis, laboratory findings, and microscopic (light, immunofluorescent, electron microscopic) appearance of the following glomerular diseases: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease); Acute proliferative (post-streptococcal, postinfectious) glomerulonephritis; Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis; Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (e.g. Goodpasture's syndrome, Wegener's granulomatosis).
  • PATH.6016 Recognize the glomerular changes associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and outline its etiology and pathogenesis, clinical features, laboratory findings and microscopic (light, immunofluorescent, electron microscopic) appearance.

Lecture roadmap

  • IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease)
  • Acute proliferative (post-streptococcal, postinfectious) glomerulonephritis
  • Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
  • Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (e.g. Goodpasture's syndrome, Wegener's granulomatosis)
Glomerular diseases are characterized by inflammation (-itis) in the glomeruli.Pathogenesis of nephritic syndrome

Nephritic syndrome — definition and the entities

PATH.6015src p.1264

The main clinical features of nephritic syndrome

  • Hematuria — red blood cells and red cell casts in urine
  • Proteinuria (usually sub-nephrotic range) with or without edema
  • Azotemia
  • Hypertension

Clinicopathological conditions with predominantly nephritic syndrome

  1. IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease)
  2. Post-streptococcal (postinfectious) glomerulonephritis
  3. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
  4. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
Trap
Nephritic vs nephrotic is a proteinuria threshold *and* a mechanism
  • Nephrotic = podocyte injury, > 3.5 g/24 hr, bland urine. Nephritic = inflammation, sub-nephrotic proteinuria, and red cell casts and dysmorphic RBCs. The two overlap in real patients — MPGN and lupus can present either way — which is exactly why the lecture keeps returning to the biopsy.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes444

Nephritic syndrome — overall pathogenesis

PATH.6015src p.1266–1267
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes445

Complement levels in glomerular diseases — the test that splits the differential

PATH.6015 · PATH.6016src p.1265 · 1269 · 1273 · 1277 · 1285
Serum complement levels can help to distinguish glomerular diseases. Normal levels indicate that production of complement components are keeping up with the consumption of complement factors. Normal levels do not exclude complement involvement in the inflammatory process of glomerular injury.PATH.6015 + 6016
DiseaseComplement pattern in this lecture
IgA nephropathyNormal C3/C4 levels — despite activation of the alternative complement pathway in its pathogenesis
Post-streptococcal GNLow serum complement levels (part of the diagnostic triad with ASO / anti-DNase B titres)
MPGN type IClassical pathway activated; the disease involves activation of both the classical and alternative complement pathways
MPGN type II (dense deposit disease)Alternate pathway activated. Decreased serum C3 with normal C1 and C4; decreased Factor B and Properdin — the components of the alternate pathway
Lupus nephritisDisease activity and lupus flares can be monitored by serial measurement of complements, anti-dsDNA antibodies, ESR, C-reactive protein
Exam Lock
Normal complement with mesangial IgA is the giveaway
  • The lecture states plainly that IgA nephropathy's pathogenesis involves activation of the alternative complement pathway, yet C3/C4 are normal — production is keeping up with consumption. If a stem gives you gross hematuria after a sore throat with normal complement, the answer is IgA nephropathy; low complement moves it to PSGN.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes446

Where the deposit sits — the anatomical key to the whole lecture

PATH.6015src p.1276 · 1278 · 1288 · 1294
Bottom Line
The clearance rule explains PSGN's natural history
  • Subendothelial deposits are rapidly cleared, accounting for the resolution of hematuria and renal failure. Later in the disease — by the time of biopsy — there are subepithelial deposits, which are cleared slowly because they are separated from circulating cells and factors. That is why the biopsy shows humps in a child who is already recovering.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes447

IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease)

PATH.6015src p.1268–1271
Characterized by the presence of prominent IgA deposits in the mesangial regions and recurrent hematuria; it is the most common type of glomerulonephritis worldwide.Definition

Pathogenesis

Genetically susceptible individuals, after respiratory / GI infection or exposure to a microbe → increased IgA synthesis→IgA is abnormally glycosylated and is identified as an antigen→Formation of immune complexes that are deposited in the mesangium→Activation of the alternative complement pathway and initiation of glomerular injury

Clinical features

  • Most common in children and young adults.
  • Episodes of gross hematuria associated with respiratory, GI, or urinary tract viral infections, with persistent microscopic hematuria between these episodes.
  • May be associated with local pain.
  • Usually non-nephrotic range proteinuria (< 3.5 g/day).
  • Normal C3/C4 levels.
  • Slow progression to chronic renal failure; 35% develop ESRD.
  • It might present with arthritis, vasculitis.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes448

IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) (cont.)

PATH.6015src p.1268–1271

Other associated conditions

  • Dermatitis herpetiformis
  • Celiac disease / gluten-sensitive enteropathy
  • HIV infection

Morphology

Light microscopy
Mesangioproliferative pattern — segmental mesangial widening and endocapillary proliferation as a result of cellular proliferation, matrix accumulation, and immune deposits
Immunofluorescence
Characteristic deposition of IgA (with C3), principally in mesangial regions. Granular and patchy appearance. Early complement components are usually absent.
Electron microscopy
Electron-dense deposits predominantly in the mesangium
Trap
Synpharyngitic vs post-streptococcal — the timing is the discriminator
  • IgA nephropathy gives gross hematuria at the same time as, or within days of, the infection; PSGN manifests 1 to 4 weeks after the child recovers. Add normal complement (IgA) vs low complement (PSGN) and the pair separates cleanly.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes449

Acute postinfectious (post-streptococcal) glomerulonephritis

PATH.6015src p.1272–1273
Characterized by glomerular deposition of immune complexes, resulting in inflammatory cell influx and damage to glomeruli.Definition

Etiopathogenesis

  • Most common underlying infections: certain nephritogenic strains of group A β-hemolytic streptococci.
  • Throat infection (pharyngitis) or skin infection (impetigo).
  • Antibody formation against the streptococcal antigenic component to form immune complexes.
  • Initially: subendothelial immune complex deposits → pathogenesis of nephritic syndrome. Later: through unknown mechanisms, subepithelial deposits form → at the time of biopsy.

Clinical features

  • Manifests usually 1 to 4 weeks after the child recovers from a group A streptococcal infection.
  • More common in children (6–10 years of age).
  • Typical case: a young child with an abrupt onset of malaise, fever, nausea, oliguria, and hematuria (smoky or cola-colored urine) 1 to 4 weeks after recovery from a sore throat.
  • Urine appears smoky brown ("Coca-cola"-colored urine).
  • Edema and hypertension are common, with mild to moderate azotemia. Severe cases can progress to nephrotic syndrome.

Diagnosis and prognosis

  • History and clinical presentation with elevated titres of anti-streptolysin O antibody or anti-DNase B, in association with low serum complement levels.
  • Less than 1% of children do not improve and develop a rapidly progressive form of glomerulonephritis and irreversible renal failure 10 to 40 years after the initial illness.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes450

PSGN morphology — three named appearances

PATH.6015src p.1274–1276
Light microscopy
Increased cellularity of the glomerular tufts that affects nearly all glomeruli — hence the term diffuse GN. The increased cellularity is caused both by proliferation and swelling of endothelial and mesangial cells and by infiltrating neutrophils and monocytes.
Immunofluorescence
Granular deposits of IgG and C3 in the mesangium and along capillary walls. "Lumpy-bumpy" pattern. "Starry sky" appearance.
Electron microscopy
Electron-dense immune complex deposits in the subepithelial space called "humps", with a neutrophil in the lumen.
Exam Lock
Three eponymous appearances, one disease
  • Lumpy-bumpy and starry sky are the immunofluorescence; humps are the electron microscopy. All three belong to post-streptococcal GN. Compare with membranous nephropathy, whose subepithelial deposits give spike and dome on silver stain light microscopy — the same anatomical compartment, different stain, different disease.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes451

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis — the two types

PATH.6015src p.1277–1279
Membrano-
Thickened basement membrane
-proliferative
Hypercellularity due to increased mesangial and endothelial cells, and infiltration of inflammatory cells

MPGN is a histologic lesion and not a specific disease entity.

FeatureType IType II
IncidenceMost common type of MPGNVery rare; also called Dense Deposit Disease
PathogenesisIgG-immune complex mediatedNon-IgG, non-immune-complex mediated
ComplementClassical pathway activatedAlternate pathway activated
DepositsSub-endothelial immune complex deposits containing IgG and complementIntramembranous dense deposits due to alternative complement overactivation (no IgG)
Light microscopyIn both cases, the basement membrane will appear to be split in light micrographs — "tram track" appearanceAs type I

Histopathology — common to both types

  • Light microscopy with silver stain shows mesangial cell proliferation, leukocyte infiltration, and accentuation of lobular architecture.
  • The glomerular capillary wall often shows a double contour, or "tram track," appearance, especially evident with silver or PAS stains. This "splitting" of the GBM is due to extension of processes of mesangial and inflammatory cells into the peripheral capillary loops.
  • These findings are seen in type 1 and type 2 disease.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes452

MPGN type I and type II — causes, clinical course and biopsy

PATH.6015src p.1280–1286

Type I MPGN

  • Primary (idiopathic) or secondary to: systemic lupus erythematosus · hepatitis B & C · cryoglobulinemia · subacute infective endocarditis · parasitic infection.
  • Pathogenesis: the disease involves activation of both the classical and alternative complement pathways.
  • Primary disease presentation is common in adolescence or young adults; secondary disease is more common in adults and is more associated with immune complex disorders.
  • Most common form of MPGN.
  • Usually presents with acute nephritic syndrome with hematuria or a varying degree of proteinuria; insidious onset of edema and nephrotic syndrome.
  • Most progress to ESRD within 10–15 years.
Type I — immunofluorescence
Granular deposits of IgG in the basement membrane. IgG and C3 are deposited in a granular pattern. Lobular appearance of tissue is evident.
Type I — electron microscopy
Electron-dense deposits in the glomerular capillary wall between duplicated (split) basement membranes and in mesangial regions.

Type II MPGN — dense deposit disease

Circulating autoantibody termed C3 nephritic factor (C3NeF)→Binds the alternative pathway C3 convertase and protects it from inactivation→Persistent C3 activation→C3 synthesis is also decreased by the liver → hypocomplementemia
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes453

MPGN type I and type II — causes, clinical course and biopsy (cont.)

PATH.6015src p.1280–1286
  • Commonly seen in children and/or young adults.
  • Usually presents with nephritic syndrome with hematuria, and/or nephrotic syndrome.
  • Poor prognosis. High incidence of recurrence following renal transplantation (90% of cases).
  • Decreased serum C3 and normal C1 & C4. Decreased Factor B and Properdin, which are components of the alternate complement pathway.
  • It can involve the classical pathway if there are immunoglobulins.
Type II — IF and EM
C3 is present in irregular granular or linear foci in the basement membranes ("dense deposits" on immunofluorescence). Electron microscopy shows dense deposits in the basement membrane — the characteristic feature of dense deposit disease.
Exam Lock
C3NeF is the mechanism you must be able to state
  • An autoantibody that stabilises an enzyme rather than blocking it: it protects the alternative-pathway C3 convertase from inactivation, so C3 is consumed continuously. Serum C3 falls with normal C1 and C4 — the signature of pure alternative-pathway consumption — and Factor B and properdin fall with it. Recurrence after transplant in 90% follows from the fact that the antibody, not the kidney, is the disease.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes454

Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis

PATH.6015src p.1287 · 1289–1290
A clinical syndrome associated with severe glomerular injury, but it does not denote a specific etiology. Characterized by a relatively rapid and progressive loss of renal function associated with severe oliguria and signs of nephritic syndrome; if untreated, death from renal failure may occur within weeks to months.Definition
  • Three types that are either isolated kidney disease or part of a systemic syndrome.
  • Common denominator in all types of RPGN is severe glomerular injury: proteinuria (nephritic), hematuria, red blood cell casts, hypertension, edema, variable degree of oliguria.

Histopathology

  • Proliferation of glomerular epithelial cells, migration of macrophages into the urinary space, and fibrin deposition due to escape of procoagulant factors — initially more cellular, later more fibrotic.
  • Crescents contain fibrin and plasma proteins with glomerular parietal cells, monocytes, and macrophages.
  • Wrinkling and disruption of basement membranes on electron microscopy.
  • Light microscopy with silver stain: areas of necrosis and crescent formation.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes455

RPGN — the three types, reproduced exactly

PATH.6015src p.1288
Type I (35%)Type 2 (40%)Type 3 (40%)
CauseAnti-GBM antibody mediated — cross reacts with alveolar basement membrane, therefore lungs are affectedImmune-complex mediatedANCA mediated
AssociationRenal limited · Goodpasture syndromeIdiopathic · Post-infectious glomerulonephritis · IgA glomerulonephritis · Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP) · Lupus nephritisIdiopathic · Wegener's granulomatosis · Microscopic polyangiitis · Churg-Strauss syndrome
ImmunofluorescenceLinear immunofluorescenceGranular immunofluorescenceNo immunofluorescence (pauci-immune)
Exam Lock
Linear · granular · nothing
  • Three immunofluorescence patterns map one-to-one onto the three mechanisms. Linear = an antibody bound continuously along the GBM (anti-GBM). Granular = discrete immune complexes. Pauci-immune = no antibody in the tissue at all, because the antibody (ANCA) is acting on neutrophils, not on the GBM. Any RPGN question resolves to this row.
Trap
Haemoptysis plus haematuria is not automatically Goodpasture
  • Anti-GBM disease cross-reacts with alveolar basement membrane, so the lungs are affected — but the ANCA vasculitides (Wegener's granulomatosis, microscopic polyangiitis, Churg-Strauss) also produce a pulmonary-renal syndrome. The immunofluorescence pattern is what separates them: linear vs pauci-immune.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes456

Lupus nephritis

PATH.6016src p.1291–1292
An autoimmune disease involving multiple organs, characterized by a vast array of autoantibodies, particularly antinuclear antibodies (ANAs), in which injury is caused mainly by the deposition of immune complexes and binding of antibodies to various cells and tissues.Definition
Epidemiology
  • 30–50% of patients have clinical manifestations of renal disease at the time of diagnosis
  • 60% of adults and 80% of children develop renal abnormalities at some point in the course of their disease
Etiology
  • Abnormal excess production of antibodies against "endogenous" nuclear antigens (dsDNA, ANA, Sm, RNA, Ro, La)
  • Immune complex (anti-dsDNA) deposited in the kidney, with subsequent complement activation, recruitment of inflammatory cells, and tissue destruction

Clinical features

  • Clinical and immunological domains (EULAR/ACR criteria).
  • Gives rise to a wide variety of renal lesions; clinical manifestations include recurrent microscopic or gross hematuria, nephrotic syndrome, RPGN, acute and chronic renal failure, and hypertension.
  • Renal involvement usually follows a protracted course with periods of remissions and exacerbations ("on and off") immunosuppressive therapy.
  • Disease activity and lupus flares can be monitored by serial measurement of complements, anti-dsDNA antibodies, ESR, C-reactive protein.
  • Immunofluorescence: positive for IgG, IgM, C3, C1q, C4 and more → "full house" pattern (everything is positive!).
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes457

Lupus nephritis — the six ISN/RPS classes, verbatim

PATH.6016src p.1293

1Minimal mesangialNormal histology with few mesangial deposits on immunohistochemistryNormal—
2MesangioproliferativeMesangial hypercellularity with expansion of mesangial matrixElevated creatinineNephritic
