Reproduced from source p. 1293. Immunofluorescence across the classes is the "full house" pattern.

Bottom Line
Lupus can imitate every disease in both glomerular lectures
  • Class 5 is membranous nephropathy. Class 4 is a proliferative nephritic picture. Class 3/4 can present as RPGN (it is listed under immune-complex-mediated RPGN, type 2). The one finding that stays lupus-specific is the "full house" immunofluorescence — IgG, IgM, C3, C1q, C4 all positive.

Summary 2 — the eight discriminators for the nephritic lecture

src p.1259–1294
  1. Nephritic = inflammation: hematuria with red cell casts and dysmorphic RBCs, sub-nephrotic proteinuria, azotemia, hypertension (fluid retention + renin from ischemic kidneys).
  2. IgA nephropathy is the most common glomerulonephritis worldwide; hematuria is synpharyngitic; complement is normal; 35% reach ESRD.
  3. PSGN follows a group A β-hemolytic streptococcal throat or skin infection by 1–4 weeks, in children 6–10; low complement + raised ASO / anti-DNase B; < 1% progress to RPGN.
  4. PSGN's three eponyms: lumpy-bumpy · starry sky (IF) · humps (EM, subepithelial).
  5. MPGN = tram track on silver/PAS in both types. Type I: subendothelial, IgG immune complex, classical pathway. Type II (dense deposit disease): intramembranous, no IgG, alternative pathway, C3NeF, ↓C3 with normal C1/C4, 90% recurrence after transplant.
  6. RPGN = crescents. Type I linear (anti-GBM, lungs affected) · Type II granular (immune complex) · Type III pauci-immune (ANCA).
  7. Lupus nephritis: "full house" immunofluorescence; class 4 (diffuse) is the most common; class 5 is membranous.
  8. Deposit site predicts everything: mesangial → IgA; subendothelial → MPGN I, lupus III/IV, early PSGN; intramembranous → dense deposit disease; subepithelial → membranous (spike and dome) and late PSGN (humps).
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes460

Block exam — the nephritic syndromes

PATH.6015

A 19-year-old develops visible haematuria on the second day of a sore throat. He has had similar episodes before, with microscopic haematuria in between. Protein is 1.1 g/24 hr; C3 and C4 are normal. What will immunofluorescence show?

  1. ALinear IgG along the GBM
  2. BGranular IgA with C3, principally in the mesangium
  3. CGranular IgG and C3 in a lumpy-bumpy pattern
  4. DFull house pattern with C1q
  5. ENo immunofluorescence (pauci-immune)
Answer
B. IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) — the most common type of glomerulonephritis worldwide, with episodes of gross hematuria associated with respiratory, GI or urinary tract viral infections and persistent microscopic hematuria between these episodes, non-nephrotic proteinuria (< 3.5 g/day) and normal C3/C4. IF shows characteristic deposition of IgA (with C3), principally in mesangial regions — granular and patchy, with early complement components usually absent. Note the timing: same-day hematuria, not 1–4 weeks later.
PATH.6015

A 7-year-old has cola-coloured urine, periorbital oedema and BP 132/88, three weeks after impetigo. C3 is low and anti-DNase B is elevated. What does electron microscopy show, and why is the child already improving?

  1. ASubendothelial deposits, which clear slowly
  2. BSubepithelial "humps"; the earlier subendothelial deposits are rapidly cleared, which accounts for resolution of hematuria and renal failure
  3. CIntramembranous dense deposits from alternative pathway overactivation
  4. DMesangial deposits with normal complement
  5. EWrinkling and disruption of the GBM with crescents
Answer
B. Post-streptococcal GN. Initially: subendothelial immune complex deposits → pathogenesis of nephritic syndrome. Later: subepithelial deposits form → at the time of biopsy. And: subendothelial deposits are rapidly cleared, accounting for the resolution of hematuria and renal failure; the subepithelial deposits are cleared slowly because they are separated from circulating factors. Diagnosis rests on elevated ASO or anti-DNase B with low serum complement.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes461

Block exam — the nephritic syndromes (cont.)

PATH.6015

Which pair of eponymous descriptions both belong to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?

  1. ASpike and dome; tram track
  2. BLumpy-bumpy; starry sky
  3. CTram track; crescents
  4. DFull house; wire loop
  5. EMaltese cross; oval fat body
Answer
B. PSGN's immunofluorescence shows granular deposits of IgG and C3 in the mesangium and along capillary walls, described as "lumpy-bumpy" and "starry sky". Spike and dome is membranous nephropathy (silver stain, previous lecture); tram track is MPGN; crescents are RPGN; Maltese cross and oval fat bodies are the lipiduria of nephrotic syndrome.
PATH.6015

A 21-year-old has nephritic syndrome; biopsy shows a tram-track GBM on silver stain, and immunofluorescence is positive for C3 but negative for IgG, C1q and C4. Serum C3 is low with normal C1 and C4. What antibody explains the findings, and what is the transplant outcome?

  1. AAnti-PLA2R; recurrence rare
  2. BC3 nephritic factor, which binds and protects the alternative-pathway C3 convertase; recurrence in 90% after transplantation
  3. CAnti-GBM antibody; recurrence in 35%
  4. DANCA; recurrence unrelated to antibody titre
  5. EAnti-dsDNA; recurrence in 60% of adults
Answer
B. MPGN type II — dense deposit disease. Circulating autoantibody termed C3 nephritic factor (C3NeF) binds the alternative pathway C3 convertase and protects it from inactivation → persistent C3 activation; C3 synthesis is also decreased by the liver, resulting in hypocomplementemia. The lecture gives decreased serum C3 and normal C1 & C4; decreased Factor B and Properdin, poor prognosis, and high incidence of recurrence following renal transplantation (90% of cases).
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes462

Block exam — the nephritic syndromes (cont.)

PATH.6015

Which statement correctly matches an RPGN type to its immunofluorescence?

  1. AAnti-GBM disease — granular immunofluorescence
  2. BANCA-associated disease — linear immunofluorescence
  3. CImmune-complex-mediated disease — pauci-immune
  4. DAnti-GBM disease — linear immunofluorescence; ANCA-associated disease — pauci-immune
  5. EAll three types show a full house pattern
Answer
D. The lecture's table: Type I (35%) anti-GBM antibody mediated → linear immunofluorescence; Type 2 (40%) immune-complex mediated → granular immunofluorescence; Type 3 (40%) ANCA mediated → no immunofluorescence (pauci-immune). Type I cross-reacts with alveolar basement membrane, therefore the lungs are affected (Goodpasture syndrome); type 3 associations are Wegener's granulomatosis, microscopic polyangiitis, Churg-Strauss syndrome.
PATH.6015

Which of these is listed as an association of immune-complex-mediated (type 2) RPGN?

  1. AWegener's granulomatosis
  2. BMicroscopic polyangiitis
  3. CHenoch-Schönlein purpura
  4. DChurg-Strauss syndrome
  5. EGoodpasture syndrome
Answer
C. Type 2 (immune-complex-mediated) RPGN associations are idiopathic, post-infectious glomerulonephritis, IgA glomerulonephritis, Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), and lupus nephritis. Wegener's, microscopic polyangiitis and Churg-Strauss are type 3 (ANCA); Goodpasture is type I (anti-GBM).
PATH.6015

What is the composition of the crescent in RPGN?

  1. AFibrin and plasma proteins with glomerular parietal cells, monocytes, and macrophages
  2. BNeutrophils and streptococcal antigen
  3. CAmyloid fibrils and mesangial matrix
  4. DIgA and C3 immune complexes
  5. EDuplicated basement membrane and mesangial cell processes
Answer
A. Crescents contain fibrin and plasma proteins with glomerular parietal cells, monocytes, and macrophages. They arise from proliferation of glomerular epithelial cells, migration of macrophages into the urinary space, and fibrin deposition due to escape of procoagulant factors, and are initially more cellular, later more fibrotic. Option 5 describes the tram track of MPGN.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes463

Block exam — the nephritic syndromes (cont.)

PATH.6016

A woman with SLE has a renal biopsy showing diffuse endocapillary proliferation with diffuse subendothelial and mesangial deposits, and creatinine of 1.9 mg/dL. Which class is this, and what immunofluorescence pattern is expected?

  1. AClass 2; IgA only
  2. BClass 4 (the most common); a full house pattern of IgG, IgM, C3, C1q and C4
  3. CClass 5; granular IgG and C3 only
  4. DClass 6; negative immunofluorescence
  5. EClass 3; linear IgG
Answer
B. Class 4 — diffuse nephritis (most common): diffuse endocapillary ± extracapillary proliferation with diffuse subendothelial and mesangial deposits, elevated creatinine. Immunofluorescence in lupus nephritis is positive for IgG, IgM, C3, C1q, C4 and more → "full house" pattern (everything is positive!). Class 5 is membranous nephritis — thickened GBM with diffuse subepithelial deposits; class 6 is global sclerosis → ESRD.
PATH.6015 · PATH.6016

Which statement about serum complement in glomerular disease is correct as this lecture states it?

  1. AA normal complement level excludes complement involvement in glomerular injury
  2. BNormal levels indicate that production of complement components is keeping up with consumption, and do not exclude complement involvement
  3. CComplement is consumed in every glomerular disease
  4. DC4 is selectively low in dense deposit disease
  5. EIgA nephropathy characteristically has a low C3
Answer
B. Serum complement levels can help to distinguish glomerular diseases. Normal levels indicate that production of complement components are keeping up with the consumption of complement factors. Normal levels do not exclude complement involvement in the inflammatory process of glomerular injury. In dense deposit disease it is C3 that falls with normal C1 and C4 — pure alternative pathway; IgA nephropathy has normal C3/C4 despite alternative pathway activation.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes464

Block exam — the nephritic syndromes (cont.)

PATH.6015

Which feature is shared by MPGN type I and type II?

  1. AIgG-containing subendothelial deposits
  2. BTram-track (double contour) appearance of the capillary wall on silver or PAS stain
  3. CClassical complement pathway activation
  4. DC3 nephritic factor
  5. EAbsence of mesangial proliferation
Answer
B. In both cases, the basement membrane will appear to be split in light micrographs — "tram track" appearance, and these findings are seen in type 1 and type 2 disease. The splitting is due to extension of processes of mesangial and inflammatory cells into the peripheral capillary loops. IgG subendothelial deposits and classical pathway activation belong to type I; C3NeF to type II.
L21 · Glomerular Diseases Part 2 — The Nephritic Syndromes465
PATH

Tubular and Interstitial Diseases

Dr. Ravi Singh · Department of Pathology. The compartment changes and so does the urine: no nephritic or nephrotic syndrome here — tubular function fails instead.

Dr. Ravi Singh · Department of Pathology  ·  source pp. 1482–1520

Learning objectives — verbatim

  • PATH.6021 Compare and contrast the relative frequency, etiology and pathogenesis, clinical presentation, course and prognosis, laboratory findings, gross and microscopic appearance for the following renal tubular diseases: Acute tubular necrosis (toxic and ischemic); Acute tubulo-interstitial nephritis (acute drug-induced interstitial nephritis); Acute pyelonephritis; Chronic pyelonephritis.
  • PATH.6022 Distinguish the common pathologies that obstruct the urinary flow (obstructive uropathy) and explain how it can lead to hydronephrosis.
  • PATH.6023 Distinguish the types of renal stones based on their biochemical composition and explain their clinical features, preventive measures and treatment modalities.

Lecture roadmap

  • Introduction to tubulointerstitial diseases
  • Acute tubular injury / necrosis
  • Tubulointerstitial nephritis — drug-induced interstitial nephritis
  • Pyelonephritis — acute and chronic
  • Obstructive uropathy
  • Nephrolithiasis
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases466

Introduction to tubulointerstitial diseases

PATH.6021src p.1487
Acute tubular injury
  • Most common cause of acute renal failure
  • Morphologic evidence of tubular injury
  • Necrosis of tubular epithelial cells
  • Can be ischemic or toxic
Inflammation — tubulointerstitial nephritis
  • Absence of nephritic or nephrotic syndrome
  • May present with defects in tubular functions like:
  • Impaired ability to concentrate urine → polyuria or nocturia
  • Salt wasting
  • Diminished ability to excrete acids
Exam Lock
What makes this lecture different from the last two
  • Glomerular disease announces itself in the glomerular urine — protein and red cell casts. Tubulointerstitial disease announces itself as failure of tubular jobs: concentrating urine (polyuria, nocturia), reabsorbing salt (salt wasting), and excreting acid (metabolic acidosis). Learn the three failures and most of the clinical pictures follow.
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases467

Acute tubular injury / necrosis — the two etiologies

PATH.6021src p.1488

Considered to be a clinical diagnosis, not a structural one. Pre-renal and intrinsic causes — can be of two types.

ISCHEMIC CAUSES — decreased blood flow due to:NEPHROTOXIC CAUSES — direct toxic damage to tubular cells due to:
Diffuse involvement of intra-renal vessels like in microscopic polyangiitis, microangiopathies (vasculitis)Endogenous toxins like myoglobin, hemoglobin, monoclonal light chains, bile/bilirubin
Decreased effective circulating volume like in hypotensive shock due to burns or acute pancreatitis; hemorrhagic shock like in GI bleeding; septic shockExogenous toxins like drugs, radiocontrast dyes, heavy metals and organic solvents
Bottom Line
Endogenous toxins are the ones examinations hide inside a story
  • Myoglobin — crush injury, rhabdomyolysis, a statin-fibrate interaction from the antihyperlipidemics lecture. Hemoglobin — a transfusion reaction or intravascular haemolysis. Monoclonal light chains — myeloma. Bile/bilirubin — obstructive jaundice. Each is a different chapter's disease that ends in the same tubule.
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases468

Pathogenesis of acute tubular injury

PATH.6021src p.1489

The critical events in both ischemic and nephrotoxic ATI are (1) tubular injury and (2) persistent and severe disturbances in blood flow.

L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases469

ATI — the three clinical stages, and what kills in each

PATH.6021src p.1491–1493
StageTiming / definitionWhat to watch for
InitiationAround 36 hours; dominated by the inciting medical, surgical or obstetric eventSlight decrease in urine output with a rise in BUN and creatinine — due to a transient decrease in blood flow and declining GFR
MaintenanceAcute kidney injury (acute renal failure) — sustained decrease in urine output between 40–400 mL/dayRising serum creatinine and BUN. Watch for electrolyte abnormalities (like hyperkalemia), acidosis, and the signs and symptoms of uremia and fluid overload.
RecoveryWith supportive care, patients usually survive and have a good chance of recovering renal function. Early recovery: steady increase in urine volume up to 3 L/day → diuresis and polyuriaTubules are still damaged, so sodium, potassium and water are lost. Watch for life-threatening HYPOkalemia and a peculiar vulnerability to infections.
Exam Lock
The potassium flips
  • Maintenance → HYPERkalemia (you cannot excrete it). Recovery → HYPOkalemia (you are losing it in a 3 L/day diuresis through tubules that still cannot reabsorb). Same patient, opposite emergency, a week apart — and this is exactly how it is asked.
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases470

ATI — diagnosis and morphology

PATH.6021src p.1490 · 1494–1495
  • Identifying the initiation agent is the key to diagnosis.
  • Patients typically present with hypotension, oliguria, and if severe, signs of uremia.
  • Serological and urine examination findings are helpful to diagnose stage, severity and complications.
Serology
  • Elevated serum creatinine and BUN
  • Metabolic acidosis (low HCO₃⁻)
  • Serum electrolyte abnormalities
Urine examination
  • Muddy brown granular casts
  • Epithelial cell casts
  • Free epithelial cells

The presence of these casts in the urine suggests acute tubular injury.

Morphology

  • Detachment of tubular epithelial cells from their underlying basement membranes, and granular casts. Congestion of peritubular capillaries is prominent.
  • Necrotic tubular epithelial cells and cellular debris in tubular lumens.
  • In both types, lumens of the distal convoluted tubules (DCT) and collecting ducts (CD) contain casts.
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases471

Tubulointerstitial nephritis — introduction and the drug list

PATH.6021src p.1496–1500
  • Causes acute kidney injury (acute renal failure) and manifests by azotemia.
  • Inflammatory damage to the tubules + interstitium due to infection (pyelonephritis) or drug-induced immune mechanisms (allergic).

Drug-induced interstitial nephritis — the culprits, verbatim

  • First identified in patients taking sulfonamides
  • Synthetic penicillins like methicillin, ampicillin
  • Rifampin
  • Diuretics like thiazides
  • NSAIDs

Pathogenesis

Drugs function as haptens and covalently bind to some plasma membrane or extracellular component of tubular cells→These modified self-antigens then become immunogenic→The resultant injury is due to IgE or cell-mediated immune reactions directed against the tubular cells or their basement membranes

Onset and presentation

  • Begins 2 to 40 days after drug exposure (average: 15 days).
  • Fever, eosinophilia (which may be transient) and skin rash.
  • Renal abnormalities — hematuria, mild proteinuria, and leukocyturia (often including eosinophils).
  • 50% of cases: rising creatinine or acute kidney injury with oliguria.
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases472

Tubulointerstitial nephritis — introduction and the drug list (cont.)

PATH.6021src p.1496–1500
Urine examination
  • Eosinophils
  • Sterile pyuria
  • WBC casts
  • Proteinuria (mild)
Serology / blood, diagnosis and treatment
  • Increased BUN and creatinine
  • Increased eosinophil count
  • Tubular dysfunction: high K⁺, low HCO₃⁻
  • Diagnosis confirmed by renal biopsy
  • Treatment: stop the offending agent; oral steroids help recovery

Histology: chronic inflammatory infiltrate in the interstitium with tubular injury, and a prominent eosinophilic infiltrate.

Exam Lock
Fever + rash + eosinophilia + sterile pyuria ≈ 15 days after a new drug
  • That tetrad is the entire diagnosis, and sterile pyuria is the finding that separates it from pyelonephritis — white cells in the urine with no growth on culture. Treatment is withdrawal of the drug; steroids help recovery.
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases473

Pyelonephritis — pathogenesis and the ascending route

PATH.6021src p.1501–1503
  • Infection and inflammation of the kidney → pyelonephritis.
  • The most common causative agent is Escherichia coli, followed by Proteus, Klebsiella, and Enterobacter.
  • In immunocompromised persons, particularly those with transplanted organs: polyomavirus, cytomegalovirus, and adenovirus.
  • Infection can reach the kidney either hematogenously or ascending from the lower urinary tract — the most common route.

Ascending infection: urethra → bladder → kidney

Remember — organisms have to enter the bladder first! From the urethra to the bladder, organisms gain entrance during urethral catheterization or other instrumentation; long-term catheterization, in particular, carries a risk of infection.

Why women
  • Shorter urethra in females
  • Absence of antibacterial properties like in prostatic fluid
  • Hormonal changes affecting bacterial adherence to the mucosa
  • Urethral trauma during sexual intercourse
What moves organisms from bladder to kidney
  • Obstruction and stasis of urine: prostate hyperplasia, tumors, stones
  • Reflux: vesicoureteric and intrarenal
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases474

Acute pyelonephritis

PATH.6021src p.1504–1508
  • Suppurative inflammation of the kidney — acute inflammation.
  • Caused by bacterial and sometimes viral (e.g. polyomavirus) infection.
  • Infection can reach the kidney by hematogenous spread or, more commonly, through the ureters in association with vesicoureteral reflux.

Clinical features

  • Sudden onset of pain at the costovertebral angle.
  • Systemic evidence of infection, such as fever, nausea, vomiting and malaise.
  • Symptoms of bladder and urethral irritation, such as dysuria, frequency, and urgency.

Laboratory investigations

  • Pyuria — urine contains many leukocytes derived from the inflammatory infiltrate.
  • Bacteriuria.
  • Leukocyte casts — typically rich in neutrophils (pus casts). This indicates renal involvement, because casts are formed only in tubules.
  • Elevated BUN, creatinine (volume depletion).
  • Diagnosis of infection is established by quantitative urine culture.

Morphology: the cortical surface shows grayish-white areas of inflammation and abscess formation; microscopically, neutrophilic exudates within tubules and interstitium.

L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases475

Acute pyelonephritis (cont.)

PATH.6021src p.1504–1508

Complications

ComplicationDetail (verbatim)
Papillary necrosisSeen mainly in diabetics, sickle cell disease, chronic urinary tract obstruction and excessive analgesic intake. Ischemic, suppurative necrosis leads to sloughing of the papillae that can obstruct the lower urinary tract → presents acutely with fever and renal colic. Grossly: areas of hemorrhagic necrosis involve the papillae; the tissue is necrotic and seen as fragmented debris.
PyonephrosisIn case of obstruction, suppurative exudate is unable to drain and fills the renal pelvis, calyces, and ureter with pus (pyo- = pus, nephro- = kidney).
Perinephric abscessExtension of suppurative inflammation through the renal capsule into the perinephric tissue (peri- = around, nephric- = kidney).
Chronic pyelonephritisSee the next slide.
Exam Lock
Papillary necrosis — the four-cause mnemonic the lecture hands you
  • Diabetes · Sickle cell disease · Chronic obstruction · Analgesic excess. The presentation is fever plus renal colic, because the sloughed papilla behaves like a stone.
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases476

Chronic pyelonephritis

PATH.6021src p.1509–1512
Chronic inflammation of tubules and interstitium along with inflammation and scarring of the calyces and pelvis.Definition

Cause — recurrent or persistent renal infections due to

  1. More commonly, superimposition of a UTI on congenital vesicoureteral reflux and intrarenal reflux — called reflux nephropathy.
  2. Superimposed infections on obstructive lesions like posterior urethral valves and kidney stones — called chronic obstructive pyelonephritis.

Clinical features

  • Polyuria and nocturia — loss of tubular function, therefore reduced concentrating ability.
  • Development of hypertension.
  • Mild proteinuria.
  • Most patients are diagnosed after gradual onset of renal insufficiency noticed on routine renal function tests (serum creatinine and urine albumin).
  • May also present with onset of nephrotic syndrome (severe proteinuria) following the development of FSGS.

Morphology

Finding
GrossAffected kidneys are asymmetrically contracted — a shrunken kidney with irregular, coarse scars. In reflux nephropathy: preferential scarring and calyceal dilatation at the poles. In chronic obstructive interstitial nephritis: diffuse dilatation of calyces and scarring.
MicroscopicFocus of chronic inflammation · tubular atrophy · interstitial fibrosis. Many of the dilated tubules may contain pink to blue, glassy-appearing casts — it looks like thyroid, hence this change is called "thyroidization".
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases477

Chronic pyelonephritis (cont.)

PATH.6021src p.1509–1512
Trap
The FSGS link is the crossover question
  • A patient with old renal scarring who later develops nephrotic-range proteinuria has developed FSGS — the hyperfiltration injury mechanism from the nephrotic lecture (reduction in renal mass → compensatory hypertrophy and hyperfiltration → intraglomerular hypertension → segmental sclerosis). Two lectures, one patient.
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases478

The cast gallery — one urine finding, one compartment

PATH.6021src p.1494–1495 · 1499 · 1505 · 1512
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases479

Obstructive uropathy and hydronephrosis

PATH.6022src p.1513–1516
  • Obstructive lesions of the urinary tract increase susceptibility to infection and stones.
  • Unrelieved obstruction almost always leads to permanent renal atrophy → hydronephrosis or obstructive uropathy.
  • Types of obstruction: sudden or insidious · partial or complete · unilateral or bilateral · at any level of the urinary tract from the urethra to the renal pelvis.
  • Caused by intrinsic lesions of the urinary tract or extrinsic lesions that compress the ureter.

Hydronephrosis — definition and mechanism

Dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces associated with progressive atrophy of the kidney due to obstruction to the outflow of urine.Definition
OBSTRUCTION — continued glomerular filtration, but urine is unable to be excreted→Filtrate diffuses back into the renal interstitium→High pressure in the pelvis is transmitted through collecting tubules into the renal cortex→Compresses renal medullary vasculature → decrease in medullary flow → causes renal atrophy→Tubular functional defects and interstitial inflammation with fibrosis
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases480

Obstructive uropathy and hydronephrosis (cont.)

PATH.6022src p.1513–1516

Clinical features

PatternPresentation
Sudden complete obstructionRenal colic
Bilateral partial obstructionEarliest manifestation is inability to concentrate urine → polyuria and nocturia
Unilateral hydronephrosisMay remain silent for long periods because the unaffected kidney can maintain adequate renal function
Timing of reliefRenal function is fully recovered if relieved fast; irreversible damage and renal failure if obstruction is not relieved by 2–3 weeks.

Morphology: marked dilation of the pelvis and calyces and thinning of the renal parenchyma.

L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases481

Nephrolithiasis / urolithiasis — the four stone types

PATH.6023src p.1517–1518
Epidemiology
  • Affects 5% to 10% of people in the United States in their lifetime
  • Stones may form anywhere in the urinary tract — most arise in the kidney
  • Men affected more often than women
  • Peak age at onset is between 20 and 30 years
Etiology
  • Idiopathic or specific disease (gout, cystinuria, hyperoxaluria)
TypeFrequencyCompositionMechanism / association
Calcium stones70%Calcium oxalate and phosphateHypercalcemia and hypercalciuria
Triple / struvite stones15%Magnesium ammonium phosphateUrea-splitting bacteria like Proteus
Uric acid stones5–10%Uric acidWith or without hyperuricemia; tendency to excrete urine at low pH
Cystine stones1–2%CystineGenetic defects in the renal reabsorption of amino acids, including cystine, leading to cystinuria

Pathogenesis

  • Increased concentration of stone constituents
  • Changes in urinary pH
  • Decreased urine volume
  • Presence of bacteria influence the formation of calculi
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases482

Stones — clinical features, treatment and prevention

PATH.6023src p.1518–1519

Clinical features

  • Silent if they remain in the renal pelvis.
  • Symptomatic if the stone passes into the ureters:
  • Renal colic — abrupt onset of flank pain radiating to the groin (intermittent), nausea, vomiting, gross or microscopic hematuria (ulceration of urothelium).
  • Superimposed UTI — urinary stasis, trauma.
  • Hydronephrosis due to obstruction of the ureter.

Treatment and prevention

Treatment options
  • IV antibiotics
  • Urosurgical intervention
Prevention — by decreasing urinary concentration of the causative substances
  • Increased fluid intake (2 L/day)
  • Low sodium diet → decreases urinary calcium excretion
  • Alkalinisation of urine to increase solubility of uric acid
Bottom Line
Prevention answers follow directly from the stone's chemistry
  • Uric acid stones precipitate at low pH → alkalinise the urine. Calcium stones follow urinary calcium → a low-sodium diet lowers calcium excretion. Struvite stones follow urea-splitting organisms → the infection is the target. Every preventive measure is the mechanism run backwards.

Block exam — tubular and interstitial diseases

PATH.6021

A 68-year-old is admitted after a ruptured AAA repair complicated by hypotension. On day 2 urine output is 180 mL, creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 3.4 mg/dL, and K⁺ is 6.1 mmol/L. Urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts. Which stage is this, and what is the immediate danger?

  1. AInitiation; volume depletion
  2. BMaintenance; hyperkalemia, acidosis, uremia and fluid overload
  3. CRecovery; hypokalemia and infection
  4. DDrug-induced interstitial nephritis; eosinophiluria
  5. EAcute pyelonephritis; urosepsis
Answer
B. This is the maintenance stage of acute tubular injury — sustained decrease in urine output between 40–400 mL/day with rising serum creatinine and BUN; watch out for electrolyte abnormalities (like hyperkalemia), acidosis and the signs and symptoms of uremia and fluid overload. Initiation is around 36 hours with only a slight fall in output; recovery brings diuresis up to 3 L/day and the opposite danger, life-threatening hypokalemia. Muddy brown granular casts and epithelial cell casts confirm ATI.
PATH.6021

Ten days after starting ampicillin for pneumonia, a 44-year-old has fever, a maculopapular rash, creatinine 2.6 mg/dL and eosinophilia. Urine shows white cells and eosinophils but no growth. Which mechanism underlies this?

  1. ADirect tubular toxicity from the antibiotic
  2. BThe drug acts as a hapten, covalently binding a tubular cell component; the modified self-antigen provokes IgE or cell-mediated injury
  3. CImmune complex deposition in the mesangium
  4. DAscending bacterial infection from the bladder
  5. EAlternative complement pathway overactivation
Answer
B. Drug-induced interstitial nephritis. Drugs function as haptens and covalently bind to some plasma membrane or extracellular component of tubular cells; these modified self-antigens then become immunogenic; the resultant injury is due to IgE or cell-mediated immune reactions directed against the tubular cells or their basement membranes. Onset is 2 to 40 days after drug exposure (average: 15 days) with fever, eosinophilia and rash, and the urine shows eosinophils and sterile pyuria.
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases486

Block exam — tubular and interstitial diseases (cont.)

PATH.6021

Which drug class named in this lecture was the FIRST in which drug-induced interstitial nephritis was identified?

  1. ANSAIDs
  2. BSulfonamides
  3. CThiazide diuretics
  4. DRifampin
  5. ESynthetic penicillins
Answer
B. First identified in patients taking sulfonamides. The lecture's full list is sulfonamides · synthetic penicillins like methicillin and ampicillin · rifampin · diuretics like thiazides · NSAIDs.
PATH.6021

A 26-year-old woman has fever 39 °C, right costovertebral angle tenderness, dysuria and frequency. Urine shows pyuria, bacteriuria and casts packed with neutrophils. Which finding proves the kidney — not just the bladder — is involved, and why?

  1. ABacteriuria, because bacteria colonise the tubules
  2. BLeukocyte (pus) casts, because casts are formed only in tubules
  3. CDysuria, because it reflects ureteric irritation
  4. DElevated BUN, because it reflects renal parenchymal loss
  5. EPositive nitrites, because they indicate upper tract organisms
Answer
B. Leukocyte casts — typically rich in neutrophils (pus casts) — indicate renal involvement, because casts are formed only in tubules. Pyuria and bacteriuria occur in lower tract infection too. The diagnosis of infection is established by quantitative urine culture, and E. coli is the commonest organism, followed by Proteus, Klebsiella and Enterobacter.
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases487

Block exam — tubular and interstitial diseases (cont.)

PATH.6021

A diabetic with recurrent pyelonephritis develops fever with renal colic; imaging shows a filling defect and CT shows fragmented necrotic tissue in the papillae. Which four settings does this lecture list for this complication?

  1. APregnancy, hypertension, myeloma, gout
  2. BDiabetes, sickle cell disease, chronic urinary tract obstruction, excessive analgesic intake
  3. CDiabetes, hypertension, transplantation, NSAIDs
  4. DSickle cell disease, cystinuria, amyloidosis, obstruction
  5. EAnalgesic use, contrast exposure, myoglobinuria, sepsis
Answer
B. Papillary necrosis is seen mainly in diabetics, sickle cell disease, chronic urinary tract obstruction and excessive analgesic intake. It is an ischemic, suppurative necrosis that leads to sloughing of the papillae, which can obstruct the lower urinary tract → presenting acutely with fever and renal colic. The other complications listed are pyonephrosis and perinephric abscess.
PATH.6021

Which histological feature is characteristic of chronic pyelonephritis?

  1. ACrescents in Bowman's space
  2. BTram-track duplication of the GBM
  3. CDilated tubules containing pink-to-blue glassy casts resembling thyroid follicles
  4. DKimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
  5. ESubepithelial humps
Answer
C. Many of the dilated tubules may contain pink to blue, glassy-appearing casts — it looks like thyroid, hence this change is called "thyroidization". The other microscopic findings are foci of chronic inflammation, tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis, and grossly an asymmetrically contracted kidney with irregular, coarse scars — polar scarring with calyceal dilatation in reflux nephropathy versus diffuse calyceal dilatation in chronic obstruction.
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases488

Block exam — tubular and interstitial diseases (cont.)

PATH.6022

A man with prostatic hyperplasia has bilateral partial obstruction. What is the EARLIEST manifestation, and how long can obstruction persist before damage becomes irreversible?

  1. ARenal colic; 24 hours
  2. BInability to concentrate urine causing polyuria and nocturia; 2–3 weeks
  3. CAnuria; 48 hours
  4. DHematuria; 6 months
  5. EHypertension; 3 months
Answer
B. Bilateral partial obstruction — the earliest manifestation is inability to concentrate urine → polyuria and nocturia. Sudden complete obstruction gives renal colic, and unilateral hydronephrosis may remain silent for long periods because the unaffected kidney can maintain adequate renal function. Renal function is fully recovered if relieved fast; irreversible damage and renal failure occur if obstruction is not relieved by 2–3 weeks.
PATH.6023

Urine culture in a patient with recurrent stones grows Proteus. Which stone type is expected, and what is its composition?

  1. ACalcium oxalate; 70% of stones
  2. BStruvite (triple) stone; magnesium ammonium phosphate
  3. CUric acid; formed at low urinary pH
  4. DCystine; from defective amino acid reabsorption
  5. ECalcium phosphate; from hypercalciuria
Answer
B. Triple / struvite stones (15%) — magnesium ammonium phosphate — are formed by urea-splitting bacteria like Proteus. Urease raises urinary pH and supplies ammonium. For comparison: calcium stones (70%) — calcium oxalate and phosphate, with hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria; uric acid stones (5–10%) — with or without hyperuricemia, tendency to excrete urine at low pH; cystine stones (1–2%) — genetic defects in renal reabsorption of amino acids including cystine.
PATH.6023

Which preventive measure does this lecture pair with uric acid stones specifically, and why?

  1. ALow sodium diet, to reduce urinary calcium excretion
  2. BAlkalinisation of urine, to increase the solubility of uric acid
  3. CAntibiotics, to eliminate urea-splitting bacteria
  4. DThiazide diuretics, to reduce urinary calcium
  5. ERestriction of dietary oxalate
Answer
B. The lecture's prevention list is increased fluid intake (2 L/day) · low sodium diet → decrease urinary calcium excretion · alkalinisation of urine to increase solubility of uric acid. Uric acid stones form because of a tendency to excrete urine at low pH, so raising the pH dissolves them — the mechanism run backwards.
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases489

Block exam — tubular and interstitial diseases (cont.)

PATH.6021

Which of the following is a NEPHROTOXIC (rather than ischemic) cause of acute tubular injury in this lecture's classification?

  1. AMicroscopic polyangiitis
  2. BHemorrhagic shock from GI bleeding
  3. CSeptic shock
  4. DMyoglobin released after crush injury
  5. EHypotensive shock following burns
Answer
D. Nephrotoxic causes = direct toxic damage to tubular cells. Endogenous toxins like myoglobin, hemoglobin, monoclonal light chains, bile/bilirubin; exogenous toxins like drugs, radiocontrast dyes, heavy metals and organic solvents. The other four options are all ischemic — diffuse involvement of intra-renal vessels (microscopic polyangiitis, microangiopathies) and decreased effective circulating volume (burns, acute pancreatitis, hemorrhagic shock, septic shock).
L23 · Tubular and Interstitial Diseases490
PATH

Renal Vascular Diseases

Dr. Ravi Singh · Department of Pathology. Hypertension damages the kidney, and the damaged kidney raises the pressure. Then: microangiopathies, cysts, and one collagen disease.

Dr. Ravi Singh · Department of Pathology  ·  source pp. 1643–1675

Learning objectives — verbatim

  • PATH.6027 Compare and contrast the pathogenesis, gross and microscopic appearance, clinical presentations, course and prognosis of benign nephrosclerosis and malignant nephrosclerosis.
  • PATH.6028 Distinguish the vascular diseases that involve the kidney with regard to etiology, pathogenesis, clinical presentation, lab investigations, course and prognosis.
  • PATH.6029 Diagnose the common cystic lesions in the kidney based on morphology, clinical features, and genetic basis and associated abnormalities.
  • PATH.6030 / PATH.6036 Explain the pathogenesis, gross and microscopic appearance, clinical presentation of Alport syndrome.

Lecture roadmap

  • Hypertension — nephrosclerosis (benign and malignant)
  • Renal artery stenosis
  • Thrombotic microangiopathies (HUS and TTP)
  • Cystic diseases of the kidney
  • Alport syndrome
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders491

Nephrosclerosis — the shared pathogenesis

PATH.6027src p.1647
Nephrosclerosis — term used for the renal pathology associated with sclerosis of renal arterioles and small arteries; it is strongly associated with hypertension.Definition

Pathogenesis

  • Medial and intimal thickening, a response to hemodynamic changes, aging, genetic defects, or some combination of these.
  • Hyalinization of arteriolar walls, caused by extravasation of plasma proteins through injured endothelium and by increased deposition of basement membrane matrix.
  • Thickened walls → affected vessels have narrowed lumens → focal parenchymal ischemia → glomerulosclerosis and chronic tubulointerstitial injury.
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders492

Benign vs malignant nephrosclerosis — the branch point

PATH.6027src p.1649 · 1653–1654
Exam Lock
Hyaline vs hyperplastic — the one-word answer
  • Benign → hyaline arteriolosclerosis. Malignant → hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis ("onion-skin") plus fibrinoid necrosis of the afferent arteriole. The mechanistic reason is in the diagrams: benign disease reduces pressure transmission downstream, while malignant hypertension causes breakthrough transmission of high pressure that injures the endothelium directly.
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders493

Benign nephrosclerosis

PATH.6027src p.1648 · 1650–1651
  • Benign as patients are asymptomatic. Usually normal or slightly reduced GFR.
  • Risk factors for ESRD: higher blood pressure · a second underlying CKD (diabetes).

Pathological features

Vascular
  • Medial and intimal thickening
  • Hyaline arteriolosclerosis
Glomerular
  • Global sclerosis
  • FSGS — compensatory hyperfiltration due to nephron loss
Tubulointerstitial
  • Tubular atrophy
  • Ischemia-mediated interstitial fibrosis

Clinical features and diagnosis

  • Patients with a long-standing history of hypertension present with a slowly progressive elevation in serum creatinine.
  • Mild proteinuria (< 1 g/day). No microscopic hematuria.
  • Few progress to end-stage renal disease.
  • Diagnosis is based on clinical features; urine analysis shows a bland urine sediment — no cells, casts or crystals — with mild proteinuria.

Don't forget the other manifestations of long-standing hypertension: LVH (left ventricular hypertrophy) · retinopathy · stroke.

Gross
Cortical surfaces have a fine, even granularity — resembles grain leather.
Trap
"Bland sediment" is the discriminator, not the creatinine
  • Almost every renal disease raises creatinine. What makes benign nephrosclerosis recognisable is what is absent: no cells, no casts, no crystals, and no microscopic hematuria, with proteinuria under 1 g/day. Compare the cast gallery from the tubular lecture — this is the one entity whose urine is empty.
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders494

Malignant nephrosclerosis

PATH.6027src p.1652–1654
  • ~5% of hypertensives (primary or secondary) → rapidly rising blood pressure (200/120 mm Hg and more).
  • Evidence of end-organ damage — renal failure, retinal hemorrhages and exudates, with or without papilledema (optic nerve swelling indicative of increased intracranial pressure).
  • Termed malignant hypertension. The renal lesions associated with it → malignant nephrosclerosis — remember, nothing to do with cancers!

Pathogenesis — where it diverges from benign disease

Medial and intimal thickening + duplication of basement membrane → luminal narrowing→SEVERE hypertension results in breakthrough transmission of high pressure→Endothelial cell injury in arterioles and capillaries→Fibrinogen, platelet activation and plasma protein leakage → fibrinoid necrosis and intravascular thrombosis

Pathological findings

  • Fibrinoid necrosis of the afferent arteriole.
  • Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis — the "onion-skin" lesion.
Bottom Line
Malignant hypertension is a thrombotic microangiopathy
  • The lecture lists malignant hypertension among the secondary causes of thrombotic microangiopathy two slides later — and the pathogenesis says why: endothelial injury → platelet activation → intravascular thrombosis. So a patient with BP 220/130, schistocytes and a falling platelet count is not two diseases; it is one.
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders495

Renal artery stenosis

PATH.6028src p.1655–1657
  • Unilateral renal artery stenosis is responsible for 2% to 5% of hypertension cases.
  • Etiopathogenesis: hypertension secondary to renal artery stenosis is caused by increased production of renin from the ischemic kidney.

Most common causes

CauseShareDetail
Atherosclerosis> 70%The typical older hypertensive with vascular disease elsewhere
Fibromuscular dysplasia> 10%More common in women and tends to occur in younger age groups — the third and fourth decades.

Pathological findings

  • Diffuse atrophy of the affected kidney due to ischemia; crowded glomeruli, atrophic tubules, interstitial fibrosis, and focal inflammatory infiltrates.
  • Hypertension due to renal artery stenosis leads to hyaline arteriolosclerosis in the CONTRALATERAL kidney.

Clinical features and investigations

  • Most patients are long-standing hypertensives; a bruit can be heard on auscultation of the affected kidneys.
  • Sometimes present with sudden onset of uncontrolled hypertension in a previously well-controlled patient, or accelerated / malignant hypertension.
  • Elevated plasma or renal vein renin, response to an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.
  • Arteriography is required to localize the stenotic lesion.
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders496

Renal artery stenosis (cont.)

PATH.6028src p.1655–1657
Exam Lock
The two kidneys look different — and that is the diagnosis
  • The stenotic kidney is protected from the systemic pressure and becomes atrophic and ischemic; the contralateral kidney takes the full pressure and develops hyaline arteriolosclerosis. Asymmetric kidneys in a hypertensive patient with a bruit is the classic picture.
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders497

Thrombotic microangiopathies (TMA)

PATH.6028src p.1658–1660
Refers to conditions presenting with renal failure due to systemic vascular lesions characterized by microvascular thrombosis, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Could be primary or secondary.Definition
Primary — those with a known etiology
  • Shiga toxin mediated hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) and atypical HUS (complement mediated TMA)
  • Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)
Secondary — develop in the background of other diseases without well-defined etiologies
  • Malignant hypertension
  • Scleroderma-associated TMA

The three mechanisms — why the triad exists

  1. Flow abnormalities → shear and mechanically damage red cells → microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA). Mechanically damaged RBCs are called "schistocytes" or fragmented RBCs.
  2. Microvascular occlusions that cause tissue ischemia and organ dysfunction.
  3. Widespread "consumption" of platelets leads to thrombocytopenia.

Caused by diverse insults that lead to thrombi in capillaries and/or arterioles in various tissue beds, including those of the kidney.

L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders498

HUS vs TTP — the pair that is always tested together

PATH.6028src p.1661–1662
Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)
Classic settingClassically seen in children one week after an episode of bloody diarrhea caused by enterohemorrhagic E. coli (O157:H7).Due to deficiency of ADAMTS13 enzyme.
Organ emphasisMore severe renal failure, less pronounced CNS involvement.CNS involvement more pronounced, renal failure less severe.
Other causes / associationsOther infections like viral, Shigella, Salmonella. Drug-induced: quinine (tonic water), gemcitabine, cyclosporine, ticlopidine, oral contraceptives.Often associated with SLE, HIV, hematological malignancy.

Clinical features and laboratory findings — common to both

  • Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia — schistocytes in the peripheral blood smear.
  • Thrombocytopenia.
  • Purpuric rash.
  • Acute renal failure — mild to moderate proteinuria, hematuria.
  • Neurological abnormalities: headache, confusion, seizure, stroke.
  • Fever.

Fibrin stain shows thrombi (red) in the glomerular capillaries — characteristic of thrombotic microangiopathic disorders.

Trap
Do not let the shared triad hide the discriminator
  • Both produce MAHA + thrombocytopenia + renal impairment + neurological signs + fever. What separates them is the weighting (kidney-dominant = HUS, brain-dominant = TTP) and the mechanism (Shiga toxin after bloody diarrhoea vs ADAMTS13 deficiency).
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders499

Cystic diseases of the kidney — the classification

PATH.6029src p.1663–1664
Inherited
  • Autosomal dominant adult polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) — polycystin proteins
  • Autosomal recessive childhood polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) — fibrocystin proteins
Acquired
  • Benign simple cysts — older age, common post-mortem finding
  • Medullary sponge kidney
Associated with systemic syndromes
  • Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL gene)
  • Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 and TSC2 genes)

Shared pathogenesis

Mutations in polycystin 1, 2 and fibrocystin→Altered tubular epithelial growth and differentiation→Cyst formation→As cysts grow, they compress surrounding parenchyma → glomerular damage · vascular damage · interstitial inflammation and fibrosis
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders500

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)

PATH.6029src p.1665–1669
Hereditary disorder characterized by multiple expanding cysts of both kidneys that ultimately destroy the renal parenchyma and cause renal failure. Clinically silent until adulthood — autosomal dominant, AD = Adulthood.Definition
Epidemiology
  • Common condition affecting roughly 1 in 400 to 1000 live births
  • Accounting for about 5% to 10% of cases of ESRD
Inheritance
  • Autosomal dominant
  • Each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the mutation
  • No "skipped generations"
  • Equally transmitted by men and women

Etiopathogenesis

GeneLocusProteinPhenotype
PKD1Chromosome 16p13Polycystin 1Most common
PKD2Chromosome 4q21Polycystin 2Milder phenotype · later onset of cysts · fewer and smaller cysts · slower progression · later age of ESRD
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders501

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) (cont.)

PATH.6029src p.1665–1669

Renal manifestations — each one is a mechanical consequence of the cysts

MechanismResult
Cysts compress renal vasculature → release of renin and aldosterone systemHypertension
Cysts rupture into the collecting ductHematuria
Cysts stretch the renal capsuleFlank / back pain
Distal tubule secretion and absorption defectsNephrolithiasis — uric acid and calcium oxalate stones

Infections are common — infected cysts and acute pyelonephritis caused by gram-negative bacteria.

Extrarenal manifestations

  • Hepatic cysts (most common)
  • Cysts in pancreas, spleen and lungs
  • Colonic diverticulae
  • Berry (intracranial) aneurysms — can rupture and cause stroke
  • Mitral valve prolapse

Gross: the kidney is markedly enlarged, with numerous dilated cysts.

L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders502

ARPKD, medullary sponge kidney, and Alport syndrome

PATH.6029 · PATH.6030 · PATH.6036src p.1670–1674

Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease

  • Autosomal recessive in inheritance. Manifests in neonates, infants and children.
  • Mutation in the PKHD1 gene on chromosome 6p21 coding for fibrocystin protein.
  • The kidney is enlarged with a smooth external surface.
  • Dilated elongated channels are present at right angles to the cortical surface, completely replacing the medulla and cortex.
  • Congenital hepatic fibrosis: common extrarenal manifestation.
  • Renal failure and death may occur in infants.

Medullary sponge kidney

  • Multiple cystic dilations of the collecting ducts in the medulla.
  • Occurs in adults.
  • Unknown etiopathogenesis.
  • Usually discovered radiographically.
  • Renal function is usually normal.

Alport syndrome

  • Inherited disease of the basement membrane collagen type IV, which is crucial for normal function of the lens, cochlea, and glomerulus.
  • Inheritance: most commonly X-linked; autosomal recessive and dominant forms also seen.
  • Genes involved: genes coding for the alpha chains in collagen type IV → COL4A4 and COL4A5.
  • Pathogenesis: defective assembly of the collagen network → defect in GBM.
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders503

ARPKD, medullary sponge kidney, and Alport syndrome (cont.)

PATH.6029 · PATH.6030 · PATH.6036src p.1670–1674
Alport syndromeDetail
Clinical featuresMales > females. Symptoms appear between 5–20 years of age; overt renal failure appears between 20–50 years in men. Most common presenting complaint: gross or microscopic hematuria along with red cell casts.
Other features — type IV collagen is widespread!1. Nerve deafness · 2. Lens dislocation · 3. Posterior cataracts · 4. Corneal dystrophy
Electron microscopyPronounced splitting and lamination of the lamina densa, often producing a distinctive "basket weave" appearance. Irregular thickening of the basement membrane with foci of rarefaction.
ImmunohistochemistryAntibodies against alpha chains — negative in basement membranes.
Bottom Line
Two "split basement membrane" appearances, two very different diseases
  • MPGN gives a "tram track" — the GBM is duplicated by interposed mesangial cell processes and the disease is inflammatory. Alport gives a "basket weave" — the lamina densa itself splits and laminates because the type IV collagen network is defective, and the disease is inherited. Deafness and lens problems settle it clinically.

Block exam — renal vascular and cystic disease

PATH.6027

A 62-year-old with 20 years of hypertension has creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, urine protein 0.6 g/day, no haematuria, and a completely bland sediment. Which vascular lesion is expected on biopsy?

  1. AFibrinoid necrosis of the afferent arteriole
  2. BHyaline arteriolosclerosis with medial and intimal thickening
  3. CHyperplastic "onion-skin" arteriolosclerosis
  4. DFibrin thrombi in glomerular capillaries
  5. EDuplication of the glomerular basement membrane
Answer
B. Benign nephrosclerosis: patients are asymptomatic with slowly progressive elevation in serum creatinine, mild proteinuria (< 1 g/day), no microscopic hematuria, and a bland urine sediment — no cells, casts or crystals. The vascular lesion is hyaline arteriolosclerosis with medial and intimal thickening, and grossly the cortex has a fine, even granularity resembling grain leather. Options 1 and 3 belong to malignant nephrosclerosis.
PATH.6027

A 41-year-old presents with BP 226/134, headache, retinal haemorrhages and papilloedema, and creatinine 3.8 mg/dL. Which mechanism explains the renal lesion?

  1. AReduced pressure transmission to arterioles protects the glomerulus
  2. BBreakthrough transmission of high pressure injures arteriolar and capillary endothelium, allowing fibrinogen and plasma protein leakage with platelet activation
  3. CImmune complex deposition activates the classical complement pathway
  4. DIncreased renin release from an ischemic kidney
  5. EADAMTS13 deficiency causes microvascular thrombosis
Answer
B. Malignant nephrosclerosis — ~5% of hypertensives develop rapidly rising blood pressure (200/120 mm Hg and more) with evidence of end-organ damage — renal failure, retinal hemorrhages and exudates, with or without papilledema. The pathogenesis: medial and intimal thickening plus duplication of the basement membrane → luminal narrowing, then severe hypertension results in breakthrough transmission of high pressure → endothelial cell injury → fibrinogen, platelet activation and plasma protein leakage → fibrinoid necrosis and intravascular thrombosis. Option 1 is the benign pathway.
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders508

Block exam — renal vascular and cystic disease (cont.)

PATH.6028

A 34-year-old woman develops severe hypertension over three months with an abdominal bruit. Angiography shows a beaded mid-renal artery. What is the mechanism of her hypertension, and what will the contralateral kidney show?

  1. AAldosterone excess; contralateral hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis
  2. BIncreased renin production from the ischemic kidney; contralateral hyaline arteriolosclerosis
  3. CCatecholamine excess; contralateral fibrinoid necrosis
  4. DVolume overload; contralateral normal histology
  5. EImmune complex nephritis; contralateral crescents
Answer
B. Renal artery stenosis from fibromuscular dysplasia — > 10% of cases, more common in women, third and fourth decades (atherosclerosis accounts for > 70%). Hypertension secondary to renal artery stenosis is caused by increased production of renin from the ischemic kidney, and hypertension due to renal artery stenosis leads to hyaline arteriolosclerosis in the contralateral kidney. Investigations: elevated plasma or renal vein renin, response to an ACE inhibitor, with arteriography required to localise the lesion.
PATH.6028

A 5-year-old is admitted with anuria, platelets 42 ×10⁹/L and schistocytes on the smear, one week after bloody diarrhoea. Which diagnosis and which organ emphasis?

  1. ATTP; CNS involvement more pronounced, renal failure less severe
  2. BHUS; more severe renal failure, less pronounced CNS involvement
  3. CMalignant nephrosclerosis; retinal involvement predominates
  4. DPost-streptococcal GN; nephritic syndrome
  5. EADPKD; haematuria from cyst rupture
Answer
B. Hemolytic uremic syndrome — classically seen in children one week after an episode of bloody diarrhea caused by enterohemorrhagic E. coli (O157:H7), with more severe renal failure and less pronounced CNS involvement. TTP is the mirror image: due to deficiency of ADAMTS13, with CNS involvement more pronounced and renal failure less severe, often associated with SLE, HIV and haematological malignancy.
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders509

Block exam — renal vascular and cystic disease (cont.)

PATH.6028

Which of these is listed as a SECONDARY thrombotic microangiopathy?

  1. AShiga-toxin-mediated HUS
  2. BAtypical (complement-mediated) HUS
  3. CTTP
  4. DMalignant hypertension
  5. EADAMTS13 deficiency
Answer
D. The lecture splits TMA into primary — those with a known etiology: Shiga-toxin-mediated HUS and atypical HUS (complement-mediated TMA), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) and secondary — develop in the background of other diseases or conditions without well-defined etiologies, like malignant hypertension and scleroderma-associated TMA. The triad in all of them is microvascular thrombosis, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia.
PATH.6029

A 38-year-old with bilateral flank masses, hypertension and haematuria has a family history of renal failure in her father and grandmother. Which extrarenal complication most threatens her life, and which gene is most commonly responsible?

  1. ACongenital hepatic fibrosis; PKHD1
  2. BBerry aneurysm rupture causing stroke; PKD1
  3. CColonic diverticulitis; PKD2
  4. DRetinal haemangioblastoma; VHL
  5. ERenal angiomyolipoma; TSC1
Answer
B. ADPKD. PKD1 on chromosome 16p13 → polycystin 1 (most common); PKD2 (4q21, polycystin 2) gives a milder phenotype with later onset. Extrarenal manifestations: hepatic cysts (most common), cysts in pancreas, spleen and lungs, colonic diverticulae, berry (intracranial) aneurysms — which can rupture and cause stroke — and mitral valve prolapse. Note the inheritance signature in the stem: no skipped generations, equally transmitted by men and women, 50% per child. PKHD1/congenital hepatic fibrosis belongs to ARPKD.
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders510

Block exam — renal vascular and cystic disease (cont.)

PATH.6029

Which cystic disease shows dilated elongated channels arranged at right angles to the cortical surface, completely replacing medulla and cortex?

  1. AADPKD
  2. BARPKD
  3. CMedullary sponge kidney
  4. DSimple benign cysts
  5. EVon Hippel-Lindau disease
Answer
B. Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease — the kidney is enlarged with a smooth external surface; dilated elongated channels are present at right angles to the cortical surface, completely replacing the medulla and cortex. It is caused by mutation in the PKHD1 gene on chromosome 6p21 coding for fibrocystin protein, manifests in neonates, infants and children, and its common extrarenal manifestation is congenital hepatic fibrosis. Medullary sponge kidney is multiple cystic dilations of the collecting ducts in the medulla, in adults, with normal renal function.
PATH.6030 · PATH.6036

A 14-year-old boy has persistent microscopic haematuria with red cell casts, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss and anterior lenticonus. What will electron microscopy show?

  1. ASubepithelial humps
  2. BTram-track duplication of the GBM
  3. CSplitting and lamination of the lamina densa in a basket-weave pattern
  4. DEffacement of foot processes without deposits
  5. EWire-loop capillary thickening
Answer
C. Alport syndrome — an inherited disease of basement membrane collagen type IV, which is crucial for normal function of the lens, cochlea, and glomerulus, caused by mutations in COL4A4 and COL4A5 and most commonly X-linked (males > females). Electron microscopy shows pronounced splitting and lamination of the lamina densa, often producing a distinctive "basket weave" appearance, and immunohistochemistry with antibodies against alpha chains is negative in basement membranes. The other features are nerve deafness, lens dislocation, posterior cataracts and corneal dystrophy.
L25 · Renal Vascular Diseases and Miscellaneous Disorders511

Block exam — renal vascular and cystic disease (cont.)

PATH.6029

Which renal manifestation of ADPKD is explained by cysts compressing the renal vasculature?

  1. AHaematuria
  2. BFlank pain
  3. CHypertension
  4. DNephrolithiasis
  5. ERecurrent infection
Answer
C. The lecture maps each manifestation to a mechanical consequence: cysts compress renal vasculature → release of renin and aldosterone system → hypertension; rupture into the collecting duct → haematuria; stretch the renal capsule → flank/back pain; distal tubule secretion and absorption defects → nephrolithiasis (uric acid and calcium oxalate stones). Infections are common as infected cysts and acute pyelonephritis caused by gram-negative bacteria.
PATH.6027

Which statement about nephrosclerosis pathogenesis is correct as this lecture states it?

  1. AHyalinization results from lipid deposition within the media
  2. BHyalinization is caused by extravasation of plasma proteins through injured endothelium and by increased deposition of basement membrane matrix
  3. CNephrosclerosis spares the glomeruli entirely
  4. DMedial and intimal thickening widen the lumen
  5. ENephrosclerosis is unrelated to hypertension
Answer
B. Hyalinization of arteriolar walls, caused by extravasation of plasma proteins through injured endothelium and by increased deposition of basement membrane matrix. The sequence continues: thickened walls → affected vessels have narrowed lumens → focal parenchymal ischemia → glomerulosclerosis and chronic tubulointerstitial injury, and nephrosclerosis is strongly associated with hypertension.
