L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis513

Classification — four axes, and the words that matter on each

MICR.83src p.1788–1789

Urinary tract infections (UTI): infections of the bladder, urethra, ureters, or kidneys.

ClassificationClinical nameDetails (verbatim)
By clinical presentationAsymptomatic bacteriuriaBacteriuria without clinical symptoms
Urinary tract infectionBacteriuria with clinical symptoms
By anatomical locationLower UTIInfections of the bladder (cystitis) and/or urethra (urethritis)
Upper UTIInfections of the kidney and ureter (pyelonephritis)
By severity of infectionUncomplicated UTIUTIs in healthy pre-menopausal, non-pregnant women without further risk factors for infection, and individuals with no history of treatment failure
Complicated UTIUTIs in individuals with risk factors for infection, structural or functional abnormalities of the urinary tract, with a history of treatment failure, or a risk of serious complications
By route of infectionAscending (most common)UTIs caused by the migration of organisms, primarily bacteria, from the perineum via the urethra to the bladder and kidney
Exam Lock
"Uncomplicated" is a definition, not an impression
  • It means a healthy, pre-menopausal, non-pregnant woman with no risk factors and no treatment failure. Everything else — men, pregnancy, catheters, stones, diabetes, structural abnormality, recurrence — is complicated, and that word changes the diagnostic pathway (urine culture required) and the complication list.
L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis514

Epidemiology and the urinary tract's own defences

MICR.85 · MICR.86 · MICR.87src p.1790–1793

Epidemiology

  • UTIs are the most commonly occurring bacterial infection in outpatient settings in the US.
  • Initial occurrence and recurrence is much more frequent in women. Prevalence increases with age.
  • Pediatric UTIs are most common in children aged 1–2 years and are commonly associated with vesicoureteral reflux (VUR).
  • Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) is the dominant infectious agent in both uncomplicated and complicated UTIs.

Protective components of the urinary system

  • Unidirectional flow of urine
  • Urine pH (4.6 – 8.0)
  • Urine composition: immunoglobulin · lactoferrin · Tamm-Horsfall protein (THP, uromodulin)
  • Tamm-Horsfall protein: the most abundant protein excreted in urine; a constitutive inhibitor of calcium crystallization; and the key urinary anti-adherence factor, serving to prevent type 1 fimbriated E. coli from binding to the urothelial receptors.
  • Normal vaginal microbiome: lactobacilli (MICR.86).

Risk factors

  • Host factors: structural or functional abnormalities of the urinary tract (BPH, congenital malformation, urinary tract calculi, neurogenic bladder, etc.)
  • Sex: female individuals
  • Hormonal changes: pregnancy, menopause
  • Underlying conditions: diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, history of previous UTI
  • Sexual intercourse
  • Lifestyle and behavioral / hygiene practices
  • Urinary catheterization: catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)
L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis515

Epidemiology and the urinary tract's own defences (cont.)

MICR.85 · MICR.86 · MICR.87src p.1790–1793
Bottom Line
Two defences, two drugs' worth of consequences
  • Tamm-Horsfall protein does two jobs the exam likes: it inhibits calcium crystallization (link to the stone lecture) and it blocks type 1 fimbriae from binding urothelium (link to UPEC virulence). Lactobacilli keep vaginal pH low; menopause and antibiotics remove them, which is one mechanism behind the hormonal risk factor.
L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis516

Clinical presentation — by level, and by demographic

MICR.83 · MICR.84src p.1794–1795
Lower urinary tract infection
  • Increased urinary frequency
  • Urinary urgency
  • Dysuria
  • Suprapubic tenderness
Upper urinary tract infection
  • Symptoms of lower UTI
  • Fever
  • Flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness
  • Fatigue, nausea, vomiting
DemographicPresentation (verbatim)
Pediatric populationUrinary incontinence · malodorous urine · irritability · poor feeding
Elderly populationAcute confusion / delirium · tachypnea, tachycardia, hypotension (urosepsis)
Pregnant womenIncreased risk of pyelonephritis
Trap
The classic symptoms are the ones most likely to be missing
  • In the very young and the very old, UTI does not present with dysuria and frequency. Irritability and poor feeding in an infant, and acute confusion or delirium in an elderly patient, are the presentations this lecture asks you to recognise (MICR.84).
L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis517

Cystitis and pyelonephritis — the two clinical entities

MICR.83src p.1796–1797

Cystitis — inflammation of bladder mucosa

  • Infectious cause: E. coli (#1 cause).
  • Clinical features: dysuria · urinary urgency and frequency · a sensation of bladder fullness or lower abdominal discomfort · suprapubic tenderness.
Acute hemorrhagic cystitis
Lower UTI symptoms with sudden onset of gross hematuria and irritative voiding symptoms. Infectious causes: E. coli, adenovirus 11, 21 (pediatric population), BK virus (hematopoietic stem cell transplant patients), influenza A virus.

Pyelonephritis

Inflammation of the renal interstitium involving destruction of the parenchyma, tubules and renal pelvis, with relative sparing of the glomeruli. Usually caused by an ascending bacterial infection but can also be from hematogenous spread.Definition
  • Clinical features: fever, chills · flank pain · costovertebral angle tenderness (usually unilateral) · symptoms of lower UTI.
  • Complications: urosepsis, renal abscess, renal papillary necrosis, recurrent bacterial pyelonephritis.

Note the phrase "with relative sparing of the glomeruli" — that is what makes pyelonephritis a tubulointerstitial, not a glomerular, disease, and why the urine shows leukocyte casts rather than red cell casts.

L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis518

Diagnosis — dipstick, microscopy, and when culture is required

MICR.91 · MICR.92src p.1798–1800
  • Clinical history and physical examination findings.
  • Urinalysis: visual, chemical (dipstick), and microscopic examination.
Components / findings
Dipstick componentsLeukocyte-esterase test · Nitrites test — nitrates → nitrites by nitrate reductase · pH · blood
Microscopic findingsPyuria (≥ 5 WBC/HPF or 8–10 WBC/mm³) · hematuria (micro- or macroscopic) · leukocyte casts
Urine cultureGold standard — 95% sensitivity and 85% specificity. Not routinely ordered in uncomplicated lower UTIs. Indications: pregnant women; suspicion for complicated or healthcare-associated UTI; pyelonephritis or urosepsis; history of recurrent UTIs; concern for multi-resistant pathogens; over 65 years.

Clinical approach

Uncomplicated UTIs
Clinical history and urinalysis.
Complicated UTIs
Clinical history, urinalysis and urine culture.
Exam Lock
Why a negative nitrite does not exclude a UTI
  • The nitrite test detects the conversion of nitrates to nitrites by bacterial nitrate reductase — an enzyme E. coli, Klebsiella and Proteus have but S. saprophyticus does not (nitrite test negative). A young sexually active woman with dysuria and a negative nitrite is the classic S. saprophyticus stem.
L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis519

Complications of UTI

MICR.87src p.1801
General
  • Pyelonephritis
  • Perinephric abscess
  • Urosepsis
  • Emphysematous pyelonephritis
Male individuals
  • Prostatitis
  • Epididymitis
  • Orchitis
  • Urethral stricture
Pregnant women
  • Increased risk of preterm labor and birth
  • Chorioamnionitis
L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis520

The four key pathogens — one lab grid

MICR.88 · MICR.89src p.1802–1815

Etiological agents. Bacteria: Escherichia coli · Staphylococcus saprophyticus · Klebsiella pneumoniae · Proteus mirabilis · Enterococci spp. · Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Viruses: adenovirus · cytomegalovirus · BK virus. Etiology varies slightly between complicated and uncomplicated UTIs.

L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis521

Virulence factors — how each organism does its damage

MICR.90src p.1807 · 1814 · 1816

Uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC)

Member of the normal enteric microbiome; Enterobacteriaceae. Most common cause of UTIs.

Bacterial cell surface virulence factors
  • Type 1 fimbriae
  • P fimbriae: pyelonephritis-associated pili (PAP)
  • LPS: O antigen and lipid A
  • K antigen
  • H antigen
Secreted virulence factors
  • α-hemolysin
  • Siderophore

Klebsiella pneumoniae

Member of the natural flora of the gastrointestinal tract, Enterobacteriaceae, and oropharynx. 3rd leading cause of UTIs, especially nosocomial UTI.

Cell surface
  • Capsule: anti-phagocytic (K antigen)
  • Lipopolysaccharide (LPS): endotoxin
  • Fimbriae type 1 — attachment to host cells; type 3 — medical devices
Secreted
  • Siderophore: increased iron binding capacity
  • Biofilm formation: resistance to host cell and antibiotic killing

Proteus mirabilis

Member of the normal enteric microbiome, Enterobacteriaceae. One of the leading causes of CAUTI.

L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis522

Virulence factors — how each organism does its damage (cont.)

MICR.90src p.1807 · 1814 · 1816
  • Fimbriae · proteases · hemolysins · LPS (lipid A; endotoxin).
  • Urease: urine urea → ammonia (rapid hydrolysis) → urine pH ↑ → precipitation of magnesium and calcium ions → magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) and calcium phosphate (apatite) calculi / stone formation.
  • Pathogenesis: urinary stones / nephrolithiasis can obstruct urinary flow and cause tissue damage. Precipitated minerals can form crystalline biofilms, also blocking urine flow (CAUTI).
Exam Lock
P fimbriae are named after the disease they cause
  • Type 1 fimbriae bind the bladder urothelium — and are the target of Tamm-Horsfall protein. P fimbriae — pyelonephritis-associated pili (PAP) are what let UPEC ascend and colonise the kidney. Same organism, different adhesin, different level of the tract.
L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis523

Staphylococcus saprophyticus, and the urease link back to stones

MICR.89 · MICR.90src p.1809–1811 · 1816
  • Member of the natural flora of the female genital tract and perineum.
  • 2nd leading cause of UTI in young, sexually active women — "honeymoon cystitis".
  • Biological features: Gram-positive cocci, non-motile, facultative anaerobe · catalase positive · coagulase negative · novobiocin resistant · nitrite test negative · urease positive.

The urease test

(NH₂)₂CO + H₂O → CO₂ + 2 NH₃. Urea agar results in the lecture: Proteus mirabilis — rapidly urease positive · Klebsiella pneumoniae — delayed urease positive · Escherichia coli — urease negative.

Urease-positive organisms — "PUNCH KiSS"

  1. Proteus
  2. Ureaplasma
  3. Nocardia
  4. Cryptococcus
  5. Helicobacter
  6. Klebsiella
  7. S. Saprophyticus
  8. S. Epidermidis
Bottom Line
One enzyme ties three lectures together
  • Urease raises urinary pH and supplies ammonium → struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones from the tubular/interstitial lecture → stones cause obstruction and stasis → obstruction and stasis predispose to pyelonephritis from the same lecture. A single Proteus stem can be asked from any of the three angles.
L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis524

Summary — urinary tract infections on one page

src p.1785–1817
AxisWhat to know
DefinitionsAsymptomatic bacteriuria = bacteriuria without symptoms. Lower UTI = bladder/urethra; upper UTI = kidney/ureter. Uncomplicated = healthy, pre-menopausal, non-pregnant woman, no risk factors, no treatment failure; everything else is complicated. Ascending is the most common route.
EpidemiologyMost common bacterial infection in US outpatients; more frequent in women; rises with age; paediatric peak 1–2 years, associated with vesicoureteral reflux; UPEC dominates both uncomplicated and complicated UTI.
DefencesUnidirectional flow · urine pH 4.6–8.0 · immunoglobulin · lactoferrin · Tamm-Horsfall protein (most abundant urinary protein; inhibits calcium crystallization; blocks type 1 fimbriae) · vaginal lactobacilli
PresentationLower: frequency, urgency, dysuria, suprapubic tenderness. Upper: the above + fever, flank pain, CVA tenderness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting. Children: incontinence, malodorous urine, irritability, poor feeding. Elderly: acute confusion/delirium, urosepsis. Pregnancy: increased risk of pyelonephritis.
DiagnosisDipstick: leukocyte esterase, nitrites, pH, blood. Microscopy: pyuria ≥ 5 WBC/HPF (8–10/mm³), haematuria, leukocyte casts. Culture is the gold standard (95% sens / 85% spec) — not routine in uncomplicated lower UTI; indicated in pregnancy, complicated/healthcare-associated UTI, pyelonephritis/urosepsis, recurrence, resistance concern, age > 65.
ComplicationsGeneral: pyelonephritis, perinephric abscess, urosepsis, emphysematous pyelonephritis. Men: prostatitis, epididymitis, orchitis, urethral stricture. Pregnancy: preterm labour and birth, chorioamnionitis.
PathogensE. coli (#1, lactose fermenter, nitrite +, urease −) · S. saprophyticus (2nd in young women, novobiocin resistant, nitrite −, urease +) · K. pneumoniae (3rd, nosocomial, capsule, mucoid, urease +) · P. mirabilis (CAUTI, swarming, H₂S +, urease +, non-lactose fermenter) · Enterococci · Pseudomonas. Viruses: adenovirus, CMV, BK virus.
VirulenceUPEC: type 1 fimbriae, P fimbriae (pyelonephritis-associated pili), LPS (O antigen, lipid A), K and H antigens, α-hemolysin, siderophore. Klebsiella: capsule (K antigen), LPS, fimbriae type 1 (host cells) and type 3 (medical devices), siderophore, biofilm. Proteus: fimbriae, proteases, hemolysins, LPS, and urease → alkaline urine → struvite and apatite stones → obstruction and crystalline biofilm.
L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis525

Block exam — urinary tract infections

MICR.89 · MICR.92

A 22-year-old woman has three days of dysuria, frequency and suprapubic tenderness after becoming sexually active. Dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase but NEGATIVE for nitrites. Which organism is most likely, and which two laboratory features confirm it?

  1. AE. coli; nitrite positive and lactose fermenting
  2. BStaphylococcus saprophyticus; novobiocin resistant and urease positive
  3. CKlebsiella pneumoniae; mucoid capsule and delayed urease
  4. DProteus mirabilis; swarming motility and H₂S positive
  5. EEnterococcus; catalase negative and bile-esculin positive
Answer
B. S. saprophyticus is the 2nd leading cause of UTI in young, sexually active women — "honeymoon cystitis", and is a member of the natural flora of the female genital tract and perineum. Its features: Gram-positive cocci, non-motile, facultative anaerobe, catalase positive, coagulase negative, novobiocin resistant, nitrite test negative, urease positive. The negative nitrite in the stem is the discriminator — the nitrite test depends on bacterial nitrate reductase, which E. coli, Klebsiella and Proteus have.
MICR.86

Which urinary protein both inhibits calcium crystallization and prevents type 1 fimbriated E. coli from binding urothelial receptors?

  1. ALactoferrin
  2. BSecretory IgA
  3. CTamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin)
  4. DAlbumin
  5. EBeta-defensin
Answer
C. Tamm-Horsfall protein (THP or uromodulin): the most abundant protein excreted in urine; a constitutive inhibitor of calcium crystallization; and the key urinary anti-adherence factor, serving to prevent type 1 fimbriated E. coli from binding to the urothelial receptors. The other listed defences are unidirectional flow of urine, urine pH 4.6–8.0, immunoglobulin, lactoferrin, and the normal vaginal microbiome (lactobacilli).
L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis526

Block exam — urinary tract infections (cont.)

MICR.84 · MICR.91

A 79-year-old nursing home resident is brought in with acute confusion, tachypnea and hypotension. Which UTI presentation does this represent, and what does this lecture say about the diagnostic approach?

  1. AUncomplicated lower UTI; urinalysis alone is sufficient
  2. BComplicated UTI with urosepsis in the elderly; clinical history, urinalysis and urine culture — culture is also indicated over age 65
  3. CAsymptomatic bacteriuria; no investigation needed
  4. DInterstitial cystitis; cystoscopy is required
  5. EAcute hemorrhagic cystitis; viral PCR is required
Answer
B. Elderly population: acute confusion / delirium; tachypnea, tachycardia, hypotension (urosepsis). This is a complicated UTI, for which the approach is clinical history, urinalysis and urine culture. The lecture also lists over 65 years among the specific indications for culture, alongside pregnancy, complicated or healthcare-associated UTI, pyelonephritis or urosepsis, recurrent UTIs, and concern for multi-resistant pathogens.
MICR.90

A man with a chronic indwelling catheter develops recurrent obstruction; urine pH is 8.4 and culture grows a swarming, H₂S-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod. Which enzyme explains the stones, and what is their composition?

  1. ANitrate reductase; calcium oxalate
  2. BUrease; magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) and calcium phosphate (apatite)
  3. Cα-hemolysin; uric acid
  4. DSiderophore; cystine
  5. ECatalase; calcium oxalate monohydrate
Answer
B. Proteus mirabilis, one of the leading causes of CAUTI. Urease: urine urea → ammonia (rapid hydrolysis) → urine pH ↑ → precipitation of magnesium and calcium ions → magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) and calcium phosphate (apatite) calculi / stone formation. And: urinary stones can obstruct urinary flow and cause tissue damage; precipitated minerals can form crystalline biofilms, also blocking urine flow.
L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis527

Block exam — urinary tract infections (cont.)

MICR.90

Which virulence factor allows uropathogenic E. coli to ascend and colonise the kidney specifically?

  1. AType 1 fimbriae
  2. BP fimbriae (pyelonephritis-associated pili)
  3. CK antigen
  4. Dα-hemolysin
  5. ESiderophore
Answer
B. The lecture names them explicitly: P fimbriae: pyelonephritis-associated pili (PAP). The other UPEC surface factors are type 1 fimbriae (bladder adherence — the target of Tamm-Horsfall protein), LPS (O antigen and lipid A), K antigen and H antigen; the secreted factors are α-hemolysin and siderophore.
MICR.88

A 5-year-old boy after allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation develops sudden gross haematuria with irritative voiding symptoms. Which organism does this lecture link to this picture?

  1. AE. coli
  2. BAdenovirus 11 and 21
  3. CBK virus
  4. DInfluenza A virus
  5. ECytomegalovirus
Answer
C. Acute hemorrhagic cystitis presents with lower UTI symptoms with sudden onset of gross hematuria and irritative voiding symptoms, and the lecture's causes are E. coli, adenovirus 11 and 21 (pediatric population), BK virus (hematopoietic stem cell transplant patients), and influenza A virus. The transplant context in the stem points to BK virus; adenovirus 11/21 is the paediatric association without transplantation.
MICR.89

Which biological feature correctly distinguishes Klebsiella pneumoniae from E. coli in this lecture's tables?

  1. AKlebsiella is a lactose fermenter; E. coli is not
  2. BKlebsiella is non-motile with a large mucoid capsule and is urease positive, whereas E. coli is motile and urease negative
  3. CKlebsiella is nitrite negative; E. coli is nitrite positive
  4. DKlebsiella is Gram-positive; E. coli is Gram-negative
  5. EKlebsiella is H₂S positive; E. coli is H₂S negative
Answer
B. Both are Gram-negative, lactose-fermenting, nitrite-positive, H₂S-negative Enterobacteriaceae. The differences the lecture gives are that Klebsiella is non-motile, has a large mucoid capsule forming pink mucoviscous colonies on MacConkey, is urease positive (delayed on urea agar) and is multidrug resistant, while E. coli is motile, urease negative==, and gives a green metallic sheen on EMB agar.
L29 · Urinary Tract Infections — Cystitis and Pyelonephritis528

Block exam — urinary tract infections (cont.)

MICR.91 · MICR.92

Which statement about urine culture in this lecture is correct?

  1. AIt has 85% sensitivity and 95% specificity
  2. BIt is the gold standard, with 95% sensitivity and 85% specificity, and is NOT routinely ordered in uncomplicated lower UTIs
  3. CIt should be ordered for every dysuric patient
  4. DIt is contraindicated in pregnancy
  5. EIt replaces urinalysis in the uncomplicated setting
Answer
B. Urine culture (gold standard) has 95% sensitivity and 85% specificity. Not routinely ordered in uncomplicated lower UTIs. Its indications are pregnant women, suspicion for complicated or healthcare-associated UTI, pyelonephritis or urosepsis, history of recurrent UTIs, concern for multi-resistant pathogens, or over 65 years. The clinical approach is uncomplicated → history and urinalysis; complicated → history, urinalysis and culture.
MICR.90

Which of the following is a Klebsiella virulence factor whose stated function is attachment to MEDICAL DEVICES rather than host cells?

  1. ACapsule (K antigen)
  2. BType 1 fimbriae
  3. CType 3 fimbriae
  4. DSiderophore
  5. ELipopolysaccharide
Answer
C. The lecture separates them: fimbriae type 1 and type 3 — attachment to host cells; type 1 → host cell, type 3 → medical devices. The capsule (K antigen) is anti-phagocytic, LPS is endotoxin, the siderophore increases iron binding capacity, and biofilm formation gives resistance to host cell and antibiotic killing — the reason Klebsiella is prominent in nosocomial UTI.
MICR.89

Which organism is NOT on the lecture's "PUNCH KiSS" list of urease-positive organisms?

  1. AProteus
  2. BCryptococcus
  3. CEscherichia coli
  4. DHelicobacter
  5. EKlebsiella
Answer
C. "PUNCH KiSS": Proteus · Ureaplasma · Nocardia · Cryptococcus · Helicobacter · Klebsiella · S. Saprophyticus · S. Epidermidis. The urea agar results the lecture illustrates make it explicit: Proteus mirabilis is rapidly urease positive, Klebsiella pneumoniae is delayed urease positive, and Escherichia coli is urease negative.

Nervous System I

Dr Frik J Kotze, Assoc. Prof., Department of Clinical Skills. History for weakness, the structure of the neurological examination, and the twelve cranial nerves.

Dr Frik J Kotze · Department of Clinical Skills  ·  source pp. 1818–1861

Learning objectives — verbatim

CLSK · Nervous System I — History and Cranial Nerves533

The seven categories of the neurological examination

CPD.0.0077 · CPD.0.0078src p.1821 · 1826–1827

Think in the following categories:

  1. Mental status
  2. Speech and language
  3. Cranial nerves
  4. Motor system
  5. Sensory system
  6. Coordination and balance
  7. Changes in mood or behavior

The diagnostic process

Symptoms — presenting complaints→Signs — physical examination findings→Where — neuro localization→Diagnosis — presentation of illness
Exam Lock
Localise before you name
  • The lecture's own four-step map puts "where" between the findings and the diagnosis. In neurology the level of the lesion — cortex, brainstem, cord, root, nerve, junction, muscle — is usually a stronger discriminator than the symptom itself, which is why the examination is organised by system rather than by complaint.
CLSK · Nervous System I — History and Cranial Nerves534

Common symptoms (complaints) in the nervous system — grouped as the lecture groups them

CPD.0.0077src p.1824–1825
CategoryComplaints
MotorWeakness · shaking or jerky movements · tremors · fainting / blacking out
SensoryNumbness / tingling
Coordination and gaitGait abnormalities (ataxia) · dizziness and vertigo
Cranial nervesHeadache · visual disturbances · hearing loss · dysphasia · dysphagia
NeurobiologicalDepression · memory disturbance

History of presenting illness

  • Chief complaint and history of presenting illness — elicit the cardinal features of the complaint; include pertinent positives and negatives.
  • If acute presentation: recent illnesses (Guillain-Barré) · trauma (cerebral hemorrhages).
  • Past medical history — emphasis on chronic diseases (hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, diabetes mellitus → cerebrovascular accident); rare conditions (berry aneurysm).
CLSK · Nervous System I — History and Cranial Nerves535

Mental status and cranial nerves I–IV, VI

CPD.0.0078 · CPD.0.0079src p.1828 · 1831–1836 · 1841–1842
Brief mental status
Level of consciousness — Glasgow coma scale
CN I (Olfactory)
Test for patency bilaterally · test for smell (not done in lab)
CN II (Optic)
Review the HEENT lecture for examination of the eye; this lecture discusses the clinical findings of the neurological component of the eye.

CN II and III — pupillary light reaction (technique)

  • Examination room should be darkened.
  • Patient looks into the distance.
  • Penlight should come from the side — do not shine light directly into the pupil.
  • Assess direct and consensual response.

CN III, IV & VI — extraocular movements

  • H-test. Start centrally · bury the sclera in each direction · support the lids on downward gaze.
  • LR6 SO4 — lateral rectus is CN VI, superior oblique is CN IV.
Neurological deficitResult
Oculomotor palsy — CN IIIPtosis (down and out) · diminished / absent light reflex
Trochlear palsy — CN IVGaze (up and outward) · head tilt and chin tuck — head tilt away from the affected eye
Abducens palsy — CN VIMedially directed eye, cannot abduct

Pupillary abnormalities — the lecture's table, verbatim

CPD.0.0079src p.1837 · 1840
DefectDescriptionCause
Marcus Gunn pupilDecreased bilateral pupillary constrictionAfferent pupillary defect (CN II damage, retinal detachment)
Argyll Robertson pupil ("prostitute pupil")Pupils accommodate but do not reactBilateral damage to the pretectal nuclei in the midbrain (neurosyphilis, diabetes mellitus)
Adie's pupilSlow, sluggish decreased reaction to lightPostganglionic parasympathetic denervation (viral infection, trauma, vasospasm due to migraine, ocular surgery, tumors)
Horner syndrome (oculosympathetic paresis)Constricted pupil (miosis), unresponsive, dilates slowly, ptosis, anhidrosisLoss of sympathetic nerve fibers (brainstem CVA, Pancoast tumor, syringomyelia)

The pupil in the comatose patient

PupilsCause
Bilateral pinpointMetabolic encephalopathy · pontine hemorrhage · drugs (morphine, heroin)
Bilateral dilated and fixedPost cardiac arrest · drugs (TCAs, atropine)
Bilateral dilated but reactiveDrugs (cocaine, LSD, amphetamine)
Unilateral dilated and fixedTemporal lobe herniation
Exam Lock
One pupil beats four in an emergency
  • Bilateral pinpoint → opioids or pons. Bilateral dilated + fixed → post-arrest or anticholinergic. Bilateral dilated + reactive → sympathomimetic. Unilateral dilated and fixed → temporal lobe (uncal) herniation — the only one in the table that is a surgical emergency of mass effect, and it links straight to the herniation figure in the pathology lectures.
CLSK · Nervous System I — History and Cranial Nerves537

Cranial nerves V, VII, VIII, IX–XII

CPD.0.0079src p.1843–1854
NerveHow the lecture says to test it
CN V (Trigeminal) — motorAsk the patient to clench teeth · assess the temporal and masseter muscles · hollow scooped-out appearance of the face
CN V — sensoryAssess sensory input only (V1, V2, V3) · examine the central areas of each branch on the right and left side of the face · use cotton to touch the divisions lightly — not stroke
CN V + VII — corneal reflex*(not done in lab)* Ask the patient to look in the other direction so you are not testing the "blink reflex", then gently but firmly touch the cornea at its junction with the sclera.
CN VII (Facialis) — motorRaise the eyebrow · frown · eye closure (including assessment against resistance to determine power) · smile · show upper and lower teeth · grimace · puff out cheeks
CN VII — sensory*(not done in lab)* Taste of anterior 2/3 of tongue
CN IX + X (Glossopharyngeal, Vagus)Assess for voice and palatal elevation · gag reflex
CN XI (Accessory)Head turn (SCM) — turning the head RIGHT uses the LEFT SCM muscle; shoulder shrug (trapezius) — test both at the same time. Assess muscle bulk and against resistance.
CN XII (Hypoglossal)Inspect at rest in the oral cavity · observe for wasting or fasciculations · extend tongue directly outwards · move tongue right and left · assess against resistance

CN VIII (Vestibulocochlear) — the whisper test, verbatim

  1. Stand 1–2 feet behind the patient so they cannot read your lips.
  2. Instruct the client to place one finger on the tragus of the left ear to obscure sound.
  3. Whisper a combination of three numbers and letters, such as 3-U-1, towards the client's right ear.
  4. Ask the patient to repeat the words back.
  5. Repeat the test using a different number/letter combination for the left ear.
  6. The patient should correctly repeat the words.
CLSK · Nervous System I — History and Cranial Nerves538

CN VII and CN XII — the two lesions students reverse

CPD.0.0079src p.1847 · 1856–1857
Upper motor neuron lesionLower motor neuron lesion
CN VII (facial)Forehead spared — the upper face has bilateral cortical innervationWhole side of the face is affected
CN XII (hypoglossal)Tongue deviates AWAY from the lesion. The affected side will be stiff with no muscle wasting or fasciculations.Tongue deviates TOWARDS the lesion side. The affected side will be wasted and have fasciculations — the lecture's mnemonic: "lick your wounds".

Cranial reflexes — afferent and efferent limbs

ReflexResponseAfferentEfferent
Pupillary light reflexConstriction of the pupilCN IICN III
Corneal reflexBlinking in response to corneal touchCN VCN VII
Jaw jerk (masseter reflex)Jaw closure on muscle stretchingCN V3 (sensory)CN V3 (motor)
GagSensation to vomit when the pharynx is touchedCN IXCN X
Bottom Line
"Lick your wounds" is worth the ten seconds
  • LMN → tongue points at the lesion (the weak side cannot push, so the healthy genioglossus wins). UMN → tongue points away. The same logic explains the pronator drift on the next lecture's motor exam: the weak side loses to gravity.

CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait540

The reflex arc, and the four components of the motor examination

CPD.0.0083src p.1951 · 1954–1955

What happens when we test a motor reflex?

Sensory receptor — detects stimulus→Afferent nerve — conveys sensory signal to spinal cord / brain→Integrative centre — integrates sensory input and produces motor output command→Efferent nerve — conveys motor signal to periphery→Motor effector — carries out response

Motor system components

  1. Inspection for body position
  2. Involuntary movements and muscle bulk
  3. Muscle tone
  4. Muscle power (strength)
Pronator drift
Arms outstretched with PALMS UPWARD and EYES CLOSED. Positive test: the arm pronates — suggests a corticospinal tract lesion in the contralateral hemisphere — or sideward drift (loss of position sense).
CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait541

Muscle tone — why we test it, and the Modified Ashworth Scale

CPD.0.0083src p.1957–1958

Why do we test muscle tone?

To detect damage to the central nervous system (brain, spinal cord) or motor pathways by evaluating the passive resistance of muscle groups.

  1. Locating lesions — UMN vs LMN
  2. Diagnosing disorders e.g. cerebral palsy, Parkinson's disease, or multiple sclerosis
  3. Assessing spasticity e.g. velocity-dependent resistance — corticospinal lesion
  4. Identifying rigidity e.g. "lead-pipe" resistance — Parkinson's disease
  5. Detecting hypotonia — cerebellar dysfunction

Modified Ashworth Scale — verbatim

GradeDescription
0No increase (resistance) in muscle tone
1Slight increase in muscle tone (resistance) at end of movement, or catch and release
1+Slight increase in muscle tone manifested as a catch followed by minimal resistance for the remainder (less than half) of ROM
2More marked resistance through most of ROM (still moves easily)
3Considerable increase in muscle tone (passive movement difficult)
4Affected part rigid in flexion or extension

Slight residual muscle tone is present in relaxed muscle; feel the muscle's resistance to passive stretch.

Trap
Spasticity and rigidity are not synonyms
  • Spasticity is velocity-dependent and belongs to the corticospinal (UMN) lesion; rigidity is "lead-pipe", constant through the range, and belongs to Parkinson's disease. Hypotonia points to the cerebellum. Three tones, three localisations.
CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait542

Deep tendon reflexes

CPD.0.0083src p.1962–1968

General principles

  • Compare each reflex on the right and left side.
  • Must be able to examine the reflex in two positions: sitting and supine (most neurological cases).
GradeMeaning
0No response
1+Diminished
2+Normal
3+Increased
4+Hyperactive

Why do we test reflexes?

  1. Locating nerve damage
  2. Differentiating motor neuron lesions — hyperreflexia (overactive): UMN damage; hyporeflexia / areflexia (weak / absent): LMN damage
  3. Assessing systemic disease — thyroid disorders or electrolyte imbalances
  4. Early detection — changes (often decreasing) long before symptoms of nerve damage become severe
  5. Monitoring health — a baseline for monitoring improvement or degradation
CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait543

Deep tendon reflexes (cont.)

CPD.0.0083src p.1962–1968
ReflexRootTechnique and normal response
BicepsC5, 6Provide support for the patient's forearm · place your thumb on the biceps tendon · strike your thumb with the reflex hammer — the only reflex where the examiner's thumb is struck. Normal: flexion of the elbow, contraction of biceps.
TricepsC6, 7Support the arm · strike the triceps tendon 5 cm above the elbow. Normal: extension of the elbow and contraction of triceps.
BrachioradialisC5–6Support the forearm · relax it in the pronated state · strike the lower end of the radius, 5 cm above the wrist. Normal: contraction of brachioradialis, flexion of elbow and slight flexion of fingers.
Knee / patellarL3–4Supine: flex the knee to 60° by placing your forearm under it. Sitting: leg hanging freely. Strike the patellar tendon midway between insertion and origin. Normal: extension of knee, contraction of quadriceps.
Ankle / AchillesL5–S1Supine: hip externally rotated, knee flexed, ankle dorsiflexed so the Achilles tendon is stretched. Or sitting / kneeling on a chair with the ankle hanging loose. Normal: plantar flexion of foot, contraction of gastrocnemius.
CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait544

Cutaneous (superficial) reflexes

CPD.0.0083src p.1969–1970 · 1973–1974
ReflexRootTechnique, normal response and significance
Plantar (Babinski)—Patient supine, knee slightly flexed, thigh externally rotated. Stroke the outer aspect of the sole with the blunt pointed end of the reflex hammer — from the heel curving towards the mid-metatarsophalangeal joint. Normal (negative): the big toe flexes at the MP joint. Positive: the big toe extends at the IP joint and the other toes dorsiflex in a fanwise manner.
AbdominalUpper T8–10, lower T10–11Patient supine; stroke the abdominal wall with a blunt object from lateral to medial in all four quadrants. Normal: umbilicus moves toward the source of stimulation; abdominal muscles contract. Absent in 20% of the population — may be significant if asymmetrical; absent in both UMN and LMN lesions.
CremastericL1–2Stroke the medial side of the thigh with a blunt object. Normal: contraction of the cremaster muscle.
BulbocavernosusS2–4Squeeze the glans penis or clitoris, or tug on an indwelling Foley catheter. Normal: contraction of the anal sphincter. In a patient with acute paralysis from trauma: absent → spinal shock; present → spinal cord severance.
Anal (anal wink, anocutaneous, perineal)S2–4Stroke the skin around the anus with a blunt sterile object. Normal: contraction of the external anal sphincter.
Exam Lock
The Babinski sign, and when it is normal
  • Present in babies up to 2 years of age — normal. After that it is a sign of a UMN lesion (corticospinal tract): the lecture lists amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Lou Gehrig disease), brain tumor or injury, meningitis, multiple sclerosis, spinal injury / defect / tumor, and stroke.
CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait545

Upper vs lower motor neuron — the table that answers most neuro-exam questions

CPD.0.0083src p.1975
CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait546

Muscle power

CPD.0.0083src p.1976–1979

What do we look for when testing power?

  1. Is there movement?
  2. Is there movement against gravity?
  3. Is there movement against gravity and resistance?

Why do we test for muscle strength?

  1. Identify the location and severity of muscle dysfunction; help to determine the cause of weakness (e.g. neurological diseases, nerve damage, or muscle disease).
  2. Rehabilitation monitoring.
  3. Evaluating function and risks — fall risk in the elderly.

Technique

  • Assess each of the patient's muscles against the resistance of the examiner.
  • Compare right with left.
  • Always start on the unaffected side.

Power is graded on the movement–gravity–resistance ladder above; myotomes are assessed for the upper and lower limb.

CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait547

Sensory examination — modality by tract

CPD.0.0083src p.1983–1986
ModalityTechnique (verbatim)
Light touchUse a small piece of gauze · touch lightly (avoid pressure) · ask the patient to respond when touch is felt.
VibrationUse the 128 Hz tuning fork, make sure the fork is vibrating, place it on the sternum to familiarise the patient with the feeling. Start at the distal phalanx of the upper and lower extremity and move proximally if nothing is felt — e.g. big toe → ankle malleolus → tibial shaft → anterior iliac crest tuberosity. Ensure the examiner holds the stem, and that the examiner's finger is below the patient's joint to also assess for the presence of the vibration.
ProprioceptionHold the distal IP joint of the thumb or big toe between your index finger and thumb. Do not hold the nail bed — it gives the patient a clue by pressure. Make small-amplitude movements of the joint. Repeat with the patient's eyes closed.
Pin prick (pain)Demonstrate both sharp and dull sensation before beginning the exam. Use a different instrument for each patient.

Suggested dermatomes: thumb (C6) · little finger (C8) · inner and outer forearms (C6, T1) · shoulder (C4) · little toe (S1) · medial and lateral side of leg (L4, L5) · thighs (L2).

CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait548

Coordination, stance and gait

CPD.0.0083src p.1988–1993
TestTechniqueAbnormality and significance
Rapid alternating movementsAsk the patient to place their hands on their thighs and then rapidly turn their hands over and lift them off their thighs for 10 seconds (alternatively strike the palmar and dorsal aspect of the hand).Inability is called dysdiadochokinesis. Adults → multiple sclerosis. Children → cerebellar tumors.
Point-to-point movementFinger to nose — patient extends the index finger, touches their nose, then the examiner's outstretched finger, repeated quickly; then with eyes closed. Heel to shin — patient supine, places the right heel on the left shin just below the knee and slides it down, repeated quickly.Inability is called dysmetria. Significance: loss of motor strength, proprioception, or a cerebellar lesion.
Stance — Romberg's testRequires 2 out of 3: (1) proprioception, (2) vision, (3) normal cerebellar and vestibular function. Patient stands with heels together, eyes open, then closes the eyes (stand close to the patient).If the patient loses their balance, the test is positive. Positive in conditions causing sensory ataxia — B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis), sensory peripheral neuropathies (diabetes mellitus), Ménière's disease.
GaitRegular gait · tandem gait · toe and heel walking.See the eight observation points below.

Key aspects to observe during gait testing

  1. Step symmetry and length: right = left
  2. Speed and cadence: assess the overall pace and rhythm
  3. Foot strike and placement: heel strike first, foot rolling through to the toes — overpronation or supination
  4. Postural alignment: excessive forward, backward, or lateral trunk leaning
  5. Joint motion: proper knee, hip, and ankle flexion / extension
  6. Arm swing: naturally and symmetrically
  7. Foot clearance: toes clear the ground during the swing phase — "foot drop"
  8. Balance: stability during turn and tandem gait
CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait549

Coordination, stance and gait (cont.)

CPD.0.0083src p.1988–1993
Bottom Line
Romberg is a proprioception test, not a cerebellar test
  • The rule of 2 out of 3 explains it: with the eyes closed you remove vision, so a patient who still has proprioception and cerebellar/vestibular function stays upright. A patient who is unsteady only after closing the eyes has lost proprioception — sensory ataxia. A cerebellar patient is unsteady with the eyes open.
CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait550

Special test — meningeal signs, with the actual test characteristics

CPD.0.0084src p.1996–1998
SignTechniqueSensitivitySpecificity
Nuchal rigidityEnsure there is no cervical vertebral injury · flex the head forward until the chin touches the chest. Normal: supple (no resistance). Abnormal: resistance to flexion. Frequently absent in a child under 2 years.30%77%
Brudzinski's signPatient supine, in extension. The examiner gently grasps the patient's head in the occipital region and attempts flexion of the neck. Flexion of the neck causes involuntary flexion of the knee and hip.5%100%
Kernig's signPatient supine. Hip and knee are flexed by the examiner up to 90°. The examiner attempts to passively straighten the leg at the knee. The patient experiences pain along the spinal cord and the pain limits passive extension of the knee.5%100%
Exam Lock
Why the numbers matter clinically
  • Brudzinski's and Kernig's signs add no diagnostic value to the diagnosis of meningitis if negative — at 5% sensitivity they miss 19 of 20 cases. They are 100% specific, so a *positive* sign is close to diagnostic. This is the cleanest example in the module of the rule that a specific test rules in (SpPin) and a sensitive test rules out (SnNout).
Source note
Evidence base cited in the lecture
  • Thomas KE, Hasbun R, Jekel J, Quagliarello VJ. *The diagnostic accuracy of Kernig's sign, Brudzinski's sign, and nuchal rigidity in adults with suspected meningitis.* Clin Infect Dis 2002;35(1):46–52. Also cited: Mehndiratta et al., Ann Indian Acad Neurol 2012;15(4):287–8; Kumar M, Das B, Kumar D, J Neurosci Clin Res 2018;3:1.

CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait552

Block exam — the neurological examination

CPD.0.0079

A 68-year-old has a left hemispheric stroke. On examination the tongue deviates to the right when protruded, with no wasting or fasciculations. Which lesion is this, and why does the tongue deviate that way?

  1. ALMN lesion of the right hypoglossal nerve; the weak side cannot push
  2. BUMN lesion affecting the left hemisphere; the tongue deviates away from the lesion and the affected side is stiff without wasting or fasciculations
  3. CBilateral LMN lesion; symmetrical wasting
  4. DCN XI lesion; the tongue is not involved
  5. ECerebellar lesion; dysmetria of the tongue
Answer
B. UMN lesion — the tongue deviates AWAY from the lesion; the affected side will be stiff with no muscle wasting or fasciculations. In an LMN lesion the tongue deviates TOWARDS the lesion side and that side is wasted with fasciculations — the lecture's mnemonic is "lick your wounds". Absence of wasting and fasciculations is what makes this UMN.
CPD.0.0079

A comatose patient has one dilated, fixed pupil. Which cause does this lecture pair with that finding?

  1. AMetabolic encephalopathy
  2. BPontine hemorrhage
  3. CTemporal lobe herniation
  4. DTCA overdose
  5. ECocaine intoxication
Answer
C. Unilateral dilated and fixed → temporal lobe herniation. The rest of the lecture's table: bilateral pinpoint → metabolic encephalopathy, pontine hemorrhage, drugs (morphine, heroin); bilateral dilated and fixed → post cardiac arrest, drugs (TCAs, atropine); bilateral dilated but reactive → drugs (cocaine, LSD, amphetamine).
CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait553

Block exam — the neurological examination (cont.)

CPD.0.0079

Which pupillary defect accommodates but does not react, and what is the anatomical lesion?

  1. AMarcus Gunn pupil; afferent pupillary defect
  2. BArgyll Robertson pupil; bilateral damage to the pretectal nuclei in the midbrain
  3. CAdie's pupil; postganglionic parasympathetic denervation
  4. DHorner syndrome; loss of sympathetic nerve fibers
  5. EThird nerve palsy; compression of the oculomotor nerve
Answer
B. Argyll Robertson pupil ("prostitute pupil"): pupils accommodate but do not react; bilateral damage to the pretectal nuclei in the midbrain — neurosyphilis, diabetes mellitus. Marcus Gunn is decreased bilateral pupillary constriction from an afferent defect (CN II damage, retinal detachment); Adie's is a slow, sluggish reaction from postganglionic parasympathetic denervation; Horner is miosis, ptosis and anhidrosis from loss of sympathetic fibres (brainstem CVA, Pancoast tumor, syringomyelia).
CPD.0.0083

On examining tone, the resistance you feel increases the faster you move the limb. Which lesion does this lecture attribute that to?

  1. AParkinson's disease — lead-pipe rigidity
  2. BCorticospinal lesion — velocity-dependent spasticity
  3. CCerebellar dysfunction — hypotonia
  4. DPeripheral neuropathy — flaccidity
  5. ENeuromuscular junction disease — fatigable weakness
Answer
B. Assessing spasticity, e.g. velocity-dependent resistance — corticospinal lesion. The lecture separates this from identifying rigidity, e.g. "lead-pipe" resistance — Parkinson's disease and detecting hypotonia — cerebellar dysfunction. Tone is graded with the Modified Ashworth Scale (0 to 4).
CPD.0.0083

A trauma patient has acute flaccid paralysis below T6. The bulbocavernosus reflex is ABSENT. What does this indicate?

  1. AComplete cord severance
  2. BSpinal shock
  3. CCauda equina syndrome
  4. DConus medullaris infarct
  5. EPeripheral nerve injury
Answer
B. Bulbocavernosus reflex (S2–4): in a patient with acute paralysis from trauma — absent → spinal shock; present → spinal cord severance. The technique is to squeeze the glans penis or clitoris, or tug on an indwelling Foley catheter, with a normal response of contraction of the anal sphincter.
CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait554

Block exam — the neurological examination (cont.)

CPD.0.0084

Which statement about Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs is correct according to the evidence cited in this lecture?

  1. ABoth are highly sensitive, so a negative sign rules out meningitis
  2. BBoth have 5% sensitivity and 100% specificity, so a negative sign adds no diagnostic value
  3. CNuchal rigidity is 100% specific and 30% sensitive
  4. DBrudzinski's sign is 77% specific
  5. EAll three signs are equally sensitive
Answer
B. Brudzinski's sign — sensitivity 5%, specificity 100%. Kernig's sign — sensitivity 5%, specificity 100%. The latter 2 add no diagnostic value to the diagnosis of meningitis if negative. Nuchal rigidity is sensitivity 30%, specificity 77%, and is frequently absent in a child under 2 years.
CPD.0.0083

A patient stands steadily with eyes open but sways and nearly falls when the eyes close. Which system has failed, and which condition fits?

  1. ACerebellum; multiple sclerosis
  2. BVestibular apparatus; benign positional vertigo
  3. CProprioception; vitamin B12 deficiency or tabes dorsalis
  4. DCorticospinal tract; stroke
  5. EBasal ganglia; Parkinson's disease
Answer
C. Romberg's test requires 2 out of 3: proprioception, vision, and normal cerebellar and vestibular function. Closing the eyes removes vision; a fall then means proprioception has failed. Positive Romberg's test in conditions causing sensory ataxia, e.g. B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis), sensory peripheral neuropathies (DM), Ménière's disease. A cerebellar patient is unsteady with the eyes open.
CPD.0.0083

Which reflex is the only one in which the examiner's own thumb is struck, and what is its root level?

  1. ATriceps, C6–7
  2. BBiceps, C5–6
  3. CBrachioradialis, C5–6
  4. DPatellar, L3–4
  5. EAchilles, L5–S1
Answer
B. Biceps C5,6: provide support for the patient's forearm, place your thumb on the biceps tendon, and strike your thumb with the reflex hammer — the only reflex where the examiner's thumb is struck. Normal response is flexion of the elbow and contraction of biceps.
CLSK · Nervous System II — Motor, Sensory, Reflexes, Gait555

Block exam — the neurological examination (cont.)

CPD.0.0083

Which modality pair is carried by the dorsal columns as this lecture assigns them?

  1. APin prick and temperature
  2. BVibration and proprioception
  3. CPain and light touch
  4. DTemperature and proprioception
  5. EPain and vibration
Answer
B. The lecture labels light touch (crude and fine), vibration and proprioception as dorsal column, and pin prick (pain) as spinothalamic tract. It also separates the testing strategy: pain, temperature and light touch: assess dermatomes; vibration and proprioception: assess fingers and toes, starting distal and moving proximally.
CPD.0.0083

A child of 18 months has an extensor plantar response with fanning of the toes. How should this be interpreted?

  1. ADefinite UMN lesion requiring imaging
  2. BNormal — present in babies up to 2 years of age
  3. CLMN lesion of S1
  4. DCerebellar disease
  5. EEvidence of spinal shock
Answer
B. Present in babies up to 2 years of age — normal. Beyond that it is a sign of a UMN lesion (corticospinal tract), and the lecture lists amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Lou Gehrig disease), brain tumor or injury, meningitis, multiple sclerosis, spinal injury/defect/tumor, and stroke.

PHAR

Antidepressant Drugs

Dr. Tiffany Clementson · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology. One hypothesis, seven classes, and two named drug-interaction emergencies.

Dr. Tiffany Clementson · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology  ·  source pp. 1862–1946
Depression is classified as major depression (i.e. unipolar depression) or bipolar depression (i.e. manic depressive illness). Depressive episodes are characterized by depressed or sad mood, pessimistic worry, diminished interest in normal activities, mental slowing and poor concentration, insomnia or increased sleep, significant weight loss or gain, psychomotor agitation or retardation, feelings of guilt and worthlessness, decreased energy and libido, and suicidal ideation, occurring most days for a period of at least 2 weeks.Reading notes

PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs558

Classification of affective disorders

PHAR.00001src p.1884
Major depressionBipolar depression
Persistent depressed or sad moodGrandiosity
Pessimistic worryDiminished need for sleep
Diminished interest in normal activitiesExcessive talking or pressured speech
Feelings of worthlessnessRacing thoughts
Preoccupation with death or suicideIncreased level of goal-focused activity
—Excessive pleasurable activities
—Distractibility

Major depression = only depression. Bipolar depression = depression + mania.

Depressive symptoms can also occur secondary to other illnesses such as hypothyroidism, Parkinson's disease, and inflammatory conditions.

PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs559

The monoamine hypothesis — how it was discovered, and where it fails

PHAR.00001src p.1885–1889

How did we discover this?

  • Reserpine, used for hypertension, was found to precipitate depression in some patients, and was shown to deplete dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine in rat brains.
  • Iproniazid and isoniazid, used for TB, were found to lift the depression of chronically ill patients — and were later shown to inhibit MAO.
Monoamine preservation leads to mood elevation. Monoamine depletion leads to depression. Therefore: "Depression may be due to lowered monoamine neurotransmitters at brain synapses. Treatment of depression may be achieved by restoring the monoamine levels or actions to normality."The monoamine hypothesis

Strengths — the hypothesis is reinforced by how the drugs work

  • Tricyclic antidepressants block monoamine reuptake.
  • MAO inhibitors block degradation of monoamine neurotransmitters.

Weaknesses of the monoamine hypothesis

  • The pharmacological actions of both the tricyclic and MAO inhibitor classes are immediate.
  • The clinical effects take weeks.
  • That discrepancy is the central weakness.
  • Depression may instead be linked to a deficiency in signal transduction — such a deficiency could lead to a deficient response of target neurons to neurotransmission and thus, depression.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs560

The monoamine hypothesis — how it was discovered, and where it fails (cont.)

PHAR.00001src p.1885–1889
Exam Lock
The strength and the weakness are the same experiment
  • Reserpine depletes monoamines and causes depression; MAOIs preserve them and relieve it. That is the case for the hypothesis. But the transporter block happens in hours while the mood change takes weeks — so monoamine levels cannot be the whole story, which is why the lecture moves to downstream signal transduction. Expect to be asked for this discrepancy by name.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs561

General features of the antidepressant drugs, and the seven classes

PHAR.00002src p.1890–1891
  • Antidepressant drugs produce remissions in about 30% of adults with major depression and a response in about 50–60%; 80% of patients will eventually respond to drug therapy.
  • Antidepressants may take 2–4 weeks to produce any improvement and 6–8 weeks to achieve substantial benefit.
  • All currently available antidepressant drugs enhance monoamine neurotransmission by one of several mechanisms. The most common mechanism is inhibition of the serotonin transporter (SERT), the norepinephrine transporter (NET), or both.
ClassDrugs
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)Isocarboxazid · phenelzine · tranylcypromine · selegiline
Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs)Amitriptyline · clomipramine · desipramine · imipramine · nortriptyline
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)Citalopram · escitalopram · fluoxetine · fluvoxamine · paroxetine · sertraline
5-HT2 antagonists / reuptake inhibitors (SARIs)Nefazodone · trazodone
Serotonin & norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs)Venlafaxine · duloxetine
Norepinephrine & dopamine reuptake inhibitors (NDRIs)Bupropion
Noradrenergic & specific serotonergic antidepressants (NaSSAs)Mirtazapine
NMDA receptor antagonistsEsketamine · ketamine (off-label)
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs562

Where each class acts — one synapse map

PHAR.00002 · PHAR.00003src p.1893–1927
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs563

Monoamine oxidase inhibitors

PHAR.00003src p.1866–1867 · 1892–1896
  • MAO inhibitors were the first modern class of antidepressants, introduced in the 1950s.
  • MAO is a mitochondrial enzyme found in nerve and other tissues, such as the gut and liver. In the neuron it functions as a "safety valve" to oxidatively deaminate and inactivate excess neurotransmitter molecules (norepinephrine, dopamine, serotonin) that may leak out of synaptic vesicles when the neuron is at rest.
  • MAO inhibitors inactivate the enzyme, so neurotransmitter molecules escape degradation.
IsozymeSubstratesRelevance
MAO-APreferentially metabolizes norepinephrine and serotoninThe antidepressant effect of MAOIs correlates predominantly with inhibition of MAO-A.
MAO-B—The MAO-B inhibitor selegiline is approved for treatment of early Parkinson's disease. Selegiline has antidepressant effects at high doses that also inhibit MAO-A.
BothBoth MAO-A and MAO-B metabolize dopamine and tyramine.This is why the tyramine reaction happens even with a "selective" agent at high dose.

Uses, pharmacokinetics and adverse effects

  • MAO inhibitors are now rarely used in clinical practice due to toxicity and potentially lethal food and drug interactions. Their primary use is in depression unresponsive to other antidepressants.
  • Well absorbed after oral administration, but antidepressant effects require at least 2–4 weeks.
  • Selegiline and tranylcypromine have an amphetamine-like stimulant effect that may produce agitation or insomnia.
  • Adverse effects: drowsiness · insomnia · nausea · orthostatic hypotension · weight gain · muscle pain · sexual dysfunction.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs564

The two MAOI emergencies — serotonin syndrome and the cheese reaction

PHAR.00006 · PHAR.00007src p.1868 · 1897–1901
Serotonin syndromeCheese reaction (tyramine-induced hypertension)
TriggerCombination of a MAOI with a serotonergic agent. An irreversible MAOI with a serotonergic agent is the most toxic combination. Any drug or combination that increases serotonin can cause it.Tyramine is contained in certain foods — aged cheeses and meats, chicken liver, soy products, pickled or smoked fish such as anchovies or herring, and red wines — and is normally inactivated by MAO in the gut. Patients on a MAOI cannot degrade dietary tyramine.
MechanismOverstimulation of 5-HT1A and 5-HT2 receptors.Tyramine causes the release of large amounts of stored catecholamines from nerve terminals.
PresentationHyperthermia, hypertension, muscle rigidity and myoclonus — "Hot (hyperthermia), Hyper(tension), and Hyperactive (myoclonus, hyperreflexia)". Life-threatening.Occipital headache, stiff neck, tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmias, seizures, and possibly stroke.
ManagementDiscontinuation of all serotonergic agents · supportive care · sedation with benzodiazepines · administration of the serotonin antagonist cyproheptadine.Phentolamine or prazosin are helpful in the management of tyramine-induced hypertension. The lecture's mnemonic: STOP (MAOI), DROP (BP), BLOCK (NE effects). Sympathomimetic drugs may also cause significant hypertension, so OTC cold preparations containing pseudoephedrine and phenylpropanolamine are contraindicated. The selegiline transdermal patch is better tolerated and safer — unlikely to cause tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis.
Exam Lock
Two syndromes, two antidotes
  • Serotonin syndrome → cyproheptadine (a serotonin antagonist) plus benzodiazepines. Cheese reaction → phentolamine or prazosin (α-blockade). Both start with stopping the offending agent, and the distinguishing features are hyperthermia + myoclonus + rigidity (serotonin) versus occipital headache + stiff neck after a meal (tyramine).
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs565

Tricyclic antidepressants

PHAR.00003 · PHAR.00004 · PHAR.00005src p.1869–1870 · 1902–1907
  • Block SERT and NET, leading to increased monoamine concentration in the cleft.
  • There is considerable variability in affinity for SERT versus NET: clomipramine has very little affinity for NET but potently binds and blocks SERT; desipramine and nortriptyline are more selective for NET.

Adverse effects — all four follow from receptor blockade

Receptor blockedAdverse effect
α1-adrenoceptorsOrthostatic hypotension and reflex tachycardia
Muscarinic receptorsBlurred vision, xerostomia, urinary retention, constipation and aggravation of narrow-angle glaucoma
H1 receptorsSedation and weight gain
Cardiac fast sodium channelsArrhythmias

Overdose and precautions

  • TCAs have a narrow therapeutic index — e.g. five- to six-fold the maximal daily dose of imipramine can be lethal.
  • Overdose can induce lethal arrhythmias. Sodium bicarbonate is useful in reversing conduction block.
  • Depressed patients who are suicidal should be given only limited quantities of these drugs and be monitored closely.
  • 7% of the Caucasian population in the USA has a CYP2D6 polymorphism associated with slow metabolism of TCAs.
  • Antihypertensive agents may exacerbate the orthostatic hypotension induced by TCAs.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs566

Tricyclic antidepressants (cont.)

PHAR.00003 · PHAR.00004 · PHAR.00005src p.1869–1870 · 1902–1907
Administer cautiously in
  • Angle-closure glaucoma
  • BPH
  • Urinary retention
  • Constipation
  • Cardiovascular disease
  • Impaired liver function
Avoid in
  • Second- or third-degree heart block
  • Arrhythmias
  • Prolonged QT interval
  • Severe liver disease
  • Recent acute myocardial infarction
Bottom Line
The lecture's own mnemonic
  • TCAs → Tachycardia · Cardiotoxicity · Anticholinergic effects · sexual dysfunction. The cardiotoxicity is the one that kills: fast sodium channel blockade → conduction block and arrhythmia → sodium bicarbonate, exactly as in the antiarrhythmic lectures' class I toxicity.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs567

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors

PHAR.00003 · PHAR.00008src p.1871–1872 · 1908–1912
  • SSRIs are the drugs of choice in treating depression and the most common antidepressants in clinical use. Fluoxetine is the prototype; escitalopram is the S-enantiomer of citalopram.
  • They specifically inhibit serotonin reuptake, leading to increased concentrations of the neurotransmitter in the synaptic cleft and greater postsynaptic neuronal activity.
  • They have little blocking activity at muscarinic, α-adrenergic and histaminic H1 receptors — which is exactly why the TCA adverse-effect list is absent.

Adverse effects

  • Nausea, GI upset and diarrhea — due to increased serotonergic activity in the gut.
  • Diminished sexual function and interest — due to increased serotonergic tone at the level of the spinal cord and above.
  • Increase in headaches and insomnia or hypersomnia.
  • Some patients gain weight, particularly with paroxetine.
  • Citalopram: QT prolongation.

Drug interactions — PHAR.00008 asks you to contrast these

Interaction riskDrugsDetail
High — strong CYP inhibitorsFluoxetine and paroxetineInhibit CYP2D6, which is responsible for the elimination of TCAs, neuroleptic drugs, and some antiarrhythmics and β-blockers.
FluvoxamineInhibits CYP1A2, CYP2C19 and CYP3A4.
LowCitalopram · escitalopram · sertralinePreferred when the patient is already on interacting drugs.
  • All SSRIs may cause a serotonin syndrome when used in the presence of a MAO inhibitor or another serotonergic drug.
  • The likelihood of fatalities from SSRI overdose is extremely low; overdoses may cause seizures.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs568

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (cont.)

PHAR.00003 · PHAR.00008src p.1871–1872 · 1908–1912
Bottom Line
The lecture's two mnemonics for this class
  • SSRIs — the 4 S's: Stomach upset · Sexual dysfunction · Serotonin syndrome · Size increase (weight gain). And for indications: SSRIs are Effective For Sadness, Panic, Compulsions — Escitalopram, Fluoxetine, Fluvoxamine, Sertraline, Paroxetine, Citalopram.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs569

SARIs, SNRIs, NDRIs and NaSSAs

PHAR.00003src p.1873–1874 · 1913–1922
ClassDrug(s)MechanismDistinguishing features
SARIs — 5-HT2 antagonists / reuptake inhibitorsTrazodone · nefazodoneCombine 5-HT reuptake blockade with 5-HT2 antagonism, which decreases the undesired actions of 5-HT2 stimulation. Both are weak inhibitors of SERT and NET and potent antagonists at the 5-HT2 receptor.Trazodone ("traZZZobone") blocks H1 and α1 receptors → extremely sedating → excellent hypnotic; its most common current use is as an unlabeled hypnotic. Rare but troublesome adverse effect: priapism. Nefazodone is associated with hepatotoxicity and is no longer commonly prescribed; it is an inhibitor of CYP3A4 (trazodone is a substrate but not a potent inhibitor).
SNRIs — serotonin & norepinephrine reuptake inhibitorsVenlafaxine · duloxetineBlock reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine.Differ from TCAs by their lack of blockade of H1, muscarinic and α1 receptors. May be effective in patients in whom SSRIs are ineffective. Venlafaxine: potent 5-HT uptake inhibitor; at higher doses inhibits norepinephrine uptake; very weakly inhibits dopamine reuptake. Duloxetine inhibits both at all doses. Relatively fewer CYP450 interactions than the SSRIs.
NDRIs — norepinephrine & dopamine reuptake inhibitorsBupropionInhibits norepinephrine and dopamine uptake and also increases their release.Used for depression if anxiety is not prominent. Assists in decreasing craving and attenuating withdrawal symptoms for nicotine in tobacco users. Not associated with sexual dysfunction, because it is not serotonergic. Overdose is associated with seizures. Mnemonic: "Boosts mood and battles cravings, but beware of seizures."
NaSSAs — noradrenergic & specific serotonergic antidepressantsMirtazapineAntagonist of central presynaptic α2 receptors → enhances release of norepinephrine and 5-HT. Antagonist at 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 receptors → decreased GI upset. H1 antagonist.Sedation and weight gain — may be useful if insomnia or agitation is prominent.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs570

NMDA receptor antagonists, and the discontinuation syndrome

PHAR.00003 · PHAR.00009 · PHAR.00012src p.1875 · 1923–1926

Esketamine and ketamine (off-label)

  • Noncompetitive antagonism at the NMDA receptor (N-methyl-D-aspartate glutamate receptor).
  • Actions: ↑ dopamine reuptake inhibition · ↑ descending serotonin pathways.
  • Works on multiple pathways — opioid, monoamine and cholinergic receptors, and voltage-sensitive Ca²⁺ channels. Despite its use as an anaesthetic, ketamine does not appear to act on GABA receptors.
  • Fast-acting; intranasal. Used in treatment-resistant depression or major depressive disorder with suicidal ideation or behavior.
  • Acute adverse events after treatment include sedation, nausea and vomiting, dissociation and hallucinations, and increased blood pressure.

Antidepressant discontinuation syndrome (PHAR.00009)

  • Abrupt discontinuation of antidepressants is associated with a discontinuation syndrome. Most often seen with SSRI discontinuation — because SSRIs are the most commonly prescribed class.
  • Symptoms: anxiety, irritability, tearfulness · dizziness · headache · lethargy · flu-like symptoms · electric-shock sensations · insomnia · nausea, vomiting, diarrhea.
  • More likely with a short half-life drug — most likely with paroxetine or venlafaxine; least likely with fluoxetine because of its long half-life.
Exam Lock
Half-life explains both the discontinuation syndrome and the washout period (PHAR.00012)
  • The same property runs in both directions. A short half-life (paroxetine, venlafaxine) means abrupt withdrawal produces symptoms. A long half-life (fluoxetine) protects against withdrawal but demands a long washout before starting a MAOI — otherwise the two overlap and you get serotonin syndrome, the reason the washout exists at all.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs571

Contrast the adverse effects — the lecture's own grid (PHAR.00004)

PHAR.00004src p.1928
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs572

Adverse effects by receptor — read the mechanism, predict the side effect

PHAR.00004src p.1929
Receptor actionAdverse effects
5-HT2 agonism & 5-HT3 agonismSexual dysfunction · GI disturbances — nausea, diarrhea · headaches, insomnia
α1 antagonismOrthostatic hypotension, reflex tachycardia
NE reuptake inhibition or NE agonismDry mouth, constipation, decreased appetite, sweating
ACh (muscarinic) antagonismBlurred vision, xerostomia, urinary retention, constipation, aggravation of narrow-angle glaucoma
H1 antagonismSedation, weight gain
Bottom Line
This table makes the whole class predictable
  • Once you know a drug's receptor profile you can generate its side effects without memorising them separately: mirtazapine is a heavy H1 antagonist → sedation and weight gain; amitriptyline blocks α1, muscarinic and H1 → the full TCA burden; SSRIs touch none of them → only the serotonergic effects remain.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs573

Choosing an antidepressant, and the clinical indications

PHAR.00010 · PHAR.00013 · PHAR.00016src p.1876–1877 · 1930–1934

Management of depression — the lecture's ladder

StepChoice
1st lineSSRI or SNRI. Fluoxetine would be a reasonable first choice for adults or children not taking other drugs that may interact with it; citalopram or sertraline for adults taking other drugs that could interact with fluoxetine.
2nd lineIf no response after 4–8 weeks of an SSRI → switch to another SSRI or an SNRI, or add a drug from a different class (e.g. SSRI + bupropion).
AdjunctiveIf monotherapy is inadequate, add a second-generation antipsychotic: quetiapine, aripiprazole, olanzapine — the three approved for adjunctive treatment of major depressive disorder.
Other classesSARI (trazodone) — alternative if anxiety is not prominent; TCAs and MAOIs for moderate to severe disease.

Clinical indications (PHAR.00013)

  1. Depression: SSRIs first choice (fluoxetine FDA-approved for children).
  2. Anxiety disorders: SSRIs for GAD, PTSD, OCD, panic and social anxiety — after major depression, anxiety disorders are the most common application of antidepressants. Bupropion is less effective.
  3. Eating disorders: fluoxetine for bulimia (not for anorexia).
  4. Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD): SSRIs — fluoxetine, sertraline.
  5. Smoking cessation: bupropion — as effective as nicotine patches.
  6. Chronic pain: TCAs and SNRIs are used for neuropathic and other pain conditions; drugs that block NE and 5-HT reuptake are often useful for pain disorders. SSRIs are not effective.
Trap
Screen for bipolar disorder before you prescribe (PHAR.00016)
  • A major depressive episode may be the initial presentation of bipolar disorder, and treating such an episode with an antidepressant alone may precipitate mania. Before starting an antidepressant, patients with depressive symptoms should be screened for evidence of bipolar disorder.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs574

Lithium — mechanism and monitoring

PHAR.00014src p.1878 · 1936–1938 · 1943
  • Lithium is the standard treatment for bipolar disorder — used prophylactically in treating manic-depressive patients and in treatment of manic episodes. Also effective in 60–80% of patients with mania and hypomania.
  • Clinically effective at a plasma concentration of 0.5–1 mM; above 1.5 mM it produces a variety of toxic effects — the therapeutic window is narrow.

Inositol depletion theory — the lecture's step-by-step

Normal Gq signalling: Gq receptor → PLC activation → PIP₂ → IP₃ + DAG → ↑ intracellular signalling → neuronal activation→Inositol recycling loop: IP₃ → IP₂ → IP₁ → inositol → PIP₂ regenerated→Lithium inhibits inositol monophosphatase (IMPase) and inositol polyphosphatase → blocks inositol regeneration→End result: ↓ inositol, ↓ PIP₂, ↓ IP₃ and DAG signalling → reduced neuronal activity (fewer manic episodes)

Monitoring and drug interactions

  • Must be regularly monitored: serum lithium concentrations · thyroid function · renal function.
  • Renal clearance of lithium is reduced by thiazide diuretics, NSAIDs, and ACE inhibitors / ARBs — these cause retention of lithium and need dose adjustments.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs575

Lithium — adverse effects, toxicity and the diabetes insipidus story

PHAR.00014src p.1879 · 1939–1943

Adverse effects — the lecture's LMNOP mnemonic

LetterEffect
LLeukocytosis
MMovement (tremor) — propranolol and atenolol can alleviate lithium-induced tremor
NNephropathy — nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
OhypO­thyroidism
PPuffiness (edema, weight gain) and Pregnancy problems

Also listed: tremor, sedation, ataxia and aphasia · seizures · weight gain · edema · dermatitis · alopecia.

Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus — mechanism and management

  • Lithium enters kidney cells via Na/Li channels → increased sodium excretion, decreased kidney response to ADH / aldosterone. ADH usually activates aquaporins to reabsorb water; lithium blocks aquaporin function → polyuria and dehydration.
  • Presentation: a patient on long-term lithium with polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia ± symptoms of dehydration.
  • Labs: elevated serum osmolality, low urine osmolality, and a water deprivation test that fails to increase urine osmolality after desmopressin.
  • Management: adjust lithium therapy or discontinue if possible; amiloride blocks ENaCs in the collecting duct → prevents lithium from entering principal cells, reducing further damage and helping restore aquaporin-2 expression. If amiloride is insufficient: thiazides or NSAIDs.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs576

Lithium — adverse effects, toxicity and the diabetes insipidus story (cont.)

PHAR.00014src p.1879 · 1939–1943

Toxicity and pregnancy

  • Acute intoxication is characterized by vomiting, profuse diarrhea and coarse tremor, progressing through motor impairment to coma, convulsions and death if the plasma concentration reaches 3–5 mM.
  • Use during pregnancy may increase the incidence of congenital cardiac anomalies. Category D. Contraindicated in nursing mothers.
Trap
The management of lithium-induced DI is deliberately counter-intuitive
  • Amiloride — a potassium-sparing diuretic from the diuretics lecture — is used because it blocks ENaC, the very channel through which lithium enters the principal cell. And thiazides, which normally *raise* lithium levels by reducing its clearance, are a second-line treatment for the polyuria. Both facts are examinable precisely because they look wrong.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs577

Alternatives to lithium

PHAR.00015src p.1880 · 1944
  • The antiepileptics valproate and carbamazepine are used.
  • Monitoring: valproic acid — liver function and CBC; carbamazepine — CBC.
  • Other alternatives — atypical antipsychotics: olanzapine, aripiprazole, quetiapine, risperidone. Antiepileptics: lamotrigine.
  • Several atypical antipsychotics are approved for treatment of acute mania or mixed episodes.
  • A combination of olanzapine with fluoxetine has been approved for treatment of depression associated with bipolar disorder.
  • Lamotrigine is approved for maintenance treatment in bipolar disorder.
