Block exam — antidepressants and mood stabilisers

PHAR.00006 · PHAR.00007

Two days after a patient on phenelzine is started on sertraline for inadequate response, she develops fever 40 °C, hypertension, muscle rigidity and myoclonus. Which receptors are overstimulated, and what specific antidote does this lecture name?

  1. Aα1 receptors; phentolamine
  2. B5-HT1A and 5-HT2 receptors; cyproheptadine
  3. CD2 receptors; dantrolene
  4. DMuscarinic receptors; physostigmine
  5. ENMDA receptors; ketamine
Answer
B. Serotonin syndrome — the combination of a MAOI with a serotonergic agent; an irreversible MAOI with a serotonergic agent is the most toxic combination. It is the result of overstimulation of 5-HT1A and 5-HT2 receptors, presenting with hyperthermia, hypertension, muscle rigidity and myoclonus — "Hot, Hyper(tensive) and Hyperactive". Management: discontinuation of all serotonergic agents, supportive care, sedation with benzodiazepines, and administration of the serotonin antagonist cyproheptadine.
PHAR.00006 · PHAR.00007

A patient on tranylcypromine eats aged cheese and develops severe occipital headache, stiff neck and BP 220/130. What is the mechanism, and which agents manage it?

  1. ASerotonin excess; cyproheptadine
  2. BTyramine cannot be degraded, releasing large amounts of stored catecholamines; phentolamine or prazosin
  3. CDirect α1 agonism by tyramine; a β-blocker alone
  4. DHistamine release; an antihistamine
  5. EDopamine excess; haloperidol
Answer
B. The cheese reaction. Tyramine is normally inactivated by MAO in the gut; patients on a MAO inhibitor are unable to degrade dietary tyramine, and tyramine causes the release of large amounts of stored catecholamines from nerve terminals, resulting in occipital headache, stiff neck, tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmias, seizures and possibly stroke. Phentolamine or prazosin are helpful in the management of tyramine-induced hypertension — STOP, DROP, BLOCK. The selegiline transdermal patch is unlikely to cause a tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs581

Block exam — antidepressants and mood stabilisers (cont.)

PHAR.00005

A 24-year-old takes a large amount of amitriptyline. ECG shows a widened QRS and ventricular arrhythmia. Which receptor/channel action explains this, and what is the treatment?

  1. AH1 blockade; diphenhydramine
  2. BMuscarinic blockade; physostigmine
  3. CCardiac fast sodium channel blockade; sodium bicarbonate
  4. Dα1 blockade; noradrenaline
  5. ESERT blockade; cyproheptadine
Answer
C. TCAs block α-adrenergic, muscarinic, histamine receptors and cardiac fast sodium channels; blockade of cardiac fast sodium channels → arrhythmias. TCAs have a narrow therapeutic index — five- to six-fold the maximal daily dose of imipramine can be lethal — and overdose can induce lethal arrhythmias. Sodium bicarbonate is useful in reversing conduction block.
PHAR.00008

A patient stable on nortriptyline is started on an SSRI and develops severe anticholinergic toxicity. Which SSRIs are most likely responsible, and by which enzyme?

  1. ACitalopram or sertraline; CYP3A4
  2. BFluoxetine or paroxetine; CYP2D6
  3. CEscitalopram; CYP1A2
  4. DFluvoxamine; CYP2D6
  5. ESertraline; CYP2C19
Answer
B. Fluoxetine and paroxetine are potent inhibitors of CYP2D6 and therefore have a high potential for drug interactions. CYP2D6 is responsible for the elimination of TCAs, neuroleptic drugs, and some antiarrhythmic and β-blockers. Fluvoxamine inhibits CYP1A2, CYP2C19 and CYP3A4. Citalopram, escitalopram and sertraline are low interaction risk. Note also that 7% of the Caucasian population has a CYP2D6 polymorphism associated with slow TCA metabolism.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs582

Block exam — antidepressants and mood stabilisers (cont.)

PHAR.00003 · PHAR.00013

Which antidepressant is preferred for a depressed smoker who is distressed by sexual dysfunction on his current drug — and what is its principal overdose risk?

  1. AMirtazapine; weight gain
  2. BBupropion; seizures
  3. CTrazodone; priapism
  4. DVenlafaxine; hypertension
  5. EParoxetine; discontinuation syndrome
Answer
B. Bupropion inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine uptake and increases their release, assists in decreasing craving and attenuating withdrawal symptoms for nicotine (as effective as nicotine patches), and is not associated with sexual dysfunction because it is not serotonergic. Its overdose is associated with seizures. It is used for depression if anxiety is not prominent and is less effective than other antidepressants for anxiety.
PHAR.00003

Which antidepressant is described as extremely sedating, is most commonly used as an unlabelled hypnotic, and can cause priapism?

  1. AMirtazapine
  2. BTrazodone
  3. CNefazodone
  4. DAmitriptyline
  5. EDuloxetine
Answer
B. Trazodone — a SARI: a weak but selective inhibitor of SERT whose primary metabolite is a potent 5-HT2 antagonist; it also blocks α1 and H1 receptors, is extremely sedating, and is an excellent hypnotic — its most common use in current practice is as an unlabeled hypnotic, with the rare but troublesome adverse effect of priapism. Nefazodone is the SARI associated with hepatotoxicity and CYP3A4 inhibition.
PHAR.00001

Why do the immediate pharmacological actions of TCAs and MAOIs count as a WEAKNESS of the monoamine hypothesis?

  1. ABecause the drugs do not actually raise monoamine levels
  2. BBecause the biochemical effect is immediate while the clinical effect takes weeks
  3. CBecause reserpine does not deplete monoamines
  4. DBecause monoamines are not present in the brain
  5. EBecause SSRIs work faster than MAOIs
Answer
B. Weaknesses of the monoamine hypothesis: the pharmacological actions of both tricyclic and MAO inhibitor classes of antidepressants are immediate; the clinical effects take weeks; discrepancy. This is why the lecture proposes that depression may be linked to a deficiency in signal transduction. The supporting evidence remains reserpine precipitating depression while depleting dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine, and iproniazid/isoniazid lifting depression while inhibiting MAO.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs583

Block exam — antidepressants and mood stabilisers (cont.)

PHAR.00014

A patient on long-term lithium develops polyuria and polydipsia. Water deprivation fails to raise urine osmolality, and desmopressin does not help. Which drug does this lecture recommend, and why?

  1. ADesmopressin at higher dose; to overcome receptor resistance
  2. BAmiloride; it blocks ENaC in the collecting duct, preventing lithium from entering principal cells and helping restore aquaporin-2 expression
  3. CFurosemide; to reduce medullary tonicity
  4. DSpironolactone; to block aldosterone
  5. EHydrochlorothiazide alone as first choice
Answer
B. Lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Lithium enters kidneys via Na/Li channels → increased sodium excretion, decreased kidney response to ADH/aldosterone; lithium blocks aquaporin function → polyuria and dehydration. Management: adjust lithium therapy or discontinue if possible; amiloride blocks ENaCs in the collecting duct → prevents lithium from entering principal cells, reducing further damage and helping restore aquaporin-2 expression; if amiloride is insufficient, thiazides or NSAIDs.
PHAR.00014

A patient stable on lithium is started on a new drug and becomes toxic. Which of these reduces lithium's renal clearance according to this lecture?

  1. AAmiloride
  2. BPropranolol
  3. CThiazide diuretics, NSAIDs, and ACE inhibitors or ARBs
  4. DCarbamazepine
  5. ELamotrigine
Answer
C. Renal clearance of lithium is reduced by thiazide diuretics, NSAIDs, and ACE inhibitors and ARBs — these cause retention of lithium and need dose adjustments. Lithium's window is narrow (effective at 0.5–1 mM, toxic above 1.5 mM), and serum lithium concentrations, thyroid function and renal function must be regularly monitored. Acute intoxication gives vomiting, profuse diarrhea and coarse tremor.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs584

Block exam — antidepressants and mood stabilisers (cont.)

PHAR.00016

A 29-year-old presents with a first major depressive episode. Why does this lecture insist on screening before prescribing an SSRI?

  1. ASSRIs cause QT prolongation in all patients
  2. BA major depressive episode may be the initial presentation of bipolar disorder, and an antidepressant alone may precipitate mania
  3. CSSRIs are contraindicated under age 30
  4. DSSRIs require a CYP2D6 genotype first
  5. ESSRIs must be preceded by a lithium level
Answer
B. A major depressive episode may be the initial presentation of bipolar disorder. Treating such an episode with an antidepressant alone may precipitate mania in patients with bipolar disorder. Before starting an antidepressant, patients with depressive symptoms should be screened for evidence of bipolar disorder. For bipolar depression the approved combination is olanzapine with fluoxetine.
PHAR · Lecture 31 · Antidepressant Drugs585
PHAR

Directed Learning Activity — Pharmacogenetics

Dr Tiffany Clementson · PCM1 Pharmacology. Three kinds of genetic variation, ten worked examples, and one summary table you should be able to reproduce.

Dr Tiffany Clementson · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology  ·  source pp. 2003–2015
Pharmacogenetics is the study of the role of inheritance in variation in drug response. It is important because adverse drug reactions are a major cause of morbidity and mortality.Definition, PHAR.0315
PHAR · DLA · Pharmacogenetics586

Learning objectives — verbatim

src p.2004
  • PHAR.0315 Define 'pharmacogenetics' and 'personalized medicine'.
  • PHAR.0316 Describe how genetic variation can affect the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic response to drugs.
  • PHAR.0317 Describe how genetic variations can play a role in idiosyncratic drug adverse effects.
  • PHAR.0318 Explain the relationship between N-acetyltransferase 2 polymorphisms and the incidence of adverse effects associated with drugs metabolized by acetylation (e.g. procainamide, isoniazid, hydralazine, sulfonamides).
  • PHAR.0319 Describe how genetic polymorphisms of butyrylcholinesterase affect metabolism of succinylcholine, resulting in prolonged neuromuscular paralysis.
  • PHAR.0320 Explain how polymorphisms of CYP2D6 are associated with interindividual variability in responses to a large number of drugs, including antidepressants, antipsychotics, antiarrhythmics, and analgesics.
  • PHAR.0321 Explain the role of TPMT in the metabolism of the anticancer thiopurines. Explain how TPMT polymorphisms are associated with increased risk of myelosuppression.
  • PHAR.0322 Explain how polymorphisms of CYP2C9 and vitamin K epoxide reductase are associated with interindividual variability in warfarin response.
  • PHAR.0323 Explain the relationship between G6PD deficiency and hemolytic anemia induced by oxidizing drugs such as sulfonamides, antimalarials, and chloramphenicol.
  • PHAR.0324 Describe how polymorphisms in the RYR1 gene trigger uncontrolled calcium release from the SR upon exposure to halogenated volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine, giving rise to a malignant hyperthermia syndrome.
PHAR · DLA · Pharmacogenetics587

Genomic variation, and the three types that matter

PHAR.0315 · PHAR.0316 · PHAR.0317src p.2005–2006
  • Many factors can influence the drug response phenotype: age, gender, underlying disease and genetic variation.
  • Interindividual differences in the genes that encode drug targets, drug transporters, or enzymes that catalyze drug metabolism can affect the success or failure of pharmacotherapy.
  • The human genome contains approximately three billion nucleotides and about 30,000 genes that may encode 100,000 or more proteins. Any two people differ on average at about one nucleotide in every 1,000 — an average interindividual difference of 3 million base pairs. The majority of these differences are single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).

Personalized medicine — the promise (PHAR.0315)

Determining an individual's unique genetic profile in respect to disease risk and drug response will have a profound impact on understanding pathogenesis, and it may enable truly personalized therapy — the possibility that knowledge of a patient's DNA sequence could be used to enhance pharmacotherapy, maximizing drug efficacy by targeting drugs only to those patients most likely to benefit while reducing the incidence of adverse drug reactions.Reading notes

Three types of interindividual genetic variation can influence pharmacotherapy

  1. Variation in proteins involved in drug metabolism or transport — pharmacokinetic variation. *(The most common factor; almost all major drug-metabolizing enzymes display clinically significant polymorphisms.)*
  2. Variation in drug targets or pathways associated with those targets — pharmacodynamic variation.
  3. Genetic variation associated with idiosyncratic adverse drug effects.
Exam Lock
The three-way split is the exam's organising principle
  • Every example in this DLA is filed under one of the three. NAT2, BChE, CYP2D6, CYP2C19 and TPMT are pharmacokinetic. VKORC1 is pharmacodynamic. Warfarin is both. G6PD and RYR1 are idiosyncratic — and the lecture notes that idiosyncratic drug reactions are not caused by differences in either drug metabolism or drug targets; they seem to result from interactions between the drug and a unique aspect of the physiology of the individual patient.
PHAR · DLA · Pharmacogenetics588

N-acetyltransferase 2 and butyrylcholinesterase

PHAR.0318 · PHAR.0319src p.2006–2008
N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2)Butyrylcholinesterase (BChE)
EnzymeA genetically polymorphic phase II enzyme that catalyzes acetylation.Plasma pseudocholinesterase — hydrolyses succinylcholine.
GeneticsSlow acetylators are homozygous for an autosomal recessive allele with lower activity levels. The rate of isoniazid acetylation is inherited (bimodal distribution).Defects in the BCHE gene; transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait. Because of the rarity of these variants, testing is not a routine clinical procedure.
ConsequenceSlow acetylators are prone to toxicity of drugs that are inactivated by acetylation.Decreased rate of metabolism of succinylcholine → prolonged paralysis. Normally the onset of blockade is within 1 minute and the duration only 5–10 minutes because of rapid hydrolysis by BChE.
ExamplesIsoniazid → neuropathy, hepatotoxicity and systemic lupus erythematosus. Hydralazine and procainamide → systemic lupus erythematosus. Sulfonamides → hypersensitivity reactions, hemolytic anemia and systemic lupus erythematosus.Succinylcholine, mivacurium.
Management / testDose adjustment and awareness of the drug-induced lupus risk.Treated with continued mechanical ventilation until muscle function returns to normal. Dibucaine number — the percent of pseudocholinesterase activity inhibited by dibucaine: wild-type homozygotes ≥ 75; heterozygotes 40–70; atypical homozygotes ≤ 20
Bottom Line
Succinylcholine is normally short-acting *because* it is destroyed in the plasma
  • The drug is not inactivated at the synapse at all — succinylcholine is not metabolized effectively at the synapse, therefore the membrane remains depolarized and unresponsive to additional impulses, and a flaccid paralysis results. Its brevity depends entirely on plasma BChE, so a BChE defect converts a 5–10 minute drug into hours of paralysis.
PHAR · DLA · Pharmacogenetics589

CYP2D6 — four metabolizer phenotypes and their opposite consequences

PHAR.0320src p.2008–2010
  • CYP2D6 is a member of the cytochrome P450 family of microsomal, phase I drug-metabolizing enzymes and contributes to the metabolism of a large number of drugs, including antidepressants, antiarrhythmics, and analgesics. The polymorphism was originally described when studying the antihypertensive debrisoquine and the oxytocic agent sparteine.
PhenotypeGenotypeConsequence
Poor metabolizersHomozygous for recessive alleles coding for enzymes with low activityAdverse drug effect with standard doses of agents that are INACTIVATED by CYP2D6 — e.g. metoprolol. Codeine is relatively ineffective, because it requires metabolism by CYP2D6 to form the more potent opioid morphine.
Extensive metabolizersHeterozygous or homozygous for the "wild type" alleleNormal response.
Ultrarapid metabolizersMultiple copies of the CYP2D6 gene — some have up to 13 copies.May require very high doses of drugs metabolized by CYP2D6, but can OVERDOSE with codeine — suffering respiratory depression or even respiratory arrest in response to standard doses.

CYP2D6 metabolizes many commonly prescribed medications, including the β-adrenergic blocker metoprolol, the neuroleptic haloperidol, the opioids codeine and dextromethorphan, and the antidepressants fluoxetine, imipramine, and desipramine. Codeine and tramadol are prodrugs metabolized to their active metabolites by CYP2D6. Tamoxifen is also a prodrug requiring activation by CYP2D6, CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 to 4-hydroxytamoxifen and endoxifen; CYP2D6 poor metabolizers have worse outcomes with respect to breast cancer recurrence.

Exam Lock
Prodrug or active drug decides which way the phenotype hurts
  • Active drug inactivated by CYP2D6 (metoprolol): poor metabolizer → toxicity. Prodrug activated by CYP2D6 (codeine, tramadol, tamoxifen): poor metabolizer → no effect; ultrarapid metabolizer → overdose. One enzyme, opposite errors, decided entirely by which side of the arrow the active molecule sits on.
PHAR · DLA · Pharmacogenetics590

CYP2C19, TPMT, and the two-gene warfarin story

PHAR.0320 · PHAR.0321 · PHAR.0322src p.2010–2012
GeneDrugThe mechanism the lecture gives
CYP2C19ClopidogrelClopidogrel is an antiplatelet prodrug; the active metabolite is an irreversible antagonist of the P2Y12 subtype of ADP receptors. Polymorphisms that decrease formation of the active metabolite reduce antiplatelet activity; poor CYP2C19 metabolizers taking clopidogrel are at increased risk for serious adverse cardiovascular events, and an alternative antiplatelet agent should be used. The enzyme handles at least 10% of commonly prescribed drugs, including some SSRI antidepressants.
TPMT6-mercaptopurine, thioguanine, azathioprineTPMT catalyzes the S-methylation of the anticancer thiopurines; methylation INACTIVATES them. Thiopurines have a narrow therapeutic window and some patients suffer life-threatening myelosuppression. Approximately 1 in 300 individuals are homozygous for a polymorphism leading to low TPMT activity; homozygotes are at increased risk for myelosuppression at standard doses and have to be treated with approximately 1/10 of the standard dose.
CYP2C9 + VKORC1WarfarinWarfarin has a narrow therapeutic window and wide interindividual variability; under-anticoagulation causes thrombosis, over-anticoagulation causes bleeding. Warfarin is a racemic mixture: S-warfarin is 3–5 times more potent than R-warfarin. The S isomer is metabolized mainly via CYP2C9; the R isomer via CYP3A4 and other isoforms. CYP2C9 is highly polymorphic — carriers of variant alleles require decreased doses (pharmacokinetic). VKORC1 polymorphisms affect warfarin dose requirement; the dose may vary two-fold (pharmacodynamic). The FDA revised the warfarin label on 16 August 2007 to state that lower initial doses should be considered for patients with genetic variations in CYP2C9 and VKORC1.
Bottom Line
Warfarin is the lecture's example of "multiple genes: pharmacokinetics + pharmacodynamics"
  • CYP2C9 changes how much drug is there (kinetics); VKORC1 changes how much the target responds (dynamics). The same drug is the worked example for both halves of PHAR.0316 — which is why it earns the only FDA label change quoted in the DLA.
PHAR · DLA · Pharmacogenetics591

Idiosyncratic effects — G6PD deficiency and malignant hyperthermia

PHAR.0317 · PHAR.0323 · PHAR.0324src p.2012–2014

Idiosyncratic drug reactions are not caused by differences in either drug metabolism or drug targets. Idiosyncratic effects seem to result from interactions between the drug and a unique aspect of the physiology of the individual patient. By definition, idiosyncratic effects are difficult or impossible to predict.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

Diminished G6PD activity impairs the ability of the cell to form NADPH, essential for maintaining the reduced glutathione pool→Decrease in cellular detoxification of free radicals and peroxides formed within the cell→Oxidation of protein sulfhydryl groups, including haemoglobin → denatured proteins forming insoluble masses (Heinz bodies) that attach to the red cell membranes→Additional oxidation of membrane proteins → rigid, nondeformable red cells removed from the circulation by macrophages in the spleen and liver
  • The most common polymorphism is a cSNP causing an amino acid substitution with a 90–95% reduction of G6PD enzyme function. That allele, A−, is present in 10–20% of Africans and is thought to provide protection against malaria.
  • Drugs that cause oxidative stress on red blood cells: sulfonamides, antimalarials (e.g. primaquine and chloroquine), and chloramphenicol. Individuals with G6PD deficiency exposed to these may develop acute and, at times, severe hemolytic anemia.
PHAR · DLA · Pharmacogenetics592

Idiosyncratic effects — G6PD deficiency and malignant hyperthermia (cont.)

PHAR.0317 · PHAR.0323 · PHAR.0324src p.2012–2014

Malignant hyperthermia

  • A potentially fatal genetic disorder of skeletal muscle triggered in susceptible individuals by volatile inhalation anesthetics (e.g. halothane) and depolarizing skeletal muscle relaxants such as succinylcholine.
  • Transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait, with a reported incidence of about 1:12,000. One of the main causes of death due to anesthesia.
  • The syndrome includes tachycardia and hypertension, severe muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, hyperkalemia, and acid-base imbalance with acidosis.
  • In most cases it is caused by a defect in the ryanodine receptor gene (RYR1). In skeletal muscle, RYRs sit in the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane and associate with the cytoplasmic domain of the dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR), a voltage-sensing plasma-membrane protein; depolarisation changes DHPR conformation, opening the RYR and releasing Ca²⁺.
Abnormal RYR1 → unregulated Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum→Sustained muscle contraction which generates heat→Aerobic metabolism produces CO₂ and cellular acidosis, and depletes oxygen and ATP→Switch to anaerobic metabolism worsens acidosis with lactate→Energy stores depleted → muscle fibres die → rhabdomyolysis → hyperkalemia and myoglobinuria

The most reliable test to establish malignant hyperthermia susceptibility is the in vitro caffeine-halothane muscle contracture test — a small piece of muscle obtained under regional or general anesthesia is attached to a device measuring force of contraction and exposed to halothane or caffeine; a response to halothane, or a response to low concentrations of caffeine, is diagnostic for malignant hyperthermia-susceptible muscle.

Trap
Malignant hyperthermia's inheritance is the opposite of most of this DLA
  • NAT2 slow acetylation and BChE deficiency are autosomal RECESSIVE. Malignant hyperthermia is autosomal DOMINANT, incidence 1:12,000 — so a single affected parent, or a family history of an anaesthetic death, is enough to change your anaesthetic plan.
PHAR · DLA · Pharmacogenetics593

PHAR · DLA · Pharmacogenetics594

Check — pharmacogenetics

PHAR.0320

A 27-year-old is given codeine after surgery and reports no analgesia whatsoever. Which phenotype explains this, and what would the same phenotype do to metoprolol?

  1. AUltrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizer; metoprolol would be ineffective
  2. BPoor CYP2D6 metabolizer; codeine cannot be converted to morphine, while metoprolol would accumulate and cause an adverse effect
  3. CPoor CYP2C19 metabolizer; metoprolol unaffected
  4. DSlow acetylator; metoprolol would cause lupus
  5. EBChE deficiency; metoprolol would be prolonged
Answer
B. Codeine is relatively ineffective in poor metabolizers because it requires metabolism by CYP2D6 to form the more potent opioid morphine. And poor metabolizers for CYP2D6 can potentially experience an adverse drug effect when treated with standard doses of agents such as metoprolol that are inactivated by CYP2D6. The mirror-image danger is the ultrarapid metabolizer, who can overdose with codeine, suffering respiratory depression or even respiratory arrest in response to standard doses.
PHAR.0319

After a brief procedure, a patient remains paralysed for two hours following succinylcholine. What is the mechanism, what is the treatment, and what test identifies it?

  1. ARYR1 mutation; dantrolene; caffeine-halothane contracture test
  2. BButyrylcholinesterase deficiency; continued mechanical ventilation until muscle function returns; the dibucaine number
  3. CSlow NAT2 acetylation; N-acetylcysteine; acetylator phenotyping
  4. DCYP2D6 poor metabolism; naloxone; genotyping
  5. ETPMT deficiency; leucovorin; TPMT activity assay
Answer
B. Patients with genetic variations in butyrylcholinesterase have a decreased rate of metabolism of succinylcholine, resulting in prolonged paralysis, treated with continued mechanical ventilation until muscle function returns to normal. The dibucaine number is the percent of pseudocholinesterase activity inhibited by dibucaine: wild-type homozygotes ≥ 75; heterozygotes 40–70; atypical homozygotes ≤ 20. Defects in the BCHE gene are transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait.
PHAR · DLA · Pharmacogenetics595

Check — pharmacogenetics (cont.)

PHAR.0321

A patient started on azathioprine develops profound pancytopenia. Which enzyme is deficient, how common is the homozygous state, and what dose adjustment does the lecture give?

  1. ANAT2; 1 in 12,000; half the standard dose
  2. BTPMT; approximately 1 in 300; about one-tenth of the standard dose
  3. CG6PD; 10–20% of Africans; avoid entirely
  4. DCYP2C9; 1 in 100; two-fold reduction
  5. EDPD; 1 in 300; no change required
Answer
B. TPMT catalyzes the S-methylation of the anticancer thiopurines 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine; methylation inactivates them. Thiopurines have a narrow therapeutic window and some patients suffer life-threatening myelosuppression. Approximately 1/300 individuals are homozygous for a polymorphism that leads to low TPMT activity; homozygotes are at increased risk for myelosuppression at standard doses and have to be treated with approximately 1/10 of the standard dose.
PHAR.0323

A patient of West African descent is given primaquine and develops acute haemolysis with Heinz bodies on the film. Which step in the mechanism is impaired first?

  1. AAcetylation of the drug by NAT2
  2. BFormation of NADPH, which is essential for maintaining the reduced glutathione pool
  3. CS-methylation of the drug
  4. DCalcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
  5. EVitamin K epoxide reduction
Answer
B. Diminished G6PD activity impairs the ability of the cell to form NADPH that is essential for the maintenance of the reduced glutathione pool → decreased detoxification of free radicals and peroxides → oxidation of sulfhydryl groups in proteins including haemoglobin → denatured proteins forming insoluble masses (Heinz bodies) → rigid, nondeformable cells removed by splenic and hepatic macrophages. The trigger drugs are sulfonamides, antimalarials (e.g. primaquine and chloroquine), and chloramphenicol, and the A− allele is present in 10–20% of Africans, thought to provide protection against malaria.
PHAR · DLA · Pharmacogenetics596

Check — pharmacogenetics (cont.)

PHAR.0322

Which combination correctly matches the two genes that alter warfarin response to their type of variation?

  1. ACYP2C9 pharmacodynamic; VKORC1 pharmacokinetic
  2. BCYP2C9 pharmacokinetic (metabolism of the more potent S-isomer); VKORC1 pharmacodynamic (the drug target)
  3. CBoth pharmacokinetic
  4. DBoth pharmacodynamic
  5. ECYP3A4 and VKORC1, both pharmacodynamic
Answer
B. Warfarin is a racemic mixture; S-warfarin is 3–5 times more potent than R-warfarin, and metabolism of the S isomer is mainly via CYP2C9 — a pharmacokinetic variation — while VKORC1 polymorphisms affect warfarin dose requirement, which may vary two-fold — a pharmacodynamic variation in the target. The FDA revised the warfarin label on August 16, 2007 to state that lower initial doses should be considered for patients with genetic variations in CYP2C9 and VKORC1.
PHAR.0324

Which statement about malignant hyperthermia matches this DLA?

  1. AAutosomal recessive, incidence 1:300, triggered by non-depolarizing blockers
  2. BAutosomal dominant, incidence about 1:12,000, triggered by volatile inhalation anaesthetics and succinylcholine, most reliably diagnosed by the in vitro caffeine-halothane contracture test
  3. CX-linked, triggered by propofol, diagnosed by RYR1 sequencing only
  4. DAutosomal dominant but only triggered by nitrous oxide
  5. EAcquired, triggered by antipsychotics
Answer
B. A potentially fatal genetic disorder of skeletal muscle triggered in susceptible individuals by volatile inhalation anesthetics (e.g. halothane) and depolarizing skeletal muscle relaxants such as succinylcholine. Transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait with a reported incidence of about 1:12,000; one of the main causes of death due to anesthesia. The syndrome is tachycardia and hypertension, severe muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, hyperkalemia, and acidosis, caused by a defect in RYR1, and the most reliable test is the in vitro caffeine-halothane muscle contracture test.
PHAR · DLA · Pharmacogenetics597

Check — pharmacogenetics (cont.)

PHAR.0318

A patient on hydralazine and procainamide develops a positive ANA with arthralgias and a malar rash. Which polymorphism increases this risk?

  1. AFast acetylation via NAT2
  2. BSlow acetylation via NAT2
  3. CCYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolism
  4. DTPMT deficiency
  5. EVKORC1 variant
Answer
B. Slow acetylators are homozygous for an autosomal recessive allele of N-acetyltransferase 2 with lower activity levels, and are prone to toxicity of drugs that are inactivated by acetylation. The lecture's examples: isoniazid may cause neuropathy, hepatotoxicity and systemic lupus erythematosus; hydralazine and procainamide may cause systemic lupus erythematosus; sulfonamides may cause hypersensitivity reactions, hemolytic anemia and systemic lupus erythematosus.
PHAR · DLA · Pharmacogenetics598
DLA

DLA 06 — Diagnostic approach to neurological disorders: confusion and memory loss

Department of Clinical Skills. Two patients, two time courses, and the questions that separate delirium from dementia.

Department of Clinical Skills  ·  source pp. 2016–2027

Learning objectives — verbatim

  • CPD.0.0095 Discuss the approach to a patient presenting with neurologic deficits of confusion and memory loss.
  • CPD.0.0096 Formulate a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with confusion and/or memory loss.
  • CPD.0.0097 List the symptoms, signs, and causes of various types of dementia and delirium.
Confusion is an impairment in attention and is characterized by an inability to maintain a coherent stream of thought or action. An "acute confusional state" is a prolonged period of confusion and is synonymous with "delirium".Introduction
DLA 06 · Diagnostic Approach — Confusion and Memory Loss599

Confusion — the framing, and why the history comes from the caregiver

CPD.0.0095src p.2016–2018
  • An acute confusional state is usually of abrupt onset, and the mental status fluctuates from alert and hypervigilant to obtunded.
  • An altered level of consciousness is common and can be the predecessor of stupor and coma if the underlying cause is not found and reversed.
  • Confusion presents a unique challenge in acquiring a direct patient history because the patient is inattentive and distractible. For that reason, most of the historical information must be acquired from caregivers and family members.
Dementia is a chronic, progressive loss of cognitive function that impairs day-to-day abilities and predisposes to confusion if the brain is challenged with even a relatively minor toxic or metabolic disturbance. A major diagnostic challenge is to determine whether the altered mental status is due solely to an acute condition or whether underlying dementia is acting as a predisposing factor.Reading notes

Interview framework — determine the acute cause AND the baseline risk factors

Timing of the episode
  • Previous episodes
  • Suddenness of onset
  • Any baseline cognitive impairment
  • Any history of seizures
Associated symptoms
  • Fever
  • Shortness of breath
  • Headache
  • Abnormal motor activity
Drug usage
  • Any recent change in drug regimen
  • Use of drugs of abuse

DLA 06 · Diagnostic Approach — Confusion and Memory Loss602

The diagnostic approach — three factors

CPD.0.0095 · CPD.0.0096src p.2020
  1. Temporal course
  2. Presence of focal neurologic symptoms
  3. Age of the patient
  • An acute onset over hours to days suggests delirium, whereas a gradual onset of cognitive dysfunction over months suggests underlying dementia.
  • If the onset is acute, rapidly search for an underlying reversible cause that may be life-threatening without treatment.
  • Focal symptoms (visual changes, headache, focal weakness, or numbness) suggest a primary CNS process — CNS infections (meningitis, abscess), strokes (ischemic or hemorrhagic), mass lesions (tumors), or seizures (with postictal state).
  • If delirium develops without focal signs or symptoms, the patient's age may help determine the likely cause: in younger patients without a focal CNS cause, consider drug use or withdrawal, unwitnessed head trauma, and unwitnessed seizures; when delirium develops in the elderly, likely causes include systemic infection and the other systemic precipitants above.
Exam Lock
"Acute on chronic" is the phrase the case turns on
  • A worsening over days to weeks on a baseline of gradual decline over months to years is highly suggestive of delirium in the setting of decreased cognitive reserve from dementia. That is not one diagnosis but two, and both need naming — the acute precipitant *and* the underlying substrate.
DLA 06 · Diagnostic Approach — Confusion and Memory Loss603

Patient 1 — worked case

CPD.0.0095 · CPD.0.0096src p.2022
A 70-year-old man lives with his daughter. She is awakened one night and finds him wandering in the kitchen with the pots in disarray. He cannot explain clearly what he is doing, and she is worried because this is a dramatic change for him.Case stem

Additional history

On focused questioning, the daughter reports that the patient has fallen occasionally over the last few weeks. He has been more confused over the last few days and has had a few episodes of urinary incontinence. Although he has had some memory problems for a year or 2, he has been unable to dress or to tend to hygiene only in the last few days. He has also had some headaches over the last few days. He has not had any fever or any change in medications.

Most probable diagnosis

  • Subdural hematoma from trauma. The history of trauma in an elderly patient leading to confusion over days to weeks suggests a subdural hematoma.
  • The patient likely also has underlying dementia, which is both a risk factor for falls and subdural hematomas.
  • The "acute on chronic" nature of a worsening over days to weeks on a baseline of a gradual decline over months to years is highly suggestive of delirium in the setting of a decreased cognitive reserve from dementia.
  • Other causes such as meningitis, seizure with postictal confusion, and cerebrovascular accident (CVA) are less likely — think first of the most likely cause and secondly of treatable causes of confusion. There is no history of fever, so meningitis is less likely. Seizures cause fluctuating symptoms and are of more rapid onset.
DLA 06 · Diagnostic Approach — Confusion and Memory Loss604

Memory loss — the major causes

CPD.0.0097src p.2023–2024

Although recall and the speed of cognitive processing decline slightly with normal aging, substantial memory loss is abnormal and reflects underlying pathology. While memory loss characteristically is the most prominent feature of early dementia, impairment in other domains of cognitive function, personality changes, or behavioral disturbances may be the earliest symptoms noted by observers.

TypeDefinition (verbatim)
MCIDepending on the definition used, between 5% and 16% per year will progress to dementia.
Alzheimer's diseaseDementia has an insidious onset and progresses steadily in the absence of focal neurologic signs or other identifiable causes. Autopsy reveals characteristic cortical degeneration with amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles.
Vascular dementiaDementia is temporally related to a stroke or due to chronic cerebral ischemia. Classically, dementia progresses in a stepwise manner, but it may be steadily progressive. It may be difficult to distinguish from Alzheimer's disease. In the early stages, subcortical signs (e.g. depression, subtle gait disturbances) and language difficulties often outweigh memory impairment, in contrast to early Alzheimer's disease, in which memory loss typically predominates.
Mixed dementiaThe coexistence of Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia.

Screening

  • Clinicians often fail to detect early dementia, in part because patients commonly deny having memory or other cognitive deficits and in part because well-preserved social skills may conceal these deficits.
  • In the absence of a complaint of memory loss, it is reasonable to screen patients for cognitive impairment approximately every 3 years from age 75 to 81, and then every other year thereafter.
  • The most widely used screening instrument is the Folstein Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). However, the MMSE does not cover executive function (reasoning, judgment, organization, and planning) and is insensitive to very early impairment.
DLA 06 · Diagnostic Approach — Confusion and Memory Loss605

Memory loss — the interview framework

CPD.0.0096 · CPD.0.0097src p.2024–2025
FeatureSpecific information
OnsetAbrupt (onset can be dated to within days or weeks; if abrupt, ask about associated events such as a fall or a new medication) or insidious (exact onset impossible to pinpoint)
DurationDays, weeks, months, or years
Overall courseStable (no progression) · steadily progressive · stepwise
Associated neurologic symptomsHeadache · focal neurologic symptoms · gait disorder
Concurrent medical conditionsUntreated or undertreated medical conditions, such as hyper- and hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, chronic ethanol abuse, HIV infection
Prescribed and over-the-counter medicationsMedications that can cause confusion, such as narcotics, benzodiazepines, tranquilizers, and anticholinergic medications (e.g. antihistamines)
Associated psychiatric symptomsPersonality changes · mood changes · behavioral problems · aggression · agitation · psychosis · paranoia
QuestionThink about…
What sort of activities or hobbies did you do 6 months ago? Have you had trouble or stopped doing any of these in recent months? Why?Impairment of daily activities due to difficulties with memory or executive function suggests dementia rather than MCI or benign age-related changes. Depression should also be considered.
In the last few months, have you lost your way while driving to a familiar destination?Loss of visuospatial functioning suggests dementia.
Which came first, memory problems or stiffness and a shuffling gait?If memory problems came first, think about Lewy body dementia or vascular dementia. If memory problems began more than a year after parkinsonian symptoms, consider Parkinson's disease with dementia.

Screening tools like the MMSE can only partially determine the severity of dementia; systematic questioning about the impact of the memory loss or dementia on daily activities should comprise part of the evaluation.

DLA 06 · Diagnostic Approach — Confusion and Memory Loss606

Patient 2 — worked case

CPD.0.0095 · CPD.0.0097src p.2026–2027

The patient's wife reports that he began to lose interest in lawnmower repair perhaps 6 to 12 months earlier. She remembers him stating that the motors had gotten too complicated in recent years. He first got lost while driving 18 months ago... In recent months, he has gotten lost twice on the way to his regular barbershop. She states, "He is not much of a talker," and she has always paid the bills "because, with a sixth-grade education, he never was very good at math." His 80-year-old older brother has had "real memory problems" since his bypass operation, and his mother, who died from a stroke, became forgetful a year or 2 before she died. The patient has a past medical history of hypertension, prostatic hyperplasia, and insomnia, for which he takes over-the-counter sleeping aids.

Most probable diagnosis

  • Vascular dementia.
  • Losing objects in the face of an unacknowledged memory problem is common among patients with early dementia.
  • In early dementia, short-term (recent) memory is more likely to be impaired than long-term memory.
  • His lack of in-depth conversations with family members may conceal forgetfulness.
  • Getting lost implies problems with orientation; his limited education is a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease.
  • Nonprescription sleeping pills often contain diphenhydramine, an anticholinergic antihistamine that may cause confusion in older persons.
Bottom Line
The over-the-counter sleeping aid is the point of the case
  • Every dementia history in this DLA ends with a medication review, and the list is specific: narcotics, benzodiazepines, tranquilizers, and anticholinergic medications such as antihistamines. A patient with cognitive decline on nightly diphenhydramine has a potentially reversible contributor sitting in the bathroom cabinet.
Source note
Source
  • Adapted from chapters 58 and 59 of *The Patient History: An Evidence-Based Approach to Differential Diagnosis* (McGraw-Hill Education) and Wolters Kluwer material. The DLA also links to an external practice-question form.
DLA 06 · Diagnostic Approach — Confusion and Memory Loss607

Check — confusion and memory loss

CPD.0.0096

An 82-year-old with a two-year history of gradual forgetfulness becomes acutely confused over four days after several falls, with new headaches and urinary incontinence and no fever. What is the leading diagnosis, and what is the term for this pattern?

  1. AMeningitis; acute delirium
  2. BSubdural hematoma from trauma; "acute on chronic"
  3. CAlzheimer's disease; steady progression
  4. DPostictal confusion; fluctuating symptoms
  5. EIschemic stroke; sudden onset
Answer
B. Most probable diagnosis: subdural hematoma from trauma. The history of trauma in an elderly patient leading to confusion over days to weeks suggests a subdural hematoma... The "acute on chronic" nature of a worsening over days to weeks on a baseline of a gradual decline over months to years is highly suggestive of delirium in the setting of a decreased cognitive reserve from dementia. There is no history of fever, so meningitis is less likely; seizures cause fluctuating symptoms and are of more rapid onset.
CPD.0.0095

A patient becomes confused over a period of seconds. Which three diagnoses does the time-course table put at the top?

  1. AInfection, renal failure, hepatic failure
  2. BSeizure, stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage
  3. CDrug-induced, hypoxia, hypoglycemia
  4. DDementia, MCI, depression
  5. ESundowning, postictal state, syncope
Answer
B. The lecture's table: sudden (over seconds) → seizure, stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage; over minutes to hours → drug-induced, hypoxia, hypoglycemia; over hours to days → infection, renal failure, hepatic failure; gradual progression over months → dementia. The three factors that drive the whole approach are temporal course, presence of focal neurologic symptoms, and age of the patient.
DLA 06 · Diagnostic Approach — Confusion and Memory Loss608

Check — confusion and memory loss (cont.)

CPD.0.0097

Which feature best distinguishes early vascular dementia from early Alzheimer's disease in this DLA?

  1. AVascular dementia always has focal signs on imaging
  2. BIn early vascular dementia, subcortical signs such as depression and subtle gait disturbances and language difficulties often outweigh memory impairment, whereas memory loss predominates in early Alzheimer's disease
  3. CAlzheimer's disease progresses in a stepwise manner
  4. DVascular dementia spares executive function
  5. EOnly Alzheimer's disease is associated with stroke
Answer
B. Vascular dementia is temporally related to a stroke or due to chronic cerebral ischemia; classically it progresses in a stepwise manner, but it may be steadily progressive. It may be difficult to distinguish from Alzheimer's disease. In the early stages, subcortical signs (e.g. depression, subtle gait disturbances) and language difficulties often outweigh memory impairment, in contrast to early Alzheimer's disease, in which memory loss typically predominates. Mixed dementia is the coexistence of both.
CPD.0.0097

A patient has parkinsonian stiffness and shuffling gait that began three years ago, with memory problems starting this year. Which diagnosis does the DLA's question point to?

  1. ALewy body dementia
  2. BVascular dementia
  3. CParkinson's disease with dementia
  4. DAlzheimer's disease
  5. EMild cognitive impairment
Answer
C. The framing question is "Which came first, memory problems or stiffness and a shuffling gait?" — if memory problems came first, think about Lewy body dementia or vascular dementia; if memory problems began more than a year after parkinsonian symptoms, consider Parkinson's disease with dementia. Here the motor features preceded the cognitive ones by years.
DLA 06 · Diagnostic Approach — Confusion and Memory Loss609

Check — confusion and memory loss (cont.)

CPD.0.0097

Which screening statement matches this DLA?

  1. AThe MMSE assesses executive function well and detects very early impairment
  2. BIn the absence of a memory complaint, screen approximately every 3 years from age 75 to 81 and then every other year; the MMSE is the most widely used instrument but does not cover executive function and is insensitive to very early impairment
  3. CScreening should begin at age 50 and be annual
  4. DScreening is unnecessary if social skills are preserved
  5. EThe MMSE fully determines the severity of dementia
Answer
B. In the absence of a complaint of memory loss, it is reasonable to screen patients for cognitive impairment approximately every 3 years from age 75 to 81, and then every other year thereafter. The most widely used screening instrument is the Folstein Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). However, the MMSE does not cover executive function (reasoning, judgment, organization, and planning) and is insensitive to very early impairment. Note the trap in option 4: well-preserved social skills may conceal deficits, which is a reason to screen, not to skip it.

Learning objectives — verbatim

Perform all steps and special tests during your small group skills practice sessions. When performing a physical exam skill, always compare both sides of the body to identify abnormalities. This is called bilateral comparison and helps distinguish between normal and abnormal findings. For small group patient simulations and assessments, the Special Tests are only performed if indicated based on the patient's clinical presentation.Directions for all examinations
SG08 · Nervous System Skills Examination (Student Workbook)611

Cranial nerve steps the workbook adds beyond the lectures

CPD.0.0104src p.2030–2038
TestTechnique (verbatim)
Near reaction / accommodation-convergence reflexHold your finger or a pencil 10 cm from the patient's eyes and ask them to look at it, then into the distance, and back to it. Watch for pupillary constriction (pupillary constrictor muscle) with near effort and convergence of the eyes (medial rectus muscles). The third component of the near reaction, accommodation (ciliary muscle) of the lens that brings the near object into focus, is not visible.
Fundoscopy (CN II) — SPECIAL TESTDarken the room. Switch on the ophthalmoscope light and turn the lens disc until you see the large round beam of white light. Shine the light on the back of your hand to check the type of light, its desired brightness, and the electrical charge of the ophthalmoscope. Turn the focusing wheel to the 0 diopter — a diopter is a unit that measures the power of a lens to converge or diverge light; at this diopter, the lens neither converges nor diverges.
Extraocular movements (III, IV, VI)Inspect for ptosis. Hold your finger vertically at least 50 cm away from the patient and ask them to follow it with their eyes without moving the head. Move your finger steadily to one side, then up and down, then to the other, describing the letter H in the air. Note any conjugate gaze or lid lag. Pause during each gaze position to detect nystagmus. Then test convergence.
Trigeminal sensory (V)Light touch sensation on forehead, cheeks and jaw. Have the patient close their eyes, use a fine wisp of cotton, and gently touch the face in the areas of the three divisions comparing sides — do not stroke. Isolated sensory loss occurs in peripheral nerve disorders, including lesions of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).
Weber test (VIII)Place the vibrating tuning fork (512 Hz) at the middle of the head or on the mid-forehead. Ask the patient in which ear the sound is best heard, or if it is equal.
Rinne test (VIII)Hold the vibrating tuning fork on the mastoid bone until the patient cannot hear the sound. When the patient can no longer hear it, quickly place the fork close to the ear and ask if they hear the vibration. The "U" of the fork should face forward, which maximizes sound.
Palatal elevation (IX, X)Ask the patient to open their mouth and say "Ah" while you look with a penlight for soft palate and pharynx movement; use a tongue depressor on the anterior tongue to increase visibility. The palate fails to rise with a bilateral lesion of CN X. In unilateral paralysis, one side of the palate fails to rise and, together with the uvula, is pulled toward the normal side.
Hypoglossal (XII)Note any fasciculations, symmetry, deviation, movement and strength. Inspect the tongue at rest, then protruded; move it side to side; push against the inside of each cheek and palpate externally for strength. Tongue atrophy and fasciculations can be seen in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
SG08 · Nervous System Skills Examination (Student Workbook)612

Cranial nerve steps the workbook adds beyond the lectures (cont.)

CPD.0.0104src p.2030–2038
Trap
The 512 Hz fork is not the 128 Hz fork
  • Weber and Rinne use a 512 Hz fork (hearing); vibration sense in the sensory exam uses a 128 Hz fork (dorsal columns). Two forks, two purposes, and the frequencies are examinable.
SG08 · Nervous System Skills Examination (Student Workbook)613

Motor, sensory and reflex steps with their root values

CPD.0.0105 · CPD.0.0107src p.2039–2045

Motor system

  • Observe the patient's body position during movement and at rest. Abnormal positions alert you to conditions such as mono- or hemiparesis from a stroke.
  • Observe for involuntary movements: ask the patient to hold hands out for a few seconds and observe for tremors, tics, chorea, or fasciculations — noting their location, quality, rate, rhythm and amplitude.
  • Inspect muscle bulk and contour.
MovementRootTechnique
Elbow flexion / extensionC5,6 / C6-8Apply resistance while the patient flexes then extends the elbow against your hands.
Wrist extensionC6-8Patient makes a fist, arms out in front; try to push down on the hands while the patient resists.
Finger abductionC8, T1Patient spreads fingers apart wide; try to force them together by pressing on the lateral aspect of the index and fourth fingers.
Grip strengthC7, C8, T1Ask the patient to make a fist around your index and middle fingers.
Ankle dorsiflexion / plantar flexionL4-5 / S1Place hands beneath both feet and ask the patient to press down against resistance, then move your fingers to the dorsal aspect and ask them to pull up against resistance.
SG08 · Nervous System Skills Examination (Student Workbook)614

Motor, sensory and reflex steps with their root values (cont.)

CPD.0.0105 · CPD.0.0107src p.2039–2045

Sensory system

  • For pain, temperature and touch sensation, compare distal to proximal areas of the extremities. Compare symmetric areas.
  • Suggested pattern — upper extremity: thumbs and fourth fingers (C6/C8) · an inner and outer aspect of the forearms (C6/T1) · shoulders (C4). Lower extremity: fifth toes (S1) · medial and lateral aspects of calves (L4/L5) · both thighs (L2/L3).
  • Light touch: explain steps and expected responses; instruct the patient to close their eyes; touch very lightly with a cotton wisp and do not stroke the skin.
  • Proprioception: with the patient's eyes closed, grasp the great toe or finger by its sides and move it up or down 3–4 times in a random sequence to see if the patient can accurately identify joint position. Examine at least one point on each hand and foot; if abnormal, continue sequentially to more proximal joints.
  • Loss of position sense, like loss of vibration sense, is seen in tertiary syphilis, multiple sclerosis, or B12 deficiency from posterior column disease.

Reflexes and clonus

ReflexRootTechnique
TricepsC6,7Patient's arm is down or supported by you; directly strike the tendon above the elbow.
BrachioradialisC5,6Patient's forearm partly pronated; directly strike the radius 1–2 inches above the wrist.
Quadriceps / patellar / knee-jerkL2-4Expose and flex the patient's knee; tap the patellar tendon just below the patella.
Ankle / Achilles jerkS1Holding the patient's foot in slight dorsiflexion, strike the Achilles tendon.
Clonus — SPECIAL TEST—Support the knee in a partly flexed position. With the other hand, dorsiflex and plantarflex the foot a few times, then sharply dorsiflex the foot and maintain it in dorsiflexion. Observe for any oscillations. Sustained clonus points to CNS disease affecting the corticospinal tract. If reflexes are symmetrically diminished or absent, demonstrate the use of reinforcement.
SG08 · Nervous System Skills Examination (Student Workbook)615

Coordination, gait and the workbook's interpretation notes

CPD.0.0103 · CPD.0.0106src p.2046–2047
TestTechnique and interpretation
Rapid alternating movementsShow the patient how to strike one hand on the thigh, raise the hand, turn it over, and strike the back of the hand down in the same place. Urge them to repeat as rapidly as possible; repeat with the other hand. Observe speed, rhythm and smoothness of action.
Point-to-point (finger-to-nose)Ask the patient to touch your index finger and then his or her nose alternately several times. Move your finger so the patient must change directions and extend the arm fully. After several repeats, ask the patient to close both eyes and try several more times.
Finger tapping (alternative)Ask the patient to tap the distal joint of the thumb with the tip of the index finger as rapidly as possible; observe speed, rhythm and smoothness.
Regular gaitAsk the patient to take a few steps away from you, then turn and walk back. Observe posture, balance, arm swing and leg movement.
Tandem walk / toes and heelsHave them walk heel to toe; walk on toes and heels.
Romberg testPatient stands with feet together with eyes open, then closes both eyes for 30–60 seconds. Observe the ability to maintain an upright posture without sway. Position yourself to grab a potentially unsteady patient.

Interpretation — the workbook's own notes

  • Ataxia is seen in cerebellar disease, loss of position sense, and intoxication.
  • Patients with Parkinson's disease walk slowly with a stooped posture, shuffling short steps, and minimal arm-swing.
  • In sensory ataxia from loss of position sense, vision compensates for the sensory loss: the patient stands well with eyes open but loses balance when they are closed — a positive Romberg sign. In cerebellar ataxia, the patient has difficulty standing with feet together whether the eyes are open or closed.
Exam Lock
The single line that separates cerebellar from sensory ataxia
  • Eyes open makes no difference in cerebellar ataxia; eyes open rescues sensory ataxia. That is the whole of Romberg, and it is why the workbook holds the eyes closed for a full 30–60 seconds rather than a moment.
SG08 · Nervous System Skills Examination (Student Workbook)616

The full examination checklist — what you are marked on

src p.2048–2049
Preparation and cranial nerves
  • Patient preparation, comfort and dignity
  • Hand hygiene (WHO handwashing protocols)
  • Exam organization
  • I Olfactory (not done in lab) · II Optic · III Oculomotor · IV Trochlear · V Trigeminal · VI Abducens · VII Facial · VIII Acoustic/vestibulocochlear · IX Glossopharyngeal · X Vagal (not done in lab) · XI Spinal accessory · XII Hypoglossal
Motor system
  • Inspection for position, bulk and contour, and involuntary movements
  • Pronator drift
  • Muscle tone — arms and forearms; thighs and legs

Reflexes, gait, sensory and special
  • Upper limb reflexes; lower limb: patellar, Achilles, plantar (Babinski), triceps
  • Clonus
  • Cutaneous stimulation reflexes: abdominal, plantar (Babinski), anal (not done in lab)
  • Gait and stance: regular gait, toe walking, heel walking, tandem walking, Romberg
  • Sensory: light touch, pain, temperature (not done in lab), vibration, proprioception
  • Coordination: rapid alternating movement, point-to-point, finger tapping
  • Special techniques: nuchal rigidity, Brudzinski sign, Kernig sign

SG09 · Cardiovascular Pharmacology 2 — Case Workbook620

Case 1 — DVT in a hospitalised man, complicated by HIT

PHAR.0344–0351src p.2051–2052
A 76-year-old hospitalized man is examined for progressive swelling and soreness of the right calf. Antipsychotic Drugs

Dr Tiffany Clementson · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology. One receptor in four places: the therapeutic effect and three families of adverse effect all come from D2 blockade.

Dr Tiffany Clementson · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology  ·  source pp. 2057–2122
Psychosis is defined as a sustained mental state of impaired contact with reality. Schizophrenia is a chronic psychotic disorder characterized by disturbed behavior, thinking, emotions, and perceptions.Definitions

PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs629

Schizophrenia — diagnosis and the three symptom domains

PHAR.00017src p.2057–2058 · 2071–2075
  • Diagnosis requires ≥ 2 of the following symptoms: delusions · hallucinations, often auditory · disorganized speech · disorganized behavior · negative symptoms (flat affect, social withdrawal). Symptoms should be present for at least 6 months for diagnosis.
Positive symptoms — an excess of normal functions
  • Hallucinations and delusions
  • Thought disorder / disorganized speech
  • Perceptual disturbances
  • Incongruous mood
  • Increased motor function / abnormal motor behavior
Negative symptoms — diminution or loss of normal functions
  • Blunted affect
  • Poverty of speech
  • Diminished motivation
  • Social withdrawal
Cognitive symptoms
  • Deficits in working memory
  • Deficits in cognitive control of behavior

The dopamine hypothesis

  • The dopamine hypothesis was the first neurotransmitter-based concept to be developed. Although it is no longer considered adequate to explain all aspects of schizophrenia, it is still highly relevant to understanding the positive, negative and cognitive dimensions — and it is essential for understanding the mechanism of action of antipsychotic drugs.
  • Drugs that increase dopaminergic activity increase or produce positive psychotic symptoms, whereas drugs that decrease dopaminergic activity reduce them.
  • Positive symptoms — overactivity of the mesolimbic pathway. Negative symptoms — hypoactivity of the mesocortical pathway.
PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs630

The four dopamine pathways — the anatomy that explains every effect

PHAR.00017 · PHAR.00019 · PHAR.00021src p.2077–2083

Nigrostriatal detail: dopaminergic neurons inhibit the GABAergic output from the striatum, whereas cholinergic neurons have an excitatory effect — which is why blocking D2 alters this balance, causing a relative excess of cholinergic influence and resulting in extrapyramidal motor effects, and why antimuscarinic drugs treat them.

PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs631

Classification — classical vs atypical, and potency within the classical group

PHAR.00018 · PHAR.00019 · PHAR.00020src p.2059–2061 · 2084–2089
First generation (classical)Atypical
ChlorpromazineClozapine — the prototype
FluphenazineRisperidone
HaloperidolOlanzapine
ThioridazineQuetiapine
—Aripiprazole
—Pimavanserin
High-potency classicalLow-potency classical
DrugsHaloperidol · fluphenazine — *"High-Flyers"*Chlorpromazine · thioridazine — *"Couch Time"*
Extrapyramidal reactionsMORE likelyLESS likely
Sedation and postural hypotensionLess likelyMORE likely

Mechanism of action

  • Classical: the efficacy of the traditional neuroleptic drugs correlates closely with their ability to block D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway.
  • Atypical: atypical antipsychotic drugs have higher affinities for other receptors than for the D2 receptor. Clozapine has high affinity for D1, D4, 5-HT2, muscarinic and α-adrenergic receptors, but is also a D2 blocker. Risperidone blocks 5-HT2 to a greater extent than D2.
  • Aripiprazole is a partial agonist at D2 and 5-HT1A receptors and an antagonist at 5-HT2A receptors.
  • Pimavanserin is an inverse agonist at the 5-HT2A receptors with no significant affinity for dopamine receptors.
PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs632

Classification — classical vs atypical, and potency within the classical group (cont.)

PHAR.00018 · PHAR.00019 · PHAR.00020src p.2059–2061 · 2084–2089

Common properties of the atypicals

  • Dual antagonism at 5-HT2A and D2 receptors; part of their action is due to 5-HT receptor blockade.
  • Less EPR · less tardive dyskinesia · less likely to cause hyperprolactinemia · more effective at treating negative symptoms · effective in refractory populations.
  • Risperidone may cause EPR (rare at therapeutic doses). Clozapine and quetiapine are the agents least likely to induce EPR.
PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs633

Actions and metabolism

PHAR.00019src p.2061 · 2090–2091
Antipsychotic actions
  • Reduce hallucinations and agitation associated with schizophrenia
  • Have a calming effect
  • Do not depress intellectual function
  • Motor incoordination is minimal
  • Onset of antipsychotic action is ≤ 24 h
Antiemetic actions
  • With the exception of aripiprazole and thioridazine, most neuroleptics have antiemetic effects.
  • Mediated by blockade of D2 receptors of the chemoreceptor trigger zone of the medulla

Metabolism

  • Most antipsychotic drugs are almost completely metabolized, mainly by CYP2D6, CYP1A2 and CYP3A4.
  • Antipsychotics do not interfere with the metabolism of other drugs.

Antipsychotics have a high therapeutic index and are generally safe agents.

Bottom Line
The antiemetic exception is a two-drug list
  • Nearly every neuroleptic is an antiemetic through D2 blockade at the chemoreceptor trigger zone — but aripiprazole (a partial agonist, so it does not fully block) and thioridazine are the exceptions. Prochlorperazine and droperidol are the agents actually used for nausea and vomiting.
PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs634

Extrapyramidal reactions — the four, with time course and management

PHAR.00021 · PHAR.00022 · PHAR.00023src p.2062–2063 · 2093–2103

Extrapyramidal reactions are associated with high D2 potency: most likely with high-potency conventional antipsychotics such as haloperidol and fluphenazine, which have high affinity for D2 receptors; less likely with low-potency conventional drugs such as chlorpromazine or thioridazine. EPRs are also less likely with conventional agents with strong anticholinergic activity, such as thioridazine and chlorpromazine. Atypical antipsychotic drugs have low potential for causing EPRs.

ReactionDescriptionManagement
ParkinsonismMimics parkinsonism: bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor and postural instabilityAntimuscarinic drugs like benztropine or trihexyphenidyl, with diphenhydramine, or with amantadine. Levodopa should never be used in these patients.
DystoniaMuscles contract involuntarily with repetitive or twisting movementsBenztropine, trihexyphenidyl, or diphenhydramine
AkathisiaRestlessnessRequires reduction of dosage or a change of the antipsychotic drug. The drugs most commonly used are clonazepam or propranolol.
Tardive dyskinesiaLate-occurring syndrome of abnormal choreoathetoid movements. The most important adverse effect of antipsychotic drugs. Patients display involuntary movements including lateral jaw movements and fly-catching motions of the tongue. Disfiguring and potentially irreversible. Probably due to long-term dopamine receptor blockade, causing dopamine receptors to up-regulate.Discontinue the antipsychotic or reduce the dose · eliminate all drugs with central anticholinergic action · the VMAT inhibitors tetrabenazine or valbenazine · a benzodiazepine may help · clozapine is recommended for patients with tardive dyskinesia who require antipsychotics.
PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs635

Extrapyramidal reactions — the four, with time course and management (cont.)

PHAR.00021 · PHAR.00022 · PHAR.00023src p.2062–2063 · 2093–2103
AntipsychoticEPR risk
Aripiprazole+
Clozapine0/+
Olanzapine+
Quetiapine0/+
Risperidone++
Chlorpromazine (low potency)++
Thioridazine (low potency)+
Fluphenazine (high potency)++++
Haloperidol (high potency)++++

Source p. 2103 — atypical agents listed first, then classical.

Trap
Anticholinergics treat three of the four — and worsen the fourth
  • Parkinsonism and dystonia respond to benztropine, trihexyphenidyl or diphenhydramine. Akathisia takes clonazepam or propranolol. But in tardive dyskinesia you must eliminate all drugs with central anticholinergic action — the opposite instruction. And levodopa is never used for drug-induced parkinsonism, because you would be feeding the psychosis.
PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs636

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, sedation and seizures

PHAR.00021 · PHAR.00024src p.2064 · 2104–2107

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (PHAR.00024)

  • Rare and life-threatening disorder.
  • Rigidity, tremor, hyperthermia · altered mental status · autonomic instability · elevated WBC, elevated CK · myoglobinemia, with potential nephrotoxicity.
  • Dantrolene or bromocriptine may be helpful.

Sedation and seizures

  • Sedation is more likely with low-potency antipsychotics and with the atypical agents. It is due to blockade of central H1 receptors.
  • Chlorpromazine and clozapine are the agents with the greatest risk of seizures — the lecture's mnemonic: "C is for C-Zures."

Autonomic effects

  • Some antipsychotics — particularly thioridazine, chlorpromazine, clozapine and olanzapine — block muscarinic receptors, producing anticholinergic effects. Antimuscarinic effects are beneficial in relation to EPRs.
  • Blockade of α1 receptors causes orthostatic hypotension and impaired ejaculation.
Bottom Line
Three hyperthermic emergencies, three antidotes — keep them apart
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (D2 blockade): rigidity, hyperthermia, ↑ CK → dantrolene or bromocriptine. Serotonin syndrome (from the antidepressant lecture): hyperthermia with myoclonus and hyperreflexia → cyproheptadine. Malignant hyperthermia (from the pharmacogenetics DLA, RYR1): triggered by volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine → dantrolene. Only dantrolene appears twice.

The organ-specific toxicities — five drugs you must be able to name on sight

PHAR.00021 · PHAR.00022src p.2065–2066 · 2109–2117
ToxicityDrugDetail (verbatim)
AgranulocytosisClozapineCauses agranulocytosis in 1–2% of patients. Regular blood cell counts are mandatory.
CardiotoxicityThioridazineCauses a high incidence of QTc- and T-wave changes and may rarely produce ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death. Associated with a significant risk of QT prolongation and lethal torsade de pointes; the FDA has issued a "black box" warning recommending its use be reserved for patients who have failed adequate courses of other antipsychotics. Mnemonic: *"QT stretched long, T-waves gone wrong, arrhythmias could come along."*
Ocular — cornea and lensChlorpromazineCauses deposits in the anterior portions of the eye (cornea and lens).
Ocular — retinaThioridazineCauses retinal deposits. Mnemonic: *"Chlorpromazine: cornea and lens. Thioridazine: deposits on the retinal end."*
SeizuresChlorpromazine and clozapineThe agents with the greatest risk.

Endocrine and metabolic effects

  • Blockade of D2 receptors in the pituitary leads to an increase in prolactin secretion. In women: amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome and infertility. In men: loss of libido, infertility and impotence. Atypical antipsychotics are less likely to produce prolactin elevations.
  • Weight gain is a significant problem during long-term use. Drugs with significant H1 antagonism induce appetite stimulation through effects at hypothalamic sites.
  • Atypical antipsychotics are associated with an increased risk of hyperglycemia, diabetes and dyslipidemia; the labels of all atypical antipsychotics must carry a warning about the increased risk of hyperglycemia and diabetes.
  • Antipsychotic drugs may impair the body's ability to regulate its own temperature; hypothermia or hyperthermia may result, depending on the ambient temperature.
PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs639

The organ-specific toxicities — five drugs you must be able to name on sight (cont.)

PHAR.00021 · PHAR.00022src p.2065–2066 · 2109–2117
Trap
The black box that applies to the whole class
  • Antipsychotics carry a Black Box Warning indicating that elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death. That is separate from thioridazine's own black box for QT prolongation — two different warnings, and both are examinable.
PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs640

Indications and choice of agent

PHAR.00026 · PHAR.00027src p.2066–2067 · 2118–2121
Psychiatric indications
  • Schizophrenia — the primary indication; antipsychotics are the only efficacious treatment for schizophrenia
  • Bipolar disorder
  • Suppression of tics in Tourette's disorder
  • Control of disturbed behavior in Alzheimer's disease
  • Adjuncts to antidepressants in treatment-resistant major depression
  • In combination with antidepressants in psychotic depression
  • Management of irritability in autistic disorder
  • Pimavanserin is approved for hallucinations and delusions associated with Parkinson's disease psychosis
Non-psychiatric indications
  • Nausea and vomiting — the agents typically used are prochlorperazine and droperidol
  • Droperidol is used in combination with fentanyl in neurolept-anesthesia

Drugs of choice (PHAR.00027)

  • Atypical drugs are preferred due to: benefit for negative symptoms and cognition · diminished risk of EPRs and tardive dyskinesia · lesser increases in prolactin levels.
  • Aripiprazole is currently the most prescribed antipsychotic in the US.
  • Clozapine, because of its potential for agranulocytosis, is reserved for refractory patients.
  • Several antipsychotics are available as long-acting injectable formulations, administered IM with a therapeutic duration of 2 to 4 weeks; these are often used to treat outpatients and individuals who are noncompliant with oral medications.

Pregnancy

  • Antipsychotic drugs are pregnancy category C. Only clozapine is category B.
  • The risk of hyperglycemia and weight gain, which may be problematic in pregnancy, is greater with atypical antipsychotics.
PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs641

Indications and choice of agent (cont.)

PHAR.00026 · PHAR.00027src p.2066–2067 · 2118–2121
Exam Lock
Clozapine is the drug of last resort and of two exceptions
  • It is reserved for refractory patients because of agranulocytosis in 1–2% with mandatory blood counts, and it carries the highest metabolic burden and one of the two highest seizure risks. Yet it is also the agent recommended for patients with tardive dyskinesia who require antipsychotics and the only category B drug in pregnancy. Learn it as the exception, not the rule.
