PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs643

Block exam — antipsychotics

PHAR.00023

A 24-year-old on haloperidol develops a sustained involuntary contraction of the neck muscles 36 hours after starting treatment. Which pathway is responsible, and what is the treatment?

  1. AMesolimbic; increase the dose
  2. BNigrostriatal; benztropine, trihexyphenidyl or diphenhydramine
  3. CTuberoinfundibular; bromocriptine
  4. DMesocortical; add an SSRI
  5. ENigrostriatal; levodopa
Answer
B. Acute dystonia, an extrapyramidal reaction. The nigrostriatal pathway projects from the substantia nigra to the basal ganglia and is part of the extrapyramidal nervous system; blockade of D2 receptors in this system may lead to disorders of movement. Since dopaminergic neurons inhibit and cholinergic neurons excite the striatal output, D2 blockade creates a relative cholinergic excess, so dystonia can be controlled with benztropine, trihexyphenidyl, or diphenhydramine. Levodopa should never be used in these patients. Haloperidol is a high-potency agent (EPR risk ++++).
PHAR.00023

A patient on long-term antipsychotic therapy develops lateral jaw movements and fly-catching motions of the tongue. Which management step does this lecture specify that is the OPPOSITE of the treatment for acute EPRs?

  1. AAdd benztropine
  2. BEliminate all drugs with central anticholinergic action
  3. CIncrease the antipsychotic dose
  4. DStart levodopa
  5. EAdd propranolol
Answer
B. Tardive dyskinesia — a late-occurring syndrome of abnormal choreoathetoid movements; the most important adverse effect of antipsychotic drugs; disfiguring and potentially irreversible; probably due to long-term dopamine receptor blockade causing dopamine receptors to up-regulate. Management: discontinue the antipsychotic or reduce the dose; eliminate all drugs with central anticholinergic action; the VMAT inhibitors tetrabenazine or valbenazine; a benzodiazepine may help; clozapine is recommended for patients who require antipsychotics.
PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs644

Block exam — antipsychotics (cont.)

PHAR.00024

A patient started on an antipsychotic three days ago has a temperature of 40 °C, lead-pipe rigidity, fluctuating blood pressure, WBC 18,000 and CK 9,000. Which two agents does this lecture name as helpful?

  1. ACyproheptadine or a benzodiazepine
  2. BDantrolene or bromocriptine
  3. CBenztropine or trihexyphenidyl
  4. DPropranolol or clonazepam
  5. ETetrabenazine or valbenazine
Answer
B. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — a rare and life-threatening disorder with rigidity, tremor, hyperthermia, altered mental status, autonomic instability, elevated WBC, elevated CK, and myoglobinemia with potential nephrotoxicity. Dantrolene or bromocriptine may be helpful. Contrast serotonin syndrome (myoclonus and hyperreflexia → cyproheptadine) and malignant hyperthermia (RYR1, anaesthetic-triggered → dantrolene).
PHAR.00021 · PHAR.00027

Which antipsychotic requires mandatory regular blood counts, and why is it nonetheless recommended in a particular circumstance?

  1. AThioridazine; QT monitoring, recommended for refractory depression
  2. BClozapine; agranulocytosis in 1–2%, yet recommended for patients with tardive dyskinesia who require antipsychotics
  3. COlanzapine; agranulocytosis, recommended in pregnancy
  4. DHaloperidol; neutropenia, recommended for Tourette's
  5. ERisperidone; thrombocytopenia, recommended for autism
Answer
B. Clozapine causes agranulocytosis in 1–2% of patients; regular blood cell counts are mandatory, and it is reserved for refractory patients. Yet it is also recommended for patients with tardive dyskinesia who require antipsychotics, is among the agents least likely to induce EPR (0/+), and is the only antipsychotic in pregnancy category B. Its costs are the metabolic burden (+++ weight gain, glucose, dyslipidaemia) and seizure risk.
PHAR.00021

Which drug is associated with retinal deposits and a black box warning for QT prolongation and torsade de pointes?

  1. AChlorpromazine
  2. BThioridazine
  3. CHaloperidol
  4. DQuetiapine
  5. EAripiprazole
Answer
B. Thioridazine is associated with a significant risk of QT prolongation and lethal torsade de pointes; the FDA has issued a "black box" warning recommending its use be reserved for patients who have failed adequate courses of other antipsychotics, and thioridazine causes retinal deposits while chlorpromazine causes deposits in the anterior portions of the eye (cornea and lens).
PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs645

Block exam — antipsychotics (cont.)

PHAR.00021

A woman on risperidone develops amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. Which pathway is blocked, and which class is less likely to do this?

  1. AMesolimbic; classical agents
  2. BTuberoinfundibular; atypical antipsychotics
  3. CNigrostriatal; low-potency agents
  4. DMesocortical; high-potency agents
  5. ETuberoinfundibular; high-potency classical agents
Answer
B. The tuberoinfundibular pathway projects from the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary; dopamine released from these neurons inhibits prolactin secretion, so blockade of dopamine receptors increases prolactin levels and may cause galactorrhea. In women: amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome and infertility; in men: loss of libido, infertility and impotence. Atypical antipsychotics are less likely to produce prolactin elevations — although risperidone is a notable atypical that still does.
PHAR.00020 · PHAR.00025

Which statement contrasting classical and atypical antipsychotics is correct?

  1. AClassical agents are more effective for negative symptoms
  2. BAtypicals have dual antagonism at 5-HT2A and D2, produce less EPR and tardive dyskinesia, are less likely to cause hyperprolactinaemia, and are more effective for negative symptoms
  3. CAtypicals have a higher affinity for D2 than for other receptors
  4. DClassical agents are effective in refractory populations
  5. EAtypicals do not block dopamine receptors at all
Answer
B. Common properties of atypical antipsychotics: dual antagonism at 5-HT2A and D2 receptors; part of their action is due to 5-HT receptor blockade; less EPRs; less tardive dyskinesia; less likely to cause hyperprolactinemia; more effective at treating negative symptoms; effective in refractory populations. Option 3 inverts the mechanism: atypicals have higher affinities for other receptors than for the D2 receptor.
PHAR.00021 · PHAR.00022

Which two agents does this lecture name as carrying the greatest risk of seizures?

  1. AHaloperidol and fluphenazine
  2. BChlorpromazine and clozapine
  3. COlanzapine and quetiapine
  4. DRisperidone and aripiprazole
  5. EThioridazine and pimavanserin
Answer
B. Chlorpromazine and clozapine are the agents with the greatest risk of seizures — the lecture's mnemonic is "C is for C-Zures." Note that sedation is a separate axis: it is more likely with low-potency antipsychotics and with the atypical agents, and is due to blockade of central H1 receptors.
PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs646

Block exam — antipsychotics (cont.)

PHAR.00021 · PHAR.00026

An 82-year-old nursing-home resident with Alzheimer's disease is agitated. What class-wide warning applies?

  1. AAntipsychotics are contraindicated over age 65
  2. BA Black Box Warning states that elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death
  3. COnly clozapine may be used
  4. DAntipsychotics have no role in dementia
  5. EThe warning applies only to atypical agents
Answer
B. Antipsychotics carry a Black Box Warning indicating that elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death. Note that control of disturbed behavior in Alzheimer's disease is nonetheless listed among the psychiatric indications — the warning shapes the risk-benefit discussion rather than forbidding use outright.
PHAR.00018 · PHAR.00026

Which antipsychotic is an inverse agonist at 5-HT2A receptors with no significant affinity for dopamine receptors, and what is its approved indication?

  1. AAripiprazole; treatment-resistant depression
  2. BPimavanserin; hallucinations and delusions associated with Parkinson's disease psychosis
  3. CQuetiapine; bipolar disorder
  4. DClozapine; refractory schizophrenia
  5. ERisperidone; irritability in autistic disorder
Answer
B. Pimavanserin is an inverse agonist at the 5-HT2A receptors with no significant affinity for dopamine receptors, and is approved for treatment of hallucinations and delusions associated with Parkinson's disease psychosis — which is precisely why the absence of dopamine blockade matters. Aripiprazole is a partial agonist at D2 and 5-HT1A and an antagonist at 5-HT2A, and is the most prescribed antipsychotic in the US.
PHAR · Antipsychotic Drugs647

Interview and Mental Status Examination

Dr. Morona Sukhoo-Pertab, MBBS · Department of Clinical Skills. The psychiatric history, the three screening instruments, and the six components of the MSE.

Dr. Morona Sukhoo-Pertab, MBBS · Department of Clinical Skills  ·  source pp. 2123–2166

Learning objectives — verbatim

  • CPD.0.0170 Summarize the diagnostic approach to a patient presenting with a psychiatric complaint.
  • CPD.0.0171 Effectively communicate with patients and families using sensitive, non-judgmental language, and recognize the emotional impact of illness on patients and families.
  • CPD.0.0172 Obtain an age- and gender-appropriate medical history for a patient with psychiatric complaints.
  • CPD.0.0173 Interpret historical data from multiple sources including the patient, family member and previous hospital records.
  • CPD.0.0174 Relay that the most common mental disorders (depression, anxiety, and substance abuse) are often co-morbid with other chronic diseases and impact course, severity, and clinical outcome.
  • CPD.0.0175 Outline the components and indications for a mental status examination.
There is NO health without mental health. Mental health is described by the WHO as "a state of well-being in which the individual realizes his or her own abilities, can cope with the normal stresses of life, can work productively and fruitfully, and is able to make a contribution to his or her community" (WHO 2001a, p.1).Opening
CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination648

Determinants, and the shape of the psychiatric interview

CPD.0.0170 · CPD.0.0171 · CPD.0.0172 · CPD.0.0173src p.2125–2135
  • Mental illnesses involve changes in emotion, thinking or behavior (or a combination of these).
  • Mental illnesses are associated with distress and/or problems functioning in social, work or family activities.
  • Exposure to adversity at a young age is an established preventable risk factor for mental disorders.
"Your patient is expected to reveal his or her deepest and most shameful secrets to a perfect stranger."Carlat, *The Psychiatric Interview*

The interview is based on information gathered from three domains

  1. Observation and interview of the patient
  2. Collateral information
  3. Information from others · the medical record

Communication skills common to the psychiatric interview

Do
  • Actively listen with appropriate verbal and non-verbal communication
  • Sensitive and nonjudgmental
  • Open ended
  • Empathy · sympathy · support
  • Defuse situations · be adjustable · patience · repair fractures
Avoid
  • Avoid jargon
  • The more leading the probe, the less valid the response
  • Miscommunication and misunderstandings in a relationship cause disconnection
CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination649

Determinants, and the shape of the psychiatric interview (cont.)

CPD.0.0170 · CPD.0.0171 · CPD.0.0172 · CPD.0.0173src p.2125–2135

Psychiatric evaluation — the order of exclusion

History and physical examination→Rule out general medical condition→Rule out substance abuse→Rule out malingering and factitious disorder→Diagnose primary mental disorder
Exam Lock
The primary psychiatric diagnosis is the last one you make, not the first
  • The lecture's own sequence puts medical illness, substances, and malingering/factitious disorder ahead of the psychiatric diagnosis. This is the same discipline as the confusion DLA, where an acute onset demands a rapid search for a reversible, life-threatening cause before dementia is invoked.
CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination650

Screening instruments — with their actual test characteristics

CPD.0.0172src p.2136–2139
InstrumentWhat it screensPerformance (verbatim)
CAGE questionnaireAlcoholBest sensitivity for alcohol dependence (91%; specificity 87.8%) and for alcohol abuse (87.5%, specificity 80.9%). It is NOT a good screening tool for assessing unhealthy alcohol use (53% sensitive).
AUDITAlcohol — developed by the WHO to assess alcohol consumption, drinking behaviors, and alcohol-related problemsScore ranges 0 to 40. A score of 8 or greater is generally considered a positive test for unhealthy alcohol use, with greater than 90% sensitivity and 80% specificity. A score of 20 or greater suggests the presence of alcohol dependence.
Well-Being IndexDepressionA score below 13 indicates poor well-being and is an indication for further testing for depression.

General appearance, vital signs and physical examination are part of the psychiatric evaluation — the lecture cites evidence that "not all patients who present to the ED with psychiatric symptoms underwent a physical examination by ED doctors".

Trap
CAGE and AUDIT do not screen for the same thing
  • CAGE is a dependence/abuse instrument — excellent for those (91% / 87.5% sensitive) and poor for unhealthy use at 53% sensitivity. AUDIT covers the broader unhealthy-use question at > 90% sensitivity, with ≥ 20 suggesting dependence. Choosing the wrong instrument is choosing to miss the patient.
CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination651

Types of mental status examination — three tools, three indications

CPD.0.0175src p.2140–2142
ToolIndicationWhat that indication means (verbatim)
Brief Confusion Assessment Method (bCAM)DeliriumA sudden disturbance in attention (i.e. reduced ability to direct, focus, sustain, and shift attention) and awareness (reduced orientation to the environment).
Mini Mental Status ExaminationCognitive impairment (dementia)Gradual decline from a previous level of performance in one or more cognitive domains (complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual-motor, or social cognition) — see DSM-5 for the full list.
Mental Status ExaminationPsychiatric presentationMood disorder · psychotic disorder · stress, trauma, OCD · somatic disorders · personality disorders.
Bottom Line
Attention vs memory is the delirium/dementia split
  • The two definitions in this table are the distinction the confusion DLA also draws: delirium is a sudden disturbance of attention and awareness; dementia is a gradual decline in cognitive domains. That is why bCAM tests attention and the MMSE tests cognition — and why the MMSE is insensitive to very early impairment and does not cover executive function.
CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination652

Components of the mental status examination

CPD.0.0175src p.2145–2146
ComponentWhat does this mean? What are you looking for?
Appearance and behaviorObserving outward portrayal
Mood and affectEmotional status
Language and speechSpontaneous speech (not written) to discern problems in output or articulation
Thoughts and perceptionContent, relevance, awareness (including response to stimuli) and organization
Insight and judgementAwareness of illness
Cognition and memoryInformation processing "new" and "old", and executive function

Appearance and behavior — elements to assess

  • Level of consciousness: vigilant, alert, drowsy, lethargic, stuporous, asleep, comatose, confused, fluctuating.
  • Appearance: body habitus, grooming habits, interpersonal style, degree of eye contact, how the patient looks compared with his or her age; well-groomed, immaculate, attention to detail, unkempt; distinguishing features (e.g. scars, tattoos); ill- or well-appearing.
  • Behavior: congenial, cooperative, open, candid, engaging, relaxed, withdrawn…
Gregory Baker was a 20-year-old man who was brought to the emergency room by the campus police of the university. He is a well-groomed young man who was generally uncooperative. He appeared constricted, guarded, inattentive, and preoccupied — consisting rocking back and forth in the chair and looking at the window behind him.Case — appearance and behavior
CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination653

Mood and affect · language and speech · thought

CPD.0.0175src p.2147–2152
DefinitionHow to elicit and describe
AffectThe patient's feeling/emotion typically in response to an external event or a thought. Reflects short-term feeling triggered by a specific event.Observe the patient's facial expression (objective). Descriptors: emotional range (broad or restricted) · intensity (blunted, flat, or normal) · congruent with mood · appropriate for a given situation.
MoodAn inner state that persists for some time, with a disposition to exhibit a particular emotion or affect. Reflects long-term feeling.Inquire from the patient (subjective).
Mood incongruenceThe individual's reactions or emotional state appear to be in conflict with the situation.Common in psychotic disorders.

Language and speech

Language
  • Comprehension: identifies objects
  • Expression: repeat words, phrases or sentences
Speech
  • Rate: fast, pressured, slow, normal
  • Volume: loud, soft, monotone, weak, strong, mumbled
  • Quantity: talkative, expansive, paucity, poverty (alogia)
  • Fluency and rhythm: slurred, clear, hesitant, mumbled

Thought process — the flow of thoughts

  • Inquire and observe for the logic, relevance, organization and coherence of conversation — the way in which ideas are assembled.
  • Normal thinking is characterized by reasonable, smooth and continuous flow from one idea to the next with a clear goal-direction (linear).
  • The spectrum the lecture illustrates: Logical → Circumstantial → Tangential → Loose association → Flight of ideas.
CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination654

Mood and affect · language and speech · thought (cont.)

CPD.0.0175src p.2147–2152

Thought content refers to the ideas, beliefs, preoccupations, plans, themes — the context. Delusions are deemed bizarre if they are clearly implausible and not understandable to same-culture peers and do not derive from ordinary life experiences.

CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination655

Suicidal ideation, and perception

CPD.0.0175src p.2153–2154

The suicidal-ideation algorithm, as the lecture draws it

Patient expresses suicidal ideation→Does the patient have a suicide plan?→Plan + access to lethal means + poor social support + poor judgement, AND cannot make a contract for safety → HOSPITALIZE→No plan/intent, or no access to lethal means, AND able to make a contract for safety → evaluate for psychiatric disorders or stressors; treat with antidepressants and treat the underlying cause; continuous monitoring

Perception

Perception is physical sensation given meaning — the integration of sensory stimuli to form an image or impression, in a manner or configuration influenced by past experience.Definition
HallucinationAssociation (verbatim)
1. Visual (most common)Occur most often in organic conditions such as Charles Bonnet syndrome, migraines, Lewy body dementia, metabolic encephalopathy.
2. AuditoryOften seen in schizophrenia.
3. TactileMost common with alcohol withdrawal or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
4. Gustatory—
5. Olfactory (phantosmia)May occur in schizophrenia and mood disorder. Consider temporal lobe epilepsy, chronic migraine headaches, brain tumor, and Parkinson's disease.
CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination656

Suicidal ideation, and perception (cont.)

CPD.0.0175src p.2153–2154
Exam Lock
The modality points at the cause
  • Auditory → schizophrenia. Visual → organic. Tactile → alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. Olfactory → temporal lobe epilepsy, tumour, migraine, Parkinson's. A patient with visual hallucinations is more likely to have a medical problem than a primary psychotic one — which is exactly why the evaluation sequence rules out medical causes first.
CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination657

Insight, judgement and cognition

CPD.0.0175src p.2155–2156

Insight and judgement

Insight
Awareness of one's own illness and/or situation. Example question: "Do you know why you are here?"
Judgement
The ability to anticipate the consequences of one's behavior and make decisions to safeguard your wellbeing and that of others.
GradeDescription of insight (verbatim)
1Complete denial of illness
2Slight awareness of being sick and needing help but denying it at the same time
3Awareness of being sick but blaming it on others, external factors, or medical or unknown organic factors
4Intellectual insight: admission of illness and recognition that symptoms or failures in social adjustment are due to irrational feelings or disturbances, without applying that knowledge to future experiences
5True emotional insight: emotional awareness of the motives and feelings within, and of the underlying meaning of symptoms

Cognitive function — localisation and the test that probes it

LocationFunctionCognitive tests
Frontal lobeExecutive functionDigit span · WORLD backwards · serial 7s · verbal (letter) fluency
Temporal lobeMemoryOrientation · immediate recall · delayed recall
Mesial temporal lobe (R > L)Facial recognitionIdentification of celebrities and politicians
Left hemisphereLanguageReading and comprehension · writing · naming · repetition
Occipital and biparietal lobesVisuospatialPentagon copy (MMSE)
Left parietalArithmeticAddition or subtraction (serial 7s)
CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination658

Cognitive testing in detail

CPD.0.0175src p.2157–2162
DomainHow to test it (verbatim)
OrientationPerson — do not limit to the patient's name only. Place — patient's residence, name of current location, city, state. Time — time of day, day of the week, month, season, date, year. Progression of loss: 1st time, 2nd place, last person.
AttentionThe ability of an individual to focus and sustain their thoughts on a specific task despite minor stimuli. Serial 7's: ask the patient to start from a hundred and subtract 7, and keep subtracting 7 — need > 5 units correctly. Spelling: spell the word W-O-R-L-D forward then backward. Consider poor math/spelling skills before calling it inattention.
Digit spanPatient repeats a series of numbers, starting with 3 and building to 8: 7-8-3 · 7-9-6-2 · 6-3-8-1-7 · 4-8-3-9-7-2 · 8-9-2-6-4-1-7 · 7-1-9-2-8-3-5-4.
MemoryThe ability to take in information, store it, and recall it later: 1. encoding (registration), 2. storage, 3. retrieval (recall or recognition). Immediate term (new learning): provide 3 words and ask the patient to repeat. Short term: ask the patient to recall the 3 words at least 5 minutes later. Long term.
Information and vocabularyThe amount of general information an individual stores in long-term memory. Specifically ask: names of presidents, names of five largest cities. Depends on educational background.
Abstract thinkingThe ability to think beyond the immediate, specific stimulus situation and to think in general, symbolic modes — the opposite of concrete (literal) thinking. Two common methods: proverbs and similarities. Deficits: schizophrenia, autistic spectrum disorder.
Constructional abilityA set of cognitive functions that allows an individual to plan, evaluate, and execute new and complex tasks. Two common methods: ask the patient to draw a clock face; copy figures of increasing complexity.
Trap
Education confounds three of these tests
  • The lecture flags it twice: attention testing asks you to consider poor math/spelling skills before calling serial 7s abnormal, and information and vocabulary depends on educational background. The confusion DLA makes the same point from the other side — a sixth-grade education was offered there as the reason a patient "never was very good at math."

CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination660

Check — psychiatric interview and MSE

CPD.0.0172

A patient's family reports heavy drinking. You want to screen for unhealthy alcohol use, not dependence. Which instrument does this lecture support, and why not the other?

  1. ACAGE, because it is 91% sensitive for dependence
  2. BAUDIT, because CAGE is only 53% sensitive for unhealthy alcohol use while AUDIT is over 90% sensitive at a cut-off of 8
  3. CWell-Being Index, because it covers substance use
  4. DThe MMSE, because alcohol causes cognitive decline
  5. EEither — they perform identically
Answer
B. The CAGE questionnaire presented the best sensitivity for alcohol dependence (91%; specificity 87.8%) and for alcohol abuse (87.5%, specificity 80.9%). It is NOT a good screening tool for assessing unhealthy alcohol use (53% sensitive). With a score that can range from 0 to 40, a score of 8 or greater on the AUDIT is generally considered a positive test for unhealthy alcohol use, with greater than 90 percent sensitivity and 80 percent specificity; a score of 20 or greater suggests the presence of alcohol dependence.
CPD.0.0175

A 58-year-old with alcohol use disorder, admitted 48 hours ago, reports insects crawling on his skin. Which hallucination modality is this, and what does this lecture associate it with?

  1. AVisual; Lewy body dementia
  2. BAuditory; schizophrenia
  3. CTactile; alcohol withdrawal or benzodiazepine withdrawal
  4. DOlfactory; temporal lobe epilepsy
  5. EGustatory; migraine
Answer
C. Tactile hallucinations are most common with alcohol withdrawal or benzodiazepine withdrawal. The rest of the list: visual (most common) occur most often in organic conditions such as Charles Bonnet syndrome, migraines, Lewy body dementia and metabolic encephalopathy; auditory are often seen in schizophrenia; olfactory (phantosmia) may occur in schizophrenia and mood disorder — consider temporal lobe epilepsy, chronic migraine headaches, brain tumor and Parkinson's disease.
CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination661

Check — psychiatric interview and MSE (cont.)

CPD.0.0175

A patient says "I know I have bipolar disorder and that my spending sprees come from the illness, but when I feel that way I still spend." Which grade of insight is this?

  1. AGrade 1 — complete denial
  2. BGrade 2 — slight awareness while denying
  3. CGrade 3 — awareness but blaming others
  4. DGrade 4 — intellectual insight without applying the knowledge to future experiences
  5. EGrade 5 — true emotional insight
Answer
D. Grade 4 — intellectual insight: admission of illness and recognition that symptoms or failures in social adjustment are due to irrational feelings or disturbances, without applying that knowledge to future experiences. Grade 5 is true emotional insight: emotional awareness of the motives and feelings within and of the underlying meaning of symptoms — the point at which the knowledge actually changes behaviour.
CPD.0.0175

Which statement about mood and affect matches this lecture?

  1. AMood is objective and observed; affect is subjective and asked
  2. BAffect is observed from facial expression and reflects short-term feeling; mood is inquired from the patient and reflects a longer-lasting inner state
  3. CBoth are assessed only by direct questioning
  4. DMood incongruence is characteristic of delirium
  5. EBlunted and flat describe mood, not affect
Answer
B. Affect: observe the patient's facial expression (objective); the patient's feeling/emotion typically in response to an external event or a thought; reflects short-term feeling triggered by a specific event. Mood: inquire from the patient (subjective); refers to an inner state that persists for some time; reflects long-term feeling. Affect descriptors are range, intensity (blunted, flat, normal), congruence and appropriateness, and mood incongruence is common in psychotic disorders.
CLSK · Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination662

Check — psychiatric interview and MSE (cont.)

CPD.0.0175

Which tool does this lecture pair with a sudden disturbance in attention and awareness?

  1. AMini Mental Status Examination
  2. BBrief Confusion Assessment Method (bCAM)
  3. CMental Status Examination
  4. DAUDIT
  5. EWell-Being Index
Answer
B. Brief Confusion Assessment Method (bCAM) — indication: delirium — a sudden disturbance in attention (i.e. reduced ability to direct, focus, sustain, and shift attention) and awareness (reduced orientation to the environment). The MMSE is indicated for cognitive impairment (dementia): gradual decline from a previous level of performance in one or more cognitive domains, and the MSE for a psychiatric presentation.
CPD.0.0175

In which order is orientation typically lost, according to this lecture?

  1. APerson, then place, then time
  2. BPlace, then person, then time
  3. CTime, then place, then person
  4. DTime, then person, then place
  5. EAll three are lost simultaneously
Answer
C. Progression of loss: 1st — time; 2nd — place; last — person. Orientation testing should not be superficial: person — do not limit to the patient's name only; place — patient's residence, name of current location, city, state; time — time of day, day of the week, month, season, date, year.
CPD.0.0175

Serial 7s and WORLD-backwards primarily probe which lobe and function, per the lecture's localisation table?

  1. ATemporal lobe; memory
  2. BFrontal lobe; executive function
  3. CLeft parietal; language
  4. DOccipital; visuospatial
  5. EMesial temporal; facial recognition
Answer
B. The table gives frontal lobe → executive function → digit span, WORLD backwards, serial 7s, verbal (letter) fluency. Others: temporal lobe → memory (orientation, immediate and delayed recall); mesial temporal lobe (R > L) → facial recognition; left hemisphere → language; occipital and biparietal → visuospatial (pentagon copy); left parietal → arithmetic. Note that serial 7s appears twice — as attention and as arithmetic.

PHAR

Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs

Dr Tiffany Clementson · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology. One chloride channel, two ways to open it, and ten drug classes arranged around it.

Dr Tiffany Clementson · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology  ·  source pp. 2167–2234
An effective anxiolytic drug should reduce anxiety and exert a calming effect with little or no effect on motor or mental functions. The degree of CNS depression should be the minimum consistent with therapeutic efficacy. A hypnotic drug should produce drowsiness and encourage the onset and maintenance of a state of sleep that as far as possible resembles the natural sleep state.Definitions, PHAR.00028
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs664

Lecture objectives — verbatim

src p.2181–2183
  • PHAR.00028 Define anxiolytic and hypnotic. Describe the differences in the dose-depression relationships for benzodiazepines.
  • PHAR.00029 List the different classes of anxiolytic and hypnotic drugs. Describe their mechanism of action, pharmacokinetic properties, adverse effects and clinical uses of the azepines and the barbiturates.
  • PHAR.00030 Explain why antidepressants are the drugs of choice for chronic anxiety.
  • PHAR.00031 Describe the structure and function of the GABAA receptor.
  • PHAR.00032 Describe the actions of agonists, antagonists and inverse agonists at the GABAA receptor.
  • PHAR.00033 Explain the uses of flumazenil.
  • PHAR.00034 Describe the pharmacokinetic properties of benzodiazepines.
  • PHAR.00035 Compare and contrast the effects of barbiturates, benzodiazepines, and non-benzodiazepine benzodiazepine-receptor agonists on induction and maintenance of sleep, and their adverse effects.
  • PHAR.00036 Describe the differences in the dose-response relationships for benzodiazepines and the barbiturates.
  • PHAR.00037 Explain why drugs acting selectively at benzodiazepine receptors have replaced barbiturates as anxiolytics and hypnotics.
  • PHAR.00038 Compare and contrast the time course of anxiety relief for benzodiazepines and antidepressants.

Hypnotic effects involve more pronounced depression of the CNS than sedation. This can be achieved with some anxiolytic drugs by increasing the dose. Newer drugs exert anxiolytic effects without causing sedation or hypnosis, and newer hypnotic drugs lack anxiolytic effects.

PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs665

The classes, and why antidepressants come first

PHAR.00029 · PHAR.00030 · PHAR.00038src p.2168–2169 · 2184–2186
  1. Antidepressants
  2. Benzodiazepines
  3. Barbiturates
  4. Non-benzodiazepine benzodiazepine-receptor agonists (Z-drugs) — zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone
  5. 5-HT1A receptor partial agonists — buspirone
  6. Melatonin receptor agonists — ramelteon
  7. Orexin receptor antagonists — suvorexant, lemborexant
  8. Beta-blockers — propranolol
  9. Alpha-blockers — prazosin
  10. Antihistaminics — doxepin, hydroxyzine, diphenhydramine, doxylamine
  11. Older sedative-hypnotics — meprobamate, chloral hydrate, paraldehyde

Antidepressants (PHAR.00030 · PHAR.00038)

  • Antidepressants are the treatment of choice for the management of chronic anxiety. An SSRI or an SNRI is the drug of choice for initial treatment.
  • The antianxiety response may take 4–6 weeks.
  • They may be used alone or in combination with a benzodiazepine during the first weeks of treatment; after 4–6 weeks the benzodiazepine can be tapered.
  • TCAs can be used if anxiety has not responded to an SSRI or SNRI.
  • They have replaced benzodiazepines as the drugs of choice for chronic anxiety due to a tolerable adverse effect profile — and because benzodiazepines carry dependence and withdrawal.
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs666

The classes, and why antidepressants come first (cont.)

PHAR.00029 · PHAR.00030 · PHAR.00038src p.2168–2169 · 2184–2186
Exam Lock
The time-course contrast is objective PHAR.00038 in one line
  • Benzodiazepines give rapid relief of acute anxiety symptoms; antidepressants take 4–6 weeks for the antianxiety response. That is exactly why the two are combined at the start and the benzodiazepine is then tapered — the fast drug covers the gap until the safe drug works.
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs667

The GABA-A receptor — structure, binding sites, and what each drug does to the channel

PHAR.00031 · PHAR.00032src p.2170 · 2190–2195

GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS. Binding of GABA to its receptor opens the chloride channel, leading to an increase in chloride influx. The influx of chloride ions causes a hyperpolarization that moves the postsynaptic potential away from its firing threshold and thus inhibits the triggering of action potentials. Two benzodiazepine receptor subtypes commonly found in the CNS have been designated BZ1 and BZ2.

PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs668

Benzodiazepines — actions, duration and metabolism

PHAR.00029 · PHAR.00034src p.2171 · 2187–2204
  • Widely used anxiolytic drugs. They replaced barbiturates in the treatment of anxiety because they are safer and more effective.
  • Benzodiazepine-induced enhancement takes the form of an increase in FREQUENCY of channel opening events, and benzodiazepines decrease the EC50 for the GABA-induced Cl⁻ influx.

Actions — "A Calm Sea Moment"

  1. Anxiety reduction
  2. Calm / sedative and hypnotic
  3. Seizures prevented (anticonvulsant)
  4. Muscle relaxant

Pharmacokinetics

  • Benzodiazepines are lipophilic, rapidly and completely absorbed after oral administration and distributed throughout the body. Onset of action is 30 to 60 minutes.
  • The half-lives are very important clinically: duration of action may determine the therapeutic usefulness.
Duration classDrugsHalf-life
Long-actingChlordiazepoxide · clonazepam · diazepam · flurazepam1–3 days
Intermediate-actingAlprazolam · lorazepam · oxazepam · temazepam10–20 hours
Short-actingMidazolam · triazolam3–8 hours
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs669

Benzodiazepines — actions, duration and metabolism (cont.)

PHAR.00029 · PHAR.00034src p.2171 · 2187–2204

Metabolism

  • Metabolized mainly in the liver. Most benzodiazepines undergo phase I reactions, mainly by CYP3A4; the metabolites are then conjugated in phase II to form glucuronides excreted in the urine. Inhibitors of CYP3A4 therefore prolong their action.
  • Desmethyldiazepam, with a half-life of over 40 hours, is an active metabolite of several benzodiazepines used clinically; it is then metabolized to the active compound oxazepam.
  • Oxazepam, lorazepam and temazepam are conjugated directly and are NOT metabolized by the P450 system.
  • Flurazepam is oxidized by liver enzymes to active metabolites with half-lives ranging from 30 to 100 hours.
Bottom Line
"LOT" — the three benzodiazepines that skip phase I
  • Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam are conjugated directly, so they are the ones whose handling does not depend on CYP3A4 or on hepatic phase I capacity. That is why the lecture names lorazepam or oxazepam for patients with advanced liver disease in the drug-withdrawal indication.
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs670

Benzodiazepines — therapeutic uses and adverse effects

PHAR.00029 · PHAR.00033src p.2172–2173 · 2205–2210
IndicationDetail (verbatim)
Anxiety disorders1. Rapid relief of acute anxiety symptoms. 2. Adjuncts to antidepressants. 3. Recommended only for short-term use. Alprazolam is effective for short- and long-term treatment of panic disorder but may cause withdrawal reactions.
Muscular disordersDiazepam is useful in the treatment of skeletal muscle spasms such as occur in muscle strain, and in treating spasticity from degenerative disorders like multiple sclerosis and cerebral palsy.
SeizuresClonazepam — used for some types of epileptic seizures. Lorazepam, midazolam and diazepam — used in status epilepticus.
Drug withdrawalUsed for management of ethanol withdrawal. Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide are commonly used; lorazepam or oxazepam are used in patients with advanced liver disease.
AnesthesiaCertain benzodiazepines are used as components of anesthesia protocols.
Sleep disordersThe most prescribed for sleep disorders are intermediate-acting temazepam and short-acting triazolam.

Adverse effects — "Sleepy And Clumsy"

  • Drowsiness and confusion · ataxia · cognitive impairment.
  • Paradoxical effects: anxiety, irritability, hostility and rage, paranoia, depression and suicidal ideation — collectively sometimes called disinhibition or dyscontrol reactions. The incidence of such reactions is rare and appears to be dose-related.
  • Dependence can develop if high doses are given over a prolonged period. Abrupt discontinuation leads to withdrawal symptoms: confusion, anxiety, agitation, restlessness.
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs671

Benzodiazepines — therapeutic uses and adverse effects (cont.)

PHAR.00029 · PHAR.00033src p.2172–2173 · 2205–2210

Flumazenil (PHAR.00033)

  • The only benzodiazepine receptor antagonist available for clinical use. It blocks the effects of benzodiazepines and Z-drugs.
  • Approved for reversing the CNS depressant effects of benzodiazepine overdose, and to hasten recovery following use of benzodiazepines in anesthetic and diagnostic procedures.
  • Rapid onset and short duration: half-life about 1 hour, due to rapid hepatic clearance — frequent administration may be necessary to maintain reversal of long-acting benzodiazepines.
  • May precipitate withdrawal in physiologically dependent patients. May cause seizures if a benzodiazepine is being used to control seizures.
Trap
Flumazenil is not a routine antidote
  • Its 1-hour half-life means a patient can re-sedate after it wears off, and it can precipitate withdrawal or unmask seizures in exactly the patients most likely to have overdosed. Note also that it reverses Z-drugs as well — they share the benzodiazepine site.
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs672

Barbiturates

PHAR.00029 · PHAR.00035src p.2174–2176 · 2211–2220
  • Formerly the mainstay of treatment to sedate the patient or to induce and maintain sleep. Replaced by the benzodiazepines and Z-drugs, because barbiturates induce tolerance and dependence, are associated with very severe withdrawal symptoms, and can cause coma in toxic doses.
Long-acting (1–2 days)
Phenobarbital
Short-acting (3–8 hours)
Pentobarbital · thiopental

Mechanism of action

  • Positive allosteric modulators of GABAA receptors; they enhance GABAergic transmission.
  • The binding site of barbiturates is different from that of the benzodiazepines.
  • In contrast to benzodiazepines, they increase the DURATION of the GABA-gated chloride channel openings.
  • At high concentrations, barbiturates also directly activate chloride channels, independent of the presence of GABA.
  • Barbiturates block glutamate receptors and inhibit voltage-activated sodium and calcium channels. The multiplicity of sites of action explains their ability to induce full surgical anesthesia and their more pronounced central depressant effects.

Actions and uses

  • Depression of CNS — any degree of CNS depression is possible, depending on the dose.
  • Respiratory depression: barbiturates suppress the hypoxic and chemoreceptor response to CO₂, and overdosage is followed by respiratory depression and death.
  • Enzyme induction: barbiturates induce P-450 microsomal enzymes in the liver.
  • Anesthesia: the ultra-short-acting barbiturates such as thiopental have been used IV to induce anesthesia (they have been replaced by other agents).
  • Anticonvulsant: phenobarbital can be used in the management of tonic-clonic seizures and status epilepticus; pentobarbital and thiopental are used in the management of status epilepticus.
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs673

Barbiturates (cont.)

PHAR.00029 · PHAR.00035src p.2174–2176 · 2211–2220

Adverse effects — the lecture's "6 Ps and an H"

  1. Poor focus — drowsiness, impaired concentration
  2. Paradoxical excitement — *"excitement rather than depression, and the patient may appear inebriated"*
  3. Pulmonary depression — respiratory depression
  4. Pain worsens — hyperalgesia
  5. Physical dependence — severe withdrawal
  6. Poisoning — respiratory and cardiovascular collapse
  7. H for Hypersensitivity (*allergic reactions occur especially in persons who tend to have asthma, urticaria, angioedema*) and Hangover (*hypnotic doses produce a feeling of tiredness well after the patient awakes, impairing the ability to function normally for many hours*)
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs674

Dose–response: the reason the class was replaced (PHAR.00036 · PHAR.00037)

PHAR.00036 · PHAR.00037src p.2215–2221

Dose–response: the reason the class was replaced (PHAR.00036 · PHAR.00037) (cont.)

The Z-drugs, and the non-GABA alternatives

PHAR.00029 · PHAR.00035src p.2177–2179 · 2222–2232

Non-benzodiazepine benzodiazepine-receptor agonists (Z-drugs)

  • Positive allosteric modulators of GABAA receptors. Act only on the BZ1 subtype of benzodiazepine receptors; only approved as hypnotics.
  • Antagonized by flumazenil. Minimal muscle-relaxing and anticonvulsant effects.
  • Little or no tolerance; low incidence of adverse effects. They have largely replaced benzodiazepines in the treatment of insomnia.
DrugOnset (min)DurationHalf-life (h)FDA-approved indication

Zolpidem ER30Intermediate1.6–5.5Insomnia characterized by difficulties with sleep onset and/or sleep maintenance
Zaleplon20Ultrashort1Short-term treatment of insomnia
Eszopiclone30Intermediate6Treatment of insomnia

Zolpidem is extensively metabolized to inactive metabolites, mainly by CYP3A4. Adverse effects include nightmares and agitation.

PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs680

Block exam — anxiolytics and hypnotics

PHAR.00031 · PHAR.00036

Which single difference in channel kinetics underlies the fact that barbiturates can cause fatal respiratory depression while benzodiazepines usually cannot?

  1. ABenzodiazepines increase duration; barbiturates increase frequency of channel opening
  2. BBenzodiazepines increase the frequency of channel opening and require GABA; barbiturates increase the duration and at high doses open the channel directly, without GABA
  3. CBenzodiazepines are competitive antagonists at GABA-A
  4. DBarbiturates act only at the benzodiazepine site
  5. EBenzodiazepines block glutamate receptors
Answer
B. Benzodiazepine-induced enhancement takes the form of an increase in FREQUENCY of channel opening events; in contrast to benzodiazepines, barbiturates increase the DURATION of the GABA-gated chloride channel openings, and at high concentrations barbiturates also directly activate chloride channels, independent of the presence of GABA. Because the benzodiazepine effect requires GABA, there is a ceiling: benzodiazepines do not produce significant respiratory depression, coma, or death unless combined with alcohol or other depressants.
PHAR.00034

A patient with alcoholic cirrhosis needs a benzodiazepine for ethanol withdrawal. Which agents does this lecture specify, and why?

  1. ADiazepam or chlordiazepoxide, because they are long-acting
  2. BLorazepam or oxazepam, because they are conjugated directly and are not metabolized by the P450 system
  3. CMidazolam or triazolam, because they are short-acting
  4. DAlprazolam, because it treats panic
  5. EFlurazepam, because its metabolites are active
Answer
B. Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide are commonly used for ethanol withdrawal, but lorazepam or oxazepam are used in patients with advanced liver disease — because oxazepam, lorazepam and temazepam are conjugated directly and are not metabolized by the P450 system. Contrast flurazepam, which is oxidized by liver enzymes to active metabolites with half-lives ranging from 30 to 100 hours.
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs681

Block exam — anxiolytics and hypnotics (cont.)

PHAR.00029

Which anxiolytic has no hypnotic, anticonvulsant or muscle-relaxant effect, no dependence, no interaction with alcohol, and takes 2–3 weeks to work?

  1. AAlprazolam
  2. BBuspirone
  3. CZolpidem
  4. DHydroxyzine
  5. ERamelteon
Answer
B. Buspirone — a partial agonist at 5-HT1A receptors; slow onset of 2–3 weeks (similar to antidepressants); no hypnotic, anticonvulsant, or muscle relaxant effects; less psychomotor impairment than benzodiazepines; no interaction with alcohol or benzodiazepines; no rebound anxiety or withdrawal on discontinuation; no dependence. It is a second-line agent in generalized anxiety disorder due to variable efficacy. Mnemonic: *"BUS rides SLOW, but safe."*
PHAR.00033

A patient who takes clonazepam for seizures presents obtunded after a mixed overdose. Why is flumazenil hazardous here?

  1. AIt has too long a half-life
  2. BIt may cause seizures if a benzodiazepine is being used to control seizures, and may precipitate withdrawal in physiologically dependent patients
  3. CIt does not reverse benzodiazepines
  4. DIt reverses opioids as well
  5. EIt causes respiratory depression
Answer
B. Flumazenil may precipitate withdrawal in physiologically dependent patients and may cause seizures if a benzodiazepine is used to control seizures. It also has a rapid onset and short duration — half-life about 1 hour due to rapid hepatic clearance — so frequent administration may be necessary to maintain reversal of long-acting benzodiazepines. It is the only benzodiazepine receptor antagonist available for clinical use, and it blocks the effects of benzodiazepines and Z-drugs.
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs682

Block exam — anxiolytics and hypnotics (cont.)

PHAR.00029

Which hypnotic is contraindicated in narcolepsy, and what is its mechanism?

  1. AZolpidem; BZ1 agonism
  2. BSuvorexant; dual orexin OX1 and OX2 receptor antagonism
  3. CRamelteon; MT1/MT2 agonism
  4. DDoxepin; H1 antagonism
  5. EEszopiclone; GABA-A modulation
Answer
B. Orexin A and B are neuropeptides that promote wakefulness through activation of the OX1 and OX2 receptors. Suvorexant and lemborexant are dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORA)... Contraindicated in narcolepsy. Their adverse effects are daytime somnolence and worsening of depression/suicidal ideation. Blocking the wake-promoting system in a patient who already cannot stay awake is the reason for the contraindication.
PHAR.00029

Which drug in this lecture is used for performance anxiety, and which for PTSD nightmares?

  1. APropranolol for performance anxiety; prazosin for PTSD nightmares
  2. BPrazosin for performance anxiety; propranolol for PTSD nightmares
  3. CHydroxyzine for both
  4. DBuspirone for performance anxiety; doxepin for PTSD nightmares
  5. EZolpidem for both
Answer
A. Propranolol and other β-adrenergic receptor antagonists can reduce the autonomic symptoms associated with specific situational phobias; propranolol is widely used to control performance anxiety (stage fright). Prazosin crosses the blood-brain barrier and antagonizes central α1 receptors, blocking stress responses; through this mechanism prazosin can improve sleep and reduce nightmares associated with PTSD.
PHAR.00035

Which statement about the Z-drugs is correct?

  1. AThey act at all benzodiazepine receptor subtypes and have strong muscle-relaxant effects
  2. BThey act only on the BZ1 subtype, are approved only as hypnotics, are antagonised by flumazenil, and have minimal muscle-relaxing and anticonvulsant effects
  3. CThey are not positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A
  4. DZaleplon has the longest half-life of the group
  5. EThey produce more tolerance than benzodiazepines
Answer
B. Z-drugs are positive allosteric modulators of GABAA receptors; act only on the BZ1 subtype of benzodiazepine receptors; only approved as hypnotics; antagonized by flumazenil; minimal muscle relaxing and anticonvulsant effects; little or no tolerance; low incidence of adverse effects; have largely replaced benzodiazepines in the treatment of insomnia. Zaleplon has the shortest half-life (1 h, ultrashort duration); eszopiclone the longest (6 h).
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs683

Block exam — anxiolytics and hypnotics (cont.)

PHAR.00034

Which benzodiazepine grouping matches the lecture's duration table?

  1. AAlprazolam long-acting; diazepam short-acting
  2. BChlordiazepoxide, clonazepam, diazepam and flurazepam long-acting (1–3 days); alprazolam, lorazepam, oxazepam and temazepam intermediate (10–20 h); midazolam and triazolam short-acting (3–8 h)
  3. CMidazolam long-acting; flurazepam short-acting
  4. DTemazepam short-acting; triazolam long-acting
  5. EAll benzodiazepines have similar half-lives
Answer
B. The lecture's table gives exactly that grouping, with half-lives of 1–3 days · 10–20 hours · 3–8 hours. It also notes the sleep-disorder favourites: intermediate-acting temazepam and short-acting triazolam, and that the onset of action of benzodiazepines is 30 to 60 minutes.
PHAR.00030 · PHAR.00038

Why have antidepressants replaced benzodiazepines as first-line therapy for chronic anxiety, and how is the transition managed?

  1. AAntidepressants work faster; benzodiazepines are stopped immediately
  2. BAntidepressants have a tolerable adverse-effect profile without dependence; a benzodiazepine may be combined during the first weeks and then tapered after 4–6 weeks
  3. CBenzodiazepines are ineffective for anxiety
  4. DAntidepressants have no delay in onset
  5. EBuspirone is always used instead
Answer
B. Antidepressants are considered first-line agents in the management of chronic anxiety. They have replaced benzodiazepines as the drugs of choice for chronic anxiety due to a tolerable adverse effect profile. The antianxiety response may take 4–6 weeks. They may be used alone or in combination with a benzodiazepine during the first weeks of treatment; after 4–6 weeks the benzodiazepine can be tapered. Benzodiazepines remain excellent for rapid relief of acute anxiety symptoms but are recommended only for short-term use.
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs684

Block exam — anxiolytics and hypnotics (cont.)

PHAR.00029 · PHAR.00035

A patient on long-term phenobarbital has subtherapeutic levels of warfarin and an oral contraceptive failure. Which barbiturate property explains both?

  1. AIncreased duration of chloride channel opening
  2. BInduction of hepatic P-450 microsomal enzymes
  3. CSuppression of the chemoreceptor response to CO₂
  4. DDirect activation of chloride channels
  5. EBlockade of glutamate receptors
Answer
B. Enzyme induction: barbiturates induce P-450 microsomal enzymes in the liver. This is one of the explicit contrasts with benzodiazepines, which have no enzyme induction, and it is the same mechanism that put barbiturates on the warfarin-inducer list in the coagulation lecture (with carbamazepine, phenytoin and rifampin).
PHAR · Anxiolytic and Hypnotic Drugs685

Neuropathology 1 — Trauma and Hydrocephalus

Dr. Adesola Adeleye · Department of Pathology. Everything in this lecture follows from one idea: the brain lives in a closed box.

Learning objectives — verbatim

  2. Lecture 2 — cerebrovascular diseases

NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus686

Revision — what makes the CNS unique, and what follows from it

PATH.7025src p.2240–2242
Gross neuroanatomy
  • Cerebrum: 2 hemispheres connected by the corpus callosum
  • Cerebellum
  • Brainstem: midbrain · pons · medulla oblongata
  • The brain is surrounded by meninges: dura, arachnoid, pia
Histology
  • Neurons — dendrites, body (soma), axon, the synapse
  • Astrocytes: supportive, nutritional
  • Oligodendrocytes: supportive, insulating (myelin)
  • Microglia: phagocytic (mononuclear)
  • Ependymal cells: line the CSF compartment and produce and carry CSF
UniquenessImplication
Closed box — bony, membranous and CSF encasementPathological increase in intracranial pressure and its consequences
Autoregulation of blood flow — ability to maintain flow locally within physiological limitsUnable to autoregulate after a limit — pathological
Blood-brain barrier — protective against chemicals in the systemic circulationSome medications cannot cross it — have to be administered locally
Limited-to-no lymphaticsImpairs resorption of edema fluid
Functional localisation — remember the homunculusFocal neurological deficits

"The closed box"

  • Brain + blood + CSF/water: everything has to fit into this one box. If one increases, intracranial pressure increases.
  • Causes of raised intracranial pressure are therefore Brain (tumor) · Blood (hemorrhage) · Water/CSF (hydrocephalus, cerebral edema).
  • The result: 1. Equilibration (up to a certain limit and speed) · 2. Herniation (with asymmetrical pressure) · 3. Diffusely raised ICP — when might perfusion become an issue?
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus687

Revision — what makes the CNS unique, and what follows from it (cont.)

PATH.7025src p.2240–2242
Exam Lock
Three compartments, three diseases, one lecture
  • Brain → tumour and oedema. Blood → the four haemorrhages. Water → hydrocephalus. Every entity in this lecture is one compartment expanding inside a rigid box, and every complication is the box's answer: equilibration, then herniation, then failure of perfusion.
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus688

Cerebral edema — the two types

PATH.7025src p.2244–2245
Accumulation of excess fluid within brain parenchyma. Water can increase in the extracellular or intracellular compartment.Definition and etiopathogenesis
Vasogenic edema (vaso: vessel; genic: arising from)Cytotoxic edema (cyto: cell; toxic: poison/harmful)
MechanismDisruption of the blood-brain barrier; fluid moves from the vascular component into the extracellular space of the brainNeuronal, glial or endothelial cell membrane injury; increase in intracellular fluid
CausesMeningitis, encephalitis, trauma and metastasisGeneralized hypoxia/ischemia insult · metabolic damage · anything that injures the cells
Aggravating factorPaucity of lymphatics greatly impairs the resorption of excess extracellular fluid—
Clinical features
  • Headache
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Altered mental status
  • Seizures
  • Neurological deficit
Complications
  • Brain herniation
  • Stroke
  • Permanent brain injury
Morphology
  • The surfaces of the gyri are flattened as a result of compression of the expanding brain by the dura mater and inner surface of the skull
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus689

Hydrocephalus — the four types

PATH.7025 · PATH.7040src p.2246–2249
Accumulation of CSF within the ventricular system. Etiology: 1) obstruction of flow, 2) impaired resorption, 3) excess production.Definition
  • Before the sutures fuse: increase in head circumference. After the sutures fuse: no increase in head circumference (closed box) → ventricular expansion and increased intracranial pressure.
Non-communicatingCommunicatingEx vacuo
EtiopathogenesisObstruction to flow of CSF in a part of the ventricle — stricture of the aqueduct of Sylvius or tumor in the 4th ventricle. Interferes with or blocks normal CSF circulation from ventricles to subarachnoid space.Poor absorption of CSF by arachnoid villi — post-meningitic scarring, subarachnoid haemorrhage, leptomeningeal carcinomatosis. Also tumour — choroid plexus papilloma or carcinoma (excess production), vestibular schwannoma.Infarctions or neurodegenerative disorders → loss of brain volume
ResultOnly the affected portion of the ventricle enlargesEntire ventricular system enlargedSecondary increase in CSF volume — compensatory, not a pressure problem

Normal pressure hydrocephalus

  • Normal pressure: normal opening pressure on lumbar puncture. Hydrocephalus: pathologically enlarged ventricular size.
  • Idiopathic; a type of communicating hydrocephalus. Theory: transient high CSF pressure leading to ventricular enlargement → distorts fibers of the corona radiata; ventricular enlargement normalizes pressure.
  • Clinical features: 1. gait disturbances · 2. dementia · 3. urinary incontinence.

Morphology: dilated lateral ventricles seen in coronal section through the mid-thalamus.

NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus690

Hydrocephalus — the four types (cont.)

PATH.7025 · PATH.7040src p.2246–2249
Bottom Line
Ex vacuo is not really hydrocephalus
  • The ventricles are big because the brain has shrunk, not because CSF is under pressure — hence "ex vacuo", filling a vacuum. Contrast NPH, where the ventricles are enlarged with a normal opening pressure but the triad of gait disturbance, dementia and urinary incontinence is real and treatable.
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus691

Pseudotumor cerebri (idiopathic intracranial hypertension)

PATH.7026 · PATH.7040src p.2251
  • Definition: pseudo- false; tumor- mass; cerebri- brain → not due to a tumor.
  • Epidemiology: overweight women of childbearing age.
  • Etiology: unknown — therefore "idiopathic intracranial hypertension". No obvious cause on neuroimaging: no masses, no bleeding within the brain, no hydrocephalus / increased ventricular size, no vasogenic or cytotoxic edema.
  • Clinical features: increased intracranial pressure characterised by headache (positional), diplopia (CN VI palsy), vomiting, and papilledema potentially leading to vision loss.
  • Treatment: lumbar punctures, acetazolamide, shunt.
Trap
Diplopia here is a false localising sign
  • The CN VI palsy in raised ICP does not localise the lesion — the abducens nerve has the longest intracranial course and is compressed by pressure alone. Combine that with papilloedema and positional headache in an overweight woman of childbearing age, and a normal scan, and the diagnosis is made by exclusion.
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus692

Cerebral herniations — the three types and their signs

PATH.7026src p.2252–2253
Displacement of brain tissue past rigid dural folds (the falx and tentorium) or through openings in the skull. Etiology: anything that raises intracranial pressure. Clinical features: compromised blood supply, infarctions, edema, and specific symptoms depending on the area involved.Definition
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus693

Cerebral herniations — the three types and their signs (cont.)

PATH.7026src p.2252–2253
TypeMechanism and consequence (verbatim)
Subfalcine (cingulate)Unilateral or asymmetrical expansion of a cerebral hemisphere displaces the cingulate gyrus under the falx cerebri → compresses the anterior cerebral artery → infarcts in the area supplied by the artery → motor and sensory deficits in the lower extremity and lower trunk.
Transtentorial (uncal)The medial aspect of the temporal lobe (uncus) is pushed down and compressed against the free margin of the tentorium. Initially: ipsilateral blown pupil and ipsilateral impaired extraocular movements due to CN III compression, and contralateral hemiparesis due to ipsilateral uncal compression.
TonsillarCerebellar tonsils displaced through the foramen magnum → brainstem compression and compromise of the respiratory and cardiac centres → death.
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus694

Transtentorial herniation — the two named complications

PATH.7026src p.2254
PhenomenonMechanism and signs (verbatim)
Kernohan phenomenonFurther displacement of the uncus → contralateral blown pupil and contralateral impaired extraocular movements, plus ipsilateral hemiparesis. This is due to compression of the contralateral cerebral peduncle against the tentorium and compression of the contralateral cranial nerve III.
Duret hemorrhagesLinear, flame-shaped hemorrhages due to stretching of the median and paramedian pontine arteries — branches of the basilar artery running on the brainstem.
Exam Lock
Why Kernohan's notch is called a false localising sign
  • In ordinary uncal herniation the signs are ipsilateral pupil, contralateral hemiparesis. When the brainstem is pushed far enough across, the opposite cerebral peduncle is crushed against the tentorium, so the hemiparesis becomes ipsilateral to the mass and the pupil contralateral — pointing the examiner to the wrong side. Recognising it is the point of the slide.
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus695

CNS trauma — the three categories

PATH.7026src p.2256–2260
Skull bone fractures
  • Sharp vs blunt force
  • Linear vs depressed vs basilar types of fractures
Brain parenchymal injuries
  • Concussion — clinical syndrome secondary to brain injury
  • Contusions and lacerations
  • Diffuse axonal injuries
  • Coup vs contrecoup injury
Vascular injuries — disruption of vessel walls
  • Epidural
  • Subdural
  • Subarachnoid
  • Intraparenchymal

Skull bone fractures

  • Force can be sharp or blunt. Injury is more likely if the head is stationary. The skull acts as a shock absorber.
  • Linear fracture — straight and sharply defined (> 80% of all fractures). Depressed fracture — fractured edges overlap. Basilar fracture — fractures in the base of the skull.

Concussion

  • Definition: clinical syndrome of reversible altered consciousness following head injury. Etiology: head trauma, like after impact with a rigid object.
  • Pathogenesis: possibly due to dysregulation of the reticular activating system in the brainstem; no permanent brain injury; no obvious findings on neuroimaging.
  • Clinical features: sudden onset of transient neurologic dysfunction — transient loss of consciousness · headache · amnesia for the event · inability to focus or concentrate.
  • Complication: chronic traumatic encephalopathy (persistent and profound neurologic deficit), typically associated with repetitive injuries (boxing, American football, ice hockey); neurodegenerative processes may occur later, associated with accumulation of protein.
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus696

CNS trauma — the three categories (cont.)

PATH.7026src p.2256–2260

Contusion and diffuse axonal injury

Detail (verbatim)
ContusionBruises to the brain surface from contact with the skull. More serious than a concussion. Pathological findings: edema, depressions and hemorrhaging. Pathogenesis — coup vs contrecoup: coup is the site of impact; contrecoup is the opposite site of impact, as a result of the brain hitting the other side of the skull. Old contusions are seen on the inferior frontal surface with a depressed yellow-brown appearance.
Diffuse axonal injuryDamage to the deep white matter regions. Etiopathogenesis: with trauma, the denser gray matter doesn't accelerate/move as fast as white matter → shearing of axons away from the cell body as they are stretched beyond the elastic point → alterations in axoplasmic flow. Pathological findings: axonal swelling and focal hemorrhagic lesions. Seen in around 50% of patients in coma after trauma, even without contusions. No lucid interval seen.
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus697

Epidural vs subdural haemorrhage — the lecture's comparison table

PATH.7026 · PATH.7041src p.2261–2265
Epidural hemorrhageSubdural hemorrhage
TraumaTrauma
Bleeding between dura mater and inner table of skullBleeding between dura mater and arachnoid mater
Associated with skull fracture (involving the pterion)Brain atrophy and mild trauma
Arterial bleed — middle meningeal arteryVenous bleed — bridging veins
Clinical: acute presentation with lucid intervalClinical: acute or delayed with slowly evolving symptoms
Imaging: lens-shaped, as it does not cross suture linesImaging: crescent-shaped, as it can cross suture lines
  • Epidural pathogenesis: laceration of the middle meningeal artery → acute arterial blood accumulation in the potential space between dura and skull (hence the name). Clinical course: initial loss of consciousness followed by a so-called "lucid interval" with recovery of consciousness → continued bleeding and expansion of hematoma → deterioration over a period of hours.
  • Subdural risk factors: in the elderly due to brain atrophy — bridging veins get stretched out and the brain has additional space to move; in infants bridging veins are thin-walled and easily ruptured. Clinical: acutely (within hours of trauma) or delayed (days to weeks), especially in the elderly after trivial head injury.

CT descriptions from the lecture: the large right epidural hematoma with a lens-shaped outline, as the smooth dura becomes indented against the underlying cortex; a large left subdural hematoma with left-to-right shift and ventricular narrowing, interdigitating with the adjacent gyri and sulci but compressing the brain.

Exam Lock
Artery, fracture, lucid interval, lens — or vein, atrophy, slow, crescent
  • The two haemorrhages differ on every line, and each line predicts the next. Arterial pressure explains the hours-long deterioration after a lucid interval; tight dural attachment at the sutures explains the lens shape. Venous, low-pressure bleeding in an atrophic brain explains days-to-weeks and the crescent that crosses sutures.
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus698
