NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus700

Block exam — trauma and hydrocephalus

PATH.7026

A 19-year-old is struck on the side of the head, briefly loses consciousness, wakes and talks normally, then deteriorates over three hours. CT shows a lens-shaped hyperdensity that does not cross the suture. Which vessel and which fracture?

  1. ABridging veins; no fracture
  2. BMiddle meningeal artery; fracture involving the pterion
  3. CAnterior cerebral artery; subfalcine herniation
  4. DPontine perforators; Duret haemorrhage
  5. EArachnoid villi; communicating hydrocephalus
Answer
B. Epidural haemorrhage. Etiology: skull fracture involving the pterion. Pathogenesis: laceration of the middle meningeal artery → acute arterial blood accumulation in the potential space between dura and skull. Does not cross the sutural margin → lens-shaped appearance on imaging. Clinical: initial loss of consciousness followed by a so-called "lucid interval" with recovery of consciousness → continued bleeding and expansion of hematoma → deterioration over a period of hours.
PATH.7026

An 84-year-old on no anticoagulant becomes progressively confused over three weeks after a minor fall. CT shows a crescentic collection crossing the coronal suture. What is the mechanism and the risk factor?

  1. AMiddle meningeal artery laceration; skull fracture
  2. BRupture of bridging veins between arachnoid and dura; brain atrophy stretching the veins and allowing extra movement
  3. CCharcot-Bouchard aneurysm rupture; hypertension
  4. DBerry aneurysm rupture; ADPKD
  5. EDiffuse axonal injury; rotational acceleration
Answer
B. Subdural haemorrhage — due to rupture of veins bridging arachnoid and dura → slower (venous) blood accumulation between dura and arachnoid membranes. Risk factor: in the elderly due to brain atrophy — bridging veins get stretched out and the brain has additional space to move; in infants bridging veins are thin-walled and easily ruptured. Can cross sutural margins and has a crescent-shaped lesion on brain imaging. Presentation may be acute (within hours) or delayed (days to weeks), especially in the elderly after trivial head injury.
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus701

Block exam — trauma and hydrocephalus (cont.)

PATH.7026

A patient with a large right temporal mass has a dilated right pupil and left hemiparesis, then over the next hour develops a dilated LEFT pupil and RIGHT hemiparesis. What has happened?

  1. ATonsillar herniation
  2. BSubfalcine herniation with ACA compression
  3. CKernohan phenomenon — the contralateral cerebral peduncle and CN III are compressed against the tentorium
  4. DDuret haemorrhage in the pons
  5. ENormal pressure hydrocephalus
Answer
C. Kernohan phenomenon: further displacement of the uncus → contralateral blown pupil, contralateral impaired extraocular movements and ipsilateral hemiparesis. This is due to compression of the contralateral cerebral peduncle against the tentorium and compression of the contralateral cranial nerve III. The initial picture — ipsilateral blown pupil and contralateral hemiparesis — is ordinary uncal herniation. Duret haemorrhages are linear flame-shaped haemorrhages from stretching of the median and paramedian pontine arteries.
PATH.7025

A 74-year-old has a magnetic gait, cognitive decline and urinary incontinence. Ventricles are enlarged and the LP opening pressure is normal. Which type of hydrocephalus is this?

  1. ANon-communicating, from aqueductal stenosis
  2. BEx vacuo, from neurodegeneration
  3. CNormal pressure hydrocephalus — a type of communicating hydrocephalus
  4. DChoroid plexus papilloma with overproduction
  5. EPseudotumor cerebri
Answer
C. Normal pressure: normal opening pressure on lumbar puncture. Hydrocephalus: pathologically enlarged ventricular size. Idiopathic; type of communicating hydrocephalus. Theory: transient high CSF pressure leading to ventricular enlargement → distorts fibers of corona radiata; ventricular enlargement normalizes pressure. Clinical features: 1. gait disturbances, 2. dementia, 3. urinary incontinence. Ex vacuo would be loss of brain volume with a secondary increase in CSF volume, not a treatable triad.
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus702

Block exam — trauma and hydrocephalus (cont.)

PATH.7025

Which mechanism produces cytotoxic rather than vasogenic cerebral oedema?

  1. ADisruption of the blood-brain barrier by a metastasis
  2. BNeuronal, glial or endothelial cell membrane injury from generalised hypoxia or ischaemia
  3. CMeningitis increasing capillary permeability
  4. DObstruction of the aqueduct of Sylvius
  5. EPoor CSF absorption by arachnoid villi
Answer
B. Vasogenic edema: disruption of the blood-brain barrier; fluid from the vascular component into the extracellular space — meningitis, encephalitis, trauma and metastasis. Cytotoxic edema: neuronal, glial or endothelial cell membrane injury; increase in intracellular fluid — in generalized hypoxia/ischemia insult, metabolic damage, anything that injures the cells. The paucity of lymphatics greatly impairs the resorption of excess extracellular fluid, which is why the brain tolerates oedema poorly.
PATH.7026 · PATH.7040

A 28-year-old woman with obesity has months of positional headache, transient visual obscurations, horizontal diplopia and papilloedema. MRI is normal. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

  1. ACommunicating hydrocephalus; ventriculoperitoneal shunt only
  2. BPseudotumor cerebri (idiopathic intracranial hypertension); lumbar punctures, acetazolamide, shunt
  3. CNormal pressure hydrocephalus; shunt
  4. DSubdural haematoma; evacuation
  5. ECerebral venous sinus thrombosis; anticoagulation
Answer
B. Pseudotumor cerebri: pseudo- false, tumor- mass, cerebri- brain → not due to a tumor. Epidemiology: overweight women of childbearing age. No obvious cause on neuroimaging: no masses, no bleeding, no hydrocephalus/increased ventricular size, no vasogenic or cytotoxic edema. Clinical features: increased intracranial pressure characterised by headache (positional), diplopia (CN-6 palsy), vomiting, and papilledema potentially leading to vision loss. Treatment: lumbar punctures, acetazolamide, shunt.
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus703

Block exam — trauma and hydrocephalus (cont.)

PATH.7026

Which injury is seen in about half of patients comatose after trauma, has NO lucid interval, and arises from differential acceleration of grey and white matter?

  1. ACerebral concussion
  2. BCerebral contusion
  3. CDiffuse axonal injury
  4. DEpidural haematoma
  5. ESubfalcine herniation
Answer
C. Diffuse axonal injuries: damage to the deep white matter regions. With trauma, denser gray matter doesn't accelerate/move as fast as white matter → shearing of axons away from the cell body as they are stretched beyond the elastic point → alterations in axoplasmic flow. Pathological findings: axonal swelling and focal hemorrhagic lesions. Seen in around 50% of patients in coma after trauma, even without contusions. No lucid interval seen. The lucid interval belongs to the epidural haematoma.
PATH.7026

Which herniation compresses the anterior cerebral artery, and what deficit follows?

  1. ATonsillar; respiratory arrest
  2. BTranstentorial; CN III palsy
  3. CSubfalcine; motor and sensory deficits in the lower extremity and lower trunk
  4. DTranscalvarial; scalp swelling
  5. ECentral; bilateral pinpoint pupils
Answer
C. Subfalcine herniation: unilateral or asymmetrical expansion of a cerebral hemisphere displaces the cingulate gyrus under the falx cerebri → compresses the anterior cerebral artery → infarcts in the area supplied by the artery → motor and sensory deficits in the lower extremity and lower trunk. The ACA supplies the medial motor and sensory cortex — the leg area of the homunculus, which is why the deficit is in the lower limb.
NCRS 36 · Neuropathology — Trauma and Hydrocephalus704
PHAR

Treatment of Parkinson Disease

Dr Malcolm Antoine Jr · PCM500 Pharmacology. Restore dopamine, or oppose acetylcholine — every drug in the lecture does one of those two things.

Dr Malcolm Antoine Jr · PCM500 Pharmacology  ·  source pp. 2268–2361
Clinically, Parkinson disease is characterized by resting tremor, muscular rigidity, bradykinesia, and gait impairment, known as the "cardinal features" of the disease. Additional features can include freezing of gait, postural instability, speech difficulty, autonomic disturbances, sensory alterations, mood disorders, sleep dysfunction, cognitive impairment, and dementia.Reading notes
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease705

Lecture objectives — verbatim

src p.objectives file
  • PHAR.00052 List the cardinal features of Parkinson's disease.
  • PHAR.00053 Discuss current hypotheses about the etiology and pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease.
  • PHAR.00054 Outline the strategy for treatment of Parkinson's disease.
  • PHAR.00055 Describe the rationale for the use of levodopa in Parkinson's disease and the rationale for its use in combination with carbidopa. Discuss how the drug combination alters levodopa's therapeutic and adverse effect profiles. Discuss the changes in control of symptoms by levodopa as the disease progresses.
  • PHAR.00056 Explain why dopamine is not used to treat Parkinson's disease.
  • PHAR.00057 Describe the rationale for the use of the different classes of drugs used in the management of Parkinson disease (dopamine receptor agonists, MAO inhibitors, COMT inhibitors, amantadine, antimuscarinics). Describe the molecular mechanism of action, adverse effects, drug interactions and contraindications of the drugs used in Parkinson's disease.
  • PHAR.00058 Discuss the choice of treatment for Parkinson's disease.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease706

Etiology and pathophysiology

PHAR.00052 · PHAR.00053 · PHAR.00054src p.2268 · 2270 · 2282–2298
  • The cause is unknown for most patients. The primary deficit is a loss of the neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta which provide dopaminergic innervation to the striatum.
  • Parkinson's disease is generally progressive, leading to increasing disability unless effective treatment is provided.
  • At least 70% of the neurons are destroyed at the time symptoms first appear. Often, 95% of the neurons are missing at autopsy.
  • The destruction of these neurons results in the core features of the disease: bradykinesia, rigidity, impaired postural balance and tremor.

The circuit

Dopaminergic neurons from the substantia nigra normally INHIBIT the GABAergic output from the striatum, whereas cholinergic neurons STIMULATE it→In PD there is destruction of the nigrostriatal neurons responsible for secreting dopamine in the striatum→Loss of the control of muscle movement

Many of the symptoms of parkinsonism reflect an imbalance between the excitatory cholinergic neurons and the diminished number of inhibitory dopaminergic neurons.

Secondary parkinsonism

  • Parkinsonian symptoms infrequently follow viral encephalitis or multiple small vascular lesions.
  • Classical antipsychotic drugs, whose major pharmacologic action is blockade of dopamine receptors in the brain, may also produce parkinsonian symptoms. These drugs should not be used in parkinsonian patients.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease707

Etiology and pathophysiology (cont.)

PHAR.00052 · PHAR.00053 · PHAR.00054src p.2268 · 2270 · 2282–2298

Strategy of treatment (PHAR.00054)

Therapy is aimed at restoring dopaminergic input in the basal ganglia and/or antagonizing the excitatory effect of cholinergic neurons, thus reestablishing the correct dopamine/ACh balance.Strategy
Exam Lock
The same nigrostriatal circuit, read in two directions
  • In the antipsychotics lecture, D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway caused drug-induced parkinsonism treated with antimuscarinics. Here the same circuit fails from the other end — loss of dopaminergic neurons — and the treatment is the same two options: give dopamine back or block the acetylcholine.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease708

Dopamine synthesis, receptors, and why dopamine itself is useless

PHAR.00053 · PHAR.00056src p.2268–2269 · 2284–2291
  • Dopamine synthesis, like that of all catecholamines in the nervous system, originates from the amino acid precursor tyrosine, which must be transported across the blood-brain barrier into the dopamine neuron. Tyrosine, like other neutral amino acids such as phenylalanine and leucine, is transported by system L across the blood-brain barrier in a Na⁺-independent manner.
  • Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting step. DOPA is converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase.
  • DOPA decarboxylase turns over so rapidly that DOPA levels in the brain are negligible under normal conditions — it is therefore possible to enhance dramatically the formation of dopamine by providing this enzyme with increased amounts of substrate. *(This one sentence is the entire rationale for levodopa.)*
  • Once synthesized, dopamine is sequestered in storage vesicles by VMAT2, an antiporter of protons and monoamines. Release occurs through exocytosis triggered by depolarization and Ca²⁺ entry.
  • Actions are terminated by reuptake into the nerve terminal or uptake into the postsynaptic cell. Metabolism occurs by the sequential actions of COMT, MAO and aldehyde dehydrogenase; in humans HVA (homovanillate) is the principal metabolite of dopamine.

Dopamine receptors

D1 receptors
↑ adenylyl cyclase
D2 receptors
↑ adenylyl cyclase · ↑ K⁺ conductance · ↑ Ca²⁺ conductance
Which matters
The benefits of dopaminergic antiparkinsonism drugs appear to depend mostly on stimulation of the D2 receptors, but D1 stimulation may also be required for maximal benefit.
Trap
PHAR.00056 in one line
  • Dopamine does not cross the blood-brain barrier — that is the whole answer to "why not just give dopamine?" Its immediate precursor levodopa does cross, using the facilitative L-transport system for neutral amino acids, and is then converted to dopamine in the brain.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease709

The drug classes

PHAR.00057src p.2271 · 2299–2308
Drugs that restore dopamine actions
  • Dopamine precursors — levodopa
  • Dopamine receptor agonists — ergot: bromocriptine; non-ergot: pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine, apomorphine
  • Inhibitors of dopamine metabolism — MAO inhibitors: selegiline, rasagiline; COMT inhibitors: tolcapone, entacapone
  • Amantadine
Antagonists of acetylcholine
  • Antimuscarinics — benztropine, trihexyphenidyl
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease710

Levodopa's journey — and the four places drugs intervene

PHAR.00055 · PHAR.00057src p.2313–2359
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease711

Levodopa and carbidopa

PHAR.00055src p.2272–2273 · 2310–2319
  • Levodopa is the levorotatory stereoisomer of dopa and the metabolic precursor of dopamine (and norepinephrine); it restores dopamine levels in the extrapyramidal centers.
  • In patients with early disease, the number of residual dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra is enough for conversion of levodopa to dopamine. With time, the number of neurons falls and there are fewer cells capable of taking up levodopa and converting it — consequently motor control fluctuation develops.
  • Relief provided by levodopa is only symptomatic and lasts only while the drug is present in the body.
  • Much of the drug is decarboxylated to dopamine in the periphery, which results in peripheral side effects: nausea, vomiting, cardiac arrhythmias, hypotension.

Carbidopa — and the numbers that justify it

  • Carbidopa is a dopa decarboxylase inhibitor that does NOT cross the blood-brain barrier. Levodopa is always given in combination with carbidopa. It decreases the metabolism of levodopa in the GI tract and peripheral tissues, thus increasing the availability of levodopa to the CNS.
  • Concomitant administration of carbidopa may reduce the daily requirements of levodopa by 75%.
Fate of the doseLevodopa aloneLevodopa + carbidopa
Reaches the brain1–3%10%
Peripheral tissues27–29%40%
Metabolized in the GI tract70%50%

Pharmacokinetics

  • Absorbed rapidly from the small intestine. Food delays the appearance of levodopa in the plasma. Certain amino acids can compete with the drug for absorption from the gut and for transport from the blood to the brain.
  • Metabolism: levodopa → 3-O-methyldopa (COMT); levodopa → dopamine (DOPA decarboxylase); dopamine → 3-methoxytyramine (COMT) or DOPAC (MAO, aldehyde dehydrogenase) → homovanillate (HVA).
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease712

Levodopa — clinical course, adverse effects, and contraindications

PHAR.00055src p.2273–2274 · 2320–2324

Clinical uses and the decline in response

  • Levodopa in combination with carbidopa is an efficacious drug regimen. In approximately 2/3 of patients this treatment substantially reduces the severity of symptoms in the first few years.
  • There is a decline in response during the 3rd to 5th year of therapy. Responsiveness may ultimately be lost completely, because of the disappearance of dopaminergic nigrostriatal neurons.
  • Levodopa does not stop progression of PD.
GI effects
  • Anorexia, nausea and vomiting
Cardiovascular effects
  • Tachycardia and ventricular extrasystoles
  • Hypotension
CNS effects
  • Visual and auditory hallucinations
  • Dyskinesias
  • Mood changes, depression, anxiety, agitation, insomnia

Fluctuations in response

Wearing-off reactions
Fluctuations RELATED to the timing of levodopa intake.
The on-off phenomenon
Fluctuations in response UNRELATED to the timing of doses. The exact mechanism is unknown. For patients with severe off-periods who are unresponsive to other measures, apomorphine may provide benefit.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease713

Levodopa — clinical course, adverse effects, and contraindications (cont.)

PHAR.00055src p.2273–2274 · 2320–2324

Interactions and contraindications

  • Vitamin B6 is a cofactor for dopa decarboxylase: it increases peripheral metabolism of levodopa and decreases its effectiveness.
  • Concomitant administration of levodopa and nonspecific MAO inhibitors, such as phenelzine or tranylcypromine, may precipitate hypertensive crisis.
  • Levodopa should not be given to psychotic patients, as it may exacerbate the mental disturbance. Coadministration of antipsychotic drugs should be avoided.
  • Contraindicated in angle-closure glaucoma.
  • Cardiac patients should be monitored because of possible arrhythmias.
  • Coadministration of an antihypertensive could increase the risk of orthostatic hypotension.
  • Patients with active peptic ulcer must be managed carefully: GI bleeding can occur with levodopa.
Trap
Levodopa and antipsychotics cancel each other in both directions
  • Antipsychotics block D2 and cause parkinsonism — so they should not be used in parkinsonian patients. Levodopa raises dopamine and can precipitate psychosis — so it should not be given to psychotic patients. That is why the antipsychotics lecture insists levodopa should never be used for drug-induced parkinsonism, and why pimavanserin (no dopamine affinity) exists for Parkinson's disease psychosis.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease714

Dopamine receptor agonists

PHAR.00057src p.2275–2277 · 2326–2336

Dopamine agonists do not require enzymatic conversion for activity; therefore they do not depend on the functional capacities of the nigrostriatal neurons. That is the entire rationale for the class.

AgentDetail (verbatim)
Bromocriptine (ergot)D2 agonist. Widely used to treat Parkinson's disease in the past; now rarely used for this purpose — superseded by newer dopamine agonists.
Pramipexole & ropinirole (non-ergot)Well tolerated; used increasingly as initial treatment for PD, particularly for younger patients. Many experts favor dopamine agonists as initial therapy in younger patients and levodopa as initial therapy in older patients, who may be more vulnerable to the adverse cognitive effects of the dopamine agonists. Dopamine agonists are less effective than levodopa in treating the motor symptoms of PD, but are less likely to cause motor fluctuations or dyskinesia.
Rotigotine (non-ergot)Available in a transdermal formulation; once-daily use.
Apomorphine (non-ergot)Rescue therapy for the acute treatment of "off" episodes in patients with a fluctuating response to dopaminergic therapy. Given subcutaneously or sublingually. Highly emetogenic: pretreatment with the antiemetic trimethobenzamide is recommended; 5-HT3 receptor antagonists are contraindicated because of the combination. Other adverse effects: QT prolongation, dyskinesias, drowsiness, sweating, hypotension. Indicated only when other measures have failed.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease715

Dopamine receptor agonists (cont.)

PHAR.00057src p.2275–2277 · 2326–2336

Adverse effects of the class

GI and cardiovascular
  • Anorexia, nausea and vomiting, constipation, dyspepsia
  • Bleeding from peptic ulceration
  • Postural hypotension
  • Cardiac arrhythmias
  • Peripheral edema
  • Ergot derivatives: painless digital vasospasm (a complication of long-term treatment)
Neuropsychiatric
  • Dyskinesias — abnormal movements similar to those produced by levodopa; treatment is reducing the total dose of dopaminergic drugs
  • Confusion, hallucinations, delusions — more common and severe than with levodopa
  • Compulsive behaviors, defined as impulse control disorders (ICDs)
Class-specific
  • Ergot agonists: headache, nasal congestion, increased arousal, pulmonary infiltrates, pleural and retroperitoneal fibrosis, erythromelalgia
  • Pramipexole, ropinirole and rotigotine: uncontrollable somnolence — this requires discontinuation of the medication
  • Drug interactions: antipsychotic drugs antagonize dopamine and may reduce the efficacy of dopamine agonists; concomitant CNS depressants could increase the risk of somnolence and confusion.
  • Contraindications: a history of psychotic illness, recent myocardial infarction, or active peptic ulceration.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease716

Inhibitors of dopamine metabolism, amantadine and antimuscarinics

PHAR.00057src p.2278–2279 · 2339–2354
Class / drugMechanismKey points
MAO-B inhibitors — selegiline, rasagilineSelegiline selectively and irreversibly inhibits MAO-B (which selectively metabolizes dopamine), retarding the breakdown of dopamine in the brain. Rasagiline is a second irreversible MAO-B inhibitor approved for PD.Enhances the effect of levodopa and allows the levodopa dose to be reduced; mainly used as an adjunct to levodopa. Selegiline is metabolized to methamphetamine and amphetamine — may cause insomnia if taken late in the day. Interactions: use of other MAO inhibitors, SNRIs, SSRIs, TCAs, St John's wort, methadone, tramadol or meperidine within 14 days could result in hypertensive crisis and/or serotonin syndrome and is contraindicated; methylphenidate, amphetamines or sympathomimetic amines can cause severe hypertension.
COMT inhibitors — tolcapone, entacaponeInhibition of dopa decarboxylase (by carbidopa) causes compensatory activation of the COMT pathway → increased plasma 3-O-methyldopa, which competes with levodopa for the active carrier that transports levodopa across the intestinal mucosa and the blood-brain barrier. Inhibiting COMT reverses this.Effects: decreased metabolism of levodopa · decreased plasma levels of 3-O-methyldopa · increased uptake of levodopa · higher dopamine levels in the brain. Fulminating hepatic necrosis is associated with tolcapone: its use in the US requires signed patient consent plus monitoring of liver function tests every 2 weeks. No such toxicity has been reported for entacapone, which is therefore preferred and is available in fixed-dose combinations with levodopa/carbidopa.
AmantadineAntiviral drug with antiparkinsonian actions. Its mode of action in PD is unclear; it may increase dopamine release and inhibit dopamine reuptake, and it is an antagonist of the NMDA receptor — suggesting an antidyskinetic effect.The effects of amantadine in PD are modest. Adverse effects: restlessness, agitation, confusion, hallucinations; at high doses acute toxic psychosis; peripheral edema (responds to diuretics); headache, heart failure, orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, urinary retention, GI disturbances. Livedo reticularis sometimes occurs and usually clears within a month of withdrawing the drug. Caution with a history of seizures or heart failure.
Antimuscarinics — benztropine, trihexyphenidylAntagonists of acetylcholine — the other half of the treatment strategy.Adjuvant therapy. May improve tremor and rigidity; little effect on bradykinesia. Can produce mood changes, xerostomia, pupillary dilation, confusion, hallucinations and urinary retention. Cannot be used in patients with glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy or pyloric stenosis.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease717

Inhibitors of dopamine metabolism, amantadine and antimuscarinics (cont.)

PHAR.00057src p.2278–2279 · 2339–2354
Bottom Line
Why a COMT inhibitor only makes sense alongside carbidopa
  • Blocking dopa decarboxylase peripherally shunts levodopa down the COMT pathway, raising 3-O-methyldopa, which then competes with levodopa for the same L-system carrier at the gut and the blood-brain barrier. The COMT inhibitor closes that escape route. Two enzymes, one substrate, and the second block is needed because of the first.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease718

Summary — choice of treatment and the whole drug list

src p.2268–2360

Choice of treatment (PHAR.00058) — verbatim

  1. Levodopa/carbidopa is the most effective treatment for PD.
  2. Dopamine agonists are less effective than levodopa; they can be used as monotherapy before introduction of levodopa or as adjuncts to levodopa in patients with motor fluctuations.
  3. Addition of a COMT or MAO-B inhibitor to levodopa can reduce motor fluctuations.
  4. Amantadine can be used as monotherapy in early PD and as an adjunct in later stages; it may modestly improve PD symptoms and can decrease levodopa-induced dyskinesia.
  5. Anticholinergics can help control tremor and drooling, but are rarely used because of adverse effects.
  6. Apomorphine can be used for rescue treatment of "off" episodes.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease719

Block exam — Parkinson disease pharmacology

PHAR.00055 · PHAR.00056

Why is levodopa given rather than dopamine, and what does adding carbidopa achieve numerically?

  1. ADopamine is destroyed in the stomach; carbidopa protects it
  2. BDopamine does not cross the blood-brain barrier while levodopa is carried across on the L-system; carbidopa raises brain delivery from 1–3% to about 10% and cuts the daily levodopa requirement by 75%
  3. CDopamine is a prodrug; carbidopa activates it
  4. DLevodopa is more potent at D2 receptors; carbidopa is a D1 agonist
  5. ECarbidopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and converts levodopa centrally
Answer
B. Dopamine does not cross the blood-brain barrier, but its immediate precursor levodopa is transported into the CNS and is converted to dopamine in the brain... Levodopa is transported into the brain by the facilitative L-transport system for neutral amino acids. Carbidopa is a dopa decarboxylase inhibitor that does not cross the blood-brain barrier... Concomitant administration of carbidopa may reduce the daily requirements of levodopa by 75%. The lecture's figures: levodopa alone 1–3% to brain; with carbidopa 10%.
PHAR.00055

A patient on levodopa/carbidopa has good mornings but predictable loss of benefit before each next dose. What is this called, and how does it differ from the on-off phenomenon?

  1. AOn-off phenomenon; it is related to dose timing
  2. BWearing-off reaction — fluctuations RELATED to the timing of levodopa intake; the on-off phenomenon is UNRELATED to dose timing and its mechanism is unknown
  3. CDyskinesia; it occurs at peak dose
  4. DAkathisia; it is drug-induced
  5. EFreezing of gait; it is a cardinal feature
Answer
B. Wearing-off reactions: fluctuations related to the timing of levodopa intake. The on-off phenomenon: fluctuations in response unrelated to the timing of doses; the exact mechanism is unknown. For patients with severe off-periods who are unresponsive to other measures, apomorphine may provide benefit. The underlying reason both develop is that with time the number of neurons falls and there are fewer cells capable of taking up levodopa and converting it to dopamine.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease721

Block exam — Parkinson disease pharmacology (cont.)

PHAR.00057

Which COMT inhibitor requires signed patient consent and liver function tests every two weeks, and why?

  1. AEntacapone; peripheral neuropathy
  2. BTolcapone; fulminating hepatic necrosis
  3. CSelegiline; amphetamine metabolites
  4. DRasagiline; hypertensive crisis
  5. EAmantadine; livedo reticularis
Answer
B. Fulminating hepatic necrosis is associated with the use of tolcapone. Accordingly, its use in the US requires signed patient consent plus monitoring of liver function tests every 2 weeks. No such toxicity has been reported for entacapone, which is therefore preferred and is available as fixed-dose combinations with levodopa/carbidopa.
PHAR.00057

A patient on pramipexole develops new compulsive gambling and episodes of falling asleep at the wheel. Which two adverse effects are these, and what does the lecture say to do about the second?

  1. ADyskinesia and akathisia; reduce the dose
  2. BImpulse control disorders and uncontrollable somnolence; the somnolence requires discontinuation of the medication
  3. CPsychosis and orthostatic hypotension; add an antipsychotic
  4. DDigital vasospasm and fibrosis; switch to an ergot agonist
  5. ESerotonin syndrome and hypertensive crisis; give cyproheptadine
Answer
B. Confusion, hallucinations, delusions. Compulsive behaviors, defined as impulse control disorders (ICDs). And: Pramipexole, ropinirole and rotigotine: uncontrollable somnolence. This requires discontinuation of the medication. Note the class contrast — ergot agonists instead cause pulmonary infiltrates, pleural and retroperitoneal fibrosis, erythromelalgia and painless digital vasospasm.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease722

Block exam — Parkinson disease pharmacology (cont.)

PHAR.00057

Which statement about dopamine agonists versus levodopa matches the lecture?

  1. ADopamine agonists are more effective for motor symptoms but cause more dyskinesia
  2. BDopamine agonists are less effective than levodopa for motor symptoms but less likely to cause motor fluctuations or dyskinesia, and are favoured as initial therapy in younger patients
  3. CDopamine agonists require conversion by residual nigrostriatal neurons
  4. DLevodopa is preferred in younger patients because of cognitive effects
  5. EBoth are equally effective at all stages
Answer
B. Dopamine agonists are less effective than levodopa in treating the motor symptoms of PD. They are less likely to cause motor fluctuations or dyskinesia. Many experts favor dopamine agonists as initial therapy in younger patients with PD, and levodopa as initial therapy in older patients who may be more vulnerable to the adverse cognitive effects of the dopamine agonists. And crucially: dopamine agonists do not require enzymatic conversion for activity; therefore they do not depend on the functional capacities of the nigrostriatal neurons.
PHAR.00057

A patient with PD on selegiline is prescribed tramadol for back pain. What is the risk, and what interval does the lecture specify?

  1. ANo risk; MAO-B inhibitors are selective
  2. BHypertensive crisis and/or serotonin syndrome; use within 14 days of an MAO-B inhibitor is contraindicated
  3. CNeuroleptic malignant syndrome; 7 days
  4. DTyramine reaction; 24 hours
  5. EHepatic necrosis; 2 weeks of LFTs
Answer
B. Use of other MAO inhibitors, SNRIs, SSRIs, TCAs, St. John's wort, methadone, tramadol, or meperidine within 14 days of an MAO-B inhibitor could result in hypertensive crisis and/or serotonin syndrome and is contraindicated. Concomitant use of methylphenidate, amphetamines, or sympathomimetic amines such as pseudoephedrine with an MAO-B inhibitor can also result in severe hypertension. Selegiline's own metabolism to methamphetamine and amphetamine also explains insomnia if taken late in the day.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease723

Block exam — Parkinson disease pharmacology (cont.)

PHAR.00057 · PHAR.00058

Which drug is an antiviral with an NMDA-antagonist action, decreases levodopa-induced dyskinesia, and can cause a reversible mottled rash?

  1. AEntacapone
  2. BAmantadine
  3. CBenztropine
  4. DApomorphine
  5. ERasagiline
Answer
B. Amantadine — an antiviral drug with antiparkinsonian actions; its mode of action in PD is unclear; it may increase dopamine release and inhibit dopamine reuptake, and it is an antagonist of the NMDA receptor, suggesting an antidyskinetic effect. Livedo reticularis sometimes occurs in patients taking amantadine and usually clears within a month of withdrawing the drug. It can be used as monotherapy in early PD and as an adjunct in later stages, and can decrease levodopa-induced dyskinesia.
PHAR.00055

Which supplement reduces levodopa's effectiveness, and by what mechanism?

  1. AVitamin B12; impairs absorption
  2. BVitamin B6; it is a cofactor for dopa decarboxylase and increases peripheral metabolism of levodopa
  3. CVitamin K; competes for the L-system carrier
  4. DFolate; inhibits COMT
  5. EVitamin D; increases renal clearance
Answer
B. Vitamin B6 is a cofactor for L-Dopa decarboxylase. Vitamin B6 increases peripheral metabolism of levodopa and decreases its effectiveness. Note the related pharmacokinetic point: certain amino acids can compete with the drug for absorption from the gut and for transport from the blood to the brain, and food delays the appearance of levodopa in the plasma.
PHAR.00053

Approximately what proportion of substantia nigra neurons are lost by the time symptoms first appear, and how much at autopsy?

  1. A30% at onset; 60% at autopsy
  2. BAt least 70% at onset; often 95% at autopsy
  3. C50% at onset; 70% at autopsy
  4. D95% at onset; 99% at autopsy
  5. E10% at onset; 50% at autopsy
Answer
B. The extent of loss of dopaminergic neurons is profound. At least 70% of the neurons are destroyed at the time symptoms first appear. Often, 95% of the neurons are missing at autopsy. This is why treatment is symptomatic — relief provided by levodopa is only symptomatic and lasts only while the drug is present in the body, and levodopa does not stop progression of PD.
PHAR · Treatment of Parkinson Disease724

Block exam — Parkinson disease pharmacology (cont.)

PHAR.00057

Which antiparkinsonian drug improves tremor and rigidity but has little effect on bradykinesia, and in whom is it contraindicated?

  1. ALevodopa; psychotic patients
  2. BBenztropine; patients with glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy or pyloric stenosis
  3. CEntacapone; liver disease
  4. DPramipexole; recent myocardial infarction
  5. EAmantadine; heart failure
Answer
B. Benztropine and trihexyphenidyl are adjuvant therapy; they may improve tremor and rigidity with little effect on bradykinesia; can produce mood changes, xerostomia, pupillary dilation, confusion, hallucinations, and urinary retention; and cannot be used in patients with glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy or pyloric stenosis. They are the antagonists of acetylcholine arm of the treatment strategy — restoring the dopamine/ACh balance from the other side.

NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases726

Introduction — ischemic vs haemorrhagic stroke

PATH.7045src p.2367
Cerebro- brain; vascular- blood vessel → brain disorders caused by pathologic processes involving blood vessels which cause an interruption of blood flow in the vessel supplying blood to a region of the brain. "Stroke": clinical designation applied to all these conditions when symptoms last more than 24 hours.Definition

BEFAST — B: loss of balance and coordination · E: sudden visual loss · F: facial drooping · A: arm and leg weakness · S: speech difficulty · T: time to call the emergency team.

Ischemic strokeHemorrhagic stroke
CauseEmbolic >> thrombotic; global hypoxia/ischemia (rare)Vascular rupture — can be intraparenchymal or subarachnoid
ImagingDiffusion-weighted MRI shows the lesion within 30 minutes of onset; CT shows the lesion within 6 to 24 hours.Both CT and MRI can identify the lesion immediately after onset.
Exam Lock
The imaging line is the reason for the CT-first algorithm
  • A CT in the first hours is often normal in ischaemic stroke but shows haemorrhage immediately. That is precisely why the emergency CT is done — not to see the infarct, but to exclude the bleed before thrombolysis. It joins the 3–4.5-hour alteplase window from the coagulation lecture.
NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases727

Hypoxia and ischemia — global, focal, and the watershed

PATH.7027src p.2368–2369
Global cerebral ischemia / hypoxiaFocal cerebral ischemia
SettingSevere systemic hypotension — myocardial infarction, shock — or decreased O₂ capacity of the blood (CO poisoning)Embolization from a distant source, or in situ thrombosis
What decides outcome(a) severity and (b) duration of insult; and the type of cell involved — neurons >> glial cells, especially pyramidal cells of the hippocampus and cerebellar Purkinje cellsCollateral blood flow plays a crucial role in limiting the damage; the major source is the circle of Willis.
SeverityMore severe neurological impairment than focal cerebral ischemiaNot as severe as global ischemia, however the effect can still be very detrimental

Watershed (border zone) infarcts

  • Occur in the regions of the brain or spinal cord that lie at the most distal reaches of the arterial blood supply — the border zones between arterial territories.
  • Greatest risk: the border zone between the anterior and the middle cerebral artery distributions.
  • Usually seen after hypotensive episodes; most commonly seen in patients resuscitated after cardiac arrest.
  • The lecture names three: cortical border zone between ACA and MCA · internal border zone between superficial and deep vessels of the MCA · cortical border zone between MCA and PCA.
Bottom Line
Selective vulnerability explains the clinical picture after cardiac arrest
  • Neurons die before glia, and among neurons the hippocampal pyramidal cells and cerebellar Purkinje cells go first — which is why survivors of arrest show memory impairment and ataxia. Add the ACA–MCA watershed and you also get the classic "man-in-a-barrel" proximal arm weakness.
NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases728

Types of ischemic stroke — four mechanisms

PATH.7027src p.2370
MechanismDetail (verbatim)
Embolic infarctionsMore common than thrombotic. Source of emboli: cardiac mural thrombus or carotid atheromatous plaque. Predisposing factors: atherosclerotic plaque, atrial fibrillation, myocardial dysfunction.
Thrombotic occlusionUsually a thrombus superimposed on atherosclerotic plaques. Can have anterograde extension. Can fragment and embolize.
Paradoxical emboliWhen a venous embolus crosses over to the arterial side due to the presence of a right-to-left shunt (patent foramen ovale, atrial or ventricular septal defect) and can lead to ischemia on the systemic side, including stroke.
Lacunar infarctsOcclusion of penetrating arteries (commonly lenticulostriate), mostly due to hypertension causing lipohyalinosis of these arteries. Lipohyalinosis can obstruct the vessel lumen → lacunar infarct, or weaken the vessel wall → Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm.
Exam Lock
Lipohyalinosis has two endings, and the lecture tests both
  • The same hypertensive small-vessel change either blocks the lumen → lacunar infarct or weakens the wall → Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm → hypertensive haemorrhage. Both happen in the lenticulostriate arteries, which is why the basal ganglia are the commonest site for each.
NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases729

Morphology of the cerebral infarct, in time

PATH.7027src p.2371–2373

Gross: swollen brain with wide gyri and narrowed sulci; eventually tissue liquefies leaving a fluid-filled cavity. Descriptions from the lecture's images: a large, discolored, focally hemorrhagic infarct in the distribution of the left middle cerebral artery; an infarct with punctate hemorrhages, consistent with ischemia-reperfusion injury; an old cystic infarct showing destruction of cortex and surrounding gliosis; and infiltration by neutrophils beginning at the edges of the lesion where the vascular supply is intact.

NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases730

Intracranial haemorrhage — the classification

PATH.7028 · PATH.7029src p.2375–2377
Intraparenchymal haemorrhageSubarachnoid haemorrhage
Hypertensive: primary intraparenchymal hemorrhage · rupture of Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm · slit hemorrhageThe most important cause is non-traumatic rupture of a berry aneurysm.
Non-hypertensive: cerebral amyloid angiopathy · vascular malformation · coagulopathy · tumor hemorrhage · hemorrhagic conversion of ischemic stroke—

Hypertensive haemorrhage

  • Due to rupture of small intraparenchymal vessels which branch off major cerebral vessels. Like Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms and lacunar infarcts, they commonly involve the lenticulostriate arteries.
  • Clinical features depend on location and size of the bleed: if very small, silent; if large or if it extends into the ventricular system, it can be fatal.
  • Typical locations: basal ganglia (most common), thalamus, pons and cerebellum.
Lipohyalinosis
In the CNS it is seen in deep penetrating arteries and arterioles that supply the basal ganglia, brainstem and hemispheric white matter. Affected vessel walls (mostly lenticulostriate arteries) are weakened, forming small microaneurysms (Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm) that are vulnerable to rupture. Histology: foamy macrophages and hyalinosis.
NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases731

Non-hypertensive intraparenchymal haemorrhage

PATH.7028 · PATH.7030src p.2378–2379
  1. Amyloid angiopathy — the hemorrhage affects larger non-penetrating vessels supplying the cortex and is therefore typically superficial / lobar in location, unlike the small penetrating vessels affected by hypertension, which are typically subcortical / deep. Amyloid deposits inside the vessel wall (subintimal and medial deposition), which weakens the vessel and increases the risk of rupture and hemorrhage.
  2. Vascular malformations — most commonly arteriovenous malformations, where there is a tangled network of arteries and veins with no interposing capillaries.
  3. Coagulopathy — antiplatelet medications, thrombocytopenia, vitamin K deficiency, anticoagulants and hemophilia increase the risk of intracranial hemorrhage by affecting factors involved in hemostasis.
  4. Tumor hemorrhage — tumor growth has a high demand on blood supply, which causes new blood vessels to form.

Arteriovenous malformations (PATH.7030)

Epidemiology
  • Most common vascular malformation
  • Affects males twice more than females (2:1 M:F)
  • Age: 10 to 30 years
Clinical features and complications
  • Manifest with seizure, intracerebral hemorrhage or even a subarachnoid hemorrhage
  • In newborns: high-output congestive heart failure because of blood shunting from arteries to veins
Trap
Lobar vs deep is the single most useful location rule
  • Hypertensive bleeds are DEEP — basal ganglia (commonest), thalamus, pons, cerebellum, from small penetrating vessels. Amyloid angiopathy bleeds are LOBAR/superficial — from larger non-penetrating cortical vessels. An elderly normotensive patient with a recurrent lobar haemorrhage is amyloid angiopathy until proven otherwise.
NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases732

Subarachnoid haemorrhage and berry aneurysms

PATH.7026 · PATH.7029src p.2381–2385
  • The most frequent cause of clinically significant non-traumatic haemorrhage is rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm.
  • 90% are in the anterior circulation, at branch points of the circle of Willis.
  • Saccular aneurysms are associated with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and other congenital diseases which can affect the connective tissue of blood vessels — these occur at a younger age.
  • They are also associated with acquired risk factors which cause degenerative changes of blood vessels, e.g. hypertension, smoking and advanced age.

Morphology

  • Saccular (sac-like) aneurysm: a thin-walled outpouching of the artery.
  • Beyond the neck, the muscular wall and internal elastic lamina are absent. The sac is lined only by thickened hyalinized intima and a covering of adventitia (seen more in acquired degeneration of the wall than in congenital causes such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome).
  • The extravasated blood enters the subarachnoid space.

Clinical features, investigations and complications

  • The risk of rupture increases with the size of the aneurysm. Arterial blood is forced into the subarachnoid space with intense pressure.
  • The patient develops an excruciating headache known as a "thunderclap headache" or "worst headache of my life" and they rapidly lose consciousness.
  • Meningismus: neck stiffness, photophobia — because blood in the subarachnoid space irritates the arachnoid meninges.
  • Investigations: CT scan showing blood in the basal cisterns, ventricles or Sylvian fissure. Lumbar puncture shows a high number of RBCs or xanthochromia — yellowish CSF due to release of bilirubin after RBC lysis.
NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases733

Subarachnoid haemorrhage and berry aneurysms (cont.)

PATH.7026 · PATH.7029src p.2381–2385
ComplicationDetail (verbatim)
RebleedCommon, and higher risk of mortality
VasospasmIn the early period after the hemorrhage. Nimodipine helps prevent vasospasm.
HydrocephalusDue to healing and meningeal fibrosis → obstruction of CSF absorption by arachnoid granulations — i.e. a communicating hydrocephalus, exactly as in the previous lecture's table
Exam Lock
Three complications, three time frames
  • Rebleed — immediately. Vasospasm — the early period after the haemorrhage (and nimodipine, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker from the antihypertensives lecture, prevents it). Communicating hydrocephalus — late, from meningeal fibrosis blocking the arachnoid granulations.
NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases734

Summary — cerebrovascular disease on one page

src p.2362–2387
EntityCause / mechanismKey features
Global ischemia / hypoxiaSevere systemic hypotension (MI, shock) or ↓ O₂ carrying capacity (CO poisoning); outcome set by severity and durationNeurons > glia; hippocampal pyramidal cells and cerebellar Purkinje cells most vulnerable; more severe impairment than focal ischemia
Watershed infarctBorder zones at the most distal reaches of arterial supply, after hypotensive episodes, classically after resuscitation from cardiac arrestGreatest risk: ACA–MCA border zone; also internal border zone (superficial vs deep MCA) and MCA–PCA
Embolic infarctMore common than thrombotic; cardiac mural thrombus or carotid atheromatous plaque; AF, myocardial dysfunctionFocal deficit in a named arterial territory
Thrombotic infarctThrombus on an atherosclerotic plaqueAnterograde extension; may fragment and embolize
Paradoxical embolusVenous embolus crossing a right-to-left shunt — PFO, ASD, VSDSystemic ischemia including stroke
Lacunar infarctHypertensive lipohyalinosis of penetrating (lenticulostriate) arteries obstructing the lumenDeep, small; the other outcome of lipohyalinosis is the Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm

Cerebral amyloid angiopathySubintimal and medial amyloid in larger non-penetrating cortical vesselsSuperficial / lobar haemorrhage in contrast to the deep hypertensive bleed

Subarachnoid haemorrhageRupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm; 90% anterior circulation, at branch points of the circle of Willis; ADPKD, Ehlers-Danlos; hypertension, smoking, ageThunderclap headache, rapid loss of consciousness, meningismus; CT blood in basal cisterns; LP with RBCs or xanthochromia; complications rebleed, vasospasm (nimodipine), communicating hydrocephalus

Block exam — cerebrovascular disease

PATH.7028

A 58-year-old hypertensive collapses with a dense left hemiplegia; CT shows a haemorrhage centred on the right putamen extending into the ventricle. Which vessels and which lesion?

  1. ACortical branches of the MCA; cerebral amyloid angiopathy
  2. BLenticulostriate arteries; Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms arising from lipohyalinosis
  3. CAnterior communicating artery; berry aneurysm
  4. DBridging veins; subdural haematoma
  5. EMiddle meningeal artery; epidural haematoma
Answer
B. Hypertensive primary intraparenchymal haemorrhage — due to rupture of small intraparenchymal vessels which branch off major cerebral vessels; like Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms and lacunar infarcts, they commonly involve the lenticulostriate arteries, with typical locations: basal ganglia (most common), thalamus, pons and cerebellum, and it can be fatal if large or if it extends into the ventricular system. Lipohyalinosis weakens the wall → Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm.
PATH.7028

An 81-year-old normotensive woman has her second lobar haemorrhage in two years. What is the mechanism, and why is the location different from a hypertensive bleed?

  1. ACharcot-Bouchard aneurysm; the lenticulostriate arteries are superficial
  2. BCerebral amyloid angiopathy — amyloid deposits subintimally and in the media of larger non-penetrating cortical vessels, so the bleed is superficial/lobar, unlike the deep hypertensive bleed from small penetrating vessels
  3. CArteriovenous malformation; AVMs are always lobar
  4. DBerry aneurysm rupture; anterior circulation predominance
  5. EHaemorrhagic conversion of an infarct; reperfusion injury
Answer
B. Amyloid angiopathy: the hemorrhage affects larger non-penetrating vessels supplying the cortex and is therefore typically superficial/lobar in location, unlike small penetrating vessels affected by hypertension which are typically subcortical/deep. Amyloid deposits inside the vessel wall (subintimal and medial deposition) which weakens the vessel and increases the risk of rupture and hemorrhage.
NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases736

Block exam — cerebrovascular disease (cont.)

PATH.7029

A 44-year-old collapses with the "worst headache of my life" and neck stiffness. CT is equivocal; LP shows xanthochromia. Which complication is prevented by nimodipine, and when does it occur?

  1. ARebleeding, immediately
  2. BVasospasm, in the early period after the haemorrhage
  3. CCommunicating hydrocephalus, late
  4. DSeizures, at any time
  5. ECerebral oedema, at 48 hours
Answer
B. Subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm. The complications: rebleed — common and higher risk of mortality; vasospasm — in the early period after the hemorrhage (nimodipine helps prevent vasospasm); hydrocephalus — due to healing and meningeal fibrosis obstructing CSF absorption by arachnoid granulations. Xanthochromia is yellowish CSF due to release of bilirubin after RBC lysis.
PATH.7029

Which associations does this lecture give for saccular (berry) aneurysms?

  1. AMarfan syndrome and Turner syndrome only
  2. BADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (congenital, younger age), plus hypertension, smoking and advanced age (acquired degeneration)
  3. COnly hypertension
  4. DOnly trauma
  5. ENeurofibromatosis type 1
Answer
B. Saccular aneurysms are associated with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and other congenital diseases which can affect connective tissue of blood vessels — these occur at a younger age. Saccular aneurysms are also associated with acquired risk factors which cause degenerative changes of blood vessels, e.g. hypertension, smoking and advanced age. 90% are in the anterior circulation, at branch points of the circle of Willis. Note the ADPKD link back to the renal-vascular lecture's berry aneurysm extrarenal manifestation.
NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases737

Block exam — cerebrovascular disease (cont.)

PATH.7027

A patient resuscitated after prolonged cardiac arrest has bilateral proximal arm weakness and profound short-term memory loss. Which two vulnerabilities explain this?

  1. ALacunar infarcts of the lenticulostriate arteries and Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms
  2. BWatershed infarction at the ACA–MCA border zone, and selective vulnerability of hippocampal pyramidal cells
  3. CAmyloid angiopathy and lobar haemorrhage
  4. DBerry aneurysm rupture and vasospasm
  5. EParadoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale
Answer
B. Border zone infarcts occur in the regions that lie at the most distal reaches of the arterial blood supply. GREATEST RISK: border zone between the anterior and the middle cerebral artery distributions. Usually seen after hypotensive episodes; most commonly seen in patients resuscitated after cardiac arrest. And in global ischemia, the cell type matters: neurons >> glial cells, especially pyramidal cells of the hippocampus and cerebellar Purkinje cells.
PATH.7027

Forty-eight hours after an ischaemic stroke, what will the histology show?

  1. AOnly red neurons with no inflammatory cells
  2. BTissue necrosis with an early influx of neutrophils, followed a few days later by macrophages
  3. CA glial scar and cystic space
  4. DNormal appearances
  5. EAmyloid within vessel walls
Answer
B. The lecture's timeline: up to 24 hours ("acute") — cytoplasmic eosinophilia, nuclear pyknosis and karyorrhexis → red neurons; 24 hours to 2 weeks ("subacute") — tissue necrosis causing early influx of neutrophils followed a few days later by influx of macrophages, later vascular proliferation and reactive gliosis; after 2 weeks ("repair") — removal of necrotic tissue and gliosis, leaving behind a glial scar and cystic space. Grossly at this point the brain is pale, soft and swollen.
NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases738

Block exam — cerebrovascular disease (cont.)

PATH.7030

A 26-year-old man presents with a seizure; imaging shows a tangle of vessels with no intervening capillary bed. Which lesion is this, and what is its presentation in a newborn?

  1. ACavernous malformation; hydrocephalus
  2. BArteriovenous malformation; high-output congestive heart failure from arteriovenous shunting
  3. CBerry aneurysm; thunderclap headache
  4. DCapillary telangiectasia; asymptomatic
  5. EAmyloid angiopathy; lobar haemorrhage
Answer
B. Arteriovenous malformations: most commonly a tangled network of arteries and veins with no interposing capillaries. The most common vascular malformation; affects males twice more than females (2:1 M:F); age 10 to 30 years. Manifest with seizure, intracerebral hemorrhage or even a subarachnoid hemorrhage. In newborns: high output congestive heart failure because of blood shunting from arteries to veins.
PATH.7045

Which imaging statement matches this lecture's comparison of ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke?

  1. ACT shows an ischaemic lesion within 30 minutes
  2. BDiffusion-weighted MRI shows an ischaemic lesion within 30 minutes; CT shows it within 6 to 24 hours; both CT and MRI identify haemorrhage immediately
  3. CMRI cannot identify haemorrhage
  4. DIschaemic and haemorrhagic strokes appear identically on CT
  5. EHaemorrhage is visible on CT only after 24 hours
Answer
B. Ischemic stroke: diffusion-weighted MRI shows the lesion within 30 mins of onset; CT shows the lesion within 6 to 24 hours. Hemorrhagic stroke: both CT and MRI can identify the lesion immediately after onset. Note also that "stroke" is the clinical designation applied when symptoms last more than 24 hours.
NCRS 38 · Neuropathology — Cerebrovascular Diseases739
PHAR

Antiepileptic Drugs

Dr Tiffany Clementson · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology. Three mechanisms — block the channel, raise GABA, lower glutamate — and a long list of drug-specific toxicities.

Dr Tiffany Clementson · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology  ·  source pp. 2389–2446
Epilepsy is a chronic disorder of brain function characterized by the recurrent and unpredictable occurrence of seizures. Seizures are finite episodes of brain dysfunction resulting from abnormal discharge of cerebral neurons. Seizures are thought to arise from the cerebral cortex. Approximately 1% of the world's population has epilepsy.Definition
PHAR · Antiepileptic Drugs740

Lecture objectives — verbatim

src p.2389 · 2399–2402
  • PHAR.00039 Define epilepsy. Describe the pathophysiology. List the major types of seizure.
  • PHAR.00040 Outline the principles of antiepileptic treatment.
  • PHAR.00041 Describe the mechanism of action of antiepileptic drugs.
  • PHAR.00042 Describe the main indications of antiepileptic drugs.
  • PHAR.00043 Define status epilepticus and explain how it is managed pharmacologically.
  • PHAR.00044 Describe the main adverse effects and contraindications of antiepileptic drugs.
  • PHAR.00045 Describe the pharmacokinetics of phenytoin.
  • PHAR.00046 List the drugs most associated with skin rash and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
  • PHAR.00047 Outline lamotrigine and carbamazepine black box warning about life-threatening skin reactions.
  • PHAR.00048 Discuss the risks of antiepileptic drugs during pregnancy.
  • PHAR.00049 List the antiepileptic drugs that induce P450 enzymes.
  • PHAR.00050 Discuss other therapeutic uses of antiepileptic drugs.
  • PHAR.00051 Describe the main non-pharmacological antiepileptic therapies.

Etiology and general treatment principles

  • Underlying genetic, structural, metabolic or unknown cause. Most cases have no identifiable cause.
  • Seizures result from abnormal electrical discharge of neurons in a localized brain area called the primary focus. Triggers can be physiologic, environmental or other precipitating factors.
  • If the underlying cause is identified and corrected, long-term antiseizure therapy may not be required.
  • Seizures can be controlled with one drug in 75% of patients. Patients may require more than one drug; some patients may never obtain total seizure control.

Exam Lock
Two EEG numbers and one negative
  • 3 Hz spike-and-wave = typical absence; 1.5–2.5 Hz diffuse spike-wave = atypical absence. And the single most useful bedside discriminator is no postictal confusion in typical absence — a child who stares, blinks and then carries straight on mid-sentence.
PHAR · Antiepileptic Drugs743

The nature of seizures, and how drugs interrupt them

PHAR.00041src p.2392 · 2410–2418
  • GABAA receptor antagonists and glutamate receptor agonists provoke seizures; GABAA receptor agonists and glutamate receptor antagonists prevent them.
  • Rapidly firing neurons require rapid depolarization, repeated action potentials and spread of electrical activity, which rely heavily on voltage-gated ion channels — so blockade of voltage-gated ion channels reduces neuronal excitability and also prevents seizures.

Antiepileptic drugs are classified based on their mechanisms of action. However, the clinical effectiveness of many drugs is only partially explained by these mechanisms, because they often act on multiple targets (pleiotropic effects). For some drugs the primary molecular target remains unclear (valproate, zonisamide); other drugs act on multiple mechanisms simultaneously (topiramate, felbamate).

Two mechanisms worth stating precisely

Na⁺ channel blockers
In seizures, neurons fire excessively and repetitively → uncontrolled high-frequency firing spreads through neural networks. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine and others stabilize the INACTIVATED state of Na⁺ channels → preventing the uncontrolled, repetitive firing that drives seizure activity.
T-type Ca²⁺ channel blockers
Absence seizures involve oscillatory neuronal activity between thalamus and cortex. The T-type Ca²⁺ current governs oscillatory responses in thalamic neurons. Ethosuximide and valproate inhibit this current and are effective in absence seizures.

Voltage-gated sodium channel blockade is thought to be the principal mechanism of action of phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine and zonisamide; it may also contribute to the effects of phenobarbital, valproate and topiramate. Primidone is metabolized to phenobarbital and phenylethylmalonamide.

PHAR · Antiepileptic Drugs744

Classification of antiepileptic drugs by mechanism

PHAR.00041src p.2415 · 2419

Detail of the synaptic column: ↑ GABAergic transmission — postsynaptic direct action on the GABA receptor (benzodiazepines, barbiturates, topiramate); presynaptic inhibition of GABA reuptake (tiagabine) or of GABA degradation (vigabatrin inhibits GABA aminotransferase). ↓ Glutamatergic transmission — postsynaptic glutamate receptor blockade (phenobarbital, topiramate, felbamate); gabapentin and pregabalin decrease glutamate release by blocking presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; levetiracetam binds synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A).

PHAR · Antiepileptic Drugs745

Principles of therapy and choice by seizure type

PHAR.00040 · PHAR.00042src p.2393–2394 · 2423–2425

Principles (PHAR.00040)

  • The aim of therapy is total seizure freedom without clinically significant adverse effects. This is achievable in more than 2/3 of patients. Correct seizure diagnosis is a precondition for the success of therapeutic decisions.
  • Treatment should be started with a single drug; the dosage titrated slowly.
  • Regular monitoring for seizure frequency and adverse effects.
  • Add combination therapy only after ≥ 2 failed monotherapy trials.
  • Newer AEDs are often approved as adjuncts but used more broadly.

Therapeutic strategy, as the lecture's algorithm runs

Newly diagnosed epilepsy → first-line drug appropriate for the seizure type, considering toxicity and patient characteristics; titrate to maximally tolerated→Seizures persist → second-choice drug: titrate to therapeutic level for seizure control BEFORE tapering and discontinuing the original agent→Seizures persist → rational combination of two drugs, or alternate drug therapy→Seizures persist → consider non-pharmacological management

PHAR · Antiepileptic Drugs747

Febrile convulsions and status epilepticus

PHAR.00042 · PHAR.00043src p.2394 · 2426–2429

Febrile convulsions

Definition and diagnostic criteria
  • Seizures occurring in young children with fever (> 38 °C)
  • Typically generalized tonic-clonic and short in duration
  • Age < 6 years · fever present (> 38 °C) · no CNS infection or inflammation · no metabolic abnormality causing seizures · no prior afebrile seizures
Management
  • Most febrile seizures are self-limited
  • Treatment required if the seizure lasts > 5 minutes
  • Diazepam: IV or rectal administration
  • Acetaminophen

Status epilepticus (PHAR.00043)

Status epilepticus is a single seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, or two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between seizures. It may be convulsive or nonconvulsive. The most common type, generalized tonic-clonic status epilepticus, is a life-threatening emergency.Definition
PhaseTimingTherapy
Phase 1 — initial (benzodiazepine) phase5–20 minutes of activityIM midazolam OR IV lorazepam OR IV diazepam. *If not responding after the first dose → phase 2.*
Phase 2 — second (antiepileptic drug) phase20–40 minutes of activityIV fosphenytoin OR IV valproic acid OR IV levetiracetam. Second-line option (less preferred): IV phenobarbital
Phase 3 — refractory phaseSeizures continuingRepeat second therapy, and proceed to refractory management

Other convulsive emergencies: drug-induced seizures in nonepileptic patients may be controlled with diazepam, lorazepam or phenobarbital.

PHAR · Antiepileptic Drugs748

Febrile convulsions and status epilepticus (cont.)

PHAR.00042 · PHAR.00043src p.2394 · 2426–2429
Exam Lock
Five minutes defines two different things
  • A febrile seizure needs treatment if it lasts > 5 minutes, and status epilepticus is defined as a single seizure lasting more than 5 minutes. The same number, and the same first drug class — a benzodiazepine — in both.

PHAR.00044 · PHAR.00045 · PHAR.00046 · PHAR.00047 · PHAR.00049src p.2395 · 2431–2438

Sodium channel blockersPhenytoinGingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, coarsening of facies. Follows zero-order kinetics (tricky to dose). Also diplopia, ataxia, drowsiness, sedation, and rash / Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

PHAR · Antiepileptic Drugs750

Adverse effects — the drug-by-drug table (cont.)

PHAR.00044 · PHAR.00045 · PHAR.00046 · PHAR.00047 · PHAR.00049src p.2395 · 2431–2438

Rash and Stevens-Johnson syndrome (PHAR.00046 · PHAR.00047)

  • Antiepileptic drugs are associated with an increased risk for Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN).
  • Lamotrigine and carbamazepine have black box warnings regarding SJS/TEN reactions. They should be discontinued at the first sign of rash.
  • High risk: phenytoin · lamotrigine · carbamazepine.

P450 (PHAR.00049)

Inducers
Carbamazepine · phenobarbital · phenytoin; oxcarbazepine is a weak P450 inducer
Inhibitor
Valproate — hepatotoxicity; inhibits cytochrome P450; inhibits the metabolism of several drugs; inhibits its own metabolism

Overdose toxicity: antiepileptic drugs are commonly taken in intentional overdoses but antiseizure drugs are rarely lethal. The most dangerous effect after large overdoses is respiratory depression. Treatment is supportive; stimulants should not be used.

PHAR · Antiepileptic Drugs751

Pregnancy, discontinuation, other uses, and non-pharmacological therapy

PHAR.00040 · PHAR.00048 · PHAR.00050 · PHAR.00051src p.2396–2397 · 2437–2445

Antiepileptic drugs and pregnancy (PHAR.00048)

  • There is good evidence of an increased risk of congenital malformations in infants born of women taking antiseizure drugs. Most pregnant patients exposed to antiepileptic drugs deliver normal infants; however, fetal exposure to older drugs — particularly valproate and phenobarbital — is associated with congenital anomalies.
  • Valproate causes a significantly higher rate of fetal malformations compared to other antiepileptic drugs.
  • Prophylactic folic acid decreases the incidence of neural tube defects.
  • Newborn haemorrhagic disease: enzyme-inducing antiepileptic drugs may increase degradation of vitamin K in the fetus, which can cause bleeding in the newborn. Vitamin K supplementation is recommended for the mother in the final month of pregnancy and for the newborn.

Discontinuing therapy

  • If a patient is seizure-free for 3–5 years, discontinuation is warranted.
  • Discontinuation should be slow. Benzodiazepines and barbiturates should be discontinued very gradually to avoid withdrawal seizures.
  • If the patient is on combination therapy, drugs should be withdrawn one at a time.
PHAR · Antiepileptic Drugs752

Pregnancy, discontinuation, other uses, and non-pharmacological therapy (cont.)

PHAR.00040 · PHAR.00048 · PHAR.00050 · PHAR.00051src p.2396–2397 · 2437–2445

Other therapeutic uses (PHAR.00050)

Antiepileptic drugOther uses
CarbamazepineNeuropathic pain · bipolar disorder

LamotrigineBipolar disorder
PregabalinNeuropathic pain
TopiramateMigraine prophylaxis
ValproateBipolar disorder · migraine prophylaxis

Non-pharmacological approaches (PHAR.00051)

  • About 1/3 of patients with epilepsy continue to have seizures on medication.
  • Surgery — resection (surgical removal of pathological lesions) or disconnection (surgical section of neuronal circuits).
  • Stimulation techniques — vagus nerve stimulation, deep brain stimulation. Intermittent electrical stimulation of the LEFT vagus nerve with an implanted pacemaker-like device reduces the number of partial seizures by 1/3. The patient can activate the device when they sense a seizure is imminent. Used as an adjunct to anticonvulsant therapy.
  • The ketogenic diet — four parts fat to one part protein and carbohydrate. The high fat content and extremely low carbohydrate content produce ketosis, which appears to have a direct antiseizure effect. How the ketogenic diet suppresses seizures remains unclear.

Block exam — antiepileptic drugs

PHAR.00039 · PHAR.00041 · PHAR.00042

A 7-year-old has 20 daily episodes of staring with eye fluttering, each under 10 seconds, with no postictal confusion. EEG shows 3-Hz spike-and-wave. Which drugs are first line, and by what mechanism?

  1. ACarbamazepine and phenytoin; Na⁺ channel blockade
  2. BEthosuximide and valproate; inhibition of the T-type Ca²⁺ current that governs thalamic oscillatory activity
  3. CLevetiracetam; SV2A binding
  4. DVigabatrin; GABA transaminase inhibition
  5. EGabapentin; presynaptic Ca²⁺ channel blockade
Answer
B. Typical absence seizures — brief loss of consciousness, abrupt staring, rapid eye blinking, usually < 10 seconds, no postictal confusion, 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharge, onset 3–5 years, often resolving by puberty. Absence seizures involve oscillatory neuronal activity between thalamus and cortex; the T-type Ca²⁺ current governs oscillatory responses in thalamic neurons; ethosuximide and valproate inhibit this current and are effective in absence seizures. Valproate is preferred if tonic-clonic seizures are also present.
PHAR.00048

A young woman with generalized epilepsy plans pregnancy. Which drug carries the highest malformation risk, and what two supplements does the lecture recommend?

  1. ALamotrigine; folic acid and iron
  2. BValproate; prophylactic folic acid for neural tube defects, and vitamin K for the mother in the final month and for the newborn
  3. CLevetiracetam; folic acid only
  4. DCarbamazepine; vitamin D and calcium
  5. ETopiramate; vitamin B6 and folic acid
Answer
B. Valproate causes a significantly higher rate of fetal malformations compared to other antiepileptic drugs — and it is listed as teratogenic: avoid in females of childbearing age. Prophylactic folic acid decreases incidence of neural tube defects. Newborn hemorrhagic disease: enzyme-inducing antiepileptic drugs may increase degradation of vitamin K in the fetus... Vitamin K supplementation is recommended for the mother in the final month of pregnancy and for the newborn.
PHAR · Antiepileptic Drugs756

Block exam — antiepileptic drugs (cont.)

PHAR.00046 · PHAR.00047

A patient started on lamotrigine two weeks ago develops a spreading rash with mucosal involvement. What is the correct action, and which other drugs share this black box?

  1. AContinue and add an antihistamine; only lamotrigine has the warning
  2. BDiscontinue at the first sign of rash; lamotrigine and carbamazepine carry black box warnings for SJS/TEN, and phenytoin is also high risk
  3. CHalve the dose; phenobarbital shares the warning
  4. DSwitch to valproate immediately; no other drug carries the warning
  5. EContinue — rash is expected with all AEDs
Answer
B. Antiepileptic drugs are associated with an increased risk for Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN). Lamotrigine and carbamazepine have black box warnings regarding SJS/TEN reactions. They should be discontinued at the first sign of rash. High risk: phenytoin, lamotrigine, carbamazepine. The lecture also notes that lamotrigine's risk is high if titrated too quickly.
PHAR.00043

A seizure has continued for 8 minutes in the emergency department. Which is the correct first-phase therapy, and what follows if it fails?

  1. AIV fosphenytoin, then IV lorazepam
  2. BIM midazolam or IV lorazepam or IV diazepam; then IV fosphenytoin, valproic acid or levetiracetam
  3. CIV phenobarbital, then general anaesthesia
  4. DOral carbamazepine, then IV valproate
  5. EIV levetiracetam, then IM midazolam
Answer
B. Status epilepticus is a single seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between seizures. Phase 1 (5–20 minutes of activity): IM midazolam OR IV lorazepam OR IV diazepam. Phase 2 (20–40 minutes): IV fosphenytoin OR IV valproic acid OR IV levetiracetam; second-line, less preferred, IV phenobarbital. Phase 3: repeat second therapy / refractory management.
PHAR.00044

Which antiepileptic requires regular eye examinations, and why?

  1. ATopiramate; acute angle-closure glaucoma
  2. BVigabatrin; permanent visual field defects
  3. CPhenytoin; diplopia
  4. DCarbamazepine; diplopia
  5. EEthosuximide; retinal deposits
Answer
B. Vigabatrin: permanent visual field defects (requires regular eye checks). Vigabatrin's mechanism is inhibition of GABA degradation — it inhibits GABA aminotransferase. Note the contrast with diplopia, which is a common, reversible dose-related effect of phenytoin, carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine.
PHAR · Antiepileptic Drugs757

Block exam — antiepileptic drugs (cont.)

PHAR.00049

Which antiepileptic INHIBITS cytochrome P450 — including its own metabolism — while the others listed induce it?

  1. ACarbamazepine
  2. BPhenobarbital
  3. CPhenytoin
  4. DValproate
  5. EOxcarbazepine
Answer
D. Carbamazepine, phenobarbital and phenytoin induce cytochrome P450; oxcarbazepine is a weak P450 inducer. Valproate is a CYP450 inhibitor: hepatotoxicity; inhibits cytochrome P450; inhibits metabolism of several drugs; inhibits its own metabolism. This is the same inducer list that appeared in the coagulation lecture as drugs that stimulate warfarin metabolism and reduce anticoagulation.
PHAR.00045

A patient on phenytoin has a small dose increase and becomes ataxic with diplopia and levels far above expectation. Which pharmacokinetic property explains this?

  1. AFirst-order kinetics with a short half-life
  2. BZero-order (saturation) kinetics
  3. CEnterohepatic recirculation
  4. DActive tubular secretion
  5. EP-glycoprotein efflux
Answer
B. Phenytoin follows zero-order kinetics of elimination (tricky to dose) — once the enzyme is saturated, a small dose increment produces a disproportionate rise in level, hence diplopia and ataxia. Its other signature effects are gingival hyperplasia, coarsening of facial features in children, hirsutism, and rash / Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
PHAR.00041

Which drug pairing of mechanism is correct as this lecture classifies them?

  1. ATiagabine inhibits GABA aminotransferase; vigabatrin blocks GABA reuptake
  2. BTiagabine inhibits GABA reuptake; vigabatrin inhibits GABA aminotransferase
  3. CGabapentin binds SV2A; levetiracetam blocks presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels
  4. DEthosuximide blocks Na⁺ channels; phenytoin blocks T-type Ca²⁺ channels
  5. EFelbamate enhances GABA reuptake; topiramate blocks SV2A
Answer
B. Inhibition of the reuptake of GABA: tiagabine. Inhibition of degradation of GABA: vigabatrin inhibits GABA aminotransferase. And on the glutamate side: gabapentin and pregabalin decrease glutamate release by blocking presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; levetiracetam binds to synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A). Ethosuximide is a T-type Ca²⁺ blocker; phenytoin is a Na⁺ channel blocker.
PHAR · Antiepileptic Drugs758

Block exam — antiepileptic drugs (cont.)

PHAR.00051

Which non-pharmacological therapy involves stimulating the LEFT vagus nerve, and by how much does it reduce partial seizures?

  1. ADeep brain stimulation; by half
  2. BVagus nerve stimulation; by about one-third
  3. CKetogenic diet; by two-thirds
  4. DCorpus callosotomy; by 90%
  5. ETranscranial magnetic stimulation; by 10%
Answer
B. Intermittent electrical stimulation of the left vagus nerve with an implanted pacemaker-like device reduces the number of partial seizures by 1/3. The patient can activate the device when they sense a seizure is imminent. Vagus nerve stimulation is used as an adjunct to anticonvulsant therapy. The other options in the lecture are surgery (resection or disconnection), deep brain stimulation, and the ketogenic diet (4:1 fat to protein and carbohydrate).
PHAR.00050

Which antiepileptic is listed as a first-line option for essential tremor?

  1. ATopiramate
  2. BGabapentin
  3. CPrimidone
  4. DLamotrigine
  5. ECarbamazepine
Answer
C. Primidone — essential tremor (first-line option); propranolol is also first line. The rest of the "other uses" table: carbamazepine — neuropathic pain and bipolar disorder; gabapentin — neuropathic pain and restless legs syndrome; lamotrigine — bipolar disorder; pregabalin — neuropathic pain; topiramate — migraine prophylaxis; valproate — bipolar disorder and migraine prophylaxis. Recall too that primidone is metabolized to phenobarbital, and its adverse effects mirror it.
PHAR · Antiepileptic Drugs759
