Neuropathology 3 — Neurodegenerative Diseases

Dr. Adesola Adeleye · Department of Pathology. Five diseases, five aggregating proteins, five anatomical addresses.

Dr. Adesola Adeleye · Department of Pathology  ·  source pp. 2447–2477

Learning objectives — verbatim

  • PATH.7034 Discuss Alzheimer disease, frontotemporal dementia, Parkinson disease, Huntington disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) in terms of their: age of onset, etiopathogenesis, morphology, clinical manifestations and prognosis.
  • PATH.7044 Discuss Parkinson disease, Huntington disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) in terms of their: age of onset, etiopathogenesis, morphology, clinical manifestations and prognosis.
Neurodegenerative disorders are the most common form of neurological disease. Characterized by progressive death of groups of neurons with functional interconnections. The common pathological process seen in most is accumulation of protein aggregates, which is the "histological hallmark" of that disease. Clinical features depend on the neural systems affected.Definition
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases760

The whole lecture as one grid

PATH.7034src p.2452–2477
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases761

Alzheimer disease — clinical picture and the two proteins

PATH.7034src p.2453–2456
  • Epidemiology: the most common cause of dementia in older adults. Familial cases (5–10%) are early onset.
  • Clinical features: early-onset memory impairment · altered mood and behavior · over time severe dysfunction — aphasia, disorientation. The motor and sensory systems are usually intact.
  • Diagnosis: dementia is diagnosed with a mental status examination; histological diagnosis is confirmed only during autopsy.
  • Cause of death: intercurrent pneumonia or other infections.
Accumulation of Aβ and tau proteins in the forms of plaques and tangles, leading to neuronal dysfunction, death and a local inflammatory reaction.Etiopathogenesis
PlaquesNeurofibrillary tangles
What aggregatesAggregation of EXTRACELLULAR Aβ peptidesAggregation of tau — develops INTRACELLULARLY, then persists extracellularly after neuronal death
SignificanceAβ generation is a critical inciting event. Mutations in the APP gene increase the risk of AD.Mutations in the tau protein gene increase risk for frontotemporal lobar degeneration.

The APP pathway, step by step

Amyloid precursor protein (APP), on chromosome 21 — hence the association with Down syndrome — is present on neuronal membranes and contains the Aβ peptide→APP is broken down by secretases — β, α, γ. α-secretase + γ-secretase → a soluble fragment and a NON-amyloidogenic breakdown product. β-secretase + γ-secretase → a soluble fragment and the Aβ peptide, the amyloidogenic breakdown product.→Aβ monomer → Aβ oligomers → Aβ aggregates and fibrils → neuronal damage and formation of extracellular plaques
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases762

Alzheimer disease — clinical picture and the two proteins (cont.)

PATH.7034src p.2453–2456

And how tau follows

  • Tau is a microtubule-associated protein present in the axons.
  • Aβ oligomers activate kinases → hyperphosphorylate tau → tau loses its ability to bind microtubules → aggregates and forms neurofibrillary tangles inside cells (intracellularly; compare with extracellular plaques), becoming extracellular after cell death.
  • The exact mechanism of neuronal damage and death by neurofibrillary tangles is not known.
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases763

Alzheimer disease — genetics and morphology

PATH.7034src p.2457 · 2459–2460
5–10%: INHERITED, EARLY ONSET90–95%: SPORADIC, LATE ONSET
Associated with gene mutations or chromosomal alterations that increase production of Aβ peptideApoE genotype on chromosome 19: three different allelic forms (ε2, ε3, ε4)
Amyloid precursor protein on chromosome 21 — Down syndromeIf homozygous for ε4: the risk of Alzheimer is much greater — a 95% chance by age 85
Presenilin 1 and 2 gene mutations on chromosomes 14 and 1, which code for the γ-secretase enzyme—
Gross
  • Atrophy, especially in the frontal, temporal and parietal lobes
  • Narrowing of gyri and widening of cerebral sulci
  • As brain tissue is destroyed, the ventricular spaces become secondarily larger — ex vacuo ventriculomegaly
Microscopic
  • Neuronal loss in the cerebral cortex
  • Gliosis — astrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy
  • Neurofibrillary tangles (intracellular) and neuritic plaques (extracellular)

From the lecture's images: a neurofibrillary tangle is present within one neuron, and several extracellular tangles are also present; silver stain highlights a neurofibrillary tangle (black) within the neuronal cytoplasm; plaques with dystrophic neurites surrounding amyloid cores; the plaque core and surrounding region are immunoreactive for Aβ, while the tangle and the neurites around a plaque contain tau.

Exam Lock
Three genes for the 5%, one allele for the 95%
  • Early-onset familial AD: APP (chr 21) · presenilin 1 (chr 14) · presenilin 2 (chr 1) — all of which increase Aβ production, and the presenilins are γ-secretase. Late-onset sporadic AD: ApoE ε4 on chr 19, with 95% risk by age 85 in ε4 homozygotes. The Down syndrome link is APP gene dosage on chromosome 21.
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases764

Frontotemporal lobar degeneration

PATH.7034src p.2461–2462
  • Definition: disorders preferentially affecting the frontal and/or temporal lobes.
  • Epidemiology: tends to present at younger ages — differentiate from Alzheimer disease.
  • Clinical features: progressive behavioral changes or language problems depending on the lobe affected primarily → memory disturbances occur LATER — differentiate from Alzheimer disease.

Etiopathogenesis — two protein subtypes

FTLD-tau
Accumulation of tau neurofibrillary tangles. One subtype that includes tau protein is Pick disease, where Pick bodies are seen intracellularly — round, homogeneous neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions that stain intensely with silver stains.
FTLD-TDP-43
Intracellular accumulation of TDP-43, a DNA/RNA binding protein. How this intracellular accumulation causes neuronal injury and death is poorly understood. Immunohistochemistry: cytoplasmic inclusions containing TDP-43 in association with loss of normal nuclear immunoreactivity.

Gross: marked frontal and temporal lobe (lobar) atrophy with knifelike thinning of the gyri.

Trap
Two features separate FTLD from Alzheimer at the bedside
  • Younger age of onset and behaviour or language first, memory later — the exact reverse of Alzheimer disease, where early memory impairment dominates and behaviour follows. Note also the protein crossover: tau gene mutations increase the risk of FTLD, not of AD.
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases765

Parkinson disease — the pathologist's view

PATH.7034 · PATH.7044src p.2464–2469

Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease both affect neurons in the basal ganglia — Parkinson's disease causes decreased intentional movement and Huntington's disease increased unintentional movement. Parkinson's: death of pigmented dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. Huntington's: death of striatal cholinergic interneurons and striatal GABAergic neurons.

  • Definition: a neurodegenerative disease due to loss of dopaminergic neurons from the substantia nigra. Clinical features: the classic triad of tremor + rigidity + bradykinesia.
  • Etiopathogenesis: the exact cause is unknown; mainly associated with aggregation of α-synuclein. Most cases are sporadic (a small percentage show mutations in the α-synuclein gene).
  • α-Synuclein is expressed at presynaptic neurons and binds to presynaptic secretory vesicles containing dopamine, causing degranulation and exocytosis of dopamine into the synaptic cleft. For unknown reasons, α-synuclein does not bind to vesicles and forms insoluble aggregates in patients with Parkinson's disease; this can be enhanced by point mutations in the α-synuclein gene. The aggregates are toxic to dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra.

Morphology

Gross
Pallor and atrophy of the substantia nigra (the nucleus of dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain) — a depigmented substantia nigra
Microscopy
Loss of the pigmented neurons associated with gliosis. "Lewy bodies" are found in the remaining neurons of the substantia nigra: single or multiple, cytoplasmic, eosinophilic inclusions; on ultrastructure, filaments composed of α-synuclein, a protein involved in synaptic transmission.

Clinical features in the pathologist's list

  • Asymmetric pill-rolling tremor.
  • Bradykinesia: generalized slowness, especially in gait (shuffling).
  • Cogwheel rigidity: an alternating pattern of resistance and relaxation as the examiner moves the limb.
  • Dementia: fluctuating cognition, hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder caused by cortical involvement. When dementia arises WITHIN 1 year of motor symptoms it is Lewy body dementia; if more than 1 year apart it is called dementia secondary to Parkinson disease.
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases766

Parkinson disease — the pathologist's view (cont.)

PATH.7034 · PATH.7044src p.2464–2469
Bottom Line
The one-year rule ties three lectures together
  • The confusion DLA asked *"which came first, memory problems or stiffness and a shuffling gait?"*; this lecture gives the answer in numbers — dementia within 1 year of motor onset = Lewy body dementia; more than 1 year apart = dementia secondary to Parkinson disease. And the antipsychotics lecture supplies the drug for the hallucinations: pimavanserin.
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases767

Huntington disease

PATH.7034 · PATH.7044src p.2470–2473
  • Definition: an autosomal dominant movement disorder associated with degeneration of the striatum (caudate and putamen). The lecture's mnemonic: CAG — Caudate loses Acetylcholine and GABA.
  • Clinical features: involuntary jerky movements (chorea) in all parts; typically writhing movements of the extremities (athetosis); cognitive changes ranging from forgetfulness to dementia.
  • Natural course: the disease is progressive; death after an average course of 15 years.

The genetics

  • The prototypical polyglutamine trinucleotide repeat expansion disorder. CAG repeats on chromosome 4: 6–35 repeats is normal; 36 or more repeats causes Huntington disease.
  • The normal gene functions as a transcription factor regulator by modulating/limiting conversion of DNA to mRNA in the nucleus. A toxic gain of function of the HTT gene impairs mitochondrial biogenesis and disrupts synthesis of proteins involved in the degradation pathway and proteolysis.
  • Ubiquitinated mutant protein and impaired proteolysis → characteristic intranuclear fragments. Development of intranuclear inclusions containing huntingtin is the pathologic hallmark of HD.
  • There is an inverse relationship between repeat number and age of onset (longer repeats = earlier onset). Repeat expansions occur during spermatogenesis → paternal transmission is associated with earlier onset in the next generation (anticipation).

Clinical correlation and morphology

  • There is correlation between the degree of degeneration of the striatum and the severity of motor symptoms, and between the degree of cortical neuronal loss and dementia.
  • Motor symptoms: chorea (involuntary jerky movements) and athetosis (writhing movements).
  • Cognitive and psychiatric: early cognitive changes include forgetfulness; difficulty organizing tasks; lack of impulse control; aggression and increased risk of suicide.
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases768

Huntington disease (cont.)

PATH.7034 · PATH.7044src p.2470–2473
Gross
The brain is small. Marked atrophy of the caudate and sometimes the putamen. Dilated lateral and third ventricles.
Microscopy
Severe loss of neurons from the striatum with gliosis; in the remaining neurons, intranuclear inclusions of ubiquitinated huntingtin protein (highlighted for ubiquitin on immunohistochemistry).
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases769

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

PATH.7034 · PATH.7044src p.2475–2477
  • Also called Lou Gehrig's disease or motor neuron disease.
  • Definition: a neurodegenerative disease due to death of LOWER motor neurons in the spinal cord and brain stem as well as UPPER motor neurons in the motor cortex.

Natural history

  • Males > females. Manifests in the fifth decade or later. Life expectancy 2–5 years after onset.
  • Most cases are sporadic; ~10% are familial (autosomal dominant inheritance).
  • Pathogenesis: uncertain, possibly due to abnormal RNA and/or protein processing. Identified mutations: chromosome 9 hexanucleotide repeat and the superoxide dismutase gene.

Clinical features

  • Begins as subtle asymmetric distal extremity weakness.
  • Loss of upper motor neurons → paresis, spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, and degeneration of the corticospinal tract in the lateral portion of the spinal cord ("lateral sclerosis").
  • Loss of lower motor neurons → denervation of muscles → muscle atrophy ("a-myo-trophy"), weakness, fasciculations.
  • Intellect, sensation, sphincter control and eye movements are SPARED.

Pathological features

  • Gross: atrophy of the entire upper motor neuron tract / corticospinal tract from motor cortex to anterior horn in the spinal cord; atrophy of the entire lower motor neuron tract from anterior horn to anterior motor spinal nerve root and peripheral motor nerve.
  • Microscopy: reduction in the number of anterior horn cell neurons, loss of myelinated fibers in the lateral corticospinal tract, and degeneration of anterior nerve roots.
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases770

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (cont.)

PATH.7034 · PATH.7044src p.2475–2477
Exam Lock
The name is the pathology
  • "A-myo-trophic" = the lower motor neuron loss (muscle atrophy, fasciculations). "Lateral sclerosis" = the upper motor neuron loss (degeneration of the corticospinal tract in the lateral cord → spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski). And the four things that are spared — intellect, sensation, sphincters and eye movements — are what distinguish it from everything else in this lecture.
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases771

NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases772

Block exam — neurodegenerative disease

PATH.7034

Which combination of gene, chromosome and mechanism belongs to early-onset familial Alzheimer disease?

  1. AApoE ε4 on chromosome 19; impaired Aβ clearance
  2. BPresenilin 1 on chromosome 14, coding for γ-secretase, increasing Aβ production
  3. CTau on chromosome 17; hyperphosphorylation
  4. DHuntingtin on chromosome 4; CAG expansion
  5. ESuperoxide dismutase; free radical injury
Answer
B. 5–10% inherited, early onset: associated with gene mutations or chromosomal alterations that increase production of Aβ peptide — amyloid precursor protein on chromosome 21 (Down syndrome), and presenilin 1 and 2 gene mutations on chromosomes 14 and 1 which code for the γ-secretase enzyme. ApoE ε4 on chromosome 19 belongs to the 90–95% sporadic, late-onset group, where ε4 homozygotes have a 95% chance by age 85.
PATH.7034

Which secretase combination generates the amyloidogenic product, and which is non-amyloidogenic?

  1. Aα + γ is amyloidogenic; β + γ is not
  2. Bβ-secretase + γ-secretase gives the Aβ peptide (amyloidogenic); α-secretase + γ-secretase gives a non-amyloidogenic product
  3. Cα + β is amyloidogenic
  4. DOnly γ-secretase matters
  5. ENeither combination produces Aβ
Answer
B. APP is broken down into different fragments by a group of secretases — β, α, γ. 1. α-secretase + γ-secretase = soluble fragment + non-amyloidogenic breakdown product. 2. β-secretase + γ-secretase = soluble fragment + Aβ peptide (amyloidogenic breakdown product). The Aβ monomer then forms oligomers → aggregates and fibrils → neuronal damage and extracellular plaques, and the oligomers activate kinases that hyperphosphorylate tau.
PATH.7034

A 58-year-old develops disinhibition, socially inappropriate behaviour and progressive word-finding difficulty; memory is relatively preserved. Imaging shows knife-edge frontal and temporal atrophy. What is the diagnosis, and which two proteins define its subtypes?

  1. AAlzheimer disease; Aβ and tau
  2. BFrontotemporal lobar degeneration; tau (Pick bodies) or TDP-43
  3. CLewy body dementia; α-synuclein
  4. DHuntington disease; huntingtin
  5. EVascular dementia; no protein
Answer
B. Frontotemporal lobar degeneration: disorders preferentially affecting the frontal and/or temporal lobes; tends to present at younger ages (differentiate from Alzheimer disease); progressive behavioral changes or language problems depending on the lobe affected primarily → memory disturbances occur later (differentiate from Alzheimer disease). FTLD-tau: accumulation of tau neurofibrillary tangles; one subtype is Pick disease, where Pick bodies are seen intracellularly. FTLD-TDP-43: intracellular accumulation of TDP-43, a DNA/RNA binding protein. Grossly: lobar atrophy with knifelike thinning of the gyri.
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases773

Block exam — neurodegenerative disease (cont.)

PATH.7034 · PATH.7044

A man develops visual hallucinations and fluctuating cognition eight months after the onset of a resting tremor. What does the lecture call this, and what is the histological hallmark?

  1. ADementia secondary to Parkinson disease; neurofibrillary tangles
  2. BLewy body dementia; Lewy bodies — cytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions of α-synuclein
  3. CAlzheimer disease; neuritic plaques
  4. DFTLD-TDP; TDP-43 inclusions
  5. EHuntington disease; intranuclear ubiquitinated inclusions
Answer
B. When dementia arises within 1 year of motor symptoms it is Lewy body dementia; if more than 1 year apart it is called dementia secondary to Parkinson disease. The hallmark: "Lewy bodies" are found in the remaining neurons of the substantia nigra — single or multiple, cytoplasmic, eosinophilic inclusions; on ultrastructure, filaments composed of α-synuclein. Grossly there is pallor and atrophy of the substantia nigra.
PATH.7034 · PATH.7044

A 38-year-old with chorea has a father who developed the same illness at 52. Which genetic principle explains the earlier onset, and what is the threshold repeat number?

  1. AMaternal imprinting; 20 repeats
  2. BRepeat expansion occurs during spermatogenesis, so paternal transmission is associated with earlier onset; 36 or more CAG repeats on chromosome 4
  3. CMitochondrial inheritance; 50 repeats
  4. DX-linked inheritance; 30 repeats
  5. ESomatic mosaicism; 10 repeats
Answer
B. CAG repeats on chromosome 4: 6–35 repeats is normal; 36 or more repeats causes Huntington disease. There is an inverse relationship between repeat number and age of onset (longer repeats = earlier onset). Repeat expansions occur during spermatogenesis → paternal transmission is associated with earlier onset in the next generation. The pathologic hallmark is intranuclear inclusions containing ubiquitinated huntingtin, and the gross picture is marked caudate atrophy with dilated lateral and third ventricles.
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases774

Block exam — neurodegenerative disease (cont.)

PATH.7034 · PATH.7044

A 55-year-old has asymmetric hand weakness, tongue fasciculations, brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response. Sensation, cognition and eye movements are normal. What is spared, and what is the prognosis?

  1. AMotor function is spared; 15 years
  2. BIntellect, sensation, sphincter control and eye movements are spared; life expectancy 2–5 years after onset
  3. COnly sensation is spared; 10 years
  4. DNothing is spared; 1 year
  5. ESphincters are affected first; 20 years
Answer
B. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Intellect, sensation, sphincter control and eye movements are spared. Manifests in the fifth decade or later; life expectancy 2–5 years after onset; males > females; most cases sporadic, ~10% familial with autosomal dominant inheritance. The mixed picture is diagnostic: loss of upper motor neurons → paresis, spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign and degeneration of the lateral corticospinal tract; loss of lower motor neurons → muscle atrophy, weakness and fasciculations.
PATH.7034

Which pairing of disease and basal ganglia consequence is correct?

  1. AParkinson's — increased unintentional movement; Huntington's — decreased intentional movement
  2. BParkinson's — decreased intentional movement from death of pigmented dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra; Huntington's — increased unintentional movement from death of striatal cholinergic interneurons and GABAergic neurons
  3. CBoth cause decreased movement
  4. DBoth affect the substantia nigra
  5. EHuntington's spares the striatum
Answer
B. Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease both affect neurons in the basal ganglia — Parkinson's disease causes decreased intentional movement and Huntington's disease increased unintentional movement. Huntington disease: death of striatal cholinergic interneurons and death of striatal GABAergic neurons. Parkinson's disease: death of pigmented dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. The lecture's mnemonic is CAG — Caudate loses Acetylcholine and GABA.
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases775

Block exam — neurodegenerative disease (cont.)

PATH.7034

Which statement about neurofibrillary tangles is correct?

  1. AThey are extracellular from the outset and composed of Aβ
  2. BThey develop intracellularly from hyperphosphorylated tau and persist extracellularly after neuronal death; tau gene mutations increase the risk of frontotemporal lobar degeneration
  3. CThey are composed of α-synuclein
  4. DThey are the hallmark of Huntington disease
  5. EThey contain ubiquitinated huntingtin
Answer
B. Neurofibrillary tangles: aggregation of tau (develop intracellularly) → persist extracellularly after neuronal death. Mutations in the tau protein gene increase risk for frontotemporal lobar degeneration. The mechanism: tau is a microtubule-associated protein present in axons; Aβ oligomers activate kinases → hyperphosphorylate tau → it loses its ability to bind microtubules → aggregates into tangles. Plaques, by contrast, are extracellular Aβ.
NCRS 40 · Neuropathology — Neurodegenerative Diseases776

Dr. Mohit Kaur · Department of Pharmacology. Eight classes, one final common pathway — and the four words that must be kept apart.

Dr. Mohit Kaur · Department of Pharmacology  ·  source pp. 2480–2607
Abuse is the excessive self-administration of any substance for nonmedical purposes. Almost all abused substances produce an effect on the brain that is perceived as desirable and will initiate drug-seeking behavior. Some drugs of abuse do not lead to addiction.Definition

The four terms — and why they are not synonyms

PHAR.00059src p.2480–2481 · 2498–2503
TermDefinition (verbatim)
AbuseThe excessive self-administration of any substance for nonmedical purposes.
AddictionBehaviors that include one or more of the following: impaired control over drug use · compulsive use · continued use despite harm · craving.
DependenceA state of adaptation manifested by the drug-class-specific withdrawal syndrome. The withdrawal syndrome can be produced by abrupt cessation, rapid dose reduction, or administration of an antagonist.
Withdrawal syndromePhysiological and behavioral changes directly related to sudden cessation or reduction in use of a drug to which the body has become adapted.
ToleranceA state of adaptation in which exposure to a drug induces changes that result in a diminution of one or more of the drug's effects over time. Tolerance may occur to both the desired and undesired effects of drugs, and may develop at different rates for different effects.

Dependence and tolerance are normal responses that often occur with the persistent use of certain medications. Physical dependence may develop with chronic use of many classes of medications, including β-blockers, α2-adrenergic agents, corticosteroids and antidepressants. The lecture's worked example: with opioids, tolerance usually develops more slowly to analgesia than to respiratory depression, and tolerance to the constipating effects may not occur at all.

Exam Lock
Dependence is not addiction
  • A patient on a β-blocker or a corticosteroid is physically dependent and will have a withdrawal syndrome if it is stopped abruptly — but has none of the four behaviours that define addiction. Getting this distinction right is the point of PHAR.00059, and it is the clinical reason opioid analgesia is not the same as opioid addiction.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse779

Neural mechanisms of addiction — three routes to the same dopamine

PHAR.00060src p.2504–2505

The mesolimbic dopamine system is the prime target of addictive drugs. As a general rule, all addictive drugs activate the mesolimbic dopamine system.

PHAR · Drugs of Abuse780

Ethanol

PHAR.00061 · PHAR.00062 · PHAR.00063src p.2482–2484 · 2509–2530
  • Ethanol is classed as a depressant because it produces sedation and sleep. However, the initial effects of ethanol are often perceived as stimulation, due to suppression of inhibitory systems.
  • Sites of action — ethanol influences several cellular functions: GABAA receptors · Kir3/GIRK channels · adenosine reuptake · glycine receptors · NMDA receptors · 5-HT3 receptors.

Withdrawal syndrome — the timeline

Tremor, nausea and vomiting, excessive sweating, agitation and anxiety→In some individuals, visual, tactile and auditory hallucinations→Generalized seizures may manifest after 24–48 hours→48–72 hours after cessation: alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens)

Management of withdrawal

  • Long half-life benzodiazepines are the preferred agents: diazepam and chlordiazepoxide. Because of their long half-life, withdrawal is smoother and rebound withdrawal symptoms are less likely.
  • Lorazepam and oxazepam are intermediate-acting drugs; they may be preferable in the elderly and those with liver failure.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse781

Ethanol (cont.)

PHAR.00061 · PHAR.00062 · PHAR.00063src p.2482–2484 · 2509–2530

Pharmacotherapy of alcohol addiction (PHAR.00063)

DrugMechanismDetail
DisulfiramInhibitor of aldehyde dehydrogenaseUsed to create aversion to drinking. If ethanol is consumed by a patient who has taken disulfiram, acetaldehyde accumulation leads to nausea, headache, flushing and hypotension. No longer commonly used.
NaltrexoneOpioid (μ) receptor antagonistAlcohol releases endogenous opioids, which activate μ receptors, resulting in dopamine release. Administration of naltrexone reduces craving for alcohol and decreases relapse to heavy drinking. FDA-approved for treatment of alcohol dependence.
AcamprosateMechanism unclear; an NMDA receptor antagonistMay work by blocking a hyperglutamatergic state in the alcoholic brain; shown to be efficacious in preventing relapse to alcohol drinking.
TopiramateFacilitates GABA function, antagonizes glutamate receptorsMay reduce cravings. Not FDA-approved for this indication.

Three drugs are FDA-approved for treatment of alcoholism: disulfiram, naltrexone and acamprosate.

Bottom Line
Naltrexone's mechanism drawn out
  • Ethanol evokes release of endorphins → activation of μ receptors inhibits the GABAergic interneuron → less GABA → the dopaminergic mesolimbic neuron is disinhibited → more dopamine. Naltrexone blocks the μ receptor → the interneuron is disinhibited → more GABA → less dopamine. That is route 1 of the addiction diagram, run forwards and then backwards.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse782

Benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and the methylxanthines

PHAR.00064 · PHAR.00065 · PHAR.00066 · PHAR.00067src p.2485–2486 · 2531–2549

Benzodiazepines and barbiturates (PHAR.00064 · PHAR.00065)

  • Benzodiazepines can cause physical dependence and addiction; addiction is rare.
  • Mechanism in the reward pathway: there are GABAA receptors on GABAergic interneurons; benzodiazepines are agonists at the GABAA receptor; activation of these receptors inhibits GABA release; the dopaminergic mesolimbic neuron is disinhibited and more dopamine is released.
  • Withdrawal syndrome: tremors, anxiety, perceptual disturbances, dysphoria, psychosis, and seizures. The syndrome can be life-threatening.
  • Management of benzodiazepine withdrawal: if the patient is on a short-acting drug they are switched to a long-acting drug — diazepam is the most used agent — and then the dose is gradually reduced.
  • Abuse problems with barbiturates resemble those seen with benzodiazepines.

Methylxanthines — caffeine, theophylline and theobromine

  • Caffeine is the most widely consumed stimulant.
  • Methylxanthines block presynaptic adenosine receptors. Activation of adenosine receptors inhibits norepinephrine release; therefore competitive antagonism of the receptors disinhibits — increases — norepinephrine release, and thus acts as a stimulant.
  • Caffeine may also block adenosine receptors on cortical neurons.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse783

Benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and the methylxanthines (cont.)

PHAR.00064 · PHAR.00065 · PHAR.00066 · PHAR.00067src p.2485–2486 · 2531–2549
DoseEffect
100–200 mg of caffeine (1–2 cups of coffee)Decrease in fatigue and increased mental alertness
1.5 g of caffeine (12–15 cups of coffee)Anxiety and tremors
2–5 g of caffeineSpinal cord is stimulated
Moderate dosesInsomnia, anxiety and agitation
High doseEmesis and convulsions
~10 g (about 100 cups of coffee)The lethal dose — induces cardiac arrhythmias. Death from caffeine is highly unlikely.

Tolerance can rapidly develop to the stimulating properties of caffeine. Caffeine withdrawal consists of feelings of fatigue and sedation. Addiction is rare.

PHAR · Drugs of Abuse784

Cocaine and the amphetamines

PHAR.00066 · PHAR.00067 · PHAR.00068src p.2487–2488 · 2550–2563
CocaineAmphetamines
ScheduleSchedule II (DEA)Schedule II (DEA)
MechanismInhibits dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake. Prolongation of dopaminergic effects in the brain's limbic system produces the intense euphoria.Increase release of catecholamines; also weak inhibitors of MAO; possible direct catecholaminergic agonists. Taken up into neurons by biogenic amine transporters; once inside, they interfere with VMAT, depleting synaptic vesicles; cytoplasmic dopamine rises and is released into the synapse by reversal of the DAT.
CNS actionsStimulation of cortex and brainstem; increases mental awareness and produces a feeling of well-being and euphoria; paranoia may occur after repeated doses; at high doses tremors and convulsions, followed by respiratory and vasomotor depression.Behavioral effects similar to cocaine, due to release of dopamine; increased alertness, decreased fatigue, depressed appetite and insomnia; at high doses, psychosis and convulsions.
Sympathetic actionsPeripherally potentiates the action of norepinephrine → tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis and diaphoresisActivate receptors through norepinephrine release
PharmacokineticsAbuse liability and dependence are greatest with IV injection and freebase ("crack") smoking. Rapidly de-esterified and demethylated to benzoylecgonine, which is excreted in the urine — detection of this substance in the urine identifies a user.—
WithdrawalDysphoria, depression, sleepiness, fatigue, cocaine craving and bradycardia. Cocaine withdrawal is generally mild; treatment of withdrawal symptoms is usually not required.Tolerance can be marked. An abstinence syndrome can occur: increased appetite, sleepiness, exhaustion and mental depression. Antidepressants may be indicated.
Therapeutic usesMany agents, mainly antidepressants and dopamine agonists, have been tested as treatments for cocaine abuse. None have demonstrated clear efficacy.Attention deficit syndrome: amphetamine and methylphenidate. Narcolepsy: amphetamine and methylphenidate. Also appetite control.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse785

Cocaine and the amphetamines (cont.)

PHAR.00066 · PHAR.00067 · PHAR.00068src p.2487–2488 · 2550–2563
Trap
Cocaine blocks the transporter; amphetamine reverses it
  • Both raise synaptic dopamine, but by opposite manoeuvres. Cocaine sits on DAT and stops reuptake. Amphetamine is carried IN by DAT, empties the vesicles via VMAT, and then makes DAT run backwards. That is why amphetamine's effect survives vesicle depletion and cocaine's does not.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse786

Nicotine

PHAR.00069src p.2489–2491 · 2565–2571
  • The active ingredient of tobacco. Second only to caffeine as the most widely used CNS stimulant, and second only to alcohol as the most abused drug. In combination with the tars and CO in cigarette smoke, nicotine represents a serious risk factor for lung and cardiovascular disease, various cancers and other illnesses. In terms of numbers affected, addiction to nicotine exceeds all other forms of addiction.
  • Pharmacokinetics: highly liposoluble, so absorption occurs readily via the oral mucosa, lungs, gastrointestinal mucosa and skin. Nicotine crosses the placental membrane and is secreted in the milk of lactating women. By inhaling tobacco smoke the average smoker takes in 1 to 2 mg of nicotine per cigarette (most cigarettes contain 6 to 8 mg).

Mechanism and actions

  • Full agonist of the nicotinic receptor. The rewarding effect involves nicotinic receptors expressed ON dopamine neurons — when nicotine excites these neurons, dopamine is released. *(This is route 2: direct stimulation.)*
  • In low doses: ganglionic stimulation by depolarization. At high doses: ganglionic blockade.
  • CNS: low doses produce some degree of euphoria and relaxation, and improve attention, learning, problem solving and reaction time. High doses result in central respiratory paralysis and severe hypotension caused by medullary paralysis. Nicotine is an appetite suppressant.
  • Withdrawal is mild — irritability and sleeplessness — yet nicotine is among the most addictive drugs and relapse is very common.

Treatment of nicotine addiction (PHAR.00069)

TherapyDetail
Nicotine replacement therapyTransdermal patch, gum, nasal spray, vapor inhaler, or lozenge for buccal absorption
Sustained-release bupropionMechanism unclear. Associated with seizures: patients with a history of seizure, stroke, brain tumor, brain surgery, or severe head injury should not take bupropion.
VareniclineA partial agonist at neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the CNS. Varenicline binds to the nicotinic receptor with greater affinity than nicotine, thus reducing the reward of smoking. The most common adverse effect is nausea.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse787

Opioids and marijuana

PHAR.00060 · PHAR.00070 · PHAR.00071 · PHAR.00072src p.2492–2493 · 2573–2590

Opioids

  • The most commonly abused opioids are heroin, morphine, codeine and oxycodone.
  • All opioids induce strong tolerance and dependence. Addiction to heroin or other short-acting opioids produces behavioural disruptions and is usually incompatible with a productive life.
  • The withdrawal syndrome is unpleasant but NOT life-threatening: dysphoria, lacrimation, rhinorrhea and yawning.
  • Mechanism: there are μ opioid receptors on GABAergic interneurons; opioids are agonists at the μ receptor; activation causes less GABA to be released; the dopaminergic mesolimbic neuron is disinhibited and more dopamine is released.
ApproachDetail
Detoxification using opioid agonistsThe illicit agent is replaced by a long-acting opioid and the dose is slowly reduced. Drugs used: methadone or buprenorphine. Methadone is a useful drug for detoxification and maintenance of the chronic relapsing heroin addict — the lecture's graph contrasts heroin's repeated high–sick swings with methadone's flat curve.
Detoxification using opioid antagonistsNaltrexone is an antagonist with a high affinity for the μ opioid receptor; it can be used AFTER detoxification for patients with high motivation to remain opioid-free.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse788

Opioids and marijuana (cont.)

PHAR.00060 · PHAR.00070 · PHAR.00071 · PHAR.00072src p.2492–2493 · 2573–2590

Marijuana (PHAR.00070–00072)

  • The smoke from burning cannabis contains many chemicals, including 61 different cannabinoids. One of these, Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9-THC, THC, dronabinol), produces most of the characteristic pharmacological effects.
  • Two cannabinoid receptor subtypes: CB1 and CB2; both are Gi protein-linked. CB1 receptors are found primarily in the brain and mediate the psychological effects of THC; CB2 receptors are present mainly on immune cells.
  • Mechanism in the reward pathway: CB1 receptors are present on GABAergic neurons; binding of THC decreases GABA release; this disinhibits dopaminergic neurons, increasing dopamine release.
  • Actions: THC can produce euphoria, followed by drowsiness and relaxation; affects short-term memory and mental activity; impairs highly skilled motor activity. Other effects: appetite stimulation, xerostomia, visual hallucinations, delusions, enhancement of sensory activity. At high doses: toxic psychosis.
  • Tolerance and mild physical dependence occur with continued, frequent use.
CannabinoidApproved indication (verbatim)
Dronabinol — the synthetic form of THCNausea and vomiting associated with cancer chemotherapy in patients who have failed to respond to conventional antiemetic treatments; also anorexia associated with weight loss in patients with AIDS
Nabilone — a synthetic derivative of THCNausea and vomiting associated with cancer chemotherapy after failure of conventional antiemetics
Cannabidiol (CBD)Seizures associated with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome, or tuberous sclerosis complex. CBD does not have activity at the CB1 or CB2 receptors.

Dronabinol and nabilone can produce psychotropic effects and often cause lethargy, drowsiness, ataxia and dry mouth; rarely, they cause euphoria.

PHAR · Drugs of Abuse789

Psychedelic agents

PHAR.00073src p.2494–2495 · 2592–2602

Psychedelic drugs affect thought, perception and mood. They don't cause marked psychomotor stimulation or depression. The class: LSD · mescaline · psilocybin · phencyclidine · MDMA.

AgentMechanismPresentation and management
LSD (with mescaline and psilocybin)The hallucinogenic actions of LSD appear to be mediated by AGONIST effects at 5-HT2 receptors in the CNS.Patients present with a combination of somatic and psychomimetic symptoms. Somatic symptoms are due to sympathomimetic effects: mydriasis, hypertension, tachycardia, increased body temperature, flushing, sweating, tremors and piloerection. Users may require medical attention because of "bad trips"; severe agitation may require treatment with a benzodiazepine. LSD does not cause addiction and there is no withdrawal syndrome.
Phencyclidine (PCP)The dissociative properties of PCP are due to NON-COMPETITIVE ANTAGONISM at NMDA receptors. It also blocks reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, causes cholinergic and anticholinergic effects, and has actions at nicotinic and opioid receptors. *Originally used as an anesthetic; withdrawn in humans due to adverse effects; retained in veterinary practice.*Patients alternate from agitation to stupor. Paranoid behavior and extreme violence may occur unexpectedly. Both vertical and horizontal nystagmus is common. Pupils may be large or small. Hypertension, tachycardia and hyperthermia. Muscle rigidity, dystonias and seizures. Hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis resulting in myoglobinuria and renal failure. There is no specific antidote; violent psychotic behavior requires sedation with parenteral benzodiazepines, and seizures should be treated with benzodiazepines. Ketamine shares many structural, pharmacologic and clinical characteristics with PCP and is a popular drug of abuse.
MDMA ("ecstasy")A derivative of amphetamine. Like amphetamines, MDMA causes release of biogenic amines by reversing the action of their transporters; it has preferential affinity for SERT and therefore most strongly increases the concentration of serotonin in the synapse.Acute effects: enhanced sensory perception, increased extroversion, emotional warmth, empathy. Adverse effects: tachycardia, dry mouth, jaw clenching, muscle aches; at higher doses visual hallucinations, agitation, hyperthermia and panic attacks. Hyperthermia, along with dehydration, may be fatal. Other complications include serotonin syndrome and seizures. Withdrawal is characterized by depression.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse790

Psychedelic agents (cont.)

PHAR.00073src p.2494–2495 · 2592–2602
Exam Lock
Nystagmus in both planes is the PCP giveaway
  • Both vertical AND horizontal nystagmus in an agitated, violent patient with hypertension, hyperthermia and rigidity is PCP, and the treatment is benzodiazepines for both the behaviour and the seizures — there is no specific antidote. Note the hyperthermia trio again: PCP, MDMA and serotonin syndrome all kill through temperature.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse791

Inhalants and anabolic steroids

PHAR.00074 · PHAR.00075src p.2496 · 2604–2606
InhalantDetail (verbatim)
Nitrous oxideSometimes used as an intoxicant by medical personnel. It produces euphoria and analgesia and then loss of consciousness. Usually taken as 35% N₂O mixed with O₂; administration of 100% N₂O may cause asphyxia and death.
Volatile organic solventsAliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons — gasoline, paint thinner, lighter fluid, glue and degreasers. Boys in early teen years from lower socioeconomic classes are the principal users. They produce a sense of exhilaration and light-headedness. Toxicity depends on the properties of individual solvents; they have been implicated in cancer, cardiotoxicity, neuropathies and hepatotoxicity.
Organic nitritesAmyl nitrite produces dilation of smooth muscle and has been used for treatment of angina. In recent years amyl nitrite and butyl nitrite have been used to enhance erection. They are NOT addictive.

Anabolic steroids (PHAR.00075)

  • Anabolic-androgenic steroids are used to increase muscle size and definition and are sometimes co-abused with other growth enhancers, such as human growth hormone.
  • In sports in which mass, physical size, or even total strength is important, the abuse of anabolic steroids provides a shortcut to attainment of the physical stature that might otherwise require much more extensive training and exercise.

PHAR · Drugs of Abuse794

Block exam — drugs of abuse

PHAR.00059

A patient on long-term propranolol develops tachycardia and tremor when it is stopped abruptly. Which term does this lecture apply, and which does it NOT?

  1. AAddiction; not dependence
  2. BPhysical dependence with a withdrawal syndrome; not addiction
  3. CTolerance; not dependence
  4. DAbuse; not tolerance
  5. EAll four terms apply
Answer
B. Dependence: a state of adaptation manifested by the drug-class-specific withdrawal syndrome... Dependence and tolerance are normal responses that often occur with the persistent use of certain medications. Physical dependence may develop with chronic use of many classes of medications. These include β-blockers, α2-adrenergic agents, corticosteroids, antidepressants. Addiction requires the behaviours impaired control over drug use, compulsive use, continued use despite harm, craving, none of which are present here.
PHAR.00062

Sixty hours after his last drink, an alcohol-dependent man becomes disoriented with visual hallucinations, fever and autonomic instability. What is this, and which agents are preferred?

  1. AAlcoholic hallucinosis; haloperidol
  2. BDelirium tremens; long half-life benzodiazepines — diazepam and chlordiazepoxide
  3. CWernicke encephalopathy; thiamine alone
  4. DSeizure; phenytoin
  5. ESerotonin syndrome; cyproheptadine
Answer
B. The lecture's timeline: withdrawal begins with tremor, nausea and vomiting, sweating, agitation and anxiety, may be followed by hallucinations, generalized seizures may appear after 24–48 h, and after 48–72 h delirium tremens may appear. Management: long half-life benzodiazepines are the preferred agents — diazepam and chlordiazepoxide — because their long half-life makes withdrawal smoother and rebound symptoms less likely; lorazepam and oxazepam are intermediate-acting and may be preferable in the elderly and those with liver failure.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse795

Block exam — drugs of abuse (cont.)

PHAR.00063

Which alcohol pharmacotherapy works by blocking μ opioid receptors, and how does that reduce dopamine release?

  1. ADisulfiram; it inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase
  2. BNaltrexone; ethanol-evoked endorphins normally inhibit the GABAergic interneuron, so blocking μ receptors restores GABA release and re-inhibits the mesolimbic dopamine neuron
  3. CAcamprosate; NMDA antagonism
  4. DTopiramate; GABA facilitation
  5. EVarenicline; nicotinic partial agonism
Answer
B. Alcohol releases endogenous opioids, which activate μ receptors, resulting in dopamine release. Administration of the opioid antagonist naltrexone reduces craving for alcohol and decreases relapse to heavy drinking. The lecture animates it: ethanol → endorphins → μ activation inhibits the GABAergic interneuron → less GABA → dopaminergic mesolimbic neuron disinhibited → more dopamine. Naltrexone blocks μ → the interneuron is disinhibited → more GABA → less dopamine.
PHAR.00066

Which mechanism distinguishes amphetamine from cocaine?

  1. ACocaine reverses the dopamine transporter; amphetamine blocks it
  2. BAmphetamine is taken into the neuron, depletes vesicles via VMAT and reverses the DAT; cocaine blocks reuptake at DAT, NET and SERT
  3. CBoth block MAO irreversibly
  4. DCocaine acts at 5-HT2 receptors; amphetamine at NMDA
  5. EAmphetamine blocks adenosine receptors
Answer
B. Cocaine inhibits dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake. Amphetamines are taken up into neurons by biogenic amine transporters; once in the neuron, amphetamines interfere with the VMAT, depleting synaptic vesicles; levels of dopamine in the cytoplasm increase and are released into the synapse by reversal of the DAT. Amphetamines are also weak inhibitors of MAO and possible direct catecholaminergic agonists.
PHAR.00066 · PHAR.00067

A urine screen identifies benzoylecgonine. Which drug does this indicate, and which routes carry the greatest abuse liability?

  1. AAmphetamine; oral
  2. BCocaine; IV injection and freebase ("crack") smoking
  3. CMDMA; oral
  4. DHeroin; intranasal
  5. EPCP; inhalation
Answer
B. Cocaine is rapidly de-esterified and demethylated to benzoylecgonine, which is excreted in the urine; detection of this substance in the urine identifies a user. Abuse liability and dependence are greatest with IV injection and freebase ("crack") smoking. Withdrawal is dysphoria, depression, sleepiness, fatigue, craving and bradycardia — generally mild, and no agent has demonstrated clear efficacy for cocaine addiction.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse796

Block exam — drugs of abuse (cont.)

PHAR.00069

A patient wants help stopping smoking but has a history of head injury with post-traumatic seizures. Which agent should be avoided, and which acts as a nicotinic partial agonist?

  1. AAvoid varenicline; bupropion is the partial agonist
  2. BAvoid bupropion because of seizure risk; varenicline is the partial agonist that binds nicotinic receptors with greater affinity than nicotine
  3. CAvoid nicotine patches; bupropion is the partial agonist
  4. DAvoid both; only patches are safe
  5. EAvoid varenicline; nicotine gum is the partial agonist
Answer
B. Bupropion is associated with seizures: patients with a history of seizure, stroke, brain tumor, brain surgery, or severe head injury should not take bupropion. Varenicline is a partial agonist at neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the CNS; it binds to the nicotinic receptor with greater affinity than nicotine, thus reducing the reward of smoking. The most common adverse effects are nausea.
PHAR.00070 · PHAR.00071

Which cannabinoid receptor mediates the psychological effects of THC, and how does THC raise dopamine?

  1. ACB2 on immune cells; by direct dopaminergic agonism
  2. BCB1 in the brain; THC binding to CB1 on GABAergic neurons decreases GABA release, disinhibiting dopaminergic neurons
  3. CCB1 on dopamine neurons; by transporter reversal
  4. DCB2 in the brain; by NMDA antagonism
  5. ENeither — THC acts at 5-HT2
Answer
B. Two cannabinoid receptor subtypes: CB1 and CB2; both are Gi protein-linked. CB1 receptors are found primarily in the brain and mediate the psychological effects of THC; CB2 receptors are present mainly on immune cells. CB1 receptors are present in GABAergic neurons; binding of THC to CB1 receptors decreases GABA release; decrease of GABA release disinhibits dopaminergic neurons, resulting in increased dopamine release.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse797

Block exam — drugs of abuse (cont.)

PHAR.00073

An agitated, violent patient has both vertical and horizontal nystagmus, hypertension, hyperthermia and muscle rigidity, and later develops myoglobinuria. Which drug, and what is the treatment?

  1. ALSD; a benzodiazepine and reassurance
  2. BPhencyclidine; there is no specific antidote — parenteral benzodiazepines for the violent behaviour and for seizures
  3. CMDMA; cyproheptadine
  4. DCocaine; a β-blocker
  5. ECannabis; supportive care only
Answer
B. Phencyclidine: patients alternate from agitation to stupor; paranoid behavior and extreme violence may occur unexpectedly; both vertical and horizontal nystagmus is common; pupils may be large or small; hypertension, tachycardia and hyperthermia; muscle rigidity, dystonias and seizures; hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis resulting in myoglobinuria and renal failure. There is no specific antidote for PCP; extreme violent psychotic behavior requires sedation with parenteral benzodiazepines; seizures should be treated with benzodiazepines. Its dissociative properties are non-competitive antagonism at NMDA receptors.
PHAR.00073

Which statement about LSD is correct?

  1. AIt is a 5-HT2 antagonist and causes a severe withdrawal syndrome
  2. BIts hallucinogenic actions are mediated by agonist effects at 5-HT2 receptors; it does not cause addiction and there is no withdrawal syndrome
  3. CIt acts at NMDA receptors like PCP
  4. DIts somatic effects are parasympathetic
  5. EBad trips require haloperidol
Answer
B. The hallucinogenic actions of LSD appear to be mediated by agonist effects at 5-HT2 receptors in the CNS. LSD does not cause addiction. There is no withdrawal syndrome. The somatic symptoms are due to sympathomimetic effects: mydriasis, hypertension, tachycardia, increased body temperature, flushing, sweating, tremors and piloerection, and severe agitation may require treatment with a benzodiazepine.
PHAR.00074

Which inhalant is explicitly described as NOT addictive, and what was its original medical use?

  1. ANitrous oxide; anaesthesia
  2. BToluene; industrial solvent
  3. CAmyl nitrite; treatment of angina
  4. DGasoline; none
  5. EButane; none
Answer
C. Organic nitrites: amyl nitrite produces dilation of smooth muscle and has been used for treatment of angina. In recent years amyl nitrite and butyl nitrite have been used to enhance erection. They are not addictive. For contrast: nitrous oxide produces euphoria and analgesia and then loss of consciousness, usually taken as 35% N₂O mixed with O₂; administration of 100% N₂O may cause asphyxia and death, and volatile organic solvents are principally used by boys in early teen years from lower socioeconomic classes.
PHAR · Drugs of Abuse798
PATH

Neuropathology 4 — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS Tumors

Dr. Adesola Adeleye · Department of Pathology. The last neuropathology lecture: myelin, nutrition and neoplasia.

Dr. Adesola Adeleye · Department of Pathology  ·  source pp. 2608–2643

Learning objectives — verbatim

  • PATH.7032 Compare multiple sclerosis (MS), post-infectious immune demyelination (ADEM, AHEM) and central pontine myelinolysis in terms of their: i) etiology, ii) age at onset, iii) distribution of lesions, iv) morphology and v) clinical course.
  • PATH.7033 Compare Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff psychosis in terms of their: i) etiology, ii) pathogenesis, iii) morphology and iv) clinical findings.

  • PATH.7043 Discuss the relevance of morphological findings and clinical presentations in diagnosis of glioblastoma multiforme and meningiomas. Correlate them with different underlying pathophysiological mechanisms, and course of the diseases and other CNS tumors.

What are demyelinating disorders?

PATH.7032src p.2613
  • Axons in the CNS are tightly ensheathed by myelin, which allows rapid propagation of neuronal impulses. Myelinated axons are the dominant component of the white matter.

Two types of myelin disorder

  1. Loss of myelination ("de-myelination") — acquired conditions with preferential damage to previously normal myelin: multiple sclerosis (MS) · post-infectious / immune (ADEM, AHEM) · myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination syndrome)
  2. Improper myelin formation ("dys-myelination")
NCRS 42 · Neuropathology — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS Tumors800

Multiple sclerosis

PATH.7032src p.2614–2618
An autoimmune demyelinating disorder characterized by disease activity separated in TIME, that produces white matter lesions that are separated in SPACE. The most common demyelinating disorder.Definition
Epidemiology
  • Affects young adults
  • F:M = 2:1
Risk factors (etiology not known)
  • Smoking
  • Low vitamin D
  • Moving to an endemic area before puberty
  • Genetic susceptibility: HLA-DRB1
  • Family history

Pathogenesis

  • Autoimmune response directed against antigens of the myelin sheath.
  • Th1 and Th17 T cells react against myelin antigens and secrete cytokines: Th1 releases IFN-γ, which attracts and activates macrophages; Th17 releases IL-17, which attracts neutrophils → inflammation causing demyelination.
  • B lymphocytes and antibodies also play a less clear role.
  • Genetic factor — the major histocompatibility complex: each copy of the HLA-DRB1*1501 allele an individual inherits brings a roughly 3-fold increase in the risk for MS.
NCRS 42 · Neuropathology — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS Tumors801

Multiple sclerosis (cont.)

PATH.7032src p.2614–2618

Morphology

Gross
Primarily a multifocal white matter disease with patchy loss of myelin. Characteristic plaque: discrete, slightly depressed, glassy-appearing, red-tan. Common near the ventricles, optic nerves, chiasm, brainstem, white matter tracts, cerebellum and spinal cord.
Microscopy
Active plaques: abundant macrophages with engulfed myelin breakdown products, and perivascular lymphocytic inflammation. Inactive plaques: inflammation disappears, leaving behind no myelin, replaced by astrocytic proliferation — gliosis.

Clinical features and laboratory findings

  • Symptoms relate to the area involved: optic neuritis, ataxia/intention tremor, weakness/spasticity and abnormal sensations.
  • Variable course with multiple relapses and remissions. Attacks are separated by time (episodic) and space — the most important clue. Gradual step-wise accumulation of neurological deficits.
  • CSF: elevated protein with increased immunoglobulin ("oligoclonal bands") and moderate pleocytosis. Electrophoresis of serum and CSF shows patterns of increased immunoglobulin-G production.
  • MRI shows white matter plaques, most commonly periventricular.
Exam Lock
Time and space — then confirm with two tests
  • The definition itself is the diagnostic criterion: activity separated in time, lesions separated in space. The two confirmatory findings are oligoclonal bands in the CSF and periventricular white matter plaques on MRI.
NCRS 42 · Neuropathology — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS Tumors802

Post-infectious demyelination, and central pontine myelinolysis

PATH.7032src p.2619–2620
Immune-mediated demyelination that occurs following a number of systemic infectious illnesses, usually mild viral diseases. May occasionally occur following vaccination. The mechanism possibly includes cross-reacting antibodies that result in myelin damage. Two patterns cause an acute-onset MONOPHASIC illness.Post-infectious demyelination
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)Acute necrotizing hemorrhagic encephalomyelitis (AHEM)
FeaturesNon-localizing symptoms (vs. MS) over 1–2 weeksSimilar but more devastating than ADEM; in children and young adults; preceded by an infection; rapid progression
OutcomeRarely fatalMore severe

Central pontine myelinolysis / osmotic demyelination

  • Non-immune damage to oligodendrocytes of the pons, typically after SUDDEN CORRECTION of hyponatremia, that may result in a rapidly evolving quadriplegia and bulbar palsy → locked-in syndrome (only eye movement unaffected).
  • The concept has been extended with the recognition that lesions occur outside the pons — so-called "extrapontine myelinolysis".
  • Pathogenesis: rapid correction of hyponatremia → fluid movement from intracellular to extracellular compartment, causing contraction of oligodendrocytes and apoptosis. Remember: oligodendrocytes form the myelin sheath by wrapping their cell bodies and dendrites around the neuron's axon, so apoptosis of oligodendrocytes → demyelination.
  • Only occurs in CHRONIC hyponatremia (> 2 days), because osmolytes — potassium, chloride and organic osmolytes such as glucose and glutamine — are pushed out of the cell over about 2 days to balance the osmotic gradient. When hyponatremia is corrected rapidly there are no osmolytes within the cell to keep fluid from rapidly moving out → oligodendrocyte contraction and apoptosis.
NCRS 42 · Neuropathology — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS Tumors803

Post-infectious demyelination, and central pontine myelinolysis (cont.)

PATH.7032src p.2619–2620
Trap
The two-day rule is why acute hyponatraemia is safe to correct quickly
  • Osmotic demyelination needs a cell that has already exported its osmolytes — which takes about two days. That is the mechanistic reason the syndrome is a complication of chronic hyponatraemia only, and it is exactly the kind of "why" the exam builds a question around.
NCRS 42 · Neuropathology — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS Tumors804

Toxic and acquired metabolic disease — thiamine and alcohol

PATH.7033src p.2622–2624
  • A relatively common cause of neurologic illness. The brain is particularly vulnerable to nutritional diseases and alterations in metabolic state because of the high metabolic demands of neurons.
  • Nutritional: vitamin deficiency — thiamine and B12. Metabolic: hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, hepatic encephalopathy. Toxic: ethanol, cocaine, medications, industrial products and environmental toxins.

Thiamine deficiency (PATH.7033)

  • Thiamine (vitamin B1) is essential for converting glucose into energy (ATP) in the brain; it acts as a co-enzyme (thiamine pyrophosphate) for key enzymes in glucose metabolism.
  • Deficiency → abrupt onset of encephalopathy called Wernicke encephalopathy, characterized by the triad: encephalopathy presenting with confusion · ocular palsies · ataxia.
  • Risks: chronic alcoholism, GI surgery, anorexia.
  • Laboratory studies: ETKAC (erythrocyte transketolase activity coefficient) > 1.25 — low transketolase activity.
  • Treatment with thiamine reverses these deficits. Delayed treatment leads to an irreversible memory disturbance called Korsakoff's syndrome — no new memories and confabulation.
  • Pathological features include foci of hemorrhage and necrosis, most commonly in the mamillary bodies.

Alcohol as a neurotoxic agent

  • Ethanol can lead to multiple neurological manifestations: peripheral neuropathy · cerebellar degeneration · seizures (from withdrawal in alcoholics) · Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (with severe malnutrition associated with alcoholism).
  • Morphology of alcoholic cerebellar degeneration: the anterior vermis is atrophic with wide spaces between folia.
Exam Lock
Wernicke is reversible; Korsakoff is what is left behind
  • Treatment with thiamine reverses the Wernicke triad. Delayed treatment leaves the irreversible memory disturbance of Korsakoff's syndrome — no new memories and confabulation. The lesion to name is haemorrhage and necrosis of the mamillary bodies.

The astrocytoma spectrum — the lecture's classification table

PATH.7031 · PATH.7043src p.2628–2631
FeaturePilocytic astrocytomaAstrocytoma, IDH-mutantGlioblastoma, IDH wild-type
GradeIII–IIIIV

Oligodendroglioma, ependymoma and medulloblastoma

PATH.7031src p.2632–2636
TumourAge and siteGeneticsMorphology and clinical
Oligodendroglioma4th–5th decade; insidious onset; most common site: cerebral hemispheres, especially frontal and temporal lobesCodeletion of 1p and 19q — good prognosis. IDH1 or IDH2 mutation — good prognosis.Clinical: several years of antecedent neurological symptoms, especially seizures. Gross: gray, cystic mass with focal hemorrhage and calcification. Microscopy: cells with round nuclei, clear cytoplasm forming halos ("fried egg" appearance) and thin-walled capillaries.
EpendymomaMost common site: ependymal cells lining the ventricular cavity, including the central canal of the spinal cord. First 2 decades — 4th ventricle. Adults — mostly in the spinal cord, with an association with neurofibromatosis 2.Ependymomas do not share the genetic alterations found in infiltrating gliomas.Microscopy: regular cells with round-to-oval nuclei and abundant granular chromatin; variable fibrillary background. Cells may form true ROSETTES with long delicate processes extending into the lumen ("canals"), and PERIVASCULAR PSEUDOROSETTES — tumor cells arranged around vessels.
Medulloblastoma (embryonal tumour)The most common CNS malignancy in children — 20% of pediatric brain tumors. Most common site: cerebellum (posterior fossa).Wnt-β-catenin pathway; MYC overexpression. IHC: a mixture of neuronal and glial markers.Neuroectodermal origin — small round blue cells, remnants of the normal progenitor cells during embryology. Microscopy: sheets of small round blue anaplastic cells, hyperchromatic nuclei, abundant mitoses, scant cytoplasm, Homer Wright rosettes. Gross: well circumscribed, gray, friable; may involve leptomeninges. Grade IV, highly malignant; prognosis generally poor if untreated, better if β-catenin is involved; very radiosensitive — 75% of patients treated are alive after 5 years.
Bottom Line
Rosettes are not one word
  • Homer Wright rosettes → medulloblastoma (cells around a fibrillary centre). True rosettes with a gland-like central lumen and perivascular pseudorosettes → ependymoma. "Fried egg" cells with perinuclear halos → oligodendroglioma. Three patterns, three tumours, and each is the fastest route to the answer on a histology stem.
NCRS 42 · Neuropathology — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS Tumors808

Meningioma, schwannoma and metastases

PATH.7031 · PATH.7043src p.2637–2640
TumourDetail (verbatim)
MeningiomaOrigin: arachnoid meningothelial cells; attached to the dura mater. Age: mostly in adults. Location: either on the external surface of the brain or the ventricular system. Clinical features: vague non-localizing symptoms plus focal symptoms due to compression of adjacent brain. Prognosis depends on size, location, surgical accessibility and histological grade. Associations: multiple meningiomas + 8th nerve schwannoma or glial tumors → neurofibromatosis type 2. Genetics: chromosome 22q. Histology: a whorled pattern of cell growth and psammoma bodies — calcifications with concentric rings; grossly parasagittal, multi-lobular, attached to the dura and compressing the underlying brain.
SchwannomaBenign encapsulated tumors that may occur in soft tissues, internal organs, or spinal nerve roots. Most commonly affected cranial nerve: the vestibular portion of the eighth nerve ("acoustic neuroma" / vestibular schwannoma) at the cerebellopontine angle. Associated with NF2. Genetics: chromosome 22q. Clinical features: hearing loss, tinnitus. Gross: circumscribed masses abutting an adjacent nerve. Histology: dense pink ANTONI A areas and loose, pale, myxoid ANTONI B areas, with hyalinized blood vessels; in Antoni A areas the nuclei align in palisading rows called VEROCAY BODIES.
Secondary (metastatic) tumoursMost commonly metastatic carcinomas; account for 25% to 50% of intracranial tumors. Most common primary sites: lung, breast, skin (melanoma), kidney and GIT. Metastases form sharply demarcated masses (usually multiple but can be single) at the grey-white matter junction. Paraneoplastic syndromes can involve the central and peripheral nervous systems; the common pattern is cerebellar degeneration (ataxia), limbic encephalitis (dementia), and sensory neuropathy.
Trap
Chromosome 22q appears twice — and links them
  • Meningioma and schwannoma both map to chromosome 22q, and multiple meningiomas plus an eighth nerve schwannoma, or glial tumours, define neurofibromatosis type 2 — which also explains the adult spinal ependymoma association a slide earlier. One syndrome, three tumours.

Block exam — demyelination, toxicology and CNS tumours

PATH.7032

A 28-year-old woman has had optic neuritis, and two years later develops leg spasticity. MRI shows periventricular white matter plaques. Which CSF finding supports the diagnosis, and which T-cell subsets drive it?

  1. AXanthochromia; Th2 cells
  2. BOligoclonal bands; Th1 releasing IFN-γ and Th17 releasing IL-17
  3. CLow glucose; cytotoxic T cells
  4. DNeutrophilia; B cells only
  5. ENormal CSF; NK cells
Answer
B. Multiple sclerosis — disease activity separated in time, producing white matter lesions separated in space. CSF analysis: elevated protein with increased immunoglobulin ("oligoclonal bands") and moderate pleocytosis; MRI shows white matter plaques, most commonly periventricular. Pathogenesis: Th1 and Th17 T cells react against myelin antigens; Th1 releases IFN-γ which attracts and activates macrophages, and Th17 releases IL-17 which attracts neutrophils → inflammation causing demyelination.
PATH.7032

A patient's chronic hyponatraemia of 112 mmol/L is corrected to 132 over 8 hours. Two days later she develops quadriplegia and bulbar palsy with preserved eye movements. What is the mechanism, and why does chronicity matter?

  1. AImmune demyelination; chronic disease sensitises the immune system
  2. BOsmotic demyelination — oligodendrocytes have exported their osmolytes over ~2 days, so rapid correction drives fluid out, causing cell contraction and apoptosis
  3. CPontine infarction; chronic hyponatraemia causes vasospasm
  4. DWernicke encephalopathy; thiamine is lost with sodium
  5. EMultiple sclerosis; hyponatraemia is a trigger
Answer
B. Central pontine myelinolysis: non-immune damage to oligodendrocytes of the pons typically after sudden correction of hyponatremia, that may result in a rapidly evolving quadriplegia and bulbar palsy → locked-in syndrome (only eye movement unaffected)... Only occurs in chronic hyponatremia (> 2 days) because osmolytes — potassium, chloride and organic osmolytes such as glucose and glutamine — are pushed out of the cell over a period of 2 days... When hyponatremia is corrected rapidly, there are no osmolytes within the cell to keep fluid from rapidly moving to the extracellular compartment → oligodendrocyte contraction and apoptosis.
NCRS 42 · Neuropathology — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS Tumors812

Block exam — demyelination, toxicology and CNS tumours (cont.)

PATH.7033

A malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder has confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. Which structure shows haemorrhage and necrosis, and what happens if treatment is delayed?

  1. AHippocampus; Alzheimer disease
  2. BMamillary bodies; irreversible Korsakoff's syndrome with inability to form new memories and confabulation
  3. CSubstantia nigra; parkinsonism
  4. DCaudate; chorea
  5. EPons; locked-in syndrome
Answer
B. Wernicke encephalopathy is characterized by the triad: encephalopathy presenting with confusion, ocular palsies, and ataxia... Pathological features include foci of hemorrhage and necrosis most commonly in the mamillary bodies... Treatment with thiamine reverses these deficits; delayed treatment leads to an irreversible memory disturbance called Korsakoff's syndrome — no new memories and confabulation. The laboratory marker is ETKAC > 1.25.
PATH.7031 · PATH.7043

A 62-year-old has a rapidly enlarging hemispheric mass that crosses the corpus callosum with haemorrhage and necrosis. Histology shows microvascular proliferation and tumour nuclei arrayed around anucleate necrotic zones. Which tumour, grade and genetics?

  1. APilocytic astrocytoma; grade I; BRAF translocation
  2. BGlioblastoma, IDH wild-type; grade IV; EGFR and PDGFR amplification, TP53 mutation, TERT promoter mutation, CDKN2A deletion
  3. COligodendroglioma; grade II; 1p/19q codeletion
  4. DEpendymoma; grade II; no infiltrating-glioma mutations
  5. EMedulloblastoma; grade IV; MYC overexpression
Answer
B. Glioblastoma, IDH wild-type — grade IV; cerebral hemispheres; EGFR and PDGFR gene amplification, TP53 mutation (resistant to apoptosis), telomerase mutation, biallelic deletion of CDKN2A, TERT promoter mutation; gross: infiltrating tumor with hemorrhage and necrosis crossing the midline ("butterfly glioma"); histology: microvascular proliferation with areas of "pseudo"-palisading necrosis.
NCRS 42 · Neuropathology — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS Tumors813

Block exam — demyelination, toxicology and CNS tumours (cont.)

PATH.7031

A 7-year-old has a cerebellar cystic lesion with a mural nodule; histology shows bipolar cells with hair-like processes and brightly eosinophilic corkscrew inclusions. Which tumour and which genetic change?

  1. AMedulloblastoma; MYC
  2. BPilocytic astrocytoma; BRAF translocation
  3. CEpendymoma; NF2
  4. DGlioblastoma; EGFR
  5. EOligodendroglioma; 1p/19q
Answer
B. Pilocytic astrocytoma — grade I; cerebellum; BRAF translocations; gross: cystic lesion with a mural nodule; histology: bipolar cells with thin hair-like ("pilo") processes in a fibrillary meshwork with eosinophilic rod-like structures — ROSENTHAL FIBERS, seen at low magnification as a biphasic pattern with alternating loose and compact regions. It is one of the three commonest paediatric tumours, with medulloblastoma and ependymoma, all in the infratentorial posterior fossa.
PATH.7031

Which histological feature belongs to ependymoma?

  1. AHomer Wright rosettes
  2. BPerivascular pseudorosettes and true rosettes with a gland-like lumen
  3. CRosenthal fibres
  4. DPsammoma bodies
  5. EVerocay bodies
Answer
B. Ependymoma microscopy: regular cells with round-to-oval nuclei and abundant granular chromatin; variable fibrillary background; cells may form rosettes with long delicate processes extending into the lumen ("canals"); also seen are "pseudo"-rosettes which are perivascular, with tumor cells around vessels. Homer Wright rosettes → medulloblastoma; Rosenthal fibres → pilocytic astrocytoma; psammoma bodies → meningioma; Verocay bodies → schwannoma.
NCRS 42 · Neuropathology — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS Tumors814

Block exam — demyelination, toxicology and CNS tumours (cont.)

PATH.7031

A 40-year-old has bilateral vestibular schwannomas and two meningiomas. Which chromosome and syndrome, and what other CNS tumour is associated?

  1. AChromosome 17; NF1; optic glioma
  2. BChromosome 22q; neurofibromatosis type 2; spinal ependymoma in adults
  3. CChromosome 3; von Hippel-Lindau; haemangioblastoma
  4. DChromosome 9; tuberous sclerosis; subependymal giant cell astrocytoma
  5. EChromosome 13; retinoblastoma; pineoblastoma
Answer
B. Meningioma: multiple meningiomas + 8th nerve schwannoma or glial tumors → neurofibromatosis type 2; genetics: chromosome 22q. Schwannoma: most commonly the vestibular portion of the eighth nerve at the cerebellopontine angle; associated with NF2; genetics: chromosome 22q. And adult ependymomas are mostly in the spinal cord, with an association with neurofibromatosis 2.
PATH.7031

Which statement about metastatic brain tumours matches this lecture?

  1. AThey account for under 5% of intracranial tumours
  2. BThey account for 25–50% of intracranial tumours and form sharply demarcated masses at the grey-white matter junction; commonest primaries are lung, breast, melanoma, kidney and GIT
  3. CThey are always solitary
  4. DThey arise most often from prostate and thyroid
  5. EThey never cause paraneoplastic syndromes
Answer
B. Most commonly metastatic carcinomas; account for 25% to 50% of intracranial tumors; most common primary sites: lung, breast, skin (melanoma), kidney and GIT; metastases form sharply demarcated masses (usually multiple but can be single) at the grey-white matter junction. Paraneoplastic syndromes can involve the central and peripheral nervous system; the common pattern is cerebellar degeneration (ataxia), limbic encephalitis (dementia) and sensory neuropathy.
NCRS 42 · Neuropathology — Demyelinating Diseases, Toxicology and CNS Tumors815

Block exam — demyelination, toxicology and CNS tumours (cont.)

PATH.7031

Which finding carries a GOOD prognosis in oligodendroglioma?

  1. AEGFR amplification
  2. BCodeletion of 1p and 19q, and IDH1 or IDH2 mutation
  3. CTERT promoter mutation
  4. DCDKN2A deletion
  5. EMYC overexpression
Answer
B. Oligodendroglioma genetics: codeletion of 1p and 19q — good prognosis; IDH1 or IDH2 mutation — good prognosis. The tumour presents in the 4th–5th decade with several years of antecedent neurological symptoms, especially seizures, most often in the frontal and temporal lobes, and shows round nuclei with clear cytoplasm forming halos ("fried egg") and thin-walled capillaries with calcification on gross examination.

DLA — Disorders in Psychiatry

Department of Clinical Skills · a directed learning activity built entirely on DSM-5 criteria. Five categories, one shared question at every branch point.

Department of Clinical Skills · Directed Learning Activity  ·  source pp. 2644–2667

Learning objectives — verbatim

  • CPD.0.0098 Discuss the typical clinical features of the following: mood disorders, psychosis, personality disorders, anxiety disorders, post traumatic and substance abuse.
  • CPD.0.01 Recognize and discuss bodily signs and symptoms that accompany classic psychiatric disorders.
  • CPD.0.0099 Determine the extent to which a general medical illness may contribute to the signs and symptoms of a psychiatric disorder.

Categories of Mental Disorders

The five
  • Mood Disorders
  • Psychotic Disorders
  • Anxiety Disorders
  • Trauma & Stress Disorders
  • Personality Disorders
How this DLA is built
  • Each category is a symptom list plus a cut-off
  • The cut-off is almost always duration or a count
  • Every branch ends in the same three screening questions

Source reference used throughout: DSM-5-TR (https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.books.9780890425596). Slide 25 of the source deck cites Shea SE, Gordon K, Hawkins A, Kawchuk J, Smith D. *Pathology in the Hundred Acre Wood: a neurodevelopmental perspective on A.A. Milne.* CMAJ. 2000;163(12):1557–9.

DLA · Disorders in Psychiatry — DSM-5 Clinical Features817

Mood disorders — the axis

CPD.0.0098src p.2646
  • Every mood diagnosis sits on one axis running from ↓ Mood (Depression) through Normal to ↑ Mood (Manic).
  • Learn the two symptom lists once. The six diagnoses are then only differences in how many symptoms, which symptom is obligatory, and how long.
↓ Mood — depression (SIG E CAPS)
  • ↓ mood
  • ↓ interest or pleasure in activities (anhedonia)
  • ↓ weight OR weight gain (more than 5% of body weight in 1 month)
  • ↓ sleep OR hypersomnia
  • Psychomotor agitation or retardation
  • ↓ energy
  • Feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt
  • ↓ ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness
  • Recurrent thoughts of death / suicide
↑ Mood — mania (DIG FAST)
  • ↑ Inflated self-esteem / grandiosity
  • Decreased need for sleep
  • ↑ talkative than usual / pressure to keep talking
  • ↑ Flight of ideas
  • Distractibility (easily drawn to unimportant or irrelevant external stimuli)
  • ↑ in goal-directed activity
  • ↑ involvement in activities that have a high potential for painful consequences
Bottom Line
The source deck spells the two mnemonics down the middle of the slide as letters: S-I-G E C-A-P-S on the depression side and D-I-G F-A-S-T on the manic side. Learn them as letters — the DSM counts symptoms, and you will be counting under time pressure.

    Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)

    CPD.0.0098src p.2647
    Exam Lock
    MDD must have
    • 5 symptoms from the depression list
    • and at least 1 is either ↓ mood / anhedonia
    • >2 weeks

    The two questions the slide attaches to MDD

    • Suicidal thoughts? — asked at every depression encounter, not only when volunteered.
    • Substance abuse? — a substance-induced depressive disorder is a different diagnosis with a different treatment.
    Trap
    Five symptoms is not enough on its own. A patient with insomnia, ↓ energy, ↓ concentration, guilt and weight loss for a month has five symptoms and no ↓ mood and no anhedonia — that is not MDD. One of the two gateway symptoms must be present.
      DLA · Disorders in Psychiatry — DSM-5 Clinical Features820

      Persistent Depressive Disorder (PDD) and PMDD

      CPD.0.0098 · CPD.0.0099src p.2648–2649
      Persistent Depressive Disorder (PDD) must have
      • ↓ mood for most of the day, for more days than not, for at least 2 years
      • + 2 other symptoms
      Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder must have
      • > 5 symptoms must be present in the final week before the onset of menses
      • start to improve after the onset of menses
      • and become absent in the week postmenses

      The screening questions the slide attaches here

      • Substance abuse?
      • Thyroid disease? — hypothyroidism reproduces the entire depressive syndrome, and it is the classic general medical illness contributing to the signs and symptoms of a psychiatric disorder.
      Bottom Line
      PDD trades severity for chronicity: fewer symptoms (2 beyond low mood), far longer clock (2 years). MDD trades the other way — more symptoms, only 2 weeks.
        DLA · Disorders in Psychiatry — DSM-5 Clinical Features821

        Bipolar I, Bipolar II and cyclothymia

        CPD.0.0098src p.2650–2652
        Bipolar I must have
        • ↑ mood and 3 other symptoms
        • >1 week
        • Substance abuse?
        Bipolar II must have
        • Hypomanic AND MDD
        • Never had a manic episode
        Cyclothymia must have
        • Hypomanic symptoms AND depressive symptoms
        • >2 years
        • Never without symptoms for >2 months
        Trap
        Bipolar I does not require a depressive episode. One manic episode of >1 week is sufficient. Bipolar II is the mirror image: the depressive episode is mandatory and a full manic episode is disqualifying.
          Exam Lock
          The cyclothymia clock
          • >2 years of oscillation, and
          • never symptom-free for more than 2 months — the gaps are what the criterion is measuring
