          Block check — mood disorders

          CPD.0.0098

          A 34-year-old reports 3 weeks of low mood, anhedonia, 6 kg weight loss, early-morning waking, poor concentration and guilt. TSH is normal and she takes no substances. Which criterion set does she satisfy?

          1. APersistent depressive disorder
          2. BMajor depressive disorder
          3. CPremenstrual dysphoric disorder
          4. DBipolar II disorder
          5. ECyclothymia
          Answer
          B. MDD must have 5 symptoms, at least 1 of which is either ↓ mood or anhedonia, for >2 weeks. She has six symptoms including both gateway symptoms, over three weeks. PDD would require ≥2 years; bipolar II requires hypomania AND MDD.
          CPD.0.0098

          A 41-year-old man has had persistently low mood for most of the day, more days than not, for the last 3 years, with low energy and poor concentration but no episode ever meeting full MDD criteria. Which is correct?

          1. AMajor depressive disorder
          2. BPersistent depressive disorder
          3. CAdjustment disorder
          4. DCyclothymia
          5. EBipolar II disorder
          Answer
          B. PDD: ↓ mood for most of the day, for more days than not, for at least 2 years, + 2 other symptoms. The diagnosis is defined by chronicity, not by severity — which is why students who count only symptoms miss it.
          DLA · Disorders in Psychiatry — DSM-5 Clinical Features824

          Block check — mood disorders (cont.)

          CPD.0.0098

          A 22-year-old has an 8-day episode of elevated mood, grandiosity, decreased need for sleep and reckless spending. He has never had a depressive episode. Which diagnosis fits?

          1. ABipolar II disorder
          2. BCyclothymia
          3. CBipolar I disorder
          4. DBrief psychotic episode
          5. EMajor depressive disorder with mixed features
          Answer
          C. Bipolar I must have ↑ mood and 3 other symptoms, >1 week. He has grandiosity, decreased need for sleep and painful-consequence activity over 8 days. A depressive episode is NOT required for bipolar I. Bipolar II would require hypomania AND MDD, and never a manic episode.
          CPD.0.0099 · CPD.0.01

          A 29-year-old woman is referred for 'depression'. She has fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance and low mood for 4 months. Which step does the DLA place BEFORE assigning a psychiatric diagnosis?

          1. AStart an SSRI and reassess in 6 weeks
          2. BAssess for thyroid disease
          3. CDiagnose persistent depressive disorder
          4. DRefer for cognitive behavioural therapy
          5. EDiagnose premenstrual dysphoric disorder
          Answer
          B. Determine the extent to which a general medical illness may contribute to the signs and symptoms of a psychiatric disorder. The source slides print Thyroid disease? directly beneath the depression criteria. Weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation are the bodily signs that accompany the classic psychiatric presentation here.

          CPD.0.0098

          Which feature would EXCLUDE bipolar II disorder?

          1. AA major depressive episode
          2. BA hypomanic episode
          3. CA single manic episode lasting 9 days
          4. DTwo years of fluctuating symptoms
          5. EA family history of bipolar disorder
          Answer
          C. Bipolar II must have hypomania AND MDD, and the patient must NEVER have had a manic episode. A 9-day manic episode is >1 week and reclassifies the patient as bipolar I.

          CPD.0.0098src p.2653
          1. Delusions
          2. Hallucinations
          3. Disorganized speech
          4. Disorganized or abnormal motor behavior
          5. Negative symptoms — diminished emotional expression; diminished purposeful activities (avolition)

          Then sort on duration

          Brief Psychotic Episode>1 day but <1 month

          Schizophrenia>6 months

          Substance abuse? is printed on this slide too — a substance-induced psychotic disorder is excluded before any of the three are assigned.

          Psychosis — the clock and the mood branch

          CPD.0.0098src p.2653–2655
          DLA · Disorders in Psychiatry — DSM-5 Clinical Features828

          Schizoaffective disorder — the second question

          CPD.0.0098src p.2654–2655
          An uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major mood episode (major depressive or manic) concurrent with schizophrenia (Criterion A of the DSM V).Source definition

          The decision the slide is drawing

          • Duration? → brief psychotic episode · schizophreniform · schizophrenia
          • Mood symptoms? → schizoaffective disorder, or mood disorder with psychotic features
          Trap
          The two mood-plus-psychosis diagnoses are separated by when the psychosis happens. In schizoaffective disorder psychosis persists in the absence of the mood episode; if psychosis occurs only during mood episodes, it is a mood disorder with psychotic features.
            DLA · Disorders in Psychiatry — DSM-5 Clinical Features829

            Block check — psychotic disorders

            CPD.0.0098

            A 24-year-old has had auditory hallucinations, disorganized speech and avolition for 10 weeks. Urine drug screen is negative. Which diagnosis fits the duration?

            1. ABrief psychotic episode
            2. BSchizophreniform disorder
            3. CSchizophrenia
            4. DSchizoaffective disorder
            5. EDelusional disorder
            Answer
            B. Schizophreniform = >1 month but <6 months. Ten weeks is past the 1-month line and well short of 6 months. Brief psychotic episode is >1 day but <1 month; schizophrenia requires >6 months.
            CPD.0.0098

            A patient has had 2 years of delusions and negative symptoms. Manic episodes have occurred concurrently at times, but the delusions clearly persist during long periods when mood is normal. Which is correct?

            1. ABipolar I disorder with psychotic features
            2. BSchizophreniform disorder
            3. CSchizoaffective disorder
            4. DBrief psychotic episode
            5. EMajor depressive disorder with psychotic features
            Answer
            C. Schizoaffective disorder: an uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major mood episode concurrent with Criterion A of schizophrenia. The discriminator is that psychosis persists when the mood episode is absent — otherwise it would be a mood disorder with psychotic features.
            DLA · Disorders in Psychiatry — DSM-5 Clinical Features830

            Block check — psychotic disorders (cont.)

            CPD.0.0098

            Which of the following is listed by the DSM as a NEGATIVE symptom in Criterion A?

            1. ADelusions of reference
            2. BDisorganized speech
            3. CDiminished purposeful activities (avolition)
            4. DAuditory hallucinations
            5. ECatatonic posturing
            Answer
            C. Criterion A lists delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized or abnormal motor behavior, and negative symptoms — diminished emotional expression and diminished purposeful activities (avolition). The other four options are all *positive* or motor features.

            Anxiety disorders — GAD and panic disorder

            CPD.0.0098src p.2656–2658
            Generalized Anxiety disorder (GAD)
            • occurring most days and for at least 6 months
            • Cannot control worry
            • 3 or more of the following symptoms
            • Restlessness.
            • Easily fatigued.
            • Difficulty concentrating
            • Irritability.
            • Muscle tension.
            • Sleep disturbance
            Panic Disorder
            • unexpected attacks of fear and intense discomfort
            • Must have 4 or more symptoms
            • Followed by 1 month of worry / maladaptive change
            • General medical condition?
            Bottom Line
            Count discipline: GAD counts 3, panic counts 4. The two numbers are the single highest-yield fact on these two slides and they are trivially swappable under exam pressure.

              Trauma- and stressor-related disorders

              CPD.0.0098src p.2659–2660

              The tree the slide draws

              • Stressor? → Life threatening → Acute stress disorder / Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
              • Stressor? → Not Life threatening → Adjustment Disorder
              • Neglect → Reactive Attachment Disorder / Social Engagement Disorder

              Key Features — shared by acute stress disorder and PTSD

              • Exposure to traumatic event — direct, close family member, witness, repeated indirect exposure
              • Intrusive Symptoms — Recurrent memories and dreams & Flashbacks
              • Avoidance
              • Changes in Mood / Cognition
              • Change in Arousal (hypervigilance)
              Exam Lock
              The only thing separating the two
              • Acute Stress disorder: >3 days but <1-month disturbance
              • Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder: >1-month disturbance
              DLA · Disorders in Psychiatry — DSM-5 Clinical Features835

              Personality disorders — three clusters

              CPD.0.0098src p.2661–2666
              Cluster A · WIRED
              • Odd, eccentric; unable to develop meaningful relationships
              • Paranoid — Distrustful and suspicious
              • Schizoid — Happy. Loners. Do not want any relationships
              • Schizotypal — Magical thinking — no hallucinations / response to external stimuli
              Cluster B · WACKY
              • Dramatic, emotional, or erratic
              • Antisocial — Criminal. No regard for others and lack remorse
              • Borderline — Rapid changes in mood, suicidal gestures
              • Narcissistic — Inflated sense of worth, demands special treatment
              • Histrionic — Theatrical, attention seeking, hypersexual
              Cluster C · WORRIED
              • Anxious or fearful
              • Avoidant — Loners but fears rejection and criticism
              • Dependent — Fears of being alone
              • Obsessive-compulsive — Rigid, perfectionist no intrusive thoughts or forced compulsions**
              DLA · Disorders in Psychiatry — DSM-5 Clinical Features837

              The three clusters side by side

              CPD.0.0098src p.2661–2666
              DLA · Disorders in Psychiatry — DSM-5 Clinical Features838

              The two pairs that get confused

              CPD.0.0098src p.2662–2666
              Schizoid vs avoidant — both are loners
              • Schizoid (Cluster A) — Happy. Loners. Do NOT WANT any relationships.
              • Avoidant (Cluster C) — Loners but FEARS rejection and criticism — they want relationships and cannot tolerate the risk
              OCPD vs OCD
              • Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (Cluster C) — Rigid, perfectionist; no intrusive thoughts or forced compulsions; ego-syntonic
              • OCD — true obsessions (intrusive thoughts) and compulsions; ego-dystonic, the patient is distressed by them
              Trap
              Do not read schizoid or schizotypal as mild schizophrenia. Schizotypal has magical thinking with no hallucinations and no response to external stimuli — the absence of true psychosis is exactly what keeps it a personality disorder.

GAD: occurring most days and for at least 6 months, cannot control worry, 3 or more symptoms from restlessness, easily fatigued, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance. She has three. Panic disorder would need discrete unexpected attacks with 4 or more symptoms.
                CPD.0.0098

                Three weeks after surviving a motor-vehicle collision, a 27-year-old has flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance of driving and hypervigilance. Which diagnosis applies today?

                1. APost-traumatic stress disorder
                2. BAcute stress disorder
                3. CAdjustment disorder
                4. DPanic disorder
                5. EReactive attachment disorder
                Answer
                B. Acute stress disorder = >3 days but <1-month disturbance; PTSD = >1-month disturbance. At three weeks the symptom set is identical to PTSD but the clock has not run out, so the diagnosis is acute stress disorder.

                CPD.0.0098

                A patient has no friends, avoids all social invitations, and states he simply prefers to be alone and is content that way. He is not distressed by the isolation. Which personality disorder fits?

                NCRS SG-10 — Renal Pathology

                Department of Pathology, St. George's University. A microscope session: eleven numbered slides and three reference slides, each one a diagnosis you must call out loud.

                Department of Pathology, SGU · Small Group 10  ·  source pp. 2668–2684

                Learning objectives — verbatim

                • PATH.6008 Compare and contrast the: relative frequency, etiology, pathogenesis, clinical presentation, course, prognosis, laboratory findings, microscopic (light, immunofluorescent, electron microscopic) appearance of the following glomerular diseases: a. Minimal change disease · b. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis · c. Membranous Nephrotic syndrome
                • PATH.6015 Compare and contrast the relative frequency, etiology, pathogenesis, clinical presentation, course, prognosis, laboratory findings, and microscopic (light, immunofluorescent, electron microscopic) appearance of the following glomerular diseases: Acute proliferative (post-streptococcal, postinfectious) glomerulonephritis · Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis · Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (e.g. Goodpasture's syndrome, Wegener's granulomatosis)
                • PATH.6021 Compare and contrast the: relative frequency, etiology, and pathogenesis, clinical presentation, course and prognosis, laboratory findings, gross and microscopic appearance for Acute pyelonephritis
                • PATH.6027 Compare and contrast the pathogenesis, gross and microscopic appearance, clinical presentations, course and prognosis of benign nephrosclerosis and malignant nephrosclerosis
                • PATH.6029 Diagnose the common cystic lesions in the kidney based on morphology, clinical features, and genetic basis and associated abnormalities
                • PATH.6035 Distinguish the common renal tumors based on the age, etiology, risk factors, pathogenesis, clinical features and complications (Paraneoplastic syndrome and metastatic) and genetic basis
                Source note
                The source deck carries this small group as image-only slides — a title, a slide number and a photomicrograph, with no written text. Reproduced here are the verbatim objectives and slide list, plus, for each numbered slide, the diagnostic criteria you are expected to state at the scope, drawn from the corresponding NCRS lectures already in this deck (Nephrotic Syndrome, Nephritic Syndrome, Tubulointerstitial Disease, Vascular Disease, UTI and Renal Tumors).

                  ReferenceWhat you are being oriented toRead for

                    NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)845

                    Slide 1 — Features of Minimal Change Disease

                    PATH.6003 · PATH.6008src p.2674
                    Light microscopy
                    • Normal glomeruli — this is the point of the slide
                    • Lipid in proximal tubular cells ("lipoid nephrosis")
                    Immunofluorescence
                    • Negative — no immune deposits
                    Electron microscopy
                    • Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes — the only abnormality
                    Exam Lock
                    Clinical anchor
                    • Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children
                    • Selective proteinuria (albumin)
                    • Dramatic response to corticosteroids
                    • Secondary associations: Hodgkin lymphoma, NSAIDs
                    Trap
                    A slide that looks normal on light microscopy is the answer, not a failed slide. If LM is normal and the child is nephrotic, you have already made the diagnosis — EM only confirms it.
                      NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)846

                      Slide 2 — Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis

                      PATH.6008src p.2675
                      Light microscopy
                      • FOCAL — only some glomeruli involved
                      • SEGMENTAL — only part of the involved tuft
                      • Sclerosis with hyalinosis; capillary lumina obliterated
                      Immunofluorescence
                      • IgM and C3 in the sclerotic segments — trapped, not immune-complex driven
                      Electron microscopy
                      • Foot process effacement (as in MCD) plus focal detachment of podocytes and denudation of GBM
                      Exam Lock
                      Clinical anchor
                      • Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, and in African-American patients
                      • Non-selective proteinuria; poor steroid response; progresses to chronic kidney disease
                      • Secondary: HIV, heroin, sickle cell disease, obesity, reduced nephron mass
                      Bottom Line
                      Because the lesion is focal, an inadequate biopsy that samples only spared glomeruli reads as minimal change disease. The steroid-unresponsive "MCD" is FSGS until proven otherwise.
                        NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)847

                        Slide 3 — Membranous Glomerulopathy

                        PATH.6007 · PATH.6008src p.2676
                        Light microscopy
                        • Diffuse thickening of the capillary wall, no hypercellularity
                        • Silver stain: "spikes and domes" — GBM material between subepithelial deposits
                        Immunofluorescence
                        • Granular IgG and C3 along the capillary wall
                        Electron microscopy
                        • Subepithelial electron-dense deposits
                        • Foot process effacement
                        Exam Lock
                        Clinical anchor
                        • Primary: autoantibody against phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) on podocytes — ~75%
                        • Secondary: hepatitis B, SLE, solid tumours (lung, colon), drugs (penicillamine, NSAIDs, captopril)
                        • Nephrotic syndrome in the adult; the most thrombogenic of the nephrotic lesions
                        Trap
                        Membranous (thick wall, no hypercellularity, subepithelial deposits) versus membranoproliferative (thick wall plus hypercellularity, tram-tracks, subendothelial deposits). The names are one syllable apart; the slides are not.
                          NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)848

                          The three nephrotic slides, compared

                          PATH.6008src p.2674–2676
                          NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)849

                          Slides 1–3 — nephrotic pattern

                          PATH.6008

                          A 5-year-old has periorbital oedema and 4+ proteinuria. The biopsy glomeruli are normal on light microscopy and immunofluorescence is negative. What will electron microscopy show?

                          1. ASubepithelial deposits with spikes
                          2. BDiffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes
                          3. CSubendothelial deposits with tram-tracking
                          4. DSegmental sclerosis with hyalinosis
                          5. ELinear deposition along the GBM
                          Answer
                          B. Minimal change disease: normal LM, negative IF, and diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes on EM. It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and shows a dramatic response to corticosteroids.
                          PATH.6007 · PATH.6008

                          Which immunofluorescence finding is expected on Slide 3 (membranous glomerulopathy)?

                          1. ANegative immunofluorescence
                          2. BLinear IgG along the GBM
                          3. CGranular IgG and C3 along the capillary wall
                          4. DIgA in the mesangium
                          5. EC3 only, in a mesangial pattern
                          Answer
                          C. Membranous glomerulopathy shows granular IgG and C3 along the capillary wall, corresponding to subepithelial electron-dense deposits and the spikes-and-domes silver pattern. Linear IgG is anti-GBM disease; IgA in the mesangium is IgA nephropathy.
                          NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)850

                          Slides 1–3 — nephrotic pattern (cont.)

                          PATH.6008

                          A steroid-unresponsive adult nephrotic patient has a biopsy showing sclerosis of part of the tuft in 3 of 20 glomeruli. Which is the diagnosis, and what makes it easy to miss?

                          1. AMinimal change disease — the deposits are subtle
                          2. BFocal segmental glomerulosclerosis — a small biopsy may sample only spared glomeruli
                          3. CMembranous glomerulopathy — the spikes need a silver stain
                          4. DMembranoproliferative GN — tram-tracks need EM
                          5. EPost-streptococcal GN — the humps resolve
                          Answer
                          B. FSGS is FOCAL (some glomeruli) and SEGMENTAL (part of the tuft), so an inadequate biopsy that samples only spared glomeruli reads as minimal change disease. FSGS is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults and responds poorly to steroids.
                          NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)851

                          Slide 4 — Post-streptococcal Glomerulonephritis

                          PATH.6015src p.2677
                          Light microscopy
                          • Diffuse global hypercellularity — endothelial, mesangial and neutrophils filling the tuft
                          • Bloodless glomeruli (obliterated lumina)
                          Immunofluorescence
                          • Granular IgG, IgM and C3 — "starry sky" / "lumpy-bumpy"
                          Electron microscopy
                          • Subepithelial "humps" — large dome-shaped deposits
                          Exam Lock
                          Clinical anchor
                          • Child, 1–4 weeks after a group A streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection
                          • Nephritic syndrome: haematuria (cola-coloured urine), RBC casts, hypertension, periorbital oedema, mild proteinuria
                          • ↓ serum C3; ↑ ASO / anti-DNase B titres
                          • Excellent prognosis in children; ~95% recover
                          NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)852

                          Slide 5 — Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis (MPGN)

                          PATH.6015src p.2678
                          Light microscopy
                          • Hypercellular AND thickened capillary walls
                          • "Tram-track" double contour of the GBM — silver stain, from mesangial interposition
                          • Lobular accentuation of the tuft
                          Immunofluorescence
                          • Type I: granular C3 with IgG and early complement (C1q, C4)
                          • Type II / dense deposit disease: C3 only, no immunoglobulin
                          Electron microscopy
                          • Type I: subendothelial deposits
                          • Type II: dense ribbon-like transformation of the lamina densa
                          Exam Lock
                          Clinical anchor
                          • Presents as a nephrotic–nephritic hybrid; slow progression to chronic renal failure
                          • Type I: immune-complex — hepatitis C (± cryoglobulins), hepatitis B, SLE, chronic infection
                          • Type II: C3 nephritic factor — an autoantibody stabilising C3 convertase → persistent complement activation and a persistently LOW C3
                          NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)853

                          Slide 6 — Rapidly Progressive GN and the anti-GBM pattern

                          PATH.6015src p.2679
                          Light microscopy — RPGN
                          • Crescents filling Bowman space — proliferating parietal epithelium, monocytes and fibrin
                          • Crescents in >50% of glomeruli defines the pattern
                          • Segmental necrosis and GBM rupture beneath the crescent
                          Immunofluorescence — anti-GBM disease
                          • SMOOTH LINEAR deposition of IgG along the GBM — the second panel of this slide
                          • Contrast: granular = immune complex (type II); negative / pauci-immune = type III ANCA
                          RPGN typeImmunofluorescenceClassic diseases
                          Type I — anti-GBMLinear IgGGoodpasture syndrome (anti-α3 chain of type IV collagen; lung + kidney)
                          Type II — immune complexGranular "lumpy-bumpy"Post-infectious GN, SLE, IgA nephropathy, Henoch-Schönlein purpura
                          Type III — pauci-immuneLittle or no stainingGranulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's) — c-ANCA/PR3; microscopic polyangiitis — p-ANCA/MPO; eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis

                          The objective names Goodpasture's syndrome and Wegener's granulomatosis explicitly — they sit at opposite ends of this table.

                          Trap
                          Crescents are a pattern, not a disease. Light microscopy tells you the kidney is failing fast; only immunofluorescence tells you which of the three mechanisms did it, and therefore whether the treatment is plasmapheresis, immunosuppression, or both.
                            NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)854

                            Immunofluorescence — the three deposit patterns

                            PATH.6015src p.2677–2679
                            NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)855

                            Slides 4–6 — nephritic pattern

                            PATH.6015

                            A 7-year-old develops cola-coloured urine and hypertension 2 weeks after a sore throat. Which set of findings is expected?

                            1. ALinear IgG on IF, normal C3
                            2. BGranular IgG and C3 with subepithelial humps and low C3
                            3. CTram-tracking with subendothelial deposits and normal C3
                            4. DNegative IF with crescents and normal complement
                            5. EIgA in the mesangium with normal complement
                            Answer
                            B. Post-streptococcal GN: diffuse hypercellularity with neutrophils on LM, granular "starry-sky" IgG/C3 on IF, subepithelial humps on EM, and a LOW serum C3 with raised ASO / anti-DNase B. Prognosis in children is excellent.
                            PATH.6015

                            Slide 5 shows a hypercellular, lobular glomerulus with a double-contoured GBM on silver stain. IF shows C3 alone with no immunoglobulin. Which is correct?

                            1. AMPGN type I, from hepatitis C immune complexes
                            2. BDense deposit disease (MPGN type II), associated with C3 nephritic factor
                            3. CMembranous glomerulopathy with PLA2R antibody
                            4. DAnti-GBM disease
                            5. EMinimal change disease
                            Answer
                            B. C3 alone with no immunoglobulin is dense deposit disease (MPGN type II), driven by C3 nephritic factor — an autoantibody that stabilises C3 convertase, producing persistent complement consumption and a ribbon-like dense transformation of the lamina densa on EM. Type I shows granular C3 with IgG and subendothelial deposits.
                            NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)856

                            Slides 4–6 — nephritic pattern (cont.)

                            PATH.6015

                            A 60-year-old with haemoptysis and rapidly rising creatinine has crescents in 70% of glomeruli and SMOOTH LINEAR IgG along the GBM. Which is the diagnosis?

                            1. AGranulomatosis with polyangiitis
                            2. BMicroscopic polyangiitis
                            3. CGoodpasture syndrome
                            4. DSLE nephritis
                            5. EIgA nephropathy
                            Answer
                            C. Linear IgG along the GBM is type I (anti-GBM) RPGN — Goodpasture syndrome, antibodies against the α3 chain of type IV collagen shared by glomerular and alveolar basement membrane, hence lung + kidney. Wegener's / GPA and microscopic polyangiitis are pauci-immune (type III) with little or no staining.
                            NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)857

                            Slide 7 — Features of Acute Pyelonephritis

                            PATH.6021src p.2680
                            Gross
                            • Discrete yellowish, raised abscesses on the cortical surface
                            • Wedge-shaped suppuration; abscesses may be confluent
                            Light microscopy
                            • Patchy interstitial suppurative inflammation
                            • Intratubular neutrophil aggregates → WBC (leukocyte) casts
                            • Tubular necrosis; glomeruli characteristically spared
                            Exam Lock
                            Clinical anchor
                            • Ascending infection — E. coli >> Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterobacter
                            • Fever, costovertebral angle tenderness, pyuria and WBC casts — the cast is what locates the infection in the kidney rather than the bladder
                            • Predisposing: vesicoureteral reflux, obstruction, instrumentation, diabetes, pregnancy
                            • Complications: papillary necrosis, pyonephrosis, perinephric abscess
                            Bottom Line
                            Glomeruli are spared in acute pyelonephritis. If a slide shows heavy interstitial neutrophils *and* glomerular damage, reconsider — you are probably not looking at pyelonephritis.
                              NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)858

                              Slides 8 and 8b — Benign and Malignant Nephrosclerosis

                              PATH.6027 · PATH.6028src p.2681–2682
                              Benign nephrosclerosisMalignant nephrosclerosis
                              SettingLong-standing benign hypertension; diabetes; ageingMalignant hypertension — diastolic >120 mmHg, often superimposed on benign
                              GrossFinely granular "grain-leather" cortical surface; symmetrically contracted kidneys"Flea-bitten" kidney — petechial haemorrhages on the cortical surface
                              Vessel lesionHyaline arteriolosclerosis — homogeneous pink hyaline thickening with luminal narrowingHyperplastic arteriolosclerosis — "onion-skinning"; fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles
                              ParenchymaPatchy ischaemic atrophy, glomerular sclerosis, interstitial fibrosisNecrotising glomerulitis; thrombi; infarcts
                              ClinicalMild ↓ GFR, mild proteinuria; rarely causes uraemia aloneMedical emergency: papilloedema, encephalopathy, retinal haemorrhage, cardiac decompensation, acute renal failure
                              Trap
                              Both slides are labelled "Slide 8" in the source deck. Read the titles: Benign Nephrosclerosis and Malignant Nephrosclerosis are separate images.
                                NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)859

                                Benign versus malignant nephrosclerosis

                                PATH.6027src p.2681–2682
                                NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)860

                                Slide 9 — Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease

                                PATH.6029src p.2683
                                Gross
                                • Massively enlarged kidneys (can reach 4 kg each)
                                • Innumerable cysts of varying size replacing the entire cortex and medulla
                                • Intervening parenchyma compressed and atrophic
                                Genetics and associations
                                • PKD1 on chromosome 16 (~85%, polycystin-1) — earlier, more severe
                                • PKD2 on chromosome 4 (~15%, polycystin-2) — later onset
                                • Extrarenal: liver cysts (most common), berry aneurysms → subarachnoid haemorrhage, mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula
                                Exam Lock
                                Clinical anchor
                                • Presents in the 4th–5th decade: flank pain, palpable kidneys, haematuria, hypertension
                                • Progresses to end-stage renal disease in ~50%
                                • Contrast autosomal recessive (ARPKD, PKHD1, chromosome 6) — presents in infancy, smooth-surfaced kidneys with radially arranged elongated cysts, with congenital hepatic fibrosis
                                NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)861

                                Slide 10 — Gross and microscopic features of renal cell carcinoma

                                PATH.6035src p.2684
                                Gross
                                • Golden-yellow, well-circumscribed mass, most often at an upper pole
                                • Variegated with haemorrhage and necrosis
                                • Invasion of the renal vein — a tongue of tumour extending into the vein and IVC
                                Microscopy
                                • Clear cell type (~70%): nests of cells with clear, glycogen- and lipid-rich cytoplasm and a delicate vascular network
                                • Papillary type (~15%): papillae with foamy macrophages and psammoma bodies
                                • Chromophobe (~5%): perinuclear halos, prominent cell membranes
                                Exam Lock
                                Clinical anchor
                                • Genetics: clear cell — VHL gene on chromosome 3p (sporadic and von Hippel–Lindau); papillary — MET
                                • Risk factors: smoking (the strongest), obesity, hypertension, chronic dialysis with acquired cystic disease
                                • Classic triad — costovertebral pain, palpable mass, haematuria — present in only ~10%
                                • Paraneoplastic syndromes: EPO → polycythaemia; PTHrP → hypercalcaemia; renin → hypertension; ACTH → Cushing syndrome
                                • Metastasis is characteristically to lung and bone, often as the presenting event
                                Bottom Line
                                Renal cell carcinoma is the tumour that invades a vein. That single gross feature — a tumour thrombus climbing the renal vein into the IVC — separates it from almost everything else you will be shown.
                                  NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)862

                                  SG-10 — the eleven slides in one table

                                  PATH.6008 · 6015 · 6021 · 6027 · 6029 · 6035src p.2668–2684
                                  SlideDiagnosisThe one finding that names it
                                  1Minimal change diseaseNormal LM, negative IF, foot-process effacement on EM
                                  2Focal segmental glomerulosclerosisFocal + segmental sclerosis with hyalinosis; IgM/C3 trapped
                                  3Membranous glomerulopathyThick wall, no hypercellularity; granular IgG/C3; subepithelial deposits and spikes

                                  NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)863

                                  Slides 7–10 — tubulointerstitial, vascular, cystic and neoplastic

                                  PATH.6021

                                  Slide 7 shows patchy interstitial neutrophils, intratubular neutrophil aggregates and normal glomeruli. Which urinary finding corresponds?

                                  1. ARBC casts
                                  2. BFatty casts
                                  3. CWBC (leukocyte) casts
                                  4. DBroad waxy casts
                                  5. EMuddy-brown granular casts
                                  Answer
                                  C. Acute pyelonephritis: patchy interstitial suppuration with intratubular neutrophil aggregates forming WBC casts, tubular necrosis, and characteristically spared glomeruli. The WBC cast is what localises the infection to the kidney rather than the bladder. RBC casts are nephritic; muddy-brown granular casts are acute tubular necrosis.
                                  PATH.6027

                                  A kidney has a 'flea-bitten' cortical surface, and arterioles show onion-skin thickening and fibrinoid necrosis. Which clinical picture accompanies it?

                                  1. AAsymptomatic mild proteinuria over decades
                                  2. BDiastolic pressure >120 mmHg with papilloedema and acute renal failure
                                  3. CNephrotic syndrome with hyperlipidaemia
                                  4. DRecurrent gross haematuria after infection
                                  5. EProgressive bilateral flank masses
                                  Answer
                                  B. Malignant nephrosclerosis: flea-bitten kidney from petechial haemorrhages, hyperplastic "onion-skin" arteriolosclerosis and fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles, occurring in malignant hypertension with diastolic pressure >120 mmHg — a medical emergency with papilloedema, encephalopathy and acute renal failure. Benign nephrosclerosis gives a finely granular grain-leather surface and hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
                                  PATH.6029

                                  A 45-year-old with bilateral flank masses and hypertension has a sudden severe headache. Which association explains this?

                                  1. ALiver cysts
                                  2. BMitral valve prolapse
                                  3. CBerry aneurysm rupture causing subarachnoid haemorrhage
                                  4. DColonic diverticula
                                  5. ERenal cell carcinoma
                                  Answer
                                  C. ADPKD extrarenal associations: liver cysts (most common), berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse and colonic diverticula. A sudden severe headache in a patient with polycystic kidneys is berry aneurysm rupture → subarachnoid haemorrhage. The gene is PKD1 on chromosome 16 in ~85%.
                                  NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)864

                                  Slides 7–10 — tubulointerstitial, vascular, cystic and neoplastic (cont.)

                                  PATH.6035

                                  A smoker presents with polycythaemia and a golden-yellow upper-pole renal mass extending into the renal vein. Which gene is most likely involved?

                                  1. AMET
                                  2. BVHL on chromosome 3p
                                  3. CPKD1 on chromosome 16
                                  4. DWT1 on chromosome 11p
                                  5. EPKHD1 on chromosome 6
                                  Answer
                                  B. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma — the VHL gene on chromosome 3p, sporadic or as part of von Hippel–Lindau. Smoking is the strongest risk factor; the golden-yellow upper-pole mass with renal vein invasion is characteristic, and EPO production causes polycythaemia. MET drives the papillary type.
                                  PATH.6008 · PATH.6015

                                  Which single question, asked at the microscope, separates membranous glomerulopathy from membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis?

                                  1. AIs the GBM thickened?
                                  2. BIs there hypercellularity in addition to the thickened wall?
                                  3. CAre the glomeruli sclerotic?
                                  4. DIs there interstitial inflammation?
                                  5. EAre there crescents?
                                  Answer
                                  B. Both thicken the capillary wall. Membranous: thickened wall with NO hypercellularity, subepithelial deposits, spikes and domes. Membranoproliferative: thickened wall WITH hypercellularity, tram-track double contours, subendothelial (type I) deposits. That is the whole discriminator on light microscopy.
                                  NCRS SG-10 · Renal Pathology (Practical Slide Review)865

                                  Learning objectives — verbatim

                                  • CPD.0.0124 Discuss common etiologies of weakness including key clinical features.
                                  • CPD.0.0118 Demonstrates effective communication and interpersonal skills in patient interactions and with any other member involved in the patient's care.
                                  • CPD.0.012 Present an age-appropriate medical history, that differentiates among etiologies of disease, for a patient presenting with numbness.
                                  • CPD.0.0125 Perform a relevant Neurological examination according to the suspected differentials and identify the discriminating clinical features to establish the diagnosis.
                                  • CPD.0.0123 Rank a list of clinical differential diagnoses based on the patient's presentation in order of highest probability to least likely.
                                  • CPD.0.0115 Provide supportive evidence from the subjective/objective sections to justify the differential diagnoses.
                                  • CPD.0.0121 Generate a list of appropriate initial investigations based on the differential diagnosis.
                                  • CPD.0.0116 Provide basic information and explain the provisional diagnosis, relevant investigations, prognosis, and treatment plan to the patient.
                                  • CPD.0.0117 Demonstrates effective teamwork and leadership.
                                  • CPD.0.0119 Demonstrate respect towards the patient, families, and all members of the health care team.
                                  • CPD.0.0122 Demonstrate the ability to document pertinent information (negative and positive) obtained from the history and physical examination in the appropriate sections of the patient note.

                                  Build the differential BEFORE the session — VINDICATE

                                  CategoryWorked examples for weakness
                                  VVASCULARStroke · TIA · Todd's paralysis (post-ictal) · hemiplegic migraine · anterior cerebral artery occlusion
                                  IINFECTIOUS / INFLAMMATORYCerebral abscess · encephalitis · venous sinus thrombosis · Lyme disease · polymyositis · dermatomyositis
                                  NNEOPLASTICSpinal cord tumour · parasagittal tumour · cauda equina tumour · metastatic cord compression · Lambert-Eaton (small-cell lung cancer)
                                  DDEGENERATIVEAmyotrophic lateral sclerosis · progressive muscular atrophy · degenerative disc disease · cervical spondylotic myelopathy
                                  IIATROGENIC / INTOXICATIONSteroid-induced myopathy · statin myopathy · drug-induced myasthenia (penicillamine, aminoglycosides, calcium channel blockers) · alcoholic myopathy · botulism
                                  CCONGENITALDuchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy · Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease · familial periodic paralysis · mitochondrial myopathy
                                  AAUTOIMMUNEMultiple sclerosis · myasthenia gravis · Guillain-Barré syndrome · transverse myelitis · vasculitis-associated mononeuritis
                                  TTRAUMATICSpinal cord injury · herniated disc · brachial plexus neuropathy · subdural / epidural haematoma
                                  EENDOCRINE / METABOLICThyroid myopathy · hyperthyroidism · adrenal insufficiency · uraemic polyneuropathy · electrolyte disturbance

                                  VINDICATE is a generator, not an answer. Run it before the session, then use the history to rank.

                                  NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness870

                                  Interview framework — evaluating a patient with weakness

                                  CPD.0.012 · CPD.0.0124src p.2690–2691
                                  1. Start with an Open Question — ask the patient to describe the weakness in their own words. Let them explain what they are experiencing before asking specific questions.
                                  2. Confirm if it is TRUE WEAKNESS — determine whether this is true muscle weakness or something else (fatigue, pain, lack of effort, or functional weakness). True muscle weakness = reduced muscle power. Fatigue or asthenia = feeling tired or lacking energy, but muscle strength may be normal.
                                  3. Understand the Time Course — when did it start? Sudden or gradual? Getting worse, improving, or staying the same?
                                  4. Identify the Distribution — which body parts? One side or both? Arms, legs, face, or all? This helps you localize the problem (brain, spinal cord, nerve, or muscle).
                                  5. Ask About Associated Symptoms — cranial nerve symptoms, fever, reflex changes.
                                  6. Review Risk Factors — trauma, hypertension, atrial fibrillation or cardiac problems.
                                  Trap
                                  Step 2 is the step students skip. Fatigue and true weakness are different conditions, but they can occur together or be confused. A patient who says "weak" and means "tired" will send you down the wrong VINDICATE branch for the whole encounter.
                                    NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness871

                                    Associated symptoms — what each answer means

                                    CPD.0.0124src p.2690–2691
                                    FindingInterpretation
                                    Cranial nerve symptoms present — facial weakness or drooping, problems with speech, swallowing or visionSuspect a lesion in the brain (above the foramen magnum)
                                    Cranial nerve symptoms absentConsider a spinal cord lesion
                                    FeverSuggests infection: cerebral abscess · venous sinus thrombosis · encephalitis
                                    Decreased or absent reflexes (LOWER motor neuron signs)Herniated disc · cauda equina tumor · early cervical cord tumor · progressive muscular atrophy · brachial plexus neuropathy · sciatic neuritis · peripheral neuropathy
                                    Hyperactive or abnormal reflexes (UPPER motor neuron signs)Spinal cord tumor · parasagittal tumor · amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) · anterior cerebral artery occlusion · spinal cord injury · transverse myelitis · multiple sclerosis

                                    Risk factors that change urgency

                                    • Trauma — any recent injury?
                                    • Hypertension — increases risk of cerebral hemorrhage and cerebral aneurysm.
                                    • Atrial fibrillation or cardiac problems — history of AF? Heart murmur? Other signs of an embolic source? These increase the risk of cerebral embolism.
                                    NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness872

                                    Focused questions — the answer-to-diagnosis table

                                    CPD.0.0124src p.2692
                                    If the patient says yes to…Think about…
                                    Are you weak on both sides of your body?Spinal cord compression (neoplasm, infection, degenerative disk disease)
                                    Is your weakness confined to just one limb or part of one limb?Peripheral neuropathy or radiculopathy · multiple sclerosis · stroke · Todd's paralysis
                                    Does your weakness involve one side of your body or your face?Stroke or TIA · hemiplegic migraine
                                    Difficulty lifting your head off the bed, standing from a sitting position, or brushing your hair? (proximal weakness)Polymyositis or dermatomyositis · diabetic amyotrophy · Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy
                                    Is it difficult for you to stand on your toes? (distal > proximal)Inclusion body myositis · polyneuropathy or radiculopathy
                                    Has your voice changed? Trouble swallowing?ALS · polymyositis or dermatomyositis · myasthenia gravis · stroke
                                    Do you have double vision (diplopia)?Mononeuritis (cranial nerve IV, VI) · myasthenia gravis · multiple sclerosis
                                    Do you have droopy eyelids?Myasthenia gravis · botulism (acute)
                                    Does your weakness get WORSE with exercise?Myasthenia gravis · mitochondrial myopathies
                                    Does your weakness get BETTER with exercise?Lambert-Eaton syndrome
                                    Numbness and tingling with the weakness?Multiple sclerosis · stroke · polyneuropathies — neurologic disorders, NOT myopathies
                                    Can you see your muscles twitching? (fasciculations)ALS
                                    Sudden eye pain (optic neuritis)? Heat exacerbates symptoms?Multiple sclerosis
                                    Rash or weight loss?Vasculitis-associated mononeuritis · dermatomyositis · malignancy · hyperthyroidism
                                    NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness873

                                    Past history, medications and exposures

                                    CPD.0.0124src p.2692–2693
                                    QuestionThink about…
                                    Do you have diabetes mellitus?Mononeuritis · polyneuropathies · stroke
                                    Hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, vascular disease, cigarette smoking or estrogen use?Stroke
                                    Hyperthyroidism or symptoms of hyperthyroidism?Thyroid myopathy · myasthenia gravis (occasionally associated)
                                    Kidney disease?Uremic polyneuropathy
                                    Rheumatoid arthritis? History of neck trauma?Cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy
                                    Ever treated for malignancy? Recent weight loss, night sweats, fatigue?Lambert-Eaton syndrome (particularly small-cell lung cancer) · spinal cord compression
                                    Are you taking any medications?Steroid-induced myopathy · statin myopathy · drug-induced myasthenia gravis (penicillamine, aminoglycosides, calcium channel blockers)
                                    Family history of similar problems?Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease · familial periodic paralysis · Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy · mitochondrial myopathy
                                    Do you drink alcohol? How much?Alcoholic myopathy
                                    IV drugs or unprotected sex? HIV infection?Distal symmetric polyneuropathy · mononeuritis multiplex · myopathies (polymyositis and zidovudine-related myopathy)

                                    Where is the lesion? The eight levels

                                    CPD.0.0125src p.2689–2693

                                    Physical examination — the SG-11 checklist

                                    CPD.0.0125src p.2693–2694
                                    Introduction — always scored
                                    • Patient preparation — dignity: ask permission, explain techniques, purpose and expectations; obtain consent to proceed
                                    • Hand hygiene, draping, position — comfort: soap and water or alcohol-based sanitizer per WHO technique and duration; proper draping; attention to comfort
                                    • Examination organization: consistent step-by-step instructions; appropriate sequence
                                    Cranial nerves (this case)
                                    • Trigeminal Nerve (V)
                                    • Facial Nerve (VII)
                                    • Glossopharyngeal and Vagus (IX, X)
                                    • Hypoglossal Nerve (XII)

                                    Motor system exam

                                    • Inspection for the position, bulk, and involuntary movements
                                    • Assess for pronator drift
                                    • Assess for muscle tone — upper extremity (arms and forearms); lower extremity (thighs and legs)
                                    • Assess for muscle strength — upper limb: shoulder abduction/adduction · elbow flexion and extension · wrist flexion and extension · finger abduction and adduction · thumb abduction · grip strength. Lower limb: hip flexion and extension · hip abduction and adduction · knee flexion and extension · ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion
                                    Reflex exam
                                    • Upper limb: biceps · brachioradialis · triceps
                                    • Lower limb: patellar · Achilles · plantar (Babinski sign)
                                    Gait and station
                                    • Regular gait
                                    • Toe walking
                                    • Heel walking
                                    • Tandem walking
                                    Sensory and coordination
                                    • Sensation, upper and lower limb: light touch · pain · vibration · proprioception
                                    • Coordination: rapid alternating movement · point-to-point movement · finger tapping
                                    NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness876

                                    Physical examination — the SG-11 checklist (cont.)

                                    CPD.0.0125src p.2693–2694

                                    Additional relevant systems for the focused 17-minute OSCE: identify one or more systems outside the main one and perform at least two relevant items — here cardiovascular (carotid bruits; heart sounds S1, S2, S3, S4, gallops and murmurs), peripheral vascular (peripheral pulses), and vital signs (remeasure BP; radial pulse rhythm and amplitude).

                                    NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness877

                                    Descriptors of weakness — say it in one word

                                    CPD.0.0122 · CPD.0.0124src p.2700
                                    TermDefinition
                                    Ascending paralysisMotor weakness begins in the feet and progressively moves up the body
                                    Descending paralysisMotor weakness begins in the face and progressively moves down the body
                                    Distal weaknessWeakness in the distal extremities (e.g., foot drop)
                                    Proximal weaknessWeakness in proximal muscles (e.g., shoulder girdle, quadriceps) resulting in difficulty standing up from a seated position or raising arms above head
                                    HemiparesisWeakness on one side of the body
                                    MonoparesisWeakness of one limb
                                    ParaparesisWeakness of both legs
                                    TetraparesisWeakness of all 4 limbs
                                    Bulbar symptomsWeakness in the muscles of the face and tongue, resulting in difficulty speaking, swallowing, and smiling
                                    Todd's paralysisReversible weakness following a seizure
                                    Upper motor neuron lesionsAbnormalities of motor pathways that descend from the central nervous system to the alpha motor neurons, resulting in spasticity, hyperreflexia, and increased muscle tone
                                    Lower motor neuron lesionsAbnormalities of the alpha motor neuron in the brainstem or spinal gray matter, resulting in muscle atrophy, hyporeflexia, and fasciculations

                                    Appendix C of the workbook. Using these terms in the SOAP note is the difference between *"leg weakness"* and *"acute ascending flaccid paraparesis with areflexia"*.

                                    NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness878

                                    Skin signs — Appendix B images

                                    CPD.0.0124src p.2699–2700
                                    SignPoints to
                                    Skin bronzingAdrenal insufficiency
                                    Gottron's papules, shawl sign, heliotrope rashDermatomyositis
                                    Erythema nodosum (tender nodules found on shins)Sarcoidosis
                                    Erythema migransLyme disease

                                    These are the four images in Appendix B. A rash on a weak patient is a diagnosis, not an incidental finding.

                                    Bottom Line
                                    Heliotrope = violaceous periorbital rash. Gottron's papules = over the knuckles. Shawl sign = over the shoulders and upper back. All three plus proximal symmetric weakness = dermatomyositis, and dermatomyositis is a paraneoplastic flag in an adult — look for the malignancy.

                                      Stroke prevention — Appendix D, the counselling content

                                      CPD.0.0116src p.2701
                                      What a stroke is
                                      • An acute brain injury caused by ischemia (blockage of blood flow to the brain) or hemorrhage (rupture of a brain blood vessel)
                                      In the United States
                                      • About 800,000 strokes occur each year; around 600,000 are first-time strokes
                                      • ~140,000 deaths annually; a leading cause of long-term disability
                                      • Annual cost approximately $56.5 billion
                                      • Risk increases with age, but 5–10% occur in people aged 18–45
                                      • Individuals assigned female at birth have a higher lifetime risk (partly due to longer life expectancy).
                                      • African Americans have higher rates of first ischemic stroke and stroke-related death, reflecting health disparities.

                                      Modifiable risk factors

                                      • Smoking · high blood pressure · diabetes · high cholesterol · physical inactivity · poor diet · obesity · excess alcohol use. The USPSTF provides guidelines on screening and managing these conditions.
                                      NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness881

                                      What the USPSTF actually recommends

                                      CPD.0.0116src p.2701–2702
                                      QuestionPosition
                                      Low-dose aspirin (81 mg daily) for primary preventionReduces risk of nonfatal stroke and heart attack; does NOT reduce overall mortality; increases GI and intracranial bleeding (risk higher in adults ≥60 years). Ages 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk → individual decision (shared decision-making). Age 60+ → not recommended for primary prevention.
                                      Screening for atrial fibrillationAFib is common, a major stroke risk factor, may have no symptoms, and can be detected by ECG or wearable devices. Blood thinners reduce stroke risk in confirmed AFib. However, the USPSTF states there is insufficient evidence to recommend routine screening.
                                      Screening for asymptomatic carotid artery stenosisThe USPSTF recommends AGAINST screening in asymptomatic adults. Narrowing causes only a small percentage of strokes; carotid endarterectomy may help selected patients but the overall benefit is small, there is a 2–3% surgical risk of stroke or death, and no strong evidence shows screening reduces stroke risk overall.
                                      Trap
                                      This is a counselling objective, not a treatment one. The examinable point is that three plausible-sounding preventive interventions are not blanket recommendations — and you must be able to say why to a patient who has read about them.
                                        NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness882

                                        Adherence versus compliance, and informed consent

                                        CPD.0.0116src p.2702
                                        Compliance
                                        • Compliance means a patient passively follows the doctor's instructions.
                                        • It implies obedience to medical authority.
                                        • The patient simply does what they are told without active involvement.
                                        Adherence
                                        • Adherence means the patient actively chooses to follow a treatment plan.
                                        • It involves patient responsibility, engagement, and lifestyle change.
                                        • Patients and healthcare providers work together in decision-making.
                                        Exam Lock
                                        Core difference
                                        • Compliance → passive obedience
                                        • Adherence → active participation
                                        NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness883

                                        Adherence versus compliance, and informed consent (cont.)

                                        CPD.0.0116src p.2702

                                        Elements of informed consent — Appendix E

                                        Area to explorePurposeExample question
                                        Decision-Making CapacityEnsure the patient can understand and make an independent decision*Can you tell me what you understand about your condition?*
                                        VoluntarinessConfirm the decision is being made freely*Do you feel pressured by anyone to make this decision?*
                                        DiagnosisEnsure the patient understands their condition*What is your understanding of what is going on?*
                                        Nature & Purpose of TreatmentClarify what the treatment involves and why it is recommended*Do you understand what this procedure/treatment involves?*
                                        Risks & BenefitsConfirm understanding of potential outcomes*What risks or side effects are you aware of?*
                                        Alternatives (including no treatment)Ensure awareness of all reasonable options*Do you understand what could happen if we choose not to treat this?*
                                        Patient PreferencesRespect how much detail the patient wants*Do you prefer a broad overview or detailed explanation?*
                                        Health Data & PrivacyPromote transparency and trust*Do you have questions about who can access your medical information?*
                                        Surrogate Decision-MakerIdentify a substitute decision-maker if the patient lacks capacity*Do you have a healthcare proxy or advance directive?*
                                        Confirmation of UnderstandingClose the loop and ensure clarity*Can you summarize your decision for me?*
                                        NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness884

                                        Motivational interviewing — Appendix G

                                        CPD.0.0116src p.2706
                                        A patient-centered counseling style used to help people change behaviors by exploring their own motivations (not forcing change). MI is about guiding, not directing. Don't argue or persuade. Let the patient talk themselves into change.Definition
                                        When to use
                                        • Substance use disorders
                                        • Patients not ready or resistant to change
                                        • Any behavior change (diet, meds, exercise, etc.)
                                        Core principles
                                        • Be nonjudgmental
                                        • Accept resistance (don't fight it)
                                        • Highlight discrepancies — show the gap between current behavior and long-term goals
                                        • Enhance motivation — help them find their own reasons to change

                                        OARS — how you talk to patients

                                        TechniqueExample
                                        OOpen-ended questions*What concerns you about your drinking?*
                                        AAffirmations*You've made a strong effort to cut back.*
                                        RReflection*It sounds like you feel stuck.*
                                        SSummarizing*So you want to be healthier but feel unsure where to start.*
                                        NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness885

                                        Motivational interviewing — Appendix G (cont.)

                                        CPD.0.0116src p.2706

                                        The four steps

                                        1. Engaging (build rapport) — nonjudgmental, open-ended questions, collaborate on agenda, identify patient strengths
                                        2. Focusing (set direction) — help the patient choose 1–2 behaviors to change
                                        3. Evoking (elicit motivation) — goal is change talk: ask about reasons to change, desire to change, commitment to change
                                        4. Planning (make a plan) — identify specific next steps, anticipate barriers, decide how to measure success
                                        NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness886

                                        Diet and lifestyle counselling — Appendices F and the WHO quick guide

                                        CPD.0.0116src p.2703–2706
                                        AHA — six messages
                                        • Maintain a healthy calorie balance
                                        • Regular physical activity: at least 150 minutes moderate, or 75 minutes vigorous, or a combination, spread through the week
                                        • Heart-healthy diet: variety of fruits and vegetables, whole grains, healthy protein (plant proteins, fish and seafood, low-fat dairy, lean unprocessed meats), non-tropical vegetable oils
                                        • Limit processed foods, added sugars, salt, and alcohol
                                        • Healthy choices in all food settings — read Nutrition Facts labels; look for the Heart-Check mark
                                        • Tobacco-free lifestyle: avoid smoking, vaping, all tobacco or nicotine products, and secondhand smoke
                                        WHO numbers to quote
                                        • ≥400 g (≈5 servings) of fruits and vegetables per day
                                        • Free sugars <10% of daily calories (ideally <5%)
                                        • Total fat <30% of calories; saturated fat <10%; trans fat <1%
                                        • Salt <5 g per day (≈1 teaspoon)
                                        • BMI 18.5–24.9 = healthy weight
                                        • ≥150 minutes of moderate physical activity per week
                                        • Alcohol: less is better, none is best — linked to over 200 health conditions

                                        Special populations: exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, then breastfeeding with complementary foods; avoid added sugar and salt in infant foods. Nutritious balanced meals in pregnancy and breastfeeding. In older adults, healthy diets maintain mobility, independence and overall health. End the visit by helping the patient choose 1–2 specific, achievable goals.

                                        NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness887

                                        Block check — SG-11 weakness

                                        CPD.0.0124 · CPD.0.0125

                                        A patient reports weakness that is worse at the end of the day and improves with rest, with ptosis and diplopia. Which localisation does this pattern indicate?

                                        1. AUpper motor neuron
                                        2. BLower motor neuron
                                        3. CNeuromuscular junction
                                        4. DMuscle
                                        5. EDorsal column
                                        Answer
                                        C. Does your weakness get worse with exercise? → myasthenia gravis (and mitochondrial myopathies). Fatigability with ptosis and diplopia and no sensory loss localises to the neuromuscular junction. Weakness that gets better with exercise is Lambert-Eaton syndrome, classically with small-cell lung cancer.
                                        CPD.0.0124

                                        A 62-year-old has progressive weakness with visible muscle twitching, brisk reflexes and a Babinski sign, plus dysarthria and dysphagia — with entirely normal sensation. Which diagnosis best fits?

                                        1. AGuillain-Barré syndrome
                                        2. BAmyotrophic lateral sclerosis
                                        3. CMultiple sclerosis
                                        4. DPolymyositis
                                        5. ECervical radiculopathy
                                        Answer
                                        B. Fasciculations → ALS, and voice change / trouble swallowing → ALS. The combination of upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski) and lower motor neuron signs (atrophy, fasciculations) with NO sensory loss is the signature. Numbness and tingling with weakness would indicate neurologic disorders such as MS or stroke, not myopathies, and would argue against ALS.
                                        NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness888

                                        Block check — SG-11 weakness (cont.)

                                        CPD.0.0124

                                        A patient has difficulty standing from a seated position and raising her arms above her head, with a violaceous periorbital rash and papules over the knuckles. What must be actively excluded?

                                        1. AMultiple sclerosis
                                        2. BAn underlying malignancy
                                        3. CCervical cord compression
                                        4. DGuillain-Barré syndrome
                                        5. ETodd's paralysis
                                        Answer
                                        B. Proximal weakness with heliotrope rash and Gottron's papules is dermatomyositis. The workbook lists rash or weight loss as pointing to vasculitis-associated mononeuritis, dermatomyositis, malignancy and hyperthyroidism — and adult dermatomyositis is a paraneoplastic presentation until proven otherwise.
                                        CPD.0.0116

                                        A 58-year-old asymptomatic man asks whether he should have a carotid ultrasound to prevent stroke. Which answer reflects the USPSTF position in Appendix D?

                                        1. AScreening is recommended for all adults over 50
                                        2. BScreening is recommended against in asymptomatic adults
                                        3. CScreening is recommended only if he has hypertension
                                        4. DScreening is recommended annually after age 65
                                        5. EThere is insufficient evidence either way
                                        Answer
                                        B. The USPSTF recommends AGAINST screening for asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis. Narrowing causes only a small percentage of strokes; endarterectomy carries a 2–3% surgical risk of stroke or death, and no strong evidence shows screening reduces stroke risk overall. *Insufficient evidence* is the USPSTF's position on atrial fibrillation screening, a different question.
                                        NCRS SG-11 · Nervous System Simulation 1 — Weakness889

                                        Block check — SG-11 weakness (cont.)

                                        CPD.0.0116

                                        Which statement correctly distinguishes adherence from compliance?

                                        1. AAdherence means passive obedience; compliance means active participation
                                        2. BCompliance means passive obedience; adherence means active participation
                                        3. CThey are interchangeable terms
                                        4. DCompliance applies to medication, adherence to diet
                                        5. EAdherence is measured objectively; compliance is self-reported
                                        Answer
                                        B. Compliance → passive obedience. Adherence → active participation. Compliance implies obedience to medical authority; adherence involves patient responsibility, engagement, and lifestyle change, with patients and providers working together in decision-making.
