                                        Approach to a patient with sensory deficits — the frame

                                        CPD.0.0135 · CPD.0.0136src p.2744–2746
                                        Sensory symptoms (numbness, tingling, loss of position sense, burning pain) can arise from lesions anywhere along the sensory pathway: peripheral nerves · dorsal root ganglia · nerve roots · spinal cord · brainstem · brain. The key to evaluation is LOCALIZATION + TIME COURSE.Appendix A

                                        Eight steps

                                        1. Determine the distribution — unilateral or bilateral? Face involved or not? Proximal or distal? One limb or multiple limbs?
                                        2. Identify which sensory modalities are affected
                                        3. Look for associated motor findings — even if the complaint is sensory, check strength
                                        4. Consider brain involvement
                                        5. Consider brainstem involvement
                                        6. Consider spinal cord lesions
                                        7. Consider peripheral nervous system
                                        8. Determine the time course
                                        NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness892

                                        Distribution and modality — the two questions that localise

                                        CPD.0.0136src p.2744–2745
                                        NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness893

                                        Steps 3–7 — the level-by-level clues

                                        CPD.0.0136src p.2745
                                        LevelClues the workbook gives
                                        Motor findings (step 3)Upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski) → brain or spinal cord · Lower motor neuron signs (atrophy, fasciculations, hyporeflexia) → roots or peripheral nerves · Fatigability → neuromuscular junction · Proximal symmetric weakness → muscle disease. Myopathy does NOT cause sensory loss.
                                        Brain (step 4)Contralateral deficits · face and hand commonly involved together (middle cerebral artery territory) · cheiro-oral pattern (hand + mouth numbness) → contralateral cortex · higher cortical sensory deficits: agraphesthesia, extinction to double simultaneous stimulation. Small strokes: pure MOTOR stroke = internal capsule; pure SENSORY stroke = thalamus.
                                        Brainstem (step 5)Crossed findings — ipsilateral FACE symptoms, contralateral BODY symptoms — plus cranial nerve deficits. Isolated limb symptoms without cranial nerve findings are uncommon in brainstem lesions.
                                        Spinal cord (step 6)Bilateral symptoms · a sensory LEVEL on exam · possible bowel/bladder dysfunction. If arm and leg are affected without the face → think spinal cord.
                                        Peripheral nervous system (step 7)Mononeuropathy (one nerve) · mononeuropathy multiplex (multiple separate nerves) · polyneuropathy (stocking-glove pattern). Radiculopathy: dermatomal sensory loss, often with pain. Plexopathy: affects multiple nerves in one limb.
                                        NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness894

                                        Step 8 — time course is extremely important

                                        CPD.0.0135src p.2737 · 2745–2746
                                        TempoCauses
                                        Hyperacute (seconds to minutes)Stroke · seizure · migraine · acute disc herniation · nerve infarct (vasculitis)
                                        Acute (hours to days)Guillain-Barré syndrome · transverse myelitis · multiple sclerosis relapse · infection (abscess)
                                        Subacute to chronic (weeks to years)Tumor · chronic inflammatory neuropathy (CIDP) · vitamin B12 deficiency · degenerative spine disease · metabolic causes

                                        From the history section — how the workbook times it

                                        • Acute: days to 4 weeks · Subacute: 4–8 weeks · Chronic: more than 8 weeks. Acute and subacute neuropathies include GBS, vasculitis, and radiculopathies related to diabetes or Lyme disease.
                                        • Pattern of illness — monophasic (one-time event)? progressive (getting worse over time)? relapsing and remitting (comes and goes)? A relapsing course can occur in CIDP and porphyria.
                                        • Most neuropathies develop slowly and progressively.
                                        NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness895

                                        Focused questions for numbness

                                        CPD.0.0135 · CPD.0.0134src p.2738–2739
                                        If the patient says yes to…Think about…
                                        Does your numbness come and go? (episodic)Multiple sclerosis
                                        Has your numbness steadily worsened? (progressive)Chronic polyneuropathies
                                        Did your numbness appear suddenly and remain constant?Stroke · compressive neuropathy or radiculopathy
                                        Has your numbness gradually improved?Multiple sclerosis (transverse myelitis variant)
                                        Are you numb on both sides of your body?Spinal cord compression (neoplasm, infection, degenerative disk disease) · axonal polyneuropathies (drugs, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, metabolic disorders) · demyelinating polyneuropathies (GBS, CIDP, toxic or drug-related)
                                        Is your numbness confined to just one limb or part of one limb?Radiculopathy · plexopathy (brachial or lumbar plexopathy, brachial neuritis, thoracic outlet compression syndrome) · multiple sclerosis · stroke
                                        Does your numbness involve one side of your body or your face?Stroke or TIA · hemiplegic migraine
                                        Is it difficult for you to stand on your toes?Polyneuropathy or radiculopathy
                                        Has your voice changed? Trouble swallowing?Stroke
                                        Do you have urinary retention / fecal incontinence?Cauda equina syndrome
                                        Weakness in association with your numbness?Multiple sclerosis · stroke · polyneuropathies — neurologic disorders, NOT myopathies
                                        Sudden eye pain (optic neuritis)? Heat exacerbates symptoms?Multiple sclerosis
                                        NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness896

                                        Focused questions for numbness (cont.)

                                        CPD.0.0135 · CPD.0.0134src p.2738–2739
                                        If the patient says yes to…Think about…
                                        Rash or weight loss?Vasculitis-associated mononeuritis · malignancy · hyperthyroidism
                                        Trap
                                        Urinary retention or faecal incontinence with lower-limb numbness is cauda equina syndrome — the one answer in this table that converts the encounter from a workup into an emergency.
                                          NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness897

                                          Past history, medications and exposures — numbness version

                                          CPD.0.0135src p.2739–2740
                                          QuestionThink about…
                                          Do you have diabetes mellitus?Mononeuritis · polyneuropathies · stroke
                                          Hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, vascular disease, smoking or estrogen use?Stroke (lacunar, pure sensory)
                                          Kidney disease?Uremic polyneuropathy
                                          Rheumatoid arthritis? Whiplash injury or other neck trauma?Cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy
                                          Ever treated for a malignancy? Weight loss, night sweats, fatigue?Spinal cord compression
                                          Are you taking any medications?Metformin (associated with B12 deficiency) · amiodarone, vincristine, INH, hydralazine
                                          Family history of similar problems?Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease · Krabbe disease
                                          Do you drink alcohol? How much?Alcoholic neuropathy
                                          IV drugs or unprotected sex? HIV infection?Distal symmetric polyneuropathy · tertiary syphilis · mononeuritis multiplex · toxic polyneuropathies (nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors) · CIDP
                                          Nutritional deficiencies?Vitamin B12 and vitamin B6 neuropathy
                                          Bottom Line
                                          Metformin → B12 deficiency → dorsal column signs. A diabetic on metformin with impaired vibration and proprioception may have two neuropathies at once — the distal symmetric polyneuropathy of diabetes and a treatable B12 deficiency layered on top.
                                            NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness898

                                            Physical examination — the SG-12 checklist

                                            CPD.0.0136src p.2741

                                            All examinations are performed with bilateral comparison (right and left side). A focused physical examination is required for all simulation case presentations. You are NOT required to perform an examination of the complete system for assessments and small groups.

                                            Sensory system exam — LOWER limb
                                            • Light touch
                                            • Pain
                                            • Vibration
                                            • Proprioception
                                            Motor system exam
                                            • Inspection for the position, bulk, and involuntary movements
                                            • Assess for pronator drift
                                            • Muscle tone — lower extremity: thighs and legs
                                            • Muscle strength — lower limb: hip flexion and extension · hip abduction and adduction · knee flexion and extension · ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion
                                            Reflexes, gait, coordination
                                            • Lower limb reflexes: patellar · Achilles · plantar (Babinski sign)
                                            • Gait and station: regular gait · toe walking · heel walking · tandem walking
                                            • Coordination: point-to-point movement (heel to shin)

                                            Additional relevant systems for the focused OSCE: abdominal (inspection for contours/distention; general palpation, light and deep), peripheral vascular (peripheral pulses, lower extremities), vital signs (radial pulse rhythm and amplitude; remeasure BP), and HEENT (inspection of the conjunctiva and mucosal membranes).

                                            Bottom Line
                                            The additional systems are not random. Conjunctival and mucosal inspection looks for pallor — and B12 or another nutritional deficiency is exactly the diagnosis that links anaemia to dorsal column numbness. Abdominal distention looks for urinary retention, which is the cauda equina flag.
                                              NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness899

                                              Sensory and cerebellar descriptors — Appendix C

                                              CPD.0.0133 · CPD.0.0136src p.2748
                                              TermWhat it meansWhat it suggests clinically
                                              StereognosisAbility to recognize an object by touch alone (e.g., identifying a coin in your hand with eyes closed)Loss suggests cortical (parietal lobe) dysfunction
                                              GraphesthesiaAbility to recognize writing traced on the skin purely by touchLoss suggests cortical sensory deficit
                                              Point LocalizationAbility to identify the exact spot on the skin that was touchedImpaired in cortical sensory lesions
                                              ExtinctionFailure to perceive one of two simultaneous touches on symmetrical body areasSuggests contralateral parietal lobe lesion
                                              DysmetriaOver- or undershooting a target (e.g., missing examiner's finger)Indicates cerebellar dysfunction
                                              Sensory AtaxiaLoss of coordination due to impaired position senseSuggests dorsal column dysfunction (e.g., neuropathy, B12 deficiency)
                                              Heel-to-Shin DysmetriaHeel overshoots the kneeSuggests cerebellar disease
                                              Intention TremorOscillating movement as the heel moves down the shin or as the finger approaches a targetIndicates cerebellar lesion
                                              Ataxic GaitUncoordinated, reeling, unstable gaitSeen in cerebellar disease or severe sensory loss
                                              HemiplegiaParalysis of one side of the bodySuggests contralateral brain lesion
                                              DysdiadochokinesiaInability to perform rapid alternating movementsClassic sign of cerebellar dysfunction
                                              Trap
                                              Sensory ataxia versus cerebellar ataxia. Both give an unstable gait. Sensory ataxia is dorsal column loss and is worse with the eyes closed (Romberg positive); cerebellar ataxia is unchanged by vision and comes with dysmetria, intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia.
                                                NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness900

                                                Screening for diabetic peripheral neuropathy — Appendix D

                                                CPD.0.0127src p.2749
                                                Why it matters
                                                • Diabetes can damage peripheral nerves. Many patients don't realize they have neuropathy because it may not be painful.
                                                • They remain at risk for foot ulcers, infections, injuries and amputation — that is why routine screening is essential.
                                                Distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSPN)
                                                • Accounts for ~75% of diabetic neuropathies
                                                • Slowly progressive; often asymptomatic at first
                                                • Major risk factor for ulcers, joint damage (arthropathy) and amputation
                                                • ~20% of long-standing Type 1; up to 50% of long-standing Type 2
                                                • Other diabetic neuropathies: autonomic neuropathy, mononeuropathies, polyradiculopathies

                                                Symptoms, if present

                                                • Numbness · tingling · poor balance · burning pain · stabbing pain · electric shock-like sensations (usually in the feet)
                                                Exam Lock
                                                ADA-recommended foot exam
                                                • Temperature or pinprick sensation
                                                • Proprioception
                                                • Ankle reflexes
                                                • Vibration sense (128-Hz tuning fork)
                                                • Light touch sensation (10-g monofilament)
                                                • Inspection for skin breakdown, poor circulation, structural abnormalities

                                                Prevention and management: tight blood sugar control — very effective in Type 1 diabetes, modestly effective in Type 2 diabetes.

                                                NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness901

                                                SG-11 and SG-12 — the shared skeleton

                                                CPD.0.0124 · CPD.0.0135src p.2685–2755
                                                StageWeakness (SG-11)Numbness (SG-12)
                                                First questionIs this TRUE weakness, or fatigue/asthenia?Where exactly, and how did it evolve? — localization + time course
                                                DistributionBoth sides → cord compression · one limb → nerve/root/MS/stroke · one side + face → stroke/TIA/hemiplegic migraine · proximal → myopathy · distal → neuropathyFace + body one side → brain or brainstem · face only → brainstem or cortex · arm + leg no face → cervical cord or medulla · bilateral → cord or neuropathy · stocking-glove → peripheral neuropathy
                                                Modality / modifierWorse with exercise → myasthenia · better with exercise → Lambert-Eaton · fasciculations → ALSPain and temperature → spinothalamic · vibration and proprioception → dorsal columns · light touch → less localizing
                                                Red flagCranial nerve signs → lesion above the foramen magnum; fever → abscess, venous sinus thrombosis, encephalitisUrinary retention / faecal incontinence → cauda equina syndrome; sensory level → cord
                                                Exam focusCN V, VII, IX/X, XII · full motor, reflexes, gait, sensation, coordinationLower-limb sensation (light touch, pain, vibration, proprioception) · lower-limb motor and reflexes · gait · heel-to-shin
                                                Then the sameProblem representation → illness script → ranked differential → investigations → closure → CIS feedback → SOAP note and critiqueIdentical structure; the roles rotate
                                                NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness902

                                                Block check — SG-12 numbness

                                                CPD.0.0136

                                                A patient has numbness of the LEFT side of the face and the RIGHT arm and leg, with diplopia. Where is the lesion?

                                                1. ARight cerebral cortex
                                                2. BLeft thalamus
                                                3. CBrainstem
                                                4. DCervical spinal cord
                                                5. ELeft brachial plexus
                                                Answer
                                                C. Brainstem lesions often produce CROSSED findings: ipsilateral face symptoms, contralateral body symptoms — plus cranial nerve deficits such as diplopia. A cortical lesion gives contralateral face + arm + leg together; a cervical cord lesion gives arm + leg without the face.
                                                CPD.0.0135

                                                A 45-year-old has bilateral stocking-distribution numbness and impaired vibration sense in both feet, developing over 2 years. He has type 2 diabetes and takes metformin. Which additional cause must be considered?

                                                1. ACauda equina syndrome
                                                2. BVitamin B12 deficiency
                                                3. CHemiplegic migraine
                                                4. DGuillain-Barré syndrome
                                                5. EBrachial plexopathy
                                                Answer
                                                B. Metformin is associated with B12 deficiency, and vitamin B12 and B6 neuropathy are listed under nutritional deficiencies. B12 deficiency causes dorsal column loss — sensory ataxia with impaired vibration and proprioception — which can layer on top of the distal symmetric polyneuropathy that accounts for ~75% of diabetic neuropathies.
                                                CPD.0.0135

                                                A patient with 3 days of ascending numbness in both legs now reports urinary retention. Which is the most urgent consideration?

                                                1. AChronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
                                                2. BCauda equina syndrome
                                                3. CMultiple sclerosis relapse
                                                4. DAlcoholic neuropathy
                                                5. ECharcot-Marie-Tooth disease
                                                Answer
                                                B. Do you have urinary retention / fecal incontinence? → cauda equina syndrome. Bilateral lower-limb sensory symptoms with bowel/bladder dysfunction is the emergency pattern; CIDP and Charcot-Marie-Tooth are chronic, and the workbook places bowel/bladder dysfunction squarely under spinal cord lesions.
                                                NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness903

                                                Block check — SG-12 numbness (cont.)

                                                CPD.0.0136 · CPD.0.0133

                                                On examination a patient cannot identify a coin placed in her hand with her eyes closed, and fails to perceive the left-sided touch when both hands are touched simultaneously. Where is the lesion?

                                                1. ADorsal columns
                                                2. BCerebellum
                                                3. CRight parietal cortex
                                                4. DPeripheral nerve
                                                5. ENeuromuscular junction
                                                Answer
                                                C. Loss of stereognosis suggests cortical (parietal lobe) dysfunction; extinction — failure to perceive one of two simultaneous touches on symmetrical body areas — suggests a contralateral parietal lobe lesion. Left-sided extinction therefore localises to the right parietal cortex.
                                                CPD.0.0135

                                                A patient develops numbness over seconds that then remains constant. Which tempo category does this fit, and what is the leading cause?

                                                1. AAcute — Guillain-Barré syndrome
                                                2. BHyperacute — stroke
                                                3. CSubacute — chronic inflammatory neuropathy
                                                4. DChronic — B12 deficiency
                                                5. ESubacute — tumour
                                                Answer
                                                B. Hyperacute (seconds to minutes): stroke · seizure · migraine · acute disc herniation · nerve infarct (vasculitis). The focused-question table also lists "did your numbness appear suddenly and remain constant?" → stroke, compressive neuropathy or radiculopathy. GBS is acute (hours to days); CIDP, tumour and B12 deficiency are subacute to chronic (weeks to years).
                                                NCRS SG-12 · Nervous System Simulation 2 — Numbness904

                                                NCRS Small Group 13 — Psychiatry Skills & Simulation

                                                Department of Clinical Skills · Creator: Dr. Michon Sukhoo-Pertab (updated August 2026). Reviewed by Dr. Najee Hill, Dr. Dawnette Gonzague and Dr. Onika Miguel. The presenting complaint is low mood / sadness.

                                                Department of Clinical Skills · Dr. Michon Sukhoo-Pertab  ·  source pp. 2756–2785

                                                Learning objectives — verbatim

                                                • CPD.0.0148 Discuss the key clinical features and typical clinical course of mood disorders.
                                                • CPD.0.0144 Present an age-appropriate medical history, that differentiates among etiologies of disease, for a patient presenting with persistent low mood.
                                                • CPD.0.0143 Assess the presence or absence of possible co-morbidities including dementia, anxiety disorder, adverse drug effects, substance abuse, and grief in any patient suspected of having a mood disorder.
                                                • CPD.0.0142 Assess a patient's risk for suicide and be able to appropriately respond to high-risk patients.
                                                • CPD.0.0167 Discuss the Full Mental Status examination according to the suspected differentials identifying the discriminating clinical features to establish the diagnosis.
                                                • CPD.0.0147 Rank a list of clinical differential diagnoses based on the patient's presentation in order of highest probability to least likely.
                                                • CPD.0.0137 Provide supportive evidence from the subjective/objective sections to justify the differential diagnoses.
                                                • CPD.0.0145 Generate a list of appropriate initial investigations based on the differential diagnoses.
                                                • CPD.0.0138 Provide basic information and explain the provisional diagnosis, relevant investigations, prognosis, and treatment plan to the patient.
                                                • CPD.0.0146 Demonstrate the ability to document pertinent information (negative and positive) obtained from the history and physical examination in the appropriate sections of the patient note.
                                                • CPD.0.0139 · CPD.0.0140 · CPD.0.0141 Teamwork and leadership; communication and interpersonal skills; respect towards the patient, families, and all members of the health care team.
                                                Source note
                                                The mental status examination itself — its six components, the descriptors and the cognitive tests — is covered in the CLSK section *Psychiatric Interview and Mental Status Examination* earlier in this deck. This section carries the workbook content that is unique to SG-13: the depressed-mood workup, suicide-risk assessment, alcohol screening, the abnormality tables the workbook adds to the MSE, and how to close the encounter with a depressed patient.

                                                  NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood907

                                                  General approach to the psychiatric patient

                                                  CPD.0.0140 · CPD.0.0144src p.2760
                                                  The distinction between symptoms and signs is less clear in psychiatry than in the rest of medicine. The psychiatric interview, which covers both, has several purposes: to obtain a history of symptoms, to assess the present mental state for signs and to establish rapport that will facilitate further management.General Approach
                                                  • Try to develop rapport early in the interview, if possible, and to consolidate it before raising a sensitive topic, although sometimes you must cover such material without delay. It is particularly important to ask about suicidal thoughts.

                                                  Getting started

                                                  QuestionRemember
                                                  Over the past month, have you been feeling down, depressed, or hopeless?Depressed patients may make the interviewer feel sad. Use your emotional response as a diagnostic clue.
                                                  Over the past month, have you been bothered by little interest or pleasure in doing things?This symptom is often more prominent than depressed mood in older adults.

                                                  In addition to the introduction, it may be useful to begin with a general question such as *"How are things at home or work?"* or *"How are you doing emotionally?"*

                                                  Bottom Line
                                                  Use your own emotional response as data. That instruction is unusual in a physical examination workbook and it is deliberate — countertransference is an observation, not a distraction.
                                                    NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood908

                                                    Interview framework for depressed mood

                                                    CPD.0.0144 · CPD.0.0145src p.2760
                                                    1. If depressed mood or anhedonia is present, inquire about additional depressive symptoms by clinical interview, or administer a depression questionnaire such as the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ). The PHQ is a 9-item, self-report questionnaire that assesses the 9 signs and symptoms specified in the DSM to diagnose major depressive disorder; the patient rates the past 2 weeks from "not at all" to "nearly every day"; total scores range 0–27 and scores ≥10 indicate a probable depressive disorder. The PHQ questionnaire is not used in this small group — use SIGECAPS.
                                                    2. Ask about impact on daily functioning, because impaired function at home, work, or in interpersonal relationships is required to diagnose clinical depression.
                                                    3. Assess for alarm symptoms of suicidality.
                                                    4. Consider secondary causes such as medications, hypothyroidism, malignancy, or autoimmune or central nervous system disorders.
                                                    5. Consider symptom pattern, duration, and associated symptoms to make a specific diagnosis.
                                                    Trap
                                                    Step 2 is the one that separates a symptom list from a diagnosis. Five symptoms without functional impairment is not clinical depression — and the workbook prints that requirement explicitly.

                                                      Once clinical depression is diagnosed: explore the patient's understanding and acceptance of the diagnosis — stigmatizing beliefs or outright rejection may interfere with treatment adherence; and ask about prior episodes and response to treatment — the risk of relapse, and hence the need for longer-term treatment, increases with the number of prior episodes.

                                                      NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood909

                                                      SIGECAPS — the eight neurovegetative symptoms

                                                      CPD.0.0148 · CPD.0.0144src p.2760
                                                      SymptomDetail
                                                      SSleep disturbance*increased during day or decreased at night
                                                      IInterest reducedloss of interest in previously enjoyable activities
                                                      GGuiltworthlessness*, hopelessness*, regret, self-blame
                                                      EEnergy loss or fatigue*
                                                      CConcentration impairment*
                                                      AAppetite change*usually decreased; occasionally increased
                                                      PPsychomotor changeretardation/lethargy or agitation/anxiety
                                                      SSuicidal thoughtspreoccupation with death

                                                      To meet the diagnosis of major depression, a patient must have 4 of the symptoms PLUS depressed mood or anhedonia, for at least 2 weeks. To meet the diagnosis of dysthymic disorder, a patient must have 2 of the 6 symptoms marked with an asterisk (*), plus depression, for at least 2 years.

                                                      Trap
                                                      This is a counting convention, not a contradiction. The DSM says *five symptoms, at least one of which is depressed mood or anhedonia*. The workbook's phrasing — *4 of the symptoms plus depressed mood or anhedonia* — counts the gateway symptom separately and arrives at the same five. Know both forms so neither wording throws you.

                                                        Reminder from the workbook: it helps to remind you of the symptoms of depression, it does not replace the standard interview or the mental status examination, and it should not be used to report the patient interview. The goal during the interview is to cover OPQRST of the main and associative symptoms.

                                                        NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood910

                                                        SWAG — separating depression from normal sadness

                                                        CPD.0.0148src p.2762–2763
                                                        Symptoms such as suicidality, severe weight loss, absence of pleasure in one's usual activities (i.e., anhedonia), and extreme guilt (the SWAG symptoms) as well as disruption in work or interpersonal relationships, help identify [mood disorders]. In severe cases, psychotic symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations may also be present in a mood disorder patient.Behavioral Science in Medicine
                                                        Exam Lock
                                                        If ONE of the following is documented, it is most likely that the patient is depressed
                                                        • S — Suicidality (serious thoughts or attempts at self-destruction)
                                                        • W — Weight loss (more than 5% of normal body weight without medical cause)
                                                        • A — Anhedonia (loss of pleasure or interest in usually pleasurable activities)
                                                        • G — Guilt (feelings of responsibility for negative life events when little or none exists)

                                                        Why mood disorders are not just strong feelings

                                                        • Variations in mood are common in everyday life. People normally feel sad when they experience a loss or disappointment and feel happy when they anticipate or experience a positive event. In contrast, patients with primary mood disorders show DISCORDANCE between life events and how they feel emotionally. There may be no change in their current social circumstances to account for their emotions, or they may feel increased, decreased, or even contradictory emotional responsiveness to a change.
                                                        Student 1
                                                        • Does poorly on an exam; remains so sad that 9 months later he has little appetite for food, has lost 20 lb (9.1 kg), and cannot enjoy his favorite activities.
                                                        • Evidence of depression
                                                        Student 2
                                                        • Does well on an exam; feels elated and believes she can mentally transmit her superior knowledge to others.
                                                        • Elevated mood and psychotic thinking that can characterize mania
                                                        NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood911

                                                        SWAG — separating depression from normal sadness (cont.)

                                                        CPD.0.0148src p.2762–2763

                                                        Dysthymia and hypomania are attenuated versions of depression and mania, respectively. The primary mood disorders are MDD and bipolar disorder (I and II) with their less severe counterparts persistent depressive (dysthymic) disorder and cyclothymic disorder. Mood symptoms occurring because of a medical condition or substance use (secondary mood disorders) are correctly diagnosed as mood disorders resulting from a general medical condition or substance-induced mood disorder.

                                                        NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood912

                                                        Alarm symptoms — asking about suicide

                                                        CPD.0.0142src p.2760
                                                        Because patients rarely volunteer thoughts of suicide, it is important to ask directly about suicidality.Alarm Symptoms

                                                        How to open the topic

                                                        • *"Have you been feeling that life is not worth living or that you would be better off dead?"*
                                                        • *"Sometimes when a person feels down or depressed, they might think about dying. Have you been having any thoughts like that?"*
                                                        • If patients have suicidal ideation, ask more detailed questions to distinguish PASSIVE from ACTIVE suicidal ideation and assess the risk for suicide.
                                                        QuestionInterpretation
                                                        Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself in some way?A response of "not at all" puts the patient at LOW risk.
                                                        Have you made any plans or considered a method that you might use to harm yourself?If yes, ask for details.
                                                        Have you ever attempted to harm yourself?Past attempts are a risk factor for future attempts.
                                                        There's a big difference between having a thought and acting on a thought. Do you think you might try to hurt yourself in the near future?A positive response puts the patient at VERY HIGH risk for suicide.
                                                        NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood913

                                                        The SAD PERSONS scale

                                                        CPD.0.0142src p.2762
                                                        NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood914

                                                        Serious general medical conditions to screen for

                                                        CPD.0.0143 · CPD.0.0145src p.2761 · 2765
                                                        Depressive symptoms can be mimicked by medical conditions and substance use. Screening for heart disease, stroke, diabetes, thyroid problems, and alcohol/drug use is crucial to clarifying the diagnosis.Alarm Symptoms
                                                        QuestionThink about
                                                        Have you lost weight despite having a normal or near-normal appetite?Malignancy
                                                        Have you felt cold when everyone else felt comfortable? Have you noticed dry skin or constipation?Hypothyroidism
                                                        Have you noticed a rash, dry eyes or mouth, difficulty swallowing food, or pain/swelling in the hands or feet?Autoimmune disorders (e.g., Sjögren syndrome)
                                                        Have you noticed a tremor or a change in gait? Have you had episodes of weakness on one side of the body?Central nervous system disorders (Parkinson's disease or recurrent strokes)
                                                        Bottom Line
                                                        This is why the SG-13 rubric asks for two additional examination skills. If your differential includes hypothyroidism, the workbook names them: inspect and palpate the thyroid gland · assess for pretibial myxedema · assess pulse for bradycardia · assess deep tendon reflexes in upper and lower extremities (Woltman sign).
                                                          NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood915

                                                          Focused questions — mapping answers onto diagnoses

                                                          CPD.0.0144 · CPD.0.0147src p.2761
                                                          QuestionThink about
                                                          How has your mood been lately? Have you been feeling down, depressed, or hopeless? How often? How long does it last?Depressed mood
                                                          Have you lost interest in your usual activities? Do you get less pleasure from things you used to enjoy?Anhedonia
                                                          How have you been sleeping? How does that compare to your normal sleep?Sleep disturbance
                                                          Has there been any change in your appetite or weight?Appetite or weight change
                                                          Have you noticed a decrease in your energy level?Decreased energy
                                                          Have you been feeling fidgety or had problems sitting still? Have you felt slowed down, like you were moving in slow motion or stuck in mud?Increased or decreased psychomotor activity
                                                          Have you been having trouble concentrating? Is it harder to make decisions than before?Decreased concentration
                                                          Are you feeling guilty or blaming yourself for things? How would you describe yourself to someone who had never met you before?Guilt or feelings of worthlessness
                                                          Have you felt that life is not worth living or that you would be better off dead?Suicidal ideation

                                                          Quality — how many symptoms

                                                          FindingDiagnosis
                                                          At least 5 DSM symptoms including depressed mood or anhedoniaMajor depressive disorder
                                                          Milder severity (<5 DSM symptoms) including depressed mood or anhedoniaDysthymic disorder · depressive disorder NOS · adjustment disorder
                                                          Mild symptoms that do not impair functionTransient dysphoria
                                                          NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood916

                                                          Time course and associative symptoms

                                                          CPD.0.0143 · CPD.0.0147src p.2761
                                                          QuestionThink about
                                                          Did these symptoms begin after the death of a loved one?Bereavement
                                                          Did these symptoms begin during a time of stress?Adjustment disorder with depressed mood
                                                          Have you ever seen or experienced a traumatic event in which you or someone else's life was in danger? How about threat of serious injury?Posttraumatic stress disorder
                                                          Have these symptoms been present on most days for at least 2 years?Dysthymic disorder or chronic major depressive disorder
                                                          Do these episodes occur at a particular time of the year?Seasonal affective disorder
                                                          Do your symptoms begin during the week prior to menses and remit within a few days of menses?Premenstrual dysphoric disorder
                                                          Have you ever had periods where your mood was very good, or too good, for no reason — with racing thoughts, reduced need for sleep, or increased energy? Did it get you into trouble, for instance by spending too much money, impulsively traveling, or taking on too many projects?Bipolar disorder
                                                          Have you ever had visions or seen things that other people could not see?Depressive disorder with psychotic features
                                                          Have you heard things that other people could not hear, such as noises or the voices of people whispering or talking?Psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder
                                                          Have you ever had a panic attack, where out of the blue you experienced intense anxiety, fear, or discomfort for no apparent reason?Panic disorder
                                                          Have you felt nervous, anxious, or on edge on more than half the days in the last month?Generalized anxiety disorder
                                                          Do you drink alcohol? Was there ever a time when you drank too much? Has drinking ever caused problems such as missing work, legal problems, or driving while intoxicated?Alcohol disorder · substance-induced mood disorder
                                                          NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood917

                                                          Time course and associative symptoms (cont.)

                                                          CPD.0.0143 · CPD.0.0147src p.2761
                                                          Trap
                                                          Always screen for a past manic or hypomanic episode in a patient presenting with depression. Missing it and starting an antidepressant alone is the classic error — and it is why this question sits in the workbook's *associative symptoms* block rather than as an afterthought.
                                                            NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood918

                                                            Screening for unhealthy alcohol use

                                                            CPD.0.0143src p.2762
                                                            NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood919

                                                            Closing the encounter with a depressed patient

                                                            CPD.0.0138 · CPD.0.0140src p.2766

                                                            Why this matters — the workbook's own data

                                                            • Patients with depression prefer to be treated by primary care providers rather than mental health specialists. NHANES data (2006) show that only 29% of persons with depression and 39% of persons with severe depression reported contacting a mental health professional in the past year. In 1997, 87% of outpatients with depression received care from a primary care clinician as compared with only 69% in 1987, with related decreases in treatment from psychologists from 30% in 1987 to 19% in 1997.

                                                            Reasons for inadequate treatment

                                                            • Patients are reluctant to accept the diagnosis of depression due to personal or cultural reasons.
                                                            • Patients refuse to start medications or discontinue them prematurely.
                                                            • Clinicians do not titrate antidepressant medications to effective doses, usually due to knowledge deficits, discomfort or clinical inertia.

                                                            What to do in the closure

                                                            • Inform patients about the illness and inform them about medications, counseling and self-management.
                                                            • Help patients establish both short-term and long-term goals. Support patients' action plans and help them learn from examining successes and failures.
                                                            • Elicit the patient's perspectives, respond with empathy, and present "small chunks" of information directed at their beliefs using simple language. Respond to non-verbals; use normalization, symptom assumption and transitioning; check frequently for understanding.
                                                            NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood920

                                                            The scripts the workbook gives you

                                                            CPD.0.0138src p.2766

                                                            Small chunks

                                                            • *"While everyone gets sad once in a while and particularly when bad things happen, depression is a different story."*
                                                            • *"Depression comes from chemical imbalances in the brain that result in a persistent sadness or loss of enjoyment and even hopelessness. These brain chemistry changes also produce poor sleep and other physical problems like low energy, change in appetite, pain in the belly or back, or headaches."*
                                                            • *"The good news is that this illness process is treatable."*
                                                            • *"Good data show that outcomes of other illnesses — such as diabetes, heart trouble, and more — improve with treatment of depression."*
                                                            • *"We usually prescribe either antidepressants and/or counseling. What do you think… are you willing to consider treatment for your depression?"*

                                                            Teach back

                                                            • *"I've given you a lot of information about depression and its treatment. Just so that I know that I was clear, would you mind telling me back what you understand?"*
                                                            • Using the phrase "so that I know that I was clear" rather than "so that I know you understand" emphasizes it is the CLINICIAN'S responsibility to ensure that the information is absorbed rather than a "test" of the patient's knowledge.
                                                            NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood921

                                                            The scripts the workbook gives you (cont.)

                                                            CPD.0.0138src p.2766

                                                            Attend to somatic symptoms

                                                            • Explicitly discuss somatic symptoms so that useful dialogue about treatment is not impeded by patients' concern that the meaning of body symptoms might be ignored or discounted. Many patients have heard of serious or fatal treatment delays because a clinician "explained away" pain or fatigue as depression.
                                                            • Maintain a multidirectional approach: evaluate physical symptoms with respect and concern and treat them conservatively and responsively, while simultaneously treating the depressive syndrome as an independent cause of suffering and disability.
                                                            • Inform patients with known chronic medical problems that depression worsens somatic symptoms — *"our minds and bodies are closely linked and often when people have depression their pain feels worse, so treating the depression can improve the back pain."*
                                                            • When patients insist on a purely somatic explanation, ask them to name their biggest concern or fear about the complaint — this elicits the underlying worry, which can then be addressed head-on.
                                                            Bottom Line
                                                            Some clinicians compare depression to other chronic illnesses with chemical deficiencies: *"Depression is a deficiency problem like diabetes. If your pancreas makes too little insulin, your sugar goes up. In depression certain parts of your brain make too little serotonin and the deficit seriously affects how you think and feel."*
                                                              NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood922

                                                              The three psychiatric evaluations — which tool, when

                                                              CPD.0.0167 · CPD.0.0169src p.2773
                                                              Confusion Assessment Method (CAM)Mini-Mental Status Exam (MMSE / Folstein)Mental Status Examination (MSE)
                                                              IndicationDelirium (acute confusional state)Dementia (cognitive impairment)Psychiatric presentation (cognitive & behavioral impairments)
                                                              Used in this small group?NoNo — see Term 2 NB SG 12Yes
                                                              OverviewQuickly and accurately detects delirium at the bedside. Sensitivity 94–100%, specificity 90–100%, negative predictive value 90–100%. Recommended for screening at-risk patients: hospitalized general medicine patients, patients post major elective surgery, and ICU patients.The best-known screening test for dementia. Assesses orientation to time and place, registration, attention and calculation, recall, language, repetition of a complex phrase, and complex commands. Maximum 30 points; patients scoring fewer than 24 are generally considered to have dementia.An important diagnostic tool in neurological and psychiatric practice, used to assess mental state and behaviors quantitatively and qualitatively: appearance and behavior · speech · mood and affect · thought process and content · perceptual disturbances · sensorium and cognition · insight and judgment at a specific point in time.

                                                              The MMSE can be used in your OSCE assessment; the 30-point questionnaire will not be provided.

                                                              NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood923

                                                              Cultural considerations in the MSE

                                                              CPD.0.0167src p.2773
                                                              • A patient's cultural background can affect many aspects of the MSE.
                                                              • Clinicians must be cognizant that their own culture and life experiences can affect their observation and interpretation of a patient's behavior. This awareness is necessary when differentiating between cultural norms and psychopathology.
                                                              • For example, seeing visions and communicating with deceased loved ones may be common experiences in one culture yet considered symptoms of a psychotic disorder in another.
                                                              • Patients from different cultures may communicate and/or manifest symptoms in a variety of ways — for example, patients from Asian cultures may be more likely to endorse somatic symptoms rather than emotional symptoms.
                                                              • A patient's behavioral presentation, including eye contact, emotional expression, and willingness to provide personal information, is also culturally shaped.
                                                              Bottom Line
                                                              The definition of a delusion already carries the cultural safeguard in it: an abnormal belief "not shared by others from the same culture or cultural sub-group." That clause is the whole reason cultural competence sits inside the MSE and not beside it.
                                                                NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood924

                                                                Thought PROCESS abnormalities — the descriptor table

                                                                CPD.0.0164src p.2776
                                                                TermDescriptionCharacteristic of
                                                                CircumstantialNonlinear thought expressed as long-winded explanations and with multiple deviations from the central topic before a central idea is finally expressedSchizophrenia · bipolar disorder · epilepsy · intellectual disability · developmental delay
                                                                Clang associationsThe use of words based on rhyme patterns rather than meaningSchizophrenia · manic states
                                                                ConfabulationFabrication of facts or events in response to questions, to fill in the gaps from impaired memoryKorsakoff syndrome from alcoholism
                                                                Flight of ideasThe quick succession of thoughts usually expressed as a continuous flow of rapid speech and abrupt changes in topicBipolar disorder (manic phase)
                                                                Incoherence / Word saladSpeech that is incomprehensible and illogical, with lack of meaningful connections, abrupt changes in topic, or disordered grammar or word use. Flight of ideas, when severe, may produce incoherenceSevere psychotic disturbances (usually schizophrenia)
                                                                Loose associations / derailmentsIncoherent thinking expressed as illogical, sudden, and frequent changes of topicSchizophrenia · other psychotic disorders
                                                                PerseverationThe inappropriate repetition or persistence of behavior, speech, or soundsPsychoses · epilepsy · dementia · Parkinson disease · traumatic brain injury · stroke
                                                                TangentialNonlinear thought expressed as a gradual deviation from a focused idea or question; multiple unnecessary details without actually answering the questionSchizophrenia · anxiety · delirium
                                                                Thought blockingThe abrupt ending of a thought process expressed as a sudden stop in the middle of answering a questionSchizophrenia · other psychoses

                                                                Circumstantial eventually arrives at the point; tangential never does. That is the single distinction most often tested from this table.

                                                                NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood925

                                                                Thought CONTENT — abnormal beliefs

                                                                CPD.0.0165src p.2777
                                                                TermDefinition
                                                                DelusionAn abnormal belief, held with total conviction, which is maintained in spite of proof or logical argument to the contrary and is not shared by others from the same culture or cultural sub-group. Types: persecutory · grandiose · jealous · erotomanic (the belief that another person is in love with the individual) · somatic (bodily functions or sensations) · unspecified, including delusions of reference — the belief that external events, objects, or people have a particular and unusual personal significance (e.g., commands from the radio or television)
                                                                Magical thinkingAn irrational belief that certain actions and outcomes are linked, often culturally determined by folklore or custom, e.g. fingers crossed for good luck
                                                                Overvalued ideasBeliefs that are held, valued, expressed and acted on, beyond the norm for the culture to which the person belongs
                                                                Thought broadcastingThe belief that the patient's thoughts are heard by others
                                                                Thought insertionThe belief that thoughts are being placed in the patient's head from outside
                                                                Thought withdrawalThe belief that thoughts are being removed from the patient's head
                                                                AnxietiesApprehensive anticipation of future danger or misfortune accompanied by feelings of worry, distress, and/or somatic symptoms of tension
                                                                CompulsionsRepetitive behaviors that the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession, aimed at preventing or reducing anxiety or a dreaded event or situation; these behaviors are excessive and unrealistically connected to the provoking stimulus
                                                                PhobiasPersistent irrational fears accompanied by a compelling desire to avoid the provoking stimulus

                                                                Clinical correlate: compulsions, obsessions, phobias, and anxieties often occur in anxiety disorders. Delusions and feelings of unreality or depersonalization are often associated with psychotic disorders. Delusions may also occur in delirium, severe mood disorders, and dementia.

                                                                NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood926

                                                                Perception — hallucination, illusion, depersonalization

                                                                CPD.0.0154src p.2777
                                                                TermDefinition and clinical correlate
                                                                HallucinationsPerception-like experiences that seem real but, unlike illusions, LACK actual external stimulation. The person may or may not recognize the experiences as false. May be auditory, visual, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or somatic. False perceptions associated with dreaming, falling asleep, and awakening are NOT classified as hallucinations. *Clinical correlate:* delirium, dementia (less commonly), posttraumatic stress disorder, schizophrenia, and substance use. Some auditory hallucinations are characteristic of schizophrenia: voices discussing the patient in the third person, or giving a running commentary on the person's activities ('Now he's opening the kitchen cupboard').
                                                                IllusionsMISINTERPRETATIONS of real external stimuli, such as mistaking rustling leaves for the sound of voices. *Clinical correlate:* grief reactions, delirium, acute and posttraumatic stress disorders, and schizophrenia.
                                                                DepersonalizationSense that one's self or identity is different, changed, unreal, lost, or detached from one's mind or body — a subjective experience of feeling unreal.
                                                                DerealizationSense that the environment is strange, unreal, or remote — a subjective experience that the surrounding environment is unreal.

                                                                People find depersonalisation and derealisation intensely unpleasant but hard to describe. They may occur in association with severe tiredness or intense anxiety but can also arise in most types of mental illness. Ask: *"Have you ever felt that you were not real, or that the world around you wasn't real?"* Depersonalization/derealization disorder is a dissociative disorder, often triggered by severe stress; diagnosis is by symptoms after other causes are ruled out; treatment is psychotherapy plus medications for comorbid depression and/or anxiety.

                                                                Trap
                                                                Hallucination = no stimulus. Illusion = a real stimulus, misread. That one line settles most exam items on this table.
                                                                  NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood927

                                                                  Block check — SG-13 psychiatry

                                                                  CPD.0.0142

                                                                  A patient with low mood answers "yes" to having considered a specific method and says he thinks he might act on it in the near future. How does the workbook classify this?

                                                                  1. ALow risk
                                                                  2. BModerate risk
                                                                  3. CVery high risk for suicide
                                                                  4. DPassive suicidal ideation
                                                                  5. EInsufficient information
                                                                  Answer
                                                                  C. "There's a big difference between having a thought and acting on a thought. Do you think you might try to hurt yourself in the near future?" — a positive response puts the patient at VERY HIGH risk for suicide. A response of "not at all" to thoughts of self-harm is what puts a patient at low risk.
                                                                  CPD.0.0142

                                                                  Applying the SAD PERSONS scale, a patient scores 8. What does the scale suggest?

                                                                  1. AHome with appropriate follow-up
                                                                  2. BAdmit or discharge with appropriate follow-up
                                                                  3. CAdmit to hospital
                                                                  4. DNo action required
                                                                  5. ERepeat the scale in one week
                                                                  Answer
                                                                  C. 0–2 home with appropriate follow-up · 3–6 admit or discharge with appropriate follow-up · 7–10 admit to hospital. The workbook adds: this is a guide only and should not be used to replace clinical judgement.
                                                                  CPD.0.0143

                                                                  Which single screening question does the workbook name as the BEST INITIAL tool for unhealthy alcohol use?

                                                                  1. AThe CAGE questionnaire
                                                                  2. BThe full 10-item AUDIT
                                                                  3. CHow many times in the past year have you had 5 (4 for women) or more drinks in a day?
                                                                  4. DHave you ever felt you ought to cut down on your drinking?
                                                                  5. EThe AUDIT-C three-item questionnaire
                                                                  Answer
                                                                  C. Step 1 is the single-item screen — "How many times in the past year have you had 5 (4 for women) or more drinks in a day?", with ≥1 time being positive — described as the best initial screening tool. CAGE is best for identifying dependence and less sensitive for early/unhealthy use; AUDIT-C is more sensitive than CAGE for early detection.
                                                                  NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood929

                                                                  Block check — SG-13 psychiatry (cont.)

                                                                  CPD.0.0164

                                                                  A patient asked about their medical history describes at length the hospitals they have stayed in, never mentioning their medical conditions. Which thought-process abnormality is this?

                                                                  1. ACircumstantial
                                                                  2. BTangential
                                                                  3. CFlight of ideas
                                                                  4. DPerseveration
                                                                  5. EThought blocking
                                                                  Answer
                                                                  B. Tangential: nonlinear thought expressed as a gradual deviation from a focused idea or question — multiple unnecessary details WITHOUT actually answering the question. Circumstantial thought also wanders but a central idea is finally expressed.
                                                                  CPD.0.0154

                                                                  A patient mistakes rustling leaves for the sound of voices. What is this, and what is it NOT?

                                                                  1. AA hallucination, because the voices are not real
                                                                  2. BAn illusion — a misinterpretation of a real external stimulus
                                                                  3. CA delusion of reference
                                                                  4. DDepersonalization
                                                                  5. EThought insertion
                                                                  Answer
                                                                  B. Illusions are misinterpretations of REAL external stimuli. Hallucinations are perception-like experiences that seem real but LACK actual external stimulation. Illusions occur in grief reactions, delirium, acute and posttraumatic stress disorders, and schizophrenia.
                                                                  NCRS SG-13 · Psychiatry Skills and Simulation — Low Mood930

                                                                  Block check — SG-13 psychiatry (cont.)

                                                                  CPD.0.0164 · CPD.0.0161

                                                                  A 68-year-old with alcohol use disorder cannot recall how he acquired a bruise and produces a detailed but fabricated story. Which term applies, and which syndrome is it characteristic of?

                                                                  1. APerseveration — dementia
                                                                  2. BConfabulation — Korsakoff syndrome from alcoholism
                                                                  3. CClang associations — manic states
                                                                  4. DLoose associations — schizophrenia
                                                                  5. ECircumstantiality — epilepsy
                                                                  Answer
                                                                  B. Confabulation: fabrication of facts or events in response to questions, to fill in the gaps from impaired memory — characteristic of Korsakoff syndrome from alcoholism. It is also the reason the workbook advises checking recent memory against answers you can verify from other sources.
                                                                  CPD.0.0144 · CPD.0.0167

                                                                  Which statement about the PHQ is correct per this workbook?

                                                                  1. AIt replaces the mental status examination
                                                                  2. BIt is a 9-item self-report tool; scores range 0–27 and ≥10 indicates a probable depressive disorder, but it is not used in this small group
                                                                  3. CIt is a 30-point clinician-administered dementia screen
                                                                  4. DIt is scored over the past 6 months
                                                                  5. EIt is the same instrument as the AUDIT-C
                                                                  Answer
                                                                  B. The PHQ is a 9-item, self-report questionnaire assessing the 9 DSM signs and symptoms of major depressive disorder over the past 2 weeks; total scores range from 0 to 27; scores ≥10 indicate a probable depressive disorder. The PHQ questionnaire is not used in this small group — use SIGECAPS. The 30-point instrument with a <24 cut-off is the MMSE, a dementia screen.
