                                                                  PATH

                                                                  NCRS SG-14 — Neuropathology

                                                                  Department of Pathology, SGUSOM. Four reference images and twelve numbered slides — the whole neuropathology block condensed into what you must recognise down a microscope or on a gross specimen.

                                                                  Department of Pathology, SGU · Small Group 14  ·  source pp. 2786–2804

                                                                  Learning objectives — verbatim

                                                                  • PATH.7020 Compare and contrast the features of cerebral edema, communicating hydrocephalus, non-communicating hydrocephalus and hydrocephalus ex vacuo in terms of i) etiopathogenesis, ii) morphologic findings and iii) clinical manifestations.
                                                                  • PATH.7040 Discuss the clinical presentation and morphological features of hydrocephalus, categorize the types of hydrocephalus and correlate them with the pathophysiological changes and disease progression.
                                                                  • PATH.7041 Evaluate the relevance of morphological findings and clinical presentations in diagnosing epidural hematoma and subdural hematoma and correlate them with different underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of brain trauma and course of the diseases.
                                                                  • PATH.7027 Distinguish cerebral infarction in terms of etiology, morphology and pathogenesis and clinical findings.
                                                                  • PATH.7042 Analyze the peculiarities of different types of cerebral hemorrhage such as intracerebral hemorrhage and subarachnoid hemorrhage in terms of their morphological appearances, clinical features and course and prognosis.
                                                                  • PATH.7034 Compare Alzheimer disease, Frontotemporal Dementia, Parkinson disease, Huntington disease and Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) in terms of their: age of onset, etiopathogenesis, morphology, clinical manifestations and prognosis.
                                                                  • PATH.7032 Compare multiple sclerosis (MS), post-infectious immune demyelination (ADEM, AHEM) and central pontine myelinolysis in terms of their: i) etiology, ii) age at onset, iii) distribution of lesions, iv) morphology and v) clinical course.
                                                                  • PATH.7031 Classify and distinguish the tumors of the central nervous system — astrocytoma, meningioma, glioblastoma, ependymoma, medulloblastoma, schwannoma, embryonal tumors and metastatic tumors — based on location, age, histopathology and clinical presentation.
                                                                  Source note
                                                                  The source deck carries this small group as image-only slides: a title, a slide number and a photograph. Reproduced here are the verbatim objectives and the twelve slide titles, plus, for each, the findings you are expected to name at the microscope or on the gross specimen, drawn from the NCRS neuropathology lectures already in this deck (Trauma and Hydrocephalus, Cerebrovascular Disease, Neurodegenerative Disease, Demyelinating Disease and CNS Tumors).
                                                                    NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)932

                                                                    Reference images 1–4 — orientation

                                                                    PATH.7020 · PATH.7027src p.2789–2792
                                                                    ReferenceWhat you are being oriented toWhy it matters downstream
                                                                    1 and 2 — Normal BrainGyral pattern, sulcal width, grey–white junction, symmetryCerebral edema is read as flattened gyri with narrowed sulci; atrophy as narrow gyri with widened sulci. You cannot call either without the normal.
                                                                    3 — Ventricular systemLateral → foramen of Monro → third → cerebral aqueduct → fourth → foramina of Luschka and Magendie → subarachnoid space → arachnoid granulationsEvery hydrocephalus question is a question about where in this chain the obstruction sits.
                                                                    4 — Blood supply of the brainAnterior, middle and posterior cerebral territories; the circle of Willis and its branch pointsInfarct territory names the vessel; berry aneurysms sit at the branch points of the circle of Willis.
                                                                    NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)933

                                                                    Slide 1 — Cerebral edema

                                                                    PATH.7020src p.2793
                                                                    Gross
                                                                    • Flattened gyri, narrowed sulci
                                                                    • Compressed ventricular cavities
                                                                    • Soft, heavy brain; the falx and tentorium become herniation routes
                                                                    Two mechanisms
                                                                    • Vasogenic — blood-brain barrier breakdown; fluid shifts into the EXTRACELLULAR space; may be localised (around tumour, abscess) or generalised
                                                                    • Cytotoxic — INTRACELLULAR fluid increase from neuronal, glial or endothelial cell membrane injury; generalised hypoxia/ischaemia
                                                                    • In practice the two coexist
                                                                    Exam Lock
                                                                    Clinical consequence — herniation
                                                                    • Subfalcine (cingulate) — compresses the anterior cerebral artery
                                                                    • Transtentorial (uncal) — CN III palsy (blown pupil), posterior cerebral artery compression, Duret haemorrhages in the midbrain/pons
                                                                    • Tonsillar — cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum; brainstem compression and respiratory arrest
                                                                    NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)934

                                                                    Slide 2 — Hydrocephalus

                                                                    PATH.7020 · PATH.7040src p.2794
                                                                    TypeMechanismMorphology and clinical
                                                                    Non-communicating (obstructive)Obstruction WITHIN the ventricular system — aqueductal stenosis, mass, colloid cyst, posterior fossa tumourVentricles upstream of the block dilate; those downstream do not. Raised intracranial pressure
                                                                    CommunicatingCSF flows out of the ventricles but is not absorbed — arachnoid granulation impairment after meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhageWhole ventricular system dilates. Raised intracranial pressure
                                                                    Hydrocephalus ex vacuoNOT a hydrocephalus at all — compensatory ventricular enlargement following loss of brain parenchyma (atrophy, infarct)Ventricles enlarge, sulci also widen, and the CSF pressure is NORMAL
                                                                    Normal-pressure hydrocephalusA communicating hydrocephalus of the elderly with normal measured pressureWet, wacky and wobbly — urinary incontinence, dementia, magnetic gait
                                                                    Trap
                                                                    Big ventricles are not a diagnosis. Wide sulci with wide ventricles = ex vacuo (atrophy). Narrow sulci with wide ventricles = true hydrocephalus under pressure. That single comparison is what the slide is testing.
                                                                      Bottom Line
                                                                      Before the cranial sutures close, hydrocephalus enlarges the head. After they fuse, the same volume raises intracranial pressure instead — which is why the presentation is macrocephaly in the infant and headache, papilloedema and vomiting in the adult.
                                                                        NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)935

                                                                        Slides 3 and 4 — Epidural and subdural haematoma

                                                                        PATH.7041src p.2795–2796
                                                                        Epidural haematomaSubdural haematoma
                                                                        VesselMiddle meningeal ARTERY — torn by a skull fracture at the pterionBridging VEINS crossing from cortex to dural sinus
                                                                        Shape on imaging / grossLens-shaped (biconvex, lentiform); does NOT cross suture lines because the dura is bound to themCrescent-shaped; CROSSES suture lines but not the midline (limited by the falx)
                                                                        CourseLucid interval, then rapid deterioration — arterial pressure fills the space quickly; a neurosurgical emergencySlower: acute after major trauma; chronic in the elderly and alcoholics after trivial injury, because brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins
                                                                        PopulationYounger patients with temporal traumaElderly, alcoholics, patients on anticoagulants, shaken infants
                                                                        Location relative to duraBetween skull and duraBetween dura and arachnoid
                                                                        Exam Lock
                                                                        The line that answers most questions
                                                                        • Artery, lens, does not cross sutures, lucid interval → EPIDURAL.
                                                                        • Vein, crescent, crosses sutures, elderly with trivial trauma → SUBDURAL.
                                                                        NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)936

                                                                        Slide 5 — Cerebral infarction

                                                                        PATH.7027src p.2797

                                                                        Etiology and mechanism

                                                                        • Thrombotic — atherosclerosis at the carotid bifurcation, middle cerebral artery origin, and basilar artery
                                                                        • Embolic — cardiac mural thrombus, atrial fibrillation, valve vegetations, atheroemboli; most often lands in the MIDDLE CEREBRAL ARTERY territory
                                                                        • Global hypoxic-ischaemic injury — watershed (border-zone) infarcts and selective vulnerability of hippocampal CA1 (Sommer sector), Purkinje cells and cortical layers 3, 5, 6
                                                                        Time after onsetMorphology
                                                                        12–24 hoursRed neurons — eosinophilic cytoplasm, pyknotic nuclei
                                                                        24–48 hoursNeutrophilic infiltration
                                                                        2–3 days to 2–3 weeksMacrophages / microglia — the dominant cell; lipid-laden and foamy
                                                                        Beyond 2–3 weeksReactive gliosis and a fluid-filled CYSTIC CAVITY with a gliotic wall

                                                                        A haemorrhagic (red) infarct implies reperfusion — usually embolic; a pale (anaemic) infarct implies persistent occlusion, usually thrombotic.

                                                                        NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)937

                                                                        Infarct timeline

                                                                        PATH.7027src p.2797
                                                                        NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)938

                                                                        Slides 6 and 7 — Intracerebral haemorrhage and subarachnoid haemorrhage

                                                                        PATH.7042src p.2798–2799
                                                                        Intracerebral (parenchymal) haemorrhageSubarachnoid haemorrhage
                                                                        CauseHypertension — rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms of penetrating arteries; hyaline arteriolosclerosis is the substrate. In the elderly and lobar in location, cerebral amyloid angiopathyRupture of a saccular ("berry") aneurysm at a branch point of the circle of Willis — most often the ANTERIOR communicating artery
                                                                        SiteBasal ganglia / putamen (~most common), thalamus, pons, cerebellumSubarachnoid space, spreading over the base of the brain
                                                                        PresentationSudden focal deficit with headache and progressive obtundation as the mass expands"Worst headache of my life" — sudden, severe, with meningism; ~⅓ have a sentinel bleed
                                                                        Risk / associationChronic hypertension; anticoagulation; vascular malformation in the youngADPKD, Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan, fibromuscular dysplasia, smoking, hypertension
                                                                        ComplicationVentricular extension; herniationVasospasm (days 4–12) causing delayed ischaemia; rebleeding; communicating hydrocephalus from arachnoid granulation scarring
                                                                        Trap
                                                                        Berry aneurysms are NOT atherosclerotic aneurysms. They are congenital-ish defects in the media at arterial branch points, they lack an internal elastic lamina and media at the neck, and they rupture — they do not usually thrombose or dissect.
                                                                          NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)939

                                                                          Slide 8 — Alzheimer disease

                                                                          PATH.7034src p.2800
                                                                          Gross
                                                                          • Cortical atrophy with widened sulci and narrowed gyri, most marked in the FRONTAL, TEMPORAL and PARIETAL lobes
                                                                          • Compensatory ventricular enlargement — hydrocephalus ex vacuo
                                                                          • Medial temporal / hippocampal atrophy early
                                                                          Microscopy
                                                                          • Neuritic (senile) plaques — extracellular Aβ core derived from amyloid precursor protein (chromosome 21)
                                                                          • Neurofibrillary tangles — INTRAcellular, hyperphosphorylated TAU, flame-shaped; they persist after the neuron dies as 'ghost tangles'
                                                                          • Amyloid angiopathy; granulovacuolar degeneration; Hirano bodies
                                                                          Exam Lock
                                                                          Genetics and clinical
                                                                          • Early-onset familial: APP (chr 21), presenilin-1 (chr 14), presenilin-2 (chr 1)
                                                                          • Risk allele: ApoE ε4 increases risk; ApoE ε2 is protective
                                                                          • Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) — virtually all develop Alzheimer pathology by age 40
                                                                          • Clinical: insidious memory loss progressing to global cognitive decline; the most common cause of dementia
                                                                          Trap
                                                                          Tangle burden correlates with cognitive decline better than plaque burden. Plaques are extracellular and made of Aβ; tangles are intracellular and made of tau. Mixing up which is which is the most common error on this slide.
                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)940

                                                                            Neurodegenerative proteins at a glance

                                                                            PATH.7034src p.2800
                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)941

                                                                            Slide 9 — Multiple sclerosis

                                                                            PATH.7032src p.2801
                                                                            Gross
                                                                            • Well-circumscribed, firm, grey-brown PLAQUES
                                                                            • Classically PERIVENTRICULAR, and at the corpus callosum, optic nerves, brainstem and spinal cord
                                                                            • Plaques of different ages coexist — that is the point
                                                                            Microscopy
                                                                            • Active plaque: demyelination with preserved axons, lipid-laden macrophages, perivascular lymphocytes
                                                                            • Inactive plaque: gliosis, loss of oligodendrocytes, axonal loss
                                                                            Diagnosis
                                                                            • Lesions separated in TIME and in SPACE
                                                                            • CSF: oligoclonal IgG bands; mildly raised protein; mild pleocytosis
                                                                            Exam Lock
                                                                            Compare — PATH.7032
                                                                            • MS — young adults, F:M 2:1, relapsing-remitting, HLA-DRB1*1501, periventricular white matter
                                                                            • ADEM / AHEM — post-infectious or post-vaccination, monophasic, children and young adults, PERIVENOUS demyelination; AHEM is the fulminant haemorrhagic form
                                                                            • Central pontine myelinolysis — too-rapid correction of hyponatraemia; symmetric loss of myelin in the BASIS PONTIS; locked-in syndrome; the >2-day rule protects against it
                                                                            NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)942

                                                                            Slides 10, 11 and 12 — Glioblastoma, meningioma, medulloblastoma

                                                                            PATH.7031 · PATH.7043src p.2802–2804
                                                                            SlideTumourLocation and ageThe diagnostic finding
                                                                            10GlioblastomaCerebral hemispheres of adults; may cross the corpus callosum as a "butterfly glioma"Pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular (endothelial) proliferation — either one makes the diagnosis of a WHO grade 4 tumour. Variegated cut surface with haemorrhage and necrosis. IDH-wildtype = primary/de novo; IDH-mutant = secondary, younger, better prognosis
                                                                            11MeningiomaAdults; attached to the DURA, compresses rather than invades the brain; more common in women (progesterone receptors), and may grow in pregnancyWhorls of meningothelial cells and PSAMMOMA BODIES (laminated calcifications). NF2 on chromosome 22. Mostly benign (WHO grade 1); a dural tail on imaging
                                                                            12MedulloblastomaChildren; CEREBELLUM — the vermis in children, lateral hemispheres in adultsSmall round blue cells with scant cytoplasm; HOMER WRIGHT rosettes; highly malignant (WHO grade 4) but exquisitely radiosensitive; "drop metastases" seeding the CSF to the cauda equina
                                                                            Bottom Line
                                                                            Rosette discipline: Homer Wright (no lumen, fibrillary centre) — medulloblastoma and neuroblastoma. Perivascular pseudorosettes — ependymoma. Flexner-Wintersteiner (true lumen) — retinoblastoma. Psammoma bodies — meningioma (also papillary thyroid, serous ovarian, mesothelioma).

                                                                              2HydrocephalusWide ventricles with NARROW sulci = true hydrocephalus; wide ventricles with WIDE sulci and normal pressure = ex vacuo
                                                                              3Epidural hematomaMiddle meningeal ARTERY; lens-shaped; does not cross sutures; lucid interval
                                                                              4Subdural hematomaBridging VEINS; crescent-shaped; crosses sutures; elderly/alcoholic, trivial trauma
                                                                              5Cerebral infarctionRed neurons → neutrophils → macrophages → gliotic cystic cavity
                                                                              6Intracerebral hemorrhageHypertensive rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms; basal ganglia / putamen
                                                                              7Berry aneurysm — subarachnoid hemorrhageSaccular aneurysm at a circle-of-Willis branch point; worst headache of life; vasospasm days 4–12
                                                                              8Alzheimer diseaseExtracellular Aβ neuritic plaques + intracellular tau neurofibrillary tangles; cortical atrophy with ex vacuo ventricles
                                                                              9Multiple sclerosisPeriventricular plaques of differing age; demyelination with preserved axons; CSF oligoclonal bands
                                                                              10GlioblastomaPseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation; butterfly glioma
                                                                              11MeningiomaDural-based; whorls and psammoma bodies; NF2, chromosome 22
                                                                              12MedulloblastomaCerebellar vermis in a child; small round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes; radiosensitive; drop metastases
                                                                              NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)945

                                                                              Block check — SG-14 neuropathology

                                                                              PATH.7020 · PATH.7040

                                                                              A CT shows enlarged lateral ventricles AND widened cortical sulci in a 78-year-old with progressive memory loss. Measured CSF pressure is normal. Which is correct?

                                                                              1. ANon-communicating hydrocephalus from aqueductal stenosis
                                                                              2. BCommunicating hydrocephalus from prior meningitis
                                                                              3. CHydrocephalus ex vacuo from cerebral atrophy
                                                                              4. DNormal-pressure hydrocephalus
                                                                              5. ECerebral edema
                                                                              Answer
                                                                              C. Hydrocephalus ex vacuo is compensatory ventricular enlargement following loss of brain parenchyma — ventricles AND sulci enlarge, and CSF pressure is normal. A true hydrocephalus under pressure expands the ventricles while compressing the sulci. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus has normal measured pressure but the clinical triad of urinary incontinence, dementia and magnetic gait and does not widen the sulci.
                                                                              PATH.7041

                                                                              A 22-year-old is struck at the temple, briefly loses consciousness, converses normally for an hour, then deteriorates rapidly. The haematoma is lens-shaped and stops at the suture lines. Which vessel is torn?

                                                                              1. AA bridging vein
                                                                              2. BThe middle meningeal artery
                                                                              3. CA berry aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery
                                                                              4. DA Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm
                                                                              5. EThe vein of Galen
                                                                              Answer
                                                                              B. Epidural haematoma: middle meningeal ARTERY torn by a fracture at the pterion; lens-shaped (biconvex) because the dura is bound at the sutures so the collection does not cross them; the arterial pressure produces the classic lucid interval then rapid deterioration. A bridging vein tear gives a crescentic subdural that does cross sutures.
                                                                              NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)946

                                                                              Block check — SG-14 neuropathology (cont.)

                                                                              PATH.7031 · PATH.7043

                                                                              A biopsy of a hemispheric mass in a 60-year-old shows serpentine necrosis with tumour cells aligned along its edge and florid endothelial proliferation. Which diagnosis?

                                                                              1. AMeningioma
                                                                              2. BMedulloblastoma
                                                                              3. CGlioblastoma
                                                                              4. DOligodendroglioma
                                                                              5. EEpendymoma
                                                                              Answer
                                                                              C. Pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular (endothelial) proliferation define glioblastoma, WHO grade 4. Grossly it is variegated with haemorrhage and necrosis and may cross the corpus callosum as a butterfly glioma. Meningioma shows whorls and psammoma bodies; medulloblastoma shows Homer Wright rosettes in a child's cerebellum.
                                                                              PATH.7034

                                                                              Which pairing of inclusion and location is correct for Alzheimer disease?

                                                                              1. ANeurofibrillary tangles are extracellular and made of Aβ
                                                                              2. BNeuritic plaques are intracellular and made of tau
                                                                              3. CNeuritic plaques are extracellular Aβ; neurofibrillary tangles are intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau
                                                                              4. DBoth plaques and tangles are made of α-synuclein
                                                                              5. EBoth plaques and tangles are intracellular
                                                                              Answer
                                                                              C. Neuritic (senile) plaques are EXTRAcellular with an Aβ core derived from amyloid precursor protein (chromosome 21); neurofibrillary tangles are INTRAcellular, made of hyperphosphorylated TAU, and persist after neuronal death as ghost tangles. α-synuclein is Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia.
                                                                              NCRS SG-14 · Neuropathology (Practical Slide Review)947

                                                                              Block check — SG-14 neuropathology (cont.)

                                                                              PATH.7031

                                                                              A 7-year-old has morning headaches, vomiting and truncal ataxia. Imaging shows a midline cerebellar mass; histology shows sheets of small round blue cells with rosettes lacking a central lumen. Which statement is correct?

                                                                              1. AIt is benign and requires no adjuvant therapy
                                                                              2. BIt is a WHO grade 4 tumour but is exquisitely radiosensitive and may seed the CSF
                                                                              3. CIt arises from arachnoid cap cells
                                                                              4. DIt typically shows 1p/19q codeletion
                                                                              5. EIt arises in the cerebral hemispheres of adults
                                                                              Answer
                                                                              B. Medulloblastoma: children, cerebellar VERMIS, small round blue cells with HOMER WRIGHT rosettes, WHO grade 4 but exquisitely radiosensitive, and characteristically produces "drop metastases" seeding the CSF to the cauda equina. Arachnoid cap cells give meningioma; 1p/19q codeletion is oligodendroglioma.
                                                                              PATH.7042

                                                                              A hypertensive 65-year-old has a sudden dense hemiparesis. Autopsy shows haemorrhage centred on the putamen. Which lesion is responsible?

                                                                              1. ARuptured berry aneurysm
                                                                              2. BRupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms
                                                                              3. CCerebral amyloid angiopathy
                                                                              4. DArteriovenous malformation
                                                                              5. EHaemorrhagic infarction
                                                                              Answer
                                                                              B. Hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage arises from rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms of the small penetrating arteries, on a background of hyaline arteriolosclerosis; the basal ganglia/putamen is the commonest site, then thalamus, pons and cerebellum. Berry aneurysm rupture produces subarachnoid haemorrhage; cerebral amyloid angiopathy produces lobar haemorrhages in the elderly.

                                                                              General Anesthetics

                                                                              Dr Mohit Kaur · Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pharmacology. The drugs with a therapeutic index of 2–4 — and the physical chemistry that decides how they behave.

                                                                              Learning objectives — verbatim

                                                                              • PHAR.00076 Define the terms "general anesthesia" and "balanced anesthesia."
                                                                              • PHAR.00077 Describe the objectives of general anesthesia, the characteristics of an ideal anesthetic, and the stages of general anesthesia.
                                                                              • PHAR.00078 List the drugs commonly used in combination with inhalation anesthetics in balanced anesthesia.
                                                                              • PHAR.00079 Describe the mechanisms of action, adverse effects, drug interactions and contraindications of general anesthetics.
                                                                              • PHAR.00080 Describe signs and symptoms of malignant hyperthermia, its pathophysiology, prevention and management.
                                                                              • PHAR.00081 Define MAC and explain how MAC is used in anesthesiology.
                                                                              • PHAR.00082 Describe how physical properties of inhaled anesthetics influence potency and onset.
