                                                                              • PHAR.00084 Compare and contrast the properties of IV general anesthetics.

                                                                              Sources cited by the lecture: Golan, Principles of Pharmacology 4e · Goodman & Gilman 12e · Whalen, Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Pharmacology 6e · Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology 16e · Rosenfeld & Loose, BRS Pharmacology 4e.

                                                                              PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics949

                                                                              General anesthesia and balanced anesthesia

                                                                              PHAR.00076 · PHAR.00077 · PHAR.00078src p.2806
                                                                              The state of "general anesthesia" usually includes
                                                                              • Analgesia
                                                                              • Amnesia
                                                                              • Loss of consciousness
                                                                              • Suppression of sensory and autonomic reflexes
                                                                              • Skeletal muscle relaxation
                                                                              An ideal anesthetic would
                                                                              • Induce anesthesia smoothly and rapidly
                                                                              • Permit rapid recovery
                                                                              • Possess wide margin of safety
                                                                              • Be devoid of adverse effects
                                                                              No single drug is capable of achieving all of the desired goals of anesthesia. Accordingly, in a method termed BALANCED ANESTHESIA, several inhaled and/or IV drugs are used in combination to produce the anesthetic state.PHAR.00076

                                                                              Why the combination is necessary — four reasons

                                                                              1. Anesthetic partial pressure for an inhalational agent in the brain is not attained rapidly, therefore patients are usually anesthetized with an IV agent.
                                                                              2. Halogenated hydrocarbon inhaled general anesthetics often exhibit inadequate degrees of analgesia, therefore a supplemental analgesic (i.e., an opioid or N₂O) is required.
                                                                              3. Neuromuscular blocking agents must be used to provide paralysis adequate for surgical access.
                                                                              4. The anesthetic plan is designed to minimize any undesirable cardiovascular and respiratory responses to these drugs. This includes drug combinations that minimize the dose of the halogenated hydrocarbon — for example N₂O 25–40%, which by itself produces minimal cardiovascular depression, is frequently used in combination with a halogenated hydrocarbon.
                                                                              PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics950

                                                                              Anesthesia protocols and the drug classes

                                                                              PHAR.00078src p.2807 · 2826–2829
                                                                              • Protocols vary depending on the type of intervention: diagnostic · therapeutic · surgical.
                                                                              • For minor procedures, so-called MONITORED ANESTHESIA CARE or CONSCIOUS SEDATION is used, employing oral or parenteral sedatives in conjunction with local anesthetics. These techniques provide profound analgesia, but with retention of the patient's ability to maintain a patent airway and to respond to verbal commands.
                                                                              • For more extensive surgical procedures, anesthesia frequently includes preoperative benzodiazepines, induction with IV thiopental or propofol, and maintenance with a combination of inhaled and intravenous drugs — often with neuromuscular blocking drugs.
                                                                              Inhaled — gases
                                                                              • Nitrous oxide (N₂O) is a gas at ambient temperature
                                                                              Inhaled — volatile halogenated hydrocarbons
                                                                              • Volatile liquids vaporized by heat supplied by a vaporizer
                                                                              • Isoflurane* · Desflurane* · Sevoflurane* (*commercially available in the United States)
                                                                              • Halothane · Enflurane · Methoxyflurane
                                                                              Intravenous
                                                                              • Propofol · Ketamine · Etomidate · Barbiturates
                                                                              • Used as adjuncts to inhaled anesthetics and as part of techniques that do not include any inhaled anesthetic (total intravenous anesthesia)
                                                                              • Also used to sedate ICU patients who must be mechanically ventilated for long periods
                                                                              PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics951

                                                                              Induction, maintenance and recovery

                                                                              PHAR.00077src p.2808 · 2830
                                                                              PhaseDefinitionWhat is happening
                                                                              InductionThe time from administration of anesthetic to the development of surgical anesthesiaIt is essential to avoid the dangerous excitatory phase (stage II, delirium) — so general anesthesia is normally induced with an IV anesthetic such as propofol. Additional inhaled or IV drugs then produce the desired depth of Stage III anesthesia; an IV skeletal muscle relaxant is co-administered to facilitate intubation and relaxation
                                                                              MaintenanceThe period during which the patient is surgically anesthetized; the patient is monitoredUsually maintained by inhaled anesthetics. Opioids such as fentanyl are often used for pain along with inhalation agents, because the latter are not good analgesics
                                                                              RecoveryTime from discontinuation of administration of anesthesia until consciousness is regainedThe anesthetic mixture is withdrawn; return to consciousness is monitored

                                                                              Induction of anesthesia may differ in infants: infants have higher alveolar ventilation and lower functional residual capacity (high MV/FRC), therefore they can be induced with an inhaled anesthetic like sevoflurane.

                                                                              PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics952

                                                                              The four stages

                                                                              PHAR.00077src p.2808
                                                                              PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics953

                                                                              Mechanism of action and the margin of safety

                                                                              PHAR.00079 · PHAR.00082src p.2809 · 2831–2833
                                                                              The actions of inhaled anesthetics are thought to be the consequence of interactions with LIGAND-GATED ION CHANNELS.Pharmacodynamics
                                                                              • A primary molecular target of many general anesthetics is the GABA_A receptor, a major mediator of inhibitory synaptic transmission. Inhaled anesthetics FACILITATE GABA-mediated inhibition at GABA_A receptors.
                                                                              • Most inhaled anesthetics also INHIBIT nicotinic receptors.
                                                                              • The GLYCINE receptor is another ligand-gated ion channel that may function as a target for inhaled anesthetics — positively modulated.
                                                                              Exam Lock
                                                                              The safety statement you should be able to quote
                                                                              • General anesthetics are among the most dangerous drugs approved for general use, as their margin of safety is small.
                                                                              • Therapeutic indices range from about 2–4 — the dose that produces circulatory failure may be only 2 to 4 times that which produces adequate anesthesia

                                                                              Common features of the inhaled agents

                                                                              • Decrease cerebrovascular resistance, resulting in increased perfusion of brain
                                                                              • Cause bronchodilation and decrease minute ventilation
                                                                              • Potency correlates with liposolubility
                                                                              • Rate of onset is inversely correlated to blood solubility
                                                                              • Recovery from their effects is due to redistribution from the brain
                                                                              PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics954

                                                                              MAC — minimum alveolar concentration

                                                                              PHAR.00081src p.2809–2810 · 2834
                                                                              The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of an anesthetic is defined as the concentration — the percentage of the alveolar gas mixture, or partial pressure of the anesthetic as a percentage of 760 mm Hg — that results in IMMOBILITY in 50% of patients when exposed to a noxious stimulus such as surgical incision.PHAR.00081
                                                                              • MAC is expressed as % of gas in a mixture required to achieve the effect.
                                                                              • MAC represents the ED50 on a QUANTAL dose-response curve.
                                                                              • Numerically, MAC is low for potent anesthetics such as halothane (MAC = 0.75) and large for less potent agents such as nitrous oxide (105.0). Therefore 1/MAC is an index of potency.
                                                                              • The MAC value for nitrous oxide is greater than 100%, indicating that at normal barometric pressure even 760 mm Hg partial pressure of nitrous oxide (100% of the inspired gas) is not equal to 1 MAC.
                                                                              • MAC gives no information about the SLOPE of the dose-response curve. In general the slopes for inhalational anesthetics are steep: although only 50% of individuals may fail to respond at 1.0 MAC, 95% of patients may fail to respond at 1.1 MAC.
                                                                              PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics955

                                                                              What changes MAC

                                                                              PHAR.00081src p.2810 · 2836
                                                                              MAC is INCREASED by
                                                                              • Anxiety
                                                                              • Thyrotoxicosis
                                                                              • Infancy — MAC is higher in infants
                                                                              MAC is DECREASED by
                                                                              • Hypothermia
                                                                              • Hypothyroidism
                                                                              • Pregnancy
                                                                              • Adjuvant drugs — opioid analgesics or sedative-hypnotics (so the inspired concentration of anesthetic should be decreased accordingly)
                                                                              • The elderly — MAC is lower in the elderly
                                                                              MAC is NOT significantly affected by
                                                                              • Sex
                                                                              • Height
                                                                              • Weight
                                                                              Exam Lock
                                                                              MAC values are ADDITIVE
                                                                              • Nitrous oxide can be used as a "carrier" gas, decreasing the anesthetic requirement of other anesthetics.
                                                                              • Example: 0.7 MAC of isoflurane + 0.3 MAC of nitrous oxide = 1 MAC.
                                                                              Trap
                                                                              Height and weight do not change MAC. It is an alveolar *concentration*, not a dose per kilogram — which is exactly why it is the standard of comparison.
                                                                                PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics956

                                                                                Potency, speed and the two partition coefficients

                                                                                PHAR.00082 · PHAR.00083src p.2811–2812 · 2840 · 2854
                                                                                PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics957

                                                                                The Meyer–Overton correlation

                                                                                PHAR.00082src p.2811 · 2838–2841
                                                                                The potency of an anesthetic can be predicted from its physicochemical characteristics. The most reliable predictor of anesthetic potency is the anesthetic's LIPOSOLUBILITY.PHAR.00082
                                                                                • A useful measure of liposolubility is the oil:gas partition coefficient, λ(oil:gas).
                                                                                • The potency of an anesthetic increases as its liposolubility increases. In other words, as λ(oil:gas) increases, the MAC decreases.
                                                                                • Definition — the partition coefficient is the ratio of the concentrations of a compound in one solvent to the concentration in another solvent. *For example, an oil:gas partition coefficient of 19 means that the concentration of anesthetic in oil is 19-fold that present in the alveolar gas when the partial pressure of the anesthetic is identical at both sites.*
                                                                                AnestheticMAC (%)λ(oil:gas)
                                                                                Nitrous oxide1041.4
                                                                                Desflurane619
                                                                                Sevoflurane2.051
                                                                                Enflurane1.798
                                                                                Isoflurane1.498
                                                                                Halothane0.75224
                                                                                Methoxyflurane0.16960

                                                                                Read the two columns in opposite directions: λ(oil:gas) rises down the table, MAC falls down the table. That is the Meyer-Overton correlation in one image.

                                                                                PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics958

                                                                                Solubility in blood and the speed of induction

                                                                                PHAR.00083src p.2811–2812 · 2845–2854
                                                                                • Achievement of a brain concentration adequate to cause anesthesia requires transfer of the anesthetic from the alveolar air to blood and then to brain.
                                                                                • The blood:gas partition coefficient λ(blood:gas) defines the relative solubility of an anesthetic for the blood compared to air. The coefficients for desflurane, nitrous oxide and sevoflurane, which are not very soluble in blood, are low; the value is greater than 10 for agents such as methoxyflurane.
                                                                                LOW blood solubility
                                                                                • Relatively few molecules of anesthetic are enough to saturate the blood, therefore the arterial anesthetic tension rises QUICKLY.
                                                                                • Once the blood compartment is saturated, additional molecules are readily transferred to other compartments — the most important being the brain
                                                                                HIGH blood solubility
                                                                                • More molecules need to dissolve in blood before the anesthetic partial pressure increases significantly, therefore the arterial tension increases more SLOWLY.
                                                                                Exam Lock
                                                                                The two sentences to memorise
                                                                                • There is an INVERSE relationship between blood solubility of an anesthetic and the rate of rise of its tension in arterial blood. A low blood:gas partition coefficient determines a FASTER onset of anesthesia.
                                                                                • Anesthetics with larger λ(oil:gas) tend to have larger λ(blood:gas) — which means MORE POTENT INHALED ANESTHETICS TEND TO HAVE SLOWER ONSETS.
                                                                                PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics959

                                                                                The five determinants of induction speed

                                                                                PHAR.00083src p.2812–2813 · 2844 · 2855–2859
                                                                                PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics960

                                                                                The other four determinants in detail

                                                                                PHAR.00083src p.2812–2813
                                                                                FactorEffect on the rate of induction
                                                                                Anesthetic concentration in the inspired airIncreases in the inspired anesthetic concentration increase the rate of induction by increasing the rate of transfer into the blood. *Example: a 3–4% concentration of halothane may be administered initially to increase the rate of induction; this is then reduced to 1–2% for maintenance when adequate anesthesia is achieved.*
                                                                                Ventilation rateThe rate of rise of anesthetic gas tension in arterial blood is DIRECTLY dependent on both the rate and depth of ventilation, and the magnitude varies with the blood:gas coefficient. An increase in pulmonary ventilation causes only a slight increase in arterial tension if the anesthetic has low blood solubility, but can significantly increase tension of anesthetics with moderate or high blood solubility — a fourfold increase in ventilation rate almost doubles the arterial tension of halothane during the first 10 minutes but increases that of nitrous oxide by only 15%.
                                                                                Pulmonary blood flowAn INCREASE in pulmonary blood flow (increased cardiac output) SLOWS the rate of rise in arterial tension, particularly for anesthetics with moderate to high blood solubility, because increased pulmonary blood flow exposes a larger volume of blood to the anesthetic; blood "capacity" increases and tension rises slowly. A decrease in pulmonary blood flow has the opposite effect.
                                                                                Arteriovenous concentration gradientThe difference between the concentration of gas in arterial and venous blood; it reflects the solubility of the gas in the TISSUES. If tissue solubility is high, a large amount is taken up by tissues and the venous concentration is low. An anesthetic which is highly soluble in tissues will have a high arteriovenous gradient and thus a SLOW onset of action AND recovery.
                                                                                Trap
                                                                                Increased cardiac output slows inhalational induction. This is counter-intuitive and it is examined precisely because it is counter-intuitive — more blood flowing past the alveolus means more blood to saturate, so alveolar and arterial tension climb more slowly.
                                                                                  PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics961

                                                                                  Elimination and metabolism

                                                                                  PHAR.00083 · PHAR.00079src p.2813–2814 · 2860
                                                                                  • The time to recovery from inhalation anesthesia depends on the rate of elimination of anesthetics from the brain. Elimination is largely the reverse process of uptake.
                                                                                  • For agents with LOW blood and tissue solubility, recovery mirrors induction, regardless of the duration of anesthetic administration.
                                                                                  • For agents with HIGH blood and tissue solubility, recovery is a function of the DURATION of administration, because the accumulated anesthetic in FAT acts as a reservoir.
                                                                                  • Nitrous oxide, desflurane and sevoflurane display recovery times significantly shorter than halothane or isoflurane.

                                                                                  Routes of elimination

                                                                                  • The major route is clearance by the LUNGS into the expired air, but metabolism by enzymes of the liver and other tissues may also contribute. *The washout of halothane during recovery is more rapid than that of enflurane, which would not be predicted from their solubilities — because* over 40% of inspired halothane is metabolized during an average anesthetic procedure, while less than 10% of enflurane is.
                                                                                  AgentMetabolism and its consequence
                                                                                  HalothaneOxidative metabolism yields trifluoroacetic acid with release of bromide and chloride ions. Under conditions of low oxygen tension, halothane is metabolized to the chlorotrifluoroethyl FREE RADICAL, capable of reacting with hepatic membrane components.
                                                                                  Isoflurane and desfluraneThe LEAST metabolized of the fluorinated anesthetics — only traces of trifluoroacetic acid appear in the urine
                                                                                  Enflurane and sevofluraneMetabolism forms FLUORIDE, which does not reach toxic levels under normal circumstances. Sevoflurane is additionally degraded by contact with the CO₂ adsorbent in anesthesia machines, yielding a vinyl ether called "compound A" that can cause renal damage if high concentrations are absorbed.
                                                                                  MethoxyfluraneOver 70% is metabolized by the liver with release of fluoride at concentrations that can be NEPHROTOXIC.
                                                                                  Nitrous oxideProbably not metabolized by human tissue.
                                                                                  PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics962

                                                                                  Elimination and metabolism (cont.)

                                                                                  PHAR.00083 · PHAR.00079src p.2813–2814 · 2860
                                                                                  Exam Lock
                                                                                  Rank order of metabolism
                                                                                  • Methoxyflurane > halothane > enflurane > sevoflurane > isoflurane > desflurane > nitrous oxide
                                                                                  PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics963

                                                                                  Organ effects of the inhaled anesthetics

                                                                                  PHAR.00079src p.2814–2815 · 2863–2867
                                                                                  SystemEffect
                                                                                  CardiovascularMost inhaled anesthetics depress normal cardiac contractility (dose-dependent) and decrease mean arterial pressure through vasodilation. Halothane and enflurane reduce arterial pressure mainly by MYOCARDIAL DEPRESSION (reduced cardiac output) with little effect on vascular resistance; isoflurane, desflurane and sevoflurane produce greater VASODILATION with minimal effect on cardiac output — so they may be better choices for patients with impaired myocardial function. Nitrous oxide is less likely to lower blood pressure than other inhaled anesthetics. Halothane SENSITIZES THE MYOCARDIUM TO CIRCULATING CATECHOLAMINES, which may lead to ventricular arrhythmias — less marked for isoflurane, sevoflurane and desflurane
                                                                                  RespiratoryAll volatile anesthetics have BRONCHODILATING properties and all are RESPIRATORY DEPRESSANTS. Isoflurane and enflurane are the most depressant; nitrous oxide is the least. Isoflurane and desflurane are PUNGENT, making them less suitable for induction in patients with bronchospasm; halothane, sevoflurane and nitrous oxide are NONPUNGENT.
                                                                                  CNSInhaled anesthetics increase cerebral blood flow because they reduce cerebral vascular resistance — this may increase intracranial pressure, clinically undesirable in patients with raised ICP from brain tumor or head injury. Nitrous oxide increases blood flow the least. At higher doses enflurane may produce a spike-and-wave pattern and mild generalized muscle twitching (tonic-clonic movements); this seizure-like activity does not have adverse clinical consequences. Nitrous oxide has low anesthetic potency but exerts marked ANALGESIC and AMNESIC actions.
                                                                                  KidneyAll inhaled anesthetics decrease glomerular filtration rate and renal blood flow.
                                                                                  LiverAll inhaled anesthetics decrease hepatic blood flow.
                                                                                  Uterine smooth muscleHalogenated hydrocarbon anesthetics are potent UTERINE RELAXANTS — usable when profound uterine relaxation is required for intrauterine fetal manipulation or manual extraction of a retained placenta. Nitrous oxide has little effect on uterine musculature.
                                                                                  PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics964

                                                                                  Nitrous oxide and closed gas spaces

                                                                                  PHAR.00079src p.2816 · 2868–2869
                                                                                  N₂O exchanges with nitrogen in air-containing cavities in the body. N₂O enters the cavity FASTER than nitrogen escapes; therefore it increases the volume and/or pressure of the cavity.Other Effects
                                                                                  Exam Lock
                                                                                  N₂O should be avoided in the following clinical settings
                                                                                  • Pneumothorax
                                                                                  • Obstructed middle ear
                                                                                  • Air embolus
                                                                                  • Obstructed loop of bowel
                                                                                  • Intraocular air bubble
                                                                                  • Pulmonary bulla
                                                                                  • Intracranial air

                                                                                  Theoretically N₂O can expand a pre-existing volvulus or pneumothorax.

                                                                                  Bottom Line
                                                                                  The rule generalises: any closed gas-filled space is a contraindication. If the question describes a cavity that cannot vent, nitrous oxide is the wrong answer.
                                                                                    PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics965

                                                                                    Toxicity — hepatic, renal and haematologic

                                                                                    PHAR.00079src p.2816 · 2871–2872 · 2883
                                                                                    ToxicityAgent and detail
                                                                                    HepatotoxicityHALOTHANE. A very small subset of individuals exposed to halothane may develop a potentially severe and life-threatening hepatitis — due to its toxic metabolite. Incidence probably in the range of one in 20,000–35,000. There is no specific treatment for halothane hepatitis and liver transplantation may ultimately be required.
                                                                                    NephrotoxicityMETHOXYFLURANE. Its nephrotoxic potential has limited its clinical use in anesthesia. Renal dysfunction is caused by INORGANIC FLUORIDE released during the extensive metabolism of the anesthetic by hepatic and renal enzymes.
                                                                                    Chronic haematotoxicityNITROUS OXIDE. Prolonged exposure to nitrous oxide decreases METHIONINE SYNTHASE activity and causes MEGALOBLASTIC ANEMIA. A potential occupational hazard for staff working in poorly ventilated dental operating suites.
                                                                                    Bottom Line
                                                                                    Methionine synthase is the B₁₂-dependent enzyme. N₂O irreversibly oxidises the cobalt in cobalamin — which is why the picture is a functional B₁₂ deficiency: megaloblastic anaemia, and with long exposure, subacute combined degeneration.
                                                                                      PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics966

                                                                                      Malignant hyperthermia

                                                                                      PHAR.00080src p.2816–2817 · 2873–2879
                                                                                      A potentially fatal genetic disorder of skeletal muscle that is triggered by halogenated hydrocarbon inhalation anesthetics (e.g., halothane, isoflurane, enflurane, desflurane, sevoflurane) and depolarizing skeletal muscle relaxants, such as succinylcholine.PHAR.00080
                                                                                      • The halogenated hydrocarbon anesthetics and succinylcholine ALONE have been reported to precipitate the response; however, most of the incidents arise from the COMBINATION of succinylcholine and a halogenated anesthetic.
                                                                                      • In humans, malignant hyperthermia is transmitted as an AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT trait, with a reported incidence of about 1:12,000.
                                                                                      • Malignant hyperthermia is one of the main causes of death due to anesthesia.

                                                                                      Mechanism

                                                                                      • Muscle cells possess Ca²⁺ channels called RYANODINE RECEPTORS (RYRs), named for their sensitivity to the plant alkaloid ryanodine. In skeletal muscle these receptors sit in the membrane of the sarcoplasmic reticulum and associate with the cytoplasmic domain of the DIHYDROPYRIDINE RECEPTOR (DHPR), a voltage-sensing protein in the plasma membrane. In response to depolarization, the DHPRs undergo a conformational change; this produces a conformational change in the associated RYRs, opening them, so that Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol.
                                                                                      • In most cases the syndrome is caused by a defect in the RYANODINE RECEPTOR GENE (RYR1). Abnormal RYR1 receptors trigger unregulated release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
                                                                                      PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics967

                                                                                      Malignant hyperthermia — the whole cascade

                                                                                      PHAR.00080src p.2873–2882
                                                                                      PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics968

                                                                                      Malignant hyperthermia — syndrome, treatment and susceptibility

                                                                                      PHAR.00080src p.2816–2817 · 2876–2882
                                                                                      The syndrome includes
                                                                                      • Tachycardia
                                                                                      • Hypertension
                                                                                      • Severe muscle rigidity
                                                                                      • Hyperthermia
                                                                                      • Hyperkalemia
                                                                                      • Acid-base imbalance with acidosis
                                                                                      Treatment
                                                                                      • DANTROLENE — prevents Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
                                                                                      • Appropriate measures to reduce body temperature
                                                                                      • Restore electrolyte and acid-base balance
                                                                                      Exam Lock
                                                                                      Establishing susceptibility
                                                                                      • The most reliable test is the in vitro CAFFEINE-HALOTHANE MUSCLE CONTRACTURE TEST — a small piece of muscle is obtained from the thigh under regional or general anesthesia, attached to a device measuring force of contraction, and exposed to halothane or caffeine
                                                                                      • A response to halothane, or a response to LOW concentrations of caffeine, is diagnostic for malignant hyperthermia-susceptible muscle
                                                                                      • Genetic testing can also be used
                                                                                      • During anesthesia, watch for TRISMUS from muscular contraction
                                                                                      Trap
                                                                                      Muscular dystrophies are a separate trap. Patients with undiagnosed Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy receiving succinylcholine and halogenated anesthetics can develop life-threatening HYPERKALEMIA and RHABDOMYOLYSIS — due to upregulation of extra-junctional ACh receptors depolarizing the whole cell. This is not malignant hyperthermia, though it is triggered by the same two drug classes.
                                                                                        PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics969

                                                                                        Block check — inhaled anesthetics

                                                                                        PHAR.00082 · PHAR.00083

                                                                                        Two agents have λ(oil:gas) values of 19 and 960 respectively. Which statement is correct?

                                                                                        1. AThe agent with λ(oil:gas) 19 is more potent and has slower onset
                                                                                        2. BThe agent with λ(oil:gas) 960 is more potent and has slower onset
                                                                                        3. CThe agent with λ(oil:gas) 960 is less potent and has faster onset
                                                                                        4. DPotency cannot be predicted from λ(oil:gas)
                                                                                        5. EBoth will have identical MAC values
                                                                                        Answer
                                                                                        B. Meyer-Overton: potency increases as liposolubility increases — as λ(oil:gas) increases, MAC decreases. λ(oil:gas) 960 is methoxyflurane, MAC 0.16 — the most potent. And because anesthetics with large λ(oil:gas) tend to have large λ(blood:gas), high potency correlates with SLOW onset (methoxyflurane λ(blood:gas) = 12, very slow onset and recovery).
                                                                                        PHAR.00083

                                                                                        A patient in septic shock has a high cardiac output. What effect does this have on inhalational induction?

                                                                                        1. AIt speeds induction because more anesthetic reaches the brain per minute
                                                                                        2. BIt slows induction because a larger volume of blood is exposed, increasing blood 'capacity'
                                                                                        3. CIt has no effect on the rate of rise of arterial tension
                                                                                        4. DIt only affects agents with low blood solubility
                                                                                        5. EIt raises MAC and therefore speeds induction
                                                                                        Answer
                                                                                        B. An increase in pulmonary blood flow (increased cardiac output) SLOWS the rate of rise in arterial tension, because increased pulmonary blood flow exposes a larger volume of blood to the anesthetic; blood "capacity" increases and tension rises slowly. The effect is greatest for agents with moderate to high blood solubility.
                                                                                        PHAR.00081

                                                                                        Which combination yields exactly 1 MAC?

                                                                                        1. A1.4% isoflurane plus 104% nitrous oxide
                                                                                        2. B0.7 MAC isoflurane plus 0.3 MAC nitrous oxide
                                                                                        3. C0.5 MAC halothane plus 0.5 MAC halothane
                                                                                        4. D2 MAC sevoflurane alone
                                                                                        5. EMAC values cannot be combined
                                                                                        Answer
                                                                                        B. MAC values are ADDITIVE. Nitrous oxide can be used as a "carrier" gas, decreasing the anesthetic requirement of other anesthetics: 0.7 MAC of isoflurane and 0.3 MAC of nitrous oxide yield 1 MAC.
                                                                                        PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics970

                                                                                        Block check — inhaled anesthetics (cont.)

                                                                                        PHAR.00081

                                                                                        Which of the following would DECREASE MAC?

                                                                                        1. AAnxiety
                                                                                        2. BThyrotoxicosis
                                                                                        3. CConcurrent opioid analgesia
                                                                                        4. DIncreased body weight
                                                                                        5. EMale sex
                                                                                        Answer
                                                                                        C. MAC is decreased by hypothermia, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, and adjuvant drugs such as opioid analgesics or sedative-hypnotics — so the inspired concentration should be decreased accordingly. MAC is increased by anxiety and thyrotoxicosis. Sex, height and weight do not significantly affect MAC.
                                                                                        PHAR.00079

                                                                                        A patient is being ventilated after a bowel obstruction. Which inhaled agent must be avoided, and why?

                                                                                        1. ASevoflurane — it produces compound A
                                                                                        2. BHalothane — it sensitizes the myocardium
                                                                                        3. CNitrous oxide — it enters closed gas spaces faster than nitrogen escapes
                                                                                        4. DIsoflurane — it is pungent
                                                                                        5. EDesflurane — it requires a special vaporizer
                                                                                        Answer
                                                                                        C. N₂O exchanges with nitrogen in air-containing cavities; it enters the cavity faster than nitrogen escapes, increasing the volume and/or pressure of the cavity. Avoid in pneumothorax, obstructed middle ear, air embolus, obstructed loop of bowel, intraocular air bubble, pulmonary bulla and intracranial air.
                                                                                        PHAR.00079

                                                                                        A dental assistant working in a poorly ventilated suite develops megaloblastic anaemia. Which agent and mechanism?

                                                                                        1. AHalothane — free radical hepatic injury
                                                                                        2. BMethoxyflurane — inorganic fluoride release
                                                                                        3. CNitrous oxide — decreased methionine synthase activity
                                                                                        4. DSevoflurane — compound A formation
                                                                                        5. EEnflurane — fluoride release
                                                                                        Answer
                                                                                        C. Prolonged exposure to nitrous oxide decreases METHIONINE SYNTHASE activity and causes megaloblastic anemia — a potential occupational hazard for staff working in poorly ventilated dental operating suites. Methionine synthase is the B₁₂-dependent enzyme, so the picture is a functional B₁₂ deficiency.
                                                                                        PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics971

                                                                                        Block check — inhaled anesthetics (cont.)

                                                                                        PHAR.00080

                                                                                        Thirty minutes into a sevoflurane and succinylcholine anaesthetic, a patient develops masseter spasm, generalised rigidity, tachycardia and a rising temperature. Which is the immediate pharmacological treatment and what is the underlying defect?

                                                                                        1. ANeostigmine — acetylcholinesterase inhibition
                                                                                        2. BDantrolene — a defect in the RYR1 ryanodine receptor gene
                                                                                        3. CNaltrexone — opioid receptor blockade
                                                                                        4. DOndansetron — 5-HT3 blockade
                                                                                        5. EAtropine — muscarinic blockade
                                                                                        Answer
                                                                                        B. Malignant hyperthermia: an autosomal dominant defect in the ryanodine receptor gene RYR1, incidence ~1:12,000, triggered by halogenated inhalation anesthetics and succinylcholine. Abnormal RYR1 receptors release calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum without control → sustained contraction, heat, acidosis, hyperkalemia and rhabdomyolysis. Treat with DANTROLENE, which prevents Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, plus cooling and correction of electrolytes and acid-base balance. Trismus during anesthesia is the sign to watch for.
                                                                                        PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics972

                                                                                        Ultra-short acting barbiturates — thiopental and methohexital

                                                                                        PHAR.00084src p.2818 · 2885–2887
                                                                                        • Thiopental is the barbiturate most commonly used for induction of anesthesia, often in combination with inhaled anesthetics.
                                                                                        • High liposolubility promotes rapid entry into the brain and results in surgical anesthesia in one circulation time (less than 1 minute).
                                                                                        • Used for induction of anesthesia and for short surgical procedures.
                                                                                        • Their anesthetic effects are terminated by REDISTRIBUTION from the brain to other tissues, but HEPATIC METABOLISM is required for their elimination from the body. *The redistribution sequence is vessel-rich group (brain, liver, kidneys) → muscle group (muscle, skin) → fat group.*
                                                                                        • They are respiratory and circulatory depressants.
                                                                                        • They DECREASE intracranial pressure — this makes thiopental a much more desirable drug for patients with cerebral swelling than the inhaled anesthetics, since intracranial pressure and blood volume are not increased.
                                                                                        • Barbiturates do not produce analgesia; some evidence suggests they may cause HYPERALGESIA.
                                                                                        • All barbiturates can cause apnea, coughing, chest wall spasm, laryngospasm and bronchospasm — a concern for asthmatic patients.
                                                                                        Bottom Line
                                                                                        Redistribution, not metabolism, ends the effect. That is why a single induction dose wears off in minutes but repeated dosing accumulates — the fat compartment fills, and then only hepatic clearance can remove the drug.
                                                                                          PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics973

                                                                                          Propofol, fospropofol and etomidate

                                                                                          PHAR.00084src p.2818–2819 · 2888–2889
                                                                                          Propofol
                                                                                          • The most popular IV anesthetic.
                                                                                          • Widely used for outpatient surgical procedures, in intensive care settings, and in balanced anesthesia
                                                                                          • Produces anesthesia at a rate similar to the barbiturates, and recovery is FASTER
                                                                                          • Postoperative vomiting is uncommon — propofol has ANTIEMETIC actions
                                                                                          • Used for both induction and maintenance
                                                                                          • Produces NO analgesia
                                                                                          • Rapidly metabolized in the liver at a rate ten times faster than thiopental
                                                                                          • Potent respiratory depressant; dose-dependent cardiovascular depressant effects
                                                                                          • Reduces intracranial pressure
                                                                                          • Causes hypotension, primarily through DECREASED PERIPHERAL VASCULAR RESISTANCE
                                                                                          • Fospropofol is a prodrug converted to propofol in vivo
                                                                                          Etomidate
                                                                                          • Primarily used for anesthetic induction of patients at risk for HYPOTENSION
                                                                                          • Causes minimal cardiovascular and respiratory depression
                                                                                          • No analgesic effects
                                                                                          • Reduces intracranial pressure
                                                                                          • Associated with nausea and vomiting
                                                                                          • Inhibits 11-beta hydroxylase → adrenocortical suppression via inhibitory effects on steroidogenesis, with decreased plasma levels of hydrocortisone; adrenal suppression with prolonged infusions
                                                                                          PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics974

                                                                                          Ketamine — the outlier

                                                                                          PHAR.00084src p.2819 · 2890–2891
                                                                                          • Produces DISSOCIATIVE ANESTHESIA, characterized by catatonia, amnesia and analgesia, with or without loss of consciousness.
                                                                                          • Mechanism of action may involve blockade of NMDA receptors.
                                                                                          • Ketamine is the ONLY IV anesthetic that possesses BOTH analgesic properties AND the ability to produce CV STIMULATION. Heart rate, arterial blood pressure and cardiac output increase. Cardiovascular stimulation is due to stimulation of the central sympathetic nervous system and to inhibition of the reuptake of norepinephrine at sympathetic nerve terminals.
                                                                                          • Ketamine INCREASES intracranial pressure. In this regard ketamine resembles inhaled anesthetics as a potentially dangerous drug when intracranial pressure is elevated.
                                                                                          • Use has been associated with postoperative disorientation, sensory and perceptual illusions, and vivid dreams ('EMERGENCE PHENOMENA'). Diazepam, midazolam, or propofol given before ketamine reduce the incidence of these adverse effects.
                                                                                          • Very useful for poor-risk geriatric patients and high-risk patients in cardiogenic or septic shock because of its cardiostimulatory properties.
                                                                                          Trap
                                                                                          Ketamine is the exception on almost every axis. Every other IV agent reduces intracranial pressure and provides no analgesia; ketamine raises ICP and does provide analgesia. Learn it as the exception and the rest of the table stays simple.
                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics975
