                                                                                            General anesthetics — the whole lecture on one page

                                                                                            PHAR.00076–00084src p.2805–2894
                                                                                            QuestionAnswer
                                                                                            What is general anesthesia?Analgesia · amnesia · loss of consciousness · suppression of sensory and autonomic reflexes · skeletal muscle relaxation
                                                                                            Why balanced anesthesia?No single drug achieves all the goals: inhaled agents are slow to induce and poor analgesics, paralysis needs a neuromuscular blocker, and combining drugs minimises the halogenated-hydrocarbon dose
                                                                                            MechanismFacilitate GABA_A and glycine receptors; inhibit nicotinic receptors
                                                                                            Potencyλ(oil:gas) ↑ → MAC ↓ (Meyer-Overton). 1/MAC = potency index. MAC = ED50 on a quantal curve; MAC values are additive
                                                                                            Speedλ(blood:gas) ↓ → faster onset. High potency correlates with slow onset. ↑ inspired concentration and ↑ ventilation speed induction; ↑ cardiac output SLOWS it
                                                                                            RecoveryRedistribution from the brain and exhalation. Low-solubility agents: recovery mirrors induction. High-solubility agents: recovery depends on duration, because fat is a reservoir
                                                                                            Signature toxicitiesHalothane → hepatitis and catecholamine sensitisation. Methoxyflurane → fluoride nephrotoxicity. Sevoflurane → compound A. N₂O → closed-space expansion and megaloblastic anaemia. Enflurane → spike-and-wave at high dose
                                                                                            Malignant hyperthermiaRYR1, autosomal dominant, ~1:12,000; triggered by halogenated agents ± succinylcholine; tachycardia, hypertension, rigidity, hyperthermia, hyperkalemia, acidosis; treat with DANTROLENE; diagnose with the caffeine-halothane contracture test
                                                                                            IV agentsThiopental — redistribution, ↓ICP, no analgesia. Propofol — most popular, antiemetic, ↓ICP, hypotension via ↓PVR. Etomidate — for the hypotensive patient, adrenal suppression. Ketamine — NMDA blocker, dissociative, the only one with analgesia and CV stimulation, ↑ICP, emergence phenomena
                                                                                            AdjuvantsBenzodiazepines (amnesia) · opioids (analgesia) · neuromuscular blockers (relaxation, competitive block reversed by neostigmine) · ondansetron (PONV) · antimuscarinics (amnesia, secretions, bradycardia)
                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics978

                                                                                            Block check — IV anesthetics and adjuvants

                                                                                            PHAR.00084

                                                                                            Which IV anesthetic would you choose to induce a hypotensive trauma patient with a normal ICP, and what is its characteristic long-term risk?

                                                                                            1. APropofol — hypertriglyceridaemia
                                                                                            2. BThiopental — hyperalgesia
                                                                                            3. CEtomidate — adrenocortical suppression through inhibition of 11-β-hydroxylase
                                                                                            4. DKetamine — emergence phenomena
                                                                                            5. EMidazolam — respiratory depression
                                                                                            Answer
                                                                                            C. Etomidate is primarily used for anesthetic induction of patients at risk for hypotension because it causes minimal cardiovascular and respiratory depression. It inhibits 11-beta hydroxylase, causing adrenocortical suppression via inhibitory effects on steroidogenesis with decreased plasma hydrocortisone — adrenal suppression with prolonged infusions.
                                                                                            PHAR.00084

                                                                                            A patient in septic shock needs induction. Which agent's cardiovascular profile makes it particularly useful, and what is the mechanism?

                                                                                            1. APropofol — decreased peripheral vascular resistance
                                                                                            2. BThiopental — direct myocardial stimulation
                                                                                            3. CKetamine — central sympathetic stimulation and inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake
                                                                                            4. DEtomidate — direct positive inotropy
                                                                                            5. EFospropofol — increased preload
                                                                                            Answer
                                                                                            C. Ketamine is the only IV anesthetic that possesses both analgesic properties and the ability to produce CV stimulation: heart rate, arterial pressure and cardiac output increase, due to stimulation of the central sympathetic nervous system and to inhibition of the reuptake of norepinephrine at sympathetic nerve terminals. Very useful for poor-risk geriatric patients and high-risk patients in cardiogenic or septic shock.
                                                                                            PHAR.00084

                                                                                            A head-injured patient with raised intracranial pressure requires induction. Which agent is specifically contraindicated by that concern?

                                                                                            1. AThiopental
                                                                                            2. BPropofol
                                                                                            3. CEtomidate
                                                                                            4. DKetamine
                                                                                            5. EMidazolam
                                                                                            Answer
                                                                                            D. Ketamine INCREASES intracranial pressure; in this regard it resembles inhaled anesthetics as a potentially dangerous drug when intracranial pressure is elevated. Thiopental, propofol and etomidate all REDUCE intracranial pressure — the lecture singles out thiopental as much more desirable than the inhaled anesthetics for patients with cerebral swelling.
                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics979

                                                                                            Block check — IV anesthetics and adjuvants (cont.)

                                                                                            PHAR.00084

                                                                                            A single induction dose of thiopental wears off in minutes. What terminates its effect, and what is required for elimination?

                                                                                            1. AHepatic metabolism terminates the effect; renal excretion eliminates it
                                                                                            2. BRedistribution from the brain terminates the effect; hepatic metabolism is required for elimination
                                                                                            3. CExhalation terminates the effect; hepatic metabolism eliminates it
                                                                                            4. DPlasma esterases terminate the effect
                                                                                            5. ERenal clearance does both
                                                                                            Answer
                                                                                            B. The anesthetic effects of the ultra-short acting barbiturates are terminated by REDISTRIBUTION from the brain to other tissues, but HEPATIC METABOLISM is required for their elimination from the body. The redistribution sequence runs vessel-rich group (brain, liver, kidneys) → muscle group → fat group.
                                                                                            PHAR.00078

                                                                                            Which adjuvant reversal pairing is correct?

                                                                                            1. ASuccinylcholine block is reversed by neostigmine
                                                                                            2. BCompetitive neuromuscular block is reversed by an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor such as neostigmine
                                                                                            3. COpioid effect is reversed by ondansetron
                                                                                            4. DBenzodiazepine effect is reversed by naltrexone
                                                                                            5. EAntimuscarinic effect is reversed by atropine
                                                                                            Answer
                                                                                            B. The effects of the COMPETITIVE neuromuscular blockers (e.g. pancuronium) can be reversed by an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor such as neostigmine — the depolarizing blocker succinylcholine cannot be reversed that way. Opioids are reversed by an antagonist such as naltrexone.
                                                                                            PHAR.00084

                                                                                            Which statement about propofol is correct?

                                                                                            1. AIt produces profound analgesia
                                                                                            2. BIt increases intracranial pressure
                                                                                            3. CIt has antiemetic actions and causes hypotension mainly through decreased peripheral vascular resistance
                                                                                            4. DIt is eliminated primarily by redistribution to fat
                                                                                            5. EIt is metabolised ten times more slowly than thiopental
                                                                                            Answer
                                                                                            C. Propofol produces NO analgesia, REDUCES intracranial pressure, has ANTIEMETIC actions so postoperative vomiting is uncommon, is rapidly metabolized in the liver at a rate ten times FASTER than thiopental, and causes hypotension primarily through decreased peripheral vascular resistance.
                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · General Anesthetics980
                                                                                            PHAR

                                                                                            Local Anesthetics

                                                                                            Dr Malcolm Antoine Jr · Department of Microbiology, Immunology & Pharmacology. One mechanism, one molecule shape, and a set of consequences that follow from acid-base chemistry.

                                                                                            Dr Malcolm Antoine Jr · Department of Microbiology, Immunology & Pharmacology  ·  source pp. 2895–2931

                                                                                            Learning objectives — verbatim

                                                                                            • PHAR.00085 Discuss the mechanism of action, adverse effects, pharmacokinetic properties, uses, drug interactions and contraindications of local anesthetics.
                                                                                            • PHAR.00086 List the significant differences between amide and ester-type local anesthetics.
                                                                                            • PHAR.00087 List the common adverse effects of local anesthetics and indicate appropriate treatments should they occur.
                                                                                            • PHAR.00088 Describe the common routes of administration of local anesthetics.
                                                                                            • PHAR.00089 Describe methods used to restrict local anesthetics to a desired site of action and indicate how these methods reduce adverse effects.

                                                                                            What a local anesthetic does

                                                                                            1. Block nerve conduction of sensory impulses from the periphery to the CNS.
                                                                                            2. Abolish sensation (and in higher concentrations motor activity) in a limited area of the body WITHOUT producing unconsciousness.

                                                                                            The small unmyelinated nerve fibers that conduct impulses for pain, temperature and autonomic activity are more sensitive to the actions of local anesthetics. Sources: Golan 4e · Goodman & Gilman 12e · Whalen, Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews 6e · Katzung 16e.

                                                                                            PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics981

                                                                                            Chemistry — three parts to every molecule

                                                                                            PHAR.00085 · PHAR.00086src p.2895 · 2904–2906
                                                                                            Lipophilic group (frequently an aromatic ring)→Intermediate chain (commonly including an ESTER or AMIDE)→Ionizable group (usually a tertiary amine)
                                                                                            • Optimal activity requires a delicate balance between the lipophilic and hydrophilic strengths of these groups. Specific stereochemical configurations can also be important; differences in the potency of stereoisomers have been documented for a few compounds.
                                                                                            • Since ESTER links (as in procaine) are more prone to HYDROLYSIS than AMIDE links, esters usually have a SHORTER duration of action.
                                                                                            • Local anesthetics are weak bases marketed as water-soluble salts, usually hydrochlorides. Their hydrochloride salts are mildly acidic — this increases the stability of the local anesthetic esters and any accompanying vasoconstrictor substance.
                                                                                            Bottom Line
                                                                                            A useful spelling trick: amide local anesthetics have two "i"s in the name — lidocaine, bupivacaine, prilocaine, ropivacaine. Esters have one: procaine, tetracaine, benzocaine, cocaine.
                                                                                              PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics982

                                                                                              The Henderson–Hasselbalch consequence

                                                                                              PHAR.00085src p.2895 · 2907–2908
                                                                                              pK − pH = log ( [Cationic form] / [Uncharged form] )Henderson-Hasselbalch
                                                                                              • Since the pK of most local anesthetics is in the range of 8.0–9.0, the LARGER fraction in the body fluids at physiologic pH will be the CATIONIC form.
                                                                                              • The CATIONIC form is thought to be the most active form at the receptor site, but the UNCHARGED form is important for rapid penetration of the biologic membranes — the local anesthetic receptor is NOT accessible from the external side of the cell membrane.
                                                                                              • This partly explains why dentists and surgeons observe that local anesthetics are much less effective in INFECTED TISSUES: these tissues have a low extracellular pH, so that a very low fraction of nonionized local anesthetic is available for diffusion into the cell.
                                                                                              PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics983

                                                                                              Two forms, one receptor — and the infected-tissue failure

                                                                                              PHAR.00085src p.2895 · 2907–2908
                                                                                              PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics984

                                                                                              Mechanism of action

                                                                                              PHAR.00085src p.2897 · 2910
                                                                                              The primary mechanism of action of local anesthetics is BLOCKADE OF VOLTAGE-GATED SODIUM CHANNELS. Local anesthetics bind to receptors near the INTRACELLULAR end of the channel and block the channel.PHAR.00085

                                                                                              What happens as the concentration rises

                                                                                              1. The threshold for excitation increases
                                                                                              2. Impulse conduction slows
                                                                                              3. The rate of rise of the action potential declines
                                                                                              4. The action potential amplitude decreases
                                                                                              5. Finally, the ability to generate an action potential is abolished
                                                                                              Exam Lock
                                                                                              Use-dependence — state-dependent block
                                                                                              • The blockade of sodium channels by most local anesthetics is VOLTAGE- and TIME-DEPENDENT.
                                                                                              • Channels in the RESTED state, which predominate at more negative membrane potentials, have a LOWER affinity for local anesthetics than ACTIVATED (open) and INACTIVATED channels, which predominate at more positive membrane potentials.
                                                                                              • Thus the effect of a given drug concentration is more marked in RAPIDLY FIRING axons than in resting fibers.
                                                                                              Bottom Line
                                                                                              Use-dependence explains why a nerve that is actively transmitting pain is blocked more readily than one at rest — the drug needs the channel to open before it can reach its binding site.
                                                                                                PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics985

                                                                                                Structure–activity: potency, duration and onset

                                                                                                PHAR.00085 · PHAR.00086src p.2898 · 2914 · 2920
                                                                                                Liposolubility
                                                                                                • Correlates with both POTENCY and DURATION of action
                                                                                                • Unfortunately, greater liposolubility also increases TOXICITY
                                                                                                pKa
                                                                                                • Generally correlates with the SPEED OF ONSET of action: the closer the pKa to body pH, the FASTER the onset
                                                                                                • Because a pKa nearer 7.4 leaves more of the drug in the uncharged form that can cross the membrane
                                                                                                ClassAgentPotency (procaine = 1)Duration of action
                                                                                                EstersCocaine2Medium
                                                                                                Procaine1Short
                                                                                                Tetracaine16Long
                                                                                                Benzocaine—Surface use only
                                                                                                AmidesLidocaine4Medium
                                                                                                Bupivacaine16Long
                                                                                                Prilocaine3Medium
                                                                                                Ropivacaine16Long

                                                                                                Clinical pharmacology — choose by duration

                                                                                                • The choice of local anesthetic for a specific procedure is usually based on the duration of action required.
                                                                                                • Short-acting: procaine, chloroprocaine
                                                                                                • Intermediate-acting: lidocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine
                                                                                                • Long-acting: tetracaine, bupivacaine, etidocaine, ropivacaine
                                                                                                PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics986

                                                                                                Actions on nerves — the order of block

                                                                                                PHAR.00085src p.2898
                                                                                                Different types of nerve fibers differ significantly in their susceptibility to local anesthetic blockade on the basis of SIZE and MYELINATION.Actions on Nerves
                                                                                                • Upon application of a local anesthetic to a nerve root, the small lightly myelinated B fibers (preganglionic autonomic), the small unmyelinated C fibers (mediating pain sensations), and the small myelinated A-δ fibers (mediating pain and temperature sensations) are blocked BEFORE larger myelinated A-α, A-β and A-γ fibers (carrying postural, touch, pressure and motor information).
                                                                                                • Thus: pain fibers are blocked FIRST; other sensations disappear NEXT; and motor function is blocked LAST.
                                                                                                PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics987

                                                                                                Which fibres go first

                                                                                                PHAR.00085src p.2898
                                                                                                PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics988

                                                                                                Pharmacokinetics — absorption and vasoconstrictors

                                                                                                PHAR.00088 · PHAR.00089src p.2896–2897 · 2916–2917
                                                                                                • Systemic absorption of injected local anesthetics from the site of administration is modified by several factors: DOSAGE · SITE OF INJECTION · DRUG-TISSUE BINDING · THE PRESENCE OF VASOCONSTRICTORS · the physicochemical properties of the drug.
                                                                                                • The duration of action of a local anesthetic is proportional to the time during which it is in contact with nerve. Consequently, procedures that keep the drug AT the nerve prolong the period of anesthesia.
                                                                                                Exam Lock
                                                                                                How a vasoconstrictor restricts the drug to its site (PHAR.00089)
                                                                                                • Preparations of local anesthetics often contain a vasoconstrictor, usually EPINEPHRINE.
                                                                                                • Vasoconstrictors reduce systemic absorption from the depot site by decreasing blood flow in these areas.
                                                                                                • As a consequence, neuronal uptake of the drug is ENHANCED due to the higher local drug concentration, and the SYSTEMIC TOXIC EFFECTS ARE REDUCED.
                                                                                                • Cocaine itself constricts blood vessels by potentiating the action of norepinephrine; therefore it prevents its own absorption.
                                                                                                • In SPINAL anesthesia, epinephrine acts directly on the cord to both enhance and prolong local anesthetic-induced spinal anesthesia by acting on α₂-adrenoceptors, which INHIBIT RELEASE OF SUBSTANCE P and reduce sensory neuron firing. Recognition of this fact has led to the use of the α₂ agonists CLONIDINE and DEXMEDETOMIDINE to augment local anesthetic effect in the subarachnoid space and on peripheral nerves.
                                                                                                • Some of the vasoconstrictor agent may be absorbed systemically, occasionally to an extent sufficient to cause untoward reactions. There may also be DELAYED WOUND HEALING, TISSUE EDEMA, or NECROSIS after local anesthesia.
                                                                                                Trap
                                                                                                The classic exam application: do not use epinephrine-containing solutions in end-artery territories — fingers, toes, nose, ears, penis — where vasoconstriction risks ischaemia and necrosis. That is exactly what the lecture's own vignette about the lacerated index finger is testing.
                                                                                                  PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics989

                                                                                                  Metabolism, excretion and the ester/amide divide

                                                                                                  PHAR.00086src p.2897 · 2919 · 2928
                                                                                                  ESTER-linkedAMIDE-linked
                                                                                                  ExamplesCocaine · procaine · chloroprocaine · tetracaine · benzocaineLidocaine · bupivacaine · prilocaine · ropivacaine · mepivacaine · etidocaine
                                                                                                  MetabolismMetabolized by TISSUE AND PLASMA ESTERASES (pseudocholinesterases). This process is FAST; metabolites are excreted by the kidneyDegraded by LIVER CYTOCHROME P450 enzymes. The three major routes of hepatic metabolism are aromatic hydroxylation, N-dealkylation and amide hydrolysis; metabolites are excreted by the kidney
                                                                                                  DurationShorter — the ester link is more prone to hydrolysisLonger
                                                                                                  Disease that changes handlingPseudocholinesterase deficiencyLIVER DISEASE — metabolism is slowed, so toxicity from the amide type is more likely in patients with liver disease. Many other drugs used in anesthesia are metabolized by the same P450 isozymes, and concomitant use of competing drugs may slow local anesthetic metabolism
                                                                                                  AllergyMetabolized to PARA-AMINOBENZOIC ACID (PABA) derivatives — these metabolites are responsible for allergic reactions in a small percentage of the populationNOT metabolized to p-aminobenzoic acid; allergic reactions to agents of the amide group are EXTREMELY RARE
                                                                                                  PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics990

                                                                                                  Toxicity by system

                                                                                                  PHAR.00087src p.2898–2899 · 2922–2928
                                                                                                  SystemToxic effects and management
                                                                                                  Central nervous systemFollowing absorption, local anesthetics may cause STIMULATION of the CNS, producing restlessness and tremor that may proceed to CLONIC CONVULSIONS. Central stimulation is followed by CNS DEPRESSION; death is usually caused by RESPIRATORY FAILURE. More serious toxic reactions are due to convulsions from excessive blood levels — prevented by administering the smallest dose required for adequate anesthesia. When large doses must be given, premedication with a BENZODIAZEPINE (e.g. diazepam) provides significant prophylaxis against seizures.
                                                                                                  Peripheral nervous systemWhen applied at excessively high concentrations, ALL local anesthetics can be toxic to nerve tissue. The mechanism of neurotoxicity is unknown, but it does NOT result from excessive sodium channel blockade.
                                                                                                  CardiovascularEffects result partly from direct actions on cardiac and smooth muscle membranes and partly from indirect effects on autonomic nerves. Local anesthetics block sodium channels and thus DEPRESS cardiac pacemaker activity, excitability and conduction; at very high concentrations they may also block Ca²⁺ channels. With the EXCEPTION OF COCAINE, they also depress the strength of cardiac contraction and cause arteriolar dilation, leading to HYPOTENSION. Cardiovascular collapse and death usually occur only after large doses, but may occasionally result from the small amounts used for infiltration anesthesia especially if BUPIVACAINE is the agent used — bupivacaine is more cardiotoxic than other local anesthetics.
                                                                                                  Cocaine — the exceptionBlockade of norepinephrine uptake results in VASOCONSTRICTION and HYPERTENSION. It may also precipitate cardiac arrhythmias. The vasoconstriction produced by cocaine can lead to ischemia and, in chronic abusers, to ulceration of the mucous membrane and even damage to the NASAL SEPTUM.
                                                                                                  BloodLarge doses of PRILOCAINE during regional anesthesia may lead to accumulation of the metabolite O-TOLUIDINE, an oxidizing agent capable of converting hemoglobin to METHEMOGLOBIN. Reducing agents such as METHYLENE BLUE may be given IV to convert methemoglobin back to hemoglobin.
                                                                                                  Allergic reactionsMore common with ESTER types, due to the PABA metabolite. Amides are not metabolized to PABA and allergic reactions to them are extremely rare.

                                                                                                  The lecture's own symptom list for systemic toxicity: cardiac arrest · respiratory arrest · coma · seizures · muscular spasms · tinnitus and auditory hallucinations · paresthesias in mouth and tongue · drowsiness. Perioral and lingual paraesthesia with tinnitus is the early warning — it precedes the convulsion.

                                                                                                  PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics991

                                                                                                  Drug interaction — procaine and the sulfonamides

                                                                                                  PHAR.00087src p.2900 · 2929
                                                                                                  Procaine is hydrolyzed in vivo to produce PARA-AMINOBENZOIC ACID, which INHIBITS THE ACTION OF SULFONAMIDES. Thus, large doses should not be administered to patients taking sulfonamide drugs.PHAR.00087

                                                                                                  Why — the footnote the lecture supplies

                                                                                                  • All sulfonamides in clinical use are synthetic structural analogs of p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA). Many bacteria are impermeable to folic acid: they must synthesize folate from PABA, pteridine and glutamate. *(Human beings cannot synthesize folic acid and must obtain preformed folate as a vitamin in the diet.)*
                                                                                                  • Because of their structural similarity to PABA, sulfas compete with it for the enzyme DIHYDROPTEROATE SYNTHETASE, preventing synthesis of bacterial folic acid — depriving the bacterial cell of cofactors for purine, pyrimidine and amino acid synthesis.
                                                                                                  • Flooding the system with PABA from procaine metabolism therefore out-competes the sulfonamide and antagonises its antibacterial effect.
                                                                                                  PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics992

                                                                                                  Local anesthetics — one page

                                                                                                  PHAR.00085–00089src p.2895–2931
                                                                                                  QuestionAnswer
                                                                                                  MechanismBlock voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, binding near the INTRACELLULAR end. State-dependent: higher affinity for activated and inactivated channels, so the effect is greater in rapidly firing axons.
                                                                                                  Which form does whatUncharged base crosses the membrane; the CATION binds the receptor. pK 8–9, so most is cation at pH 7.4. Low pH (infected tissue) → less uncharged drug → the block fails.
                                                                                                  Potency and durationLiposolubility ↑ → potency ↑, duration ↑, and toxicity ↑
                                                                                                  OnsetpKa closer to body pH → faster onset
                                                                                                  Order of blockB (preganglionic autonomic) and C (pain) and A-δ (pain, temperature) first; A-α/β/γ (postural, touch, pressure, motor) last. Pain first, motor last.
                                                                                                  Ester vs amideEsters — plasma/tissue esterases, short, PABA metabolite → allergy. Amides — hepatic CYP450, longer, allergy extremely rare, toxicity ↑ in liver disease. Amides have two "i"s.
                                                                                                  Restricting the drug to its siteAdd a vasoconstrictor (epinephrine): ↓ systemic absorption, ↑ neuronal uptake, ↓ systemic toxicity. In spinal anesthesia epinephrine also acts on α₂-adrenoceptors to inhibit substance P release — hence clonidine and dexmedetomidine as adjuncts. Risks: delayed wound healing, tissue edema, necrosis. Cocaine vasoconstricts by itself.
                                                                                                  Signature toxicitiesCNS: stimulation → convulsions → depression → respiratory failure; prophylax with a benzodiazepine. CV: bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic. Blood: prilocaine → o-toluidine → methemoglobinemia, treat with methylene blue. Allergy: esters, via PABA. Cocaine: vasoconstriction, hypertension, arrhythmias, nasal septal damage.
                                                                                                  Drug interactionProcaine → PABA → antagonises sulfonamides (which compete with PABA for dihydropteroate synthetase).
                                                                                                  PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics993

                                                                                                  Block check — local anesthetics

                                                                                                  PHAR.00085

                                                                                                  A 75-year-old man undergoes carpal tunnel release under local anaesthesia with bupivacaine. Which best explains the pharmacologic effect of this drug on the membrane of his neurons?

                                                                                                  1. AActivation of the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase
                                                                                                  2. BDecreased permeability to Ca²⁺
                                                                                                  3. CDecreased permeability to Na⁺
                                                                                                  4. DIncreased glutamate reuptake
                                                                                                  5. EInhibition of the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ antiporter
                                                                                                  Answer
                                                                                                  C. The primary mechanism of action of local anesthetics is blockade of VOLTAGE-GATED SODIUM CHANNELS — they bind receptors near the intracellular end of the channel and block it, decreasing Na⁺ permeability. Calcium channel block occurs only at very high concentrations and is not the primary effect. *(This is the lecture's own vignette.)*
                                                                                                  PHAR.00089

                                                                                                  A 30-year-old construction worker needs a laceration of his right index finger sutured. Which agent is CONTRAINDICATED in the local anesthetic solution?

                                                                                                  1. AEpinephrine
                                                                                                  2. BBupivacaine
                                                                                                  3. CLidocaine
                                                                                                  4. DProcaine
                                                                                                  5. EEtidocaine
                                                                                                  Answer
                                                                                                  A. Vasoconstrictors such as epinephrine reduce systemic absorption by decreasing blood flow — but in an end-artery territory such as a digit that same vasoconstriction risks ischaemia and necrosis. The lecture explicitly lists delayed wound healing, tissue edema, or necrosis among the vasoconstrictor's adverse effects. *(This is the lecture's own vignette.)*
                                                                                                  PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics994

                                                                                                  Block check — local anesthetics (cont.)

                                                                                                  PHAR.00085

                                                                                                  A dentist reports that lidocaine fails to anaesthetise an abscessed tooth. What is the pharmacological explanation?

                                                                                                  1. ASodium channels are downregulated in infection
                                                                                                  2. BThe low extracellular pH of infected tissue shifts the drug to the ionized form, so little uncharged drug diffuses into the cell
                                                                                                  3. CInfection increases hepatic CYP450 metabolism of lidocaine
                                                                                                  4. DBacterial esterases hydrolyse the amide link
                                                                                                  5. EInflammatory oedema dilutes the drug below its threshold concentration
                                                                                                  Answer
                                                                                                  B. The cationic form is the most active form at the receptor site, but the UNCHARGED form is required for penetration of biological membranes because the receptor is not accessible from the external side. Infected tissues have a LOW extracellular pH, so a very low fraction of nonionized local anesthetic is available for diffusion into the cell.
                                                                                                  PHAR.00087

                                                                                                  A patient develops cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen after a large dose of a local anesthetic for regional block. Which drug and which treatment?

                                                                                                  1. ABupivacaine — intravenous lipid emulsion
                                                                                                  2. BLidocaine — sodium bicarbonate
                                                                                                  3. CPrilocaine — intravenous methylene blue
                                                                                                  4. DCocaine — a benzodiazepine
                                                                                                  5. EProcaine — an antihistamine
                                                                                                  Answer
                                                                                                  C. Large doses of PRILOCAINE during regional anesthesia may lead to accumulation of the metabolite O-TOLUIDINE, an oxidizing agent capable of converting hemoglobin to METHEMOGLOBIN. Reducing agents such as METHYLENE BLUE may be given IV to convert methemoglobin to hemoglobin.
                                                                                                  PHAR.00086 · PHAR.00087

                                                                                                  A patient has a documented allergy to procaine. Which statement guides your choice?

                                                                                                  1. AAll local anesthetics are contraindicated
                                                                                                  2. BEsters are safe because they are hydrolysed rapidly
                                                                                                  3. CAmide local anesthetics are not metabolized to PABA and allergic reactions to them are extremely rare
                                                                                                  4. DOnly benzocaine is safe because it is used topically
                                                                                                  5. ECocaine may be substituted because it vasoconstricts
                                                                                                  Answer
                                                                                                  C. Ester-type local anesthetics are metabolized to p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) derivatives, and these metabolites are responsible for allergic reactions in a small percentage of the population. Amides are NOT metabolized to PABA, and allergic reactions to agents of the amide group are extremely rare. Procaine is an ester, so an amide such as lidocaine is the substitute.
                                                                                                  PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics995

                                                                                                  Block check — local anesthetics (cont.)

                                                                                                  PHAR.00087

                                                                                                  During an axillary block a patient reports circumoral tingling and tinnitus, then becomes restless with tremor. What is happening, and what would have reduced the risk?

                                                                                                  1. AAn allergic reaction; antihistamine premedication
                                                                                                  2. BEarly systemic local anesthetic toxicity; premedication with a benzodiazepine when large doses must be given
                                                                                                  3. CMethemoglobinemia; methylene blue
                                                                                                  4. DVasovagal syncope; supine positioning
                                                                                                  5. EEpinephrine absorption; beta blockade
                                                                                                  Answer
                                                                                                  B. Following absorption, local anesthetics may cause CNS stimulation — restlessness and tremor that may proceed to clonic convulsions — followed by CNS depression, with death usually caused by respiratory failure. Serious reactions are prevented by administering the smallest dose required; when large doses must be given, premedication with a benzodiazepine such as diazepam provides significant prophylaxis against seizures. Paresthesias in the mouth and tongue and tinnitus are listed among the early toxic symptoms.
                                                                                                  PHAR.00087

                                                                                                  Which local anesthetic raises blood pressure rather than lowering it, and why?

                                                                                                  1. ABupivacaine — direct myocardial stimulation
                                                                                                  2. BCocaine — blockade of norepinephrine uptake causing vasoconstriction
                                                                                                  3. CLidocaine — reflex tachycardia
                                                                                                  4. DRopivacaine — alpha-1 agonism
                                                                                                  5. ETetracaine — histamine release
                                                                                                  Answer
                                                                                                  B. With the exception of COCAINE, local anesthetics depress the strength of cardiac contraction and cause arteriolar dilation leading to hypotension. Cocaine's blockade of norepinephrine uptake results in VASOCONSTRICTION and HYPERTENSION; it may also precipitate cardiac arrhythmias, and its vasoconstriction can cause ischemia and, in chronic abusers, ulceration of the mucous membrane and damage to the nasal septum.
                                                                                                  PCM1 Pharmacology · Local Anesthetics996

                                                                                                  Learning objectives — verbatim

                                                                                                  • CPD.0.0237 Discuss the key clinical features and typical clinical course of the following diseases: Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT), Cellulitis, superficial Thrombophlebitis, Ruptured Baker's Cyst, and Venous Insufficiency.
                                                                                                  • CPD.0.0238 Present an age-appropriate medical history, that differentiates among etiologies of disease, for a patient presenting with calf pain.
                                                                                                  • CPD.0.0239 Rank a list of discrete and clinical differential diagnoses based on the patient's presentation in order of highest probability to least likely.
                                                                                                  • CPD.0.0240 Provide supportive evidence from the subjective/objective sections to justify differential diagnosis.
                                                                                                  • CPD.0.0241 Generate a list of appropriate initial investigations based on the differential diagnosis.
                                                                                                  • CPD.0.0242 Provide basic information and explain the provisional diagnosis, relevant investigations, prognosis, and treatment plan to the patient.
                                                                                                  • CPD.0.0243 Demonstrate teamwork and respect toward all members of the health care team.
                                                                                                  • CPD.0.0244 Demonstrate the ability to document pertinent information (negative and positive) obtained from the history and physical examination in the appropriate sections of the patient note.

                                                                                                  CPD.0.0243 · CPD.0.0244src p.2933 · 2935
                                                                                                  #TaskDescriptionTime
                                                                                                  1Preparation of ExamSoftStudents open the Examplify application on their laptop and input the provided password. Click start exam and continue when instructed.3–5 min

The Data Evaluator discusses missing data at a time-out at the end of the HPI and at the end of the ROS.15 min
                                                                                                  4Physical examinationThe Examining student performs the relevant physical examination without the use of a rubric; the PE evaluator observes and corrects.10 min

                                                                                                    Prebrief / pre-activity questions

                                                                                                    1. What are common etiologies (vascular) for lower leg pain?
                                                                                                    2. What are the clinical features of intermittent claudication?
                                                                                                    3. How do you differentiate between neurogenic and arterial claudication?
                                                                                                    4. How can you differentiate between arterial insufficiency and thromboangiitis obliterans during history and physical examination?
                                                                                                    5. What is Raynaud's phenomenon and how does it present?
                                                                                                    6. What investigations can be used to confirm the diagnosis of arterial insufficiency?
                                                                                                    Bottom Line
                                                                                                    Bilateral calf pain with a blood pressure of 160/94 in a patient sent to an outpatient clinic is the vignette telling you the answer is vascular and the risk factor is hypertension. Read the vitals before you read the complaint.

                                                                                                      Calf pain interview framework

                                                                                                      CPD.0.0238src p.2937
                                                                                                      1. FIRST: is this ACUTE or CHRONIC? — a new, sudden problem, or ongoing for weeks to months?
                                                                                                      2. Characterize the pain using OPQRST-T
                                                                                                      3. Screen for vascular risk factors
                                                                                                      4. Identify alarm features

                                                                                                      OPQRST-T

                                                                                                      Ask
                                                                                                      OOnsetWhen did the pain start? Was it sudden or gradual?
                                                                                                      PPositionWhere exactly is the pain? One leg or both? Does it move anywhere?
                                                                                                      PPrecipitating factorsWhat were you doing when it started? Did exercise or rest trigger it?
                                                                                                      QQualityWhat does the pain feel like — cramping, sharp, dull, throbbing, tight, burning?
                                                                                                      RRadiationDoes the pain travel anywhere — foot? thigh?
                                                                                                      SSeverityOn a scale of 0–10, how bad is it?
                                                                                                      TTemporal courseConstant or intermittent? Getting better, worse, or staying the same?
                                                                                                      TTransforming factorsWhat makes it worse (walking? standing?) and what makes it better (rest? elevation?) — this is the question that separates the diagnoses
                                                                                                      • Associated symptoms: swelling? redness? warmth? numbness? shortness of breath?
                                                                                                      • Vascular risk factors: diabetes · hypertension · hyperlipidemia · smoking history · family history of early heart disease
                                                                                                      NCRS PVS Simulation 2 & SOAP Assessment I — Calf Pain1001

                                                                                                      Alarm features

                                                                                                      CPD.0.0237src p.2937
                                                                                                      Alarm symptomConsider
                                                                                                      Fever + calf swelling + shortness of breath + chest pain (worse with breathing)Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) → Pulmonary Embolism
                                                                                                      Red, warm, swollen calfCellulitis or DVT

                                                                                                      These symptoms may suggest a serious condition and require urgent evaluation.

                                                                                                      Trap
                                                                                                      Cellulitis and DVT look the same from the doorway. Both give a red, warm, swollen calf. The history — fever and a portal of entry versus immobility, malignancy and previous DVT — is what separates them, and getting it wrong in either direction is dangerous.
                                                                                                        NCRS PVS Simulation 2 & SOAP Assessment I — Calf Pain1002

                                                                                                        Focused questions — calf pain

                                                                                                        CPD.0.0238 · CPD.0.0239src p.2938
                                                                                                        QuestionThink about…
                                                                                                        Does the pain occur with walking? Is the pain relieved with rest? Does the pain reoccur at the same distance every time?Intermittent claudication (consider the underlying cause)
                                                                                                        Is the pain unilateral?Lumbar spinal stenosis · deep vein thrombosis · popliteal artery entrapment syndrome
                                                                                                        Do you have pain in the thighs, buttocks, or hips?Lumbar spinal stenosis
                                                                                                        Is the pain relieved by leaning forward and aggravated by bending backwards?Spinal stenosis
                                                                                                        Have you ever had a nonhealing ulcer?Peripheral artery disease (PAD)
                                                                                                        Do you have erectile dysfunction?Leriche (aortoiliac occlusive disease) syndrome
                                                                                                        Do you have any changes in your skin such as dryness or hair loss?Peripheral arterial disease
                                                                                                        Are your fingers or toes blue or discolored?Stasis dermatitis in chronic venous insufficiency · Raynaud's phenomenon in Buerger's disease and rheumatological disease — SLE / systemic sclerosis
                                                                                                        Are there neurological deficits in the lower limb such as weakness and numbness? Is there absence of trauma?Spinal stenosis · Buerger's disease · popliteal artery entrapment
                                                                                                        Risk factors for atherosclerosis — diabetes, hyperlipidemia, smoking, hypertension?Peripheral arterial disease
                                                                                                        Is there a family history of blood clots? Do you take oral contraceptives?Deep vein thrombosis
                                                                                                        Do you smoke? Do you take anabolic steroids or hormones for body building?Smoking is the major risk factor for Buerger's disease
                                                                                                        Did you have swelling behind your knee prior to the calf pain? Do you have osteoarthritis of the knee?Dissecting Baker cyst

                                                                                                        Wells criteria as the workbook asks them

                                                                                                        Physical examination — the checklist

                                                                                                        CPD.0.0240src p.2939
                                                                                                        1. Patient preparation, comfort & dignity
                                                                                                        2. Hand hygiene
                                                                                                        3. Exam organization
                                                                                                        4. Examination of the relevant system
                                                                                                        Lower limb — inspection
                                                                                                        • Size, symmetry, and note any swelling
                                                                                                        • Color of skin and nail beds
                                                                                                        • Distribution of hair on the lower legs, feet and toes
                                                                                                        • Leg for varicosities
                                                                                                        • Any pigmentation, rashes, scars, or ulcers
                                                                                                        Lower limb — palpation and tests
                                                                                                        • Assess for temperature
                                                                                                        • Palpate the peripheral pulses bilaterally: popliteal · dorsalis pedis · posterior tibial
                                                                                                        • Assess for pitting edema
                                                                                                        • Assess for capillary refill
                                                                                                        • Buerger's test
                                                                                                        • Calf measurement
                                                                                                        Additional systems
                                                                                                        • Recheck blood pressure
                                                                                                        • Auscultate for heart sounds (S1, S2, S3, S4 and gallops)
                                                                                                        • Assess for sensation in the lower extremities
                                                                                                        Bottom Line
                                                                                                        Buerger's test and calf measurement are the two that get skipped and are on the rubric. Buerger's test — elevate to 45° looking for pallor, then hang the leg down looking for reactive hyperaemia — is the bedside test for arterial insufficiency; the calf circumference difference feeds straight into the Wells score (>3 cm).

                                                                                                          Causes of leg pain by system — Appendix A

                                                                                                          CPD.0.0237 · CPD.0.0239src p.2941
                                                                                                          SystemCommon causes of leg pain
                                                                                                          MusculoskeletalMuscle strain, muscle cramps, ligament sprain, tendinitis, shin splints, stress fracture, osteoarthritis, trauma/fracture, compartment syndrome, primary bone tumors (osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma), bone metastases, multiple myeloma
                                                                                                          NervousSciatica, herniated disc, peripheral neuropathy (e.g. diabetes), spinal stenosis, popliteal nerve entrapment
                                                                                                          VascularDeep vein thrombosis (DVT), peripheral artery disease (PAD), varicose veins, chronic venous insufficiency, arterial embolism, Buerger's disease
                                                                                                          HematologicSickle cell crisis, hemophilia (bleeding into joints/muscles), severe anemia
                                                                                                          InfectiousCellulitis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, abscess
                                                                                                          Autoimmune / inflammatoryRheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, polymyositis, vasculitis
                                                                                                          PediatricGrowing pains, Osgood–Schlatter disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis
                                                                                                          Metabolic / electrolyteHypokalemia, hypocalcemia, gout, vitamin D deficiency
                                                                                                          Referred painLumbar spine disorders, hip joint pathology, kidney stones (radiating pain)
