                                                                                                          Screening for PAD and abdominal aortic aneurysm — Appendix C

                                                                                                          CPD.0.0241 · CPD.0.0242src p.2942–2943
                                                                                                          PAD — epidemiology
                                                                                                          • About 236 million people worldwide have atherosclerotic lower extremity PAD. MOST DO NOT HAVE classic symptoms like calf pain with walking (claudication).
                                                                                                          • More common with increasing age, in high-income countries, and in people with diabetes, smoking history, high cholesterol, high blood pressure, or known atherosclerosis (coronary, carotid, renal arteries)
                                                                                                          Why detect it
                                                                                                          • It signals high cardiovascular risk
                                                                                                          • It increases the risk of heart attack and stroke 3-fold
                                                                                                          • It predicts functional decline
                                                                                                          Exam Lock
                                                                                                          The ankle-brachial index (ABI) — the main screening test
                                                                                                          • Abnormal: <0.90
                                                                                                          • Easy, reliable, done in the office
                                                                                                          • High specificity (99%) · lower sensitivity (15–20%)
                                                                                                          • USPSTF: does NOT recommend routine screening (insufficient evidence)
                                                                                                          • AHA: screening with ABI is REASONABLE in high-risk patients

                                                                                                          Abdominal aortic aneurysm

                                                                                                          • An AAA is an abdominal aorta diameter ≥3 cm.
                                                                                                          • More common in older adults and in individuals assigned male at birth.
                                                                                                          • Major risk factors: older age · smoking · family history · atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease · hypertension · high cholesterol.
                                                                                                          Trap
                                                                                                          High specificity, low sensitivity is exactly why the ABI is a good confirmatory test and a poor screening test — a normal ABI does not exclude PAD, which is also why the USPSTF stops short of recommending routine screening.
                                                                                                            NCRS PVS Simulation 2 & SOAP Assessment I — Calf Pain1012

                                                                                                            Calf pain — the five diagnoses this simulation is built around

                                                                                                            CPD.0.0237src p.2932–2943
                                                                                                            DiagnosisKey clinical featuresTypical clinical courseFirst investigation
                                                                                                            Deep venous thrombosisUnilateral calf swelling and tenderness, often subtle; calf >3 cm larger; pitting oedema; collateral superficial veins. Risk: immobility, surgery, trauma, pregnancy, malignancy, previous DVT, oral contraceptives, family historyMay progress; the danger is PULMONARY EMBOLISM, especially from proximal DVTWells score → D-dimer or compression ultrasound; anticoagulation
                                                                                                            CellulitisWarm, red, swollen, tender skin with fever; erysipelas is raised and sharply demarcatedAcute; spreads along skin and can seed lymphatics (red streaks, tender nodes = acute lymphangitis)Clinical diagnosis; antibiotics
                                                                                                            Superficial thrombophlebitisRedness, tenderness and a PALPABLE CORD along a superficial vein (often the saphenous); risk from immobility, venous stasis, IV linesAcute over days; usually benign but can extend to the deep systemUltrasound to exclude deep extension; walking and supportive care
                                                                                                            Ruptured (dissecting) Baker cystSwelling BEHIND THE KNEE preceding the calf pain; known osteoarthritis of the kneeSudden calf pain and swelling mimicking DVT once the cyst rupturesUltrasound — it is the test that separates it from DVT
                                                                                                            Chronic venous insufficiencyDiffuse aching legs, worse later in the day and with prolonged standing; oedema, BROWN pigmentation (haemosiderin), stasis dermatitis, possible ulcers (medial malleolus)Chronic and progressive; relieved by elevation and walkingVenous duplex to assess valve competence; compression therapy
                                                                                                            NCRS PVS Simulation 2 & SOAP Assessment I — Calf Pain1013

                                                                                                            Block check — PVS Simulation 2

                                                                                                            CPD.0.0238 · CPD.0.0241

                                                                                                            A patient reports calf pain that comes on after walking exactly two blocks every time and stops after standing still for two minutes. Pedal pulses are weak and the skin is cool and hairless. Which is the diagnosis and the confirming test?

                                                                                                            1. ALumbar spinal stenosis; MRI lumbar spine
                                                                                                            2. BPeripheral arterial disease; ankle-brachial index
                                                                                                            3. CDeep vein thrombosis; compression ultrasound
                                                                                                            4. DChronic venous insufficiency; venous duplex
                                                                                                            5. ECompartment syndrome; compartment pressures
                                                                                                            Answer
                                                                                                            B. Vascular (arterial) claudication: pain on walking, at a REPRODUCIBLE distance, relieved by standing still for 1–3 minutes, with cool hairless skin, weak pulses and pallor on elevation. The screening test is the ankle-brachial index — abnormal <0.90, specificity 99%, sensitivity 15–20%. Neurogenic claudication is relieved by sitting or leaning forward, with normal pulses.
                                                                                                            CPD.0.0238

                                                                                                            A 62-year-old has leg pain relieved by leaning forward on a shopping trolley and worsened by standing upright. Pedal pulses are normal. Which diagnosis?

                                                                                                            1. APeripheral arterial disease
                                                                                                            2. BLumbar spinal stenosis
                                                                                                            3. CDeep vein thrombosis
                                                                                                            4. DBuerger disease
                                                                                                            5. ELeriche syndrome
                                                                                                            Answer
                                                                                                            B. "Is the pain relieved by leaning forward and aggravated by bending backwards?" → spinal stenosis. Flexion opens the canal; extension narrows it. Normal pulses argue against an arterial cause, and the workbook also links thigh, buttock or hip pain to lumbar spinal stenosis.
                                                                                                            NCRS PVS Simulation 2 & SOAP Assessment I — Calf Pain1014

                                                                                                            Block check — PVS Simulation 2 (cont.)

                                                                                                            CPD.0.0237 · CPD.0.0238

                                                                                                            A 35-year-old heavy smoker has ischaemic ulceration of two toes with claudication of the feet and Raynaud phenomenon. What is the diagnosis and the single most important intervention?

                                                                                                            1. APeripheral arterial disease; statin therapy
                                                                                                            2. BThromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease); smoking cessation
                                                                                                            3. CChronic venous insufficiency; compression stockings
                                                                                                            4. DAcute arterial occlusion; embolectomy
                                                                                                            5. EErythema nodosum; treat the underlying cause
                                                                                                            Answer
                                                                                                            B. Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease): inflammatory occlusion of small and medium vessels in SMOKERS, affecting the digits and toes, aggravated by exercise and smoking, relieved by rest and SMOKING CESSATION, with ischaemic ulcers and gangrene that may involve multiple limbs. The workbook lists Raynaud's phenomenon in Buerger's disease among the associated features and names smoking as the major risk factor.
                                                                                                            CPD.0.0237 · CPD.0.0238

                                                                                                            A patient with known knee osteoarthritis reports a swelling behind the knee for weeks, then sudden calf pain and swelling. Which diagnosis must be considered alongside DVT?

                                                                                                            1. ACompartment syndrome
                                                                                                            2. BRuptured Baker cyst
                                                                                                            3. CAcute lymphangitis
                                                                                                            4. DErythema nodosum
                                                                                                            5. ESuperficial thrombophlebitis
                                                                                                            Answer
                                                                                                            B. "Did you have swelling behind your knee prior to the calf pain? Do you have osteoarthritis of the knee?" → dissecting Baker cyst. It mimics DVT exactly once it ruptures, which is why ultrasound is the discriminating investigation.
                                                                                                            NCRS PVS Simulation 2 & SOAP Assessment I — Calf Pain1015

                                                                                                            Block check — PVS Simulation 2 (cont.)

                                                                                                            CPD.0.0237 · CPD.0.0241

                                                                                                            Using the workbook's Wells questions, which item SUBTRACTS points?

                                                                                                            1. AEntire leg swollen
                                                                                                            2. BPrevious DVT
                                                                                                            3. CIs another diagnosis more likely?
                                                                                                            4. DCalf swelling >3 cm
                                                                                                            5. EBedridden >3 days or major surgery in the past 4 weeks
                                                                                                            Answer
                                                                                                            C. "Is another diagnosis more likely?" scores –2 points. Every other listed item — paralysis, bedridden >3 days or major surgery within 4 weeks, local tenderness, cancer, entire leg swollen, calf swelling >3 cm, pitting oedema, previous DVT and collateral superficial veins — scores +1.
                                                                                                            CPD.0.0237

                                                                                                            A patient with an aching, swollen leg that is worse at the end of the day has brown pigmentation over the medial ankle and relief with elevation. Which diagnosis?

                                                                                                            1. ADeep vein thrombosis
                                                                                                            2. BChronic venous insufficiency
                                                                                                            3. CPeripheral arterial disease
                                                                                                            4. DCellulitis
                                                                                                            5. ECompartment syndrome
                                                                                                            Answer
                                                                                                            B. Chronic venous insufficiency: venous valve failure causing chronic congestion — diffuse aching legs, worse later in the day, aggravated by prolonged standing, relieved by ELEVATION and WALKING, with edema, brown pigmentation and possible ulcers. Arterial disease is the opposite: elevation aggravates it and dangling relieves it.
                                                                                                            CPD.0.0241 · CPD.0.0242

                                                                                                            Which statement about the ankle-brachial index reflects the guideline positions in Appendix C?

                                                                                                            1. AThe USPSTF recommends routine ABI screening for all adults over 50
                                                                                                            2. BThe USPSTF does not recommend routine screening, while the AHA considers ABI screening reasonable in high-risk patients
                                                                                                            3. CBoth the USPSTF and the AHA recommend universal screening
                                                                                                            4. DThe ABI has high sensitivity and low specificity
                                                                                                            5. EAn ABI above 0.90 confirms peripheral arterial disease
                                                                                                            Answer
                                                                                                            B. USPSTF: does NOT recommend routine screening (insufficient evidence). AHA: screening with ABI is reasonable in high-risk patients. Abnormal is <0.90, with HIGH SPECIFICITY (99%) but LOWER SENSITIVITY (15–20%). Most of the 236 million people with PAD worldwide do not have classic claudication.
